title: Maternal mean arterial pressure and serum inhibin A as early predictors of hypertensive disorders in low-risk pregnant women attending a University Teaching Hospital in Lagos, Nigeria: A prospective cohort study.
authorString: Kuku OJ, Okunade KS, Olorunfemi G, Oluwole AA, Ngene NC.

journal.title: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics

abstractText:
Objective

This study evaluates the role of maternal mean arterial pressure (MAP) and serum inhibin-A level as early predictors of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) among low-risk pregnant women attending a University Teaching Hospital in Lagos, Nigeria.

Methods

This was a prospective cohort study of 254 consecutively consenting, low-risk, normotensive, and non-proteinuric pregnant women at 13-19 weeks of gestation. Receiver operating characteristics (ROC) curves and validity tests were used to determine the performance of serum levels of inhibin A, MAP, and a combination of both in predicting HDP (gestational hypertension and preeclampsia).

Results

The mean age and parity of the participants was 30.3 ± 4.9 years and 1 (0-2), respectively. The area under the ROC curves of serum inhibin A (0.9981, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.9946-1.000) was higher than for MAP (0.7531, 95% CI 0.6641-0.8421), in predicting the composite endpoint of HDP. The optimum cut-offs for predicting HDP as calculated from Youden's index were 476.8 pg/mL (sensitivity = 100% and specificity = 98.7%) for serum inhibin A and 81.3 mm Hg (sensitivity = 100% and specificity = 50.1%) for MAP. There was no statistically significant difference between the combined predictive ability of inhibin A and MAP compared to that of serum inhibin A alone for predicting HDP (AUC of 0.9984 vs. 09981, P-value = 0.7259.

Conclusion

This study demonstrated that serum inhibin A alone and MAP have good and moderate performance, respectively, in predicting HDP in the low-risk cohort of Nigerian pregnant women. The combination of serum inhibin A and MAP has a similar predictive performance as serum inhibin A alone.

title: The Situation-Specific Theory of Caregiver Contributions to Heart Failure Self-Care: An Update.
authorString: Vellone E, de Almeida Neto OP, Della Bella V, Alvaro R, Riegel B.
abstractText: Heart failure (HF) self-care remains suboptimal in a large proportion of patients, and informal caregivers play a crucial role in supporting and helping patients to perform self-care behaviors. The Situation-Specific Theory of Caregiver Contributions to Heart Failure Self-Care, originally published in 2018, provided the first theoretical framework describing this process. Eight years after its initial formulation, substantial new empirical evidence, updated clinical guidelines, and advances in nursing knowledge call for a revision of the theory. To present an updated version of the Situation-Specific Theory of Caregiver Contributions to Heart Failure Self-Care, incorporating new evidence on contributors and mechanisms contributing to outcomes associated with caregiver contributions (CC) to HF self-care. The update followed the integrative approach proposed by Im and Meleis, drawing on 3 sources: the original theory, an integrative literature review of studies published between 2018 and 2026 (N = 17 studies), and the clinical insights and accumulated experience of the research team. The updated theory introduces a new definition of CC to HF self-care as a dynamic, relational, and context-sensitive dyadic process. New contributors at the caregiver (eg, health status), patient (eg, therapeutic complexity), and dyadic levels (eg, type of relationship) were identified. Caregiver self-efficacy was confirmed as the central mediator of the process. Three new potential moderators were added alongside culture: beliefs, cohabitation, and ability to use technology. Outcomes were expanded to include dyadic-level effects. The theoretical propositions were updated and refined, and a new conceptual framework graphic is presented. This updated theory offers a more comprehensive, multilevel, and context-sensitive framework to guide research, clinical practice, and interventions targeting the patient-caregiver dyad in HF.

title: Nurse-led inferior vena cava assessment using handheld ultrasound within a cardiologist-supported home-care workflow.
authorString: Suzuki Y, Oohashi F, Ogawa M, Yamane M, Matsumoto D, Matsumoto M.
abstractText: Volume assessment in older adults receiving home-based care is challenging because body weight, edema, and symptoms may be insufficient indicators, particularly in patients with cognitive impairment. We describe a 95-year-old woman with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, severe tricuspid regurgitation, atrial fibrillation, and dementia. Trained visiting nurses acquired standardized inferior vena cava (IVC) images during home visits and shared them with a cardiologist through a secure cloud-based platform. At the initial assessment, the maximum IVC diameter was 19.3 mm and the IVC collapsibility index was 29%; at 3 weeks, these values were 11.0 mm and 54.5%, respectively. Because IVC findings alone cannot establish volume status, they were interpreted alongside weight loss and reduced skin turgor, and oral fluid intake was encouraged based on the overall clinical assessment. Follow-up laboratory data were unavailable, and hydration status could not be objectively confirmed. This case illustrates the feasibility of a cardiologist-supported home-care workflow integrating nurse-performed IVC assessment and remote cardiologist review. Its clinical utility requires further evaluation.

title: Effect of In-line Clinical Decision Support to Improve Accuracy of American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status Documentation: A Two-center Evaluation of a Quality Intervention.
authorString: Murphy ZR, Colquhoun DA, Mentz GB, Burns ML, Mathis MR, Jiao Y, Shah NJ, Wixson MC, Haydar B, Klumpner TT.
abstractText:
Background

American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA; Schaumburg, Illinois) Physical Status (PS) classification is a widely used ordinal scale that captures comorbidity burden but has significant interrater variability. Previous efforts to enhance ASA PS documentation with clinical decision support are limited by inaccurate problem lists, poor user experience, or consideration of select comorbidities. The authors developed and implemented clinical decision support which uses the anesthesia clinicians' documentation to highlight potential underclassification at time of ASA PS assignment.

Methods

Building upon examples from the ASA Committee on Economics and institutional consensus, the authors identified 51 conditions warranting an ASA PS of at least III. This was embedded in clinical decision support and implemented at the authors' large academic medical center (site 1). The authors compared the percentage of patients assigned an ASA PS III or greater before (May 22, 2023, to May 22, 2024) and after complete implementation (August 14, 2024, to August 14, 2025). A second large midwestern academic medical center served as a contemporaneous external control (site 2). Using a difference in difference analysis, the authors constructed odds ratios for assignment of ASA PS III in all patients and selected subpopulations.

Results

The study included 251,944 anesthetics from site 1 and 286,172 from site 2. Baseline characteristics were similar between sites. At site 1, the proportion of patients classified as ASA PS III or higher increased from 52.9 to 61.7% (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.42; 95% CI, 1.38 to 1.45). Site 2 experienced a small absolute increase from 47.2 to 48.4% (aOR, 1.05; 95% CI, 1.03 to 1.07). Among patients at site 1 with 50 conditions addressed by the latter phase of the clinical decision support, the proportion classified as ASA PS III or greater increased from 83.6 to 94.0% (aOR, 3.54; 95% CI, 3.34 to 3.76).

Conclusions

Implementation of the authors' in-line real-time clinical decision support was associated with a significant increase in the percentage of patients with ASA PS III or greater.

title: Maternal exposure to sleep aids and risk of specific birth defects in the Birth Defects Study To Evaluate Pregnancy exposureS.
authorString: Howley MM, Werler MM, Tracy M, Williford EM, Papadopoulos EA, Ailes EC, Reefhuis J, Fisher SC, Birth Defects Study To Evaluate Pregnancy exposureS.
abstractText:
Study objectives

Insomnia symptoms are often reported during pregnancy, prompting use of pharmacologic treatments. We explored associations between treatments used during the month before through the third month of pregnancy ("early pregnancy") and risk of birth defects using Birth Defects Study to Evaluate Pregnancy exposureS (BD-STEPS) data from 2014-2021.

Methods

Pregnancies affected by birth defects ("cases") were identified from surveillance systems in seven states; liveborn infants without birth defects ("controls") were randomly selected from the same catchment areas. Mothers of cases and controls reported early pregnancy exposures via interview, including use of prescription, over-the-counter, or herbal sleep aids. For defects with ≥5 exposed cases, we used Firth's logistic regression to estimate propensity score-adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusting for maternal age, race/ethnicity, education, body mass index, previous live birth, history of depression/anxiety, early pregnancy use of antipsychotics, anxiolytics, antidepressants, opioids, cigarettes, alcohol, and prenatal vitamins, occurrence of stressful events, occupation outside the home, health insurance, and site.

Results

Overall, 237 (7%) cases and 140 (8%) controls reported early pregnancy sleep aid use. We calculated aORs for 12/22 defects, which ranged from 0.52 for d-transposition of the great arteries to 1.61 for coarctation of the aorta. All CIs included the null.

Conclusions

Results suggest sleep aids do not increase risk of most defects studied, but increased risk for coarctation of the aorta cannot be ruled out. Small numbers limited analyses. Studies examining the severity of underlying sleep disorders and impacts of specific sleep aids would be beneficial.

title: Evaluation of exercise on quality of Life and aerobic capacity in women with heart failure: A systematic review and Meta-Analysis.
authorString: Leite HF, Valenti VE, Souza IS, Zangirolami-Raimundo J, Candeloro BM, Laporta GZ, Raimundo RD.
abstractText: Women with heart failure (HF) present distinct clinical and hormonal characteristics and remain underrepresented in exercise-based randomized trials. Given the reduction in aerobic capacity and quality of life observed in this population, this study aimed to evaluate the effects of exercise training on these outcomes in women with HF. This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, CINAHL, and LILACS through October 2025. Randomized controlled trials including adult women with HF undergoing structured exercise interventions were selected. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed for peak oxygen uptake (VO₂peak), six-minute walk distance (6MWT), and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ) scores. Four randomized trials met the inclusion criteria. Exercise training significantly improved VO₂peak and increased 6MWT distance. However, pooled analysis of MLHFQ did not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement. The certainty of evidence was moderate for VO₂peak and very low for 6MWT and MLHFQ due to risk of bias and imprecision. Exercise training improves aerobic capacity in women with HF with moderate-certainty evidence. Evidence supporting functional capacity and quality-of-life improvements remains highly uncertain. Further adequately powered, women-specific randomized trials are needed.

authorString: Yang Y, Peng K, Zhong J, Zhang J, Liu X, Yang J, Liu L, Gu J, Sun P, Chen C, Yu Y, Yuan J, Zhu Y, Liu H, Ma D, Miao C, Ji F.
abstractText: To determine whether discontinuing versus continuing angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) on the morning of surgery reduces perioperative hypotension in older patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery. Multicentre, randomised, double blind, placebo controlled trial. Five tertiary teaching hospitals in China, November 2020 to December 2023. 2036 older patients (60-80 years) using ACE inhibitors or ARBs for at least two weeks and scheduled for non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia. Patients were randomised to receive their usual ACE inhibitor or ARB or a placebo in identical capsules on the morning of surgery. The primary outcome was the incidence of perioperative hypotension (mean blood pressure <65 mm Hg or a ≥30% decrease from baseline requiring treatment). Secondary outcomes included duration of hypotension, requirement for a vasopressor, intraoperative fluid volume, postoperative hypotension, and 30 day complications (neurocognitive disorders, major cardiocerebral events) or mortality. 2012 patients (mean age 68.8 years; 54.4% male) completed the study: 1004 were included in the antihypertensive group and 1008 in the no antihypertensive group. The incidence of perioperative hypotension was lower in the no antihypertensive group (314/1008, 31.2%) versus antihypertensive group (457/1004, 45.5%): adjusted odds ratio 0.52 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.43 to 0.63); absolute risk difference -14.4% (95% CI -18.5% to -10.1%); P<0.001. The duration of hypotension and requirement for a vasopressor were both reduced in the no antihypertensive group: adjusted mean difference -1.3 minutes (95% CI -1.8 to -0.8 minutes) and 28.5% v 41.1%; adjusted odds ratio 0.54 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.66). Intraoperative fluid volume, postoperative hypotension, 30 day complications, and mortality did not differ significantly between groups. Discontinuing ACE inhibitors or ARBs on the morning of surgery in older patients with hypertension statistically significantly reduced perioperative hypotension and the requirement for vasopressors without increasing 30 day complications or mortality. This simple strategy provides high certainty evidence for preoperative drug management in this patient population. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2000039376.

title: Recent recommendations for the diagnosis and management of liver cirrhosis and its complications.
authorString: Hähner JM, Peiffer KH, Praktiknjo M, Uschner FE, Trebicka J, McCoy MS.
abstractText: Progression of liver cirrhosis is a dynamic transition toward decompensation driven by portal hypertension (PH), while systemic inflammation (SI) mediates organ dysfunction and failure, acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF), and short-term mortality. The recent publication of the Baveno VIII consensus and of harmonized organ failure definitions calls for a reassessment of current concepts and recommendations. PubMed/MEDLINE and Web of Science were searched from April 2026 to September 2026 for consensus documents, randomized trials, and large cohort studies on cirrhosis and its complications. Earlier landmark studies were included when they underpinned current recommendations, without any claim to completeness. Noninvasive risk stratification in compensated advanced chronic liver disease, prevention of first decompensation, the clinical phenotypes of decompensation, management of variceal bleeding including preemptive TIPS, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, renal dysfunction, and ACLF are included together with practical guidance for triage and transfer to expert and transplant centers. Management is shifting from reactive treatment of individual complications toward mechanism-based, preemptive care guided by dynamic risk assessment. Harmonized ACLF definitions and biomarkers of systemic inflammation should now enable trials of disease-modifying therapy, the field's largest unmet need.

title: Trevogrumab (anti-GDF8) with or without garetosmab (anti-activin A) for prevention of muscle loss during semaglutide-induced weight reduction in people with obesity (COURAGE): a two-part, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial.
authorString: Mosenzon O, Rosenstock J, Raya JG, Grimsby JS, Calle RA, Cannon K, Haggag AZ, Bays H, Sarkar N, Templeton A, Fanous M, Lighter J, Vavere A, Yancopoulos GD, Hirshberg B, COURAGE Trial Investigators.
abstractText:
Background

Rapid weight loss, as induced by GLP-1 receptor agonists, is accompanied by pronounced muscle loss. GDF8 (myostatin) and activin A (ActA), acting via ActRIIA/B receptors, are negative regulators of muscle mass. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of antibodies blocking GDF8 (trevogrumab) and ActA (garetosmab) on semaglutide-induced weight and muscle loss.

Methods

COURAGE is a two-part, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial. This multicentre (60 sites), US-based trial enrolled participants aged 18-80 years with obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2). In part A, participants were treated for 26 weeks with semaglutide (titrated to 2·4 mg subcutaneously weekly) in addition to a randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) concomitant treatment: placebo, trevogrumab 200 mg, trevogrumab 400 mg, or trevogrumab 400 mg and garetosmab 10 mg/kg. Trevogrumab was administered subcutaneously weekly and garetosmab was administered intravenously every 4 weeks. Part A also included a subsequent semaglutide withdrawal period, at which point participants (randomly assigned at baseline 1:1 within each group) received either trevogrumab 400 mg or placebo for an additional 26 weeks. In part B, participants were treated with semaglutide for 52 weeks and randomly assigned (1:2:2) to concomitant treatment with placebo, trevogrumab 25 mg, or trevogrumab 75 mg. Groups were stratified according to sex, BMI (<35 kg/m2vs ≥35 kg/m2), and participation in an exploratory MRI substudy assessing thigh muscle volume. Study participants, the principal investigators, and study site personnel were masked to all randomisation assignments throughout the study. Primary endpoints were percent change in lean mass, fat mass, and bodyweight from baseline to week 26 (part A) or week 52 (part B). Efficacy and safety analyses were done in all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of a study drug (efficacy, as randomly assigned; safety, as treated). COURAGE is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06299098, and is currently active, not recruiting.

Findings

975 participants were enrolled between June 21, 2024, and April 14, 2025. Mean age was 49·0 years (SD 13·2) and mean BMI was 36·7 kg/m2 (SD 5·0); 627 (64%) of 975 participants were female and 348 (36%) were male. In part A (n=605, of whom n=599 received at least one dose of study drug), a substantial decrease in lean mass was observed in the semaglutide plus placebo group at week 26 (-6·6% [95% CI -7·4 to -5·7]); the estimated treatment difference (ETD) versus semaglutide plus placebo was +3·1% (95% CI 1·9 to 4·3) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 200 mg, +2·7% (1·5 to 4·0) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg, and +4·5% (3·1 to 5·9) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg. In part B (n=376), lean mass percent change from baseline to week 52 for semaglutide plus placebo was -7·3% (-8·8 to -5·8); the ETD versus semaglutide plus placebo was +1·5% (-0·3 to 3·3) for semaglutide plus trevogrumab 25 mg, and +3·1% (1·3 to 4·9) for semaglutide plus trevogrumab 75 mg. Change from baseline in fat mass in part A was -15·6% (-17·4 to -13·9) in the semaglutide plus placebo group; the ETD was significant in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg group (-3·4% [-5·9 to -0·9]) and the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (-11·7% [-14·4 to -9·0]) in part A. No other groups in part A nor any in part B had significantly different changes in fat mass compared with semaglutide plus placebo. Percent change in bodyweight in part A was -10·6 (-11·6 to -9·7) in the semaglutide plus placebo group; the ETD was significant for the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (-2·7 [-4·1 to -1·2]). No other groups in part A nor any in part B had significantly different changes in bodyweight compared with semaglutide plus placebo. Semaglutide plus trevogrumab (25 mg, 75 mg, 200 mg, or 400 mg) was generally well tolerated with a safety profile similar to semaglutide plus placebo; however, semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg had a high incidence of serious adverse events (14 [9%] of 149) and treatment discontinuations (48 [32%] of 149). Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most commonly reported, and they occurred with similar incidence across treatment groups. Muscle spasms occurred more frequently in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (61 [41%] of 149) compared with the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 200 mg or 400 mg groups (23 [8%] of 299) and semaglutide plus placebo groups (seven [5%] of 151). Most adverse events were mild to moderate in severity. Two deaths occurred during the study, both in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group; a causal association between treatment and these events was not identified.

Interpretation

This study establishes proof of concept for GDF8 inhibition by trevogrumab alone as a generally well tolerated strategy to preserve lean mass during GLP-1 receptor agonist-induced weight loss. Although the addition of ActA inhibition by garetosmab further improved body composition and weight loss, the combination did not have favourable safety and tolerability. Further study is required to understand whether improved body composition during weight loss might preserve physical function and overall metabolic health.

Funding

Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

title: One-Year Outcomes of Pulmonary Vein Isolation With a Novel Cryoballoon in Asian Population.
authorString: Miyazaki S, Yamauchi Y, On YK, Kimura M, Ando K, Ashikaga K, Inaba O, Tanaka Y, Sasaki T, Kwon CH, Kusano K, Yoshida Y, Duffy M, Kwek J, Ebady R, Kayser T, Nitta J, and the POLAR SMART Investigators.
abstractText: Cryoballoon ablations for pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) to treat atrial fibrillation (AF) are well established. The POLAR SMART study was designed to collect prospective real-world data on acute and 12-month safety and effectiveness of the POLARx cryoballoon for de novo PVI. POLAR SMART is a prospective, non-randomized, multicenter study (NCT05282823) with patients enrolled across 19 centers (Japan and South Korea) and followed up to 12 months. AF ablation was performed in 293 patients, 181 receiving only PVI. In the PVI-only cohort, acute PVI was achieved in 95.0% of patients, and 98.2% of pulmonary veins (PV) with the cryoballoon. Procedure time and fluoroscopy time were 75 ± 25 min and 18.5 ± 11.1 min, respectively. Time to isolation was 42 ± 32 s, with nadir temperature of -56.6 ± 6.9°C. The study met the primary safety endpoint with an event-free rate of 97.3%. The study effectiveness event-free rate at 12 months was 75.6% for entire cohort and 81.1% for PVI-only cohort (POLARx, n = 116; 79.3% and POLARx FIT, n = 65; 84.4%). AF recurrence in PVI-only cohort was 7.2% for POLARx and 6.2% for POLARx FIT. Ablation procedure increased heart rate (HR) significantly for entire cohort (p < 0.001). The optimal HR value at predischarge for 12-month outcome was calculated with 70 bpm (Predicted Probability 0.83). The effect of increased HR remained stable after 12 months for patients ablated with POLARx FIT. The POLARx and POLARx FIT cryoballoon systems are safe and effective for PVI in real-world use. POLARx FIT ablation was associated with a sustained HR increase over 12 months.

title: Anticoagulation in Subclinical Atrial Fibrillation: An Evidence-Based Framework for Individualized Management.
authorString: Ariaga A, Olleik F, Kowey PR.
abstractText: The increasing use of wearable monitoring technologies and cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) has led to frequent incidental detection of subclinical atrial fibrillation (SCAF), yet the role of long-term anticoagulation remains uncertain. Growing evidence indicates that SCAF is a separate clinical entity on the continuous spectrum of atrial disease and not just a precursor to clinical disease. We propose that anticoagulation in SCAF should be guided by integrating arrythmia burden, baseline clinical risk and the degree of structural atrial cardiomyopathy in addition to life expectancy and patient preferences. This review synthesizes data from observational studies, randomized clinical trials, and post-hoc analyses to provide a comprehensive and practical framework for individualized anticoagulation, and risk-benefit considerations.

title: Rationale and Design of the BradycArdia paCemaKer with AV interval modulation for Blood prEssure treAtmenT (BACKBEAT) Pivotal Trial.
authorString: Burkhoff D, Fischer A, Evans SJ, Mika YH, Stagg A, Kandzari DE, Russo AM, Townsend RR, Merkely B, Lindenfeld J, Love C, Mahfoud F, Doros G, Reddy V, BACKBEAT Investigators.
abstractText:
Background

Atrioventricular interval modulation (AVIM) is a novel pacing algorithm incorporated into a dual-chamber cardiac pacemaker that enables treatment of hypertension while simultaneously treating bradyarrhythmias. Prior clinical studies have shown that AVIM reduces 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure (aSBP). The BACKBEAT (BradycArdia paCemaKer with AV interval modulation for Blood prEssure treAtmenT) pivotal trial is designed toassess the safety and efficacy of AVIM in a prospective, randomized controlled trial.

Study design and objective

BACKBEAT is a global, multicenter, prospective, randomized, double-blinded clinical trial enrolling approximately 316 subjects across up to 130 sites. Eligible participants include patients implanted with, or scheduled to be implanted with, a dual-chamber pacemaker who have uncontrolled hypertension, defined as office systolic blood pressure (oSBP) ≥135 mmHg and aSBP ≥130 mmHg despite stable medical therapy. All eligible subjects will receive AVIM therapy RAMware downloaded to their device and will be randomized to active treatment (AVIM ON) or control (AVIM OFF), in addition to continued medical therapy. The primary efficacy endpoint is the between-group difference in the change of mean 24-hour aSBP from baseline to 3 months post-randomization. The primary safety endpoint is the proportion of subjects in the treatment group free from unanticipated serious adverse device effects at 3 months. Blinding will continue through 12 months to assess longer-term outcomes. At the end of the 12-month blinded phase, subjects may cross over to the alternate group before entering a 2-year follow-up phase.

Conclusion

BACKBEAT will provide rigorous evidence regarding the safety and efficacy of AVIM therapy for hypertension in patients with a dual-chamber pacemaker.

title: Home-Based, Digitally Assisted Dyadic Tai Chi Intervention for Patients With Chronic Heart Failure and Their Caregivers: Development of an Intervention and Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
authorString: Zhang Y, Ngai FW, Cao L, Lu X, Zhang W, Wei L, Xie YJ.
abstractText: Chronic heart failure (CHF) imposes a dual and dynamically interrelated burden on patients and family caregivers, whose health and illness management behaviors are interdependent. Exercise interventions that actively engage the patient-caregiver dyad as the unit of rehabilitation in the home setting remain underdeveloped. This study aimed to develop a home-based, digitally assisted, dyadic tai chi (HDTC) intervention and evaluate its feasibility, acceptability, safety, and preliminary effects among dyads of patients with CHF and their caregivers. This sequential, multiphase study comprised intervention development followed by a single-center, assessor-blinded, parallel-group pilot randomized controlled trial. Phase 1 integrated literature review, theoretical frameworks, and stakeholder focus group interviews to develop and refine the HDTC intervention. In phase 2, eligible adults with CHF (aged 18-75 years; New York Heart Association class I-III) and their primary caregivers were recruited from a tertiary medical center in Qingdao, China, from October 14 to November 12, 2024, and followed for 12 weeks. Forty dyads were allocated 1:1 to the 12-week HDTC intervention plus usual care or usual care alone (n=20 per group). Outcome assessors and the data analyst were blinded to group allocation. Feasibility, acceptability, and safety were the primary focus of the pilot trial. Patient, caregiver, and dyadic health outcomes were preliminarily explored at baseline and 4 and 12 weeks. All 40 randomized dyads were included in the intention-to-treat analyses. The HDTC intervention comprised an online educational seminar, nurse-led dyadic coaching, preliminary face-to-face tai chi training, and supervised HDTC practice. The recruitment rate was 83.3% (40/48), mean session attendance was 73.7% (SD 8.6%), and 70% (14/20) of participants achieved high adherence rate (≥75% attendance). All intervention dyads rated the intervention as acceptable. No intervention-related adverse events were identified. Exploratory generalized estimating equation analyses suggested greater improvements from baseline to 12 weeks in the intervention group than in the control group in functional capacity (β=38.858; P=.001), together with greater reductions in Minnesota Living With Heart Failure Questionnaire scores (β=-1.850; P=.002), sedentary time (β=-1.025; P=.01), and fear of activity (β=-6.550; P=.01). Caregiver burden also decreased (β=-4.350; P<.001), while mutuality improved more for both patients (β=10.508; P<.001) and caregivers (β=6.450; P<.001). The HDTC intervention was feasible and acceptable, with preliminary improvements across patient, caregiver, and dyadic outcomes. By integrating shared patient-caregiver participation with digitally supported home-based tai chi, the HDTC intervention extends patient-centered rehabilitation toward a dyad-oriented model. If confirmed in a fully powered trial, this approach may offer a practical strategy for expanding home-based cardiac rehabilitation. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06876441; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06876441.

title: Theraphosid (Tarantula) Bite Envenomation in Humans: A Systematic Review of the Reported Epidemiology.
authorString: Alexander DD.

journal.title: Toxicon : official journal of the International Society on Toxinology

abstractText: Despite the ubiquity of Theraphosidae (tarantulas) in the pet trade, the clinical literature on theraphosid envenomation is heterogeneous, geographically uneven, dominated by selective self-report, and frequently obscured by taxonomic misidentification. PubMed/MEDLINE and supplementary sources were screened against pre-specified criteria for published reports of human theraphosid bites (PRISMA). Forty-two reports (1889-2026) entered the primary synthesis: 39 were localizable to 17 countries, one did not state the bite country, and two were international hobbyist compilations. Reporting concentrated in South Asia, in captive-keeper bites in Europe and North America, and in Australia. Among Old World species (native to Africa, Asia, and Australasia), African, South Asian, and Southeast Asian lineages were repeatedly associated with intense local pain, delayed generalized muscle cramping, creatine kinase elevation, and, rarely, transient atrial fibrillation, whereas Australian bites caused severe local pain without cramping. New World bites (species native to the Americas) predominantly produced minor local effects, with rare systemic exceptions (suspected anaphylaxis, prolonged cramping, thrombocytopenia). Only 8 of 42 reports had identification by a named arachnologist, zoologist, or institutional laboratory. No validated antivenom and no death attributable to a verified Theraphosidae bite were identified; two deaths attributed to the genus Chilobrachys in a 1997 Indian report lack documented taxonomic and causal confirmation. Most reported theraphosid bites were minor, but the literature cannot estimate population-level risk without defined denominators. Some Old World bites were high-acuity events, and the literature has emphasized less heterogeneity in Old World envenomations than exists. Priorities include standardized species identification, prospective registries, and consistent severity reporting.

title: Beyond Coronary Artery Disease: Etiologies and Outcomes of the Shark-Fin ECG Pattern: A Systematic Review.
authorString: Avidan Y, Arena R, Atwan H, Schliamser JE, Smith SW, Danon A, Weizman B.
abstractText:
Background

The shark-fin sign (SFS) is a rare, high-risk electrocardiographic pattern reported in commonly linked with obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD).

Objective

To characterize the electrocardiographic patterns, etiologies, and clinical outcomes associated with the SFS.

Methods

We systematically reviewed PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, and Cochrane from inception through May 20, 2026, including all studies with participant-level data.

Results

Eighty-five papers involving 104 patients were included; 66.3% had non-obstructive etiologies. The obstructive CAD patients were predominantly male (97.1%), while other etiologies were predominantly female (60.8%). Among CAD cases, the left main coronary artery (LMCA)/proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD) was the culprit in 75.0%, and SFS localization matched coronary anatomy in 91.4%. VT/VF and death each occurred in 37.1%, with adverse outcomes confined to those with LMCA/LAD lesions. Among other etiologies, Takotsubo syndrome (TTS, 31.7%), vasospasm (14.4%), myocarditis (6.7 %) and neurologic emergencies (4.8%) were the most frequently reported. VT/VF occurred in 43.4% and 27.5% died. Among patients with TTS, 63.6% experienced VT/VF or death, compared with ventricular arrhythmias in 66% of patients with vasospasm.

Conclusion

SFS is a high-risk ECG pattern rather than a diagnosis and warrants urgent etiologic evaluation and cardiac monitoring. Most published data are derived from patients without established CAD. LMCA/LAD disease, TTS, and coronary vasospasm were associated with particularly high-risk hospitalizations. Primary non-cardiac causes should also be considered when clinically suspected.

title: Effectiveness and safety of intravenous terlipressin as an add-on treatment for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn: a study protocol of a multicentre pragmatic randomised controlled trial in China.
authorString: Zhang P, Chen Z, Li H, Huang L, Shi Y, Zhang S, Mu D, Shi J, Zeng L, Zhang L.

title: Predictive value of systemic inflammatory indices for new-onset atrial fibrillation after acute myocardial infarction: an interpretable machine learning study.
authorString: Meng X, Wen Y, Zhan G, Xia Y, Wang X, Ma C, Xia Y, Yang X, Gao L.
abstractText: New-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) after acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is associated with adverse outcomes. Inflammation contributes to atrial fibrillation (AF) onset and progression. We developed an interpretable machine learning (ML) framework integrating complete blood count (CBC)-derived inflammatory indices with routine clinical parameters for NOAF risk assessment. We retrospectively analyzed 3,077 AMI patients without prior AF (2018-2023). Multivariable logistic regression, restricted cubic splines (RCS), and threshold analyses evaluated six inflammatory indices: neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR), systemic inflammation response index (SIRI), and aggregate index of systemic inflammation (AISI). Boruta and LASSO selections were intersected. Eight ML models were evaluated, with Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) for interpretation. NOAF incidence was 7.73%. Six indices were associated with NOAF in separate adjusted models (all p < 0.05). Estimated change points were approximately 5.5 (NLR), 1217 (SII), 2.9 (SIRI), and 430 (AISI). The support vector machine (SVM) achieved the highest mean training out-of-fold (OOF) area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC; 0.357) and a held-out test PR-AUC of 0.407. Mean absolute SHAP values were highest for left atrial diameter (LAD), age, and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP); SIRI ranked first among inflammatory features. Fixed-feature ablation showed modest PR-AUC and Brier-score improvements, uncertain ROC-AUC gains, and no consistent net benefit on decision-curve analysis. CBC-derived inflammatory indices were associated with NOAF, but their incremental predictive value beyond routine clinical variables remains uncertain. Given moderate predictive performance and no external validation, multicenter validation is needed before clinical implementation.

title: Not all plaque burden is Equal: CACS- versus SIS-derived risk stratification within CAD-RADS categories in mild-to-moderate coronary disease.
authorString: Palmisano A, Serra D, Bruno E, Vignale D, Colombo A, Bartoli A, Pisu F, Gambato G, Esposito A.
abstractText: To assess the prognostic value of plaque burden based on CACS and SIS categories over CAD-RADS. In this retrospective, single-center study, 2850 adults who underwent elective CCTA between 2016 and 2020 were screened. A total of 1818 patients were enrolled based on very low-to-intermediate pre-test risk, good image quality (Likert score ≥4), and ≥3 years of follow-up. Clinical data were collected, and CAD-RADS 2.0 with CACS-based plaque burden (CACS-P score) and SIS-based plaque burden (SIS-P score) was quantified. Prediction of 5-point MACE composite outcome (late unplanned coronary revascularization, non-fatal myocardial infarction, hospitalization for heart failure, hospitalization for angina, all-cause mortality) and 2-point MACE composite outcome (non-fatal myocardial infarction and all-cause mortality) was evaluated using survival analysis and multivariable models. During a median available follow-up of 62 months, 178/1818 patients (9.8%) experienced a 5-point MACE and 96/1818 (5.3%) experienced myocardial infarction/death within the fixed 36-month analysis horizon. Both CAD-RADS severity and plaque burden scores were associated with adverse outcomes. Integration of the CACS-based P-score identified revealed heterogeneity in risk estimates within CAD-RADS categories. For the primary endpoint, CAD-RADS 3/P0 showed HR point estimates of similar magnitude to those observed in CAD-RADS 4-5/P0 and CAD-RADS 4-5/P3-P4 (HR 15.95 [95% CI:3.95-64.36], HR 16.21 [3.23-81.31], and HR 14.13 [5.70-35.01], respectively). For myocardial infarction/death, CAD-RADS 2-3/P0 showed HR point estimates of similar magnitude to those observed in CAD-RADS 4-5/P1-P2. Conversely, SIS-P provided limited additional within category risk stratification. CACS-based P score may refine risk stratification in patients with mild-to-moderate stenosis.

title: 2026 iCARDIO Alliance Global Implementation Guidelines on Heart Failure.
authorString: Chopra V, Abraham WT, Amir O, Anker SD, Atherton JJ, Bacal F, von Bardeleben RS, Brito D, Burgos LM, Butler J, Costanzo MR, Damasceno A, Ezekowitz JA, Hameed I, Harikrishnan S, Lala A, Piña IL, Saldarriaga C, Sim D, Teerlink JR, Tsabedze N, Tsutsui H, Yu J, Zhang Y, Zubaid M, Balankhe N, Cleland JGF, Figtree G, Filippatos G, Fudim M, Gamra H, Gomez-Mesa JE, Gulati M, Januzzi JL, Konstam MA, Lindenfeld J, Mentz RJ, Monroe R, Ogola E, Pinto FJ, Rajadhyaksha GC, Ramos CE, Rosano G, Rossel V, Sato N, Schulze PC, Sindone A, Sulaiman K, Vaduganathan M, Van Spall HGC, van Veldhuisen DJ, von Haehling S, Wang TD, Zamorano P, Böhm M, Coats AJS, Zieroth S.
abstractText: This is the updated 2026 version of the iCARDIO Alliance Global Implementation Guidelines on Heart Failure - originally published in 2025. In these guidelines, we aim to consider inconsistencies in healthcare access, varying infrastructure, resource constraints and diverse local practices as well as practical and political issues that restrict the global applicability of currently available guidelines. There is a need for universal recommendations that address the unique challenges faced by patients and healthcare providers worldwide. Our iCARDIO Alliance Global Implementation Guidelines emphasize the incorporation of novel therapies, while integrating standard of care with the most up-to-date evidence to enable clinicians to optimize patient care. This document is about heart failure (HF), including acute and chronic heart failure, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction as well as HF with improved ejection fraction and cardiomyopathies. Context-specific recommendations tailored to individual patient needs are highlighted providing a thorough evaluation of the risks, benefits, and overall value of each therapy, aiming to establish a standard of care that improves patient outcomes and reduces the burden of hospitalization in this susceptible population. These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations that represent a group consensus considering the many other published guidelines that have reviewed many of the issues discussed here, but they also make new recommendations where new evidence has recently emerged. Most importantly these guidelines also provide recommendations on a number of issues where re-source limitations may put constraints on the care provided to HF patients. Such "economic adjustment" recommendations aim to provide guidance for situations when "Resources are somewhat limited" or when "Resources are severely limited". Hence, this document presents not only a comprehensive but also concise set of recommendations to guide all aspects of HF management with a unified strategy for the pharmacological, non-pharmacological, invasive and interventional management of this significant global health challenge that is applicable to the needs of healthcare around the globe.

title: Perioperative dynamics of selenoproteins and risk of cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury.
authorString: Xie X, Xue W, Wang Z, Li Z, Feng W, Zhang H, Zhang W.
abstractText: Cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI) affects over 20% of patients and is associated with perioperative mortality and long-term renal impairment. Reliable early biomarkers remain limited. Selenoproteins, including glutathione peroxidases (GPX1, GPX3) and selenoprotein P (SEPP1), are critical for redox homeostasis, but their perioperative changes in CSA-AKI remain unclear. This study aimed to characterize selenoprotein dynamics and explore their association with renal function and CSA-AKI. In this prospective observational cohort study, 99 adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery were enrolled, serum and urine samples were collected preoperatively and at 24/48 h postoperatively. SEPP1, GPX1, GPX3, and KIM-1 were measured. Mixed-effects, correlation, and logistic regression assessed selenoprotein dynamics and associations with CSA-AKI, with an exploratory model including age and preoperative SEPP1. Among 89 analyzed patients, 22 (24.7%) developed AKI. Univariable analyses showed that lower perioperative SEPP1 levels, attenuated urinary SEPP1 increases, and greater serum GPX1 decreases were associated with higher odds of CSA-AKI; older age, hypertension, and longer operation time were also associated with CSA-AKI. Postoperatively, serum SEPP1 declined markedly, remaining lower in AKI patients. Urinary SEPP1 increased significantly in non-AKI patients. Changes in GPX1 and GPX3 differed between AKI and non-AKI groups. Serum SEPP1 correlated positively with eGFR and inversely with creatinine and cystatin C. An exploratory model incorporating age and preoperative serum SEPP1 yielded an apparent AUC of 0.818. In summary, perioperative alterations in selenoproteins (GPX1, GPX3, SEPP1) are closely linked to CSA-AKI. Preoperative SEPP1 combined with clinical variables may enable early risk prediction and support timely intervention.

title: Elevated Lipoprotein(a) Is Associated With Heart Failure in Patients With Peripheral Artery Disease.
authorString: Hoshina R, Akahori H, Tanaka H, Yoshihara N, Miki K, Kawai K, Ishihara M.

journal.title: Circulation journal : official journal of the Japanese Circulation Society

abstractText:
Background

The prognostic value of lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] in peripheral artery disease (PAD) remains uncertain.

Methods and results

We retrospectively studied 138 patients with intermittent claudication undergoing endovascular therapy. Patients were classified by Lp(a) level (≥30 vs. <30 mg/dL). The primary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Elevated Lp(a) was associated with a higher incidence of MACE (31.1% vs. 9.6%; P=0.002), predominantly driven by heart failure. It independently predicted MACE (HR 4.23) and heart failure (HR 5.12), but not cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke.

Conclusions

Elevated Lp(a) was associated with heart failure-driven MACE after endovascular therapy in patients with PAD.

title: Comparative Clinical and Procedural Outcomes Among Three Pulsed Field Ablation Systems for Atrial Fibrillation: A Prospective Real-World Study.
authorString: Tscholl V, Chiba T, Wakili R, Rottner L, Leistner DM, Roth E, Baldauf CS, Benachi C, Shamloo AS, Hättasch R, Nagel P, Lucas J, Huemer M, Landmesser U, Dagres N, Hohendanner F, Hindricks G, Attanasio P.
abstractText:
Background

Pulsed Field Ablation (PFA) is a non-thermal ablation technology for atrial fibrillation. Several PFA systems are available, with distinct catheter designs and energy delivery protocols. Direct comparisons between PFA systems remain limited.

Objective

This study compared the procedural characteristics, safety, and efficacy of three contemporary PFA technologies in routine clinical practice.

Methods

Consecutive patients undergoing their first pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) using the circular multielectrode array catheter (CMAC)(PulseSelectTM), the variable-loop circular catheter (VLCC)(VaripulseTM) or the lattice-tip catheter (LTC)(AfferaTM) were prospectively included. Freedom from any atrial arrhythmia (AA) was evaluated using 12-lead electrocardiography and 24-hour Holter at 3, 6 and 12 months, followed by routine clinical follow-up.

Results

A total of 198 patients (CMAC:91, VLCC:50, LTC: 57) were included. Acute PVI was achieved in all patients (median age, 68 [61.0, 76.0] years; 127 male (64.1%); 97 paroxysmal (49.0%)). The procedure and ablation times were longest in the LTC group. During a mean follow-up of 352.4±207.2 days, the estimated 12-month freedom from AA recurrence beyond the 8-week blanking period was comparable among the CMAC, VLCC, and LTC groups (76.9%, 71.6%, and 78.8%; log-rank p=0.72). In adjusted multivariable Cox regression, PFA system choice was not associated with AA recurrence (LTC vs. CMAC: HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.39-1.52, p=0.45; VLCC vs. CMAC: HR 1.16, 95% CI 0.58-2.34, p=0.67). One major complication (0.51%, ischemic stroke (CMAC)) occurred.

Conclusion

In this prospective real-world study, PVI with the CMAC, VLCC, and LTC showed comparable efficacy and safety outcomes, while procedural profiles differed.

title: Frailty in older adults hospitalized for decompensated heart failure: prevalence, multidomain assessment and prognostic value.
authorString: Daniel FB, Arevalo-Lorido JC, Mayoral-Testón N, Elena VJ, Nieves SG, Jorge MC, José ZM, Luisa MS, Isabel A, González-Fernández María R.
abstractText: Frailty is a condition that affects prognosis and quality of life. It is not typically included in the routine assessment on admission for decompensated heart failure (dHF). Our objective was to determine its prevalence and prognosis in people admitted for dHF, with different scales of physical frailty and to evaluate its presence in its other domains. This prospective study analyzed individuals >65 years admitted for dHF grouped according to Fried phenotype. Prevalence and prognosis (mortality or readmission at 1 year) were calculated using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression models. A total of 228 patients were included (mean age 80.8+7.7 years, 52.2% women). Of them, 0.9% were robust, 16.6% were prefrail, and 82.5% were frail. Frail patients were significantly older and more were female (p < 0.001). They had a high prevalence of comorbidity, physical frailty, and nutritional impairment; moderate cognitive impairment; poor quality of life; high fall risk; and a low level of autonomy. During follow-up, 27.2% died and 56.4% were readmitted for dHF. Survival was significantly lower among patients with frailty determined by physical assessment scales and accumulation of deficits (p < 0.001). They had a significantly worse prognosis according to the Fried (HR 1.70, 95%CI 1.03-2.79) and FRAIL (HR 1.48, 95%CI 1.02-2.14) scales. Frailty is highly prevalent among individuals admitted for dHF, particularly in the clinical, functional, and psycho-cognitive domains. Despite a multidomain assessment, prognostic value was mainly driven by physical frailty scales. It is necessary to integrate the interdisciplinary assessment of frailty into routine clinical practice.

title: TIPS for refractory hepatic hydrothorax in patients with cirrhosis: impact of clinical response on survival.
authorString: Tizzani M, Caviglia GP, Téllez L, Geisselbrecht S, Vizzutti F, Reincke M, Becchetti C, Maruzzelli L, Saltini D, Rudler M, Ferdinande K, Pompili E, Larrue H, Tosetti G, Nardelli S, Campion D, Donate J, Tiede A, Aspite S, Schultheiss M, Solcia M, Olavarría A, Birolo G, Bugianesi E, Svegliati-Baroni G, Viganò M, Piano S, Toniutto P, Riggio O, La Mura V, Bureau C, Caraceni P, Senzolo M, Thabut D, Schepis F, Miraglia R, Airoldi A, Bettinger D, Marra F, Maasoumy B, Albillos A, Marzano A, Alessandria C, “TIPS for refractory hydrothorax in cirrhosis” study investigators team.

journal.title: Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association

abstractText: Refractory hydrothorax (RH) significantly impairs quality of life and clinical outcomes in patients with cirrhosis. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) has been suggested as a potential treatment, but evidence is limited. We assessed TIPS effectiveness and impact on survival in patients with RH. Consecutive patients with cirrhosis undergoing TIPS for RH over a 16-year period across 18 European centers were included. Clinical response was assessed up to 12 months after TIPS and was classified as complete (CR: disappearance of symptoms and no further thoracenteses), partial (PR: decrease of symptoms and ≥50% reduction of thoracenteses) or no response (NR: minor or no relief in symptoms and <50% reduction or same/increased number of thoracenteses). Overall, 147 patients were included. TIPS achieved CR in 88 patients (60%). Mortality rates were 1.54, 5.34, and 11.4 deaths per 100 patient-months in patients with CR, PR, and NR, respectively. Time-dependent cause-specific Cox models showed a significant lower risk of death in CR patients compared with both those with PR (HR = 0.33, 95% CI 0.15-0.73; p = 0.006) and NR (HR = 0.15, 95% CI 0.06-0.37; p < 0.001). At multivariable analysis, CR remained independently associated with improved survival (HR = 0.30, 95% CI 0.14-0.64; p = 0.002). Among patients with cirrhosis and RH selected to undergo TIPS, clinical CR was achieved in a substantial proportion and was independently associated with improved survival.

title: Oral Anticoagulant Choice Across Indications in Cirrhosis: A US Nationwide Cohort Study.
authorString: Tanaka T, Holcombe AL, Clore G, Sun Msba M, Bixby AL, Lai JC, Axelrod D.

journal.title: Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association

abstractText: Comparative data on oral anticoagulant safety and efficacy across indications in cirrhosis remain limited. We compared outcomes following direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) versus warfarin initiation in a nationwide US cohort. The primary cohort (Epic Cosmos; 2019-2024) compared propensity score-matched DOAC and warfarin initiators across atrial fibrillation (AF), deep vein thrombosis with or without pulmonary embolism (DVT/PE), and portal vein thrombosis (PVT). Competing-risk regression models evaluated death, liver transplantation (LT), and hemorrhagic and ischemic outcomes. An ancillary cohort (US transplant registry-Medicare linkage; 2021-2022) evaluated INR-driven MELD inflation as a mediator among waitlisted patients. Among 93,663 initiators in the primary cohort, DOAC versus warfarin initiation in AF was associated with similar mortality and LT rates but lower overall major bleeding and non-gastrointestinal bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage. In DVT/PE and PVT, DOAC versus warfarin initiation was associated with higher mortality (DVT/PE: sHR 1.21 [95%CI 1.10-1.34]; PVT: sHR 1.43 [1.24-1.65]) and markedly lower LT rates (DVT/PE: sHR 0.25 [0.17-0.38]; PVT: sHR 0.23 [0.17-0.32]); gastrointestinal bleeding was higher with DOACs than warfarin in PVT (sHR 1.26 [1.06-1.50]). Multiple sensitivity analyses corroborated these findings. In the ancillary cohort (n=284), warfarin-associated INR elevation partially mediated LT access differences (percentage mediated: 29%). In cirrhosis, DOAC versus warfarin initiation was associated with similar mortality but favorable bleeding outcomes in AF. However, in venous thrombosis, DOAC initiators had higher mortality and lower LT access than warfarin initiators; warfarin-related INR inflation partly explained LT disparities. These findings support indication-specific treatment and reconsideration of INR handling in the US LT allocation system amid increasing DOAC use.

title: Characteristics and Outcomes of Patients with Atrial Fibrillation Undergoing Peripheral Vascular Interventions.
authorString: Said S, Presser E, Kostiuk V, Alameddine D, Cardella JA, Tonnessen BH, Ochoa Chaar CI.
abstractText: Atrial fibrillation (Afib) is a common dysrhythmia in patients with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and can alter antithrombotic management. However, the characteristics and outcomes of patients with Afib undergoing peripheral vascular interventions (PVI) is not well characterized. The Vascular Quality Initiative registry for PVI (2011-2024) was reviewed. The characteristics of patients with Afib were compared to patients without Afib. Perioperative and long-term outcomes were compared including reintervention, major amputation, mortality, and the composite outcome of MALE or mortality (MALE = reintervention or amputation), stratified by indication. Regression analysis was used to determine the independent association of Afib with outcomes. There were 118,095 patients analyzed (14% with Afib). Patients with Afib were older, more often male, white, and less likely to have history of smoking. Compared with patients without Afib, patients with Afib had higher comorbidities including cerebrovascular disease, coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension (P<0.001). Preoperatively, Afib patients were more likely to be on anticoagulants (63% vs. 11%; P<0.001), whereas patients without Afib were more likely to be on antiplatelets (80% vs. 68%; P<0.001). Afib patients were more likely to be treated for CLTI (70% vs. 57%; P<0.001). Postoperatively, patients with Afib had significantly higher rates of 30-day mortality in both the claudication (1.0% vs. 0.3%; P<0.001) and CLTI subgroups (4.1% vs. 1.5%; P<0.001). Logistic regression showed that Afib was independently associated with higher odds of 30-day mortality in CLTI (odds ratio = 1.55 [95% CI, 1.33-1.80]; P<0.001). At 18-month follow-up, patients with Afib had significantly higher rates of mortality for claudication (16% vs. 7%; P<0.001, adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) = 1.28 [95% CI, 1.16-1.42]; P<0.001) and CLTI subgroups (40% vs. 22%; P<0.001, aHR = 1.28 [1.23-1.34]; P<0.001). Among patients with CLTI, the composite outcome (MALE or mortality) was significantly higher in patients with Afib (33% vs. 30%; P<0.001), with a trend toward higher risk after adjustment (HR = 1.05 [95% CI, 0.99-1.12]; P=0.094), whereas rates were similar in claudication (14% vs. 15%; P=0.78). Patients with Afib undergoing PVI present with a higher burden of comorbidities, have different antithrombotic medications, and are more likely to be treated for CLTI compared to patients without Afib. Afib was independently associated with a significant increase in perioperative and long-term mortality but did not seem to be associated with limb outcomes.

title: Ascites fluid PMN counts below the SBP threshold predict 30-day mortality in a national hospitalized cirrhosis cohort.
authorString: Silvey S, Patel N, O'Leary JG, Bajaj JS.
abstractText: Complications in patients with cirrhosis often result from bacterial and bacterial product translocation. This translocation can occur because of portal hypertension, alterations in the gut microbiome, and immune dysregulation. We aimed to re-evaluate admission ascites PMN/mm3 count as a biomarker of 30-day mortality. We identified veterans with cirrhosis using validated ICD-9/10 codes who had a paracentesis ≤24 hours of their index hospitalization in the Veterans Affairs Corporate Data Warehouse from 2009 to 2024. In multivariable analysis, we determined the prognostic significance of ascites PMN/mm3 <100, 100-249, and ≥250. The 4111 veterans who met the inclusion criteria were mostly older (66 y) men (96.3%) with alcohol-associated liver disease (31.1%) who experienced 16.9% 30-day mortality. Most patients (~80%) had an ascites PMN/mm3 count <100. A roughly linear relationship between 30-day mortality was seen until the threshold of 100 PMN/mm3 was reached, when the relationship plateaued. The OR for 30-day mortality of a PMN/mm3 count 100-249 was 1.93 (95% CI: [1.55-2.38], p<0.001) after adjusting for age, CCI, liver disease etiology, admission lactulose use, SBP prophylaxis, serum WBC count, MELD-Na, and serum albumin. The 30-day mortality risk was not statistically different from the higher threshold of ≥250 PMN/mm3 (p=0.53). Admission ascites PMN/mm3 count ≥100, compared with <100, independently predicts a doubling in 30-day mortality in a national cohort of hospitalized patients with cirrhosis. Larger prospective studies are needed to examine the optimal ascites fluid PMN (polymorphonuclear neutrophil) thresholds that increase mortality risk.

title: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing and health-related quality of life in children with idiopathic or heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension.
authorString: Dubois V, El Louali Suzanne F, Quennelle S, Soulatges C, Dulac Y, Guitarte A, Vincenti M, De La Villeon G, Sophie G, Ovaert C.
abstractText:
Background

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive disease causing elevated pulmonary vascular resistance, right ventricular (RV) failure, and premature death. Idiopathic and heritable PAH impair functional capacity and health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) assesses exercise limitation and disease severity, yet its relationship with HRQoL has not been investigated in pediatric PAH.

Research design and methods

A retrospective multicenter study across three French tertiary pediatric cardiology centers was conducted (June 2023-April 2025). Children with idiopathic or heritable PAH who underwent CPET and completed the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL 4.0) were included. Key CPET parameters were analyzed, and associations to HRQoL scores assessed via Spearman correlation.

Results

Among 19 children (median age 11 years, median follow-up 32 months), exercise capacity was reduced (peak VO2 29 ml/kg/min; 74.5% predicted; Z-score -2.9), with ventilatory inefficiency (VE/VCO₂ slope 40). QoL scores were lower than normative values. No significant correlation was found between CPET parameters and HRQoL scores.

Conclusion

Children with idiopathic or heritable PAH present exercise limitation and impaired HRQoL, though CPET parameters were not correlated with HRQoL scores, reflecting limited statistical power. Larger studies are needed to clarify this relationship.

title: Colchicine use was associated with reduced all-cause mortality in patients with diabetic gout without prior coronary artery disease: A propensity-matched nationwide cohort study.
authorString: Shin Y, Cha JJ, Kim JH, Joo HJ, Park JH, Yu CW, Park M, Lee Y, Hong SJ.
abstractText: Colchicine has been associated with reduced cardiovascular events in secondary prevention, but evidence for primary prevention is limited. We examined the association between colchicine use and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and gout without prior coronary artery disease. From the Korean National Health Insurance Service database, we identified 48,295 patients with diabetes and gout without prior coronary artery disease between 2015 and 2019. We compared 28,964 colchicine users with 19,331 non-users by 1:1 propensity score matching, which produced 17,337 matched pairs. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and nonfatal stroke. The primary composite outcome occurred in 12.52% of colchicine users versus 15.03% of non-users (hazard ratio [HR] 0.71; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.66-0.75; P < 0.001). All-cause mortality was significantly reduced in colchicine users (8.01% vs. 11.07%; HR 0.58; 95% CI 0.53-0.62; P < 0.001). No significant differences were observed for myocardial infarction (HR 1.15; 95% CI 0.96-1.37; P = 0.121) or stroke (HR 0.91; 95% CI 0.81-1.01; P = 0.076). In a landmark analysis at 365 days that addressed immortal time bias, the associations with all-cause mortality (HR 0.67; 95% CI 0.62-0.73; P < 0.001) and with the composite outcome (HR 0.76; 95% CI 0.71-0.81; P < 0.001) remained significant, whereas stroke (HR 0.99; 95% CI 0.87-1.12; P = 0.823) and myocardial infarction (HR 1.15; 95% CI 0.95-1.40; P = 0.144) did not differ between the two groups. In patients with diabetes and gout without prior coronary artery disease, colchicine use was associated with lower all-cause mortality. The reduction in the composite outcome was driven by mortality rather than by myocardial infarction or stroke.

title: Multi-omics characterization of white matter free water reveals genetic and vascular determinants of neurological disorders.
authorString: Cheng C, He Y, Cao X, Xiang S, Fang Y, Wang M, Shao Z, Yao Y, Huang H, Xu S, Luo X, Zong X, Wang W, Hao X, Wang M.

journal.medlineAbbreviation: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
journal.title: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
journal.isoabbreviation: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

abstractText: White matter free water (FW-WM), quantified using diffusion MRI, reflects extracellular water content and microstructural alterations within water matter, but its genetic architecture and clinical relevance remain largely uncharted. We conducted a multi-omics study integrating 42,039 individuals from the UK Biobank and Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohorts to characterize tract-specific FW-WM across genetic, phenotypic, and proteomic dimensions. Genome-wide association analyses identified 27 independent loci and prioritized 88 genes, which were enriched in the genomic functional elements of vascular endothelial cells, pericytes, and astrocytes. Notably, 20 loci (74%) were novel compared to conventional white matter metrics. Both genetic predisposition to higher FW-WM and imaging-derived FW-WM were associated with a spectrum of neurological disorders. Specifically, imaging-derived FW-WM showed strong associations with stroke (OR = 3.14) and dementia (OR = 4.15), while higher baseline FW-WM predicted progression from MCI to AD (HR = 2.58). Bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses further supported genetically predicted associations between hypertension and FW-WM, which were together associated with increased risks of stroke and cognitive impairment. Integrative proteomic analyses further nominated PEAR1 and ANGL3 as candidate proteins potentially linking hypertension-related vascular processes to FW-WM variation. Together, these findings provide a multi-omics characterization of FW-WM that connects genetic susceptibility, vascular factors, and neurological outcomes, supporting FW-WM as a tract-specific imaging phenotype with potential utility for neurological risk stratification.

title: Development and validation of an explainable artificial intelligence model to predict in-hospital adverse events for patients with acute myocardial infarction.
authorString: Tian X, Ji M, Wang T, Yang Y, Yuan P, Zhang Y, Zhu C, Xia J, Gu Y, Liu H.
abstractText: In-hospital adverse events after acute myocardial infarction (AMI) can occur abruptly and adversely affect short-term prognosis. We developed and externally validated explainable machine learning models to predict a composite of in-hospital atrial fibrillation (AF), ventricular fibrillation (VF), cardiac arrest (CA), or death using routinely available admission data. We retrospectively analyzed 7,496 patients from the MIMIC-IV database as the development cohort and 2,776 patients from Xuanwu Hospital as the external validation cohort. Predictors included demographics, medical history, and admission laboratory tests. Logistic regression, random forest, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), multilayer perceptron, and TabNet models were evaluated using five-fold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using discrimination, classification, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Latent class analysis identified three outcome clusters with distinct event-probability profiles. XGBoost achieved the best performance for the composite outcome in the development cohort (AUROC, 0.798). Predictive performance was moderate to good for AF and in-hospital death, with AUROCs of up to 0.834 and 0.870 in the development cohort and 0.803 and 0.849 in the external validation cohort, respectively. Discrimination was lower for VF and CA. SHapley Additive exPlanations highlighted neutrophil and leukocyte counts, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, renal function, glucose, glycated hemoglobin A1c, and prior AF as important predictors. These explainable models may support early risk stratification and help guide monitoring intensity and timely intervention in patients with AMI.

title: Graph-Based Minimally Supervised Risk Stratification for Prognosis Prediction in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction.
authorString: Saleem R, Brady EM, Aziz F, Free R, Cao TH, Dattani A, Maxwell CB, Squire IB, Jones DJL, Ng LL, Anjum A, McCann GP.

journal.title: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics

abstractText: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is associated with poor outcomes, with 5-year survival after hospitalisation as low as 35-40%. Despite its growing prevalence, effective treatments remain limited. A major barrier to therapeutic success is the substantial biological and clinical heterogeneity within HFpEF, suggesting that distinct patient profiles may require different management strategies. This study investigates whether graph-based machine learning methods can identify distinct patient clusters within the HFpEF population and assess their relationships with clinical characteristics and outcomes. We analysed a multimodal dataset of 133 symptomatic HFpEF patients, comprising more than 240 K attributes derived from comprehensive cardiovascular assessment. These included cardiac MRI, echocardiography, circulating biomarkers of fibro-inflammation, and high-resolution proteomics. Five conventional unsupervised clustering methods were first applied but failed to produce clinically coherent groups, largely due to the complexity and multimodality of the data. To address this, we implemented a minimally supervised Graph Neural Network (GNN) that incorporated limited label information while modelling relationships between patients. This approach produced five clusters with potential clinical relevance. Importantly, cluster membership remained significantly associated with survival after adjustment for established clinical risk factors, including age, sex, BNP levels, symptom burden, and kidney function. Internal validation yielded an accuracy of 0.706 and an $F1$-score of 0.613, indicating reasonably consistent performance and suggesting that graph structure may aid generalisation and class-wise prognostic prediction. Overall, the findings show that minimally supervised graph-based learning can more effectively capture the underlying structure of multimodal HFpEF data than traditional methods. Visualisation and cluster quality metrics further support the effectiveness of the GNN approach.

title: [German Society of Cardiology position paper-how to treat patients with electrical storm: executive summary].
authorString: Meyer C, Arya A, Bode K, Dagres N, Deneke T, Jungen C, Veltmann C, Eckardt L.
abstractText: Electrical storm (ES), defined as at least three sustained episodes of ventricular arrhythmia within 24 h, is a life-threatening state of electrical and frequently hemodynamic instability associated with a high risk of mortality. Recurrent ventricular arrhythmias indicate prognostically relevant disease progression even before overt ES develops. Accordingly, ES often represents the culmination of a continuum of increasing electrical instability that should ideally be prevented or interrupted at an early stage. Characterization of the underlying arrhythmogenic substrate, arrhythmogenic triggers, and the arrhythmia itself, together with assessment of the overall hemodynamic status, forms the basis for risk stratification, diagnostic evaluation, and targeted treatment of ES. For the first time, the German Cardiac Society (DGK) position paper integrates these three dimensions-substrate, trigger, and arrhythmia (STA)-into the STA triad. Most episodes of ES occur in patients with structural heart disease, particularly ischemic or nonischemic cardiomyopathy with advanced heart failure; primary electrical or inherited arrhythmia syndromes are less common. The NHII-MED (neuroendocrine dysfunction, heart failure/hemodynamics, ischemia/coronary pathology, inflammation/infection, medication/metabolic factors, electrolyte imbalances, drugs/alcohol) framework was introduced to facilitate systematic trigger identification and management. Core components of specialized acute treatment include correction of reversible causes, device management including implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) reprogramming, antiarrhythmic drug therapy, sedation, catheter ablation, autonomic modulation, optimization of treatment for the underlying cardiac disease, and, when required, mechanical circulatory support. The overarching therapeutic objective is to prevent further ventricular arrhythmias and repetitive ICD therapies. This executive summary of the DGK position paper addresses the associated clinical challenges and contemporary management options.

title: Disturbed flow-induced mitochondrial remodeling regulates endothelial cell death in atherosclerosis.
authorString: Hu L, Sun C, Song J, Xu Z, Li X, Zhang X, Zhou K, Wu M, Liu L.

journal.title: Apoptosis : an international journal on programmed cell death

abstractText: Endothelial cell death is a critical event contributing to the initiation and progression of atherosclerosis (AS). Atherosclerotic lesions preferentially develop at arterial bifurcations and curvatures, where endothelial cells are continuously exposed to disturbed flow and experience pathological mechanotransduction. Although apoptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis have been implicated in endothelial injury under adverse h​aemodynamic conditions, how biomechanical stimuli are converted into specific cell death responses remains incompletely understood. Emerging evidence indicates that distinct disturbed-flow patterns and exposure conditions can elicit context-dependent mitochondrial remodeling, involving changes in network dynamics, subcellular positioning, quality control, and redox homeostasis. In this review, we discuss how haemodynamic stimuli may regulate endothelial cell death in AS through mitochondrial remodeling, while emphasizing that mitochondrial responses vary with the magnitude, directionality, and duration of flow. We further discuss emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at reducing endothelial cell death under adverse haemodynamic conditions by restoring atheroprotective flow, modulating endothelial mechanotransduction, and preserving mitochondrial homeostasis, thereby providing new perspectives for the prevention and treatment of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

title: Cilengitide limits syndromic and sporadic thoracic aortic aneurysm by targeting specific αV integrin.
authorString: Rega S, Bouhuis S, Brusati M, Maverna T, Fanotti N, Casaburo M, Vodret S, Riccitelli F, Celotto F, Lambroia L, Climent M, Elia L, Vescio M, Pattini L, Santoro R, Myasoedova V, Poggio P, Bonalumi G, Udugampolage NS, Taurino J, Pini A, Zacchigna S, Pompilio G, Perrucci GL.
abstractText: Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is one of the major causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide, still lacking an etiologic therapy. Aberrant activation of TGF-β and dysregulation of mechanotransduction signalling in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) play a key role in the pathology. However, a precise picture of molecular mechanisms in the disease is still unclear. Integrins containing the αV subunit are central in pro-fibrotic pathways mediated by TGF-β and mechanotransduction signalling pathways, but their role as a potential therapeutic target in syndromic and sporadic TAAs still needs investigation. We showed higher expression levels of αV integrin in both types of human TAAs and that the αV integrin inhibitor Cilengitide limits pro-fibrotic events in patient-derived VSMCs. In vivo results defined Cilengitide as the most effective and promising drug for the treatment of TAAs in humans.

title: Outcomes of extended septal myectomy for hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy in an Asian cohort.
authorString: Shetty V, Kulsum S, Shetty DP, Singhvi A, Padmanabhan D, Kumawat K, Raghuraman B, Gunaseelan V, Bheemaiah R, Makwana R, Mehra S, Shukla D, Raj V, Narayan P.
abstractText: BackgroundHypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) is a complex cardiac disorder often treated with septal myectomy, the gold-standard surgical intervention that improves symptoms and survival. Long-term outcome data with paired echocardiographic follow-up from the Indian subcontinent remain limited.MethodsThis was a retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients undergoing extended septal myectomy for HOCM at a single tertiary referral centre between 2014 and 2024, analysed from a prospectively maintained clinical registry. Demographic, clinical, echocardiographic, operative and follow-up data were analysed. Survival was estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method.ResultsA total of 399 patients underwent extended septal myectomy (mean age 41.2 ± 16.5 years; 282/399, 70.7% male; 46/399, 11.5% aged under 18 years). Septal hypertrophy was mainly mid-septal (255/399, 63.9%), with basal (110/399, 27.6%) and apical (34/399, 8.5%) involvement. Myectomy was isolated in 247/399 patients (61.9%) and combined with a concomitant procedure in 152/399 (38.1%); 15/399 patients (3.8%) had undergone a prior cardiac intervention, including alcohol septal ablation in 1/399 (0.3%) and previous cardiac surgery in 9/399 (2.3%). In-hospital mortality was 6/399 (1.5%). Mean follow-up was 5.4 ± 3.1 years, and median follow-up was 5.9 years (interquartile range 2.5-6.7); vital status was complete for all patients. Survival was 98.1% (95% CI 96.7-99.5) at 5 years and 95.9% (95% CI 92.7-99.0) at 10 years.ConclusionsExtended septal myectomy provides excellent structural, functional, and survival outcomes, comparable to leading centres. It should remain the preferred surgical treatment for symptomatic HOCM.

title: Targeting Systemic Immune Dysregulation in Cardiovascular Disease: From Mechanisms to Precision Therapeutic Strategies.
authorString: Li H, Ou Y, Zhu X, Fan G, Li L.
abstractText: Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality despite advances in conventional pharmacological therapy. Persistent inflammation and immune dysregulation contribute to residual cardiovascular risk, disease heterogeneity, and variable therapeutic responses. Increasing evidence links cardiovascular injury to systemic immune and immunometabolic disturbances arising from the kidney, liver, brain, hematopoietic and lymphoid organs, gut, and adipose tissue. This review summarizes how systemic immune disturbances contribute to cardiovascular remodeling through altered immune-cell activation, impaired inflammatory resolution, metabolic stress, and pathological immune memory. We discuss the contributions of kidney-, liver-, neuroimmune-, gut-adipose-, and hematopoietic-associated abnormalities to major cardiovascular phenotypes, including heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, cardiorenal syndrome, metabolic cardiomyopathy, and aging-associated cardiovascular disease. These systemic abnormalities converge on common cardiovascular effector mechanisms, including endothelial dysfunction, inflammatory-cell recruitment, macrophage activation, fibroblast remodeling, extracellular matrix deposition, and cardiomyocyte dysfunction. We further examine emerging pharmacological strategies targeting systemic immune dysregulation, including cytokine inhibition, inflammasome modulation, metabolic interventions, and therapies targeting maladaptive immune memory. Although several approaches have demonstrated clinical benefit, effective translation requires identification of biologically defined patient subgroups, reliable biomarkers, and appropriate assessment of therapeutic response and safety. Integrating immune profiling with cardiovascular pharmacotherapy may facilitate a transition from nonspecific anti-inflammatory approaches toward precision modulation of pathological immune networks.

title: Cell death: from basic principles to translational developments.
authorString: Xu L, Liu R, Han Q, Wang T, Wang S, Xue L, Liu H, Sun J, Zhang Y, Zhuang C.
abstractText: The precise regulation of cell death is indispensable for embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, and the pathophysiology of human disease. Dysfunctions in regulated cell death (RCD) pathways constitute a critical aetiological factor in diverse pathologies, including oncogenesis, neurodegenerative disorders, autoimmune conditions, and ischaemic injury. Substantial efforts to therapeutically target these mechanisms are therefore needed. In this review, we present a systematic analysis of the molecular machinery underlying distinct RCD processes, including apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and multiple forms of metal-dependent cell death.
