Diagnostic accuracy was assessed using sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Results

The final seven-variable ARC included age >60 years, abrupt onset pain, severe pain, hypotension/shock, neurological deficit, pulse deficit, and known aortic disease. Patients were classified as positive if any ARC variable was present and negative only if all variables were absent. In the derivation cohort, ARC achieved a sensitivity of 99.2% (95% CI 99.1-99.3). In the ADvISED/PROFUNDUS cohort (4598 patients, 10.2% AAS prevalence), sensitivity was 100% (95% CI 99.2-100) with specificity 23.7% (95% CI 22.4-25.0). In the DAShED cohort (5346 patients, 0.3% prevalence), sensitivity was 100% (95% CI 76.8-100) and specificity 36.4% (95% CI 35.1-37.7), ruling out 36.3% of patients without missing any AAS cases.

Conclusions

ARC is an externally validated, pragmatic clinical rule demonstrating high diagnostic sensitivity in a large external validation cohort. When incorporated into existing diagnostic pathways, ARC has the potential to reduce unnecessary testing while maintaining diagnostic performance. Further prospective validation is required to confirm its clinical utility.

title: CABG in uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis complicated by thyroid storm: A case report.
authorString: Sathanantham DK, Pillai MN, Ramaratnam S, Agarwal A, Nair JTK.

journal.medlineAbbreviation: Turk Gogus Kalp Damar Cerrahisi Derg
journal.title: Turk gogus kalp damar cerrahisi dergisi
journal.isoabbreviation: Turk Gogus Kalp Damar Cerrahisi Derg

abstractText: Cardiac surgery in patients with active thyrotoxicosis carries substantially increased perioperative risks. We report a case of urgent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) in a 43-year-old man with severe biochemical thyrotoxicosis and critical left main coronary artery disease who presented with non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. Urgent off-pump CABG was performed with intra-aortic balloon pump support. Within 48 hours of surgery, the patient developed a thyroid storm characterized by fever (40 °C), tachycardia (140-180 beats/min), encephalopathy, and jaundice. The condition was successfully treated with anti-thyroid drugs and intravenous hydrocortisone. The patient recovered fully and was euthyroid at follow-up. Early recognition and prompt multidrug treatment of postoperative thyroid storm are life-saving.

title: Dual-Valve Infective Endocarditis Caused by Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii in a Patient with Bicuspid Aortic Valve: A Case Report
authorString: Zhao H, Wang S, Wu D, Cao Z, Zhang Y.
abstractText: Background Infective endocarditis (IE) caused by carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) is rare and associated with substantial mortality. When it arises on a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV), simultaneously involves the aortic and mitral valves, and presents with persistently negative blood cultures, diagnosis and management become exceptionally challenging. Case presentation A 52-year-old man presented with a four-month history of fever and positive rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies, initially raising suspicion of rheumatoid arthritis. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a BAV (right–left cusp fusion), a large mitral anterior leaflet vegetation (1.5 × 1.3 cm), and aortic valve vegetations. Splenic and cerebral infarctions were subsequently identified. Blood cultures remained repeatedly negative in the context of antecedent antimicrobial exposure. He underwent double mechanical valve replacement with vegetation debridement, and intraoperative valve tissue culture grew CRAB, prompting adjustment to a high-dose sulbactam-based regimen. He recovered and was discharged. To our knowledge, this combination of culture-negative CRAB native-valve IE, BAV, dual-valve involvement, and diagnosis solely by intraoperative tissue culture has not previously been reported. This case illustrates a plausible anatomical mechanism linking BAV to concomitant aortic–mitral involvement, highlights the diagnostic value of intraoperative tissue culture and the importance of timely surgical evaluation, and underscores the potential for positive rheumatoid serology to complicate the diagnostic process.

title: Inflammatory Markers for Predicting Post-operative Acute Kidney Injury in Patients with Acute Type A Aortic Dissection
authorString: Yu X, Nie Y, Zhao Y, Wang Q, Li Z, Zhu S, Zhang L.
abstractText: Background Acute kidney injury (AKI) is one of the most common peri-operative complications of acute aortic dissection. It contributes to in-hospital mortality and exerts adverse impacts on patients’ long-term survival. Objective To explore the predictive value of inflammatory markers for post-operative acute kidney injury in patients with acute type A aortic dissection. Methods Clinical data of 135 patients diagnosed with acute type A aortic dissection admitted to Anhui Provincial Chest Hospital from November 2022 to September 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. Patients were divided into the AKI group and non-AKI group. Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were applied to evaluate the predictive performance of inflammatory markers for AKI. Results Among the 135 enrolled patients, 69 (51.1%) developed post-operative AKI. Compared with the non-AKI group, the AKI group presented significantly higher interleukin-6 (IL-6), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR). Logistic regression showed that IL-6 (OR = 1.13, 95%CI: 1.01–1.04, P  < 0.01), NLR (OR = 1.28, 95%CI: 1.13–1.47, P  < 0.01) and PLR (OR = 1.02, 95%CI: 1.01–1.03, P  = 0.013) were independent risk factors for AKI in patients with acute type A aortic dissection. ROC curve analysis demonstrated that NLR, PLR and IL-6 possessed favourable predictive accuracy. Conclusion IL-6, NLR and PLR are correlated with AKI occurrence in patients with acute type A aortic dissection and have good reference value for predicting post-operative AKI.

title: Disparities in RSV Hospitalisations Among Children Under 2 Years in NSW, Australia.
authorString: Soenong H, Hossain S, Oei JL, Munasinghe S, Dronavalli M, Lee E, Page A, Yeo KT.

journal.title: Journal of paediatrics and child health

abstractText:
Aim

To estimate RSV hospitalisation rates among children ≤ 2 years in New South Wales (NSW), Australia over two decades; to examine how rates varied by age, prematurity and selected co-morbidities and to describe temporal, seasonal and geographic patterns in RSV hospitalisation across NSW.

Methods

RSV hospitalisation rates were calculated using linked population data for all children ≤ 2 years in NSW from 2002 to 2020 (n = 1 770 628). Infant and maternal factors were analysed as covariates using a univariate log-binomial model to determine RSV admission risk between groups. Geographical distributions were visualised using heatmaps according to location at birth.

Results

The overall RSV hospitalisation rate during 2004-2020 was 11.2 per 1000 child-years (95% CI 11.1-11.4) while during the contemporary pre-pandemic period of 2016-2019, the rate was 15.4 (15.1-15.7). Compared to children born term without comorbidities (8.41 admissions per child-years at risk [7.96-8.88]), rates of RSV hospitalisations were significantly higher among premature children (23.8 [23.2-24.5]) and children with any co-morbidities (48.2 [46.1-50.4]). Children with primary immunodeficiency (8.12 [6.78-9.72]), bronchopulmonary dysplasia (6.54 [6.06-7.06]), Down syndrome (5.10 [4.38-5.93]) and congenital heart disease (3.70 [3.53-3.88]) had persistently elevated hospitalisation rates into the second year of life. Hospitalisation rates were higher in Greater Sydney and subtropical northeastern coastal NSW where RSV activity began earlier and was less seasonally defined than temperate regions.

Conclusions

Strategies to protect premature children and those with comorbidities against RSV are warranted up to 2 years of age given the persistently elevated RSV risk. Regional RSV epidemiology should be considered when developing immunisation strategies.

title: Data-driven estimation of the onset of heat-related mortality in five Indian cities
authorString: Robles Fontan MM, Krishna B, Mahajan A, Meade RD, Tiwari A, Balsari S, Buckee C, Irizarry RA.
abstractText:
Background:

Extreme heat is an increasingly pressing public health threat, particularly in South Asia. Yet the temperatures at which mortality risk begins to increase in Indian cities remain poorly characterized. Operational heat wave definitions are based on meteorological criteria and may not reflect epidemiologically relevant temperature thresholds. Widely used distributed lag non-linear models are designed to flexibly estimate expected mortality as a function of temperature, but do not directly target the onset of excess risk from heat, a quantity central to early warning and planning.

Methods:

We conducted a multi-city time-series study of daily mortality and temperature data in Ahmedabad (2001-2010), Chennai (2012-2017), Delhi (2011-2015), Kolkata (2011-2018), and Mumbai (2011-2015). We developed a data-driven structured modeling framework that permits likelihood-based inference for city-specific temperatures at which heat-related mortality first exceeds seasonal background levels, a parameter that is challenging to estimate and perform statistical inference from short and noisy series. Using these health-based thresholds, we also estimated heat-associated excess deaths.

Results:

In all five cities, the onset of excess mortality occurred at temperatures substantially lower than those implied by current operational heat wave definitions. The proposed framework yielded stable and interpretable threshold estimates and confidence intervals across heterogeneous climates and time-series lengths and identified a larger burden of heat-associated mortality than would be captured using standard meteorological criteria.

Conclusions:

Data-driven estimation of mortality-based heat thresholds provides epidemiologi- cally relevant targets for early warning systems and heat action plans. Reliance on meteorological definitions alone may delay intervention and underestimate population risk in rapidly warming regions.

title: Congenital Heart Block: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management.
authorString: Kaywood AJ, Ahmadi A, Frishman WH.
abstractText: Congenital heart block (CHB) is a rare but potentially life-threatening form of conduction disease that manifests in utero or shortly after birth, resulting from disruption of the normal electrical conduction pathway between the atria and ventricles. The severity of CHB varies depending on the degree of atrioventricular conduction impairment, ranging from first-degree atrioventricular block, characterized by prolonged conduction, to complete third-degree block, in which atrial and ventricular activity are entirely dissociated and function independently. The most common etiology is passive transplacental transfer of maternal anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB autoantibodies, most frequently in the setting of maternal systemic lupus erythematosus or Sjögren syndrome, even when the mother is clinically asymptomatic. Less commonly, CHB arises in association with structural congenital heart disease, most notably left atrial isomerism and corrected transposition of the great arteries. The clinical spectrum ranges from an incidental prenatal finding to fetal hydrops and in utero death, with third-degree CHB carrying a perinatal mortality rate of approximately 15-30%. This review integrates current evidence on the pathophysiology, maternal autoimmune contributions, diagnostic approach, and management strategies for CHB, with an emphasis on the emerging roles of fetal surveillance, pharmacologic interventions, and postnatal pacing.

title: Retrograde Open Mesenteric Stenting Failure Requiring Aorto-Mesenteric Bypass in Acute-on-Chronic Mesenteric Ischemia: A Case Report.
authorString: Kaddouri L, Bouallala A, Benabdelaziz E, Chaouch N.
abstractText:
Introduction

Chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) is a rare pathology, most commonly associated with multivessel atherosclerosis, whose diagnosis is often delayed due to nonspecific symptoms. Endovascular treatment is the first-line treatment option, although its results may be limited by restenosis or intrastent thrombosis. Open surgery remains an important option in cases where endoluminal treatment has failed. The aim of this paper is to illustrate, through a clinical case, the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges associated with severe CMI.

Case presentation

A 69-year-old female patient, a long-term smoker being treated for peripheral arterial disease, presented with postprandial abdominal pain that had been present for 6 months, accompanied by severe malnutrition. The CT angiogram revealed occlusion of the celiac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery, with the development of extensive collateral circulation. Initial endovascular revascularization via stenting was performed in a patient presenting with gastrointestinal distress that had required segmental resection of necrotic ileojejunal loops. The course of the disease was characterized by a recurrence of symptoms and stent thrombosis, leading to surgical revascularization via an aorto-mesenteric bypass. The postoperative course was favorable, with the mesenteric angina gradually subsiding, significant weight gain, and lasting functional improvement.

Conclusions

This case highlights the limitations of endovascular treatment alone in severe multivessel disease and confirms the value of a personalized treatment strategy incorporating open surgery to optimize long-term outcomes.

title: CORRIGENDUM: Discontinuation of Tafamidis in Wild-Type Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy Patients.
authorString: Baba Y, Ochi Y, Kubo T, Kawaguchi J, Yamasaki N, Kitaoka H.
abstractText: [This corrects the article DOI: 10.1253/circrep.CR-25-0181.].

title: Cell Reprogramming: Therapeutic Advances and Challenges.
authorString: Li A, Wang Z, Lyu Z, Tuo Z, Li X, Wu RC, Wang J, Wusiman D, Wang Y, Zhang Q, Xiong W, Zhou B, Feng D.
abstractText: Cell reprogramming, which forcibly alters cell fate, offers a novel therapeutic strategy for various refractory diseases. Unlike previous reviews focused on a single disease context or a single reprogramming modality, this review is organized around therapeutic applications. It summarizes advances in direct reprogramming, partial reprogramming, and cell fusion-induced reprogramming and further compares their mechanisms, challenges in clinical translation, and safety boundaries. In oncology, reprogramming cancer cells into antigen-presenting cells elicits durable antitumor immunity and remodels the tumor microenvironment, whereas converting cancer cells into nonmalignant somatic cells can reduce their malignant phenotype and tumorigenic potential. In neurodegenerative diseases, direct reprogramming has converted fibroblasts or astrocytes into functional dopaminergic and cortical neurons both in vitro and in vivo. In mouse models of progeria and natural aging, partial reprogramming strategies markedly extend lifespan, ameliorate multiorgan pathology, and enhance tissue regenerative capacity. However, the strength and reproducibility of these findings vary across experimental models, and reported therapeutic benefits do not necessarily establish complete, stable, or safe cell-fate conversion. Against this predominantly preclinical background, ER-100 is the first regenerative therapy based on partial epigenetic reprogramming to receive Food and Drug Administration Investigational New Drug approval and enter clinical testing. It therefore provides an important reference point for the transition from animal studies to human trials. Cell fusion-induced reprogramming has context-dependent roles in tumor immunity. Fusion between tumor cells and immune cells may promote malignant progression. In contrast, dendritic cell-tumor cell fusion vaccines and chimeric exosomes can activate antitumor immune responses in preclinical models and early clinical studies. Major barriers to clinical translation include low reprogramming efficiency, an incompletely defined safety window, and the need to select in vivo or ex vivo strategies according to disease context. In addition, insufficient delivery efficiency, poor targeting, and long-term tumorigenic risk remain important constraints on clinical application. Looking ahead, single-cell multiomics and artificial intelligence may help optimize reprogramming factor combinations, while nonviral systems may improve targeted delivery. Integration with tissue engineering may further facilitate clinical translation across oncology, aging, regenerative medicine, autoimmune diseases, and neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: GLP-1 based therapy of obesity and type 2 diabetes.
authorString: Holst JJ.
abstractText: GLP-1 is 30-amino acid peptide that is secreted from the intestine in response to food intake. The release mechanism involves luminal exposure to as well as absorption and metabolism of the major nutrients. It functions mainly as a part of the ileal brake mechanism whereby nutrient entry in distal segments of the small intestine inhibit gastrointestinal secretion and motility as well as appetite and food intake, signalling nutritional abundance. It also functions as a second line incretin hormone. It acts on the brain via sensory vagal afferents, but also interacts with exposed neurons expressing the GLP-1 receptor in the circumventricular organs, in turn activating brain nuclei involved in appetite regulation and reward. High doses of GLP-1 cause nausea and vomiting, but slow dosing titration mitigates this. GLP-1 Receptor Agonists owe their actions to these physiological mechanisms and therefore represent powerful antidiabetic agents (A1c levels below 5.7%) and cause major weight loss (up to 20%), but also appear to reduce the systemic low-grade inflammation of obesity and type 2 diabetes and to exert beneficial action on the blood vessels, providing the GLP-1RAs with preventive effects on cardiovascular, hepatic, renal and central nervous system complications. Orally active GLP-1rAs have also been developed. It is emphasized that GLP-1RA therapy should be accompanied by lifestyle changes for efficacy and to prevent side effects of the weight loss. In addition, any prescription of a GLP-1RA should include a plan to mitigate adverse effects of treatment termination. Nevertheless, GLP-1RAs represent a major breakthrough in the therapy of metabolic disease and are now included among the essential medicines of the WHO.

title: Electrical Storm Triggered by Conus Branch Occlusion During Elective Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in Very Severe Aortic Stenosis: Rescue With Balloon Aortic Valvuloplasty Under Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation.
authorString: Kodama T, Honda N, Hiromatsu S, Masuda S.

journal.title: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions

abstractText: We report a case of very severe aortic stenosis (AS) in which side-branch occlusion during elective percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) precipitated life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias and hemodynamic collapse. The patient was a 72-year-old man with very severe AS who was scheduled to undergo a valve intervention. Preprocedural coronary angiography revealed a significant, newly developed stenosis in the right coronary artery, and an elective PCI was performed prior to valve treatment. Following intravascular lithotripsy and drug-eluting stent implantation, occlusion of the conus branch occurred, triggering recurrent ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. Despite initiation of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and intra-aortic balloon pump support, the patient's hemodynamic status did not improve. Because excessive afterload due to very severe AS was considered the principal pathophysiological mechanism, emergency balloon aortic valvuloplasty was performed. This resulted in rapid hemodynamic stabilization and complete resolution of ventricular arrhythmias. This case illustrates that even a minor side-branch occlusion during PCI can lead to catastrophic outcomes in patients with very severe AS. Furthermore, it highlights that mechanical circulatory support alone may be insufficient, and that prompt relief of valvular obstruction is essential. Careful consideration of the indications and sequence of coronary intervention through discussions with a heart team is warranted for patients with very severe AS.

title: CD34<sup>+</sup> Progenitors Promote Ageing-Associated Valve Sclerosis through the PDGFR-JNK-JUNB Pathway.
authorString: Yang X, Wu H, Ren G, Zhang Y, Wen Z, Zhu P, Ying Z, Jiang L, Tao T, Zhang B, Zhu L, Wang H, Zhang H, Xu Q, Cheng J, Ye H.
abstractText: Aortic valve sclerosis (AVS), characterised by fibrocalcific remodelling without significant hemodynamic obstruction, represents a critical window for early clinical intervention; however, its underlying cellular drivers during ageing remain poorly understood. Here, genetic lineage tracing and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) techniques were used to examine the temporal and spatial functions of CD34<sup>+</sup> valvular interstitial cells (VICs) in ageing-associated AVS. Human scRNA-seq datasets were used in combination with natural ageing and D-galactose (D-gal)-induced mouse models, and a significant age-dependent downregulation of CD34 in VICs was identified. Lineage tracing and bone marrow (BM) chimeras confirmed that non-BM CD34<sup>+</sup> progenitor VICs (prog-VICs), rather than bone marrow-derived cells, serve as the origin of periostin<sup>+</sup> myofibroblast-like VICs (myo-VICs) during ageing. Functionally, the systemic or non-BM-specific ablation of CD34<sup>+</sup> cells or the CD34<sup>+</sup>Periostin<sup>+</sup> transitional subpopulation markedly attenuated age-related leaflet thickening and fibrotic remodelling. Mechanistically, the JNK-JUNB signalling pathway, mediated by PDGFR, was found to be crucial for the pathological transdifferentiation of CD34<sup>+</sup> prog-VICs into periostin<sup>+</sup> myo-VICs. Non-BM CD34<sup>+</sup> prog-VICs were found to aggravate senescence-associated AVS; thus, targeting the PDGFR-JNK-JUNB axis or preserving the prog-VIC identity may offer therapeutic avenues to arrest early calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) progression.

title: Global research trends of artificial intelligence in echocardiography (1984-2025): a bibliometric analysis.
authorString: Al Saikhan L.
abstractText:
Background

Echocardiography has evolved substantially since its introduction in 1954. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers transformative potential for image acquisition, quantification, interpretation, and reporting. Despite growing research interest, a comprehensive evaluation of the historical trends and evolution of AI in echocardiography is lacking. The study aimed to conduct a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of the global research landscape in this field.

Methods

A systematic literature search was conducted using the Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection databases for publications on AI in echocardiography from inception through November 10, 2025; no language filter was applied. Data analysis was performed using Microsoft Excel, Microsoft Access, and IBM SPSS Statistics. In addition, bibliometric mapping and data visualization were conducted.

Results

Overall, 2682 publications received 35,083 citations (mean, 13.08 citations per publication), spanning 1984-2025. Original articles, conference papers, and review articles accounted for 87.4% and 98.5% of total publications and citations, respectively. Publication output remained limited until approximately 2015, rose gradually thereafter, and accelerated markedly after 2018, with similar output in 2024 and 2025. The United States led in both publication volume and total citations, followed by China and the United Kingdom. The United States also had the highest collaboration link strength, and seven of the top 10 institutions were in North America (six in the United States and one in Canada). Mayo Clinic ranked first, with 142 publications and 3604 citations, and had the earliest first indexed publication among the top institutions (1992). The journal JACC: Cardiovascular Imaging ranked first in both total citations (1,911) and citations per publication (36.75). "Echocardiography," "deep learning," "artificial intelligence," and "machine learning" were the most frequently used terms. The thematic evolution showed continuity of algorithmic-centric themes (1984-2019) with emerging clinically oriented themes (2020-2025).

Conclusions

This comprehensive bibliometric analysis highlights the rapid expansion of AI research in echocardiography, characterized by an accelerating publication output and emerging clinically oriented research topics. These findings reflect growing research interest in integrating AI into echocardiographic practice and highlight the need for future research prioritizing multicenter validation, clinical translation, and equitable real-world implementation.

title: Genetically predicted lipoprotein(a), first and recurrent venous thromboembolism, and coagulation proteins: evidence against causal relationships.
authorString: Daghlas I, Gill D.
abstractText: Lipoprotein(a) exhibits in vitro antifibrinolytic properties, though it remains uncertain whether this translates into an effect on thromboembolic disease risk. We applied Mendelian randomization (MR) to evaluate the relationship between genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) levels, venous thromboembolism (VTE), and circulating coagulation protein levels. We instrumented lipoprotein(a) using two genetic variants (rs10455872 and rs3798220) that explain 36% of circulating lipoprotein(a) variance. The primary outcomes were first (81,190 cases) and recurrent VTE (1,775 cases). Comparator outcomes included coronary artery disease (181,522 cases) and calcific aortic stenosis (13,765 cases). We performed MR analyses to estimate the association of a genetically predicted 100 nmol/L increase in lipoprotein(a) with each outcome. In exploratory analyses, we tested associations with levels of 35 coagulation proteins in the UK Biobank (n = 46,218) and deCODE (n = 35,559) cohorts. Genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) was associated with a small reduction in risk of first VTE (odds ratio [OR] 0.98, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.96-0.99, P = 0.002), though this was not supported by colocalization (posterior=12%), suggesting that the MR association was driven by genetic confounding. There was no association with recurrent VTE (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.91-1.16, P = 0.68). In contrast, genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) was strongly associated with increased risk of coronary artery disease (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.29-1.33) and calcific aortic stenosis (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.30-1.40). After multiple testing correction, genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) had no significant association with any coagulation proteins. Human genetic evidence does not support a clinically meaningful role for lipoprotein(a) in VTE risk. These findings support targeting of lipoprotein(a)-lowering therapies toward atherosclerotic and valvular diseases rather than thromboembolic indications.

title: Advances in engineered 3D cardiac tissue for functional biosensing, disease modeling, and regenerative medicine.
authorString: Zhang C, Sun W, Liu X, Xiong W, Xiao W, Yang Y, Langari FM, Daoud A, Sun C, Chen W, Tang W, Liu X, Maynes JT, Sun Y, Dou W.
abstractText: Three-dimensional (3D) engineered cardiac tissues are miniaturized in vitro cardiac models to recapitulate essential aspects of native heart physiology for applications in drug testing, disease modeling and regenerative therapy. Building on advances in microfabrication, biomaterials, bioelectronics and stem cell biology, these systems reproduce myocardial architecture, mechanical dynamics, electrical conductivity, and disease-specific phenotypes. Existing reviews treat biofabrication, biomaterials, functional biosensing, disease modeling, and cardiac regenerative therapy as separate topics, while few have framed these components within a unified micro- and nanoengineering framework that links tissue architecture, functional biosensing, and application-driven performance. This review addresses this gap by highlighting recent advances in biofabrication strategies for precise control over tissue architecture and cellular microenvironments and discusses the incorporation of microelectronic, optical, and mechanical biosensors for real-time, multiparametric monitoring of tissue contractility and electrophysiological activity. We further summarize representative applications in disease modeling such as cardiomyopathies, ischemic injury, and drug-induced cardiotoxicity, as well as the development of bioengineered cardiac constructs and patches as transplantable grafts to restore myocardial function. Finally, key challenges and future directions toward predictive, scalable, and translational cardiac microphysiological systems are discussed.

title: miR-144-5p in extracellular vesicles: A promising candidate diagnostic biomarker for carotid artery plaques.
authorString: Shao L, Xie Z, Yang M, Xu H, Chen L.

journal.title: Clinica e investigacion en arteriosclerosis : publicacion oficial de la Sociedad Espanola de Arteriosclerosis

abstractText:
Background

Extracellular vesicle-derived microRNAs (EV-miRNAs) play critical regulatory roles in atherosclerosis, but their expression profiles and key regulatory molecules in carotid artery plaques remain insufficiently elucidated.

Methods

EV-miRNA sequencing data (SRP515368) of human carotid plaque and marginal tissues were analyzed via DESeq2, WGCNA and LASSO regression to screen diagnostic miRNAs. PPI network analysis and GO/KEGG enrichment was performed on target genes. ApoE-/- mice with perivascular carotid collars and high-fat feeding were established as plaque models; qRT-PCR validated miR-144-5p expression in plaque tissues, while ELISA detected serum inflammatory markers IL-1β and TNF-α for correlation analysis.

Results

A total of 801 differentially expressed EV-miRNAs were screened. WGCNA combined with LASSO identified hsa-miR-144-5p as the sole predictive marker with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.907. Its targets were enriched in cell adhesion, migration, inflammation and vascular remodeling pathways. qRT-PCR confirmed significant miR-144-5p upregulation in mouse carotid plaques (P<0.0001), which was strongly positively correlated with serum IL-1β and TNF-α (r≥0.89, P<0.01).

Conclusion

hsa-miR-144-5p, derived from extracellular vesicles, acts as a novel high-performance biomarker in carotid plaques and is closely related to the inflammatory progression of the plaque. This provides molecular evidence for the development of diagnostic signatures and precise therapeutic targets against carotid atherosclerosis.

title: Segmental arterial mediolysis: An underrecognized rare vascular disease requiring an interprofessional diagnostic and therapeutic pathway.
authorString: Mojica Crespo R, Morales Crespo MM.
abstractText: Segmental arterial mediolysis (SAM) is a rare, non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic arteriopathy that predominantly affects the visceral circulation and may cause dissection, aneurysm, hemorrhage, or ischemia. Its diagnosis is challenging because imaging findings overlap with fibromuscular dysplasia, vasculitis, connective tissue disorders, atherosclerosis, and mycotic aneurysm. This narrative review synthesizes the available evidence into an interprofessional diagnostic and therapeutic pathway. The proposed framework links radiological suspicion with structured exclusion of major mimics, multidisciplinary vascular assessment, treatment selection, management of hemodynamic instability, and longitudinal imaging surveillance. Conservative management is appropriate for stable patients without active hemorrhage, whereas endovascular treatment is generally preferred when intervention is required and anatomically feasible, with surgery reserved for failed stabilization or uncontrolled bleeding. Because current evidence is largely observational and case-based, the pathway should be regarded as a literature-based framework requiring prospective validation rather than a validated clinical guideline.

title: Mitochondrial protein import stress augments α-synuclein aggregation and neural damage.
authorString: Coyne LP, Rana A, Wang X, Mauro J, Bhagwagar S, Umino Y, Solessio EC, Middleton F, Chen XJ.
abstractText: Genetic and environmental factors are known to converge on mitochondria to cause Parkinson's disease. The underlying mechanism is incompletely understood. In addition to bioenergetic defects, nonbioenergetic pathways have been largely unexplored. Validating the nonbioenergetic mitochondrial stressors as independent pathogenic factors is challenging because most mouse models of mitochondrial stress are confounded by bioenergetic defects. Here, we show that expression of Ant1<sup>P.A114P,A123D</sup>, previously shown to cause mitochondrial protein import clogging in cultured human cells, does not affect the overall bioenergetic capacity, yet it induces proteostatic stress responses in the cytosol that suggests accumulation of unimported precursor proteins. In a Parkinson's disease model expressing α-synuclein (A53T), Ant1<sup>P.A114P,A123D</sup> increased the size of α-synuclein aggregates, increased aggregation of mitochondrial preproteins, heightened neuroinflammation, and worsened motor coordination defects. Importantly, we found no evidence of bioenergetic defects in either α-synuclein (A53T) or α-synuclein (A53T) + Ant1<sup>P.A114P,A123D</sup> mice. These data suggest that Ant1<sup>P.A114P,A123D</sup> likely induces mitochondrial protein import stress, and contributes to neural damage through cytosolic proteostatic stress and altered aggregation dynamics of neuropathogenic proteins independent of bioenergetics.

title: Impairment of LEM-domain function in LEMD2-associated cardiomyopathy.
authorString: Chen R, Abdelfatah N, Maimaitiniyazi W, Urlaub D, Bihler T, Gordon PMK, Fielding C, Belke D, Wang Z, Gerull B.

journal.title: Journal of molecular and cellular cardiology

abstractText: LEMD2 is an inner nuclear membrane protein that interacts with LMNA and contributes to nuclear membrane integrity and chromatin organization. Pathogenic LEMD2 variants are associated with progressive cardiomyopathy, but the relationship between Lemd2 protein abundance and disease severity remains unclear. Using computational modeling, we designed a Lemd2 in-frame deletion (p.Glu8_Leu9del, ΔE8_L9) within the LEM domain, predicted to alter its conformation, and generated knock-in (KI) mouse by CRISPR/Cas9. Western blot analysis demonstrated that the ΔE8_L9 deletion was associated with a near-complete loss of Lemd2 protein. Findings were considered alongside those previously reported for the Lemd2 p.L13R KI model, which retains ~68% of Lemd2 protein, to describe the cardiac phenotype and nuclear phenotypes associated with two distinct LEM-domain mutations. ΔE8_L9 homozygous mice exhibited postnatal growth retardation and rapidly progressive dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) with systolic dysfunction and myocardial fibrosis by postnatal day 21 (P21), whereas the reported p.L13R model exhibited later-onset DCM. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed dense intranuclear chromatin aggregates and peripheral heterochromatin accumulation in cardiomyocytes. Bulk RNA sequencing identified downregulation of DNA replication- and DNA repair-related pathways at P1.5 and upregulation of mechanical stress-, senescence-, and immune response-related pathways at P21. Consistently, ΔE8_L9 hearts exhibited increased γ-H2AX-positive DNA damage and a numerically lower percentage of Ki-67-positive cardiomyocytes. The ΔE8_L9 model is associated with marked Lemd2 protein reduction, nuclear membrane abnormalities, altered chromatin architecture, DNA damage, and early-onset DCM.

title: Cardiovascular Disease Risk Screening for Endocrine-Disrupting Chemicals Based on Machine Learning.
authorString: Zhang J, Yang H, He H, Li Y, Wang W.
abstractText: Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) interfere with human and animal endocrine systems and are common in plastics, personal care products, and pesticides. EDC exposure has been associated with cardiovascular disease (CVD), particularly in middle-aged and older adults. We developed a computational framework to screen 1,106 EDCs for potential CVD risk, using population biomarker data on 39 environmental contaminants (ECs) from a published epidemiological study for model calibration and benchmarking. Structural clustering identified 677 candidate EDCs. A three-stage framework combining positive-unlabeled (PU) learning and stacking then identified 167 EDCs with potential CVD risk. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) identified descriptors contributing to these predictions. Adverse outcome pathway (AOP) analysis, molecular dynamics simulations, and statistical methods were combined to calculate atherosclerosis effect scores and construct a priority control list. The list included 50 high-risk EDCs, with pesticides, aromatic amines, and nitrogen-containing heterocycles as prominent chemical groups. TabNet and sensitivity analysis identified molecular features associated with the predicted risk levels. The framework integrates published epidemiological data with theoretical simulations to support EDC prioritization and environmental risk management. Independent external validation is needed before applying the model to uncharacterized EDCs.

title: N-glycoproteomic profiling reveals aberrant ITGB1 glycosylation in hyperoxia-induced bronchopulmonary dysplasia.
authorString: Zhao C, Liu J, Tong C, Chen C, Liu Y, Chen Y, Wang L, Peng H.
abstractText:
Background

Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a prevalent chronic lung disease in preterm infants, characterized by arrested alveolarization. Extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling and receptor signaling are critical for alveolarization and are strictly regulated by protein N-glycosylation. However, the specific role of the vital post-translational modification in BPD pathogenesis remains unexplored. The present research aims to delineate a N-glycoproteomic landscape and elucidate the glycosylation-associated pathogenic mechanisms in a murine BPD model.

Methods

To establish BPD models, newborn mice were exposed to continuous hyperoxia (85% O2) for 14 days. Lung developmental impairment was quantified using Radial Alveolar Count (RAC) and Mean Linear Intercept (MLI). A comprehensive dual-omics profiling strategy was conducted, utilizing an Orbitrap Exploris 480 platform for global proteomics and a timsTOF Pro mass spectrometer for N-glycoproteomics. Key molecular targets were further validated by lectin histochemistry, Western blot, and AlphaFold-based spatial structure modeling.

Results

Hyperoxia exposure successfully induced BPD-like lung injury, substantiated by a marked decline in RAC coupled with a concurrent elevation in MLI (P < 0.001). Conjoint omics analysis identified 612 N-glycoproteins and 1105 modification sites. After normalizing to global protein abundance, we revealed distinct glycosylation alterations, characterized by the identification of 16 upregulated and 100 downregulated modification sites. Furthermore, lectin histochemistry confirmed an overall reduction and redistribution of core-mannose N-glycans on the cell surface in BPD lungs. Bioinformatics analysis demonstrated that differentially glycosylated proteins were predominantly enriched in ECM-receptor interactions, integrin-mediated cell adhesion, and PI3K-Akt signaling. Subsequent Protein-Protein Interaction network analysis revealed Integrin beta-1 (ITGB1) as a crucial hub node; notably, we identified a marked downregulation of its site-specific N-glycosylation. Spatial modeling pinpointed a crucial, disease-associated aberrant glycosylation site at Asn212, located merely 17.3Å from the MIDAS binding pocket. This site-specific hypo-glycosylation is postulated to unmask the ITGB1 interface, potentially perturbing physiological ligand binding.

Conclusion

This study provides the first exhaustive N-glycoproteomic map of hyperoxia-induced BPD. Our results highlight dysregulated N-glycosylation, particularly the site-specific hypo-glycosylation of ITGB1 at Asn212. Based on computational predictions, it is hypothesized to severely disrupts the ECM-receptor networks and integrin affinity, which correlates with potentially driving alveolarization arrest. These insights provide a novel post-translational perspective on BPD pathogenesis and offer new avenues for future investigation into potential therapeutic targets.

title: Risk Prediction for Heart Failure in Patients with Cancer: Current Models and Future Directions.
authorString: Agdamag AC, Manaila-Nabi AS, Nandar PP, Tang WHW.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

Cancer survivors have an elevated risk for developing heart failure due to prior chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and other overlapping co-morbid conditions. With the advancement in cancer treatment, there is an increasing number of survivors who are at an even higher risk of developing heart failure. There is a growing need for heart failure specific risk prediction models in this population to facilitate early diagnosis and timely management. This review aims to summarize most recent findings on heart failure risk prediction among patients with history of cancer.

Recent findings

Current risk prediction models focus on heart failure risk at the time of cancer treatment and shortly thereafter. There is limited data on heart failure risk among long term survivors.

title: Interleukin-6, soluble interleukin-6 receptor, and outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve implantation: an exploratory biomarker substudy of a prospective multicenter cohort.
authorString: Procyk G, Tyrna P, Młynarczuk-Biały I, Budzianowski J, Olasińska-Wiśniewska A, Kochman J, Gąsecka A.
abstractText:
Background

Severe aortic stenosis can be treated with transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Identifying clinical and laboratory factors that predict clinical outcomes after TAVI may facilitate more informed decision-making. We aimed to assess the incidence of major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) within 12 months after TAVI and long-term survival according to baseline interleukin-6 (IL-6) and soluble interleukin-6 receptor (sIL-6R) levels.

Methods and results

In this biomarker substudy of a prospective multicenter cohort, we evaluated clinical outcomes after TAVI according to baseline IL-6 signal and sIL-6R concentration. We included only patients with an available baseline stored plasma sample. Patients were stratified into high and low IL-6 and sIL-6R groups. Two primary end points were analyzed: (i) 12-month MACCE, and (ii) long-term overall survival. Secondary end points included the individual components of MACCE. Stored baseline plasma was available for measurements in 62 patients who underwent TAVI between December 2018 and September 2021 across three clinical sites. Patients with high IL-6 had a higher 12-month MACCE risk in age- and sex-adjusted Firth penalized Cox regression analysis (HR 3.31; 95%CI 1.02-11.04, P = 0.0458) but not in unadjusted analysis (log-rank P = 0.07). The association was not robust to alternative cutoffs and the age- and sex-adjusted continuous analysis of IL-6 also did not show a statistically significant association (hazard ratio per 1-SD increase, 1.52, 95% CI, 0.86 to 2.46, P = 0.13). No significant associations were observed in the primary models between IL-6 and long-term overall survival or between sIL-6R and either primary end point.

Conclusions

High IL-6 signal at baseline may be associated with increased 12-month MACCE risk after TAVI, although this finding was sensitive to IL-6 categorization and was not statistically significant in continuous analysis. Baseline sIL-6R concentration was not significantly associated with the analyzed clinical outcomes. These findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

title: A Validated Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy Claims-Based Coding Algorithm: ValidATTR-US.
authorString: Jimenez JI, Fahed G, Cai N, Udall M, Kitakata H, Alexander KM.
abstractText:
Introduction

Lack of a validated United States (US) claims-based method for identifying transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) limits the reliability and comparability of real-world evidence. We developed and validated a US claims-based coding algorithm (ValidATTR-US) to identify patients with ATTR-CM.

Methods

ValidATTR-US was developed by optimizing previously published algorithms using International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes and refining them using the STAnford Research Repository (STARR, claims/electronic health record-linked database; N = 61,908) to define the index cohort (n = 694). The Stanford ATTR-CM Patient Registry (N = 634) served as the validation cohort for cross-referencing the index cohort. Index cohort inclusion criteria were age ≥ 60 years at diagnosis and ≥ 2 ATTR-CM diagnosis codes (ICD-10-CM, E85.[0, 1, 2, 4, 82]) on separate days and ≥ 2 cardiac-related codes or ≥ 1 tafamidis claim. Exclusion criteria were multiple myeloma (C90), light chain amyloidosis (E85.81), hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (Z94.84), and organ-limited amyloidosis (E85.4) when co-occurring with cerebral amyloid angiopathy (I68.0), end-stage renal disease (N18.6), or skin disorders (L99). Performance metrics included accuracy ({true positives [TPs] + true negatives [TNs]}/total sample), specificity (TNs/{TNs + false positives [FPs]}), and sensitivity (TPs/{TPs + false negatives [FNs]}).

Results

Accuracy was 99.51% (95% confidence interval [CI] 99.45-99.56%), specificity 99.70% (99.65-99.74%), and sensitivity 80.76% (77.47-83.76%) for detecting patients with ATTR-CM (TP, n = 512; TN, n = 61,092; FP, n = 182; FN, n = 122). Individual ICD-10-CM codes were strongly predictive of ATTR-CM case status (area under the curve [AUC] 0.84) and genotype classification (AUC 0.88).

Conclusion

ValidATTR-US is the first US claims-based ATTR-CM coding algorithm validated against a clinically confirmed ATTR-CM registry. Broader application may improve identification of patients with ATTR-CM in real-world datasets and help characterize prevalence and treatment patterns. Graphical abstract available for this article.

title: Aging modifies the immunological signature of pesticide exposure: increased circulating sTREM-1 and sTREM-2 in rural workers.
authorString: do Carmo Neto JR, Barradas MC, Tomaz AA, de Oliveira Matos A, de Oliveira AA, do Carmo Dietz J, da Silva ABA, Xavier DF, Dos Santos Dantas PH, Silva-Sales M, de Melo E Silva D, Sales-Campos H.

journal.title: International archives of occupational and environmental health

abstractText: Pesticides pose significant risks to human health through both environmental and occupational exposure. In agricultural contexts, occupational exposure is particularly prevalent and has been linked to the activation of inflammatory pathways and dysregulation of the immune response. Nevertheless, the acute and chronic impacts of pesticide exposure on biomarkers of innate immunity remain poorly characterized. In this context, the soluble forms of TREM-1 and TREM-2 have emerged as sensitive indicators of inflammation and/or been associated with neurodegenerative disorders, respectively, however, they have not yet been explored as occupational biomarkers of pesticide exposure. Thus, this study aimed to evaluate the influence of age, duration of exposure, and type of pesticide on circulating levels of sTREM-1 and sTREM-2 in a cross-sectional cohort of 168 rural workers from the state of Goiás, Brazil, stratified according to type of exposure and age (≤ 50 and ≥ 51 years). Serum levels of sTREM-1 and sTREM-2 were determined by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA). Sociodemographic and exposure-related variables were evaluated using parametric and nonparametric statistical tests, depending on the data distribution. Older individuals had significantly higher levels of sTREM-1 and sTREM-2, regardless of the type of pesticide they were exposed to. Age was correlated with increased biomarker concentrations, while the number of pesticides seemed not to influence these molecules. Longer exposure to pesticides was positively associated with higher levels of both biomarkers. Lifestyle factors (smoking and alcohol consumption) and history of previous pesticide poisoning modulated these effects in specific subgroups. These findings indicate that aging plays a central role in modulating sTREM-1 and sTREM-2 levels in pesticide-exposed populations, potentially modifying the immune effects associated with different types and combinations of compounds. In this context, TREM-related markers emerge as promising indicators of chronic immune activation in environmental and occupational settings.

title: Transforming cardiac amyloidosis care: navigating the evolving diagnostic and therapeutic landscape.
authorString: Kieviet LC, Ahmetagic D, Muller SA, Guglielmo M, Nijveldt R, van der Harst P, van der Meer MG, Oerlemans MIFJ.

journal.title: Netherlands heart journal : monthly journal of the Netherlands Society of Cardiology and the Netherlands Heart Foundation

abstractText: Amyloidosis comprises a group of systemic disorders caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded precursor proteins, leading to progressive organ dysfunction. Cardiac amyloidosis, particularly transthyretin-related amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) has transitioned from a rare and underdiagnosed condition to a treatable disease, driven by major advances in diagnostic imaging, increased disease awareness, and the approval of disease-modifying therapies. These therapies target transthyretin (TTR) stabilization and amyloid production or deposition and have led to an evolving therapeutic landscape. As therapeutic efficacy is greatest in earlier disease stages, timely recognition is crucial. Effective management of ATTR-CM requires structured screening of high-risk populations, multidisciplinary collaboration, and longitudinal follow-up. This review provides a practical, clinician-focused framework that addresses clinical presentation and "red flags" to facilitate early detection. It offers a comprehensive overview of the diagnostic pathway, including (AI-enabled) electrocardiography analysis, (non-)invasive imaging modalities, biomarkers, and genetic testing. Additionally, emerging therapeutic strategies are discussed, encompassing supportive heart failure management, amyloid-specific treatments such as TTR stabilizers and gene silencers, and novel approaches including fibril depletion and gene-editing therapies. As the therapeutic paradigm shifts from disease stabilization toward potential reversal, early diagnosis and personalized treatment strategies are essential to improve prognosis and quality of life in patients with cardiac amyloidosis.

title: Cardiac amyloidosis: the role of multimodality imaging.
authorString: Achten A, Jonkhof I, Knackstedt C, Slart RAHJA.

journal.title: Netherlands heart journal : monthly journal of the Netherlands Society of Cardiology and the Netherlands Heart Foundation

abstractText: Cardiac amyloidosis is an increasingly recognized cause of heart failure, driven by advances in diagnostic techniques and the emergence of disease-modifying therapies. Early and accurate diagnosis is essential as timely treatment influences prognosis. Although endomyocardial biopsy remains the reference standard, non-invasive imaging has become central to the diagnostic pathway and disease evaluation.This review summarizes the contemporary role of multimodality imaging in cardiac amyloidosis. Echocardiography remains the first-line imaging modality and can provide important diagnostic clues, including increased ventricular wall thickness and apical sparing on strain analyses. CMR enables detailed tissue characterization, allowing non-invasive assessment of myocardial amyloid burden and disease progression. Bone scintigraphy has revolutionized the diagnosis of transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy by enabling a reliable non-biopsy diagnosis after exclusion of light-chain amyloidosis. Emerging PET tracers may further improve early detection, quantification of amyloid burden, and monitoring of treatment response.The integration of multimodality imaging has fundamentally changed the diagnostic and therapeutic landscape of cardiac amyloidosis, facilitating earlier recognition, improved risk stratification, and longitudinal disease monitoring. As novel therapies continue to emerge, advanced imaging techniques are expected to play an increasingly important role in personalized management and evaluation of therapeutic response.

title: Three-Dimensional Immunofluorescence Analysis of Psoriatic Plaques Before and After Pulsed Dye Laser Treatment: Reduced T-Cell Content Without Changes in Nerve Fiber or Blood Vessel Density.
authorString: Doppegieter M, Beek NV, Vos J, Neumann HAM, Aalders MCG, Bakker ENTP, van Leeuwen TG.
abstractText:
Objectives

Pulsed dye laser (PDL) treatment for psoriasis has demonstrated its potential for treatment-free remission periods exceeding 1 year. The mechanism leading to remission is not fully understood, but PDL is known to heat the vasculature in the skin. We hypothesized that heat diffuses from the vasculature to the surrounding environment, including perivascular nerves and T-cells, leading to an interruption of the neurogenic inflammatory cycle that drives psoriasis.

Methods

We compared histological features of the vasculature, nerves, and leukocyte infiltrate in 120 biopsy sections (80 µm thick) from 20 patients, collected before and after two PDL treatments. The alterations in vasculature were categorized into three distinct classifications: papillary vasculature, reticular vasculature, and total vasculature. Nerve fibers were divided into free epidermal nerve fibers, perivascular nerve fibers around capillaries, and reticular nerves. The densities of these structures, as well as the volume of the epidermal and dermal leukocyte infiltrate, were calculated from the three-dimensional (3D) fluorescence microscopy images.

Results

Two sessions of PDL treatment significantly reduced CD3+ leukocyte infiltrate in the skin. Furthermore, pruritus and epidermal thickness were also significantly reduced. Vascular and nerve fiber density did not significantly differ before and after two treatments.

Conclusions

Using 3D immunofluorescence microscopy to quantify T-cells, vasculature and nerve fibers, we found that two PDL treatments were associated with a significant reduction in CD3+ T-cells, even in patients whose clinical severity did not improve, while vascular and nerve fiber density remained unchanged. Perivascular heat diffusion and potential alterations in vascular integrity may contribute to this reduction, but this hypothesis requires confirmation in future studies.

title: Long Term Outcomes of Pediatric Patients After Catheter Ablation for Possible Arrhythmia Induced Cardiomyopathy.
authorString: Doi Y, Tien M, Davis A, Pflaumer A.
abstractText: Arrhythmia induced cardiomyopathy (AiCM) is reversible, and catheter ablation has become the standard treatment for most arrhythmias. However, as the diagnosis of AiCM can be made only in retrospect, management is often challenging. A single center retrospective study included patients who had ablation for presumed AiCM after January 2011 to assess the outcomes of ablation, and the final diagnosis. 22 patients (11 female) were included in the study with the following distribution of arrhythmias: Atrial Ectopic Tachycardia (AET) = 8, Permanent Junctional Reciprocating Tachycardia (PJRT) = 6, Ventricular Tachycardia = 3, Premature Ventricular Contraction = 1, Atrial Flutter = 1, Atrioventricular Reciprocating Tachycardia = 1. There were two patients where an EP study did not show a specific arrhythmia substrate and the patients proceeded in the transplantation pathway. Of the 20 patients with confirmed tachycardia, four (20%) had complete normalization of function with+ medical management. The remaining 16 patients (80%) achieved no or partial functional recovery, with ablation playing even more important role in these patients. One AET patient showed no recovery of function despite successful ablation, consequently requiring heart transplant due to later confirmed gene-positive cardiomyopathy. Overall, 19 patients (95%) showed normal cardiac function at the end of study period with diagnosis of AiCM. There was one significant complication with AV block due to RF ablation on ECMO in a newborn with PJRT. While medical management can achieve functional recovery in some pediatric AiCM cases, most patients will require catheter ablation with 88% success rate. However, once functional recovery is achieved, long term outcome is excellent. Very rarely ventricular function will not recover despite successful ablation as genetic cardiomyopathies can present with secondary arrhythmia.

title: Coronary Plaque Phenotypes According to Physiological Disease Severity and Pullback Pressure Gradient.
authorString: Nishi T, Sasahira Y, Kume T, Koto S, Okamoto H, Yamada R, Koyama T, Tamada T, Neishi Y, Uemura S.

journal.title: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions

abstractText:
Background

Coronary pressure pullback characterizes both the overall physiological severity and longitudinal distribution of coronary artery disease. However, the respective relationships of physiological disease severity and longitudinal disease distribution with local and vessel-wide plaque phenotypes remain incompletely understood.

Aims

To investigate the relationships of physiological disease severity and longitudinal disease distribution with coronary plaque characteristics assessed by optical coherence tomography (OCT).

Methods

We studied 216 patients with left anterior descending coronary artery disease who underwent OCT and angiography-based physiological assessment. Quantitative flow ratio (QFR) represented overall physiological disease severity, whereas the pullback pressure gradient (PPG) index characterized longitudinal disease distribution. Associations with local OCT characteristics and whole-vessel burden of plaque features were assessed using regression models, with physiological indices standardized per 1 SD increase.

Results

Median QFR and PPG were 0.88 [0.73-0.95] and 0.76 [0.69-0.83], respectively. Lower QFR was strongly associated with greater maximum lipid arc (β per 1 SD increase, -39.16°; 95% CI, -52.01 to -26.31; p < 0.001). PPG was not associated with maximum lipid arc in univariable analysis (β, -9.18°; p = 0.19). After accounting for QFR, however, higher PPG was associated with greater lipid arc index (β, 112.26 °·mm; p = 0.012) and smaller minimum lumen area (β, -0.42 mm2; p = 0.011), with a similar association observed for maximum lipid arc (β, 16.60°; p = 0.045). Conversely, lower PPG was associated with greater whole-vessel counts of adverse plaque features in unadjusted analyses, but these associations were attenuated after accounting for QFR.

Conclusions

At comparable physiological disease severity, a more focal physiological pattern was associated with greater local lipid concentration and lumen compromise, whereas a more diffuse pattern was associated with greater whole-vessel counts of plaque features in unadjusted analyses. These findings suggest that physiological disease severity and longitudinal disease distribution provide complementary information on the spatial phenotype of coronary atherosclerosis.

title: Endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition in atherosclerosis and its implications for biomaterial design.
authorString: Zhou M, Chen F, Bai Z, Shi J, Qu P, Gu Y, Li G, Liu F, Shu Q, Cheng P.
abstractText: Endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) contributes to endothelial dysfunction and plaque remodeling in atherosclerosis, but its therapeutic implications depend on cell state and tissue context. Lineage tracing and single-cell studies support a continuum of EndMT-associated changes involving potentially overlapping inflammatory, matrix-producing, matrix-degrading, and osteogenic programs. This functional diversity complicates broad inhibition: some programs promote disease progression, whereas others may help maintain tissue structure. This review examines how the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of EndMT and its mechanical, inflammatory, metabolic, and epigenetic regulation guide cargo selection, targeted delivery, and release control. We evaluate nucleic acid nanocarriers, engineered extracellular vesicles, and biomaterials for local interventions, distinguishing evidence of endothelial delivery and modulation of EndMT-associated programs from evidence of selective reprogramming of established pathological states. Current studies support delivery and program modulation, but evidence for state-selective reprogramming remains insufficient. The central question is whether interventions can limit pathological programs while preserving endothelial barrier function and plaque structure. Addressing this question requires separate assessments of delivery selectivity and pharmacodynamic selectivity, supported by functional evidence beyond lesion accumulation or improved marker profiles alone.

title: Generation of Human Cardiomyocytes With Adult-Like Metabolism by a Chemically Defined Medium for Mitochondrial Disease Modeling.
authorString: Tu C, Caudal A, Liu Y, Belbachir N, Kojic A, Stern B, Ren L, Hu E, Cunningham N, Yu B, Chen YI, Jurney P, Napierala JS, Napierala M, Ritterhoff J, Tian R, Wu JC.
abstractText:
Background

Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC cardiomyocytes) as a model for cardiac disease have become increasingly important, bolstered by the Food and Drug Administration's initiative to promote novel alternative methods for biomedical research. A key limitation of metabolically immature iPSC cardiomyocytes is their limited ability to accurately recapitulate mitochondria-dependent pathologies, such as Friedreich ataxia-associated cardiomyopathy. Adult cardiomyocytes are characterized by a high density of interfibrillar mitochondria, abundant respiratory complexes (I-V) that form supercomplexes, and efficient utilization of fatty acids to drive mitochondrial respiration. These unique metabolic structures and functions are largely missing in iPSC cardiomyocytes. Further, whether iPSC cardiomyocytes can efficiently utilize fatty acids for respiration in the presence of glucose, a unique adult feature, remains unclear.

Methods

We developed a chemically defined, 11-component maturation medium (MM11) designed using a bioinformatics-guided strategy that identified high-fidelity transcriptional markers of adult cardiac metabolic maturity. Human iPSC cardiomyocytes were treated with MM11 for 2 weeks and evaluated at the molecular, structural, and functional levels, with an emphasis on mitochondrial maturity. We benchmarked our results with isolated primary adult human cardiomyocytes. Last, we tested whether this method could enable us to more accurately model Friedreich ataxia cardiomyopathy.

Results

MM11 treatment increased expression of metabolic pathways, including mitochondrial respiration and fatty acid metabolism, at the transcript and protein levels. Ultrastructural analyses revealed the formation of interfibrillar mitochondria and mitochondrial respiratory supercomplexes, a feature never shown in previous reports. Functionally, MM11-treated iPSC cardiomyocytes exhibited substantially increased oxidative phosphorylation and a metabolic preference for fatty acid utilization in the presence of physiologic substrates, as determined by oxygen consumption assays and 13C isotope tracing.

Conclusions

MM11 promotes robust metabolic maturation of human iPSC cardiomyocytes, enabling sophisticated mitochondrial architecture and substrate utilization. These metabolically matured cardiomyocytes more faithfully model mitochondria-dependent cardiac pathologies, including ischemia-reperfusion injury and Friedreich ataxia cardiomyopathy, improving the use of iPSC cardiomyocytes for mechanistic studies of human heart disease.

title: Recent Advances in High-Entropy Nanozymes: From Fabrication to Applications.
authorString: Ai Y, Zhang W, Wang P, Xu W, Guo H, Sun HB, He MQ, Ren F, Liang Q.
abstractText: Nanozymes are artificial enzymes designed to circumvent the inherent limitations of natural enzymes. They have emerged as a transformative paradigm in biomimetic catalysis. High-entropy nanozymes (HEAzymes) are nanomaterials that consist of high-entropy alloys, oxides, sulfides, and other high‑entropy compounds that exhibit enzyme-like catalytic activity. HEAzymes have recently garnered substantial attention as a next-generation nanozyme. The rapid evolution of this field has been propelled by synergistic advances in nanotechnology, biotechnology, catalysis, and computational modeling, offering unprecedented opportunities for rational design and broad-spectrum applications. This review provides a comprehensive and timely overview of state-of-the-art developments in HEAzymes, systematically spanning synthetic methodologies, catalytic mechanisms, and multifunctional applications. We classify fabrication strategies into thermodynamically driven and kinetically controlled routes, elucidate enzyme-mimetic catalytic behaviors and their underlying mechanistic principles, and critically examine recent advances in antioxidative, therapeutic, biosensing, energy-related, and emerging applications. Finally, we discuss prevailing challenges and outline prospective directions to guide future research. By spotlighting the frontier of HEAzyme research, this review aims to foster interdisciplinary collaboration and catalyze continued innovation in nanozyme science.

title: Genetic effects on serum and urine metabolites across ancestries and their links to disease
authorString: Steinbrenner I, Zhang R, Scherer N, Lee Y, Nguyen NQH, Waterhoelter A, Rodriguez-Hernandez Z, Borisov O, Zakharenko D, Surapaneni A, Monteiro-Martins S, Li Y, Kelly TN, Chen J, He J, Koettgen A, Boerwinkle E, Coresh J, Grams ME, Li C, Yu B, Schlosser P.
abstractText: Genome-wide association studies of the metabolome have predominantly examined European-ancestry populations using a single biofluid, constraining both the discovery of metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs) and the resolution of causal variant finemapping. Here, we report a multi-ancestry genome-wide association study of 1,955 serum and urine metabolites in 4,431 European American and African American participants from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study. We identify 969 mQTLs for 553 metabolites, 30% unreported in studies of matched biofluid and ancestry, and replicate 91-99% of testable mQTLs in two independent cohorts. In the African American sample with balanced sample sizes, 36% of metabolites with mQTLs are serum-specific, 39% urine-specific, and 25% shared, demonstrating complementary genetic architecture. Only 23 of 632 candidate ancestry-specific mQTLs show heterogeneous effects beyond variant availability and power, yet allele frequency differences expose functional variants such as an SLC28A1 splice variant, virtually absent in Europeans, that increases urine uridine excretion, implicating impaired CNT1-mediated renal nucleoside reabsorption. Multi-ancestry finemapping improves credible set resolution, and colocalization with the Million Veteran Program phenome links the catalog to cardiometabolic, kidney and liver traits consistent with prioritized gene function. Integrating biofluids and ancestries enhances genetic discovery and mechanistic characterization of the human metabolome.

title: CD8+ T-cells protect against experimental atherosclerosis through antigen specific interactions in the plaque
authorString: de Vlieger EA, de Jong MJ, Molenaar J, Lindenbergh PP, Liu K, Hamelynck RM, Foks AC, Bot I, van de Sluis BA, Sluetter B.
abstractText: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease with a significant adaptive immune component. CD8+ T cells accumulate in plaques and display signatures of antigen-specific activation. However, whether this accumulation is driven by local antigen recognition and what functional consequences follow, remains poorly understood. Here we address this gap of knowledge using loss- and gain-of-function experiments. Atherosclerotic Rag-/-Ldlr-/- mice received adoptively transferred wildtype or antigen-restricted CD8+ T cells alongside CD4+ T cells to distinguish antigen-specific from antigen-independent responses. In a complementary model, ApobOVA-TGxLdlr-/- mice, expressing an ovalbumin-tagged variant of the atherosclerosis-associated ApoB100 protein, enabled OT-I CD8+ T cells to function as atherosclerosis-antigen-specific CD8+ T cells. T-cell distribution, activation and phenotype were assessed systemically and within lesions, plaque burden and composition were quantified histologically. Wildtype CD8+ T cells accumulated significantly more in aortic lesions compared to antigen-restricted CD8+ T cells, and exhibited increased activation, exhaustion and cytokine secretion, indicating that plaque-infiltrating T cells are predominantly antigen-specific. Perturbing antigen-specific CD8+ T-cell interactions significantly decreased plaque stability index, suggesting a protective role for antigen-specific CD8+ T cells. In ApobOVA-TGxLdlr-/- mice, OT-I T cells accumulated at high frequency in the liver, consistent with hepatic ApoB100-expression, and were found in circulation and aorta. Histological analysis revealed reduced plaque burden in OT-I recipients, reproducing an atheroprotective effect of antigen-specific CD8+ T-cell responses. Plaque reduction coincided with reduced TUNEL, but similar Caspase 3 staining, suggesting OT-I transfer results in reduced secondary necrosis. In line with this, CD47 expression in OT-I recipient mice was reduced and in vitro, OT-I but not antigen non-specific CD8+ T cells reduced expression of CD47 on OVA-presenting foam cells. CD8+ T-cell accumulation in experimental atherosclerosis is driven primarily by antigen-specific interactions and such responses are associated with plaque stabilization and reduced lesion formation, potentially through induction of apoptosis and prevention of secondary necrosis

title: Inflammatory biomarkers and prevalent coronary atherosclerosis among Ugandan adults with and without HIV
authorString: Migisha R, Byakika-Kibwika P, Kangwagye P, Muhwezi A, Erem G, Longenecker CT, Ghoshhajra B, Bibangambah P, Nassanga R, Masette G, Atwiine F, Tindimwebwa E, Gilbert RF, Reynolds Z, Randhawa M, Thondapu V, Takigami A, Passell E, Acan M, Ochieng A, Okello S, Asiimwe S, Siedner MJ.
abstractText: Background Chronic inflammation is implicated in coronary atherosclerosis, particularly among people with HIV, who may experience persistent immune activation despite antiretroviral therapy. However, most evidence linking inflammatory biomarkers to coronary artery disease (CAD) comes from populations outside sub-Saharan Africa. We assessed associations between inflammatory biomarkers and CAD among older adults with and without HIV in southwestern Uganda. Methods We analyzed adults aged ≥ 40 years in a community-based cohort in rural southwestern Uganda. CAD was assessed using coronary artery calcium scanning and contrast-enhanced coronary computed tomography angiography. Biomarkers included indicators of macrophage activation (sCD163), hypercoagulability (D-dimer), systemic inflammation (C-reactive protein), gut epithelial integrity (fatty acid binding protein 2), and hematologic inflammatory indices derived from complete blood counts. We fitted Firth penalized logistic regression models to estimate crude, HIV-stratified, and multivariable-adjusted associations. Receiver-operating-characteristic analyses assessed whether select biomarkers improved discrimination beyond the atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk score. Results Among 585 participants, mean age was 57.7 years, 287 (49.1%) had HIV, and 45 (7.7%) had CAD. Most biomarkers, including C-reactive protein, D-dimer, fatty acid–binding protein 2, and complete blood count–derived inflammatory indices, were not associated with CAD after multivariable adjustment and false-discovery-rate correction. Higher sCD163 was inversely associated with CAD in the adjusted overall model (odds ratio per 1-standard-deviation increase, 0.63; 95% confidence interval, 0.47–0.87; q = 0.048), but this finding was not consistent across HIV strata. Adding sCD163 to the ASCVD risk score did not improve discrimination for CAD. Conclusions In this cohort of older adults in rural Uganda, inflammatory biomarkers showed limited associations with CAD and did not improve discrimination beyond conventional risk assessment. These findings support emphasis on established cardiovascular risk assessment among older Ugandans, and further investigation into the pathogenesis of CVD risk in this population.

title: Phenotyping of Exercise Response in FORMs of Arrhythmogenic CardioMyopathy: PERFORM-ACM.
authorString: Wernhart S, Haykowsky MJ, Federle D, Shir M, Mastella G, Rattka I, Steger A, Diebold I, Martens E, Trenkwalder T, Laugwitz KL, Halle M, Rattka M.

journal.medlineAbbreviation: Am J Physiol Heart Circ Physiol
journal.title: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology
journal.isoabbreviation: Am J Physiol Heart Circ Physiol

abstractText: Patients with arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) are advised to perform no more than moderate-intensity exercise, but whether such exercise acutely alters hemodynamic, electrophysiological, or cardiac biomarker profiles is unknown. We investigated whether moderate-intensity isometric, resistance, or aerobic exercise induces exercise pulmonary hypertension (exPH, mean pulmonary artery pressure to cardiac output slope >3 mmHg/L/min), troponin T elevation, or changes in late potentials (LP) in definitive or probable ACM. Twenty patients (13 definitive, 7 probable ACM; age 42.2 ± 10.7 years) underwent exercise right heart catheterization during isometric handgrip (HG) and bicep curl (BC) (1 minute each at 70% of maximal voluntary contraction), followed by 2 × 20 minutes of supine cycling (CYC) at the first ventilatory threshold. Central hemodynamics and cardiac biomarkers were measured during each condition, and high-density right ventricular electroanatomical mapping was performed before and after exercise. exPH did not occur in either group (all <3 mmHg/L/min), whereas troponin T rose progressively without group differences (p=0.880). LP within the "arrhythmogenic triangle" decreased in probable (mean change -1.95 ± 1.59%) but increased in definitive ACM (mean change 2.72 ± 2.16%, p<0.001). In conclusion, moderate-intensity HG, BC, and CYC exercise were not associated with exPH in probable or definitive ACM. Despite similar hemodynamic and biomarker responses, post-exercise LP diverged between groups, decreasing in probable but increasing in definitive ACM. This observation warrants validation in larger cohorts with better control for baseline substrate and longitudinal clinical outcomes.

title: Incremental yield of genetic retesting in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
authorString: de Castro D, Ochoa JP, Fernández-Ávila AI, Cabrera-Romero E, Jiménez-Barceló JA, Armesto-Rivas J, Bernabé-García Á, Gómez-González C, Torres-Juan L, Briceño-Hinojo A, Carillo-Mora LM, Méndez-Fernández I, Heine-Suñer D, Ripoll-Vera T, Espinosa-Castro MÁ, Sabater-Molina M, Garcia-Pavia P.
abstractText:
Background and aims

Modern genetic testing in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) includes newly described HCM-associated genes and full intronic regions of certain classic sarcomeric genes. This study evaluated genetic retesting in HCM patients with a prior negative test and identified predictors of a positive result to guide retesting.

Methods

This multicentre study included patients with HCM who previously had negative next-generation sequencing (NGS)-based genetic testing at four centres. Subjects were retested using an updated NGS-based HCM panel.

Results

Of 508 retested HCM patients (median age 70 years; 66.9% male; median maximal left ventricular wall thickness 18 mm; median interval from initial genetic test 6.6 years), 46 (9%) had 48 HCM-related variants: 14 in new HCM-associated genes, 3 in deep intronic MYBPC3 regions, 18 intermediate-effect variants, and 13 (8 reclassified) in classic HCM-associated genes. In multivariable analysis, the presence of late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) [odds ratio (OR) 3.52; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.38-10.25], the Mayo HCM score (OR 1.46 per 1 point increase; 95% CI 1.08-2.01), and the Toronto HCM score (OR 1.18 per 1 point increase; 95% CI 1.08-1.30) were independent predictors of detecting HCM-related variants at retesting. The diagnostic yields in patients with LGE and a high Toronto score (≥13 points), and with LGE and a high Mayo score (≥4 points), were 80% and 50%, respectively.

Conclusions

In patients with HCM and prior negative genetic testing, retesting identified HCM-related variants in 9% of individuals, allowing counselling and risk stratification. Late gadolinium enhancement, combined with the Mayo and Toronto scores, may be used to guide which patients should be prioritized for genetic retesting.

title: Inflammation and early atherosclerosis beyond traditional risk factors: an imaging study.
authorString: Mendieta G, Pocock SJ, Taylor D, García-Alvarez A, Fuster JJ, García-Lunar I, Iglesies-Grau J, Fernández-Jiménez R, Mass V, Devesa A, Sánchez-González J, Pérez-Herreras C, Ibanez B, Fuster V.
abstractText:
Background and aims

Understanding how inflammation contributes to subclinical atherosclerosis (SA) plaque burden, beyond the impact of established cardiovascular risk factors, holds significant implications for the success of preventive strategies focused on the reduction of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. The aim of this study was to investigate the relative contribution of inflammation, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDLc), and systolic blood pressure (SBP), as determinants of SA plaque burden in a cohort of middle-aged, asymptomatic individuals, using non-invasive imaging techniques.

Methods

Participants from the Progression of Early Subclinical Atherosclerosis (PESA) study (median age 45 years) underwent longitudinal screening every 3 years (baseline, 3- and 6-year visits) involving serial blood testing [including white blood cell (WBC) count, fibrinogen, oxidized LDLc, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein], physical examinations and imaging assessments with three-dimensional vascular ultrasound of peripheral arteries, and coronary artery calcium quantification. Global plaque volume (GPV, mm3; bilateral carotid plus femoral plaque burden) at 6-year follow-up was the primary outcome.
