authorString: Harris KW, Syme S, Kasparian NA, Chang JC, Arnold RM, Bulls HW, Divanovic A, Colosimo C, Weinberg JG, Burke JG.

title: Ischemic electrocardiographic changes and initial misdiagnosis of acute aortic syndromes: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
authorString: Yan H, Lin S, Chen P.
abstractText:
Background and aims

Ischemic electrocardiographic (ECG) changes can mimic acute myocardial infarction and obscure acute aortic dissection (AAD) or other acute aortic syndromes (AAS), but their association with initial misdiagnosis has not been synthesized. We assessed whether ischemic changes on the earliest prediagnostic ECG were associated with initial misdiagnosis.

Methods

We searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure through July 1, 2026, for observational studies of confirmed AAD/AAS reporting 2 × 2 data for initial misdiagnosis by ischemic ECG status. Unadjusted odds ratios (ORs) were pooled with a random-effects model using restricted maximum-likelihood estimation and Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Heterogeneity, prediction intervals, leave-one-out sensitivity, QUIPS risk of bias, and GRADE certainty were assessed.

Results

Seven retrospective cohorts from four countries included 724 cases; 609 had analyzable ECG data, including 179 initial misdiagnoses. Ischemic ECG changes were not significantly associated with initial misdiagnosis (pooled unadjusted OR, 1.419; 95% CI, 0.608-3.312; P = 0.351; 95% prediction interval, 0.223-9.039; I2 = 62.9%). All leave-one-out 95% CIs included 1.0. Excluding the principal contributor to heterogeneity yielded an OR of 1.050 (95% CI, 0.591-1.865) with negligible residual heterogeneity. No QUIPS domain was at high risk; GRADE certainty was moderate after downgrading for serious imprecision.

Conclusions

Current evidence did not demonstrate a significant association, but wide confidence and prediction intervals and unadjusted retrospective data leave important effects unresolved. Prospective multicenter studies with standardized ECG timing, harmonized diagnostic criteria, and multivariable adjustment are needed.

title: Urgent Reno-Hepatic Artery Bypass for Acute on Chronic Mesenteric Ischemia Following Robotic Low Anterior Resection for Rectal Cancer in a Patient with Severe Stenosis of the Hepatosplenomesenteric Trunk.
authorString: Hanada K, Nishiyama A, Fukuhara N, Okada H, Yamada H.
abstractText:
Introduction

Acute mesenteric ischemia, including acute exacerbation of chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI), is a life-threatening condition associated with a 50% in-hospital mortality risk and requires immediate diagnosis, revascularization, and resection of necrotic organs. In colorectal surgery, mesenteric artery stenosis can lead to anastomotic leakage which increases morbidity and mortality. Here, we describe a case of acute exacerbation of CMI caused by severe stenosis of the hepatosplenomesenteric trunk (HSMT) and ligation of the left colic and inferior mesenteric arteries in an earlier rectal surgery that was successfully treated with urgent reno-hepatic artery bypass.

Case presentation

An 80-year-old woman was referred to our department with acute exacerbation of CMI after multiple procedures for rectal cancer. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed severe stenosis with calcification at the origin of the HSMT and hypoenhancement of the right hepatic lobe, spleen, and small intestine. Percutaneous antegrade endovascular stenting failed because the lesion was severely calcified. We opted to perform urgent open surgery, including revascularization and resection of the necrotic organs. A bypass from the right renal artery to the proper hepatic artery was selected because of the high risk of failure associated with retrograde open mesenteric stenting, the limited length of available saphenous vein, the risk of anastomotic failure secondary to infection, the patient's poor general condition, and the degree of calcification precluding aortoiliac clamping. Postoperatively, the patient developed Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and disseminated intravascular coagulation, both of which were successfully managed and resolved in the ICU. On POD 24, the patient underwent duodeno-jejunal anastomosis, ileostomy closure, and colostomy. The patient tolerated oral intake well 80 days after arterial bypass surgery and was discharged on POD 147 on single antiplatelet therapy.

Conclusions

Although hepato-renal artery bypass is typically used for renal revascularization, reno-hepatic bypass can be useful for mesenteric revascularization in patients with anatomical variations, peritonitis, or severe aortoiliac calcification.

title: Association of Homocysteine With All-Cause and Cardiovascular Mortality in Individuals With Advanced Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome: A Nationwide Prospective Cohort Study.
authorString: Shang H, Li X, Zhang X, Wan J, Yan P, Wang T, Liu J, Niu L.

journal.title: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research

abstractText: BACKGROUND Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome reflects the overlap of cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and metabolic disorders. The prognostic relevance of homocysteine (Hcy) in advanced CKM syndrome remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the associations of serum Hcy levels with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in adults with advanced CKM syndrome. MATERIAL AND METHODS This prospective cohort study included 3658 adults with advanced CKM syndrome from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1999-2006. Hcy was analyzed continuously and by tertiles. The primary analyses used survey-weighted Cox proportional hazards models to estimate hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Restricted cubic splines assessed potential nonlinear associations. RESULTS During a mean follow-up of 153.4 months, 2008 all-cause deaths and 686 cardiovascular deaths occurred. After full adjustment, each 1-unit increase in Hcy was associated with higher all-cause mortality (HR 1.01, 95% CI 1.00-1.02; P=0.014), and the highest vs lowest Hcy tertile was associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.19-1.72; P<0.001). For cardiovascular mortality, associations were directionally positive but not statistically significant after full multivariable adjustment for either continuous Hcy (HR 1.01, 95% CI 1.00-1.02; P=0.053) or the highest vs lowest tertile (HR 1.34, 95% CI 0.96-1.86; P=0.082). Restricted cubic spline analysis suggested nonlinear associations. CONCLUSIONS Higher Hcy was independently associated with increased all-cause mortality in adults with advanced CKM syndrome. The association with cardiovascular mortality was directionally positive but did not reach statistical significance after full multivariable adjustment.

title: Genomic analysis of extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from a dog with a severe episode of self-trauma and urinary tract infection.
authorString: Repossi CP, Paiva SC, Simões MN, Fernandes BM, Silva JVO, de Araújo TA, Ferraz CM, Senhorello ILS, Rossi GAM, Furlan JPR.
abstractText: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales are emerging pathogens of major importance in veterinary medicine. This study describes the clinical, microbiological, and genomic characteristics of ESBL-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from a dog with paraparesis and concurrent pyelonephritis, chronic cystitis, and a self-traumatized limb lesion. A 12-year-old mixed-breed female dog underwent repeated antimicrobial therapy during hospitalization. Urine obtained by cystocentesis and wound samples were cultured, and ESBL-producing strains were characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequence-based analysis. CTX-M-55-producing E. coli sequence type (ST) 457, phylogroup F, O11:H25, and fimH145, was recovered from urine and wound samples, while the wound sample also yielded a CTX-M-15- and SHV-2-producing K. pneumoniae ST39, KL149:OL2α.2. The two closely related E. coli strains differed by 96 single nucleotide polymorphisms, despite sharing the same ST, resistome, plasmid replicons, and virulence profile. ESBL-positive strains carried multiple virulence genes, with the E. coli strains classified as extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli strains. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae ST39 in an animal in Brazil. The co-occurrence of ESBL-producing E. coli ST457 and K. pneumoniae ST39 in the same dog highlights the potential for companion animals to harbor clinically relevant multidrug-resistant lineages and reinforces the need for continuous antimicrobial resistance monitoring and antimicrobial stewardship in this sector.

title: Exosome-Mimetic Nanotheranostics for Spatiotemporally Adaptive Sepsis Therapy: A Chemical Orthogonality Design Framework.
authorString: Zhao X, Liu Y, Shou Y, Xu Z, Bai X, Gao F, Li Z, Wang Y.
abstractText: The host immune status frequently shifts from hyperinflammation toward immunosuppression-although the two states can overlap from onset and vary by tissue compartment and patient-while multiple organs undergo sequential injury. Sepsis progresses along a highly dynamic trajectory. This complexity demands therapeutic platforms that adapt to evolving pathological cues. Exosome-mimetic nanoplatforms combining the biointerfacial properties of exosomes respond independently to specific pathological signals-reactive oxygen species, pH, and dysregulated enzymes. By chemical orthogonality, we mean the independent activation of distinct functional modules by distinct pathological cues without cross-interference. We deconstruct properties of natural exosomes with the chemical tunability of synthetic nanomaterials; this can meet this demand if their design moves beyond structural mimicry toward programmable responsiveness. Here we argue these platforms should be engineered as spatiotemporally programmable systems, with distinct diagnostic and therapeutic functions encoded by chemically orthogonal modules, sepsis pathophysiology translated into actionable chemical design requirements, and examine how membrane engineering, compositional programming, and stimulus-responsive chemistries achieve trajectory-matched sensing, drug release, and immune reprogramming within a single nanosystem, distinguishing systems with uncoupled multi-function execution from simple co-delivery. It should be stated at the outset that no platform described to date fully achieves module independence; the framework therefore defines a design target and research agenda rather than a description of current capabilities. The analysis is based on a systematic screening of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Scopus (2010-2025), from which the included publications were re-examined against explicit criteria for classifying orthogonal multi-function execution versus co-delivery (Search Strategy and Classification Criteria). We also identify the translational barriers unique to chemically programmable nanotheranostics, including in vivo orthogonality fidelity, manufacturing complexity, and regulatory ambiguity. Applications are re-evaluated through the lens of chemical orthogonality. By connecting the dynamic biology of sepsis with orthogonal chemical design, this review offers guidance for developing exosome-mimetic nanomedicines and a transferable paradigm for other complex diseases.

title: Case Report: Suspected Lower Limb Congestive Injury Associated with Decreased Compliance of the External Iliac Vein After Laparoscopic Myomectomy.
authorString: Chen B, Chen H, Tong J, Xu L, Wang Y.
abstractText:
Background

The incidence of lower extremity deep vein thrombosis following gynecologic laparoscopy is 4.0%, whereas postoperative well-leg compartment syndrome (WLCS) is much rarer, with a reported incidence of only 0.03%-0.20%. Both conditions can present with postoperative lower limb swelling and pain. We report a case of postoperative lower limb swelling and pain that suspected to be caused by venous congestion injury secondary to decreased compliance of the external iliac vein, a condition that has not been previously reported in the literature.

Case presentation

A 44-year-old woman underwent an 8-hour gynecologic laparoscopic procedure in the Lloyd-Davies position. Thirty minutes after surgery, she developed acute swelling, pain, and numbness of the right lower limb. Deep vein thrombosis was initially suspected, but treatment was ineffective. Unilateral well-leg compartment syndrome (WLCS) was subsequently considered, and her symptoms were relieved following supportive treatment, including dehydration therapy and elevation of the affected limb. Repeated review of the surgical video suggested lower limb congestive injury potentially associated with decreased compliance of the external iliac vein. The patient also experienced persistent postoperative symptoms resembling venous intermittent claudication, consistent with the clinical manifestations of impaired external iliac venous outflow.

Conclusion

This case highlights the need for increased attention to the condition of the external iliac vascular sheath during gynecologic laparoscopic surgery. Swelling and thickening of the vascular sheath, resulting in decreased compliance of the venous wall, may lead to severe venous congestion injury of the lower limb and may require timely intraoperative intervention when necessary. This case may provide a reference for the clinical diagnosis and management of postoperative lower limb swelling and pain following gynecologic laparoscopic surgery.

title: Longitudinal changes in cardiac structure and function among young adults with perinatal HIV infection or HIV exposure.
authorString: Williams PL, Yu W, Van Dyke RB, Sawyer G, Gerschenson M, Attia EF, Colan SD, Lipshultz SE, Cardiac Toxicity Study of the Pediatric HIV/AIDS Cohort Study (PHACS) network.
abstractText:
Objective

To evaluate the cardiac status of young adults with perinatal HIV (PHIV) compared to those perinatally HIV-exposed but uninfected (PHEU), and changes in their cardiac structure and function over 10+ years.

Design

United States-based longitudinal study conducted in 2018-2022 in young adults with PHIV or PHEU who had a prior echocardiogram performed 2008-2010.

Methods

Echocardiograms were performed in 158 young adults (99 PHIV, median age 23.9 years; 59 PHEU, 22.1 years) and Z-scores for measures of left ventricular (LV) systolic function and structure were calculated. Within-participant changes in Z-scores since their previous echocardiogram were computed. Adjusted linear regression models were used to compare PHIV and PHEU for each echocardiogram Z-score and for within-participant changes in Z-scores over time. Among PHIV, multivariable models were used to evaluate the association of HIV disease and antiretroviral treatment measures with current Z-scores and Z-score changes.

Results

At follow-up, no differences were observed between PHIV and PHEU for any left ventricular (LV) parameter. However, both cohorts had substantially lower LV ejection fraction Z-scores (means = -0.79) than on their prior echocardiogram. Significantly larger decreases over time were observed for PHIV versus PHEU for LV end-diastolic dimension and end-diastolic and end-systolic volume Z-scores. Among PHIV, lower nadir CD4% was associated with lower ejection fraction Z-score and with larger decreases in ejection fraction Z-scores over time.

Conclusion

We observed no evidence of progression to greater LV hypertrophy over ~10 years, but the lower observed ejection fraction could indicate underlying cardiac dysfunction. Continued follow-up of young adults with PHIV and PHEU using current cardiac imaging techniques is warranted.

title: Fructose, Advanced Glycation, And Metabolic Dysfunction: Molecular Pathways Linking Oxidative Stress, Inflammation, And Masld
authorString: Sodré AFP, Lopes ER, Sloan KP, Sloan LA, Curi R, Haber JFS, Indiane L, Dall'Antonia CT, Bishayee A, Valenti VE, Hirata M, Hirabara SM, Pithon-Curi TC, Cominato L, Tanaka M, Goulart RdA, Barbalho SM.
abstractText: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent metabolic disorder closely associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and cardiovascular complications. Excessive fructose consumption may contribute to MASLD development and progression by promoting hepatic de novo lipogenesis, advanced glycation end product (AGE) formation, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation. This review aims to critically examine the molecular pathways linking fructose metabolism and AGE–RAGE signaling to hepatic injury and cardiovascular dysfunction, highlighting their interconnected roles within the liver–heart axis. Fructose metabolism increases the availability of lipogenic substrates and reactive carbonyl intermediates, favoring lipid accumulation and AGE generation. Subsequent activation of the receptor for AGEs (RAGE) stimulates oxidative and inflammatory signaling, including reactive oxygen species production and NF-κB activation. These processes may impair antioxidant defenses, promote mitochondrial dysfunction, activate hepatic stellate cells, and contribute to steatohepatitis and fibrosis. Beyond the liver, AGE–RAGE signaling is implicated in endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, atherosclerosis, and adverse cardiac remodeling. Intestinal barrier disruption and inflammatory mediator release may further amplify these interconnected metabolic disturbances. We also discuss experimental and clinical evidence concerning fructose intake, hepatic and cardiovascular outcomes, and emerging therapeutic approaches targeting glycation, oxidative stress, and inflammation. However, heterogeneity in dietary exposures, study designs, and clinical endpoints limits causal interpretation. By integrating metabolic, inflammatory, and vascular mechanisms, this review identifies potential therapeutic targets and research priorities for understanding and mitigating fructose-associated cardiometabolic injury in MASLD. Particular attention is given to the distinction between mechanistic findings and human evidence, as well as the need for larger studies.

title: Expanding mutational landscape and clinical phenotype of the CASK-related neurological disorders.
authorString: Pekerbas M, Bulut K, Yigit A, Sahin B, Salman B, Akman B, Ozzeybek E, Senol HB, Ozyilmaz B, Gunes S, Tekin IM, Kilic E, Alanay Y, Topcu Y, Kara B, Mammadova N, Dundar M, Hazan F, Durmaz A, Aykut A, Akin H, Turkdogan D, Ozturk G, Iyisenyurek S, Uctepe E, Yesilyurt A, Celik T, Ekici B, Gencpinar P, Hiz S, Karaca E, Ozbek U.
abstractText: CASK-related disorders comprise two main phenotypes: severe microcephaly with pontocerebellar hypoplasia (MICPCH), typically caused by truncating variants, and milder X-linked intellectual disability (XLID), usually associated with missense variants. We aimed to characterize this molecular spectrum within an underrepresented national cohort. We evaluated 18 affected individuals from 16 unrelated families with CASK variants identified through exome or genome sequencing. Clinical, neurodevelopmental and neuroimaging findings were systematically reviewed. Selected missense variants were evaluated by in silico prediction tools and structural modeling. We identified 16 distinct CASK variants, 11 of which are novel, including frameshift, stop-gain, splice-site, and missense variants, as well as one large deletion. Consistent with known genotype-phenotype correlations, null alleles resulted in the severe MICPCH phenotype, while presumed hypomorphic alleles were associated with XLID. However, unlike previous reports, our MICPCH patients exhibited a higher frequency of dysmorphic facial features (86%), skeletal anomalies (57%) and sensorineural hearing loss (43%). Furthermore, contrary to the literature suggesting a milder epilepsy in females due to X-inactivation, 63% of our female patients with MICPCH presented with recurrent seizures. This cohort broadens both the molecular and phenotypic spectrum of CASK-related disorders. Findings reinforce that truncating variants predominantly cause MICPCH, while missense variants can lead to various outcomes depending on domain-level structural impact. We demonstrate that the CASK phenotypic spectrum is broader than previously recognized, frequently involving distinctive facial dysmorphism, skeletal defects and hearing impairment, suggesting that CASK plays a critical role not only in synaptic function but also in wider developmental processes.

title: Preoperative Tympanometry and the Presence of Middle Ear Effusion at the Time of Tympanostomy Tube Placement.
authorString: Prabhakar AR, Frelier M, Trautmann D, Johnson RF.
abstractText:
Objectives

To evaluate the relationship between preoperative tympanometry and intraoperative middle ear effusion in children undergoing tympanostomy tube placement.

Methods

Retrospective cohort study of children undergoing tympanostomy tube placement at a tertiary academic medical center from January to April 2021. Preoperative tympanometry was categorized as Type A, B, or C per Jerger classification. The primary outcome was middle ear effusion visualized at myringotomy. Secondary outcomes included effusion resolution among Type B ears and effusion development among Type A and C ears. Risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals were estimated using modified Poisson regression fit via generalized estimating equations, clustered by patient, with robust standard errors.

Results

A total of 268 children contributing 520 ears were included. Effusion was present at surgery in 44.0% of Type A ears, 72.4% of Type B ears, and 68.3% of Type C ears. Effusion risk was significantly higher for Type B (RR 1.65, p < 0.001) and Type C (RR 1.55, p = 0.002) compared with Type A. Among Type A and C ears, 51.2% had effusion at surgery. Differences in effusion rates across tympanogram types were no longer significant at intervals greater than 60 days. Type A ears were more commonly from children with recurrent AOM, among whom 41.2% had effusion intraoperatively.

Conclusions

Tympanogram type predicted intraoperative effusion probability, though nearly half of Type A ears had effusion confirmed at surgery. The predictive value of tympanogram type diminished at intervals greater than 60 days between assessment and surgery, suggesting tympanometry is most informative when surgery follows promptly after evaluation.

Level of evidence

4.

title: Delayed Diagnosis of Bilateral Congenital Choanal Obstruction in a 4-Year-Old Girl: Transnasal Repair with Temporary Stenting and Short-Term Outcome: A Case Report.
authorString: Abdulle ZA, Mohamud MA, Alpha MK, Mohamed MI, Warsame AA, Abdulle AA, Job A, Sheikdon AH, Hassan LM, Farah AM, Obita OK.
abstractText: Choanal atresia is a rare congenital cause of nasal obstruction. Complete obstruction is termed atresia, whereas partial narrowing is more accurately described as choanal stenosis. We report a 4-year-old girl with lifelong bilateral nasal obstruction, persistent mouth breathing, snoring, poor sleep, easy tiredness, intermittent rhinorrhoea, breastfeeding difficulty during infancy, and recurrent respiratory tract infections. Clinical assessment showed absent right-sided and markedly reduced left-sided nasal airflow. Bedside testing demonstrated no right-sided cotton-wisp movement or misting and minimal movement and misting on the left; a size 8F suction catheter could not be advanced beyond 3.5 cm on the right and met posterior resistance on the left. Preoperative flexible nasal endoscopy was not obtained because financial constraints limited access to the procedure. Computed tomography demonstrated complete right-sided choanal atresia with incomplete left-sided congenital choanal stenosis. The child underwent transnasal repair under general anesthesia using direct visualization with a Killian nasal speculum and headlight, puncture and serial dilatation of the posterior choanal obstruction, and temporary bilateral stenting. The stents were removed after six weeks. During four weeks of follow-up after stent removal, the child had improved nasal breathing and clinically patent bilateral nasal airways. This case highlights delayed recognition of asymmetric bilateral congenital choanal obstruction and the practical diagnostic and operative adaptations required in a resource-limited setting. The outcome should be interpreted as favorable in the short term because objective postoperative endoscopic confirmation and long-term follow-up were not available.

title: Transcatheter Solution to Atypical Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Drainage in a Single Ventricle Patient.
authorString: Evans RE, Stirling J, Soszyn N, Penford G.
abstractText:
Background

Partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD) is typically incompatible with single ventricle physiology if left unrepaired before cavopulmonary connection. This report describes a rare anatomical variant and novel interventional solution.

Case summary

An 8-month-old female with hypoplastic left heart variant developed profound cyanosis following bidirectional Glenn because of unrepaired PAPVD of the right upper pulmonary vein to the superior vena cava (SVC). Retrospective 3-dimensional reconstruction of the patient's neonatal computed tomography angiogram revealed a small interlobar vessel between the anomalous pulmonary vein and the anatomically normal right lower pulmonary vein. This interlobar vessel's gross dilatation and anatomical features permitted percutaneous device occlusion of the PAPVD connection to the SVC, isolating SVC return to the cavopulmonary circulation while preserving unobstructed pulmonary venous return to the atrium.

Discussion

Surgical and interventional solutions are reviewed in the context of this unusual anatomical variant.

Take-home messages

In the uncommon circumstance of an unrecognized anomalous pulmonary vein with connections to both systemic and pulmonary venous circulations, consideration may be given to interventional occlusion of the PAPVD connection to the systemic vein. Retrospective application of contemporary 3-dimensional reconstruction tools can add great value in delineating complex or unusual anatomy.

title: Comprehensive 3-Year Pediatric Resident Resuscitation Simulation Curriculum on the Care of the Severely Ill Pediatric Patient.
authorString: Kent J, Rogers A.

journal.title: MedEdPORTAL : the journal of teaching and learning resources

abstractText:
Introduction

Pediatric residents must be able to manage severely ill patients by the end of training. Simulation provides training in low-frequency, high-risk clinical situations. A longitudinal simulation curriculum could provide consistent training for residents to develop these essential skills.

Methods

We utilized Kern's 6 steps of curriculum development. A needs assessment identified content gaps. We implemented a 3-year, 9-case resuscitation simulation curriculum for pediatric residents targeting shock (septic, hypovolemic, obstructive), arrhythmias (supraventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, asystole), and respiratory failure (with bradycardia, seizures, hypoventilation). Each year, participants completed 3 simulation cases over 3 hours utilizing high-technology manikins. Patients ranged from 10 days to 10 years. We assessed the curriculum using Kirkpatrick's model, including reaction data assessing for change in self-reported confidence recognizing and managing targeted clinical events from pre/postsurveys, free-text responses noting areas of improved knowledge on postsurveys, and chart review of code events assessing for behavior change if residents led actual codes.

Results

Ninety-two pediatric residents completed the curriculum. Participation was associated with improved confidence recognizing and managing targeted clinical events (pre: median 3-4, interquartile range [IQR] 3-5; post: 4-5, IQR 4-5; P < .05). Themes of lessons learned included increased knowledge in clinical management, crisis resource management skills, and local resources. Residents were more likely to assume the code leader role in actual patient codes postcurriculum (10% pre vs 40% post).

Discussion

Participation in the curriculum was associated with increased resident confidence recognizing and managing targeted content, improved knowledge, and greater resident participation as code leaders in actual codes.

title: Economic evaluation and healthcare resource utilization in heart transplant in adults with congenital heart disease.
authorString: Gupta T, Alshawabkeh L.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

This review is timely and relevant because the population of adults with congenital heart disease (ACHD) in the United States continues to grow, and as more individuals survive into adulthood, heart failure has become the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in this population. There is a growing need to understand the economic impact of healthcare utilization and financial burden for patients with ACHD and end-stage heart failure.

Recent findings

Recent literature highlights that adults with complex congenital heart disease face disproportionately high financial burden with lifetime direct and indirect costs reaching up to $3.35 million per patient. These costs include frequent hospitalizations, surgeries, diagnostic testing, and ongoing medical care, as well as lost income for patients and families. The cost burden increases further towards the end of life, and ACHD patients with heart failure experience longer hospital stays, and higher healthcare costs compared to non-ACHD populations. Early referrals can mitigate some of the increasing cost by implementing multidisciplinary care strategies and timely interventions to potentially improve the trajectory of ACHD patients with heart failure.

Summary

The findings underscore the need for early referral to specialized, high-volume ACHD and heart transplant centers and the development of multidisciplinary care pathways to improve outcomes and reduce costs for ACHD patients with advanced heart failure.

title: Association of Wound Exudate Severity on Time to Complete Healing in Diabetic Foot Ulcers: A Real-World Retrospective Cohort Analysis (ExAct DFU Study).
authorString: Armstrong DG, Gahlon G, Veličković V, Han Y, Sanaeifar N, Corman SL, Gloviczki P, Kottner J, Rothman KJ.

journal.title: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy

abstractText:
Purpose

To quantify the association between exudate amount and time to complete diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) healing.

Patients and methods

A retrospective cohort study was conducted among adults in United States outpatient wound care centers with DFUs in the Net Health WoundExpert electronic health record database using available data from 2002-2020. Wounds were followed from first clinic visit until healing or censoring. Exudate amount (none, mild, moderate, heavy) was treated as a time-varying exposure and updated at each clinic visit; the outcome was time to complete healing. Covariates selected for confounding control included demographics, clinical characteristics, and wound-specific factors. To account for time-varying confounding and informative censoring, stabilized inverse probability of treatment and censoring weights were estimated to fit marginal structural models using weighted Royston-Parmar flexible parametric survival models. We estimated hazard ratios (with wound healing as the outcome) and healing probabilities and summarized absolute effects using restricted mean survival times (RMST).

Results

A total of 8,176 patients with 14,743 DFUs were included (median follow-up: 55 days; mean age: 62 years; 66% male). Higher exudate burden was associated with reduced healing, with adjusted hazard ratios of 0.24 (0.22-0.26), 0.14 (0.13-0.16), and 0.08 (0.06-0.10) for mild, moderate, and heavy exudate, respectively, compared with wounds without exudate (with healing as the endpoint, lower hazard ratios indicate worse outcomes). RMST analyses indicated progressively longer unhealed duration with increasing exudate, with heavy exudate associated with an additional 227 days unhealed by 52 weeks vs no exudate.

Conclusions

Higher exudate levels were strongly associated with substantially slower DFU healing. Exudate amount may serve as an important prognostic marker and target for intervention in DFU care.

title: Beyond the Reach of Standard Prophylaxis: <i>Mycoplasma hominis</i> and <i>Ureaplasma Spp</i>. in Postoperative Urological, Andrological and Renal Transplant Infections.
authorString: Mai Ba Tien D, Nguyen Hoang T, Tong Duc M, Thavixay O, Bui Duc T.
abstractText: Genital mollicutes, namely Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma urealyticum and Ureaplasma parvum, colonize the lower urogenital tract of a substantial minority of healthy adults yet are rarely considered in postoperative urological, andrological or renal transplant infection. This narrative review examines the diagnostic and prophylactic gap they create. Their lack of a cell wall makes Gram staining uninformative and confers intrinsic resistance to beta-lactams and glycopeptides. Routine microbiology also has limited sensitivity: Ureaplasma spp. generally require specialized culture or molecular detection, whereas M. hominis may grow slowly on enriched routine media but is easily overlooked. Reported disease ranges from sterile pyuria and graft pyelonephritis to perinephric or prostatic abscess, encrusting uropathy, recurrent struvite calculi and hyperammonemia syndrome. Commonly recommended perioperative agents provide little or no reliable activity against these organisms. Acquired resistance is strongly regional: among Ureaplasma isolates from North America and Germany, reported resistance to several key agents remains below 8%, whereas Vietnamese surveillance found ciprofloxacin resistance of 76.0% in U. urealyticum and 88.0% in M. hominis; doxycycline and josamycin retained greater activity but were not uniformly active. We propose five pragmatic clinical triggers, compartment-directed sampling and region-aware empiric management while emphasizing that these recommendations rest predominantly on case-level evidence. Prospective surgical studies are needed to define incidence, diagnostic thresholds and the role of screening.

title: Integration of multimodal large language models into point-of-care ultrasound documentation: A pilot study.
authorString: Boivin Z, Jaffa E, Agaraj I, Danta M, Park GY, Liu RB, Moore CL, Baloescu C.

journal.title: The American journal of emergency medicine

abstractText:
Introduction

There are no studies evaluating the potential to deploy artificial intelligence in the interpretation of cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) documentation. Telexy Health developed an image interpretation and documentation system using multimodal model extensions with video capabilities (MLLM) and deployed it on the POCUS manager QpathE. This study evaluated the MLLM's agreement to experts in identifying cardiac POCUS views and interpreting normal and abnormal examinations.

Methods

This was a retrospective pilot study using cardiac POCUS studies stored in QPathE. The MLLM was applied to POCUS examinations until 350 examinations were reached, 100 normal, and 250 with pathology. MLLM view identification and interpretation were recorded using Qualtrics, with expert image review serving as the gold standard.

Results

The MLLM was applied to 370 examinations, with 20 failures. View identification agreed with expert review in 151 examinations (43.1%). Cohen's kappa showed fair agreement for apical four-chamber views between expert and MLLM, with moderate agreement for parasternal long axis, parasternal short axis, subxiphoid, and inferior vena cava views. The MLLM agreed with expert interpretation 86 of 100 normal examinations; the agreement varied by pathology with pericardial effusion, ejection fraction, aortic outflow tract, chamber size, and inferior vena cava having an agreement of 8%, 4%, 70%, 0%, and 12% respectively.

Conclusion

While agreement in image interpretation was poor, this vendor agnostic workflow demonstrated the ability to integrate an MLLM model into image interpretation. While it should not be incorporated into clinical practice in this state, future model improvement may enable automated POCUS interpretation and documentation.

title: De novo SETD5 missense variants in individuals with MRD23 cluster within the protein's SET domain.
authorString: Marom D, Hilhorst-Hofstee Y, Kant SG, Kharbanda M, Osborne F, Robertson L, Zunz Henig N, Mory A, Weiss O, Deciphering Developmental Disorders (DDD) Study, Hamiel U, Elhanan E, Wilnai Y, Chernuha V, Baris Feldman H, Kurolap A.
abstractText: SETD5 heterozygous loss-of-function (LoF) variants and 3p25.3 deletions containing the SETD5 gene cause intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal dominant 23 (MRD23). We report five patients with an MRD23 phenotype caused by SETD5 missense variants. We studied patients with de novo SETD5 missense variants. A comprehensive literature search was conducted to reveal additional reports of SETD5 missense and LoF variants. Phenotypes and protein localization of missense variants were reviewed and compared to those reported for SETD5 LoF variants and 3p25.3 deletions. Computational analysis of the potential effect of SETD5 missense variants was performed. Six patients with de novo SETD5 missense variants were identified across five centers, gathered through the Deciphering Developmental Disorders (DDD) study database; four additional individuals with missense variants were reported in the DDD database. A comprehensive literature search revealed 12 unique individuals with missense variants, and 104 individuals with LoF variants or 3p25.3 deletions. One of the variants, p.Arg348Gln, recurred independently in three unrelated individuals. All patients with likely pathogenic missense variants shared dysmorphic features, GDD and autism, consistent with MRD23, but no major congenital anomalies, apart from hydrocephalus, which was a novel feature observed. Heart defects were reported only in the LoF group. Unlike LoF variants, which are scattered throughout the entire SETD5 coding region, pathogenic missense variants were confined to the protein's SET domain. We show that disease-causing missense variants in SETD5 cluster at the protein's SET domain. This expands the mutation spectrum of the SETD5-related neurodevelopmental phenotype, providing a framework for improving both postnatal and prenatal genetic diagnostics.

title: Combined antegrade-retrograde technique in urgent carotid stenting for true lumen compression after total arch replacement
authorString: Ng Y, Zhuang T, Ling T, Chu Y.

title: Response to "Emodin in Skeletal Muscle Ischemia-Reperfusion: Model Validity and Analytical Concerns" [Response to Letter].
authorString: Yiğit D, Oktar GL, Demirtaş H, Özer A, Küçük A, Yığman Z, Tekin E, Arslan M.

title: Beyond precision therapy: the need for precision clinical decision-making in recurrent pericarditis.
authorString: Bečić T, Radić M, Radić J.

title: Biocompatible nanoscale contrast agents for MRI and CT scans: current progress and clinical potential.
authorString: Gravandi MM, Davoodi Karsalari P, Hajihashemi A, Sadeghizadeh S, Golabchi MR, Mohammadbeigi G, Geravandi M, Mohebbi N.
abstractText: Conventional contrast agents for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) have long served as the backbone of diagnostic imaging. Yet, their well-recognized limitations, including nephrogenic systemic fibrosis and progressive gadolinium deposition with Gd-based chelates, contrast-induced nephropathy with iodinated agents, and serious hypersensitivity reactions with approved iron oxide formulations, continue to drive the search for safer alternatives. Nanoparticle-based contrast agents (NCAs) have emerged as a compelling next generation of imaging tools, offering a degree of rational design simply not achievable with small-molecule agents. By independently tuning core composition, hydrodynamic size, surface chemistry, and morphology, NCAs can be engineered to enhance relaxivity or X-ray attenuation, extend vascular residence time, direct clearance toward renal or hepatobiliary pathways, and carry targeting ligands for site-specific delivery. This review covers the principal NCA classes, iron oxide nanoparticles, gadolinium- and manganese-based nanomaterials, gold and copper nanostructures, carbon dots, lanthanide-doped upconversion nanocrystals, and quantum dots, examining their physicochemical design, pharmacokinetics, biocompatibility, and diagnostic performance across oncological and vascular applications. A recurring theme is the central role of size: Particles below the ≈6 nm glomerular filtration threshold undergo renal excretion and exhibit lower bioaccumulation risk, while larger formulations follow hepatobiliary routes with implications for long-term tissue retention. Surface coating, protein corona formation, and mononuclear phagocyte system recognition are discussed as equally decisive determinants of in vivo behavior, often outweighing core composition in their influence on clearance and tolerability. Across material classes, preclinical evidence consistently shows favorable safety profiles for well-engineered NCAs, with minimal hemolysis, low immunogenicity, and absence of histological organ injury at imaging-relevant doses, a meaningful contrast to the adverse effect profiles of conventional agents. On the efficacy side, targeted NCA formulations have demonstrated promising results across multiple tumor types, including breast, brain, liver, lung, and renal cancers, with receptor-specific designs enabling molecular-level lesion characterization that conventional agents cannot provide. Multimodal and theranostic constructs, combining MRI or CT contrast with concurrent therapeutic function, further illustrate the flexibility that nanoparticulate platforms offer. Blood-brain barrier penetration for neurooncological applications and the emerging potential of magnetic particle imaging as a future translational direction for platforms based on superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles are also discussed. The translational gap between preclinical promise and clinical reality remains the field's most honest challenge, rooted in the scarcity of long-term human safety data, the lack of standardized preclinical evaluation frameworks, and the demanding requirements of good-manufacturing-practice production at scale. Addressing these gaps, through unified safety pipelines, harmonized reporting standards, and early-phase trials that connect imaging performance to clinical outcomes, is what will ultimately determine whether NCAs fulfill their considerable potential in diagnostic medicine.

title: Preprocedural transesophageal echocardiography before cardioversion in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy-associated atrial fibrillation and thromboembolic risk.
authorString: Laffaye TA, Ibrahim R, Dacek E, Pavlas VI, Sharma S, Sorajja D, Siontis KC, Ommen SR, Geske JB, Arsanjani R, Ayoub C.

title: Long-Term Survival of Liver Transplantation in Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease: Insights From National Claims Data.
authorString: Tu W, Nephew L, Li Y, Jiang S, Li Y, Nguyen CM, Su J, Chalasani N, Gawrieh S, Liangpunsakul S.
abstractText:
Background

Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) is a leading indication for liver transplantation (LT) in the United States. While post-transplant outcomes are well established, the relative survival benefit of LT compared to non-LT remains underdefined.

Methods

Using Optum's de-identified Clinformatics Data Mart Database, we identified adults with ALD between 2017 and 2024. We used logistic regression to evaluate factors associated with LT, and Cox regression to compare survival between LT recipients and non-recipients.

Results

Among 373,025 patients with ALD, 3453 underwent LT. Female sex (adjusted OR = 0.805; 95% Confidence Interval (CI): 0.750-0.866), African-American race (adjusted OR = 0.542; 95% CI: 0.462-0.636), older age, and non-liver comorbidities, and all types of metastatic cancer were associated with lower odds of LT; non-metastatic liver cancer, however, was associated with increased odds of LT (adjusted OR = 4.147; 95% CI: 3.659-4.699). The 8-year restricted mean survival time was 2600 days (~7.12 years) for LT recipients and 1799 days (~4.93 years) for nonrecipients. The median survival among deceased patients was 1000 days with LT vs. 355 days without LT. LT was associated with a lower adjusted mortality risk (HR, 0.365; 95% CI: 0.333-0.401).

Conclusion

LT confers a substantial survival advantage for patients with ALD, beyond what is achieved without transplantation. However, significant sex and race-based disparities persist, underscoring the need for policy interventions to promote equitable access and optimized candidate selection.

title: Clinical and Invasive Hemodynamic Correlates of the TAPSE/sPAP Ratio in Pulmonary Hypertension.
authorString: Yaşar S, Eravci Ö, Dinç C, Yağci AF, Eşki S, Yildirim E, Görmel S, Çelik M.
abstractText:
Background

Right ventricular (RV) adaptation to increased pulmonary afterload is a major determinant of prognosis in pulmonary hypertension (PH), yet comprehensive validation of simple noninvasive markers against invasive hemodynamic parameters remains limited. We investigated whether the tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion to systolic pulmonary artery pressure (TAPSE/sPAP) ratio reflects the clinical, echocardiographic, and invasive hemodynamic spectrum of PH.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed 209 consecutive patients with right heart catheterization-confirmed PH who underwent comprehensive clinical assessment, transthoracic echocardiography, and invasive hemodynamic evaluation between 2016 and 2024. Patients were stratified into quartiles according to the TAPSE/sPAP ratio, and clinical, laboratory, echocardiographic, and hemodynamic characteristics were compared.

Results

The mean age was 58.8 ± 16.5 years, and 61% of patients were female. Lower TAPSE/sPAP ratios were associated with older age, higher NT-proBNP and serum uric acid levels, and lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (all p < 0.05). Decreasing TAPSE/sPAP ratios were also associated with larger right atrial and right ventricular dimensions, lower TAPSE, and higher tricuspid regurgitation velocity and estimated sPAP (all p < 0.001). Invasive hemodynamic assessment demonstrated progressively higher right ventricular systolic pressure, mean pulmonary artery pressure, and pulmonary vascular resistance (all p < 0.001), whereas mixed venous oxygen saturation increased across quartiles (p = 0.036).

Conclusions

The TAPSE/sPAP ratio is a practical, noninvasive marker that closely reflects right ventricular remodeling and invasive hemodynamic impairment in pulmonary hypertension. Lower TAPSE/sPAP ratios identify patients with more advanced RV-pulmonary arterial uncoupling and may improve bedside hemodynamic risk stratification.

title: Clinical Presentation and Immunological Characteristics of Plastic Bronchitis in Children With Severe MPP.
authorString: Wang H, Yuan L, Sun C, Zeng Z, Dong X.
abstractText: Plastic bronchitis (PB) complicating severe Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia (SMPP) increases respiratory failure risk and worsens outcomes. However, clinical and immunological features of PB concurrent with SMPP remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterize clinical, immunological, and radiological features of SMPP children with PB and identify independent predictors of PB. A retrospective analysis compared clinical, immune, and imaging data between SMPP children with and without PB. Risk factors were identified and assessed for diagnostic relevance. SMPP children with PB showed prolonged fever duration, higher peak temperature, and more severe respiratory symptoms compared with children with SMPP alone. Immunological findings included decreased peripheral CD4<sup>+</sup>/CD8<sup>+</sup> ratio, elevated serum IgM, increased bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) monocyte percentage (M%), and elevated cytokines IL-6, IL-8, and IFN-γ. Univariate and multivariate analyses identified MP resistance, number of affected lung lobes, serum IgM, CD4<sup>+</sup>/CD8<sup>+</sup> ratio, and BALF M% as independent predictors of PB in SMPP children. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis demonstrated that fever duration and the number of affected lung lobes showed diagnostic discrimination for PB, with their combination yielding an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.836. The CD4<sup>+</sup>/CD8<sup>+</sup> ratio, serum IgM level, and BALF M% showed moderate diagnostic discrimination individually, and their combined model yielded an AUC of 0.736. A comprehensive model integrating macrolide resistance, the number of affected lung lobes, CD4<sup>+</sup>/CD8<sup>+</sup> ratio, serum IgM level, and BALF M% achieved an AUC of 0.868. SMPP children complicated by PB exhibit significant immune dysregulation and extensive pulmonary pathology. Clinical (MP resistance and number of affected lung lobes) and immunological (IgM level, CD4<sup>+</sup>/CD8<sup>+</sup> ratio, and BALF M%) markers may facilitate early PB diagnosis and timely treatment.

title: Sex-Specific Risk Thresholds of Binge-Drinking Frequency for Advanced Fibrosis in MetALD and ALD: Analysis of the NHANES Cohort.
authorString: Dunn W, Vatsalya V, Diaz LA, Arab JP, Arrese M, John B, Alkhouri N, Singal AK.
abstractText:
Background and aim

New nomenclature of steatotic liver disease (SLD) is based on daily alcohol intake. Data are unclear on binge drinking in this definition.

Methods

Continuous National Health Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) (1999-2020) cohort in adults characterized relationships between binging (≥ 4 drinks for women and ≥ 5 for men) and advanced fibrosis (FIB-4 ≥ 2.67). Survey-weighted logistic regression models were fitted for men and women adjusted for demographics, metabolic risk factors, income-poverty ratio, smoking, education, number of drinks, and caffeine intake. Adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (Cis) were obtained at each binging threshold compared to no binging.

Results

Among 43,447 participants, binge drinking was reported less than monthly in 6248 (31.1 million US representative), monthly to less than weekly in 2778 (13.1 million), and weekly or more in 3285 (14.4 million) participants. Binge drinking was associated with advanced fibrosis only in women with aOR (95% CI) of 3.34 (1.38-8.11) for monthly-to-weekly and 3.20 (1.12-9.19) for weekly or more binging. As benchmarks, the adjusted odds ratios (aORs) were 2.85 (95% CI: 1.94-4.19) for metabolic dysfunction and alcohol associated (MetALD) and 7.46 (4.00-13.9) for alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD).

Conclusion

Binging monthly or more is associated with fibrosis in women, with an effect comparable to daily alcohol use at MetALD level (> 20 g/d). Novel findings suggest infrequent binging to be associated with hepatic fibrosis in women, support sex-specific framework for MetALD, and need to integrate binging into risk stratification. These data have sex-specific public-health awareness on harms of binge drinking.

title: Prognostic Implications of High HFpEF Probability in Patients With Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension.
authorString: Wang Y, Li X, Huang Z, Duan A, Wang Q, Gao L, Li S, Zhao Q, Yang T, Zhao Z, Luo Q, Liu Z.
abstractText:
Background

Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) and left heart disease, particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), show overlapping clinical features despite distinct pathophysiology.

Objectives

The HFpEF-ABA algorithm (age, body mass index, atrial fibrillation) was used to characterize HFpEF pretest probability in patients with CTEPH and evaluate its association with left heart disease and clinical worsening.

Methods

Among 466 patients with CTEPH stratified by HFpEF-ABA score (low < 25%, intermediate 25%-74%, high ≥ 75%), Spearman's correlation assessed associations with common left heart disease comorbidities. Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox regression evaluated associations with clinical worsening, with restricted cubic splines assessing the dose-response relationship and non-linearity. Subgroup analyses by sex, smoking, alcohol use, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and obstructive sleep apnea assessed the consistency. We also evaluated whether adding the HFpEF-ABA score improved COMPERA 2.0 discrimination for clinical worsening.

Results

Intermediate and high HFpEF probability was found in 52.4% (n = 244) and 9.0% (n = 42), respectively. After adjustment, each standard deviation increase in HFpEF probability was associated with an approximately 73% increase in clinical worsening (p < 0.001). Results were consistent for HFpEF probability (p < 0.05), with no significant subgroup interactions. Adding HFpEF-ABA with COMPERA 2.0 improved discrimination, increasing the C-index increasing from 0.532 to 0.634 (p = 0.012).

Conclusions

Assessing HFpEF probability in patients with CTEPH identifies those at high risk for this comorbidity and improves the precision when integrated with existing risk models.

title: Noninvasive Diagnosis of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Outside Guideline-Defined High-Risk Populations: Evolving Perspectives in the Era of MASLD.
authorString: Kang TW, Song BG.
abstractText: Noninvasive imaging-based diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in high-risk patients currently relies on the radiological hallmark of arterial-phase hyperenhancement followed by delayed washout. These criteria were designed to achieve both a high positive predictive value and sufficient specificity when applied to well-defined target populations. However, the incidence of HCC is rising globally among individuals outside the traditional high-risk groups, including those with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, formerly known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease) and genetic predispositions. This shifting epidemiology poses challenges to the current noninvasive diagnostic strategies and the binary classification of patients as either "at high-risk" or "not at high-risk," which heavily depends on established risk factors such as chronic hepatitis B, chronic hepatitis C, and liver cirrhosis. Consequently, HCC in non-high-risk individuals is often diagnosed at more advanced stages, underscoring the urgent need for reliable and noninvasive diagnostic tools tailored to this demographic population. These challenges present opportunities for the radiology community to play a proactive role in addressing them. Given the heterogeneous risk factors among low- and intermediate-risk populations, integrated strategies incorporating imaging features, fibrosis stage, serum biomarkers, individualized risk models, and artificial intelligence-assisted cross-sectional imaging may help improve the noninvasive diagnosis of non-cirrhotic or metabolically driven HCC. This review summarizes the current performance and limitations of noninvasive diagnosis outside the conventional high-risk populations in the era of MASLD and highlights emerging diagnostic strategies that warrant further investigation as evidence continues to accumulate.

title: All In: A Casino-Themed Emergency Medicine Conference Day.
authorString: Hassan S, Langan D, Bukvic A, Weizberg M, Hahn B.

journal.title: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstractText:
Audience

The target audience includes individuals involved in the education and training of emergency medicine (EM) residents, such as program directors, assistant program directors, core faculty, and academic attendings, as well as learners including residents, physician assistant (PA) fellows, and medical students (MS).

Introduction

Gamification has increasingly been incorporated into emergency medicine (EM) residency education to enhance learner engagement, motivation, and active participation. Prior studies have demonstrated benefits of game-based learning across multiple areas of medical education, including improved knowledge retention, teamwork, communication, and learner satisfaction.1-4 However, most gamification interventions in EM involve isolated activities rather than comprehensive, multi-station conference curricula. To address this gap, we developed a casino-themed, multi-station educational conference designed to reinforce core EM knowledge, procedural skills, and clinical reasoning through competitive, team-based learning. The intervention incorporated simulation, rapid-response scenarios, board-style trivia, and wagering poker chips during a protected half-day residency conference.

Educational objectives

By the end of this educational intervention, participants will be able to: 1) demonstrate airway management skills through simulation, including equipment setup and timely interventions for both adult and pediatric cases, 2) interpret various electrocardiograms (EKGs) in high-pressure scenarios, 3) analyze cases and apply evidence-based management in various rapid-response scenarios, 4) demonstrate rapid recall of EM knowledge by answering board-style trivia questions, and 5) demonstrate increased confidence in team-based decision-making, effective communication under pressure, and leadership in high-stress emergency situations.

Educational methods

This prospective educational innovation was delivered as a single, four-hour casino-themed EM conference session featuring interactive stations modeled after casino games and held during the residency program's weekly Wednesday educational conference. The session featured interactive, competition-based stations designed to replicate high-pressure ED scenarios. Learners rotated through four game-based stations: "Play Your Cards Right" for rapid-recall trivia using EM board-style questions, "Diagnostic Craps" for EKG interpretation and management, "High Stakes Airways" for hands-on airway management using mannequins and rapid sequence intubation scenarios, and "Rapid Response Roulette" for discussion of ED cases focusing on team dynamics, leadership, resuscitation, and escalation of care. The games were designed to reflect real-world ED challenges, with content and expectations tailored to postgraduate years (PGY) levels. Participants wagered poker chips based on confidence in their responses, reinforcing self-assessment and accountability. This method encouraged active participation, peer-to-peer learning, and application of clinical reasoning in high-pressure scenarios.

Research methods

The casino-style conference featured six tables each with an EM attending facilitator. Participants included EM residents, physician assistant (PA) fellows, and medical students. Learners started with 15 poker chips and engaged in four game-based sessions over four hours. The games "Play Your Cards Right," "High Stakes Airways," "Diagnostic Craps," and "Rapid Response Roulette" incorporated either case-based simulation, procedural skill stations, rapid decision-making, EKG interpretation, and/or evidence-based medicine (EBM) trivia. Learners wagered chips based on confidence, with gains/losses tied to performance. Faculty provided real-time feedback and facilitated discussions. Pre- and post-conference surveys (Appendix A) assessed educational value, skill improvement, confidence, and clinical applicability. Instructors also evaluated feasibility and effectiveness. The study was Institutional Review Board exempt.

Results

Of the 33 learners who attended the conference, 32 completed surveys (97% response rate) including 26 EM residents (10 PGY-1, 8 PGY-2 and 8 PGY-3), 4 medical students, and 2 physician assistants. One hundred percent of participants answered "yes" when asked if they would recommend this type of conference to peers and 100% preferred this learning style to traditional didactics. Eighty-eight percent of the respondents reported they are "very likely" to incorporate skills learned from this activity into future practice.Facilitators rated the game-based learning activities as highly effective teaching tools, with 92% rating 4 or 5 (on a 5-point scale). Facilitators were also asked if they found the games easy to implement, and 83% answered rating a 4 or a 5 (on a 5-point scale). Responses derived from the open-ended questions emphasize the conference's effectiveness in engaging participants, providing meaningful learning experiences and fostering a positive and well-organized environment.

Discussion

This casino-style, game-based learning conference was highly rated for both educational value and engagement. Participants reported increased confidence in managing emergency scenarios, particularly in EKG interpretation and team-based critical decision-making. The format was viewed as feasible and effective, with most participants preferring game-based learning over traditional didactics, supporting its continued use in EM education.

Topics

Gamification, EM education, simulation, active learning, residency training.

title: Ventricular Pulsed Field Ablation: State-of-the-art Review of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence.
authorString: Martinez-Gomez E, Asirvatham SJ, Siontis KC.
abstractText: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is a paradigm shift in the field of cardiac electrophysiology. The well-demonstrated success with atrial PFA is generating enthusiasm for ventricular applications of PFA, for which the clinical experience is still in its infancy, however. This study is a systematic review and critical appraisal of the published preclinical and clinical evidence on ventricular PFA, involving a total of 111 primary articles (55 preclinical and 56 clinical). An increasing number of PFA platforms and catheters are being used in the ventricle in clinical practice. This appraisal evaluates the impact of ablation parameters in association with lesion depth and volume, and synthesises the available studies of safety and efficacy outcomes for ablation of ventricular tachycardia and premature ventricular complexes with PFA, as reported in case reports and case series from around the world. The cumulative published evidence amounts to a total of 434 patients ablated with PFA for ventricular arrhythmias, with generally favourable acute and long-term results, while the understanding of safety constraints continues to be explored.

title: Clinical and ethical considerations for pediatric cardiac xenotransplantation candidates.
authorString: Contorno E, Takemoto S, Javed H, Sreenivasan S, Kim S, Schmitz M, Rajab T.
abstractText: Children with complex congenital heart disease face substantial mortality and morbidity, while access to heart transplantation remains constrained by donor scarcity. Limited mechanical circulatory support options further complicate bridging to transplantation, particularly in small infants. Cardiac xenotransplantation could provide a source of size-appropriate grafts, but its potential benefit depends upon many patient factors. This review examines clinical outcomes, pediatric preclinical evidence, and ethical considerations relevant to candidate selection, with particular attention to the single-ventricle pathway. Gene-edited porcine hearts have supported pediatric-sized nonhuman primates for months, with survival beyond 24 months in one recipient and a proof-of-concept transition to allotransplantation. Initial use as a bridge to allotransplantation may be most defensible in selected children with a poor prognosis under available palliation or mechanical support who could benefit from transplantation. Partial-heart xenotransplantation offers a separate potential application for living valve replacement. Ethical evaluation must address parental permission, the child's developing autonomy, and lifelong infection surveillance. Clinical translation requires evidence and safeguards matched to the proposed recipient population and a credible plan for subsequent treatment if xenograft function fails.

title: An asymptomatic pulmonary arteriovenous fistula presenting with a Campylobacter rectus brain abscess as the initial manifestation: a case report.
authorString: Li J, Ji X, Zhang H, Liao Y, Li J.
abstractText:
Background

Brain abscess is a severe infectious disease of the central nervous system associated with high rates of mortality and morbidity. Pulmonary arteriovenous fistula (PAVF) is a rare but important cause of cryptogenic brain abscesses. The pathogens associated with PAVF-related brain abscesses are typically oral anaerobes or facultative anaerobes, most commonly non-hemolytic streptococci and Streptococcus intermedius. To our knowledge, no case of a monomicrobial Campylobacter rectus (C. rectus) brain abscess in a patient with asymptomatic PAVF has been reported.

Case presentation

Herein, we report the case of a 57-year-old man with a C. rectus brain abscess in association with an asymptomatic PAVF. The patient presented to our hospital with fever and headache. Magnetic resonance (MR) imaging revealed a 5 × 2 cm brain abscess in the right temporal and occipital lobes, surrounded by extensive edema. Enhanced computed tomography (CT) scanning of the lungs revealed both nodules and PAVF. Blood culture and cardiac ultrasound failed to detect any abnormalities. Piperacillin-tazobactam and meropenem were administered for anti-infection, although the headache persisted. He was subsequently transferred to neurosurgery to resect the abscess by craniotomy; postoperative pus culture confirmed the presence of C. rectus.

Conclusions

For brain abscesses caused by oral anaerobes such as C. rectus, screening for right-to-left shunting diseases such as PAVF may be considered when no other source is identified.

title: Navigating the Road to Specialization in Adult Congenital Heart Disease.
authorString: Gupta T, Amir R, Frischhertz BP, Clark D, Broda CR, Lin J, Aboulhosn JA, Saef J.
abstractText: Adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) has evolved from a pediatric-focused field to a growing adult cardiovascular subspecialty, driven by advances in surgery and medical therapy that now allow nearly 2 million adults in the United States to live with congenital heart disease. Despite these advances, an estimated workforce of board-certified ACHD cardiologists remains insufficient for the growing patient population, underscoring a continued mismatch between workforce needs and the trainee pipeline. This manuscript reviews contemporary pathways to ACHD sub-specialization, including a combined internal medicine and pediatrics ('Med-Peds') residency followed by adult or pediatric cardiology, internal medicine followed by adult cardiology, and pediatrics followed by pediatric cardiology, each culminating in dedicated ACHD fellowship. For each route, the article outlines key strengths, limitations, and typical curricular emphases, and describes how Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education-recommended clinical blocks can be tailored to remediate background-specific gaps while preserving a common competency-based endpoint. By clarifying training structures, expectations, and career implications, this work seeks to demystify the pathway to ACHD cardiology and encourage workforce interest in caring for this rapidly growing, high-need population.

title: Multimodal Imaging in Anomalous Aortic Origin of the Coronary Arteries: Contemporary Approaches to Risk Stratification.
authorString: Nayfeh M, Karla AR, Parra D, Dalal AS, Flack EC, Kronenberg MW, Barker C, Dove ML, Long CN, Orr Y, Wroblewski AP, Shah AS, Janssen DR, Greene EB, Beckerman Z, Ruiz T, Hughes S, Wells J, Stouffer JA, da Nobrega de Alencar R, Henry C, Well A, Carr JJ, Nicholson G, Hernanz-Schulman M, Doan TT, Mery CM, Lima BB.
abstractText: Multimodal cardiac imaging has fundamentally reshaped the evaluation of anomalous aortic origin of the coronary artery, yet risk stratification remains challenging because anatomy, symptoms, and physiological demands vary widely across patients. This review summarizes contemporary anomalous aortic origin of the coronary artery classification and emphasizes anatomic features associated with higher risk, including interarterial and intramural courses, adverse ostial morphology, and compression related to the intercoronary pillar or myocardial bridges, which contribute to both fixed and dynamic ischemia. The complementary roles of echocardiography, coronary CT angiography with CT-derived fractional flow reserve, nuclear myocardial perfusion imaging, cardiac magnetic resonance, and hybrid anatomic-functional imaging are discussed, with attention to the specific clinical contexts in which each modality is most informative. Finally, we discuss the Vanderbilt management approach that integrates age, symptoms, detailed anatomic assessment, and functional testing to guide observation, exercise recommendations, invasive evaluation, and surgical intervention, with particular focus on individualized counseling and safe return-to-play decisions in young and athletic patients.

title: Association between chronic sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors use and right ventricular function in hemodynamically stable patients with acute pulmonary embolism.
authorString: Moady G, Maman S, Dragu R, Levi-Gofman L, Atar S.
abstractText:
Background

Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is a common cardiovascular disorder associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, with prognosis largely determined by the extent of right ventricular (RV) involvement. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors improve outcomes in patients with heart failure (HF) and exert favorable effects on left ventricular (LV) remodeling; however, their effects on RV function in acute PE remain largely unexplored. We hypothesized that chronic treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors would be associated with a lower incidence of clinical congestion and a more favorable clinical course in patients with acute PE.

Methods

We retrospectively compared 30 patients receiving chronic SGLT2 inhibitor therapy with 90 controls following 1:3 matching for multiple variables, including age, sex, comorbidities, and background medical therapy. Echocardiographic and clinical outcomes were compared between the groups, including tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), systolic pulmonary artery pressure (SPAP), and clinical congestion.

Results

Patients receiving SGLT2 inhibitors had higher TAPSE values (19.4 ± 2.7 vs. 17.3 ± 5, 95% Confidence interval (CI) 0.7-3.5, p = 0.004), fewer signs of clinical congestion [6.7% vs. 25.6%, Odds ratio (OR) 0.21, 95% CI 0.05-0.94, p = 0.03], lower troponin, [14.5 (5.3-51), vs. 64.5 (20-177), 95% CI (33-108), p < 0.001], and lower N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels, [158 (96-443) vs. 1000 (333-3433), 95% CI (467-1153) pg/mL, p < 0.001]. No significant between-group difference was observed in 1-year readmissions due to dyspnea or clinical congestion [OR 0.34, 95% CI (0.1-1.2), p = 0.13].

Conclusions

Among hemodynamically stable patients with acute PE, chronic SGLT2 inhibitor therapy was associated with more favorable RV function during the index event; however, this association did not translate into improved long-term clinical outcomes. These findings warrant confirmation in prospective studies.

title: Dynamic tissue-specific mosaicism in constitutional non-supernumerary ring chromosome 21 with a Down syndrome-like phenotype: a case report and genotype-phenotype analysis.
authorString: Martínez Anaya D, Zinser Sainas A, Cruz Cruz M, Yáñez-Félix AL, Salas Labadía C, Orta Barcenas CA, Sosa Sánchez DA, Yokoyama Rebollar E, Pérez-Vera P.
abstractText:
Introduction

Ring chromosome 21 (r (21)) is a rare constitutional rearrangement involving terminal deletions and significant phenotypic heterogeneity. High-resolution genomic analyses have demonstrated that ring chromosomes may harbor complex genomic imbalances and dynamic mosaicism. However, the contributions of ring chromosome instability, tissue-specific mosaicism, and complex dosage imbalance to the clinical phenotype remain poorly understood.

Case presentation

We report an 8-month-old boy with developmental delay, congenital heart disease, hearing impairment, structural brain abnormalities, and dysmorphic features suggestive of Down syndrome (DS), although lacking the complete classical phenotype. Cytogenomic analyses identified a constitutional non-supernumerary r (21) associated with a 18.77-Mb duplication of 21q21.2-q22.3 and a 3.09-Mb terminal deletion of 21q22.3. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) resolved the ring chromosome structure, identifying four instability-derived clones, and demonstrated tissue-specific mosaicism across lymphocytes, oral mucosa epithelial cells, and urinary sediment epithelial cells, with a duplicated monocentric r (21) as the predominant clone. Comparison with the four previously reported constitutional non-supernumerary r (21) cases revealed a recurrent combination of Down syndrome critical region (DSCR) duplication and terminal 21q deletion, despite substantial phenotypic variability.

Discussion and conclusion

This study expands the clinical and cytogenomic spectrum associated with constitutional non-supernumerary r (21). Tissue-specific mosaicism and recurrent genomic imbalances suggest that the DS-like phenotype cannot be explained solely by dosage alterations involving the classical or highly restricted DSCR. Our findings suggest a mechanism in which dynamic ring chromosome instability, and the cumulative dosage imbalance of multiple chromos​ome 21 genes, contribute to the phenotypic variability observed in these patients. Additional well-characterized cases are essential for refining the genotype-phenotype correlations of this rare genomic disorder.

title: Post-Traumatic Basal Ganglia Infarction Due to Perforator Injury: A Narrative Review Focusing on Pathogenetic Mechanisms and Differential Diagnosis in Children and Adults.
authorString: Kim MS.
abstractText: Post-traumatic basal ganglia (BG) infarction due to lenticulostriate artery (LSA) injury is rare. Most cases occur in young children, and only 6 adult patients with post-traumatic BG infarction due to LSA injury have been reported. Brain motion during a head injury may disrupt the junction between the mobile extracerebral and fixed intracerebral portions of the LSA, resulting in vasospasm, stretching, or shearing injury and subsequent infarction in both children and adults. Most pediatric patients present with BG infarction, whereas 4 of the 6 reported adult patients had associated intracranial hemorrhage. Severe stretching forces may rupture the LSA wall, resulting in BG hemorrhage. In children, common conditions predisposing to this type of stroke include viral infections (e.g., varicella) and mineralizing angiopathy of the LSA. None of the 6 adult patients had risk factors for stroke. In adults, branch atheromatous disease-related lacunar stroke (LS) and cerebral small vessel disease-related LS are important differential diagnoses of post-traumatic BG infarction. Magnetic resonance angiography in a 14-year-old boy and a 25-year-old woman demonstrated suspicious LSA injury. In forensic medicine, differentiating traumatic from spontaneous BG infarction is particularly important in adults. Therapeutic strategies for both children and adults include the early use of antiplatelet agents.

title: Point-of-care ultrasound in dogs with clinical signs due to heartworm disease.
authorString: Ames MK.
abstractText: Estimates suggest that over 1 million dogs in the United States are infected with heartworm (Dirofilaria immitis). Although dogs often have no, or only mild clinical signs with heartworm infection, some dogs develop life-threatening cardiopulmonary disease. Point-of-care ultrasound is a useful tool to assess dogs with severe heartworm disease and varies from a quick 'fluid check' to more comprehensive exams that utilize standardized views. Ultrasound is commonly used to diagnose cavitary effusions and intracardiac heartworms. With more advanced training, ultrasound can be used to identify interstitial lung abnormalities and evaluate the morphology of the right heart.
