title: Geographic Variation in Active Perinatal Management and Outcomes for Extremely Preterm Infants in New South Wales: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
authorString: Williams N, Li C, Nassar N, Gordon A.

journal.medlineAbbreviation: Aust N Z J Obstet Gynaecol
journal.title: The Australian & New Zealand journal of obstetrics & gynaecology
journal.isoabbreviation: Aust N Z J Obstet Gynaecol

abstractText:
Background

Perinatal management of infants born at 22-25 weeks' gestation varies internationally and may influence survival and long-term outcomes. In New South Wales (NSW), no contemporary statewide guideline exists.

Aims

To evaluate rates of active delivery room management and associated survival and neurodevelopmental outcomes among infants born at 22-25 weeks' gestation in NSW.

Materials and methods

Population-based cohort study of all live births at 22 + 0-25 + 6 weeks in NSW (2011-2019) using linked administrative and clinical datasets. Active management was defined as provision of respiratory support or higher in the delivery room. Primary outcomes were survival to 1 year and moderate or severe neurodevelopmental impairment (NDI) at 2-3 years.

Results

Among 1285 live-born infants, 69.0% received active management, increasing from 61.7% in 2011 to 74.5% in 2019 (p < 0.001). Rates varied across local health districts (54.9%-83.5%). One-year survival was 44.9% overall (64.4% among actively managed infants) and increased with gestational age. Of 577 children eligible for follow-up, 440 (76.3%) underwent assessment at 2-3 years, of whom 18.4% had moderate or severe NDI. Maternal transfer to a tertiary centre was associated with a lower adjusted hazard of death (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.63-0.98) but not with NDI.

Conclusions

Active management and survival increased over time; however, marked regional variation persists. Development of a statewide clinical practice guideline could support equitable, evidence-based care for extremely preterm births.

title: Wearable Technologies to Improve Physical Activity, Sedentary Breaks, Training, Sleep, and Safety: The ECSS-Wearable Technologies Special Interest Group Calls for Interdisciplinary Collaboration.
authorString: Düking P, Giurgiu M, Halson S, Schilling R, Sperlich B, Kanning M, von Haaren-Mack B, Ferrauti A, Vetrovsky T, Reichert M.
abstractText: Wearable technologies ("wearables") are lightweight sensor-based devices that detect, analyze, and transmit physiological, biomechanical or environmental data, and are increasingly used across physical activity, sedentary behavior, athletic training, safety and sleep research. Applications include for example large-scale physical activity surveillance, ambulatory assessment, and real-time feedback during athletic training. Despite promising use cases such as heart rate variability-informed endurance training or gait retraining via biomechanical feedback, critical challenges remain. These include insufficient data quality, inadequately evaluated and inaccessible algorithms, limited interoperability between systems, difficulties translating sensor data into actionable insights, and insufficient wearable technology literacy among users. The Wearable Technologies Special Interest Group of the European College of Sport Science (ECSS-WT-SIG) identifies the need for interdisciplinary collaboration to address these challenges. Key priorities include developing regulatory frameworks, promoting standardized and open data infrastructure, improving wearable literacy of users, and conducting rigorous intervention studies under real-world conditions. The ECSS-WT-SIG calls on researchers, industry partners, NGOs, and other stakeholders to collectively advance the scientific and practical application of wearables in physical activity, sedentary behavior, training, sleep, and safety research.

title: Evaluating the Delivery of a Remote Osteoarthritis Peer Mentorship Programme for People Experiencing Socioeconomic Disadvantage.
authorString: Mason S, Anderson AM, Lavender EC, Eckersley L, Barry S, Conner M, Green H, McHugh GA.
abstractText:
Introduction

Hip and knee osteoarthritis can cause difficulty with daily activities and are particularly common in people experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage. Supported self-management programmes, such as peer mentorship, can be a valuable way to support people to actively participate in managing their condition. The aim of this study was to develop, deliver and evaluate a remote peer mentorship programme to support self-management of hip and/or knee osteoarthritis among people experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage.

Methods

The current study is a process evaluation of a complex intervention involving participants with diagnosed osteoarthritis and self-reported socioeconomic disadvantage. Prior to participating in the remote self-management programme, mentees completed a baseline questionnaire. Following programme completion, mentees and peer mentors were invited to take part in a semi-structured interview, with mentees also invited to a follow-up interview. Quantitative data from baseline questionnaires were analysed using descriptive statistics, and an inductive-deductive approach was undertaken to analyse qualitative data. Data were integrated through narrative using a contiguous approach.

Results

Thirty mentees participated in the remote peer mentorship programme, delivered by 13 trained peer mentors. Twenty-two mentees participated in an initial interview, 17 participated in a follow-up interview, and 12 peer mentors were interviewed. Four inter-related themes were developed that explored engagement, remote delivery, acceptability and self-management progress. The process evaluation identified factors that influenced engagement with the programme such as competing priorities, the role of the peer mentor, and motivation.

Conclusions

Remote peer mentorship for people with osteoarthritis experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage is largely acceptable, with the potential for meaningful impact.

title: The Effects of a Short Foot Exercise Device on Foot Posture, Pain, Balance, and Walking Speed for Individuals With Foot Pain.
authorString: Hughes YB, Jendro AM, Dilley AG, Parke EA, Schmitt AC.

journal.title: Journal of foot and ankle research

abstractText:
Introduction

Weak intrinsic foot muscles may lead to foot pain, altered foot posture, single-leg balance issues, and altered gait. Short foot exercises can strengthen intrinsic foot muscles, which can improve foot posture and single-leg balance. This study tested the efficacy of a training device designed to strengthen intrinsic foot muscles, the FootCore MAX, for decreasing pain, improving single-leg balance, improving foot posture, and increasing comfortable walking speed.

Methods

Thirteen participants with chronic foot pain (10 female; 25.4 ± 4.3 yrs; body mass index 26.7 ± 6.8) performed 6 weeks of at-home short foot exercise using the FootCore MAX training device. Pre- and post-training visits included questionnaires, single-leg balance testing, foot posture measures, and comfortable and fast walking speeds. Participants also rated their foot pain before and after each lab visit.

Results

Foot and Ankle Outcome Score pain subscore decreased 30% (37 ± 18 to 26 ± 15, p = 0.040) after 6 weeks of training. Foot and Ankle Disability Index scores decreased 25% (4 ± 4 to 4 ± 3, p = 0.032), indicating disability decreased. Foot and Ankle Ability Measure total scores improved by 14% (72 ± 15 to 82 ± 16 p = 0.015), indicating ability improvement. Visual analog pain rating scores showed a significant interaction between both the beginning and end of lab visits as well as pre- and post-training (p = 0.002), suggesting pain scores were influenced by the training, as pain scores significantly increased from the beginning to the end of the pre-training lab visit (12 ± 11 to 27 ± 14, p = 0.001), but not from beginning to end of the post-training lab visit (14 ± 13 to 16 ± 18, p = 0.314). Preferred gait speed significantly increased with training (1.06 ± 0.33 to 1.16 ± 0.20, p = 0.008). Neither fast walking speed, balance, or foot postural measurements changed from pre- to post-training (p > 0.05).

Conclusion

Six weeks of short foot exercise training with the FootCore MAX can improve foot pain and increase comfortable gait speed.

title: Dietary Management and Mental Health Considerations in Adult Gastroparesis: A Cross-Sectional Survey of Dietitians.
authorString: Fagan GP, Bear DE, Lomer MCE.

journal.title: Journal of human nutrition and dietetics : the official journal of the British Dietetic Association

abstractText:
Introduction

Gastroparesis is a complex gastric motility disorder for which diet is recommended as a primary management strategy. Gastroparesis is associated with significant physical and psychological burden, with anxiety and depression commonly reported. Furthermore, gastroparesis overlaps with eating disorders (EDs), complicating management. Clinical guidelines for gastroparesis management acknowledge this overlap and recommend screening for EDs, however little is known about current dietetic practice in managing this intersection. This study aimed to explore dietitians' experiences, practice and confidence in managing adult patients with gastroparesis in the context of EDs.

Methods

A cross-sectional online survey of dietitians with experience managing gastroparesis was conducted and distributed via professional networks and social media. The survey explored demographics, dietary strategies, perceived effectiveness, barriers to implementation and mental health support, particularly in relation to EDs.

Results

A total of 87 surveys were completed. There was wide variation in dietary strategies used; small-particle diets were the least commonly implemented, while artificial nutrition support was used more frequently and perceived as more effective. Confidence in managing gastroparesis varied, with particularly low confidence in screening for EDs, regardless of years of experience (Mann-Whitney U = 851.4, p = 0.790). Only 20% of respondents screen for EDs more than half the time, and just 8% reported input from a mental health professional in their multidisciplinary teams.

Conclusion

A variety of dietary strategies are used by dietitians to manage gastroparesis, of which food-first are perceived as less effective in improving symptoms and nutritional status. Screening for EDs is inconsistent, and access to mental health support is limited. This demonstrates a need for improved dietary management of gastroparesis, better mental health resources and standardised practices to improve patient care.

title: Chronic Exercise Accelerates Disease Progression in a Rat Model of Desminopathy.
authorString: Langer HT, Haritonow N, Joshi AS, Avey AM, Bizieff A, Mohammad H, Zbinden-Foncea H, Hellerstein M, Hahn K, Stenzel W, Baar K, Mossakowski AA.

journal.title: Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle

abstractText:
Background

Desminopathy is a progressive myopathy and the most common intermediate filament disease in humans. Desmin is an essential part of the filamentous network that aligns myofibrils, anchors nuclei and mitochondria and connects the z discs to the sarcolemma. We challenged a rat model with a mutation in R349P Des, analogous to the most frequent R350P DES missense mutation in humans, through eccentric-biassed exercise training.

Methods

R349P Des rats (Des) and their wild type (WT) and heterozygous (HET) littermates were subjected to 4 weeks of downhill running. At the end of 4 weeks, muscles were collected and assessed histologically and biochemically.

Results

Des rats demonstrated significantly lower running capacity compared to wild type and heterozygous littermates (p < 0.0001), which exacerbated over the course of the study (p < 0.001). Running performance in Des rats decreased by ~50% after 4 weeks of downhill running. Desmin-positive skeletal muscle aggregates, a histopathological hallmark of desminopathy, were ~2-fold higher after downhill running in the Des group (p < 0.05). On a protein level, we found a differential exercise response of Des compared to WT affecting various cellular pathways concerning autophagy, proteasomal activity, energy metabolism and cytoskeletal proteins.

Conclusions

Our results suggest an impaired ability of Des muscle to adapt to chronic eccentric-biassed exercise and a subsequent exacerbation of the functional and histopathological phenotype.

title: Disulfide bond status links the open and closed conformations of prothrombin.
authorString: Schreuder M, Butera D, Kumar S, Pozzi N, Hogg PJ.

journal.title: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society

abstractText: Emerging evidence indicates that structural changes in proteins can influence autoimmune recognition. Antibodies targeting the central blood coagulation protein, prothrombin, are frequently detected in patients with the autoimmune disorder, antiphospholipid syndrome. Prothrombin exists as a dynamic equilibrium between closed and open conformations, and the open conformation is more antigenic. Using differential cysteine alkylation and mass spectrometry, we demonstrate that prothrombin circulates as an array of partially disulfide-bonded protein states. Immunoprecipitation of prothrombin from pooled plasma with an antibody that recognizes the open conformation resulted in enrichment of prothrombin molecules containing unformed disulfide bonds. Genetic ablation of disulfides revealed that individual bonds modulate the equilibrium between prothrombin's open and closed conformations. Unformed disulfide bonds in the kringle-1 (C65-C143 and C114-C138), kringle-2 (C191-C231), and protease domain (C293-C439, C493-C507, and C521-C551) were associated with a shift in the protein's structure toward a more open conformation, as assessed by enhanced chymotrypsin accessibility and increased binding to the open conformation antibody. These findings indicate that the disulfide bond status of prothrombin contributes to the open and closed conformational equilibrium.

title: Beyond Membrane Fusion: SNARE Proteins as Regulators of Signaling and Gene Expression.
authorString: Roux C, Descoteaux A.
abstractText: Soluble NSF Attachment Protein Receptor (SNARE) proteins are key mediators of membrane fusion and intracellular vesicular trafficking. Growing evidence indicates that SNAREs also participate in the regulation of signaling pathways and gene expression. While some SNAREs have been localized to the nucleus or shown to shuttle between the cytoplasm and nucleus, others modulate the nuclear translocation and activity of transcription factors. These findings add to the view of SNAREs as mediators of membrane fusion and identify them as regulators of signaling and gene expression. Understanding these noncanonical functions may provide novel insights into the complexity of gene expression regulation in both physiological and pathological conditions.

title: How Can We Help People With Long-Term Health Conditions Understand and Engage in Physical Activity Maintenance From Healthcare to Community Settings? Perspectives of Patients, Carers and Professionals.
authorString: Gavin JP, Holt L, Chiu X, Dando C, McDonough S.

journal.title: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy

abstractText:
Introduction

Physical activity (PA) is vital for managing long-term health conditions (LTCs), yet maintaining regular PA remains a global challenge. Partnerships between healthcare, leisure, and community services can provide accessible PA opportunities, but current pathways focus on initiating, rather than maintaining PA. Understanding factors influencing progression along PA pathways and engagement of professionals is essential.

Methods

Four focus groups of people with LTCs (n = 21; aged 39-82 years) were complemented by interviews with 19 professionals (aged 26-66) and five carers (aged 20-78 years). Inductive thematic analysis was used to generate understanding about recommendations for an integrated PA maintenance pathway, before mapping themes to the COM-B (Capability, Opportunity, Motivation, Behaviour) model.

Results

Key themes were: i) limited access to, and information about PA services; ii) a need for improved intersectoral collaboration; and iii) opportunities and barriers to developing a PA maintenance pathway. Primary care and community centres were deemed reliable and accessible locations to advertise local opportunities, but without digital platforms, lacked recency and condition-appropriate activities. Intermediaries emerged as community navigators, working intersectorally with knowledge of local communities, and behaviour change techniques to support maintenance. However, funding cuts limited intersectoral working.

Conclusion

Maintaining PA among people with LTCs and carers requires a coordinated, intersectoral pathway between healthcare and community services, which extends beyond initial consultation and referral. Investment in collaborative infrastructure, accessible digital systems, and sustainable funding is lacking. However, community-based intermediaries trained in digital tools, can play a pivotal role in supporting maintenance by connecting individuals with appropriate opportunities and providing ongoing behaviour change.

title: Qualitative Insights From Public Interviews in the United Kingdom on the Acceptability of Risk-Based Eligibility Criteria for Lung Cancer Screening.
authorString: Katsampouris E, Hutton G, Scott SE, Duffy SW, Johansson M, Robbins HA, Quaife SL.

journal.title: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy

abstractText:
Background

Targeted lung cancer screening programmes in the United Kingdom use multivariable risk models to identify high-risk individuals. However, public acceptability of targeting screening by risk using eligibility criteria, such as age and smoking history, remains unclear, including the psychological and behavioural consequences of eligibility disclosure.

Aim

To explore UK public attitudes toward the acceptability of current risk-based eligibility criteria for lung cancer screening and the anticipated psychological and behavioural responses to eligibility disclosure.

Methods

A qualitative study was conducted as the second phase of a sequential explanatory design. Semi-structured telephone interviews were held with 28 UK adults aged 45-77 years between January-April 2024. Participants were purposively sampled for diversity in demographics, smoking history, and prior acceptability questionnaire responses. Interviews were analysed using applied thematic analysis informed by the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability.

Results

Criteria were generally acceptable when perceived as evidence-based and logical, particularly age and smoking history. However, participants expected flexibility, suggested expanding inclusion criteria and had concerns about fairness and discrimination especially regarding ethnicity and education. Eligibility was anticipated to motivate screening attendance but also cause worry; the prospect of ineligibility often led to feelings of exclusion, anxiety, and disappointment. Participants emphasised the need for clear, evidence-based communication of the rationale and individual risk, alongside alternative options or support for those who are ineligible.

Conclusions

Clear and transparent communication of the rationales underpinning eligibility criteria, provided by the screening programme and trusted health professionals, are essential for improving public acceptability and individual understanding of eligibility status. These strategies should also mitigate against potential stigma, perceived discrimination, and over-reassurance, while ensuring appropriate safety-netting and risk management for those who are ineligible. Tailored messaging and pathways may optimise engagement, trust, and psychological wellbeing within lung cancer screening programmes.

Patient or public contribution

The research team sought the views of eight public and patient representatives with lung cancer experience (either personally or being a carer) during study conception. They endorsed the research objectives, helped to develop participant-facing interview questions and gave feedback on the appropriateness of the design, agreeing that in-depth interviews would best capture perceptions of the acceptability of risk-based eligibility criteria.

title: Mitochondrial Transplantation Preserves Regenerative Capacity of Denervated Skeletal Muscle by Disrupting a Ca<sup>2+</sup> Overload-Mitophagy-Ferroptosis Circuit.
authorString: Ding H, Huang J, Zhang J, He Z, Luo J, Lin Z, Yang L, Su Y, Zhang M, Wen F, Lin Y, Chang C, Dai H, Ge X, Xu J.

journal.title: Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle

abstractText:
Background

Denervation-induced muscle atrophy progresses during the interval between nerve injury and reinnervation, and depletion of muscle satellite cells (MuSCs) contributes to impaired functional recovery. Although mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired quality control are implicated in muscle wasting, whether excessive mitochondrial turnover drives MuSC failure after denervation remains unclear. This study aimed to identify the pathogenic mechanisms underlying MuSC depletion and determine whether mitochondrial transplantation therapy (MTT) preserves regenerative capacity.

Methods

A sciatic nerve transection model was established in mice to induce denervation-associated muscle atrophy. Mitochondria isolated from differentiated MuSCs were transplanted into denervated gastrocnemius muscles beginning 6 h after injury and repeated every 3 days for 6 weeks. RNA sequencing, calcium imaging, mitochondrial ultrastructural analysis, mito-mKeima-based mitophagic flux assessment, flow cytometry and molecular analyses were performed to investigate disease mechanisms and therapeutic effects. In vitro calcium overload models combined with Mdivi-1 treatment and Pink1 knockdown were used to define the regulatory pathway linking calcium stress, mitophagy and ferroptosis.

Results

Denervated muscle exhibited early calcium dyshomeostasis (Fluo-4 AM fluorescence increased 6.7-fold vs. Sham, p < 0.0001) and mitochondrial dysfunction within 3 days, followed by iron accumulation (nonheme iron increased 1.5-fold, p = 0.0046) and ferroptotic changes by 2 weeks. Mechanistically, sustained calcium overload activated the Ampk-Tsc2-mTorc1 pathway in MuSCs, inducing Pink1-dependent excessive mitophagic flux. Mito-mKeima flow cytometry confirmed increased mitophagic flux after denervation, with approximately tenfold elevation at Day 3 and persistent activation at 2 weeks. Excessive mitophagy promoted Fth1 degradation (reduced by 47.5%, p = 0.0181) and increased Tfr1 expression (1.9-fold, p = 0.0035), thereby enhancing ferroptotic susceptibility. Inhibition of mitochondrial fission or Pink1 knockdown reduced iron accumulation (Fe2+ fluorescence reduced by 58.3% and 69.2%, respectively, both p < 0.01) and protected MuSCs from ferroptosis. MTT restored mitochondrial homeostasis by reducing calcium overload (73.7% decrease vs. A23187, p < 0.0001), increasing ATP production (36.9%, p < 0.01), suppressing excessive mitophagic flux, normalizing iron metabolism (39.9% reduction, p = 0.0015) and preserving MuSCs (30.0% increase vs. DN_PBS, p = 0.0196). Consequently, MTT attenuated denervation-induced muscle fibre atrophy and improved functional recovery following delayed nerve repair.

Conclusions

This study identifies an early pathogenic cascade linking calcium overload, excessive mitophagic flux and ferroptotic susceptibility as a critical driver of MuSC dysfunction during denervation-induced muscle wasting. MTT preserves regenerative capacity by interrupting this degenerative circuit and restoring mitochondrial quality control, providing a potential therapeutic strategy for denervation-associated muscle atrophy and other muscle wasting disorders.

title: Burden of acute diseases associated with group A Streptococcus in Australia 2000-2022: a critical review and online database.
authorString: Stacey I, Junaid M, Stiles S, Bowen AC, Pearson G, Fulurija A, Katzenellenbogen JM.

journal.title: Australian health review : a publication of the Australian Hospital Association

abstractText:
Objective

To review the burden of acute diseases frequently associated with group A Streptococcus (Strep A) infections in Australia using a methodological lens for the period 2000 to 2022, to inform future disease surveillance.

Methods

Critical review of contemporary published and grey literature reporting Strep A epidemiology, with creation of an online, searchable 'living' database.

Results

Data were extracted from n = 77 burden of disease studies on frequently associated Strep A conditions and added to the database. Studies were temporally and geographically fragmented, yielding heterogenous estimates of laboratory-confirmed Strep A disease burden. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations were frequently studied, where disease burden estimates were high relative to non-Indigenous populations. Strep A skin infection prevalence was reported at values ranging from 4.2 to 90%, depending on study design; pharyngitis rates were 4 to 32 cases per 100 person-years. Invasive Strep A rates were 1.6 cases per 100,000 population (higher in Indigenous populations), had high case fatality and increased over the study period. ARF and ASPGN rates within the Indigenous population were 49.3 and 124 per 100,000 people, respectively.

Conclusions

Contemporary evidence of laboratory confirmed superficial Strep A disease burden was sparse. Passive surveillance of conditions fully attributable to Strep A, such as acute rheumatic fever and acute post-Streptococcal glomerulonephritis, may indicate underlying trends in Strep A infection rates, but cannot provide estimates of absolute Strep A prevalence. This review supports Strep A point of care testing to establish accurate burden of disease estimates, which are critical for evaluating the efficacy of Strep A prevention strategies.

title: Before the Trial: Taxonomic Inference, AIDS, and the Limits of Evidence Appraisal.
authorString: Arthur F.

journal.title: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice

abstractText:
Rationale

Evidence-based medicine (EBM) was founded to inform decisions about the care of individual patients. Its most developed appraisal tools, however, are calibrated primarily to the reliability of estimates produced within already constituted reference classes. This creates a reference-class problem: a trial may be internally valid, and its effect estimate may be appraised with methodological rigour, while the clinical category that supplied the enroled population remains taxonomically unresolved.

Aims and objectives

This article aims to distinguish adjudicatory inference from taxonomic inference and to show why both are required for clinically useful evidence appraisal. It argues that bedside inference depends not only on the validity of an estimate, but also on the adequacy of the reference class to the patient and to the mechanism of action.

Methods

The article uses the early AIDS sequence as a conceptual and historical case study. It reconstructs the inferential steps by which an initially anomalous pattern became an operational and then mechanism-confirmed reference class.

Results

The AIDS sequence demonstrates six distinct taxonomic inferential operations: anomaly recognition, eliminative induction, causal-network tracing, cross-pathway consilience, operational case definition, and marker validation. Each produced a specific intermediate product that the next operation presupposed. Anomaly recognition warranted investigation because the signal violated a well-grounded clinical expectation; consilience across structurally independent transmission routes - sexual contact, blood products, transfusion, vertical transmission - generated inferential force no single study could produce; and the 1982 case definition was epistemically powerful not because it estimated a parameter but because it made the phenomenon countable and investigable. These operations are appropriately evaluated by criteria distinct from standard EBM appraisal: anomaly specificity, rival-explanation pressure, cross-pathway independence, and marker discriminatory performance replace risk of bias, precision, and consistency. The virological and therapeutic adjudication that later transformed HIV/AIDS care depended on the prior success of this taxonomic sequence.

Conclusion

The implication is not anti-EBM but a scope clarification. EBM is strongest when the reference class is taxonomically adequate. In syndromic and mechanism-latent fields, certainty ratings should be understood as conditional on reference-class adequacy. Taxonomic appraisal should therefore be developed alongside estimate appraisal, so that medicine can evaluate not only what a trial found, but whether it was conducted in the right class of patients for the bedside inference it is asked to support.

title: Understanding Barriers to Surgical Care: A Qualitative Study of Black Individuals With Hand Dysfunction.
authorString: Thompson NT, Baxter NB, Cole-Price A, Byrnes ME, Hooper RC.

journal.title: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy

abstractText:
Objective

To identify barriers influencing treatment decision-making among Black individuals with carpal tunnel syndrome and to explore mechanisms contributing to disparities in hand surgery utilisation.

Summary background data

Racial disparities exist in a variety of surgical subspecialties, including hand surgery. Little information on why these disparities exist or how to improve disparities from the patient's perspective is known.

Methods

We conducted a study utilising virtual semi-structured interviews, focusing on participants' interactions with healthcare providers, the impact of hand dysfunction, and participants' experiences with racism and discrimination. Using an interpretive description approach, we captured major themes in the coded data.

Results

The sample included 28 Black individuals with carpal tunnel syndrome. We identified three key themes: (1) Racism predisposes Black participants to inequitable care: participants experienced intergenerational drag, microaggressions, discrimination, and mistrust related to historical injustices. Participants engaged in code-switching to navigate biases and have their symptoms validated. (2) Social and systemic factors enable access to care: participants experienced economic instability, limited paid leave, unreliable transportation, inequitable workplace policies, and lack of social support. (3) Inadequate assessment of needs and access to care among Black participants: Participants struggled to navigate the referral process and obtain timely diagnostic testing. Many participants also described how providers misinterpreted their symptoms, which strained relationships with providers.

Conclusions

Racism and discrimination contribute to Black individuals' reluctance to undergo hand surgery. Improving disparities in surgery requires systemic and interpersonal solutions that optimise resource allocation, improve the surgical referral process, mitigate bias in healthcare interactions, and strengthen patient support networks. Understanding the drivers of racial disparities from patients' perspectives is necessary to develop actionable, patient-centred solutions.

Patient or public contribution

Prior to study initiation, three structured community engagement sessions were conducted to collaborate with Black community members to co-develop and iteratively shape our research question and study design. Our community research collaborators assessed study relevance, refined key study objectives, and informed interview guide domains.

title: Per-Channel Complex B 1 + Mapping for Parallel Transmit Ultra-High Field MRI.
authorString: Yuan Y, Chen J, Rodgers CT.
abstractText: Ultra-high field (UHF, B<sub>0</sub> ≥ 7 T) MRI provides substantial gains in signal-to-noise ratio, spatial resolution and contrast. Routine clinical deployment has been limited by challenges of transmit field ( B1+ ) inhomogeneity and specific absorption rate (SAR). Parallel transmission (pTx) can mitigate these challenges but it requires per-channel complex B1+ maps to design effective pTx pulses. We review established and emerging approaches to obtain these maps. We begin by summarising the underlying physical principles and theory. Then we describe methods for magnitude B1+ mapping such as actual flip-angle imaging (AFI), saturation-prepared B1+ mapping (e.g., satTFL) and dual refocusing echo acquisition mode (DREAM) that are the basis of widely-applied per-channel complex B1+ mapping methods, as well as methods of pedagogical and/or historical relevance. Next, we describe how relative B1+ mapping with low-flip angle gradient-recalled echo (GRE) scans can determine the relative phases (and relative magnitudes) of B1+ for each channel. We recap the important interferometric approach that is now widely used. We explain how magnitude and phase maps are combined into complex per-channel B1+ maps. We discuss remaining arbitrary factors such as the position-dependent transmit reference phase. We discuss recent practical implementations such as Sandwich TFL, 3DREAM, compressed-sensing SA2RAGE and respiratory-resolved B1+ mapping. We explore the workflow improvements that could accrue if per-channel B1+ maps do not need to be acquired for every subject. This includes deep-learning-based approaches to synthesize B1+ maps from the normal localiser scans, the universal pulses (UPs) approach to precalibrate pulses and variants such as standardised universal pulses (SUPs), Fast-Online Customised (FOCUS) and machine-learning online customisation. We hope to encourage greater openness and harmonisation of these critical calibration steps for parallel transmit pulse design. This will become increasingly important as 7-T pTx MRI is adopted for multisite cross-vendor clinical research studies and to deliver the full scientific potential of new extremely high field human MRIs.

title: Beyond the Plasma Membrane: Nuclear G Protein-Coupled Receptors With a Focus on Angiotensin Receptors.
authorString: de Tezanos Pinto F, Valsecchi WM, Conte O, Bruna-Haupt E, Gironacci MM.
abstractText: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) have traditionally been described as seven-transmembrane receptors located at the plasma membrane. However, it is now well established that these receptors can also signal from intracellular membrane compartments, including endosomes, mitochondria, the Golgi apparatus, and nuclear membranes. Importantly, such intracellular signaling can generate distinct functional outcomes even when similar G protein-mediated pathways and second messenger systems are engaged. In this context, increasing evidence indicates that angiotensin receptors, which are GPCRs, are not restricted to the cell surface but can also localize to intracellular compartments, particularly the nucleus. This intracellular distribution supports the concept of an intracrine renin-angiotensin system, in which nuclear angiotensin receptors may directly regulate gene expression and cellular function. Thus, nuclear GPCR signaling represents an additional layer of complexity in angiotensin receptor biology, extending beyond classical membrane-initiated pathways. This review focuses on nuclear angiotensin receptors, their signaling properties, and their functional relevance in regulating cellular responses.

title: Suicide-Related Medical Claims, Downstream Healthcare Costs, and the Economic Impact of Enhanced Outpatient Services.
authorString: Graupensperger S, Bentley KH, Brown M, Chekroud A, Hawrilenko M.
abstractText:
Objective

Suicide-related medical claims are often followed by sustained healthcare utilization. This study quantified post-crisis cost trajectories and examined whether coordinated outpatient mental health care was associated with lower downstream spending.

Methods

We analyzed longitudinal medical claims from 13 employers. In Aim 1, individuals with a suicide-related claim (n = 5574) were matched to demographically and clinically similar controls without such claims (n = 16,632). In Aim 2, individuals who used an employer-sponsored mental health program within 1 month of a suicide-related claim (n = 248) were matched to non-users (n = 248).

Results

Relative to matched controls, individuals with suicide-related claims incurred more than double the monthly costs during the year following the suicide-related claim, corresponding to adjusted excess of $547 per month ($6564 annually), not including the month of the index claim. Among those with a suicide-related claim, early program engagement was associated with 37% lower monthly spending over Months 1-12 post-claim ($720 less per month; $8637 annually).

Conclusions

Suicide-related claims are associated with sustained economic burden for employers and health plans. Early coordinated outpatient mental health care was associated with lower subsequent healthcare spending, especially spending in acute, high-cost settings. These findings highlight the potential economic value of structured behavioral health services following suicide-related claims.

title: Body Adiposity as a Risk Factor for Portal Vein Thrombosis in Patients With Cirrhosis.
authorString: Campos-Varela I, Cespedes C, Quiroga S, Palacio E, Pons M, Roson N, Dodge JL, Vargas-Accarino E, Dopazo C, Cardenas G, Vargas V, Castells L, Simon-Talero M.

journal.title: Liver international : official journal of the International Association for the Study of the Liver

abstractText:
Background & aims

Adipose tissue alterations are linked to adverse outcomes in patients with cirrhosis, but their role in portal vein thrombosis (PVT) is unclear. We aimed to evaluate the association between body composition and PVT.

Methods

Cross-sectional study including patients with cirrhosis. Body adiposity was assessed by computed tomography (CT) at the third lumbar vertebra including visceral (VATI), subcutaneous (SATI) and total adipose (TATI) tissue indexes, bioimpedance analysis (BIA) including visceral fat area (VFA), total body fat (TBF) and total body fat percentage (TBF%), and anthropometry.

Results

In total, 245 patients with cirrhosis (median age 62 years, 74% male) were included, 17% with PVT. Adiposity was generally higher for PVT versus non-PVT groups but was only significant for BIA-derived TBF [median 25.5 kg (IQR 17.9-35.5) vs. 21.4 (15.1-30.5), p = 0.05]. In logistic regression models adjusted for sex, smoking, spleen size and Child-Pugh score, PVT was associated with higher adiposity by BIA-derived measures (aOR per standard deviation increase: TBF 1.52, 95% CI 1.09-2.11; p = 0.01; TBF% 1.47, 95% CI 1.01-2.14; p = 0.04; VFA 1.41, 95% CI 1.01-1.97; p = 0.047), CT-derived TATI (aOR per standard deviation increase: 1.44, 95% CI 1.02-2.05; p = 0.04) and anthropometry (aOR per standard deviation increase: waist circumference 1.44, 95% CI 1.01-2.08; p = 0.049; hip circumference 1.48, 95% CI 1.04-2.12; p = 0.03). Larger spleen size was consistently associated with a 46%-57% increase (per standard deviation) in likelihood of PVT across models (all p < 0.05).

Conclusion

PVT was associated with both greater adiposity and larger spleen size, suggesting that, in addition to portal hypertension, adiposity may be a risk factor for PVT development through an inflammatory/prothrombotic role among patients with cirrhosis.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Magnetic Resonance Elastography Versus Vibration-Controlled Transient Elastography for Liver Fibrosis Staging in Steatotic Liver Disease.
authorString: Gruenewald LD, Booz C, Gotta J, Reschke P, D'Angelo T, Ziegengeist NS, Torgashov K, Hempfling L, Mahmoudi S, Reisbeck L, Hammerstingl RM, Zeuzem S, Görgülü E, Pathil-Warth A, Onay M, Herrmann E, Dahmer I, Idris R, Vehreschild MJGT, Schregel K, Sommer CM, Ciesek S, Eichler K, Vogl TJ, Sinkus R, Haberkorn S, Koch V.
abstractText: Gravitational magnetic resonance elastography (GT-MRE) enables comprehensive biomechanical liver characterization and may overcome limitations of conventional elastography techniques. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of two- and three-dimensional (2D and 3D) GT-MRE compared with 2D acoustic MRE (AC-MRE) and vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE) for liver fibrosis staging. In this prospective study, patients with suspected or known steatotic liver disease underwent GT-MRE (2D and 3D, gradient-echo sequences) and AC-MRE (2D, spin-echo echo-planar imaging) at 1.5 T, plus VCTE with a median interval to MRE of 37 days (IQR, 20-124 days; range, 0-372 days). Statistical analyses included generalized additive models, ordinal logistic regression, and decision tree-based classification. Diagnostic performance was assessed using cumulative receiver operating characteristic analysis and corresponding areas under the curve (AUCs). Ninety-one participants (median age, 55 years [IQR, 45-64]; 41 women) were included, of whom 35 (38%) had histopathological correlation. In the biopsy-confirmed subgroup, 3D GT-MRE-derived viscoelastic parameters showed promising exploratory performance for early fibrosis classification. Wave attenuation achieved AUCs of 0.91 for F0 versus ≥ F1 and 0.99 for ≤ F1 versus ≥ F2, while phase angle yielded an AUC of 0.88 for F0 versus ≥ F1, with numerically higher AUCs than conventional stiffness-based metrics. For advanced fibrosis thresholds, all modalities performed well (AUC ≥ 0.84). Obuchowski measures for 3D-derived parameters were 0.95-0.96. Internally cross-validated multiparametric modeling achieved an accuracy of up to 92%. VCTE measurements plateaued beyond F3, whereas AC- and GT-MRE metrics continued to increase with fibrosis severity. 3D GT-MRE-derived viscoelastic parameters showed promising performance for liver fibrosis classification and provided biomechanical information complementary to conventional stiffness measurements. Given the limited biopsy-confirmed sample and marked class imbalance at F0, these findings require validation in larger independent cohorts before clinical implementation.

title: Dapagliflozin for Renal Protection in Heart Transplant Recipients: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
authorString: Holmen S, Manintveld O, Damman K, Haugen Löfman I, Szymanski M, Braun O, Lando M, Bjørkelund E, Brugts JJ, Taverne YJHJ, Ter Maaten JM, Thorvaldsen T, Melin M, van der Meer MG, Fagerland MW, Ravnestad H, Gude E, Andreassen AK, Gullestad L, Broch K.
abstractText:
Background

Progressive kidney disease is common in heart transplant recipients due to calcineurin inhibitor exposure and pre-existing comorbidities. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors may attenuate the decline in kidney function, but evidence in heart transplant recipients is limited.

Methods

The DAPAgliflozin for Renal protection in Heart Transplant recipients (DAPARHT) trial is a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted at six heart transplant centers in Northern Europe. We randomized adult heart transplant recipients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥25 mL/min/1.73 m² at least one year after transplantation 1:1 to receive dapagliflozin 10 mg or matching placebo once daily. The primary endpoint was the slope of the eGFR from 2 weeks after treatment initiation to the end of the 12-month blinded treatment period.

Results

Between June 2022 and September 2025, we randomized 430 participants, of whom 217 were allocated to dapagliflozin and 213 were allocated to placebo. We included the 424 patients with at least one eGFR measurement after baseline in the full analysis set. Their mean age was 53 ± 14 years and 29& were women. The eGFR at baseline was 67 ± 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. The median time from transplantation was 7 (3 - 13) years. Dapagliflozin improved the chronic slope of the eGFR compared with placebo. The change in the eGFR from 2 weeks to 12 months after treatment initiation was 2.0 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.0 - 3.1) mL/min/1.73 m2 in the dapagliflozin group and 0.3 (95% CI -0.8 - 1.4) mL/min/1.73 m2 in the placebo group for a between-group difference of 1.7 (95% confidence interval 0.1 - 3.3) mL/min/1.73 m²; p = 0.03. There were no unexpected safety signals and similar rates of adverse events, including infections, between groups.

Conclusions

In heart transplant recipients, dapagliflozin, compared with placebo, improved the slope of the eGFR from 2 weeks to 12 months of treatment.

title: Iron Repletion in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: The IRONMET-HFpEF Randomized Trial.
authorString: Lewis GD, Horick NK, Moreno F, Lim K, Cocca-Spofford D, Ikoma T, Gupta P, Camphausen C, Caccamo L, Soydara C, McGinnis S, Newlands C, Williams S, Minasian A, Iskenderian N, Landsteiner I, Iyer B, Joseph J, Delgado A, Tattersfield H, Moore E, Platt V, Lee S, Malhotra R.
abstractText:
Background

Iron deficiency is present in >50% of patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and is associated with reduced exercise capacity and survival. Whether iron repletion improves exercise capacity as objectively measured by peak oxygen uptake ([Formula: see text]) is unknown. The IRONMET-HFpEF trial (Impact of Intravenous Iron Repletion on Mechanisms of Exercise Intolerance in HFpEF) sought to determine whether ferric derisomaltose (FDI) compared with placebo improves peak [Formula: see text] in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction with iron deficiency.

Methods

This was a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial of patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and iron deficiency, defined as ferritin <100 ng/mL or <300 ng/mL with transferrin saturation <20%. Participants were enrolled between December 2021 and April 2026. Single-dose ferric derisomaltose (1000 mg; n=44) or placebo (n=21) was administered once intravenously. The primary end point was the change in peak [Formula: see text] from baseline to 12 weeks with an analysis of covariance model including terms for treatment group, baseline peak [Formula: see text], and sex. Secondary end points included changes in [Formula: see text] at the anaerobic threshold, 6-minute walk test distance, New York Heart Association class, health status assessed by the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire-Overall Summary Score, and iron biomarkers at 12 weeks.

Results

Among 65 randomized participants (median age, 68 years [interquartile range, 58-76 years], 72% women, transferrin saturation 16.0±7.4%, ferritin 57.8±48.9 ng/mL), 64 (98.5%) completed the study. The median baseline peak [Formula: see text] was 12.7 mL·kg-1·min-1 (interquartile range, 10.6-15.8 mL·kg-1·min-1) in the FDI group and 12.2 mL·kg-1·min-1 (11.6-14.6 mL·kg-1·min-1) in the placebo group. At 12 weeks, peak [Formula: see text] improved by 1.2 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI, 0.6-1.7) in the FDI group and was unchanged (0.1 mL·kg-1·min-1 [95% CI, -0.7 to 0.9]) in the placebo group (least-squares mean difference, 1.1 mL·kg-1·min-1 [95% CI, 0.2-1.9]; P=0.02). [Formula: see text] at the anaerobic threshold, 6-minute walk test distance, and New York Heart Association class also improved in the FDI compared with the placebo group (all P<0.05), whereas the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire-Overall Summary Score did not differ significantly between groups (FDI group, +4.4 [95% CI, -2.4 to 11.2]; P=0.20). FDI increased transferrin saturation (9.4% [95% CI, 4.9%-13.9%]) and ferritin (183 ng/mL [95% CI, 128-238]) compared with the placebo group (PLSMD<0.001 for both). There were no serious adverse events related to FDI administration.

Conclusions

In the largest trial to date of iron repletion in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction with iron deficiency, FDI improved multiple measures of exercise capacity.

Registration

URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT04945707.

title: Single-cell profiling of human plaques reveals cellular and molecular signatures of symptomatic atherosclerosis
authorString: Ray A, Živković L, Zhang L, Batool R, Marei A, Dichgans M, Tsilimparis N, Georgakis MK.
abstractText: Atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability drives ischemic cardiovascular events, yet the cellular and molecular signatures distinguishing symptomatic from asymptomatic human plaques remain poorly defined. Here, we compared 53 symptomatic and asymptomatic human carotid plaques using single-nucleus (snRNA-seq; 17 samples, 19,100 nuclei; AtherOMICS biobank) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; 36 samples, 68,983 cells; four public datasets), analysed independently and combined by meta-analysis. Across sequencing approaches, symptomatic plaques showed cell-state shifts toward later or terminal states in osteochondrogenic smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and CD4⁺ T cells, as well as transcriptional changes toward inflammatory and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in endothelial cells (ECs), T cells, and fibroblasts. Nuclear profiling uncovered a depletion of fibroblasts in symptomatic plaques, marked by downregulation of  RGS5 . Integrating these transcriptomic signatures with genome-wide association data for coronary, cerebrovascular, and peripheral atherosclerotic disease, we found that genetic risk was enriched primarily in vascular wall cells (SMCs, fibroblasts, ECs), rather than immune cell types. The analyses further nominated higher  TWIST1 expression in ECs (colocalized with risk across four atherosclerotic phenotypes), lower  GUCY1A1 expression in fibroblasts and macrophages, and higher  MRAS expression in T cells as candidate driver mechanisms linking genetic risk to symptomatic plaque transition. These findings provide novel insights into cellular and molecular phenotypes associated with plaque vulnerability and identify potential driver mechanisms of symptomatic plaque transformation that could inform therapeutic development.

title: [Post-resuscitation care 2025: neurological prognosis of post-cardiac arrest brain injury].
authorString: Vámos Z, Horváth LL, Nagy Z, Kiss D, Papp Á.
abstractText: Post-cardiac arrest brain injury represents a central component of the post-resuscitation syndrome, driven not only by the initial hypoxic-ischemic insult but also by reperfusion injury after the return or start of mechanical circulation. Complex neuronal damage accounts for a substantial proportion of mortality among successfully resuscitated patients, making reliable neurological prognostication a key objective of post-resuscitation care and clinical decision-making. The 2025 European Resuscitation Council guidelines emphasize a structured, multimodal approach to neuroprognostication. Prognosis should not rely on a single parameter; instead, it requires the integrated interpretation of clinical findings, electrophysiological data, neuroimaging results, and circulating biomarkers. This strategy aims to reduce falsely pessimistic predictions, prevent premature withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy, and avoid the unnecessary prolongation of futile intensive care in cases of irreversible brain injury. In the early phase of return of spontaneous circulation, neurological assessment may be confounded by several factors, including residual sedation, neuromuscular blockade, metabolic disturbances, and cardiorespiratory instability. Therefore, accurate prognostication depends on the correction of reversible conditions and stabilization of physiological parameters before definitive conclusions are drawn. Importantly, neurological outcome assessment is inherently time-dependent, and appropriate timing is essential for safe and evidence-based decision-making. Overall, the 2025 recommendations advocate standardized, multidisciplinary, and stepwise neuroprognostication as a cornerstone of post-resuscitation management, prioritizing patient-centered care while minimizing uncertainty and supporting long-term neurological recovery whenever possible. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(45): 1799-1809.

title: Early third-trimester maternal cardiac function and morphometry in high-risk pregnancies that subsequently developed fetal growth restriction and/or pre-eclampsia.
authorString: Martinez-Egea J, Daza M, Pumarola C, Lopez-Tinajero MF, Testa L, Cardiel A, Galan C, Figueras F, Meler E.

journal.title: Ultrasound in obstetrics & gynecology : the official journal of the International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology

abstractText:
Objective

To evaluate maternal cardiovascular function and cardiac morphology in early third-trimester pregnancies at high risk for fetal growth restriction (FGR) and compare findings between pregnancies that subsequently developed FGR and/or pre-eclampsia (PE) and uncomplicated pregnancies.

Methods

This prospective cohort study included singleton pregnancies at high risk for FGR referred to the Maternal-Fetal Medicine Department at the Hospital Clinic of Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain, between August 2022 and August 2024, for a routine second-trimester fetal anomaly scan. The patients were assessed between 27 + 0 and 28 + 6 weeks' gestation and were only included in the analysis if they did not have a diagnosis of FGR or PE at the time of evaluation; those who subsequently developed FGR and/or PE were identified during follow-up. Maternal echocardiography was performed to assess cardiac output (CO), stroke volume (SV), systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and structural parameters including left ventricular (LV) wall thickness and chamber volumes. Results were compared between pregnancies that subsequently developed FGR (with or without PE), pregnancies that subsequently developed isolated PE and uncomplicated pregnancies. Multivariable analysis was performed using quantile regression of the medians for CO and SVR, adjusted for body mass index (BMI), with FGR and PE assessed independently.

Results

A total of 948 patients were included in the final analysis, of whom 129 developed FGR and/or PE (including 59 that developed FGR (with or without PE) and 70 that developed isolated PE) and 819 had uncomplicated pregnancies. Median mean arterial pressure (MAP) was higher in the FGR (with or without PE) group (82.0 mmHg) and the isolated-PE group (84.8 mmHg) than in the uncomplicated group (79.7 mmHg; P = 0.027 and P < 0.001, respectively), with the isolated-PE group showing the highest MAP values (isolated PE vs FGR (with or without PE), P = 0.047). Median heart rate was elevated in the isolated-PE group (82.5 bpm) compared with the FGR (with or without PE) group (77.0 bpm; P = 0.03). In the multivariable analysis, FGR and PE were associated independently with lower CO and higher SVR prior to their development. Median SV was reduced in the FGR (with or without PE) group (59.7 mL) and the isolated-PE group (61.1 mL) compared with the uncomplicated group (64.2 mL; P = 0.030 and P = 0.016, respectively). Median BMI-indexed CO was also lower in the FGR (with or without PE) group (0.18 (L/min)/(kg/m2)) and the isolated-PE group (0.17 (L/min)/(kg/m2)) compared with the uncomplicated group (0.19 (L/min)/(kg/m2); P = 0.005 and P = 0.001, respectively). Median SVR was elevated in the FGR (with or without PE) group (1393 dynes × s/cm5) and the isolated-PE group (1339 dynes × s/cm5) compared with the uncomplicated group (1252 dynes × s/cm5; P < 0.001 and P = 0.01, respectively). Compared with the uncomplicated group, the isolated-PE group showed greater median LV myocardial thickness at end diastole (0.50 vs 0.47 cm; P = 0.003), interventricular septal thickness at end diastole (0.92 vs 0.89 cm; P = 0.031), posterior wall thickness at end diastole (0.98 vs 0.94 cm; P = 0.013) and relative wall thickness (0.45 vs 0.42; P = 0.001). Moreover, the FGR (with or without PE) group had a smaller median LV end-diastolic diameter (4.27 cm) compared with the uncomplicated group (4.48 cm; P = 0.003), indicating that preload may be reduced in patients who developed FGR (with or without PE). LV mass indexed for BMI was similar across groups.

Conclusions

Maternal cardiovascular alterations may precede the development of FGR and PE and differ by phenotype. Pregnancies that subsequently developed FGR and/or PE showed reduced CO, but those that developed FGR reflected lower preload without tachycardia, while those that developed isolated PE showed hypertensive features with a compensatory rise in heart rate. Maternal echocardiography may aid early risk stratification and guide tailored surveillance and therapy in pregnancies at high risk for FGR. © 2026 International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology.

title: [The novelties of adult advanced life support and post-resuscitation therapy according to the 2025 European Resuscitation Council guidelines].
authorString: Válint A, Bárszki L, Bukor B, Pávó M, Zima E, Kovács E.
abstractText: The European Resuscitation Council published its updated Guidelines for Resuscitation in 2025. The revised guidelines highlight advanced life support and post-resuscitation care, as well as post-resuscitation rehabilitation, as the third and fourth links in the updated Chain of Survival. In this review, we summarize the key updates and principal messages of the new guideline on advanced life support and post-resuscitation care. Although the Advanced Life Support guidelines do not represent a paradigm shift, they place a stronger emphasis on delivering high-quality, timely resuscitation. High-quality chest compressions remain the cornerstone of resuscitation, complemented by early, safe, and correctly performed defibrillation with minimal interruptions, appropriate drug administration, and prompt identification and treatment of the underlying cause of cardiac arrest. The updated guidelines also address emerging topics, including cardiopulmonary resuscitation-induced consciousness, the specific considerations for cardiac arrest occurring in closely monitored patients, and the introduction of physiology-guided resuscitation. Similarly, the post-resuscitation care guidelines introduce no major changes compared with previous recommendations. Instead, they reinforce the importance of delivering high-quality post-resuscitation care, with particular emphasis on neuroprotection. The key components of the stabilization, diagnostic, and optimization phases include an ABCDE approach to patient assessment, optimization of oxygenation, ventilation, and hemodynamic status, seizure management, prevention of fever during the first 72 hours after return of spontaneous circulation, and identification and treatment of the underlying cause of cardiac arrest. The indications for immediate coronary angiography following successful cardiopulmonary resuscitation have been further refined, and the guidelines also clarify the diagnostic approach when a non-cardiac cause of cardiac arrest is suspected. Greater emphasis is placed on multimodal neuroprognosis and post-resuscitation rehabilitation. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(45): 1810-1824.

title: [Advanced airway management of patients with preserved circulation in Hungarian emergency departments].
authorString: Sóti Á, Ádám K, Hetzman L, Fenyves BG, Bognár Z, Varga C.
abstractText:
Introduction

Advanced airway management of patients with preserved circulation (not in cardiac arrest) is a critical, high-risk procedure in emergency care. Internationally, safety improves through standardized procedures, equipment, documentation, and training.

Objective

To map current practice in Hungarian emergency departments regarding who performs the procedure, the degree of regulation, the available drugs and devices, documentation practices, and training.

Method

We conducted a cross-sectional online questionnaire survey. Based on the department-head registry of the Hungarian Society of Emergency Medicine, we sent the questionnaire to the heads of all 44 Hungarian emergency departments. Data were collected between May and July 2026 and analyzed using descriptive statistics.

Results

The response rate was 52% (23/44). In 96% of the departments, the procedure was routinely performed by emergency care providers. A written protocol existed in 48% of the departments (mandatory in 17%). Propofol, a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent, and a bougie were available in all departments. Non-invasive ventilation was available in 96% of departments, videolaryngoscopes in 74%, and capnographs in 78%; however, only 39% mandated capnography. In 52% of the responding departments, no dedicated procedural documentation was produced, and 57% had no regular topic-specific training.

Discussion

In the responding departments, the procedure was performed predominantly by emergency clinicians, and the basic pharmacological and equipment requirements were largely met. However, organizational safeguards for patient safety - a uniform protocol, mandatory capnography, structured documentation, and regular training - were often lacking, indicating both deviations from international recommendations and clear targets for improvement.

Conclusion

In the responding Hungarian emergency departments, the airway management practice for patients with preserved circulation was highly heterogeneous and insufficiently standardized. Priorities for improvement include a uniform protocol, mandatory capnography, structured documentation and a national registry, and regular training. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(45): 1835-1842.

title: Autonomic and Cortical Signatures of Sleepiness After Prolonged Sleep Deprivation: Pupillary Reflex, Hippus Oscillations, and Visual Evoked Potentials.
authorString: Różanowski K, Jankowski M.
abstractText:
Study objectives

To define physiologically interpretable visual biomarkers of progressive sleepiness during 48-hour total sleep deprivation and determine whether pupillary and cortical visual measures detect changes not captured by brief behavioral or resting cardiovascular assessments.

Methods

Twenty-four healthy adults completed one rested baseline assessment and eight supervised deprivation sessions across 48 hours of continuous wakefulness. The protocol included digital pupillometry during the pupillary light reflex (PLR) and Pupillary Sleepiness Test (PST), pattern-reversal and flash visual evoked potentials (VEPs), Stanford Sleepiness Scale (SSS) ratings, selected psychophysiological tasks, and resting blood pressure and heart rate measurements.

Results

PLR latency, reaction duration, and time to minimum diameter changed early, indicating slowed reflex timing. With advanced deprivation, DDil1 and DDil2 (pupil diameters at predefined early and late stages of redilation) decreased, identifying them as recovery-phase markers beyond classical PLR indices. The absolute Pupillary Unrest Index (PUI), measuring spontaneous pupillary oscillations (hippus), rose during the first deprivation night and remained elevated; the pupil-size-normalized rPUI followed slightly later, whereas mean pupil diameter was less informative. VEPs added a cortical layer: peak latencies of the pattern-reversal P100 and N135 and flash N3 and P3 components were delayed after prolonged wakefulness. SSS ratings increased progressively, while brief psychophysiological task performance and resting cardiovascular measures remained comparatively stable.

Conclusions

Prolonged wakefulness was reflected by a temporally organized visual biomarker profile spanning phasic pupillary reflex timing, dilation-phase recovery, tonic pupillary instability, and late cortical visual-response slowing. These findings support a candidate multimodal, non-invasive framework for objective assessment of progressive sleepiness.
