The final random forest model retained eight predictors: Killip class, inorganic phosphorus, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, left ventricular ejection fraction, absolute neutrophil count, total protein, alanine aminotransferase, and potassium. The model achieved an AUROC of 0.82 (95% CI 0.73–0.90) in internal validation and 0.90 (95% CI 0.85–0.95) in external validation. At the reported operating point, sensitivity was 0.488 and specificity was 0.991.

Conclusions:

An eight-variable random forest model derived from routinely collected EMR data showed good discrimination and preserved ranking performance in an independent hospital cohort. The model is best considered an early in-hospital risk-stratification tool; prospective validation with a prespecified prediction time is required before clinical implementation.

title: Cardiovascular Manifestations of Lyme Disease.
authorString: Manolis AA, Manolis TA, Vouliotis A, Manolis AS.
abstractText: Lyme disease is a tick-borne zoonosis caused by Borrelia burgdorferi that can involve multiple organ systems, including the cardiovascular (CV) system, noted in ~1-10% of untreated patients. This can produce atrioventricular (AV) or bundle branch block, atrial fibrillation, and myopericarditis in the acute phase, and dilated cardiomyopathy in the chronic phase. Myocardial involvement may lead to ventricular tachyarrhythmias and sudden death. AV block is reported in ~90% of cases, and in 30-60% of cases, it may necessitate cardiac pacing, at least temporarily, as most cases of high-degree AV blocks resolve with antibiotic therapy within 1 week. Occasionally, aortic dissection may occur. Although Lyme carditis, in the form of myocarditis, pericarditis, and less often endocarditis, is generally self-limited with early appropriate therapy, there is also the potential for lasting CV sequelae, such as persistent AV block (noted in 90% of cases), dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure, and the rare occurrence of coronary artery involvement and aneurysmal changes. Patients with Lyme disease should receive oral tetracycline or penicillin, which can decrease the incidence of late-stage disease; however, some patients may fail early treatment. In cases of aseptic meningitis and radiculoneuritis, IV penicillin will be needed. As Lyme disease has now replaced syphilis as the "Great Imitator," physicians should be at vigilance for the disease, especially in endemic areas, and be familiarized with the particular skin rash of erythema chronicum migrans, an expanding skin lesion with the characteristic "bull's-eye" appearance patch with a center of clear skin and a distinct peripheral outer erythematous ring.

title: Association of pre-transplant right ventricular function parameters with long-term cardiovascular outcomes following kidney transplantation.
authorString: Lawrence C, Mansuri RF, Ahmed RS, DeLonais-Parker A, Shah Z, Lyu Y, Sriram A, Roe J, Treiber E, Desanti K, Lentine KL, Benjamin MM.

journal.title: The international journal of cardiovascular imaging

abstractText: The hemodynamic effects of end-stage kidney disease and associated pulmonary hypertension may impair right ventricular (RV) function and influence cardiovascular (CV) outcomes after kidney transplantation (KT). We aimed to evaluate the association between pre-transplant echocardiographic RV function parameters, including RV strain, and long-term CV outcomes following KT. In this retrospective cohort study, we included adult KT recipients at a single Midwest academic center from 2015 to 2024 who had adequate-quality pre-transplant echocardiograms and follow-up at our institution. RV function parameters included tricuspid annular systolic velocity (S'), tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), fractional area change (FAC), RV index of myocardial performance (RIMP), and RV free wall strain measured by two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as a composite of CV death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular accident, heart failure hospitalization, coronary revascularization, or sustained ventricular arrhythmias. Among 371 patients (mean age 53.5 ± 13.1 years; 56% male) followed for a median of 4.9 years (IQR, 3.1-6.4), 79 (21.2%) experienced MACE. On univariable Cox analysis, RIMP and RV strain parameters were associated with MACE, whereas S', TAPSE, and FAC were not. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed lower MACE-free survival in patients with abnormal mid and apical RV strain, whereas the basal and dichotomized average-strain comparisons were not significant. In multivariable models, only average, mid, and apical RV strain remained independently associated with MACE. Pre-transplant RV strain was independently associated with long-term MACE after KT and may aid CV risk stratification. Further studies are needed to validate these findings.

title: NAD+ as a metabolic immune checkpoint in cancer.
authorString: Izadpanah R, Alt EU.
abstractText: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) functions in cancer as a compartmentalized signaling currency, coupling tumor cell fitness to immune competence within the tumor microenvironment (TME). In malignant cells, NAD+ sustains redox balance, poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP)-dependent DNA repair, sirtuin-mediated chromatin remodeling, and metabolic stress adaptation. In immune effector cells, the same metabolite governs mitochondrial integrity, effector persistence, and resistance to exhaustion. This duality is the basis of the explanation advanced here for why first-generation inhibitors of nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), the rate-limiting salvage pathway enzyme, failed clinically when deployed as cytotoxic monotherapies without an immunometabolic rationale. This review synthesizes the field around a central premise: NAD+ operates as a context-dependent metabolic immune checkpoint whose therapeutic value depends on where in the tumor immune ecosystem the pathway is perturbed and whether checkpoint blockade is deployed concurrently. The therapeutic landscape is reorganized around five pharmacological classes, which differ in how far each has been tested: (i) NAMPT catalytic inhibitors, evaluated clinically and withdrawn; (ii) bifunctional NAMPT/programmed death-ligand (PD-L1) compounds and proteolysis-targeting chimera (PROTAC)-mediated NAMPT degradation, both preclinical; (iii) NAD+ precursor-based immunorestorative strategies, including ex vivo rescue of age-associated chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell dysfunction through NMN/CD38 inhibitor combinations; (iv) adenosinergic axis targeting, in which anti-CD38 and anti-CD73 agents are approved or in trials while the proposed triple-blockade of CD38, CD73, and PD-1/PD-L1 remains untested; and (v) combinations with PARP and indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) inhibitors, which rest on mechanistic rationale. A tripartite pharmacological taxonomy distinguishes intracellular (iNAMPT), extracellular (eNAMPT), and vesicle-associated (vNAMPT) NAMPT as discrete drug targets. The analyses examines how TME acidification, precursor competition, and extracellular NAD+ catabolism through the CD38-CD203a-CD73 noncanonical adenosine axis reshape immune fitness, and why biomarker-guided separation of tumor-directed NAD+ depletion from immune-directed NAD+ restoration is required for rational clinical translation. Throughout, findings that are experimentally established are separated from those that remain contested or hypothetical, and the criteria under which the checkpoint designation is analytically useful, together with the conditions under which it is not, are stated explicitly.

title: Integrated clinical, biochemical, cardiac imaging, and transcriptional changes under MEK inhibition in complicated Noonan syndrome.
authorString: Gazzin A, Fornari F, Reynolds G, Isella C, Uliveto C, Massuras S, Motta M, Mignini L, Cardaropoli S, Brusco A, Tartaglia M, Medico E, Ferrero GB, Villar AM, Riggi C, Mussa A.

journal.title: European journal of human genetics : EJHG

abstractText: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a major contributor to morbidity and mortality in Noonan syndrome (NS), with a high risk of heart failure and arrhythmias. Lymphatic dysplasia represents another clinically significant manifestation often associated with significant morbidity. Emerging evidence suggests that MEK inhibitors may target these severe complications. Seven pediatric patients with molecularly confirmed NS and severe, treatment-refractory HCM and/or lymphatic effusions received oral trametinib treatment under compassionate use. Clinical, biochemical, and echocardiographic parameters were longitudinally assessed to evaluate efficacy and safety. Transcriptomic analysis of RAS/MAPK pathway-related gene expression was performed in a subset of patients at baseline, one week after treatment initiation, and during prolonged therapy. Trametinib treatment was maintained at doses ranging from 0.0075 to 0.033 mg/kg/day for 3-45 months. All patients showed a rapid decrease in NT-proBNP levels, followed by significant reductions in interventricular septal thickness and, when present, left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. In patients with lymphatic dysplasia, trametinib was associated with sustained reduction of pleural effusions and improved respiratory status. Treatment discontinuation led to progressive clinical and biochemical worsening, with improvement after reintroduction, when performed. Transcriptomic analysis demonstrated early modulation of RAS/MAPK pathway signatures in most patients. Adverse events were mild (grade 1), predominantly dermatological, and manageable with dose adjustments. These findings provide additional clinical and molecular evidence supporting trametinib treatment as a targeted therapeutic strategy for cardiac and lymphatic manifestations in NS. Prospective studies are needed to define long-term safety, optimal dosing, and treatment duration of MEK inhibition in NS and other RASopathies.

title: Burden of Albuminuria in US Adults and its Association with Obesity, Sex and Mortality: A Cross-sectional Analysis of NHANES 2003-2020.
authorString: Batool A, Thorgerson A, Wang X, Gaddy A, Ozieh M, Dawson AZ, El-Meanawy A.

journal.title: American journal of physiology. Renal physiology

abstractText:
Introduction

Albuminuria is an early marker of kidney disease diagnosis, severity and progression. Obesity, a major public health concern in the United States, may contribute to the development of albuminuria; however, the obesity-albuminuria relationship remains incompletely defined. We hypothesized that albuminuria is more prevalent in obese individuals and is associated with poor survival.

Methods

We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of NHANES survey cycles from 2003 to 2020, with linked mortality data through 2016. The study included 59,717 participants aged ≥18 years with available urinary albumin creatinine ratio (uACR) and BMI ≥18 kg/m2. BMI was categorized into normal weight, overweight and obese. Albuminuria was defined as UACR ≥30 mg/g and categorized into three severity grades (mild, moderate, and severe). Logistic regression models were used to assess the association between obesity and albuminuria, and adjustment by sociodemographic and clinical factors was assessed. Survival across albuminuria severity grades was examined.

Results

Among individuals with albuminuria the prevalence of obesity was significantly higher than those without albuminuria (40.2% vs 32.9%; p<0.001). Individuals with albuminuria were relatively older and had higher prevalence of diabetes and hypertension as compared to the no albuminuria group. Obesity was significantly associated with higher odds of albuminuria (OR 1.36; 95% CI 1.23-1.50) when controlling for sociodemographic and clinical factors. We also observed higher odds of albuminuria in individuals who were males (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.37-1.82), ages 18 to 44 years (OR 1.46, 95% CI 1.26-1.68), and ages 45 to 64 years (OR 1.79, 95% CI 1.49-2.14). The Individuals with albuminuria had poorer survival, with stark decline in a stepwise manner across albuminuria severity grades.

Conclusion

Obesity is strongly associated with albuminuria in U.S. adults. Albuminuria is linked to survival disadvantage, underscoring the importance of screening among individuals with obesity and early initiation of nephro-protective therapies in individuals with albuminuria.

title: Cold-Inducible RNA-Binding Protein Alleviates Hypertensive Renal Injury Through the KEAP1-NRF2 Pathway.
authorString: Zhang Y, Li Q, Luo M, Hua D, Sheng Y, Wang L, Li P.
abstractText: Angiotensin II (Ang II) plays crucial roles in renal dysfunction, fibrotic changes, apoptosis, and oxidative stress. CIRBP, a cold-inducible RNA-binding protein, functions to maintain cellular homeostasis. However, its role in renal damage elicited by Ang II remains unclear. Here, we investigated the mechanisms through which Cirbp overexpression alleviates renal damage caused by Ang II, and Cirbp deletion induces basal renal injury. Transcriptomic analysis identified the involvement of Cirbp in hypertension-related renal injury. Across the animal and cell models, Cirbp overexpression attenuated Ang II-induced renal dysfunction, fibrosis, apoptosis, and inflammation, whereas Cirbp deficiency aggravated basal injury and increased renal susceptibility to injury. CIRBP activated the KEAP1-NRF2 antioxidant pathway to mitigate redox stress. This renoprotective effect was reversed following the application of the NRF2 inhibitor ML385, but was resumed by the NRF2 agonist RA839. Together, CIRBP modulates redox imbalance during Ang II-mediated renal damage through KEAP1-NRF2 signaling.

title: Chest Pain in Vain: Spontaneous Portal Vein Thrombosis.
authorString: Makstutis S, Collins S.
abstractText: A 53-year-old man with a patient-reported history of ultrasound-diagnosed fatty liver disease presented with sudden-onset severe chest pain and a brief loss of consciousness, followed by progressive abdominal pain and a single episode of bloody diarrhoea. Admission investigations approximately 24 hours after the chest pain episode showed a D-dimer of 14,502 µg/L and high-sensitivity troponin I below 3 ng/L. An arterial-phase computed tomography (CT) aortogram showed no aortic dissection but did not establish portal venous patency. Following specialist thoracic radiology review, the aortogram was considered satisfactory to exclude pulmonary embolism down to the segmental level, and dedicated pulmonary angiography was not performed. Portal venous-phase CT performed 72 hours after the aortogram demonstrated extensive portal, superior mesenteric, and splenic vein thrombosis, with equivocal caecal and ascending colonic changes. Symptoms improved during anticoagulation. Repeat CT three months later showed resolution of thrombosis, with all three affected veins patent. This case illustrates the importance of selecting an imaging protocol appropriate to the evolving clinical presentation. An unrevealing arterial-phase examination did not exclude portal venous thrombosis. The relationship between the thrombosis and the initial chest pain and collapse remains uncertain, as does the contribution of the patient's reported fatty liver disease.

title: Diagnostic Pitfall: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease-Associated Pulmonary Hypertension Presenting With Postpartum Right-Sided Heart Failure in a 21-Year-Old-Case Report.
authorString: Alla SSM, Khetan MS, Alla D, Ganguru SL, Appala S, Sree K, Shah RJ, Seth A, Rawtani NA, Aamir MR, Emmanuel NW.
abstractText: Mixed connective tissue disease is a multisystem autoimmune condition characterized by overlapping clinical and serological features related to anti-U1-RNP antibodies of at least two connective tissue diseases. It may present with myocarditis, pericarditis, pulmonary arterial hypertension, and, less commonly, heart failure. We present a 21-year-old female with bilateral foot swelling, cough, and shortness of breath 3 months after a vaginal delivery. On examination, she was hypotensive (90/70 mmHg), with an elevated jugular venous pressure, a pulmonary systolic murmur with loud P2, and a tricuspid regurgitation murmur. Bronchial breath sounds and fine crepitations were present in both lower lung fields. She was evaluated initially for suspected postpartum cardiomyopathy. Transthoracic echocardiography was suggestive of a probable moderate to severe PAH. High-resolution computed tomography showed bilateral moderate pleural effusions, honeycombing with partial atelectasis of the underlying lung, and cardiomegaly. Computed Tomography Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) showed findings likely consistent with probable mild pulmonary hypertension. An antinuclear antibody panel was performed and was positive for anti-U1-RNP, SS-A, SS-B, and Jo-1 antibodies. She was started on Lasix 40 mg, Aldactone 25 mg, lisinopril 10 mg, and heparin. Treatment with 20 mg of prednisolone was started and gradually tapered. Her anasarca and dyspnea improved, and she was discharged with follow-up arranged with cardiology and rheumatology. Timely identification of MCTD-associated pulmonary hypertension and its cardiovascular complications is essential and allows early commencement of treatment, which further prevents the patients from developing heart failure.

title: Prenatal Diagnosis of Laterality Disorder Associated With NME7 Variants.
authorString: Hardy V, Ortegat M, De Clippel K, Sznajer Y, Wuyts W, Blaumeiser B, Steenhaut P.
abstractText: Situs inversus totalis (SIT) is a rare congenital laterality disorder characterized by a mirror-image reversal of the thoracic and abdominal organs. Although isolated SIT is generally associated with a favorable prognosis, prenatal diagnosis requires careful evaluation to exclude associated structural malformations and syndromic presentations, as well as genetic investigation to identify a possible underlying etiology and improve prognostic assessment. The genetic basis of SIT is complex and remains incompletely understood. To date, genotype-phenotype correlations for SIT-associated genetic variants remain poorly established. We report the prenatal and postnatal clinical course of a fetus with isolated SIT carrying a homozygous intragenic deletion of the NME7 gene, identified by whole-exome sequencing. A primigravida woman was referred at 22 + 2 weeks of gestation after dextrocardia was identified during the second-trimester morphology scan. Detailed ultrasound and fetal echocardiography were performed to assess organ laterality and exclude associated structural abnormalities. An invasive diagnostic procedure (amniocentesis) was performed, including chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and trio whole-exome sequencing. Ultrasound confirmed isolated SIT, characterized by dextrocardia, a right-sided stomach, and a left-sided liver and gallbladder. Echocardiography revealed normal cardiac anatomy and function. CMA identified a maternally inherited Xp22.33 deletion encompassing the entire SHOX gene, which was detected in the mother but not in the father and was considered an incidental finding. Trio whole-exome sequencing identified a homozygous, likely pathogenic intragenic deletion involving exons 2-7 of the NME7 gene. Targeted parental DNA analysis confirmed that both parents were heterozygous carriers of the deletion. The pregnancy was continued based on the present molecular findings, since the implication of NME7 variants seemed to be responsible for a non-syndromic form of SIT. A healthy female infant was delivered at term. Postnatal evaluation confirmed SIT with a small atrial septal defect with no hemodynamic impact and no other associated anomalies.  This case highlights the additional diagnostic value of whole-exome sequencing in fetuses with apparently isolated laterality abnormalities. It adds to the currently limited evidence linking NME7 variants to isolated SIT. This case also emphasizes the importance of multidisciplinary assessment and genetic counseling to optimize diagnosis, prognostic evaluation, parental counseling, and postnatal management.

title: Asthma Exacerbations Following Wildfire Smoke PM<sub>2.5</sub> Exposure Among U.S. Adults.
authorString: Huang Y, Luo L, Leng S, Zhang S, Lavin RP, Buenemann M, Lin Y, Campen M, Gong X.
abstractText: Asthma exacerbation can be triggered by various forms of air pollution, including PM2.5 from wildfire smoke. This study aims to investigate the association between wildfire smoke PM2.5 exposure and asthma exacerbations in adults during the warm months (April-August) between 2006 and 2019. Using a case-crossover design, we analyzed 18,935 asthma exacerbation events and four matched control periods per event from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) All of Us research program. We used the conditional logistic regression to estimate the association (odds ratios [ORs]) between wildfire smoke PM2.5 exposure and asthma exacerbation, considering lag periods of 0-7 days and adjusting for temperature, precipitation, and humidity. Significant positive associations were observed across all lag periods, with adjusted ORs ranging from 1.27 (95% CI: 1.22-1.33) to 1.38 (95% CI: 1.32-1.44). Stratified analyses showed higher odds of asthma exacerbation among older adults, non-Hispanic Whites, midwestern residents, and those exposed in May. These findings highlight the potential contribution of wildfire smoke PM2.5 to asthma exacerbations in adults and the importance of targeted public health strategies to reduce exposure during wildfire events.

title: Molecular Mechanism of Aerobic Exercise Regulating YAP to Improve TAC-Induced Heart Failure.
authorString: Xu C, Cao L, Chen Z, Li X, Shi R, Wang Y.
abstractText: The Yes-associated protein (YAP) pathway regulates cardiomyocyte proliferation, apoptosis, and immune homeostasis, with dual cardiac pathophysiological roles: aberrant activation worsens heart failure (HF), while targeted inhibition of YAP restores myocardial health. This study explores how aerobic exercise and Verteporfin intervention mediate YAP signaling to mitigate HF. The study uses a pressure overload-induced HF animal model to evaluate the effects of aerobic exercise, YAP inhibition, and their combination. Aerobic exercise preserved YAP abundance and suppressed phosphorylation-YAP overexpression in TAC-induced heart failure. This improves mitochondrial ultrastructure and cardiac function. YAP inhibition attenuates maladaptive remodeling by modulating macrophage polarization, downregulating M1 and upregulating M2 markers. The combination of aerobic exercise and YAP inhibition synergistically reduces fibrosis, hypertrophy, inflammation, and restores cardiac function. These findings identify YAP as a key target for exercise-mediated cardioprotection, and the potential mechanism may be through protecting mitochondrial integrity and immune homeostasis. This study offers novel insights into exercise-regulated YAP signaling as a therapeutic strategy for pressure overload-induced HF.

title: Understanding left atrial pressure: basic physiology, hemodynamics, and current echocardiographic assessment.
authorString: Inoue K, Yamashita S, Kinoshita M, Tamaki S, Yamaguchi O.
abstractText: Left atrial pressure (LAP) is a major determinant of pulmonary congestion and a key hemodynamic parameter in patients with heart failure and atrial fibrillation. LAP has traditionally been regarded as a surrogate of left ventricular (LV) filling pressure. However, growing evidence indicates that LAP reflects integrated interactions between left atrial (LA) mechanics, LV diastolic and systolic function, and extrinsic mechanical restraints throughout the cardiac cycle. Understanding the physiological basis of the LAP waveform provides important insights into the LA booster pump, reservoir, and conduit functions, as well as LA-LV interactions. Recent advances in echocardiography have expanded the noninvasive assessment of LAP beyond conventional Doppler indices. Contemporary approaches integrate the values of transmitral flow, mitral annular velocity, pulmonary venous flow, LA volume, and LA reservoir strain to provide a more comprehensive noninvasive assessment of LAP. In particular, LA reservoir strain has emerged as a promising marker of LAP and atrial mechanics. Additionally, exercise stress echocardiography and preload stress testing can reveal occult abnormalities in LAP responses that are not apparent at rest, particularly in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Abnormal LAP also plays a central role in the pathophysiology of atrial fibrillation, atrial remodeling, and stiff LA physiology. This review summarizes the physiological determinants of LAP, the hemodynamic significance of the LAP waveform, and contemporary echocardiographic approaches for the assessment of LAP, and the impact of extrinsic mechanical restraints on LAP, with particular emphasis on the clinical relevance of LA-LV interactions in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and atrial fibrillation.

title: Body composition in octogenarians with chronic kidney disease. Role of gender.
authorString: Cigarrán Guldris S, Sanjurjo Amado A, Rios Guillermo J, González Parra E, Barril Cuadrado G.
abstractText:
Introduction

The population with chronic kidney disease (CKD) is undergoing marked ageing, and octogenarian patients represent a growing group with distinctive clinical and functional characteristics. In this context, alterations in fluid status and body composition (BC) limit the usefulness of body mass index, necessitating a more accurate assessment with bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA). The aim of this study was to evaluate gender-related differences in body composition in octogenarian patients with CKD in a prospective observational cohort study with a 14-year longitudinal follow-up of clinical events.

Methods

A total of 724 patients were included (46.4% women), with a mean age of 84.7 years and a mean estimated glomerular filtration rate of 36.6 ml/min/1.73 m2. Vectorial tetrapolar BIA was used to analyse body composition parameters, hydration status, and bioelectrical variables, while muscle strength was assessed by handgrip dynamometry. In addition, risk of progression to kidney replacement therapy, fracture risk, cardiovascular risk, and age-adjusted comorbidity were evaluated.

Results

The results revealed clinically relevant gender differences. Women exhibited lower comorbidity and a lower risk of initiating kidney replacement therapy, but a significantly higher risk of osteoporotic and hip fractures. From a BC perspective, women showed higher adiposity and a greater proportion of ECW, together with lower muscle mass, lower TBW and ICW, and reduced muscle strength. Men presented greater muscle mass and strength but a higher prevalence of dynapenia. Overall sarcopenia was infrequent in the cohort.

Conclusion

These findings highlight a marked sexual dimorphism in body composition and functional status among octogenarians with CKD, with important clinical implications for risk stratification and individualized management in this population.

title: The CAST technique: A novel capture-assisted Safari tracking maneuver for radial pigtail repositioning after TAVI.
authorString: Ouerghi K, Benard T, Dang Van S, Rouleau F, Pinaud F, Mateus V, Camarzana A, Abi Khalil W, Delepine S, Aubourg C, Fouquet O.
abstractText:
Introduction

Right radial access is increasingly used as the sole secondary arterial access during minimalist transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). However, unfavorable right subclavian-aortic arch angulation or marked supra-aortic tortuosity may prevent spontaneous advancement of a radial pigtail catheter into the descending aorta.

Technique

We describe the CAST (Capture-Assisted Safari Tracking) technique, a simple and reproducible maneuver for repositioning a radial pigtail catheter into the descending aorta using the Safari XS guidewire already in place during TAVI. The technique consists of four sequential steps: encounter, capture, pull-down, and release. The Safari XS guidewire acts as a traction rail, allowing the pigtail loop to be captured and guided in a controlled manner toward the descending aorta.

Result

This maneuver enables successful repositioning of the pigtail catheter into the descending aorta despite unfavorable supra-aortic anatomy, without requiring additional arterial access or dedicated equipment.

Conclusion

The CAST technique is a simple, reproducible, and equipment-free maneuver that can overcome selected difficulties encountered with radial access during minimalist TAVI. It may reduce repeated catheter and guidewire manipulation and avoid the need for additional femoral access.

title: Air Embolism During Cryoballoon Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation Under Different Respiratory Management Strategies.
authorString: Fukaya H, Matsuura G, Oikawa J, Shinkai W, Traiwa M, Ogiso S, Murayama Y, Saito D, Arakawa Y, Kobayashi S, Nakamura H, Ishizue N, Kishihara J, Ako J.
abstractText:
Background

Coronary air embolism is a rare but potentially fatal complication during catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation (AF). Use of large-bore sheaths, such as those required for balloon-based catheter ablation, in the setting of unstable respiratory control may increase the risk.

Methods

We retrospectively evaluated consecutive patients who underwent first-time cryoballoon ablation (CBA) for AF from January 2017 to December 2024. Patients were divided into two groups according to respiratory management strategy: adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV, n = 266) and laryngeal mask with mechanical ventilation (LM, n = 225). The incidence of complications was compared, with a primary focus on air embolism.

Results

A total of 491 patients (median age 68 years, 71.3% male) were included. Coronary air embolism occurred in 5 patients (1.9%) in the ASV group and in none of the patients in the LM group (absolute risk difference, 1.9%; 95% CI, -0.1% to 4.3%; p = 0.066). In one patient with coronary air embolism, brain MRI performed on the day of the procedure incidentally revealed an asymptomatic acute cerebral embolic lesion. Other complications included two cases of cardiac tamponade in the ASV group and two cases of transient phrenic nerve palsy in the LM group.

Conclusions

Coronary air embolism was numerically less frequent in patients undergoing cryoballoon ablation with laryngeal mask ventilation than in those managed with ASV, although the difference did not reach statistical significance. Further prospective studies are warranted to clarify the potential role of respiratory management in procedural safety.

title: Elevated plasma phenylacetylglutamine is independently associated with heart failure: A cross-sectional biomarker study.
authorString: Lei Y, Fang Q, Wu Q, Lu J, Jiang J, Zhou L, Wang S, Ouyang D, Chen L, Li Z, Li X.

journal.title: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry

abstractText: Phenylacetylglutamine (PAGln), a microbial metabolite generated from dietary phenylalanine, has emerged as a candidate mediator in cardiovascular disease, but whether it holds diagnostic value for heart failure (HF) is unclear. We designed a cross-sectional case-control study at Xiangya Hospital, enrolling 104 participants (65 stable HF patients and 39 non-HF controls), to address this question. Plasma PAGln was quantified by ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS). Concentrations were significantly higher in the HF group than in controls (median 1.7 vs. 1.2 μM, P = 0.001). After multivariable adjustment for age, sex, body mass index, lifestyle factors, comorbidities, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, every 1-SD increase in log-transformed PAGln raised HF odds by 95% (odds ratio [OR] 1.95, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07-3.56, P = 0.030). The top tertile carried 4.57-fold greater odds than the bottom tertile (OR 4.57, 95% CI 1.08-19.45, P = 0.040). On receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, PAGln achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.658 (95% CI 0.551-0.764) with 46.2% sensitivity and 84.6% specificity. PAGln tracked positively with LDL-C, total cholesterol, and fasting glucose, and inversely with estimated glomerular filtration rate. Notably, the highest PAGln levels were seen in HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), with a significant difference between non-HF and HFrEF subgroups (P = 0.01). Collectively, our results indicate that elevated plasma PAGln is independently linked to HF and may reflect disease severity, supporting its potential as a complementary metabolic biomarker for HF evaluation.

title: CAD PVAT-derived exosomes impair endothelial barrier function through the miR-183-5p/TPM1 axis.
authorString: Gan L, Shu L, Yang J, Zhang T, Zhang X, Wang Z, Qiao B, Du Y.
abstractText: Crosstalk between perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) and vascular endothelial cells plays an important role in vascular homeostasis and atherosclerosis. However, the contribution of PVAT-derived exosomes to coronary endothelial barrier dysfunction remains incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated the effects of PVAT-derived exosomes obtained from patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) and non-CAD surgical controls on human coronary artery endothelial cells and explored the underlying molecular mechanism. Compared with exosomes from non-CAD controls, CAD PVAT-derived exosomes increased endothelial permeability, disrupted F-actin organization, reduced junctional protein expression, and decreased nitric oxide production and endothelial nitric oxide synthase phosphorylation. miR-183-5p was enriched in CAD PVAT-derived exosomes, and miR-183-5p overexpression reproduced several features of endothelial dysfunction. Dual-luciferase reporter assays identified tropomyosin 1 (TPM1) as a direct target of miR-183-5p. Importantly, inhibition of miR-183-5p attenuated CAD PVAT-exosome-induced endothelial dysfunction, whereas TPM1 overexpression partially reversed the detrimental effects of miR-183-5p. Together, these findings suggest that the miR-183-5p/TPM1 axis contributes to CAD PVAT-exosomes mediated endothelial barrier dysfunction and may represent a potential link between PVAT dysfunction and atherosclerosis.

title: A Novel Disaccharide 1-Lactulose Ameliorates Acute Liver Injury by Suppressing Oxidative Damage and Promoting Hepatocyte Proliferation.
authorString: Zhang X, Geng X, Zhang K, Xiao S, Yang S, Gu X, Yan C, Min X, Liu Z, Wang W, Lyu Q, Wang Y, Liu W.
abstractText: Acute liver injury (ALI), arising from diverse etiologies such as drug exposure and viral infection, represents a major global health concern characterized by extensive hepatocyte damage. Protecting injured hepatocytes is a central therapeutic objective, yet clinically available agents that directly target and preserve these cells remain scarce. Here, we synthesized 1-Lactulose, a novel disaccharide, and demonstrated its specific binding to asialoglycoprotein receptor 1 (ASGPR1), a hepatocyte-surface transport receptor, by molecular docking and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). In vitro, 1-Lactulose protected AML-12 cells against H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>- and acetaminophen (APAP) -induced injury, as evidenced by restored cell viability, reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, elevated superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity and glutathione (GSH) content, and enhanced proliferation of damaged hepatocytes. Notably, these protective effects were attenuated by Asgpr1 silencing, suggesting that the protective effect of 1-Lactulose is at least partially dependent on ASGPR1. Treatment with 1-Lactulose consistently attenuated liver injury, suppressed oxidative stress, and promoted hepatocyte proliferation in three mouse models of ALI induced by APAP, CCl<sub>4</sub>, and ethanol. Mechanistically, 1-Lactulose downregulated Nox4 and upregulated Pdgfra in both AML-12 cells and injured liver tissues, which was associated with attenuated oxidative damage and enhanced hepatocyte proliferation. Collectively, these findings suggest that 1-Lactulose is an ASGPR1-binding hepatoprotective disaccharide that protects against ALI across multiple etiologies through dual modulation of Nox4 and Pdgfra, supporting it as a promising therapeutic candidate for the treatment of ALI.

title: The RGS4-Gαq/11 axis in vascular homeostasis: Mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
authorString: Xiong J, You J, Xia M, Li Y, Yuan Y, Li M, Wang L, Zheng Y, Luo M.
abstractText: Vascular homeostasis, a dynamic equilibrium maintained by the circulatory system, is fundamental to cardiovascular health. Its dysregulation underlies the pathogenesis of major cardiovascular disorders, including hypertension. G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), a versatile family of seven-transmembrane proteins, play a central role in maintaining vascular homeostasis. Upon activation, certain GPCRs couple to Gαq/11 proteins and initiate multiple downstream signaling pathways, thereby regulating vascular tone, structural remodeling, and inflammatory responses. Regulator of G protein signaling 4 (RGS4) functions as a key GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that markedly accelerates GTP hydrolysis by Gαq/11, thereby promoting the timely termination of Gαq/11-mediated signaling. RGS4 therefore plays an important role in maintaining the balance of G protein signaling in the vasculature. Based on the three-dimensional structure of RGS4 (PDB ID: 1AGR), this review systematically delineates the GAP catalytic mechanism of RGS4 and its interactions with downstream effectors, including Gαq/11 and PLCβ. It discusses the pathological role of the RGS4-Gαq/11 signaling axis in major cardiovascular disorders. In addition, from a structural pharmacology perspective, this review surveys the druggable features of RGS4 and reviews previously published in silico docking and molecular dynamics studies of its representative inhibitors, intending to inform potential therapeutic strategies targeting the RGS4-Gαq/11 axis in cardiovascular disease.

title: Prevalence of coronary artery disease on coronary CT angiography in asymptomatic, predominantly high-risk Indian adults: A single-centre cross-sectional study.
authorString: Zaidi R, Thanuja K, Kothari R, Gowda S, Ambi RG, Narayan P, Raj V.
abstractText:
Background

Coronary artery disease (CAD) in South Asians often develops at a younger age and may not be adequately detected by conventional risk stratification or coronary artery calcium scoring (CACS). In this study we assessed the prevalence of CAD in asymptomatic, predominantly physician-referred individuals undergoing coronary CT angiography (CCTA).

Methods

This single-centre cross-sectional study included 1750 asymptomatic individuals, predominantly physician-referred for cardiovascular risk assessment, who underwent CCTA between 2019 and 2024. Clinical risk factors, Framingham risk score (FRS), and CACS were recorded. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify independent predictors of CAD. Prevalence of CAD in low FRS and CACS was further analysed.

Results

CAD was detected in 1084 individuals (62%), including 787 (45%) with non-obstructive and 297 (17%) with obstructive disease, while coronary calcification (CACS >0) was seen in 957 (54.6%) patients. Increasing FRS scores were associated with increased CAD prevalence (p < 0.001). Increasing CACS was also associated with CAD severity (p < 0.001). On multivariable logistic regression, independent predictors of CAD included age (OR 1.09 per year, 95%CI 1.08-1.11), male sex (OR 2.20, 95%CI 1.55-3.13), diabetes (OR 2.07, 95%CI 1.56-2.76), hypertension (OR 1.47, 95%CI 1.09-1.98), obesity (OR 1.45, 95%CI 1.00-2.10), and elevated LDL/HDL ratio>4 (OR 1.93, 95%CI 1.22-3.04).

Conclusion

In this selected cohort of asymptomatic, predominantly high-risk Indian adults referred for CCTA, subclinical coronary atherosclerosis was common, including among individuals with low Framingham risk or zero coronary calcium. Whether detecting such disease with CCTA improves outcomes or is cost-effective requires prospective, outcome-based evaluation.

title: Nutrient-mediated protection against environmental pollutant-induced heart defects: mechanisms and opportunities.
authorString: Zhang M, Yang X, Nie X, Wu L, Jiang Y, Chen T.

journal.title: Food and chemical toxicology : an international journal published for the British Industrial Biological Research Association

abstractText: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is the most prevalent birth defect worldwide, yet effective prevention strategies remain limited. Accumulating evidence implicates environmental pollutants as significant contributors to abnormalities in cardiac development. The molecular initiating events encompass xenobiotic-receptor-mediated signalling and direct toxicant-biomolecule interactions. These initial events trigger a series of downstream pathogenic cascades that ultimately result in cardiac developmental defects. Nutrients with biological activity and generally favorable safety profiles at recommended dietary intake levels offer considerable potential as preventive agents against pollutant-induced cardiac malformations. Notably, combined nutrient interventions may exert superior synergistic protective effects relative to single-nutrient approaches. This narrative review comprehensively summarizes the molecular initiating events and subsequent pathogenic pathways involved in pollutant-induced cardiac developmental abnormalities. We further critically evaluate the preclinical evidence and signalling targets of nutrients, and propose a scientific framework for the development of precision prenatal nutritional strategies to reduce the burden of environment-related CHD.

title: Enterococci as Emerging Pathogens in Infective Endocarditis and Cardiac Device Infections: Future Implications.
authorString: Dhand A, Frishman WH.
abstractText: Enterococci are emerging as important pathogens in an era of an aging population with high healthcare and antibiotic exposure, along with an increasing utilization of prosthetic valves, transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), and cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs). Contemporary cohorts place enterococci among the three leading causes of infective endocarditis, with highest risk after TAVR, where enterococci account for 15% to 30% of cases in several registries. Enterococci cause a smaller proportion of CIED infections, but present late with lead or valve involvement. Enterococcus faecalis currently causes majority of enterococcal endocarditis. Its endovascular tropism, adhesion to damaged tissue and prosthetic surfaces, biofilm tolerance, and association with occult infective endocarditis during bacteremia make it the principal cardiac species of concern. Enterococcus faecium represents a distinct future threat. Hospital-adapted lineages combine prolonged intestinal colonization, environmental persistence, mobile resistance elements, ampicillin resistance, frequent vancomycin resistance, and biofilm capacity. Absolute burden may rise because the population-at risk-living with cardiac foreign devices is expanding. Future monitoring therefore requires linked, species-level surveillance that connects bacteremia, imaging, recurrence, resistance, and genomic data.

title: Electrocardiogram-based artificial intelligence to predict incident heart failure with preserved versus reduced ejection fraction.
authorString: Khurshid S, D'Souza V, Friedman SF, Roshandelpoor A, Ribeiro P, Cunningham JW, Lau ES, Shahid A, Kany S, Strom JB, Waks JW, Maddah M, Ellinor PT, Ho JE.
abstractText:
Background

Heart failure is classically divided into two subtypes based on the ejection fraction (EF): HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), each with varying risk mitigation strategies. Electrocardiogram-based artificial intelligence (AI) may facilitate HF subtype-specific risk prediction, to enable tailored prevention.

Methods and results

Based on a previously validated HF prediction architecture, we developed an ECG-based AI model to predict 10-year risk of incident HFrEF (LVEF <50%) versus HFpEF (LVEF ≥50%) (Electrocardiogram to Heart Failure Subtype, "ECG2HF-Subtype"). ECG2HF-Subtype was developed in 98,190 individuals in Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH), and validated in three test sets: MGH, Brigham and Women's Hospital (BWH), and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), among individuals without prior HF. HF was identified using a validated natural language processing model, and subtypes were classified by LVEF proximate to incident HF. Discrimination was quantified using time-dependent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and average precision (AP), with comparisons to age and sex, and a multinomial logistic regression classifier including PREVENT-HF variables. In aggregate, models were evaluated in MGH (n=16,739, age 56±17, 54% women), BWH (n=75,195, 56±16, 59%) and BIDMC (n=30,133, 56±17, 54%). ECG2HF-Subtype consistently discriminated incident HFrEF (MGH 10-year AUROC 0.89 [0.86-0.91], 10-year AP: 0.11 [95%CI 0.09-0.15], cumulative incidence 1.73%; BWH: 0.88 [0.87-0.89], 0.13 [0.11-0.14], 2.23% BIDMC: 0.88 [0.86-0.89], 0.14 [0.12-0.17], 2.19%) and HFpEF events (MGH 10-year AUROC 0.83 [0.81-0.85], 10-year AP: 0.10 [95% CI 0.09-0.13], cumulative incidence 3.17%; BWH: 0.79 [0.77-0.80], 0.06 [0.06-0.07], 2.75%), BIDMC: 0.81 [0.80-0.82], 0.10 [0.09-0.12], 3.49%), with consistently greater AUROC versus age and sex. When compared to PREVENT-HF variables, ECG2HF-Subtypes had favorable discrimination of HFrEF (e.g., 10-year AUROC in MGH+BWH 0.86 [0.84-0.88] vs. 0.78 [0.76-0.80]), and modestly lower for HFpEF (10-year AUROC in MGH+BWH 0.78 [0.76-0.80] vs. 0.81 [0.79-0.82]).

Conclusions

By predicting risk of HFpEF and HFrEF, AI-enabled ECG analysis may enable targeted prevention to reduce HF-related morbidity.

title: ACEs and CKL diseases in middle and old age: Multistate model and MR analysis of a national cohort.
authorString: Ai Z, Yang C, Zhang J, He J, Lin H, Ai L.
abstractText:
Background

Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with chronic diseases, but evidence regarding their impact on cardiovascular, kidney, and liver (CKL) diseases and multimorbidity remains limited. This study examines the association between ACEs and the onset of CKL diseases, and explores the potential mediating role of depressive symptoms.

Methods

The study included 7184 middle-aged and older adults aged ≥45 years without CKL disease at baseline from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, 2011-2018). Cox models were used to assess the association between ACEs and new-onset disease; multistate models were employed to analyse the risk of disease transition; mediation analysis was conducted to examine the mediating role of depressive symptoms. Two-sample Mendelian randomization was further applied as an independent triangulation analysis of the association between genetic liability to depression and selected outcomes.

Results

During a median follow-up of 84 months, there were 1428, 547, 379 and 300 new cases of CVD, CKD, CLD and CKL multimorbidity, respectively. The risk of CVD, CKD, CLD and CKL multimorbidity was increased by 30% [95% confidence interval (CI): 1.15, 1.45], 37% (95% CI: 1.13, 1.66), 35% (95% CI: 1.07, 1.70) and 46% (95% CI: 1.12, 1.89), respectively, with a graded association observed across ACE categories (all P-trend <0.05). ACEs were significantly associated with the initial transition from health to CKL disease. Depressive symptoms acted as a potential mediator, and Mendelian randomization provided genetic evidence on the association between depression and selected cardiovascular outcomes.

Conclusion

ACEs were associated with higher risks of CVD, CKD, CLD and CKL multimorbidity in middle-aged and older adults, with depressive symptoms as a potential mediator. ACE history and depressive symptoms may help identify high-risk individuals, supporting further exploration of integrated management strategies for chronic diseases.

title: Quality is in the eye of the beholder: A qualitative description study to explore the perceptions of researchers and practitioners on the quality of implementation science tools.
authorString: Bhuiya AR, Herrington I, Mathura D, Chambers D, Curran J, Dobbins M, Fahim C, Florez ID, Graham ID, Holroyd-Leduc J, Honsberger J, Hynes MT, Légaré F, Li LC, Lokker C, Leung FH, Makarski J, Munce S, Perrier L, Puchalski Ritchie LM, Rac VE, Sklar B, Sibley KM, Squires JE, Straus SE, Kastner M.
abstractText:
Objective

Implementation science (IS) tools (collectively referring to theories, models, frameworks, and tools that support TMF use) provide guidance for implementing, disseminating, sustaining, and scaling up health interventions, programs, and policies. However, little is known about the quality of IS tools. The study explored how implementation researchers, practitioners, and researcher-practitioners define and perceive quality in relation to IS tools.

Study design and setting

We employed a qualitative description methodology informed by a pragmatic theoretical worldview. Eligible participants were individuals with experience developing or using IS tools, and who primarily work in Canada, the United States, Australia, or Europe. They were recruited through purposeful and snowball sampling. Data was collected through virtual, semi-structured focus groups and individual interviews on Zoom. They were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and de-identified. An inductive, codebook thematic analysis was used to analyze the data. Three researchers independently coded an initial set of transcripts to develop a coding template. One researcher coded the remaining transcripts, and another audited the coding for consistency and congruence. Three researchers generated themes and sub-themes. The Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR) was used to report our findings.

Results

We conducted 10 focus groups and 11 individual interviews with 35 total participants (19 researchers, 9 researcher-practitioners, and 7 practitioners). Approximately half were from Canada, and most identified as women. Across the roles, the quality of IS tools were perceived to be multidimensional (e.g., scientific rigour, practical utility) and context-dependent (e.g., type of IS tool). Participants' perceptions of quality were influenced by their training and experiences. Other selection factors such as relevance appear to have a greater influence than the perceived quality of an IS tool. Participants described the importance in the quality of IS tool application. They suggested multiple considerations for improving the quality, development, selection, application, and evaluation of IS tools.

Conclusion

The quality of IS tools was perceived to be multidimensional and context-dependent. Varying perspectives on the role of quality of IS tools in selection and application indicate a need for clearer conceptualization. Our findings highlight the importance of future research aimed at improving the application of IS tools.

title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies in cardiovascular development: Implications for congenital heart disease and regenerative medicine.
authorString: Xu M, Li X, Zhou D, Deng X, Tang X, Zhao L, Wu S, Gong T, Li X, Guo R, Wang Y.
abstractText: Cardiac development constitutes a highly coordinated spatiotemporal process involving the precise regulation of numerous key genes and signaling pathways at specific anatomical sites and developmental stages. How distinct embryonic lineages coordinate with complex spatiotemporal microenvironments through cell fate transitions and the remodeling of developmental niches to regulate cardiac chamber specification, conduction system development, valvulogenesis, and vascular formation remains a fundamental question in understanding cardiovascular development. Elucidating these processes in greater depth is essential for understanding the mechanisms underlying congenital heart disease (CHD) and for advancing cardiac regenerative research. In recent years, advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies have overcome traditional research bottlenecks, providing novel perspectives for elucidating cardiovascular cell heterogeneity, lineage relationships, developmental trajectories, and cell-cell interactions. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in the application of single-cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies in cardiovascular development research, focusing on the developmental characteristics of three major tissue compartments, namely the myocardium, endocardium, and epicardium, and further outlines their applications in elucidating the mechanisms of CHD and in the field of cardiac regeneration. In the future, the deep integration of single-cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies with lineage tracing and functional genomics is expected to further elucidate the regulatory mechanisms of cardiovascular development and advance precision diagnostics and regenerative therapeutic strategies for these diseases.

title: Targeting CREB1 in cardiac diseases therapy.
authorString: Yarmohammadi F, Shackebaei D, Karimi G.
abstractText: Cyclic AMP-responsive element-binding protein 1 (CREB1) family is integral to the regulation of gene expression in response to diverse cellular signals, functioning as both an activator and a repressor depending on the cellular contest. The activity of CREB1 is tightly regulated by phosphorylation, alternative splicing, and co-activator interactions, enabling it to integrate multiple signaling pathways and precisely control processes. In the cardiac diseases, CREB1 emerges as a critical regulator. Evidence indicates that CREB1 upregulation reduces cardiomyocyte apoptosis and enhances cardiac function post-infarction. At the same time, its downregulation is linked to impaired contractility and dilated cardiomyopathy, highlighting its role as both a protective factor in cardiac pathology. This review examines the central CREB1-related signaling cascades, such as the CREB1/the homeodomain-interacting protein kinase 3 (HIPK3)/microRNA-17-3p/the adenylate cyclase type 6 (ADCY6) and CREB1- the bone morphogenetic proteins 10 (BMP10)-Smad1/5/8 axes, delineating their upstream activators and downstream targets in cardiac disease. Collectively, these findings underscore the therapeutic potential of targeting CREB1 and its regulatory networks for the management of diverse cardiac conditions.

title: The pathological role of chemokines and chemokine receptors in diabetic vascular disease.
authorString: Lan TY, Chen C, Chen JW, Chang TT.
abstractText: Diabetic vascular diseases, which include microvascular and macrovascular diseases, are a common complication of diabetes mellitus. Both chemokines and their receptors are involved in the pathophysiological process of diabetic vascular diseases, given their diverse functions. Crucially, when evaluating these chemokine networks, it is essential to distinguish descriptive clinical and bioinformatic biomarker observations from functional causal mechanisms established through in vitro and in vivo interventional studies, as observational concentration changes alone do not inherently demonstrate a direct pathogenic role or identify a therapeutic target. In this review, we examine recent studies and provide an overview of the mechanisms underlying chemokine-mediated signaling in diabetic microvascular and macrovascular diseases. We conclude that while circulating chemokines primarily serve as diagnostic or prognostic biomarkers, specific functional chemokine axes represent viable therapeutic targets for diabetic vascular complications.

title: Decoding the immunoregulatory logic of mesenchymal stromal cells in tissue regeneration: mechanisms, context dependence, and therapeutic translation.
authorString: Rezaei M, Behzadifar MM, Tavassoli Razavi F, Hoseinzadeh A, Baharlou R.
abstractText: Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) have attracted increasing attention as therapeutic agents in regenerative medicine because of their immunomodulatory and reparative properties. Increasing evidence indicates that a major component of MSC-mediated tissue repair involves modulation of local immune responses through complex cellular and paracrine interactions rather than direct differentiation into tissue-specific cells. This review provides a mechanistically structured analysis of the biological properties of MSCs and their context-dependent effects on innate and adaptive immune compartments, with particular emphasis on MSC-mediated regulation of T-cell responses, including induction of regulatory T cells, suppression of effector T-cell activity, and emerging but incompletely defined evidence of an exhaustion-like or dysfunction-associated T-cell phenotype characterized by increased expression of inhibitory receptors such as TIM-3. Importantly, we distinguish established immunomodulatory effects from emerging or hypothesis-generating evidence and emphasize that increased inhibitory-receptor expression alone does not establish bona fide T-cell exhaustion. We further examine how MSC-immune cell interactions, including macrophage reprogramming, efferocytosis, and regulation of T-cell and other immune-cell responses, may contribute to inflammatory resolution, angiogenesis, fibrosis control, apoptosis reduction, and endogenous tissue repair. The roles of the MSC secretome, cytokines, growth factors, and extracellular vesicles are critically discussed, with particular attention to the distinction between small extracellular vesicles and exosomes and to methodological factors affecting their functional interpretation. We summarize preclinical and clinical applications of MSC-based therapies across cardiac, hepatic, renal, pulmonary, and neurological disorders, while distinguishing tissue protection and functional improvement from demonstrated restoration of tissue architecture and regeneration. Finally, we discuss next-generation strategies, including genetic engineering, preconditioning, three-dimensional culture, and cell-free approaches, together with key translational challenges related to potency assessment, manufacturing, product heterogeneity, route-specific safety, and clinical implementation. Overall, this review proposes a context-sensitive immunological framework linking MSC-mediated immune regulation to tissue repair, while highlighting the mechanistic uncertainties and evidence gaps that currently limit translation from experimental findings to clinically reproducible regenerative outcomes.

title: Impact of oral diuretic monitoring duration prior to discharge on 30-day heart failure readmission rates.
authorString: Suleiman NM, Marshall VD, Konerman MC, Stein A, Adie SK.

journal.title: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care

abstractText:
Background

Current guidelines recommend transitioning patients with heart failure (HF) to oral diuretics prior to discharge, yet data guiding the optimal duration of oral diuretic monitoring remains limited. Prior retrospective studies assessed discharge-day oral diuretics or used a 24-hour monitoring cutoff.

Objectives

This study aimed to evaluate time on oral diuretic prior to discharge and 30-day HF readmission.

Methods

This single center retrospective study included patients admitted for acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) between 1/2020-9/2022. The primary end-point was 30-day HF readmission. Logistic regression models were used to estimate odds of readmission across varying durations of oral diuretic therapy (<24, 24-47, 48-71, and ≥72 h). Inverse propensity score weights (IPTW) were applied to control for confounder variables. Statistical significance was assessed using 95% confidence intervals (CI).

Results

A total of 466 patients were included (mean age 67.2 + 16.2 years; 56.2% male). IPTW results showed no significant difference in readmission rates for patients on diuretics < 24-hour group compared to 24-47 h (odds ratio (OR) 0.78 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.36, 1.67], 48-71 h (OR 0.78 [CI 0.36, 1.69]), and ≥72 h (OR 0.99 [CI 0.45, 2.15]). There was no significant difference in readmission rates when comparing <24 h versus ≥24 h of oral diuretic therapy (OR 0.85 [CI 0.43, 1.68]).

Conclusion

In patients with ADHF, extending oral diuretic monitoring beyond 24 h before discharge was not associated with reduced 30-day HF readmissions. Future studies should investigate the relationship between time on oral diuretics and overall response prior to discharge.

title: Effect of a nurse-led supported self-care intervention on cardiometabolic outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes: a quasi-experimental study.
authorString: Brito GS, Palasson RR, Dias TG, Arruda GO, Marcon SS, Batiston AP, Teston EF.
abstractText:
Background

Supported self-care interventions are increasingly used in diabetes management; however, evidence regarding their impact on cardiometabolic outcomes in primary care remains limited.

Objective

To examine changes in cardiometabolic indicators following a nurse-led supported self-care intervention in adults with type 2 diabetes.

Methods

A single-group pre-post study derived from a larger quasi-experimental project was conducted between March and November 2023 at a Family Health Unit in Central-West Brazil. Participants received three monthly nurse-led supported self-care consultations and two telephone follow-ups. Clinical and anthropometric measures were assessed at baseline, during the intervention, and post-intervention, whereas HbA1c, triglycerides, TyG, and TyG-WC were assessed at baseline and post-intervention. Data were analyzed using Friedman, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and McNemar tests, as appropriate.

Results

Twenty-nine participants completed follow-up and were included in the final analysis. Significant reductions were observed in waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, TyG, and TyG-WC. No significant change in HbA1c was observed between baseline and post-intervention.

Conclusions

The nurse-led supported self-care intervention was associated with favorable within-participant changes in selected anthropometric and cardiometabolic measures, particularly those related to central adiposity and cardiovascular risk. However, no significant improvement in HbA1c was observed. Controlled studies are needed to determine whether these changes can be attributed to the intervention.

title: Integrated Prenatal Cardiopulmonary Assessment Using Fetal Echocardiography in Isolated Left-Sided Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia.
authorString: Yamoto M, Inamura N, Toyoshima K, Terui K, Nagata K, Sato Y, Okuyama H, Maruyama H, Yokoi A, Kim K, Masumoto K, Okazaki T, Koike Y, Yazaki Y, Kawaguchi Y, Sato Y, Usui N.
abstractText:
Objective

Prenatal severity assessment in congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) primarily relies on lung-based parameters such as the observed-to-expected lung-to-head ratio (o/eLHR) and liver position; however, these markers do not fully reflect fetal cardiopulmonary adaptation. We investigated the prognostic significance of fetal echocardiographic parameters and integrated these in prenatal prediction models in left-sided CDH.

Methods

This nationwide multicenter retrospective study included fetuses with prenatally diagnosed isolated left-sided CDH. Gestational age-adjusted Z-scores were generated for fetal cardiac dimensions. Receiver operating characteristic analyses were performed to evaluate prognostic performance for survival.

Results

A total of 363 fetuses were included, with an overall survival rate of 74.9%. Non-survivors demonstrated significantly smaller right pulmonary artery and mitral valve dimensions than survivors. Among fetal echocardiographic parameters, the mitral-to-tricuspid valve ratio (MTR) demonstrated the strongest predictive performance, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.77. In fetuses evaluated at ≤ 29 weeks' gestation, an exploratory model combining MTR with o/eLHR and liver-up status achieved an apparent AUC of 0.827.

Conclusion

Fetal echocardiographic parameters were associated with survival in CDH. Integrated prenatal cardiopulmonary assessment incorporating MTR may provide complementary prognostic information although independent external validation is required.

title: AI-Identified Reasons for Nonescalation of Lipid-Lowering Therapy for Secondary Prevention.
authorString: Somani S, Kim DD, Ramaraju V, Ngo S, Babu C, Bouladian S, Chen T, King S, Perez-Guerrero E, Ronaghi S, Hwang J, Maron DJ, Hernandez-Boussard T, Alsentzer E, Rodriguez F.
abstractText:
Importance

Despite guideline recommendations for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) goals in secondary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), lipid-lowering therapy (LLT) remains underused. Identifying treat-to-target strategy adoption and reasons for LLT nonescalation are critical to close guideline-discordant care gaps.

Objective

To determine whether large language models (LLMs) can identify a treat-to-target strategy use and extract reasons for LLT nonescalation from clinical notes when LDL-C concentration is above goal.

Design, setting, and participants

This was a retrospective cohort study of patients from January 1, 2019, through May 15, 2025. Notes from most recent clinical encounters were retrieved and split into development, test, and inference sets. The setting was a large, integrated health system in Northern California. Adults aged 18 to 90 years with 2 or more clinician-billed encounters for ASCVD and with LDL-C level greater than or equal to 70 mg/dL at the most recent encounter were included in note-based analyses.

Exposures

Documented LDL-C targets and LLT management decisions.

Main outcomes and measures

Model performance was evaluated on LDL-C target documentation, LDL-C target value, LLT adjustment, and reasons for nonescalation against clinical annotations. Outcome prevalence was assessed on the inference set.

Results

A total of 28 113 unique patients with ASCVD-related encounters were identified, of whom 13 810 (49.1%; mean [SD] age, 70.9 [11.4] years; 7904 male [57.2%]) had above-goal LDL-C level. Model-annotator and interannotator reliability were not statistically different across outcomes, and micro-weighted F1 scores ranged from 0.80 to 0.98. Of the 13 394 patients with above-goal LDL-C level and 13 354 relevant notes in the inference set, a treat-to-target strategy was identified in 3756 (28.1%) of all relevant notes, most commonly targeting an LDL-C level less than 70 mg/dL (2280 [17.1%]). LLT was not escalated in 11 842 of all relevant notes (88.7%), with 4788 (40.4%) containing at least 1 LLT nonescalation reason, most often due to patient-reported adverse effects (1683 [12.6%]), LDL-C level close to goal (922 [6.9%]), patient preference to avoid LLT (914 [6.8%]), preference for lifestyle changes (811 [6.1%]), and deferral to repeat laboratory tests (617 [4.6%]).

Conclusions and relevance

Results of this study show that after using a state-of-the art LLM, nearly 9 in 10 ASCVD encounters with above-goal LDL-C level did not have patient LLT escalated, most often because of adverse effects, patient preference, preference for lifestyle changes, therapeutic inertia (eg, repeat laboratory tests), and near-goal LDL-C level. These findings highlight an avenue for personalizing system-level digital health interventions to help discover and minimize guideline-discordant care gaps in secondary prevention of ASCVD.

title: A prospective cohort study on the performance of chat-bot artificial intelligence in infective endocarditis management compared to infectious diseases consultation.
authorString: Denti L, Rezzonico LF, Oltolini C, Vecchi M, Bernasconi DP, Bellomo C, Ripa M, Bartoletti M, Giovannenze F, Di Gennaro E, Bana NB, Merli M, Chiamenti M, Travi G, Crippa F, Capitanio S, Cannata A, Tortorella R, Spanò F, Torti C, Vismara C, Moreo A, Moioli MC, Puoti M.

journal.medlineAbbreviation: Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis
journal.title: European journal of clinical microbiology & infectious diseases : official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology
journal.isoabbreviation: Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis

abstractText:
Background

The role of artificial intelligence in managing complex infectious diseases (ID) remains poorly understood. This study assessed the quality and safety of the management plan recommended by ChatGPT-4o in patients with infective endocarditis (IE).

Methods

Prospective, single-center study enrolling adults with IE over an 8-months period. Clinical data for each patient, using ESC guidelines and Duke-ISCVID criteria as external knowledge or fine-tuning data, were provided to ChatGPT-4o asking for a management plan (diagnosis, diagnostic work-up, antimicrobial therapy, follow-up). The recommendations provided by local ID specialists (IDSs) and ChatGPT-4o were rated by three independent IDSs using a standardized scoring system. Evaluations were compared using McNemar-Bowker test and the inter-grader agreement was assessed.

Results

Fifty patients with IE were included, mostly with definite IE (86%) sustained by Gram-positive bacteria (80%). ChatGPT-4o initial diagnoses were identical to IDSs in ≥ 90% of cases with an optimal inter-grader agreement. Despite low inadequacy (0%-12%), the appropriateness of work-up proposed by ChatGPT-4o was significantly lower than that of IDSs because it was not specific enough in almost half of cases. The percentages of optimal antimicrobial therapy suggested by ChatGPT-4o were lower than those of IDSs (34%-66% vs. 72%-86%) and a trend towards lower adequacy was retrieved (inadequate 2%-18% vs. 2%-8%, harmful 0%-14% vs. 0%-2%), albeit the agreement between graders was moderate-low. The follow-up appropriateness was good (53%-82%).

Conclusion

While helpful in diagnosing IE, the application of ChatGPT-4o based on current guidelines requires further development in decision-making tasks, as antimicrobial therapy, and should not be employed independently.

title: Systolic pressure gradient across myocardial bridge mediates the effect of bridge depth on clinical symptoms.
authorString: Sun W, Song M, Li J, Yu X, Wei T, Zhai Z, Yang J, Zhang A, Qu X.
abstractText:
Objective

The relationship between myocardial bridging (MB) morphology and function and the pathways to clinical symptoms remained unclear. This study investigated the association between delta coronary computed tomographic angiography-derived fractional flow reserve (ΔCT-FFR) and angina-equivalent symptoms in left anterior descending MB without coronary atherosclerosis using photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT).

Materials and methods

This retrospective cohort included 180 patients with deep MB (depth > 2 mm) and no plaques. All underwent PCD-CT angiography. CT-FFR was computed by machine learning; systolic (ΔCT-FFRsys) and diastolic (ΔCT-FFRdia) trans-bridge pressure gradients were derived. MB depth and length were measured. Associations with symptoms were assessed by logistic regression and mediation analysis.

Results

Symptomatic patients (n = 81) had greater depth (median 3.30 mm vs. 2.45 mm), longer length (mean 36.06 mm vs. 26.10 mm), higher ΔCT-FFRsys (3.81% vs. 1.62%) and ΔCT-FFRdia (3.45% vs. 2.15%) than asymptomatic patients (n = 99) (all p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis identified depth (OR = 1.77, 95% CI: 1.27-2.46, p = 0.001) and ΔCT-FFRsys (OR = 1.16, 95% CI: 1.05-1.27, p = 0.002) as independent predictors. Mediation analysis indicated that ΔCT-FFRsys significantly mediated the effect of depth on symptoms (indirect effect = 0.1881, 95% CI: 0.1023-0.2897).

Conclusions

MB depth and ΔCT-FFRsys were independent risk factors for symptoms, and ΔCT-FFRsys appeared to mediate the morphological-clinical symptoms link. These findings suggested that integrated assessment, particularly ΔCT-FFRsys, might be a new non-invasive imaging biomarker for clinically identify symptomatic MB and understand its potential pathogenic mechanisms.

Key points

Question The precise relationship between myocardial bridging morphological and functional features and clinical symptoms, and whether underlying key mediating factors exist, remains currently incompletely determined. Findings Depth, length, and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient of myocardial bridging independently predicted symptoms, with the gradient significantly mediating the relationship between morphology and clinical presentation. Clinical relevance Noninvasive assessment of depth and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient can assist in identifying patients with symptomatic myocardial bridging, serving as potential imaging biomarkers and providing insights into the underlying pathophysiology of symptom presentation.

title: Human‑Scale Lymphatic Modeling to Guide Lymphatic Interventions: Application to a Soft Robotic Assist Device.
authorString: Escher A, Rosalia L, Bosoni E, Roche ET, Granegger M.
abstractText:
Purpose

The lymphatic system is essential for maintaining tissue-fluid homeostasis. In conditions of elevated venous pressures (e.g., congestive heart failure or congenital single-ventricle heart disease after Fontan palliation), increased capillary filtration and impaired lymphatic drainage disrupt this balance, predisposing patients to lymphatic overload and edema. The lack of human-scale computational models capturing lymphatic pumping and coupled tissue-fluid exchange limits the development of effective interventions.

Methods

We developed a human-scale lumped-parameter model that combines multi-lymphangion thoracic duct pumping with a Starling-based tissue-fluid balance model, enabling integrated simulation of central lymphatic function and tissue-fluid homeostasis. The framework was used to evaluate surgical and device-based lymphatic interventions. Model predictions were combined with virtual fitting using MR-derived anatomy from three Fontan patients to demonstrate translational applicability and design an extravascular soft robotic lymphatic assist sleeve, whose performance was characterized in hydraulic benchtop experiments.

Results

The model reproduced physiologic thoracic duct flow (~3.1L/day) and predicted interstitial fluid accumulation under venous hypertension (up to ~ 18 mL/min net accumulation). Surgical (lymphatic decompression) and device-based (extravascular sleeve) interventions increased thoracic duct flow and reduced simulated tissue-fluid accumulation (47% and 76.5% reduction, respectively), with the sleeve providing frequency-dependent augmentation. Virtual fitting confirmed anatomical feasibility of device implantation in all three Fontan patients. Benchtop testing demonstrated pressure step-ups from 5.5 to ~ 17 mmHg and flow augmentation from 2.5 to ~ 18 mL/min at actuation frequencies of 20-60 bpm.

Conclusion

Our human-scale computational framework offers mechanistic insights into lymphatic dysfunction under elevated venous pressure and provides a platform for the design and evaluation of lymphatic interventions.

title: Mitochondrial translation deficiency limits the cardiac benefit of ketogenic diet in early-onset cardiomyopathy.
authorString: Kartal O, Dogan SA.
abstractText: Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy is a devastating disorder with no effective treatment. Ketogenic diet (KD) has shown therapeutic benefit in some mitochondrial disease models but failed or caused harm in others, suggesting its efficacy depends on the underlying genetic defect. KD has ameliorated cardiomyopathy in models where the electron transport chain retains structural integrity, yet it has not been tested in a model with a primary defect in mitochondrial translation. We therefore examined KD in heart- and skeletal muscle-specific Dars2 knockout mice (hmKO), a model of fatal early-onset mitochondrial cardiomyopathy caused by loss of mitochondrial aspartyl-tRNA synthetase, which is essential for translation of all 13 mitochondrial DNA-encoded oxidative phosphorylation subunits. Male hmKO mice and wild type littermates received either a ketogenic or normal chow diet from weaning until the humane endpoint. KD induced a partial shift toward cardiac fatty acid metabolism and activated mitochondrial biogenesis signaling. However, these adaptations did not improve survival, cardiac hypertrophy, skeletal muscle atrophy, motor performance, respiratory chain complex abundance, enzyme activities, or cardiac ATP levels. KD reduced antioxidant gene expression, without increasing protein carbonylation, and amplified the mitokine response, with increased GDF15 and FGF21 in the heart and serum. These findings show that substrate availability alone cannot restore cardiac bioenergetics when mitochondrial translation capacity is severely impaired. Instead, mitochondrial translation machinery defines a critical boundary for metabolic interventions in mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. Our results argue that the therapeutic potential of KD in mitochondrial disease is mechanism-dependent and should not be generalized across genetically and bioenergetically distinct forms of mitochondrial cardiomyopathy.

title: Agreement between fully automated artificial intelligence and cardiac radiologists for coronary stenosis and plaque assessment in an asymptomatic screening cohort.
authorString: Shin C, Yoon G, Cha SJ, Pak S, Schöbinger M, Kim H, Ko SM.

journal.title: The international journal of cardiovascular imaging

abstractText: This retrospective single-center study evaluated segment-level agreement between experienced cardiac radiologists and a research AI platform for coronary stenosis and plaque assessment on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA). Asymptomatic individuals undergoing CCTA at a health screening center were studied, excluding those with prior revascularization, coronary anomaly, or total occlusion. Stenosis grade and plaque composition were independently assessed by the AI platform and two cardiac radiologists at the segment level, with disagreements between the two radiologists resolved by consensus. Agreement was evaluated using Cohen's κ, quadratic weighted κ for ordinal grading, observed agreement, and positive and negative agreement for dichotomized significant stenosis. The cohort comprised 172 participants and 2,582 segments. Significant stenosis was uncommon (18/2,582, 0.7%), with moderate agreement (κ = 0.412; observed agreement 98.5%; positive agreement 0.418; negative agreement 0.992). Agreement was fair for ordinal stenosis grade (κ = 0.397; quadratic weighted κ = 0.573; observed agreement 84.0%) and plaque composition (κ = 0.330; observed agreement 81.8%). Stenosis-grade agreement was lower in plaque-containing than plaque-free segments, an exploratory finding given marked differences in subgroup size and prevalence. Myocardial bridging and image quality were not major descriptive determinants of discordance. In this low-prevalence cohort, AI-based CCTA analysis showed high negative agreement for radiologist-defined significant stenosis but limited concordance for grading and plaque characterization. Reflecting low prevalence and few positive cases, the findings do not establish independent rule-out performance but support prospective evaluation of AI as an expert-supervised pre-reading or triage adjunct, with positive, ambiguous, or plaque-containing findings requiring expert review.
