authorString: Cerveri P, Taconnè M, Corino V, Mainardi L.
abstractText: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) produces heterogeneous electrical phenotypes whose continuous organization, longitudinal evolution and clinical relevance remain poorly defined. We developed complementary variational-autoencoder representations to map HCM ECG morphology relative to physiological variation and characterize within-subject change. Using 5,194 normal-reference ECGs and 2,594 longitudinal visits from 650 individuals with HCM, we found that HCM overlapped the physiological manifold but extended towards its periphery, while an HCM-oriented manifold largely reorganized shared electrical modes. Mixed-effects models identified longitudinal drift in selected phenotypic axes. A lateral/frontal QRS-force coordinate remained time-dependent after censoring septal reduction therapy, atrial fibrillation and pacing, and lower values were associated with subsequent heart-failure risk in baseline and time-updated analyses. A time-conditioned change VAE identified four interpretable within-subject modes aligned with longer-term trajectories. Sarcomeric genotype was associated with phenotype position but not trajectory rate.

title: 2D U-NET Deep Learning Architecture for Atherosclerotic Lesion Segmentation and Quantification
authorString: Giles W, Venetianer Z, Patel N, Neughebauer MB, Abramson AM, Granger AT, Tustison NJ, Shi W.
abstractText: Mice are commonly used for experimental atherosclerosis research, and a common procedure involves morphometric analysis of atherosclerotic lesions on Oil Red O-stained cross-sections of the aortic root. However, manual measurement of atherosclerotic lesion sizes on numerous histological sections is tedious and time-consuming. Here, we developed a deep learning model based on convolutional neural network to quantify atherosclerotic lesions in cross-sectioned aortic roots of mice. Microscopy images were taken from cross-sectioned aortic roots of genetically diverse F2 mice derived from BALB/cJ and LP/J  Apoe knockout mice and fed 12 weeks of a Western diet. Aortic cross-sections were stained with Oil Red O and hematoxylin and images captured. Atherosclerotic lesions were manually segmented in 2553 images using Zeiss AxioVision. These images were split into 1,533 for training the U-NET model, 510 for validation, and 510 images for testing. The developed model was evaluated for its performance to measure atherosclerotic lesions by comparing with manual measurement in test images. The model achieved a high degree of accuracy, with an Fl score of 0.82, a Jaccard score of 0.72, a Recall of 0.80, a precision of 0.87, and a correlation coefficient value of 0.98. While manual lesion measurement took approximately 5 minutes per image, the model performed the task in ~3.35 seconds, reducing measurement time by 98.9%. The developed 2D U-NET model provides a new platform for rapid and accurate quantification of atherosclerotic lesion sizes on Oil Red O-stained sections.

title: Neural Crest-Derived Endocardial Cells Required for Heart Valve Development
authorString: Merriman AF, Costa MW, Pelonero A, Huang Y, Nishino T, Li F, Jinagal SL, Lam A, Brand A, Yu V, Hu Y, Gao F, Kathiriya IS, Anwar S, Bunker M, Ranade SS, Gifford CA, Bruneau BG, Ye CJ, Srivastava D.
abstractText: Abnormalities in cardiac valves, which maintain unidirectional blood flow through the heart, affect 2–3% of people worldwide and are the most common form of structural heart disease  1 .Yet the cell types that make up the valve, and how they communicate to direct development and homeostasis, remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a rare, essential population of highly secretory valve endocardial cells in mouse and human that derive from migrating neural crest cells. Ablation of these cells in mice caused perinatal lethality with thickened leaflets, stenosis, and regurgitation, mirroring human valve disease. This subset of endocardial cells uniquely expresses the secreted signaling protein parathyroid hormone-like hormone (  Pthlh ). Global disruption of Pthlh caused valve stenosis and lethality and neural crest-specific deletion produced similar valve disease, with impaired maturation of valvular interstitial cells and disrupted bone morphogenetic protein signaling. These findings identify a previously unrecognized cell type and signaling pathway essential for valve morphogenesis, with implications for the pathogenesis and treatment of human valve defects.

title: High-fat diet promotes exhaustion-associated T-cell remodeling across vascular and lymphoid tissues in atherosclerosis-prone mice
authorString: Yarahmadi P, Xie Y, Huynh DTN, Lai J, Ling Q, Huang X, Nguyen PK.
abstractText:
Background

Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease driven by lipid accumulation and immune dysregulation. How chronic dietary lipid exposure reshapes T-cell states across vascular and lymphoid tissues, and whether these changes resolve after dietary normalization, remains incompletely defined. This study examined diet-associated T-cell remodeling and the contribution of macrophage-mediated stimulation

Methods

ApoE-deficient mice received a vegetarian diet (VD) or high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 or 24 weeks; a dietary reversal group received HFD for 12 weeks followed by VD for 12 weeks. CD45-positive cells from aorta, blood, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow underwent single-cell RNA sequencing with matched T-cell receptor sequencing. T-cell states were annotated using canonical markers, and exhaustion-and naive-associated transcriptional programs were quantified using UCell scores. Analyses assessed T-cell composition, clonal expansion, and predicted macrophage–T-cell communication, with splenic flow-cytometric validation.

Results

HFD was associated with enrichment of exhaustion-associated states, with the highest exhaustion scores in the aorta. At 24 weeks, the pooled exhausted-cell proportion was 15.7% under HFD versus 10.6% under VD. Dietary reversal restored this proportion to 10.6%, while residual transcriptional changes persisted in a tissue-dependent manner. Flow cytometry corroborated increased inhibitory receptor expression and co-expression. Aortic macrophages exhibited inflammatory and antigen-presentation programs alongside increased predicted communication with T cells. Aortic T-cell activation and clonal expansion accompanied these changes, and clonotype size correlated with exhaustion score (Spearman correlation coefficient = 0.57, p = 0.029).

Conclusion

Chronic HFD is associated with multicompartment T-cell remodeling, with prominent vascular exhaustion-associated programs and tissue-dependent recovery after dietary normalization. These findings suggest that dietary lipid exposure may leave a durable adaptive immune imprint across organs during atherosclerosis.

title: Platelet-endothelial crosstalk drives distinct endothelial dysfunction in bicuspid aortic valve disease
authorString: Weiss L, Chelvanambi S, Harrison A, Kasai T, Nakamura Y, Turner ME, Blaser MC, Billaud M, Aikawa M, Singh SA, Aikawa E.
abstractText:
Background

Bicuspid aortic valves (BAV) predispose individuals to premature development of aortic stenosis (AS). The abnormal hemodynamic environment of BAV affects both platelets and valvular endothelial cells (VECs), but whether platelet-derived signals contribute to valve morphology-specific endothelial dysfunction remains unknown.

Methods

Platelets and VECs were obtained from patients with BAVs or tricuspid aortic valves (TAVs) undergoing valve replacement for AS. Platelets were activated to generate platelet releasate (PR). PR composition and its effects on VECs were investigated using complementary molecular, multi-omic, functional, and computational approaches.

Results

BAV and TAV patients exhibited markedly distinct PR profiles, which translated into differential endothelial responses. Strikingly, BAV-derived PR elicited a substantially more pronounced endothelial dysfunction phenotype, characterized by widespread molecular reprogramming and functional alterations. Integrated multi-omics uncovered mitochondrial dysfunction as a central feature of BAV PR-induced endothelial injury, accompanied by activation of pathways spanning endothelial remodeling, migration, and immune-cell recruitment. These molecular signatures translated into mitochondrial depolarization, altered mitochondrial dynamics, enhanced VEC migration, and increased neutrophil adhesion and chemotaxis. Finally, computational ligand-receptor and ligand-target analyses identified candidate signaling axes linking platelet-derived mediators to endothelial reprogramming, highlighting potential therapeutic targets.

Conclusions

We provide the first direct evidence that platelet activation contributes to AS initiation through the induction of endothelial dysfunction and that these effects are amplified in BAV. These findings identify platelet-VEC crosstalk as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking abnormal valve hemodynamics to disease onset. Targeting platelet-derived mediators may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for AS, specifically in BAV.

Graphical Abstract

Translational Perspective

Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) confers a substantial risk of premature aortic stenosis, yet no pharmacological therapy to halt disease development exists. Our findings position platelet-endothelial crosstalk as a mechanistic link between the abnormal hemodynamic environment of BAV and valvular endothelial dysfunction. Platelet-derived mediators promoted endothelial remodeling, mitochondrial dysfunction, and a migratory phenotype, with more marked effects in BAV. These observations suggest that platelets actively contribute to the initiation and progression of calcific aortic valve disease rather than solely reflecting advanced stenosis. Targeting shear-dependent platelet-endothelial signaling may therefore provide new opportunities for sought-after disease-modifying therapeutic strategies in (BAV-associated) aortic stenosis.

title: Engineered synbiotic microspheres enable system-level reprogramming of the gut-immune-vascular axis in chronic inflammatory vascular disease.
authorString: Shen L, Zhai M, Yang Z, Yu J, Pang Z, Fang Z, Ding X, Xu J, Hu Y, Fang S, Shu G, Yang Y, Lv L, Zhang S, Xu J, Wu J, Chen W, Lu C, Chen M, Ji J.
abstractText: Chronic inflammatory vascular diseases are increasingly recognized as systemic disorders sustained by maladaptive cross-organ immunometabolic coupling, yet current therapeutic strategies remain largely lesion-centered and fail to address upstream drivers of disease persistence. Here, we identify the gut-immune-vascular axis as a system-level pathogenic unit that integrates gut microbial dysbiosis, intestinal barrier dysfunction, metabolic imbalance, and vascular immune activation into a self-reinforcing pathological circuit. Through integrated clinical profiling and cross-species validation, we demonstrate that disruption of this axis is characterized by coordinated probiotic depletion, expansion of proinflammatory taxa, translocation of microbial endotoxins, accumulation of microbiota-derived metabolites, and macrophage polarization toward a proinflammatory phenotype along the gut-vascular continuum. To therapeutically target this axis, we engineer enzyme-responsive synbiotic microspheres that codeliver probiotics, a microbial metabolic pathway inhibitor, and a prebiotic within a protective polymeric matrix, enabling site-specific intestinal activation and coordinated microbiota-metabolic modulation. This engineered system restores intestinal barrier integrity, reprograms microbial ecology and metabolite output, suppresses immunometabolic dysfunction, and robustly attenuates pathological vascular remodeling across cellular, murine, and large-animal models, with in-stent restenosis serving as a representative disease context. Collectively, this work establishes axis-oriented immunometabolic reprogramming as a generalizable therapeutic paradigm and highlights engineered synbiotic platforms as scalable tools for system-level intervention in chronic inflammatory diseases.

title: Direct regulation of a tRNA modification enzyme by ppGpp links stress signaling to translational control and biofilm development.
authorString: Trinquier AE, Slama F, Liu J, Pham L, Stolt L, Wang JD.
abstractText: Transfer RNA (tRNA) modifications influence decoding efficiency and translational fidelity, yet how they are integrated into bacterial signaling networks remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a direct connection between stress signaling and codon-specific translational regulation. We show that the alarmone guanosine tetraphosphate (ppGpp) directly inhibits MnmE (TrmE), a conserved tRNA-modification GTPase required for methylaminomethyl (mnm) modification of wobble uridine. High-resolution ribosome profiling in Bacillus subtilis revealed that loss of MnmE selectively increases ribosome pausing at AAG codons and reprograms translation of a subset of genes, including small open reading frames. Among these is a previously unrecognized AAG-containing leader peptide that controls expression of the biofilm repressor AbrB. Consistent with this mechanism, mnmE mutants exhibit constitutive extracellular matrix production and bypass the biofilm defect of a relA mutant. Together, these findings establish a pathway linking ppGpp signaling, tRNA modification, codon-specific translation, and multicellular development.

title: Comprehensive Evaluation of an Adenine/Phosphate-Induced CKD Model for the Study of Aortic Valve Calcification.
authorString: Blot G, de Berny Q, Louvet L, Vasseur L, Avondo C, Delattre J, Spicher P, Batteux B, Mensah DG, Bohbot Y, Tribouilloy C, Naudot M, Collet L, Chatelain D, Choukroun G, Benachour H, Kamel S, Bennis Y, Hénaut L.
abstractText:
Background

Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) is prevalent in chronic kidney disease (CKD), yet no pharmacological therapies exist. Preclinical models rarely incorporate CKD-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD) features, limiting translational potential. We aimed to develop a comprehensive preclinical approach to study CKD-associated CAVD, suitable for standardized assessment of therapies on valvular, cardiac, vascular, and skeletal outcomes.

Methods

Eight-week-old male Sprague Dawley rats were assigned to a control group (n=17) fed standard chow or an adenine-phosphate group (AP, n=21) fed chow supplemented with 0.3% adenine and 1.15% phosphate. Diets were enriched with 20% lactose and 19% casein to facilitate phosphate absorption and calcium solubility. Cardiac function was evaluated by echocardiography at baseline, week 5, and 9, with concurrent blood sampling. Aortic valve (AV) calcification was assessed by Alizarin Red and Osteosense staining, and aortic calcium quantified using O-Cresolphthalein Complexone. Gene expression in the aorta and left ventricle (LV) was analyzed by RNA-seq at week 9, and bone microarchitecture assessed by micro-CT.

Results

AP rats showed progressive increases in serum creatinine, calcium-phosphorus product, and uremic toxins. By week 9, they exhibited significant AV calcification, with reduced valve area and cusp separation. Relative wall thickness and LV histology were preserved, though transcriptomics revealed early priming toward inflammation and fibrosis. AP rats' aortas showed calcification, osteogenic features and reduced systolic expansion. Bone analysis revealed cortical thinning and increased porosity, while trabecular bone showed reduced trabecular number, increased trabecular spacing, and compensatory thickening. Together with elevated PTH and FGF23 levels, these changes suggest high bone turnover due to secondary hyperparathyroidism and are correlated with the extent of AV calcification.

Conclusions

These results underscore the model's translational relevance, addressing multiple facets of CKD-MBD and supporting its use for preclinical screening of novel therapies targeting CKD-associated cardiovascular calcification.

title: Fluorescence-based biosensing with DNA nanostructures and DNA origami: from programmable architectures to quantitative readouts.
authorString: Kim S, Choi MY, Jeong H, Ahn HR, Choi JH.
abstractText: DNA nanotechnology and DNA origami have emerged as promising platforms for biosensing by exploiting the programmability of DNA sequences and structural self-assembly. Diverse DNA nanostructures, including three-way junctions (TWJs), dendritic assemblies, hydrogels, and tetrahedral DNA nanostructures (TDNs), provide structurally defined frameworks for the organization of functional components. DNA origami further enables highly programmable and precise spatial positioning by folding long DNA scaffolds with multiple staple strands. Their high biocompatibility and nanoscale spatial addressability allow the controlled organization of fluorophores, quenchers, aptamers, nanoparticles, and other functional components, which is particularly advantageous for fluorescence-based sensing strategies that rely on precise spatial control of these components. In this review, we first introduce the fundamental principles of fluorescence-based biosensing, including Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) and plasmon-enhanced fluorescence (PEF). Then categorize DNA nanostructure-based fluorescence biosensors according to their structural architectures and sensing mechanisms. DNA origami-based platforms are subsequently classified based on their signal transduction strategies. Representative studies are discussed in terms of their design principles and sensing performance. We further critically discuss the remaining challenges, including structural stability, scalability, signal reproducibility, and clinical translation, and provide perspectives on the future development of next-generation fluorescence biosensing platforms enabled by programmable DNA architectures.

title: Comprehensive Risk Assessment in the Lipoprotein(a) Landscape: Practical Algorithms for Multi-Modal Risk Stratification.
authorString: Steuerwald M, Underberg J.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a common, causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Clinicians continue to face questions regarding how overall risk should be refined once Lp(a) is identified.

Recent findings

International guidelines are beginning to universally recommend Lp(a) measurement at least once in adulthood, which will make the discovery of elevated Lp(a) a more common finding in routine practice. Despite this, Lp(a) remains absent from conventional risk equations. Additional stratification tools including assessment of subclinical atherosclerosis can be further applied to help distinguish inherited susceptibility from expressed disease. All of this together should support a more informed shared decision regarding the intensity of preventive therapy in these cases. We aim to provide a flexible framework that integrates Lp(a), contemporary risk equations, imaging, and selective genetics to produce actionable risk phenotypes which can guide the intensity of preventive decisions today.

title: Salivary extracellular vesicle-associated miR-5006-5p in periodontitis: validation and functional insights.
authorString: Nik Mohamed Kamal NNS, Mohamad S, Raja Awang RA, Shahidan WNS.
abstractText:
Background

Periodontitis is an oral cavity disease arising from chronic inflammation of the periodontal tissues. microRNAs (miRs) have been demonstrated to play an important role in regulating the immune-inflammatory response; however, the function of miR-5006-5p from extracellular vesicles (EVs) in periodontal inflammation has not been investigated.

Methods

Previous microarray results were validated using RT-qPCR. Bioinformatic analyses using DIANA microT-CDS and miRDIP consistently predicted BMPR2, IL1R1, and NFKB1 as target genes of miR-5006-5p. HGF cells were transfected with miRs mimics, and miRs and target genes expression were assessed by RT-qPCR.

Results

Validation by RT-qPCR replicated the previous microarray findings. miR-5006-5p over-expression in HGF cells significantly down-regulated BMPR2 gene, making it as the putative target gene and potentially regulated target gene for the miR. KEGG pathway mapping revealed that all three genes; BMPR2, IL1R1, and NFκB1, were involved in a shared fluid shear stress and atherosclerosis pathway.

Conclusion

These consistent findings from miR microarray, RT-qPCR validation, bioinformatic analyses, and in vitro experiments support an association between miR-5006-5p and periodontitis and suggest a potential role in regulating mechanoinflammatory signalling pathways.

title: Coronary Atherosclerosis in Masters Athletes: Contemporary Evidence and Clinical Implications.
authorString: Davis BM, Kim JH.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

A growing body of evidence suggests that Masters athletes have a higher prevalence of coronary artery calcification and plaque compared to more sedentary, but low-risk individuals. This clinical paradox has sparked interest in understanding underlying mechanisms, prognostic importance, and clinical management of coronary atherosclerosis in highly-trained Masters athletes.

Recent findings

Data from multiple observational studies evaluating coronary atherosclerosis in Masters athletes have demonstrated a higher-than-expected prevalence of calcified plaque. More recent studies have also identified a greater burden of mixed plaques in Masters athletes, the prognostic significance of which remains uncertain. In parallel, contemporary exercise guidelines for Masters athletes with coronary atherosclerosis have evolved and emphasize shared decision-making, while also taking into account the Masters athlete's overall cardiovascular risk profile. In this review, we summarize the contemporary evidence on the epidemiology and plaque features of coronary atherosclerosis in Masters athletes, including sex differences and the impact of exercise intensity and traditional cardiovascular risk factors. We review potential mechanisms, including the effects of hemodynamic stress, oxidative stress, inflammation, calcium homeostasis, and genetic factors, as well as their interaction with classic risk factors. Finally, we review current clinical approaches to risk assessment and treatment options, highlighting recent shifts toward personalized assessments and shared decision-making.

title: Delays From Clinical Manifestations to Diagnosis of Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy: A National Retrospective Cohort Study.
authorString: Mitchell JD, Udall M, Hennum L, Dao HD, Zeldow B, Nagelhout E, Alexander KM, Cheng RK.

journal.title: Journal of the American Heart Association

abstractText:
Background

Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) is a progressive, life-threatening condition. Timely and accurate diagnosis remains a challenge. We assessed time from first recorded clinical manifestation to ATTR-CM diagnosis in the United States and characterized manifestations associated with diagnostic delays.

Methods

Retrospective analysis of US claims data (Komodo Healthcare Map, July 1, 2016-June 30, 2024). Patients were required to have ≥3 years of continuous enrollment before diagnosis.

Results

Among 7509 patients, mean age 75.9 years, 63.2% male, 54.5% White, and 28.6% Black. Patients had a median of 8 manifestations before diagnosis; median observed time from first recorded manifestation to diagnosis was 5.2 years, shorter for variant versus wild-type ATTR-CM (4.4 versus 5.2 years). Within 3 years before diagnosis, patients had a mean of 12.04 (95% CI, 11.75-12.35) primary care physician visits and 14.45 (95% CI, 14.10-14.80) specialists of interest visits, most commonly with cardiologists and ophthalmologists. In adjusted analyses, variant ATTR-CM was associated with shorter time to diagnosis (β, -0.41 years [95% CI, -0.56 to -0.26]), whereas comorbidities, including hypertension (β, 0.46 years [95% CI, 0.27-0.64]), were associated with longer delays.

Conclusions

The diagnostic trajectory for ATTR-CM can be prolonged and challenging, leading to more advanced disease at diagnosis and increased burden. Raising awareness may provide an opportunity for earlier diagnosis.

title: Liposome-based responsive MRI contrast agents.
authorString: Duncan AM, Ellis CM, Smith JP, Davis JJ.
abstractText: Liposomes present a promising architecture for the design of responsive MRI CAs. The ability to co-encapsulate diagnostic and therapeutic payloads further allows for (targeted) imaging and treatment of disease in vivo. Tuneable control over embedded motifs, or modification of the bilayer phospholipids themselves, can support a programmable response to disease microenvironments. In this review we summarise the design and underpinning theoretical principles relevant to the production of next-generation diagnostically potent responsive liposome-based MRI CAs.

title: Biomarker trajectories and risk of relapse in giant cell arteritis: a multicenter study.
authorString: Pichon S, Leurs A, Mortain L, Behal H, Dalhi N, Jouvray M, Koether V, Ledoult E, Chepy A, Hachulla E, Sobanski V, Launay D, Lambert M.
abstractText:
Objective

The relative value of plasma fibrinogen (PF) compared with C-reactive protein (CRP) for longitudinal monitoring in giant cell arteritis (GCA) is uncertain. We assessed their performance as biomarkers of disease activity and predictors of relapse.

Methods

We conducted a multicenter retrospective study of 465 patients diagnosed with GCA between 2000 and 2023 fulfilling GiACTA inclusion criteria. Baseline demographic, clinical, laboratory, imaging, and treatment data were collected. In a subset of 135 patients diagnosed from 2017 to 2022, CRP and PF were collected until relapse or up to 2 years. Associations between biomarker dynamics and relapse were analyzed using joint modeling.

Results

Among 465 patients, 34.2% experienced ≥ 1 relapse within 5 years. At diagnosis, headache, jaw claudication and aortic FDG uptake on PET-CT were associated with higher relapse risk. PF normalization at 1 month was associated with a lower relapse risk over 2 years (HR 0.14, 95% CI 0.07-0.28; p < 0.001). PF at month 1 showed good discrimination for relapse (AUC 0.82, bootstrap 95% CI 0.69-0.91), with an exploratory ROC-derived cut-off of 3.77 g/L (bootstrap 95%CI, 3.45-3.97) yielding a sensitivity of 71.8%, and a specificity of 90.0%. Individual trajectories of CRP and PF were heterogeneous and identified distinct phenotypes associated with different relapse risks.

Conclusion

In our GCA cohort, relapse risk was associated with cranial manifestations and aortic uptake on PET-CT at diagnosis. PF normalization at 1 month was identified as an early marker of a lower relapse risk, although this biomarker requires external validation. CRP and PF trajectories identified distinct phenotypes associated with different relapse risks, supporting further evaluation of longitudinal biomarker-guided follow-up.

title: Aortic Mycetoma with <i>Exserohilum</i>.
authorString: Zhuang J, Kandil O, Farina JM, Shubeilat J, Kumar G, Sell-Dottin K.
abstractText: We present the first reported case of aortic mycetoma due to Exserohilum, a dematiaceous mold. The patient presented with neurologic symptoms 2 months after root-sparing ascending aortic aneurysm repair with aortic valve replacement. Multimodal imaging revealed irregular densities in the aortic lumen and graft, consistent with infectious thrombus. Redo aortic aneurysm repair and aortic valve replacement was performed, and a culture of the extracted thrombus confirmed the diagnosis.

title: Extensive Dural Metastasis as Initial Presentation of Metastatic Prostate Cancer: A Case Report With Durable Disease Control Following Multimodal Treatment.
authorString: Wasilewski D, Felsberg J, Tzamalis T, Muhammad S.
abstractText: Central nervous system involvement in prostate cancer is rare, particularly in the form of dural or pachymeningeal metastases. We report the case of a 72-year-old man presenting with visual disturbances without hemianopsia, and right-sided headache since several weeks caused by an extensive right temporal dural-based lesion with intracranial extension. A minimally invasive frontotemporal burr-hole biopsy was performed for histopathological clarification. Histological and immunohistochemical analyses confirmed metastatic prostatic adenocarcinoma with expression of cytokeratin 8, NKX3.1, PSA, and PSMA. Subsequent systemic staging demonstrated metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer with pulmonary, lymphatic, and extensive osseous metastases. The patient underwent focal radiotherapy (36 Gy in 12 fractions) to the dural lesion and systemic treatment with androgen deprivation therapy and enzalutamide. Due to dizziness and sweating, enzalutamide dosage was reduced from 160 to 80 mg/day with maintained therapeutic response. At approximately 15 months of follow-up, the patient remained neurologically stable with durable local disease control on cranial MRI, marked biochemical response (PSA decline from 177 to 0.6 ng/mL), and no evidence of systemic progression. This case highlights the importance of considering metastatic prostate cancer in the differential diagnosis of dural-based intracranial lesions in elderly men and demonstrates that individualized multimodal treatment can achieve durable disease control even in rare metastatic presentations.

title: Epithelioid Angiosarcoma Masquerading as Multiple Myeloma: A Diagnostic Pitfall.
authorString: Fahy J, Dhar G, Kandakumar L, Kitaoka S, Phyu EE.
abstractText: Multifocal osteolytic lesions in an older adult, particularly in the presence of hypercalcaemia and a monoclonal paraprotein, raise strong suspicion of multiple myeloma. However, coexisting pathological processes may produce a convincing but misleading clinical picture. We describe a case involving a man in his 80s who presented with back pain, hypercalcaemia and multifocal lytic vertebral lesions, together with an elevated kappa/lambda free light-chain ratio and a monoclonal serum band. Multiple myeloma was initially considered the leading diagnosis. Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy, however, demonstrated only a low-volume kappa-restricted plasma-cell neoplasm, with approximately 3%-4% plasma cells. Further examination identified small foci of cytokeratin-positive cohesive cells, initially raising concern for metastatic carcinoma. The discrepancy between the extensive radiological disease burden and limited plasma-cell findings prompted targeted biopsy of an L3 lytic lesion. This demonstrated a separate population of atypical epithelioid cells expressing pancytokeratin (AE1/3), ERG and CD31, which supported vascular differentiation despite aberrant cytokeratin expression. Following a multidisciplinary review of the clinical, radiological and histopathological findings, a likely diagnosis of epithelioid angiosarcoma was made. A low-volume kappa-restricted plasma-cell neoplasm was again identified in the background. The patient's condition deteriorated rapidly, and he died before the final diagnosis was confirmed. This case demonstrates how epithelioid angiosarcoma can masquerade as multiple myeloma, particularly when a coexisting plasma-cell neoplasm provides a plausible but incomplete explanation for extensive lytic bone disease. Discordance between radiological disease burden and pathological findings should prompt reconsideration of the working diagnosis and timely targeted biopsy of radiologically abnormal tissue.

title: Intramyocardial Granulomatous Histoplasmosis Presenting as Narrow-Complex Ventricular Tachycardia.
authorString: Goyal S, Li S, Keefe A, Mamillapalli H, Dykoski R, Haddadin F, Claymore B, Tholakanahalli VN.
abstractText:
Background

Cardiac histoplasmosis is rare, typically manifesting as pericarditis or endocarditis; tissue-proven intramyocardial granulomatous histoplasmosis has not been previously described.

Case summary

A 77-year-old man with immunosuppression presented with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and recurrent narrow-complex tachyarrhythmias attributed to supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Echocardiography showed a hyperechoic basal septal mass. Autopsy confirmed a 1.8 × 1.1 cm partially hyalinized necrotizing granuloma of the high interventricular septum containing Histoplasma on silver staining. Retrospective aVR algorithm analysis reclassified the arrhythmia as ventricular tachycardia (VT), anatomically concordant with the granuloma.

Discussion

Granulomatous histoplasmosis of the upper interventricular septum can produce high septal VT mimicking SVT, expanding the differential of granulomatous myocarditis in immunocompromised hosts.

Take-home messages

Histoplasmosis should be included in the differential of granulomatous myocarditis, particularly in immunocompromised patients from endemic regions. Systematic use of the Vereckei aVR algorithm can prevent misclassification of relatively narrow-complex VT as SVT and guide management.

title: Idiopathic Middle Aortic Syndrome Causing Pediatric Resistant Hypertension: Beyond Coarctation.
authorString: Arain M, Amanullah M.
abstractText:
Background

Middle aortic syndrome (MAS) is a rare cause of severe hypertension in children, characterized by segmental narrowing of the distal thoracic and abdominal aorta. Early recognition is essential to prevent irreversible end-organ damage.

Case summary

A 12-year-old girl presented with resistant hypertension, headache, facial edema, blurred vision, and postprandial abdominal pain. Marked upper-to-lower limb blood pressure discrepancy, with absent femoral pulses. Computed tomography angiography demonstrated long-segment thoracoabdominal aortic narrowing extending to the iliac arteries, consistent with MAS. Because of unfavorable anatomy for endovascular treatment. Thoracoabdominal extra-anatomic aorto-aortic bypass with polytetrafluoroethylene graft was successfully performed.

Discussion

This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of idiopathic MAS and demonstrates that individualized management based on vascular anatomy can achieve excellent outcomes.

Take-home messages

Cross-sectional vascular imaging should be considered in children with resistant hypertension and diminished femoral pulses. Open aorto-aortic bypass remains effective when endovascular treatment is unsuitable.

title: Diagnostic challenge in distinguishing intestinal endometriosis-associated carcinoma from primary colorectal adenocarcinoma: a case report.
authorString: Tojo N, Kataoka H, Izumi Y, Tarumi Y, Mori T.
abstractText: Malignant transformation of intestinal endometriosis is rare and may closely mimic primary colorectal adenocarcinoma. A 43-year-old woman with a history of ovarian endometriosis presented with melena and a rectosigmoid tumor with uterine invasion and multiple lymph node metastases. Histopathological examination revealed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with intestinal endometriosis but no definitive transition between the endometriosis and the carcinoma, supporting an initial diagnosis of primary colorectal adenocarcinoma. Five years later, biopsy of a recurrent vaginal stump lesion showed an adenocarcinoma positive for estrogen receptor, paired box gene 8, and cytokeratin 7 and negative for cytokeratin 20 and caudal-type homeobox transcription factor 2. Retrospective immunohistochemical evaluation of the original tumor demonstrated a similar phenotype, supporting a Müllerian origin and malignant transformation of intestinal endometriosis. This case illustrates the difficulty of determining tumor origin based on morphology alone and highlights the diagnostic value of immunohistochemistry.

title: Photon-counting computed tomography in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: correlation of iodine concentration with histopathological and clinical parameters.
authorString: Saeed S, Helbing J, Niehoff J, Haag NP, Katz M, Muecke R, Saehn MJ, Elhabash S, Lang SA, Moenninghoff C, Kroeger JR, Borggrefe J, Surov A, Woeltjen MM.
abstractText:
Objectives

Photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) enables quantitative assessment of tissue iodine distribution. This exploratory study investigated associations between PCCT-derived iodine parameters and clinical, serologic, and histopathologic characteristics of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).

Materials and methods

This retrospective single-center study included 27 patients with histologically confirmed PDAC who underwent pretreatment contrast-enhanced PCCT. Iodine concentration was measured independently by two blinded readers in arterial and portal-venous phases using a whole-tumor ROI on the largest axial section and a solid-component ROI. Absolute iodine concentration, tumor-to-aorta normalized iodine ratios, and phase-to-phase Δ iodine were evaluated. CA 19 - 9 was analyzed continuously using Spearman rank correlation; cutoff-based and clinicopathologic subgroup comparisons were considered secondary exploratory analyses and were re-analyzed using two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. All p-values are nominal.

Results

CA 19 - 9 was available in 24 patients (median 123.5 U/mL; IQR 55.3-1962). Higher CA 19 - 9 was associated with lower portal-venous absolute iodine concentration in the solid tumor component (Spearman ρ=-0.45, 95% CI -0.77 to -0.04; nominal p = 0.028) and with the arterial whole-tumor normalized iodine ratio (ρ=-0.58, 95% CI -0.84 to -0.14; nominal p = 0.010). At the 100 U/mL cutoff, portal-venous solid-component absolute iodine concentration was higher below the cutoff (1.77 ± 0.57 vs. 1.19 ± 0.50 mg/mL; nominal p = 0.017). After two-sided re-analysis, previously reported differences by T category, Ki-67, and tumor-cell count did not reach nominal significance. Interreader reliability was excellent across iodine parameters (ICC range 0.960-0.989).

Conclusion

In this small exploratory cohort, selected absolute and normalized iodine measurements showed nominal inverse associations with CA 19 - 9, whereas associations with tumor stage and histopathologic parameters were not consistent after conservative two-sided re-analysis. PCCT iodine measurements were highly reproducible between readers. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger independent cohorts before any incremental clinical value can be inferred.

title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging Morphometric Analysis of the Lumbar Spine and Its Vascular and Muscular Relations: Anatomical Variability and Surgical Planning.
authorString: Alvim F, Pinho AR, Pereira PA, Silva MR.
abstractText:
Background

Lumbar region anatomical variability significantly affects the safety of minimally invasive spine (MIS) approaches, yet quantitative patient-specific data remain limited.

Objective

The primary goal was to characterize vascular, muscular, and skeletal variability in Portuguese patients with lumbar disc disease and assess implications for MIS surgical corridors. A secondary objective was to explore associations between muscle area and disability.

Study design

Cross-sectional observational study.

Methods

Lumbar magnetic resonance images from 46 adults were analyzed for vertebral and disc morphometry (L1-S1), psoas and intrinsic back muscles area (at the level of L4-L5 intervertebral disc), psoas-intervertebral disc overlap, psoas-vessel distances (abdominal aorta or the left common iliac artery), and iliac vessel spacing at L5 to S1 (distance between the left common iliac vein and the right common iliac artery). Sex and age were analyzed as comparative and correlational variables.

Results

Men showed significantly larger muscle areas (P < 0.001). The ante-psoas corridor narrowed caudally, with L4 to L5 being the most unfavorable level for oblique lateral interbody fusion (32.6% negative overlap). Psoas-vessel distances decreased from L1 to L5 and correlated positively with age. The aortic bifurcation was most frequently located at mid-L4 (50%).

Conclusion

Marked anatomical variability influences MIS feasibility, particularly at the L4 to L5 level. Individualized preoperative imaging assessment is essential to ensure safe surgical planning and technique selection.

Clinical relevance

Preoperative MRI assessment of patient-specific lumbar vascular and muscular anatomy may help identify anatomical constraints relevant to minimally invasive lumbar fusion and support individualized surgical approach selection, particularly at the L4-L5 level.

Level of evidence: 3

title: Workflow-friendly free-breathing whole-chest cardiovascular MRI using inner-volume balanced T1 relaxation-enhanced steady-state.
authorString: Edelman RR, Pursnani A, Planek MI, Iyer SK, Leloudas N, Clarke D, Koktzoglou I.

journal.title: Journal of cardiovascular magnetic resonance : official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance

abstractText:
Background

Free-breathing cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) may provide useful volumetric information. This study evaluated acquisition time and the feasibility of incorporating highly accelerated free-breathing inner-volume balanced T1 relaxation-enhanced steady-state (bT1RESS) imaging into a standard CMR protocol during the post-contrast interval before late gadolinium enhancement (LGE).

Methods

A prototype ECG-gated, navigator-gated inner-volume bT1RESS sequence was added to 1.5T CMR examinations in 45 patients; 30 were included in the paired comparison with breath-hold bT1RESS. Series-start timing was assessed in 14 of the 45 patients. Three readers assessed image quality. Aortic diameters were compared between bT1RESS protocols and, in an additional cohort of 15 subjects, with CEMRA. Agreement was assessed separately at five aortic levels using Bland-Altman analysis.

Results

Median inner-volume bT1RESS acquisition time was 1.82minutes (range, 0.78-3.72). In the series-start timing subset, median intervals from perfusion/CEMRA start to TI scout and first LGE series were 6.49minutes (n=13) and 8.46minutes (n=14), respectively. Reader preferences favored the inner-volume over breath-hold bT1RESS protocol. In the CEMRA comparison, mean differences (inner-volume bT1RESS minus CEMRA) ranged from 0.00 to 0.93mm; the lower and upper 95% limits of agreement ranged from -2.47 to -1.16mm and from 2.06 to 3.02mm, respectively.

Conclusion

Inner-volume bT1RESS provided rapid volumetric cardiovascular imaging within the evaluated post-contrast workflow. A primary benefit is the capability for 3D vessel measurement without a separate first-pass CEMRA acquisition. The technique may also help identify coronary artery origins, characterize morphological abnormalities in congenital heart disease and other cardiovascular disorders, and help to detect and characterize extracardiac lesions. Larger studies are needed to establish reproducibility and diagnostic performance.

title: Morphometric Characterization and Anatomical Variations of Coronary Ostia in Human Hearts: Implications for Coronary and Aortic Interventions
authorString: Kumar A.
abstractText: Background Coronary ostial morphology and position show considerable anatomical variation and are clinically relevant during coronary angiography, catheter-based interventions, aortic valve procedures, and aortic root surgery. Objective To evaluate the morphometric characteristics and anatomical position of the right and left coronary ostia and their clinical significance. Methods Sixty embalmed human heart specimens preserved in 10% formalin were examined. The number, shape, dimensions, and position of the coronary ostia were documented relative to the upper margin of the corresponding aortic cusps, sinotubular junction, and aortic valve commissures. Ostial and cusp dimensions were measured using a digital Vernier caliper. Results The mean diameter of the right coronary ostium was 4.78 mm (range, 2.7–8.8 mm), compared with 5.02 mm (range, 3.1–10.6 mm) for the left. Mean ostial height from the aortic root was 13.70 mm on the right and 14.17 mm on the left. Most right coronary ostia (86.7%) were located above the upper cusp margin, whereas 90% of left coronary ostia were at cusp level. Most ostia were below the sinotubular junction (right, 81.7%; left, 85%). Right coronary ostia were predominantly near Commissure I (58.3%), while left ostia were mainly central (56.7%) or near Commissure II (31.7%). Conclusion Coronary ostia demonstrate distinct side-specific variations in diameter, height, and spatial position. These morphometric findings provide useful anatomical reference data for coronary catheterization, aortic root surgery, coronary revascularization, and transcatheter aortic valve procedures.

title: Structure-specific variation in pediatric echocardiographic Z scores across the nutritional spectrum: four body-surface-area nomograms and a BMI-adjusted GAMLSS model
authorString: Amstein R, Metcalfe V, Trincado C, Passi-Solar Á, Larios G.
abstractText: Purpose Z score nomograms, the standard for interpreting pediatric echocardiographic dimensions, derive mostly from eutrophic populations. We assessed whether cardiac structure Z scores vary with body mass index Z score (BMIz) across four body-surface-area (BSA)-based nomograms, and whether a BMI-adjusted reference mitigates this bias. Methods Retrospective study of 1883 children aged 5–18 years with structurally normal echocardiograms (2016–2021). Eleven cardiac structure diameters were analyzed and Z scores computed with four nomograms (Pediatric Heart Network, Detroit, Toronto, Italy) and, for ten structures, with a fifth based on generalized additive models for location, scale and shape (GAMLSS) adjusted for body size, BMI and age. Associations with BMIz used linear regression in three nested models with false discovery rate correction. Results Overall, 25.8% were overweight and 15.8% had obesity. Absolute diameters increased with BMIz in every structure (p < 0.001), yet Z scores of most left-sided structures were inversely associated with it, most strongly for the four aortic levels (β − 0.325 to − 0.182, significant in all 45 nomogram-by-model comparisons) and for left ventricular end-diastolic diameter. Ventricular walls showed no consistent pattern; right-sided annuli varied non-monotonically. Under GAMLSS these associations were abolished in the most affected structures, persisted in the sinotubular junction and walls, and reversed in sign in the pulmonary annulus. Conclusion Z scores of most left-sided structures were lower in obesity than their absolute dimensions suggest, so interpretation must account for nutritional status and the reference. Persisting bias follows model construction: the three structures whose GAMLSS equations omit BMI are exactly those still biased.

title: Treadmill prehabilitation attenuates jejunal inflammation and enhances cytoprotective protein expression in murine gut ischemia-reperfusion.
authorString: Higashizono K, Takahashi K, Fukatsu K, Narita T, Takayama H, Noguchi M, Murakoshi S, Seto Y.
abstractText:
Introduction

Whether preoperative exercise protects the intestine itself is unclear. We hypothesized that treadmill prehabilitation acts on the intestine as ischemic preconditioning, and examined intestinal injury and cytokine responses after gut ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) and jejunal cytoprotective protein expression before ischemia.

Methods

Two experiments were conducted in male C57BL/6J mice. In Experiment 1, mice were randomly allocated to a sedentary or an exercise group; exercised mice completed 1 week of acclimation and 3 weeks of treadmill running. One day after the final session, the superior mesenteric artery was occluded for 45 min. Jejunal and ileal cytokines were measured in 24 mice, and mucosal injury was graded by the Chiu classification in 22 mice, at 3 or 6 h after reperfusion. In Experiment 2, separate cohorts completed 0 (SED, n = 5), 1 (EX1, n = 5), 2 (EX2, n = 4) or 3 (EX3, n = 5) weeks of running, and jejunal HSP70, Bcl-2 and p62 were quantified by western blotting without I/R.

Results

Injury scores were lower in exercised mice (jejunum at 3 h, 1.10 ± 0.22 vs 2.60 ± 0.50; main effect of exercise, P = 0.0025 [jejunum] and P < 0.0001 [ileum]). Jejunal IL-12 at 3 h (adjusted P = 0.042) and IL-6 at 6 h (adjusted P = 0.015) were lower in exercised mice, whereas in the ileum a main effect of exercise was found for IL-12 (P = 0.037) without adjusted between-group differences. HSP70/β-actin was higher in EX1-EX3, and p62/β-actin lower in EX2-EX3, than in SED (Bonferroni-corrected threshold, P < 0.017). Training duration was associated positively with HSP70/β-actin (R² = 0.55, P = 0.0003) and Bcl-2/β-actin (R² = 0.31, P = 0.014) and negatively with p62/β-actin (R² = 0.31, P = 0.014); group comparisons for Bcl-2 were not significant.

Conclusion

Treadmill prehabilitation was accompanied by less mucosal injury and a smaller early jejunal inflammatory response after gut I/R, and the jejunum before ischemia differed in cytoprotective and autophagy-related protein expression according to training duration, consistent with ischemic preconditioning of the intestine.

title: Genetic dissection of cell type-specific congenital heart disease variants reveals ETS1 control of vascular smooth muscle cell fate.
authorString: Li X, Fu M, Jia S, Wu Z, Pang L, Xiong K, Wang Y, Li W, He A, Ai S.
abstractText: Numerous congenital heart disease (CHD) risk variants lie in cis-regulatory elements, yet the impact of variants in repressed and bivalent chromatin on cell type-specific heart development is unclear. Here, we generated a single-cell multiomic atlas of human cardiac differentiation by jointly profiling H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and transcriptomes in individual cells, classifying cis-regulatory elements into six chromatin states, enabling prioritization of 610 CHD-associated noncoding variants enriched in lineage- and state-specific regulatory elements, including repressive and bivalent regions. CRISPR knockin of selected variants perturbed nearby gene expression and impaired cardiac differentiation. Dissection of a Polycomb-marked variant near ETS1 (ETS proto-oncogene 1) revealed local H3K27me3 loss, H3K27ac gain, and ETS1 up-regulation, which redirects differentiation toward second-heart-field progenitors with epithelial characteristics at early stages and, ultimately, highly migratory ETS1+ vascular smooth muscle cells. Together, our work establishes a single-cell chromatin-state framework for interpreting noncoding CHD risk variants and uncovers an ETS1-driven program linking Polycomb-deregulated noncoding variation to aberrant vascular smooth muscle fate commitment during human cardiogenesis.

title: Severe hypoxemia caused by right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale associated with right coronary artery malperfusion secondary to acute aortic dissection: a case report.
authorString: Takao N, Mori S, Takehana K, Takazawa T.
abstractText:
Background

Right coronary artery malperfusion associated with acute type A aortic dissection can cause right ventricular failure. However, hypoxemia due to a right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale secondary to elevated right-sided cardiac pressure has rarely been described in this setting.

Case presentation

An 80-year-old woman with acute type A aortic dissection presented with hypoxemia unexplained by pulmonary disease. Transesophageal echocardiography suggested that right ventricular dysfunction associated with right coronary artery malperfusion had contributed to right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale. Following ascending aortic replacement, she developed hypoxemia after separation from cardiopulmonary bypass. Transesophageal echocardiography showed persistent right ventricular dysfunction and worsening of the shunt. Intraoperative optimization of cardiovascular medications improved hemodynamics, reduced the shunt, and improved oxygenation.

Conclusions

This case suggests that intracardiac right-to-left shunting should be considered in patients with acute aortic dissection and unexplained hypoxemia, and that transesophageal echocardiography may guide perioperative management.

title: Multisite Peripheral Photoplethysmography Captures Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump Counterpulsation and Weaning State in Cardiogenic Shock.
authorString: Nakada K, Burton T, Sadrzadeh-Afsharazar F, Chiba H, Douplik A, Matsuyama T, Saiko G.
abstractText:
Background

Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) counterpulsation raises aortic diastolic pressure every cycle (1:1) or alternate cycles (1:2, weaning). Whether they reach peripheral photoplethysmography (PPG) is unknown; 1 report described 1:1 only.

Case summary

An 82-year-old man in IABP-supported cardiogenic shock had finger and thenar PPG on 1:1, 1:2, removal, and twice afterward. An augmented diastolic peak appeared on every finger beat on 1:1 and alternate beats on 1:2, barring ectopy, and none afterward. Perfusion index reached a nadir at removal and rose through recovery; finger-thenar coherence followed a similar trend.

Discussion

Peripheral PPG encoded assist ratio and weaning state. The augmented peak was proportionally larger at the finger than in the aorta, raising the hypothesis that it reflects root- and arch-supplied territories.

Take-home message

Ordinary peripheral PPG carries a beat-resolved signature of IABP counterpulsation and of the weaning course, without vascular access.

title: Urinary complications following Bricker urinary diversion in gynecologic cancer: A retrospective analysis of 77 cases.
authorString: Jaafar E, El Hajj H, Maulard A, Mal PA, Scherier S, Dabreteau T, Do K, Zaccarini F, Parier B, Espenel S, Leary A, Pautier P, Genestie C, Morice P, Gouy S.
abstractText:
Introduction

To evaluate postoperative urinary complications and their management in patients undergoing Bricker urinary diversion for gynecologic cancers, with a focus on identifying risk factors, especially uretero-ileal strictures.

Material and methods

We conducted a retrospective single-center study of 77 patients who underwent Bricker urinary diversion for gynecologic cancers between 2000 and 2020. All surgeries were performed by the same gynecologic oncologic team.

Results

Primary tumor sites included the cervix and uterine body in 87% of patients, with others involving the vagina, vulva, and adnexa. Preoperative pelvic radiotherapy was performed in 71%, and para-aortic/pelvic radiotherapy in 10%. Over a median follow-up of 21 months, uretero-ileal strictures occurred in 30%, and fistulas in 6%. Preoperative nephrostomy was significantly associated with a higher rate of strictures (p = 0.001), while preoperative ureteral stenting was associated with a reduced risk (p = 0.005). All patients with strictures or fistulas were initially managed with ureteral stenting; nephrostomy was subsequently required in 56% of stricture and 80% of fistula cases. Surgical treatment was eventually needed in 17% and 60%, respectively. Additional risk factors for strictures included preoperative chemotherapy (p = 0.023) and intraoperative evidence of chronic enteritis (p = 0.013). No significant differences were observed in overall or recurrence-free survival between patients with and without strictures (p > 0.05).

Conclusions

Uretero-ileal strictures occurred in 30% and fistulas in 6% of patients undergoing Bricker urinary diversion. Preoperative ureteral stenting may help reduce stricture risk, and appropriate bowel segment selection is essential to minimize complications.

title: From a Team of Experts to an Expert Team in Congenital Cardiology: Making Distributed Expertise Usable.
authorString: McMahon CJ, Kim J, Lewin M, Penny D, Taylor MD, Rossano J.
abstractText: Congenital heart disease care depends on specialised expertise distributed across clinicians, disciplines, patients and families. But bringing knowledgeable individuals together does not guarantee that their distinct contributions shape a decision. In complex congenital heart disease, multidisciplinary deliberation must reconcile anatomy, physiology, procedural feasibility, longitudinal risk and patient priorities, often amid uncertainty. We distinguish a team's possession of expertise from its collective capability to make that expertise usable. This distinction affirms, rather than questions, individual clinical judgement, professional responsibility and shared accountability for patients. We propose a testable conceptual framework in which relevant expertise becomes accessible, is expressed and understood, receives appropriate weight, and can revise the team's understanding or decision. Congenital cardiology examples include choices between catheter-based and surgical intervention, anticipation of intensive-care needs, and consideration of treatment burden and family goals. Constructive disagreement may reveal overlooked information or competing interpretations, while patients and families contribute essential knowledge about daily life and acceptable trade-offs. Existing team-science research supports the framework's rationale, but its ability to improve congenital heart outcomes has not been demonstrated. We outline a developmental cycle-map, observe, practise, review, adapt and re-map-through which programmes might examine how expertise enters decisions, identify missed contributions and learn across changing membership. Evaluation should combine prospective measures of decision quality and implementation with appropriately risk-adjusted clinical outcomes, patient and family experience, and longer-term trajectories. The objective is not consensus for its own sake, but better use of knowledge already available to care teams.

title: Association Between Prenatal Risk Stratification and Access to Care for Neonatal d-Transposition of the Great Arteries.
authorString: Suh Ro S, Nam J, Jergel A, Chanani NK, Wolf M, Clarke S, Michelfelder E.
abstractText: To evaluate how prenatal risk stratification impacts transfer times to the cardiac unit for newborns with d-transposition of the great arteries (d-TGA) in a high-volume, free-standing children's center. This is a retrospective study examining all prenatally diagnosed d-TGA newborns at a single center without in-house delivery capacity from 1/1/2013 to 3/1/2026. We evaluated two time periods based on implementation of level of care (LOC) assignments at our center (2013-2018 versus 2018-2026). The primary outcome was time from birth to arrival in the cardiac intensive care unit (CICU). Univariable and multivariable models were performed to include fetal echocardiographic and clinical covariates. Of 106 d-TGA newborns, 52 (49%) had a BAS within 24 h of arrival to the CICU, of which 24 (23%) required an emergent BAS within 2 h of CICU arrival. The multivariable model demonstrates that LOC implementation led to shorter median times from birth to CICU after adjusting for fetal echocardiographic markers and clinical covariates such as birthweight, gestational age and PaO2 on initial arterial blood gas (-180.7 min, 95% CI -351.9 to -9.5, p = 0.039). Risk stratification by LOC assignment is critical in access to life-saving care and shortening transport times for prenatally diagnosed d-TGA newborns, especially for free-standing children's hospitals.

title: The experiences of siblings in the congenital heart journey: a qualitative study.
authorString: Modi H, Van Diest H, Morris M, Geis A, Ilangovan S, Barnhill B, Well A, Affolter J, Ulack C, Colucci J, Carberry K, Mery CM, Fraser CD.
abstractText:
Introduction

Despite growing interest in the quality of life of individuals with single-ventricle CHD, the experiences of their siblings remain largely underexamined and heavily reliant on parent-reported outcomes. This study explores the experiences of siblings of individuals with single-ventricle CHD through a qualitative analysis of self-reported narratives.

Methods

Siblings of individuals with single-ventricle CHD aged 9 years and older participated in age-based Experience Group sessions. Trained facilitators used semi-structured, open-ended questions to prompt discussion. Qualitative data were coded using inductive thematic analysis to identify salient themes across narratives.

Results

Eighteen siblings participated. Participants (50%, n = 9 female) ranged in age from 9 to 59 years (median age 22 years); most (72%, n = 13) were older than their sibling with single-ventricle CHD. Five themes emerged: 1) adapting to their sibling's physical limitations, 2) assuming supportive roles in the family, 3) navigating complex and often conflicting emotions, 4) deepening their understanding of the condition over time, and 5) finding normalcy throughout their childhood.

Conclusions

This study provides valuable insights into the nuanced experiences of siblings of individuals with single-ventricle CHD, underscoring the key roles they play in the care journey and describing the unique experiences that have shaped them. These findings can inform tailored, family-centred care models that intentionally include siblings in psychosocial assessment, support interventions, and age-appropriate medically related education and communication.

title: Characteristics and Mechanisms of Septal Myocardial Injury and Repair Following Left Bundle Branch Area Pacing.
authorString: Fu B, Jiang Y, Jin H, Li H, Huang H, Cheng S, Weng S, Yang J, Li Z, Chen G, Ning X, Wang H, Gu M, Niu H, Hu Y, Vernooy K, Prinzen FW, Hua W.
abstractText:
Background

Left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP) requires screwing the lead deep into the interventricular septum. Multiple attempts are often required to achieve proper capture of the conduction system.

Objective

This study aimed to evaluate the impact of deep screwing attempts on septal myocardial injury and repair and to explore the underlying mechanisms.

Methods

Prospective LBBAP implantation was performed in 41 patients with bradycardia. Serum creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB) and left ventricular (LV) global longitudinal strain (GLS) were used to evaluate myocardial damage. Mechanisms of septal damage were explored in 24 LBBAP canines using histopathological and molecular changes.

Results

Compared to patients with ≤ 3 attempts, those with >3 attempts had a higher incidence of CK-MB elevation (6 vs. 44%, P=0.004), a less negative LV endocardial (-17.9 vs. -13.6 %, P<0.001), and mid-myocardial GLS (-15.3 vs. -12.4 %, P<0.001). In animal study, molecular changes associated with >3 attempts featured amplified HMGB1-centered sterile inflammation and enhanced CD206+ macrophage-mediated profibrotic remodeling. Canines with >3 attempts were characterized by three markedly thickened concentric reparative layers around the lead-inner thrombus layer, middle fibrous sheath layer, and outer reactive fibrotic layer. Interestingly, removal of the pacing lead after >3 attempts resulted in only mild scattered fibrosis, with markedly attenuated CD206+ macrophage-mediated profibrotic pathway.

Conclusions

LBBAP with >3 deep septal screwing attempts was associated with a higher risk of septal myocardial injury and markedly thickened concentric reparative layers, underpinned by more pronounced sterile inflammation, profibrotic remodeling, and foreign body reaction.

title: Local Conformal Auditing Exposes and Restores Reliability of AI-ECG Atrial Fibrillation Detection Under External Deployment Shift.
authorString: Abbasi T, Abbas A, Mehmood UH.
abstractText:
Background

AI-enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) can detect atrial fibrillation (AF), but safe deployment depends on calibration, subgroup reliability, and explicit error guarantees, not on discrimination alone.

Objective

To test whether the conformal-prediction coverage guarantee of an AF ECG classifier survives external deployment shift, and whether a small local labeled audit restores it without retraining.

Methods

A four-class 12-lead rhythm classifier trained on PTB-XL (Germany; 7,831 ECGs, 7,164 patients) was evaluated unchanged on Chinese (Chapman-Shaoxing; n=2,289) and US (Georgia; n=1,990) cohorts. We measured discrimination, expected calibration error (ECE), 90%-target split-conformal coverage, subgroup coverage, label-free shift corrections, local recalibration across audit sizes, and an AF auto-clear policy with finite-sample risk control.

Results

AF AUC remained 0.998 (95% CI 0.997-0.999) in China but fell to 0.936 (0.919-0.952) in the US cohort. ECE rose from 0.051 to 0.197 and 0.237, and source-calibrated coverage fell from 0.901 to 0.758 and 0.722 (both P<0.001). Coverage was lower in Chinese men than women (0.707 vs 0.822; difference 0.115, 95% CI 0.081-0.148). Label-free corrections failed. Local recalibration restored mean coverage to 0.90 with 50 labeled ECGs but with wide variability (95% simulation interval 0.82-0.97), narrowing to 0.86-0.94 at 200 ECGs. Local AF risk control certified auto-clearing of 68% of held-out ECGs in China but abstained in the US cohort.

Conclusion

AI-ECG uncertainty can fail silently despite high AUC. A local conformal audit detects when uncertainty estimates are untrustworthy and recalibrates the uncertainty layer without changing the classifier, converting trust into a measurable, subgroup-aware, task-specific guarantee.

title: Intraprocedural evaluation of residual mitral and tricuspid regurgitation after transcatheter edge-to-edge repair.
authorString: Pasquini A, Cammalleri V, Pica A, Filice M, Tavernese A, Stefanini A, Di Lisi D, Ilardi F, Lisi M, Malagoli A, Mandoli GE, Margonato D, Salerno G, Pastore MC, Sperlongano S, Badano LP, Agricola E, D'Andrea A, Cameli M, Benfari G, SIC (Italian Society of Cardiology) Echocardiography Study Group.
abstractText:
Aims

Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) has emerged as an established therapeutic option for selected patients with severe mitral (MR) and tricuspid regurgitation (TR), supported by expanding clinical evidence. However, intraprocedural assessment of residual regurgitation remains challenging because of dynamic hemodynamic changes, device-related artefacts, and limitations of conventional echocardiographic parameters.

Methods and results

This review summarizes current evidence on multiparametric echocardiographic and hemodynamic assessment during mitral (M-TEER) and tricuspid (T-TEER) procedures, with a focus on the evaluation of residual regurgitation, the immediate physiological response, markers of cardiac remodeling and their prognostic implications. Accurate quantification of residual MR and TR requires an integrated multiparametric approach. Residual regurgitation is associated with clinical outcomes and reverse remodeling. Conventional two-dimensional measures are limited by altered post-procedural jet geometry and multiple residual jets. Three-dimensional vena contracta area provides improved visualization and quantification of residual regurgitation, enabling summation of multiple jets. However, its quantitative accuracy has been validated only to a limited extent and thresholds after TEER are not standardized. Volumetric quantification is independent of jet geometry but remains insufficiently validated intraprocedurally. Atrial pressures, venous flow and forward flow describe the physiological response rather than regurgitant severity.

Conclusion

Intraprocedural evaluation of residual MR and TR after TEER requires expert integration of multiple echocardiographic measures of regurgitation with complementary assessment of its physiological consequences and hemodynamic parameters. Advanced 3D imaging plays an increasingly central role in improving procedural assessment and post-interventional risk stratification, but standardized and validated criteria for quantifying residual regurgitation after TEER are still lacking.
