Medicinal Cyathula roots possess anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and metabolic regulatory activities; however, their molecular mechanisms against DN remain poorly understood.

Objective

In this study, a network pharmacology strategy, combined with molecular docking, was employed to elucidate the pharmacological basis underlying the medicinal properties of Cyathula roots in DN treatment.

Methods

An integrative computer-aided strategy combining network pharmacology, protein- protein interaction (PPI) analysis, Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses, and molecular docking was employed to elucidate the therapeutic mechanisms of medicinal Cyathula roots in DN.

Results

A total of 41 phytochemical constituents were initially retrieved, of which 10 bioactive compounds satisfied the pharmacokinetic screening criteria (oral bioavailability ≥30% and druglikeness ≥0.18). Network topology analysis highlighted PPARG, TNF, MMP9, AGTR1, REN, and other hub genes as key regulators of inflammatory responses, insulin resistance, lipid metabolism, and renin-angiotensin signaling.

Discussion

Cyasterone and precyasterone exhibited the highest network connectivity, suggesting that they may represent the principal bioactive constituents responsible for the multitarget therapeutic effects of medicinal Cyathula roots. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses further indicated significant involvement in pathways associated with insulin resistance, adipocytokine signaling, diabetic cardiomyopathy, and the renin-angiotensin system.

Conclusion

Collectively, these findings provide a systems-level understanding of the multitarget mechanisms of medicinal Cyathula roots against DN and offer a computational framework for future experimental validation and natural product-based drug discovery.

title: Modified Dioscorea pills ameliorate cognitive impairment induced by chronic cerebral hypoperfusion via restoring the hippocampal neurovascular unit.
authorString: Xu Q, He D, Li H.
abstractText:
Objective

Chronic cerebral hypoperfusion (CCH) is a major cause of progressive cognitive decline and vascular dementia in older adults. Modified Dioscorea Pills (MDP), a traditional Chinese medicinal formula, has demonstrated clinical efficacy for dementia treatment. However, the effects and molecular mechanisms of MDP on the hippocampal neurovascular unit (NVU) in CCH remain unclear. This study aimed to explore whether MDP alleviates CCH-induced cognitive impairment by protecting and restoring the hippocampal NVU in rats.

Methods

A rat CCH model was established via bilateral common carotid artery occlusion (BCCAO). Forty SPF-grade male Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly divided into Sham, CCH model and MDP treatment groups. Rats received intragastric administration of normal saline or MDP concentrated decoction for 45 consecutive days. The Morris Water Maze test was used to assess learning and memory functions. Immunohistochemistry was applied to detect the expression of apoptosis-, inflammation-, neuron-, synapse-, glia-, myelin- and endothelial-related proteins, as well as microvessel density (MVD). Western blot was used to quantify Ang-1, Ang-2, Tie2 and VEGF levels. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed to observe neuronal and synaptic ultrastructure. Pearson correlation analysis was used to evaluate the correlations among NVU-related indicators.

Results

MDP significantly improved learning and memory deficits in CCH rats. MDP downregulated NF-κB p65 expression and the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, consistent with the attenuation of neuroinflammation and apoptosis-associated signaling, inhibited excessive gliosis, and upregulated neuronal, synaptic and myelin-related protein levels. MDP further activated the Ang/Tie2/VEGF pathway and reduced the abnormally elevated CD34 expression and microvessel density (MVD), indicating that MDP promoted vascular stabilization and remodeling of the excessive immature microvasculature rather than further pathological angiogenesis. TEM confirmed that MDP relieved neuronal nuclear damage and synaptic destruction. Correlation analysis revealed statistically significant associations among multiple components of the hippocampal NVU, whereas inflammation-related markers were negatively associated with NVU integrity.

Conclusions

MDP ameliorates CCH-induced cognitive impairment by comprehensively restoring the structure and function of the hippocampal NVU. The mechanisms involve attenuation of neuroinflammation and apoptosis-associated signaling, protection of neurons and synapses, inhibition of pathological gliosis, restoration of oligodendrocyte-lineage integrity, and stabilization and remodeling of the hippocampal microvasculature. This work provides preclinical evidence for the clinical application of MDP in CCH and vascular dementia.

title: Understanding and translating evolutionary adaptations in animals exposed to contaminated diets to guide strategies against human foodborne disease: a prioritisation framework.
authorString: Abaidullah M, Ji Y, Huang Q, Scarpa M, Li J, Xiao X, Xu D.
abstractText:
Background

Humans face increasing vulnerability to foodborne and infectious diseases despite medical advances, while certain animal lineages cope with pathogen-laden diets and environments under the particular ecological pressures that selected their defences. Animals are not universally resistant, and wildlife and livestock outbreaks of Salmonella, Campylobacter, Vibrio and mycotoxins are documented; but certain lineages have evolved tolerance or rapid-clearance mechanisms with minimal pathology. This disparity arises from evolutionary adaptations in animals, contrasting with human reliance on hygiene and antibiotics, which contribute to antimicrobial resistance and zoonotic spillovers, while modern sanitation has also delivered dramatic reductions in waterborne disease mortality.

Aim of review

This review aims to synthesize evidence on animal disease resistance mechanisms and translate these insights into clinical strategies for improving human health, addressing gaps in comparative biology and combating emerging threats like antimicrobial resistance. We introduce the Biomimetic Immunity Continuum, a translational framework for comparative immunology built on an explicit selection rule that rejects candidate adaptations as well as ranking them; four are rejected here. It maps animal defence pillars (genetic, ecological, behavioural, physiological, microbiome) along a spectrum from prevention to molecular tuning to therapeutic replacement, prioritizing feasibility, reversibility, safety, and scalability. These criteria are applied as three exclusion gates and four ranked criteria, with candidates ordered on the limiting step rather than on a composite numerical score. We predict that, among adaptations acting on conserved or reachable human pathways, translational potential depends more on conservation, accessibility, safety and deliverability than on the size of the phenotype in the source animal. Throughout, we distinguish avoidance (reduction of exposure), resistance (reduction of pathogen or toxin burden), tolerance (reduction of health cost per unit burden) and resilience (the composite property emerging when these operate together), because these axes carry different translational and safety implications.

Key scientific concepts of review

Animals employ multifaceted defences: genetic (e.g., immune gene evolution), ecological (e.g., habitat avoidance), behavioural (e.g., grooming), physiological (e.g., vultures' hyperacidic stomachs neutralizing anthrax), immunological (e.g., epigenetic reprogramming), and microbial (e.g., microbiome-mediated exclusion). These synergize to prevent infections, as seen in bats tolerating high viral loads with minimal immunopathology. Candidate human applications differ widely in maturity: trained immunity via BCG and defined live biotherapeutic products are already in human use, dietary interventions mimicking animal microbiomes have reached controlled trials, and heat-shock induction has human data but no controlled trial against a foodborne endpoint. We separate mechanistic inspiration from candidate intervention throughout, and the evidence level attached to each proposal says which it is. Bridging evolutionary and clinical science offers candidate approaches to disease prevention. Every proposal is classified by translational maturity on a five-level scale from approved human use to source-species observation alone; this records maturity rather than certainty or demonstrated efficacy. Animal exemplars are included only where they meet stated relevance criteria for foodborne hazards as defined by the World Health Organization, which treats infectious and chemical hazards together.

title: Mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles in diabetes: immunomodulation and therapeutic prospects.
authorString: Ma L, Hou N, Zhang X, Zhao X, Liu Q, Zhang Y, Dong J, Li Z, Wang Q.
abstractText: Diabetes mellitus is characterized by chronic hyperglycemia, immune dysregulation, and progressive multi-organ injury. Mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles(MSC-EVs) have emerged as cell-free mediators capable of transferring bioactive cargo and modulating immune, metabolic, and regenerative responses. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the roles of MSC-EVs in diabetes, focusing on immune-cell regulation, pancreatic β-cell protection, metabolic homeostasis, and major complications, while also considering EV isolation, engineering, delivery, and clinical translation. Preclinical studies indicate that MSC-EVs can modulate T-cell, macrophage, dendritic-cell, B-cell, natural killer-cell, innate lymphoid-cell, and complement-associated responses; reduce inflammatory and oxidative injury; protect β cells from apoptosis; improve insulin signaling; and promote tissue repair in diabetic wounds, kidney disease, retinopathy, neuropathy, cardiovascular injury, bone metabolic disorders, and erectile dysfunction. These effects are mediated by preparation-specific cargo and signaling pathways, including miRNAs, proteins, programmed death-ligand 1(PD-L1)/PD-1 signaling, Phosphoinositide 3-kinase/Protein Kinase B(PI3K/Akt)-related pathways, and phosphatase and tensin homolog(PTEN)/AKT signaling. The review also distinguishes direct diabetes-specific evidence from mechanistic background derived from non-diabetic models. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous across MSC sources, EV preparations, experimental models, doses, and delivery strategies, and current clinical evidence is still limited. Registered investigations should therefore be distinguished from studies reporting clinical outcomes, and product-specific efficacy should not be inferred from trial registration alone. Overall, MSC-EVs represent a promising but not yet established therapeutic platform for diabetes. Future translation will require standardized terminology and characterization, scalable manufacturing, reproducible potency assessment, optimized targeting and dosing, long-term safety evaluation, and well-designed product-specific clinical trials.

title: Adverse effects of FDA-approved RNA therapeutics: a cross-platform analysis of RNA design, delivery systems, and safety profiles.
authorString: Stamatopoulou V, Kouvela A, Ahtypi K, Douka E, Kominatou C, Meimaroglou A, Spyropoulou K, Taxari S, Theodoridou S, Plotas P.
abstractText: RNA therapeutics have emerged as a promising and effective tool to treat a wide range of genetic, metabolic, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases by directly modulating the gene expression or directing transient protein production. Currently, more than 20 RNA-based drugs have been approved by the FDA, and due to their recent introduction into the clinical practice, long-term safety data remain limited and comparisons of adverse effects across platforms are lacking. This review focuses on the three major RNA therapeutic platforms, including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), small interfering RNA (siRNA) and messenger RNA (mRNA) and intends to provide a cross-platform analysis of their adverse effects. We searched studies published up to June 2026 in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar using terms related to RNA therapeutics, individual drug names, safety and toxicity outcomes. Clinical trials, extension studies, pharmacovigilance reports, regulatory documents, and prescribing information were considered for each FDA-approved ASO, siRNA and mRNA agent. The observed safety profiles are associated with an interaction between RNA modality and additional determinants, including chemical modification, delivery system, route of administration, biodistribution, target tissue, and clinical context. Innate immune activation represents a potential shared mechanism, whereas sequence-dependent off-target effects, delivery-associated reactions, administration-related complications, and organ-specific toxicities differ in relevance and mechanism among ASO, siRNA, and mRNA therapeutics. Although most reported adverse effects are mild to moderate, important research gaps regarding long-term safety, pediatric use and rare adverse effects still exist, underscoring the need for further optimization of RNA drug design and delivery technologies, as well as continued pharmacovigilance.

title: Novel techniques in the prophylaxis and treatment of type II endoleaks: a narrative review.
authorString: Pietrzak K, Koperski M, Gutowska K, Terlecki P.
abstractText:
Background

Type II endoleaks (T2ELs) are a frequent complication after endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR), posing a risk of aneurysm expansion. This review evaluates modern techniques for T2ELs management, moving beyond traditional embolization methods.

Methods

Recent controlled trials and observational studies were analyzed to trace evidence on conventional and novel techniques employed in managing T2ELs.

Results

Novel techniques, such as transcaval embolization (TCE) and laser-assisted transgraft embolization (LATE), have demonstrated encouraging early technical and clinical outcomes, although the available evidence remains limited. In addition, shape memory polymer (SMP) embolization resulted in significant sac shrinkage in >85% of patients and prevented clinically significant T2ELs.

Conclusions

TCE, LATE, and prophylactic SMP embolization are promising alternatives to conventional methods, offering high technical success and the potential to reduce reinterventions. Larger studies are needed to confirm long-term outcomes and define optimal use.

title: Inflammatory bowel disease and the heart: how trained immunity shapes cardiovascular outcomes.
authorString: Liang S, Han L.
abstractText: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), comprising Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is a chronic relapsing intestinal inflammatory disorder. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of death in patients with IBD, with elevated risks of myocardial infarction, heart failure, stroke, and venous thromboembolism that are independent of traditional risk factors. Disease activity and histological inflammation independently predict major adverse cardiovascular events, and Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis differ in cardiovascular risk profiles. This residual risk points to immune mechanisms that remain unclear. Trained immunity (TI), an innate immune memory induced by epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming, may link chronic intestinal inflammation to cardiovascular injury. This review integrates epidemiological and mechanistic evidence, outlines cardiovascular risk features in IBD, examines the molecular basis of TI and its roles in atherosclerosis, myocardial injury, and heart failure, and evaluates candidate biomarkers and targeted therapeutic strategies. We also discuss current limitations and challenges in clinical translation and propose future research directions, to inform mechanistic studies and clinical interventions for IBD-associated CVD.

title: Strategies to reduce microvascular obstruction and infarct size in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
authorString: Rossignoli C, Portolan L, Pesarini G, Fezzi S, Galli V, Pacchioni A, Tavella D, Ribichini F, Scarsini R, Magistri M.
abstractText: Microvascular obstruction (MVO) remains a major challenge in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), as adequate myocardial reperfusion may not be achieved despite successful epicardial recanalization with primary percutaneous coronary intervention (pPCI). MVO results from multiple interacting mechanisms, including distal embolization, ischemia-reperfusion injury, inflammation, oxidative stress, and microvascular dysfunction, and is associated with larger infarct size and worse clinical outcomes. This review summarizes current and emerging strategies for the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of MVO in STEMI. Advances in cardiac imaging and invasive or angiography-derived assessment of the coronary microcirculation may improve early identification and risk stratification. Therapeutic approaches include pharmacological and device-based strategies targeting thrombotic burden and distal embolization, reperfusion injury, inflammation, and oxidative stress. However, despite encouraging results for selected interventions, available evidence remains heterogeneous and no specific therapy has become standard of care for MVO. These findings highlight the need to move beyond a uniform approach to MVO. Integration of early diagnosis with identification of the predominant pathophysiological mechanism may provide a framework for future phenotype- and endotype-guided therapeutic strategies delivered within the appropriate therapeutic window. Whether such an approach can improve myocardial reperfusion and clinical outcomes after STEMI requires evaluation in adequately powered prospective trials.

title: Cross-cohort blood transcriptome analysis identifies an eight-gene diagnostic index and inflammatory programs in acute myocardial infarction.
authorString: Pan C, Chen Z, Li J, Xie S, Fan X.
abstractText:
Background

Globally, acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is the foremost cause of cardiovascular fatality, with dysregulated immune-inflammatory cascades serving as master regulators of both acute cardiomyocyte necrosis and subsequent maladaptive remodeling. Despite the prognostic potential of individual immune biomarkers, no multi-omics machine learning (ML)-derived immune gene signature has been established for predicting AMI outcome.

Methods

Peripheral blood transcriptomes from four Gene Expression Omnibus datasets (GSE59867 as the discovery cohort; GSE48060, GSE60993, and GSE66360 as independent validation cohorts; total 348 participants) were subjected to study-wise differential expression analysis and marker-based immune scoring without cross-platform batch harmonization. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and nested machine learning (L2-regularized logistic regression, linear support vector machine (SVM), random forest, and gradient boosting) were used to derive an eight-gene diagnostic index. Signature performance was evaluated in three independent validation cohorts, contextualized at the single-cell resolution (GSE121893), and experimentally supported by in vitro reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) using American Type Culture Collection (ATCC)-authenticated cell lines (THP-1 TIB-202 and EA.hy926 CRL-2922).

Results

AMI specimens showed marked enrichment of pro-inflammatory M1-like macrophages, neutrophils, and exhausted CD8+ T cells compared to healthy donors. The WGCNA turquoise module exhibited the strongest phenotypic correlation (r = 0.78, p < 0.001). Convergent machine learning analysis yielded an eight-gene diagnostic index (BAX, EDA2R, MCEMP1, SOCS3, ASGR2, RNASE1, ADM, and KPNA5) with a repeated out-of-fold area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.984 in the discovery cohort and independent validation AUCs of 0.863, 0.655, and 0.876. Two exploratory binary-outcome analyses (6-month heart failure progression and 18-month recurrent events) yielded AUCs of 0.819 and 0.569, respectively; these small-sample results are descriptive only and do not support Kaplan-Meier or hazard ratio claims. In vitro RT-qPCR in ATCC-authenticated THP-1-derived macrophages (lipopolysaccharide/ATP stimulation) and EA.hy926 cells (hypoxia/reoxygenation) confirmed elevated levels of CXCL10 (3.82 ± 0.31-fold), IL6 (4.15 ± 0.44-fold), NLRP3 (2.94 ± 0.28-fold), and CASP1 (3.47 ± 0.38-fold) under AMI-relevant stimulation conditions (n = 3 independent biological replicates).

Conclusions

An eight-gene diagnostic index (BAX, EDA2R, MCEMP1, SOCS3, ASGR2, RNASE1, ADM, and KPNA5), derived using nested machine learning and validated in three independent cohorts, achieved robust discriminative accuracy for AMI diagnosis. Elevated inflammatory transcripts (CXCL10, IL6, NLRP3, and CASP1) confirmed by in vitro RT-qPCR in ATCC cell lines reflect concurrent inflammasome activation and immune dysregulation, offering a mechanistic rationale for precision immune-targeted intervention strategies.

title: Remnant-cholesterol-inflammatory-index as a novel predictor of cardiometabolic risk and cardiovascular mortality in elderly patients with severe aortic stenosis.
authorString: Mazzone A, Gaggini M, Foffa I, Del Turco S, Minichilli F, Berti S, Vassalle C.
abstractText:
Background

Inflammaging activates a vicious cycle common to the progression of structural cardiovascular alterations, cardiometabolic diseases as well as degenerative aortic stenosis (AoS). The remnant cholesterol inflammatory index (RCII) is a new recently proposed biomarker that combines remnant cholesterol and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, resembling inflammaging. However, the role of RCII in terms of cardiometabolic risk and cardiovascular mortality in AoS elderly patients has not been evaluated still now.

Aim

to assess the association between RCII and cardiovascular risk factors and mortality in AoS elderly patients.

Results

RCII levels correlated with systemic inflammation biomarkers (closer correlation with interleukin-6), glucose, creatinine, vascular endothelial growth factor and frailty in AoS patients. Inverse correlations were observed with albumin (typically reduced in inflammatory states) and with HDL concentration. The Kaplan-Meier survival estimates showed significantly worse survival in patients with elevated RCII levels (p<0.01) (mean follow-up 19 ± 4 months). In an exploratory multivariable Cox analysis, higher RCII was associated with cardiovascular mortality (HR = 3.5, 95% CI: 1.0-12.0).

Conclusion

RCII is associated with cardiometabolic risk and adverse prognosis in elderly patients with AoS, providing an additional perspective on the prognostic implications of the coexistence of lipid abnormalities and low-grade inflammation in this population. However, the limited number of cardiovascular deaths warrants cautious interpretation of this estimate. Moreover, external validation, standardized thresholds, serial measurements, and comparison with established risk models are needed before RCII clinical implementation.

title: A nomogram integrating YTHDC2 expression and clinicopathological parameters for predicting endometrial cancer recurrence: a multicenter retrospective study.
authorString: Gong Y, Hou L, Xiong J, Tian C, Tu Y, Jiang P, Yuan R.
abstractText:
Background

Endometrial cancer (EC) is one of the most common gynecological malignancies worldwide, with persistently rising incidence and mortality. Reliable molecular biomarkers for predicting EC recurrence remain lacking. This study aimed to develop a nomogram integrating YTHDC2 expression with clinicopathological parameters to predict postoperative recurrence-free survival (RFS) in EC patients.

Methods

A total of 520 stage I-III EC patients undergoing initial standard surgical treatment were enrolled as the training cohort, and 243 patients from three independent hospitals constituted the validation cohort. Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses were performed to identify independent prognostic factors for RFS in the training cohort, and a nomogram was constructed accordingly. Internal validation was conducted using the concordance index (C-index) and calibration curves in the training cohort, and external validation was performed in the validation cohort. Risk stratification was based on the Nomogram-predicted 3-year RFS probability, and Kaplan-Meier curves were used to evaluate the clinical utility of the model. The nomogram's discriminative performance was further compared with three published EC prediction models.

Results

Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses identified age (HR = 2.02, P = 0.006), International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) stage (HR = 4.20, P < 0.001), lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI; HR = 1.81, P = 0.022), CA125 level (HR = 1.66, P = 0.048), depth of myometrial invasion (HR = 1.68, P = 0.039), histological type (HR = 3.42, P < 0.001), p53 protein status (HR = 2.61, P < 0.001), and YTHDC2 high expression level (HR = 0.26, P < 0.001) as independent prognostic factors for RFS. A nomogram incorporating these eight factors was constructed to predict RFS in EC. Internal and external calibration curves demonstrated good agreement between predicted and observed outcomes. The model achieved a C-index of 0.892 in the training cohort and 0.859 in the validation cohort, significantly outperforming single-indicator models. It also surpassed three published EC prediction models in both cohorts. The nomogram consistently outperformed single-indicator models in predicting 1-, 3-, and 5-year RFS.

Conclusion

The nomogram integrating YTHDC2 expression with clinicopathological parameters demonstrated favorable accuracy in predicting RFS for patients with EC and may effectively guide long-term prognostic management.

title: Longitudinal immune trajectories following SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in long-term care facility residents: an unsupervised analysis approach.
authorString: Palmieri A, Damiano C, Leone P, Trevisan C, Malara A, Zucchelli A, Incalzi RA, Prato R, Fortunato F, Baldovin T, Coin A, Minchella P, Giordano S, Palamara AT, Onder G, Fedele G.
abstractText:
Background

Residents of Long-Term Care Facilities (LTCFs) represent a highly vulnerable population characterized by immunosenescence, multimorbidity, and heterogeneous immune responses to repeated SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and infection. Conventional analyses based on single clinical variables often fail to capture this complexity. We evaluated longitudinal humoral immune responses in institutionalized older adults to identify data-driven antibody profiles and characterize cluster-specific waning kinetics.

Methods

In a prospective multicenter cohort of 388 Italian LTCF residents followed across four time points (T0-T3 over 12 months), longitudinal anti-Spike (anti-S) and anti-Nucleocapsid (anti-N) IgG levels were measured alongside demographic and vaccination data. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was used for dimensionality reduction, followed by K-means clustering. Optimal cluster number was determined using internal validation metrics (Silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, and Davies-Bouldin indices) and bootstrap stability analysis. Linear mixed-effects models were applied to describe cluster-specific antibody waning trajectories.

Results

A longitudinal analysis was conducted on 388 LTCF residents. Three antibody trajectory profiles emerged: (i) a Vaccine-Driven profile (n = 130), characterized by moderate anti-S titers and progressive antibody decline; (ii) a Hybrid Immunity profile (n = 125), characterized by evidence of prior infection and remarkably stable antibody concentrations throughout follow-up despite limited uptake of the 2023/2024 booster; and (iii) a High-Peak Hybrid Responder profile (n = 133), exhibiting the highest baseline anti-S titers followed by the steepest rate of antibody waning. Across the cohort, 12 of 388 residents (3.1%) developed documented symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection during follow-up, with no COVID-19-related deaths and no significant difference in infection incidence among profiles. Bootstrap stability analysis showed a mean Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) of 0.74 (SD 0.20).

Conclusion

Unsupervised machine learning effectively resolves the complex heterogeneity of SARS-CoV-2 humoral responses in LTCF residents into data-driven trajectory patterns. These findings illustrate the utility of data-driven approach for describing humoral dynamics while distinguishing observational antibody kinetics from direct estimates of clinical protection.

title: Pretreatment neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio is associated with clinical phenotypes and infection-related mortality in microscopic polyangiitis: the multicentre REVEAL cohort study.
authorString: Hatta M, Watanabe R, Shiomi M, Masuda Y, Okazaki A, Matsuda S, Kotani T, Taniguchi T, Iwasaka S, Kadoba K, Manabe A, Jo K, Fujiki Y, Miyake H, Oka H, Sumitomo S, Yamamoto W, Nakatani S, Tsuda A, Watanabe T, Asai K, Hashimoto M.
abstractText:
Background

Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) remains associated with substantial early mortality despite advances in immunosuppressive therapy, highlighting the need for simple biomarkers that facilitate LR) has been associated with disease activity and prognosis in antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (AAV), its phenotype-specific significance in newly diagnosed MPA remains unclear. We investigated whether pretreatment NLR is associated with clinical phenotype, disease course, and long-term outcomes in MPA.

Methods

Among 418 patients with MPA enrolled in the multicentre REVEAL cohort between 2005 and 2025, 340 newly diagnosed treatment-naïve patients fulfilling the 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria were included. Patients were stratified into tertiles according to pretreatment NLR. Baseline characteristics, temporal outcomes, and survival were compared. Infection-related mortality was further evaluated after stabilised inverse probability weighting (IPW).

Results

Higher pretreatment NLR was associated with greater disease severity, including higher Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score (P < 0.001) and Five-Factor Score (P = 0.03), more frequent diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (P = 0.015), poorer renal function (P = 0.003), and more intensive remission-induction therapy, including methylprednisolone pulse therapy and rituximab. In contrast, interstitial lung disease was more common in patients with lower NLR (P = 0.001). Despite these baseline differences, disease activity, glucocorticoid tapering, and cumulative organ damage became comparable after treatment initiation. Pretreatment NLR was not associated with relapse-free survival (P = 0.44) but was associated with poorer overall survival (P = 0.012) and higher infection-related mortality (P = 0.002). After adjustment using IPW, the association with overall survival was no longer statistically significant, whereas the increased risk of infection-related mortality remained significant (HR 3.47, 95% CI 1.32-9.09, P = 0.034).

Conclusion

Pretreatment NLR reflected distinct inflammatory phenotypes and was independently associated with infection-related mortality in patients with newly diagnosed MPA. As an inexpensive and widely available marker, pretreatment NLR may have potential as a prognostic biomarker, although further validation is required to establish its clinical utility.

title: Perioperative prothrombin time activity trajectories and subsequent mortality after surgical repair of acute type A aortic dissection.
authorString: Yan H, Shen X, Weng H, Li W, Yang S.
abstractText:
Background

Perioperative prothrombin time activity (PTA) changes rapidly during surgical repair of acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD), but single measurements do not capture heterogeneous longitudinal patterns. We sought to identify recurring perioperative PTA trajectories, characterize their clinical context, and examine their association with subsequent all-cause mortality.

Methods

This single-center retrospective cohort included 284 adults who underwent ATAAD repair from 2021 through 2023. Group-based trajectory modeling used the last preoperative and observed postoperative day (POD) 1-7 PTA measurements. Patients required at least three observed PTA measurements for trajectory modeling. Mortality analyses began immediately after POD7. The primary Cox model adjusted for age and sex; Firth regression addressed sparse events. Incremental information beyond last preoperative PTA was evaluated by a prespecified likelihood-ratio comparison.

Results

The trajectory cohort comprised 268 patients with 1,895 observations and 27 deaths after POD7. Four perioperative PTA trajectory groups were identified: moderate-stable [87 (32.5%)], low-declining [50 (18.7%)], preserved-rapidly-declining [61 (22.8%)], and high-preserved [70 (26.1%)]. Cumulative mortality differed globally (log-rank P = 0.00210), and trajectory group remained associated with subsequent mortality in the age- and sex-adjusted Cox model (global P = 0.0322) and Firth sensitivity analysis (global P = 0.0481). The prespecified direct low-declining-versus-preserved-rapidly-declining comparison did not demonstrate a clear difference. Adding trajectory group to age, sex, and last preoperative PTA did not show clear incremental information (likelihood-ratio P = 0.304; Firth P = 0.380). After exclusion of mechanical-valve recipients, the principal trajectory structure was largely preserved, although this sensitivity analysis did not exclude treatment-related effects on PTA.

Conclusion

Four reproducible perioperative PTA trajectories characterized distinct longitudinal patterns and were associated with mortality after the POD7 landmark. These trajectories should be interpreted as composite perioperative patterns reflecting both disease and treatment context rather than as intrinsic coagulation states. They were not ordered mortality-risk tiers and did not show clear incremental prognostic information beyond last preoperative PTA. External validation is required.

title: The gut-brain-vascular axis: converging neuroinflammatory and hypertension-mediated pathways from gut dysbiosis to cognitive decline.
authorString: Mehta S, Loomba P, Musselmani H, Ly J, Nguyen S, Niemann A, Kolli S, Sant D.
abstractText: Hypertension and cognitive decline are major public health burdens, and both have been associated with gut microbiome dysbiosis. We propose the gut-brain-vascular axis as a testable synthesis in which dysbiosis may contribute to cognitive decline through two converging routes: direct neuroinflammatory signaling and hypertension-mediated cerebrovascular injury. In the proposed direct route, intestinal barrier dysfunction, lipopolysaccharide translocation, altered microbial metabolites, microglial activation, and vagal signaling may promote neuroinflammation. In the indirect route, dysbiosis-associated metabolites, immune activation, autonomic imbalance, and endothelial injury may contribute to hypertension, which is linked to cerebral small vessel disease, impaired cerebral autoregulation, neurovascular uncoupling, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction. The component relationships are supported to different degrees, but the complete temporal pathway and an interaction between the two routes have not been established in humans. This narrative review synthesizes gut-hypertension, gut-cognitive, cerebrovascular, shared-mechanism, and therapeutic evidence and identifies the study designs needed to test the framework. Longitudinal cohorts and trials that measure microbiome, blood pressure, cerebrovascular, and cognitive outcomes together are required to determine whether the proposed routes occur independently, sequentially, or interactively.

title: Macrophages as orchestrators of gut-organ axis crosstalk: immunometabolic reprogramming and host-directed therapy in sepsis.
authorString: Zeng W, Zhang Y, Fan L, Xun Y, Jiang Z, Dai F.

journal.title: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

abstractText: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome driven by a dysregulated host response to infection. Among the numerous contributory factors, the gut microbiota and its metabolites are increasingly recognized as potential modulators of systemic inflammation, acting through multiple gut-organ axes. Within this network, macrophages serve as central integrators that transduce microbial signals into organ-specific inflammatory or reparative outcomes. Disease evolution is critically determined by immune-metabolic reprogramming of macrophages. This reprogramming comprises tricarboxylic acid cycle truncation, lipid remodeling, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammasome activation. These processes are closely intertwined with NFκB, cGAS-STING, TLR/MyD88, and aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling. Gut-derived metabolites, particularly short-chain fatty acids and indole derivatives, shape macrophage functions in distal organs. These mechanisms predominantly operate during the acute phase of sepsis, driving early organ injury. In contrast, sepsis survivors often enter a distinct chronic phase, characterized by persistent immune dysregulation. Trained immunity, through metabolic-epigenetic rewiring, may underlie this long-term dysfunction in survivors. Preclinical promise has been demonstrated by host-directed therapies that target macrophage metabolism. Nevertheless, major challenges impede clinical translation. These include inadequate preclinical models, the absence of validated real-time biomarkers for immune-metabolic phenotyping, and marked heterogeneity among patients. This review positions macrophages as actionable sentinels in gut-organ crosstalk during acute sepsis, and further explores their role in chronic sequelae, underscoring the need for biomarker-guided stratification and precision immune-metabolic editing to overcome barriers in both settings.

title: Macrophage polarization drives viral reservoirs in HIV-1 infection.
authorString: Glokpon AEC, Gbenoudon SJ, Abana CZ, Nartey PA, Klutse J, Lamptey H, Bonney EY, Kyei GB.
abstractText: Macrophages are cells of the myeloid lineage that play a very important role in innate immunity and tissue homeostasis. They have the capacity to respond to aggression from pathogenic agents and are the target of HIV-1 infection via their CD4 receptor and the CCR5 and CXCR4 co-receptors. In People With HIV (PWH), macrophages constitute a virological reservoir, making treatment with Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) difficult as they are resistant to the cytopathic effect induced by the virus, resist apoptosis and are in parts of the body with limited access, such as the brain. During HIV infection, macrophages are activated and polarized with the aim of eliminating the virus. Based on their polarization, they are classified into three main groups during HIV infection: M1 and M4 macrophages, which are classically activated, and M2 macrophages, which are activated alternatively. M2 macrophages are subdivided into several subtypes: M2a, M2b, M2c and M2d. M1 and M4 macrophages are pro-inflammatory and are stimulated by pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-2, IL-1r and TNF-α. M2 macrophages are anti-inflammatory and are stimulated by anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-4, IL-10 and IL-13. Macrophages constitute a very significant and long-lasting viral reservoir due to their intrinsic longevity. Furthermore, the accumulation of virions within Virus-Containing Compartments (VCCs) maintains the latent virus, thereby demonstrating their role as a critical, stable and long-lasting reservoir. However, the reservoir establishment and the persistence of the virus in polarized macrophages have not been fully explored. In this review, we examined macrophage polarization dynamics during HIV infection and explained how polarized macrophages contribute to the establishment of viral reservoirs. We also discuss how the acquisition of specific phenotypes may be a key factor in HIV reservoir formation. Thus, providing important information to guide reactivation of HIV from macrophages, a critical step in the Shock-and-Kill HIV cure strategy.

title: The contribution of the CTRP family and its receptors to fibrotic diseases.
authorString: Tanaka S, Nozawai H, Chi HH, Ueno H, Tsuruzoe Y, Sakaguchi N, Tsukamoto R, Fujiyoshi S, Lee SI, Murayama MA.
abstractText: Adiponectin and other 15 members of the complement C1q/tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-related protein (CTRP) are proteins secreted primarily from adipose tissue; furthermore, recent studies have revealed their expression in various other tissues. Beyond their roles as adipokines, CTRPs critically regulate fibrogenic responses in renal and cardiovascular tissues. Adiponectin exerts its biological functions via AdipoR1, AdipoR2, and Cadherin-13 (known as T-cadherin), while several CTRPs share AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 as functional receptors. This review summarizes the current understanding of the protective effects of the CTRP family in fibrotic diseases. Future studies utilizing gain-of-function and loss-of-function animal models with single or double genetic mutations will elucidate the detailed molecular mechanisms, including the identification of functional receptors, involved in CTRP-mediated regulation of fibrotic diseases.

title: Between algorithmic alerts and bodily sensations: a qualitative study of post-PCI patients' experiences with wrist-worn heart health information.
authorString: Tong A, Luo R, Jin P, Wu C.
abstractText:
Background

Smart wrist-worn devices are increasingly used by patients after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to monitor heart rate, rhythm-related alerts, sleep, activity, and other health-related data. However, limited qualitative evidence exists on how post-PCI patients interpret and respond to such information in daily life.

Objective

This study aimed to explore how patients with coronary heart disease after PCI understand, evaluate, and respond to heart rate, heart rhythm, and health-related information generated by smart wrist-worn devices.

Methods

A qualitative descriptive design was adopted. From January to May 2026, purposive sampling was used to recruit 23 post-PCI patients who had used smartwatches or smart bands in daily life. Semi-structured interviews were conducted, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Data collection and analysis were conducted concurrently until data saturation was achieved.

Results

Four themes were developed: (1) cardiac status became continuously datafied; (2) calibrating risk between alerts and sensations; (3) device information awaited medical interpretation; and (4) from self-management to disease burden. Patients did not simply accept or reject device-generated data. Instead, they interpreted alerts by comparing them with bodily sensations, previous cardiac events, stent implantation experiences, follow-up results, and healthcare professionals' explanations. Device information could enhance awareness of medication use, follow-up, and lifestyle management. However, when alerts lacked medical interpretation or follow-up response, they also increased uncertainty, worry, repeated self-monitoring, and perceived disease burden.

Conclusions

Smart wrist-worn devices may support daily observation and clinician-patient communication in post-PCI management, but they should not be regarded as substitutes for clinical examinations or professional judgment. Clearer interpretive boundaries, stratified guidance, and follow-up response pathways are needed to help patients appropriately understand and act on device-generated information.

title: Case report: Harel-Yoon syndrome (<i>ATAD3A</i> p.Arg528Trp) with relative cognitive preservation despite severe motor impairment.
authorString: Zamudio Soledad PN, Montoya JS, Poveda-Rodriguez DS, King Chio Cho LM, Reyes MA, Bernal Pacheco O.
abstractText:
Background

Harel-Yoon syndrome (HAYOS) is a rare neurometabolic disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the ATAD3A gene, a key regulator of mitochondrial dynamics and cellular homeostasis. Although a broad phenotypic spectrum has been described, the relationship between genotype and long-term functional outcomes remains incompletely understood.

Case presentation

We report two adult sisters with genetically confirmed HAYOS who exhibited early-onset hypotonia progressing to spasticity, craniofacial dysmorphism, optic atrophy, and sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Neuroimaging revealed mild cerebellar atrophy, and electrophysiological studies showed a chronic sensorimotor polyneuropathy with axonal loss and conduction slowing. Initial exome sequencing revealed a variant of uncertain significance in COL5A1, whereas subsequent targeted familial Sanger sequencing confirmed the heterozygous ATAD3A NM_001170535.3:c.1582C>T (p.Arg528Trp) variant in both sisters. Parental segregation could not be assessed because their father died before genetic evaluation and their mother declined further clinical evaluation and targeted segregation testing for the familial ATAD3A variant. Despite severe progressive motor impairment leading to wheelchair dependence, both patients completed formal education and had low-average IQ scores (88 and 82) at single adult assessments.

Conclusion

These cases expand the phenotypic spectrum of HAYOS by demonstrating that severe progressive motor disability may coexist with relative cognitive preservation at adult assessment, limited cardiac or metabolic involvement, and long-term survival. Our findings highlight the diagnostic challenges posed by the ATAD3 locus and underscore the importance of comprehensive genetic evaluation in suspected mitochondrial disorders. Rather than representing a globally mild phenotype, these patients show a motor-severe but cognitively and systemically attenuated presentation, with implications for prognosis, genetic counseling, and clinical management.

title: Immune-driven remodeling in calcific aortic valve disease: mechanisms and immunotherapeutic opportunities.
authorString: Zhang X, Si Y, Liao L, Wu Y.
abstractText: Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) is a prevalent degenerative valvular disorder in the aging population, for which no pharmacological therapy has proven effective in halting or reversing disease progression. Over the past decade, CAVD has been increasingly recognized not as a passive degenerative process of calcium deposition, but as an active, inflammation-driven disease characterized by osteogenic remodeling. This process is initiated and sustained by endothelial injury, lipid retention, immune cell infiltration, and phenotypic transition of valvular interstitial cells. Growing evidence indicates that innate and adaptive immune responses may contribute to disease amplification. Innate immune cells propagate local inflammatory signaling through inflammasome activation, extracellular vesicle communication, protease release, and neutrophil extracellular trap formation, while adaptive immune cells further shape disease progression by sustaining cytokine networks that promote fibrosis and osteogenic reprogramming within the valvular microenvironment. Based on these mechanistic insights, this review further discusses emerging translational strategies aimed at targeting key pathogenic processes in CAVD, including modulation of inflammatory signaling, restoration of adaptive immune homeostasis, regulation of extracellular matrix remodeling and antifibrotic pathways, inhibition of VIC osteogenic differentiation, as well as development of patient stratification and local drug delivery approaches. Collectively, these strategies may provide a conceptual framework for earlier, non-surgical interventions for CAVD.

title: Nonlinear association of cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein, and glucose index with the risk of prediabetes and diabetes in normal-weight middle-aged and older Chinese adults: a multicenter retrospective cohort study.
authorString: Ding J, Cai Z, Wang X, Qin L, Chen W.
abstractText:
Background

The relationship between the cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein, and glucose (CHG) index and dysglycemia is widely recognized in the general population; however, this relationship has been much less examined among normal-weight, middle-aged and older adults-a subgroup routinely marginalized in metabolic research. Accordingly, the current study was designed to evaluate the relationship of the CHG index with incident prediabetes and diabetes specifically among this population.

Methods

The study cohort comprised 19,981 Chinese adults (age ≥45 years, BMI 18.5-23.9 kg/m2) without prediabetes or diabetes at baseline, sourced from a multicenter retrospective analysis of nationwide screening data (2010-2016). The CHG index was calculated as Ln[(TC × FPG)/(2 × HDLC)] (mg/dL). The primary outcome was incident- prediabetes and diabetes. To evaluate the association, we applied Cox proportional hazards models, along with smooth curve fitting and two-piecewise regression.

Results

During an average follow-up of 3.19 years, a higher CHG index was significantly linked to a greater risk of the outcome. After adjustment (Model 3), the hazard ratio (HR) for the CHG index as a continuous variable was 2.20 (95% CI: 1.90-2.54). Compared with Quartile 1, the HRs for Quartiles 2, 3, and 4 were 1.42, 1.86, and 1.91, respectively (all p < 0.0001). A significant nonlinear relationship was identified (log-likelihood ratio test, p < 0.001), with the inflection point located at a CHG index of 5.07. To the left of the inflection point, each unit increase in CHG index was associated with a 6.39-fold increase in risk (HR: 6.39, 95% CI: 4.73-8.64), while no significant link was observed to the right (HR: 1.02, 95% CI: 0.79-1.31).

Conclusion

This study indicates a nonlinear positive association between the CHG index and the risk of incident prediabetes and diabetes among normal-weight middle-aged and older Chinese adults. Future research employing large prospective cohorts is warranted to fully explicate the mechanisms and establish a causal nexus.

title: Routine cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance for clinical phenotyping and serial assessment of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a retrospective single-center clinical analysis.
authorString: Wang J, Xie Y, Zeng C, Nie L, Yang Y.
abstractText:
Background

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is difficult to confirm because symptoms are non-specific, comorbidities are prevalent, and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is normal by definition. We evaluated whether markers from routine cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) improved phenotyping and diagnostic discrimination in HFpEF and whether they changed after treatment optimization.

Methods

In this retrospective single-center, observational analysis, 126 adults evaluated between January 2023 and December 2025 were included: 72 with adjudicated HFpEF, 27 hypertensive controls without heart failure, and 27 healthy volunteers. All had available 1.5-T cine CMR studies that underwent blinded analysis of LV volumes, LVEF, left ventricular mass index (LVMI), left atrial volume index (LAVI), right ventricular ejection fraction, and feature-tracking global longitudinal strain (GLS). Interobserver reproducibility was quantified. The primary analysis estimated the discrimination of LAVI, LVMI, and GLS for HFpEF; a multiparametric model was developed using Firth-penalized logistic regression with bootstrap optimism correction. Forty-six patients with HFpEF had repeat CMR available at approximately 6 months after individualized treatment optimization and were included in the serial analysis.

Results

LVEF was preserved and similar across groups. HFpEF was associated with higher LVMI, marked LAVI enlargement, and less negative GLS, with large effect sizes for LAVI and GLS. LAVI and GLS were the strongest single discriminators [apparent area under the curve (AUC) 0.83 and 0.85, respectively]; the multiparametric model achieved an apparent AUC of 0.87 that fell to 0.84 after optimism correction and did not exceed GLS alone. LAVI and less negative GLS remained independent predictors after adjustment. At 6 months, LAVI decreased (mean change -4.8 mL/m2), and GLS became more negative (-1.3 percentage points), exceeding measurement variability, whereas LVEF was unchanged.

Conclusions

Routine cine CMR identified atrial remodeling, ventricular hypertrophy, and impaired longitudinal deformation despite preserved LVEF, and appeared capable of detecting selective short-term temporal changes rather than definitive treatment-induced reverse remodeling. It is a practical adjunct for phenotyping and hypothesis-generating serial assessment, pending external validation.

title: MicroRNAs as a potential missing link between environment and type 1 diabetes development.
authorString: Ciężki S, Jamiołkowska-Sztabkowska M, Walicka M, Bossowski A, Głowińska-Olszewska B.
abstractText: The pathogenesis of type 1 diabetes (T1D) is multifactorial and remains incompletely understood. Although genetic susceptibility plays a major role, epidemiological evidence indicates an important contribution of non-genetic factors. Viral infections, dietary factors, alterations in gut microbiota, pollutants and early-life exposures have all been associated with T1D risk, but the molecular mechanisms linking these exposures to disease development remain unclear. MicroRNA dysregulation has been reported in T1D and is associated with immune regulation, pancreatic β-cell function, insulin secretion and cell survival. At the same time, environmental and early-life exposures can alter microRNA expression. These two lines of evidence raise the hypothesis that environmentally responsive microRNAs may represent molecular points of convergence between environmental influences and pathways relevant to T1D. In this narrative review, we examine evidence linking environmental and early-life exposures to microRNA alterations and evaluate the potential relevance of these changes to T1D-related immune and β-cell pathways. Across human studies and T1D-relevant experimental models, environmental and early-life exposures have been associated with alterations in microRNA expression, with several microRNAs recurring across distinct environmental contexts. Among these, miR-155, miR-146a and miR-375 emerge as candidate convergent regulatory nodes linking environmental responses with immune and β-cell pathways relevant to T1D. However, direct evidence that environmentally induced alterations in these microRNAs mediate T1D development in humans is still lacking. These findings may also have clinical relevance. Circulating microRNA signatures could complement existing biomarkers in T1D, but consistent analytical methods and replication in independent cohorts are still needed before routine use. Therapeutic targeting of microRNAs remains experimental. Overall, the reviewed evidence points to environmentally responsive microRNAs as candidate molecular links between environmental exposures and immune and β-cell pathways relevant to T1D, although a causal role in disease development has not been established.

title: Single-cell transcriptome sequencing analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells reveals immune signatures in patients with polymyalgia rheumatica.
authorString: Cai T, Qin Q, Jiang Y, Liu Z, Song R, Zhang JA.
abstractText:
Background

Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an auto-inflammatory disease or autoimmune disease that involves multiple immune cells. In this study, single-cell transcriptome sequencing (scRNA-seq) combined with cellular communication analysis were used to investigate immune characteristics of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) in PMR patients.

Methods

Three newly diagnosed PMR patients were recruited; their PBMCs were isolated and sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 sequencing platform. The PBMCs scRNA-seq data of three normal controls were downloaded from the 10× Genomics platform for joint analysis.

Results

Relative to healthy controls, PMR patients exhibited a reduced abundance of circulating T cells, alongside an expanded megakaryocyte/platelet compartment. At the T cell subset level, PMR was associated with an increased proportion of pro-inflammatory KIR+NK-like T cells, while CD4+ central memory T cells, effector memory T cells, and Th1 cells showed reductions in relative abundance. Circulating NK cell subsets were disproportionately represented in PMR patients; notably, the CD56dimCD16hi-ISG subset was exclusively detected in PMR cases. While no statistically meaningful shifts were observed in the global proportional distribution of B cells, the unswitched memory B cell compartment was absent in PMR patients. Multiple monocyte subsets annotated for elevated inflammatory and interferon-stimulated gene signatures, including CD14_Monocyte-ISG and CD16_Monocyte-IFITM1, were uniformly expanded in the PMR cohort. Functional enrichment analysis showed that the co-stimulation, cytotoxicity, antigen processing and presentation, and inflammation promotion of various immune cells in PMR patients were all enhanced. Key inflammatory pathways were widely activated, including the interferon-γ signaling pathway, interleukin-1β production, and NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity. Cellular communication analysis revealed more interactions but slightly weaker strength in PMRs, with increased communication in TGF-β and CD48 pathways.

Conclusions

This preliminary study may help to further elucidate the pathogenesis of PMR and provide a theoretical basis for identifying diagnostic markers and discovering new therapeutic targets.

title: Case Report: Long-term survival in FIGO stage IVB small cell carcinoma of the ovary, pulmonary type following complete cytoreduction and platinum re-challenge.
authorString: Chae HJ, Choi YS, Lee JI, Jeong YY.
abstractText:
Background

Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, pulmonary type (SCCOPT), is a rare and highly aggressive malignancy with poor prognosis. Long-term survival in advanced-stage disease has rarely been reported.

Case presentation

A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with FIGO stage IVB SCCOPT accompanied by extensive peritoneal carcinomatosis and a solitary liver metastasis. No pulmonary lesion suggestive of primary lung malignancy was identified on CT, PET/CT, or chest radiography. She underwent aggressive primary cytoreductive surgery achieving complete macroscopic resection (R0), followed by four cycles of cisplatin and etoposide (EP). Sixteen months after diagnosis, isolated intracranial recurrence with multiple brain metastases were successfully treated with radiotherapy. Twenty-one months after diagnosis, systemic recurrence involving multiple liver metastases and a spinal metastasis was treated with six cycles of EP re-challenge, resulting in a marked radiologic response and subsequent durable disease control. The patient remained alive without clinical evidence of disease progression at the latest follow-up, 104 months after diagnosis.

Conclusions

This case suggests that prolonged survival may be achievable in selected patients with advanced SCCOPT through aggressive multimodal treatment. Complete cytoreductive surgery, platinum-based chemotherapy, including EP re-challenge following a prolonged platinum-free interval and previous response to platinum-based chemotherapy, and timely local treatment of metastatic lesions may contribute to durable disease control.

title: Fucoidan from <i>Pearsonothuria graeffei</i> alleviates dyslipidemia in ApoE<sup>-/-</sup> mice by regulating reverse cholesterol transport and promoting bile acid synthesis.
authorString: Zhao T, Yu Y, Wang Y, Zhang L, Xiao J, Chen S, Li S.
abstractText:
Background

The fucoidan extracted from sea cucumber Pearsonothuria graeffei (Fuc-Pg) has beneficial anti-inflammatory and lipid-lowering effects, suggesting its potential anti-atherosclerotic properties.

Methods

ApoE-/- mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks. Fuc-Pg (20 mg/kg and 80 mg/kg) was administered by oral gavage once daily.

Results

The results indicated that Fuc-Pg intervention reduced aortic plaques, suppressed systemic inflammation, and alleviated dyslipidemia in ApoE-/- mice. Mechanistically, Fuc-Pg reduced lipid absorption by decreasing CD36 and microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) expression levels in the small intestine, enhanced reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) by increasing hepatic LDLR and ABCG5, and facilitated bile acid synthesis by increasing CYP7A1 and CYP27A1 expression. Increased fecal lipid and hepatic bile acid levels further confirmed that Fuc-Pg exerted preventive effects in ApoE-/- mice by reducing lipid absorption.

Conclusion

Fuc-Pg alleviated atherosclerosis by modulating cholesterol metabolism and reducing lipid absorption. This study elucidates the nutritional application of fucoidan as a functional food ingredient and explores its potential mechanism.

title: Association between the perivascular fat attenuation index and CCTA-defined anatomically significant left anterior descending coronary artery stenosis: relationship with serum inflammatory biomarkers.
authorString: Ahongjiang Y, Abudukaiyoumu A, Abulimiti G, Tuerxun H, Mutailifu A.
abstractText:
Objective

To investigate whether lesion-specific perivascular fat attenuation index (FAI) is associated with CCTA-defined anatomically significant (≥50%) left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) stenosis and to evaluate the diagnostic performance of a composite model integrating serum inflammatory biomarkers.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed 160 patients with suspected coronary artery disease (CAD) who underwent coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA). Patients receiving anti-inflammatory medications were excluded. Lesion-specific perivascular FAI was measured around the LAD. The prespecified primary outcome was CCTA-defined anatomically significant LAD stenosis (≥50%), analysed as a binary variable. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors, and the final model was internally evaluated with stratified 5-fold cross-validation, 10-fold cross-validation, and 1,000-bootstrap resampling. Model building was repeated within each resample. Calibration (slope, calibration-in-the-large, Brier score) and incremental discrimination (DeLong test) were assessed.

Results

Patients with CCTA-defined anatomically significant stenosis (≥50%) had higher, less negative FAI values, higher hs-CRP and LDH levels, and a lower ApoA1/ApoB ratio than those with stenosis <50% (all P < 0.05). FAI correlated with stenosis both as a continuous percentage (ρ = 0.54, P < 0.001) and as a binary ≥50% variable (ρ = 0.64, P < 0.001), with less negative FAI values accompanying more severe stenosis. The final model identified FAI (OR = 1.055, 95% CI: 1.014-1.098), hs-CRP (OR = 1.063, 95% CI: 1.005-1.125), LDH (OR = 1.014, 95% CI: 1.005-1.023), and the ApoA1/ApoB ratio (OR = 0.209, 95% CI: 0.070-0.624) as independent predictors. The composite model achieved an AUC of 0.915 (95% CI: 0.865-0.965); internal validation yielded AUCs of 0.872 (5-fold), 0.881 (95% CI: 0.826-0.936; 10-fold), and 0.895 (95% CI: 0.848-0.942; bootstrap). On formal DeLong testing for correlated ROC curves, the composite model showed significantly better discrimination than hs-CRP alone (P  =  0.020) and than FAI alone (P < 0.001).

Conclusions

Higher, less negative perivascular FAI values were associated with CCTA-defined anatomically significant LAD stenosis. A composite model integrating FAI, hs-CRP, LDH, and the ApoA1/ApoB ratio showed high apparent diagnostic accuracy and remained stable across multiple internal validation strategies. Because this was a single-centre retrospective study without external validation or outcome data, these findings should be regarded as preliminary and hypothesis-generating; the model is not ready for clinical use.

title: Recent achievements of the National Center Biobank Network (NCBN) bioresources through Japanese fiscal year 2025.
authorString: Omae Y, Tokunaga K.
abstractText: The National Center Biobank Network (NCBN) is constituted by a network of biobanks from five National Centers and the Japan Institute for Health Security (JIHS). The NCBN primarily collects samples from patients with various diseases, amassing a total of more than 250,000 participants and 800,000 human biospecimens as of the end of March 2026. The primary sample types are blood and DNA, with spinal fluid and frozen tissue samples also collected depending on the characteristics of the disease. These samples are accompanied by highly specialized and traceable clinical information supported by advanced medical care and expertise. Moreover, some samples are accompanied by whole-genome sequencing data. Consequently, these resources provide a unique platform for translational research, biomarker discovery, and genomic medicine in Japan. In the present review, we provide a detailed account of the recent achievements of NCBN biobanks and their biospecimens and genomic data.

title: Tissue Doppler S wave velocities are associated with changes in pro-brain natriuretic peptide levels following transcatheter aortic valve implantation.
authorString: Gharra S, Elbaz-Greener G, Planer D, Yagel O, Leibowitz D.

journal.title: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice

abstractText:
Background

Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is an effective treatment for severe aortic stenosis. Despite its efficacy, TAVI carries risks of complications in elderly patients. Prior research indicates that failure to reduce NTproBNP levels post-TAVI increases the risk of mortality and recurrent hospitalizations. The tissue Doppler S wave is an index of longitudinal left ventricular function which may predict poor outcomes following TAVI.

Objective

The aim of the study was to examine whether pre-TAVI S wave velocities are associated with hemodynamic response to TAVI as assessed by changes in NTproBNP levels.

Methods

This prospective observational study enrolled patients scheduled for elective TAVI who underwent echocardiographic evaluation including TDI S wave measurements. Blood levels of NTproBNP were assessed both before and 3 months after the procedure. Subjects were defined as responders or non-responders (NR) with response defined as a ≥ 30% reduction in NTproBNP levels post-procedure.

Results

185 subjects (mean age 79 ± 9 yrs., 47% male) were included in the study. Response to TAVI was observed in 78 (42%) of the cohort. The NR group had a significantly higher incidence of hypertension (62.3% vs. 37.7%, P = 0.017). Median S wave was 6.96 (3.8-13.7) cm/s in the responders and 5.88 (3.77-12.1) cm/s in the NR (p = 0.001), a finding which remained significant on multivariate analysis (p = 0.004; OR 1.31 95%CI 1.09-1.59).

Conclusions

This study demonstrates that for the first time that the TDI S wave is a significant predictor of NTproBNP reduction following TAVI. Further research is needed to validate these results in larger populations.

title: Real-world comparative effectiveness and safety of direct oral anticoagulants versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation.
authorString: Suwatcharangkoon S, Rattanasiri S, Unwanatham N, Numthavaj P, Limpijankit T, McKay GJ, Attia J, Thakkinstian A.

journal.medlineAbbreviation: Int J Cardiol Cardiovasc Risk Prev
journal.title: International journal of cardiology. Cardiovascular risk and prevention
journal.isoabbreviation: Int J Cardiol Cardiovasc Risk Prev

abstractText:
Background and purpose

Long-term oral anticoagulants (OACs), either vitamin K antagonists or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), are essential for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF). However, comparative real-world evidence among DOACs in upper-middle-income settings remains inconsistent. This study compared the effectiveness and safety of DOACs with warfarin in reducing stroke or systemic embolism (SSE), major bleeding, and all-cause mortality in patients with AF.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with non-valvular AF newly prescribed OACs between 2010 and 2021 using the Ramathibodi Hospital database. Inverse probability weighting (IPW) was applied to balance baseline covariates and emulate a RCT. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using IPW-adjusted Cox proportional hazards models.

Results

Among 5580 patients, 4237 received warfarin, 414 dabigatran, 428 rivaroxaban, 413 apixaban, and 88 edoxaban. Compared with warfarin, apixaban (HR 0.35; 95% CI 0.18, 0.67) was associated with significantly lower risks of SSE. Dabigatran (HR 0.43; 95% CI 0.23, 0.81) and rivaroxaban (HR 0.47; 95% CI 0.25, 0.90) significantly reduced the major bleeding risk. No DOAC was associated with reduced all-cause mortality. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings.

Conclusion

Apixaban showed the most favorable profile with significant reductions in SSE and trend toward lower major bleeding compared with warfarin, supporting its preferential use for stroke prevention in this setting.

title: Translational maturity of artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography varies across cardiovascular diseases.
authorString: Chen H, Huang J, Hou X.
abstractText: Electrocardiography is a widely available and low-cost cardiovascular test, and artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) can identify latent electrical phenotypes beyond conventional interpretation. However, high retrospective discrimination does not necessarily translate into clinically reliable or actionable benefit. This critical narrative review evaluates the translational maturity of AI-ECG across arrhythmias, acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, valvular heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and cardiac amyloidosis. PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched from January 1, 2022, through July 10, 2026, with earlier landmark studies added by backward citation tracking. Seventy-seven publications informed the review. Evidence was appraised using five clinically oriented criteria: intended use, reference-standard reliability, external validation and transportability, clinical actionability, and effects on workflow or patient outcomes. AI-ECG has progressed furthest in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction triage and reduced-left-ventricular-ejection-fraction screening, where prospective or randomized studies have demonstrated workflow or diagnostic-yield benefits, whereas acute myocardial infarction rule-out has reached prospective multicenter diagnostic validation. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy screening has also advanced through international validation and prospective implementation. By contrast, occlusion myocardial infarction detection, prediction of occult or future atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, long-term heart-failure prediction, and cardiac amyloidosis remain primarily validation-stage or risk-enrichment applications. Across domains, broader adoption is constrained by label quality, calibration, transportability, operating-threshold selection, and limited patient-outcome evidence. AI-ECG is therefore best positioned as clinician-supervised decision support linked to explicit downstream testing and care pathways.

title: Early applications of apple vision pro in clinical medicine and medical education: a scoping review.
authorString: Hu Y, Wang Y, Zuo X, Hu H, Min B, Wang C, Tang Z, Xiao N, Huang C, Wang C.
abstractText: The Apple Vision Pro (AVP), a next-generation spatial computing device, has demonstrated potential applications in multidisciplinary clinical diagnosis, treatment, and medical education, by leveraging its unique technical architecture and performance advantages. In clinical practice, its fundamental advantages of three-dimensional (3D) visualization, real-time image integration, and immersive interaction have been preliminarily employed in disease diagnosis and treatment, surgical planning, precise operations, and postoperative rehabilitation across multiple disciplines. In medical education, AVP surpasses the limitations of conventional models, offering a novel methodology for anatomy education, clinical skills development, specialized practical training, and collaboration of distance learning, thereby alleviating persistent challenges such as unequal distribution of teaching resources, low efficiency in skills and specialized training, and the high cost of distance education. However, AVP faces some limitations, including limited hardware portability, insufficient system compatibility, a lack of specialized medical applications, high costs, and incomplete medical certification. Currently, most evidence derives from feasibility studies, case reports, and opinion pieces. Only two Stage 2b confirmatory studies were identified. Thus, high-level evidence for clinical benefit remains scarce. Readers should interpret all reported benefits as preliminary technical demonstrations rather than established clinical outcomes. Future advancements necessitate iterative development of lightweight hardware design, development of specialized medical software, cross-system optimization, and establishment of standardization protocols. Moreover, more randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and multicenter studies are urgently needed to fully explore and validate its intrinsic value in precision medicine and the equitable allocation of medical resources.

title: Letter to the editor on: "Meta-analysis of the histopathological features of surgically removed aortas classified according to the SCVP and AECVP consensus documents".
authorString: Singh GP, Vaishnav B.
