title: Artificial Intelligence Detection of Aortic Valve Calcification on Routine Noncontrast Chest CT: A Real-World Cohort.
authorString: Koren O, Patel V, Wimpfheimer O, Kukuev A, Chu P, Jain H, Suruga K, Shitan H, Hassid S, Ng D, Hofstetter S, Makkar RR.
abstractText:
Background

Routine noncontrast chest computed tomography (CT) may reveal aortic valve calcification (AVC) outside aortic stenosis evaluation. Its prevalence, burden, and documentation remain uncertain. Artificial intelligence (AI) may enable systematic detection.

Objectives

The study aims to evaluate AVC prevalence and burden, clinical correlates, radiology documentation, and AI-assisted case finding.

Methods

This retrospective single-center study screened 511 consecutive noncontrast, non-electrocardiographically gated chest CT examinations in adults aged ≥50 years. After 15 protocol exclusions and 56 software-designated nonevaluable examinations, 440 underwent quantification by 2 blinded readers. AVC was defined as >10 AU using a 130-Hounsfield-unit threshold adjusted for blood-pool attenuation and image noise when needed. Locked HealthAVC V1.0 was a secondary comparator.

Results

Manual quantification identified AVC in 172 of 440 scans (39.1%; 95% CI: 34.6%-43.7%); 97 of 440 (22.0%) had ≥100 AU. Inter-reader agreement at >10 AU was 99.5% (kappa = 0.990). Age (adjusted OR: 1.92 per 5 years; 95% CI: 1.63-2.26) and male sex (adjusted OR: 2.09; 95% CI: 1.32-3.30) were associated with AVC. Reports documented 27 of 172 positive scans (15.7%; 95% CI: 11.0%-21.9%). AI detected 169 of 172 manually confirmed cases (98.3%) among 440 evaluable scans, including 142 of 145 undocumented cases. Of 496 submitted scans, 56 (11.3%) were nonevaluable. End-to-end sensitivity counting positive rejected scans as missed was 89.9%. Among 86 AI-positive patients with echocardiography, 10 (11.6%) had mild-or-greater aortic stenosis.

Conclusions

AVC was common but infrequently documented on routine chest CT. AI detected most cases among evaluable scans; 11.3% were nonevaluable, yielding 89.9% end-to-end sensitivity. Prospective studies should assess clinical pathways.

title: Circadian rhythm dysregulation and ferroptosis in hypertension: mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
authorString: Zeng H, Lin J, Chen J.
abstractText: Hypertension exhibits a pronounced circadian rhythm; however, the mechanisms by which circadian disruption translates temporal imbalance into sustained vascular and renal injury remain unclear. Increasing evidence suggests that circadian misalignment may promote endothelial dysfunction, vascular remodeling, and renal injury through ferroptosis driven by oxidative stress dysregulation, thereby increasing the risk of hypertension. Based on current evidence, this review proposes that circadian disruption induces a temporal mismatch between oxidative stress generation and antioxidant defense, thereby lowering the threshold for ferroptosis in cardiovascular and renal tissues. This process may amplify hemodynamic stress, impair endothelial integrity, and disturb renal sodium handling, ultimately contributing to the development and progression of hypertension. Although direct causal evidence remains limited, this review integrates circadian biology with ferroptosis and provides a mechanistic link between time-dependent physiological regulation and structural organ damage, highlighting a potentially promising strategy for future hypertension intervention.

title: Matrix bound nanovesicles from decellularized pericardium facilitate angiogenesis.
authorString: Di Francesco D, Di Varsavia C, Regano I, Di Nunno L, Casarella S, Clemente N, Mantovani D, Boccafoschi F.
abstractText: Therapeutic angiogenesis is a regenerative medicine approach which aims to induce revascularization for tissue repair. Among the existing strategies used to promote angiogenesis, biomaterials derived from decellularized tissues and composed of extracellular matrix (dECM) possess intrinsic angiogenic and regenerative potential. Recently, a bioactive component of such ECM materials has been identified; specifically, matrix bound nanovesicles (MBV). MBV have been shown to possess highly bioactive and tissue-specific cargo, and the ability to induce a potent immunomodulatory and regenerative response. However, their angiogenic potential has not been studied yet. Herein, the angiogenic properties of MBV derived from bovine pericardia dECM is evaluated. MBV show cytocompatibility toward endothelial cells, enhancing their functional phenotype and inducing the expression of angiogenic markers. In the presence of MBV, endothelial cells form three-dimensional monolayered endothelial vessel-like structures in tube formation assay. MBV also enhance endothelial sprouting in aortic ring assay. Finally, in hind limb ischemia in vivo model, MBV prevent tissue necrosis and restore vascularization and tissue function. These results demonstrate the angiogenic potential of MBV from pericardia ECM and represent a promising approach for therapeutic angiogenesis in regenerative medicine applications.

title: Progress in NK cell-based immunotherapy for solid tumors and an exploration of its cardiovascular safety.
authorString: Chen J, Shen J, Fu X, Jiang M, Liu R, Qiao Q, Hu Y.

journal.title: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

abstractText: Natural killer (NK) cell-based immunotherapy has become a research focus in cellular immunotherapy in recent years,which has advanced rapidly in the treatment of solid tumors. NK cells are key effector cells of innate immunity and can kill abnormal target cells without prior sensitization. A broad consensus holds that NK cell-based immunotherapy may become a new strategy for solid tumor treatment with lower risk and lower cost than T-cell-based immunotherapy. However, its translation from theory to clinical application remains constrained by relevant risks, and research on its cardiovascular safety is still largely absent. This review summarizes the latest research progress of NK cell-based immunotherapy in solid tumors and discusses its cardiovascular safety.

title: Case Report: <sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT findings and SUVmax characterization in a dog with apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma.
authorString: Shim B, Kim Y, Lee S.
abstractText: Apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA) is a malignant epithelial tumor in dogs that commonly metastasizes to regional lymph nodes. Although <sup>18</sup>F-fluorodeoxyglucose (<sup>18</sup>F-FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) has been mentioned as a staging modality for this tumor, detailed imaging findings and maximum standardized uptake values (SUVmax) have not previously been reported. A 10-year-old castrated male Maltese was referred for a right anal sac mass and suspected lymph node metastasis. Preoperative <sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT revealed increased uptake in the primary mass (SUVmax 7.3), the internal iliac lymph node (SUVmax 6.35), and the lumbar aortic lymph node (SUVmax 4.3), with no evidence of distant metastasis. Therefore, the dog was therefore classified as Stage IIIa. Based on these findings, intra-abdominal lymphadenectomy and right anal sacculectomy were performed. Histopathology confirmed AGASACA in the primary mass and morphologically similar metastatic adenocarcinoma in the resected lymph nodes. To our knowledge, this is the first report of <sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT findings and SUVmax values in a dog with AGASACA and histologically confirmed lymph node metastases. These findings suggest that PET/CT may provide complementary metabolic information for preoperative nodal staging.

title: Osseous and Vascular Course Anomalies in Nontraumatic Vertebral Artery Dissection: A Per-Vessel Case-Control Study.
authorString: Shono K, Matsubara S, Sato Y, Shikata E, Shirakawa N.
abstractText:
Background

Vertebral artery (VA) dissection (VAD) is a common cause of stroke in young and middle-aged adults. Although many cases are idiopathic, we hypothesized that overlooked osseous and vascular course anomalies (hereafter, structural anomalies) may be associated with VAD. In this study, we investigated the prevalence of these structural anomalies in patients with nontraumatic VAD using per-vessel analysis.

Methods

In this retrospective single-center case-control study, we analyzed structural anomalies in 13 consecutive patients (26 vessels) diagnosed with nontraumatic VAD at our institution between January 2022 and December 2025. For comparison, all eligible control patients during the same period whose computed tomography angiography field of view fully included the cervical region required to assess high-entry VA were included (50 patients, 100 vessels). The anatomic relationship between the VA and adjacent cervical osseous structures was evaluated using 3-dimensional computed tomography angiography. Primary end points were arcuate foramen presence, high-entry VA, and craniovertebral junction malformation with persistent first intersegmental artery. Images were independently evaluated by 2 neurosurgeons.

Results

Structural anomalies were identified in 76.9% (20/26) of the vessels in the VAD group, compared with 11.0% (11/100) in the control group (P=1.21 × 10-10; odds ratio, 25.75 [95% CI, 7.99-96.9]). At the patient level, structural anomalies were present on the ipsilateral side in 12 out of 13 patients (92.3%) and on the contralateral side in 8 out of 13 (61.5%); this paired difference did not reach statistical significance (exact McNemar test, P=0.219). The arcuate foramen (50.0%) and high-entry VA (19.2%) were the most common sites in the VAD group. Interrater reliability was excellent (raw agreement, 99.0%; κ=0.95 [95% CI, 0.86-1.00]).

Conclusions

The findings support the possibility that some VADs traditionally considered idiopathic may be associated with mechanically mediated injury within a broader spectrum related to the concept of bony stroke.

title: Apparent Diffusion Coefficient Composition and Tissue Heterogeneity as Predictors of Functional Outcomes After Endovascular Thrombectomy in Patients With Large Ischemic Core.
authorString: Kim H, Seo BS, Ryu WS, Choi KH, Kim JT, Park MS.
abstractText:
Background

Recent trials established endovascular thrombectomy efficacy in large ischemic cores, yet outcomes remain heterogeneous despite similar infarct volumes, suggesting that current volumetric assessments may not fully capture tissue viability. We examined whether tissue composition quantified by apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) distribution and tissue heterogeneity within baseline diffusion-weighted imaging lesions are associated with functional outcomes in large-core patients after successful endovascular thrombectomy.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed patients with large vessel occlusion with large ischemic cores (diffusion-weighted imaging candidate volume ≥50 mL) achieving successful reperfusion after endovascular thrombectomy. We quantified ADC tissue composition as proportions within 3 ADC ranges relative to total diffusion-weighted imaging lesion volume: low (<540), mid (540-700), and high (>700 × 10-6 mm2/s). Separately, tissue heterogeneity was assessed using Shannon entropy, a metric quantifying ADC distribution heterogeneity. The primary outcome was 3-month good functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale score of 0-3), analyzed via adjusted logistic regression.

Results

Among 126 patients (age, 70.8±12.4 years; 60.3% men; diffusion-weighted imaging candidate volume, 93.7±41.2 mL), 39.7% achieved a good functional outcome. Both tissue heterogeneity (adjusted odds ratio, 1.45 per 0.1-unit increase, 1.09-1.93, P=0.011, area under the curve, 0.671) and mid-ADC fraction (adjusted odds ratio, 1.78 per 5% increase, 1.20-2.63, P=0.004, area under the curve, 0.688) were associated with good functional outcomes. Neither low-ADC nor high-ADC fractions showed significant associations with functional outcomes.

Conclusions

Higher mid-ADC (540-700 × 10-6 mm2/s) fraction and greater tissue heterogeneity predicted favorable outcomes in patients with large ischemic core, indicating that tissue composition within the ischemic core, beyond its volume, is associated with functional outcome after reperfusion. Among large-core patients who achieved successful reperfusion, ADC-based tissue characterization may help predict functional outcome.

title: Association between Blood Biomarkers and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity: A Retrospective Study from Indonesia.
authorString: Liana P, Mahrami PZ, Rahmawati E, Yuniza Y, Oktariana D, Umar TP.

journal.title: Saudi journal of medicine & medical sciences

abstractText:
Background

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease, and laboratory parameters are essential for monitoring disease activity.

Objectives

To determine the association between blood biomarkers and SLE disease activity in an Indonesian tertiary hospital.

Methods

This retrospective study included adult patients with SLE treated at a tertiary hospital in Indonesia between January 2022 and August 2024. Patients were categorized into mild (inactive) or moderate-severe (active) disease activity groups, based on the MEX-SLEDAI score. Demographic and laboratory variables were collected. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was done to assess discriminatory performance. Multivariate logistic regression was conducted to identify independent indicators of moderate-severe disease activity.

Results

A total of 110 patients were included: 52 with active and 58 with inactive SLE. Between the groups, patients with active SLE had significantly lower hemoglobin (P < 0.001), hematocrit (P < 0.001), and platelet count (P = 0.019). In addition, significant differences were found for differential leukocyte counts and inflammatory hematological parameters, except the systemic immune-inflammation response index. ROC analysis showed that neutrophil percentage and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio had the highest discriminatory performance (for both, AUC = 0.819), with optimal cut-offs of >68% (sensitivity: 67.3%; specificity: 87.9%) and >2.83 (sensitivity: 75.0%; specificity: 84.5%), respectively. In multivariate logistic regression, platelet count (P = 0.048) and eosinophil percentage (P = 0.026) were found to be independently associated with moderate-severe SLE activity.

Conclusions

This study found that low platelet count and eosinopenia were independently associated with moderate-severe SLE disease activity, while neutrophil percentage and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio demonstrated good discriminatory performance for distinguishing between active and inactive SLE.

title: Emergency department extracorporeal membrane oxygenation: Current concepts, systems-based implementation, and future directions.
authorString: Özlüer YE, Savaş AM, Serin M, Kocailik A.
abstractText: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has emerged as a time-critical resuscitative strategy for carefully selected patients with refractory cardiac arrest and other reversible causes of circulatory or respiratory failure. As the role of emergency department ECMO (ED ECMO) continues to expand, emergency physicians have become integral members of multidisciplinary extracorporeal resuscitation teams. This review aims to summarize the current evidence on ED ECMO while highlighting practical considerations for program implementation, workflow optimization, and future directions. This invited narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence regarding the indications, patient selection, cannulation strategies, pericannulation management, and postcannulation physiological challenges of ED ECMO, with particular emphasis on extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation. In addition to published literature, practical aspects of ED ECMO implementation, including multidisciplinary team organization, operational governance, workflow optimization, quality metrics, and institutional experience, are discussed. Emerging concepts such as artificial intelligence-assisted decision support, digital twin-enabled system modeling, and regional implementation strategies are also reviewed. Current evidence indicates that successful ED ECMO depends not only on technical proficiency but also on timely patient selection, standardized protocols, efficient multidisciplinary coordination, and optimized operational systems. Contemporary implementation frameworks emphasize integrated governance, continuous quality improvement, and structured performance metrics to enhance clinical effectiveness. Emerging digital technologies, including artificial intelligence and systems modeling, may further improve patient selection, operational efficiency, and program scalability. ED ECMO should be regarded as a comprehensive, systems-based resuscitation strategy rather than a standalone rescue procedure. Future progress is likely to depend on the integration of evidence-based patient selection, standardized workflows, multidisciplinary collaboration, intelligent operational systems, and continuous quality improvement. The development of regional ED ECMO networks supported by robust emergency medical service infrastructure may improve timely access to extracorporeal resuscitation and optimize patient outcomes.

title: Temporal changes in monocyte subsets and cytokine production capacity of mononuclear cells following myocardial infarction.
authorString: Los J, Hol IH, Mensink FB, Östman M, Cetinyurek-Yavuz A, Cornel JH, van Geuns RM, Riksen NP, El Messaoudi S.

journal.title: Journal of molecular and cellular cardiology plus

abstractText: Following myocardial infarction (MI), recruited monocytes play an essential role in tissue repair and scar formation. However, the temporal changes in circulating monocyte subsets and their functional characteristics remain incompletely understood. We investigated systemic inflammation and circulating monocyte heterogeneity in 72 patients during the first 12 weeks after MI. Systemic inflammation was markedly increased immediately after MI, as reflected by significant elevated C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels. During follow-up, the proportion of classical monocytes decreased, whereas the relative abundance of non-classical monocytes increased. In the acute phase, cluster of differentiation 11b expression on intermediate monocytes was elevated, while peripheral blood mononuclear cells produced lower levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and IL-1Ra. Together, the results support the presence of a relatively more inflammatory monocyte profile during the acute phase of MI.

title: Balloon-Augmented Bicuspid Scallop Intentional Laceration to Induce Circularization of the Aortic Implant (BA-BISILICA) During TAVR.
authorString: Shahmoradi V, Shah VN, Shaya GE, Ipek EG, Rier JD, Harvey JE, Davies RE, Park JY, Tolerico PH, Bruce CG.
abstractText:
Objective

Sievers type 1 bicuspid aortic valve anatomy, characterized by a calcified raphe, eccentric calcification, and elliptical annular geometry, may impede complete transcatheter heart valve (THV) expansion during transcatheter aortic valve replacement. A stepwise transcatheter electrosurgical leaflet-laceration technique is described to optimize THV deployment.

Key steps

Cerebral embolic protection is established. A steerable guiding system is positioned adjacent to the calcified raphe. An electrified guidewire is used to traverse the fused leaflet. Balloon augmentation is performed. A "flying V" rail configuration is created. Electrosurgical raphe laceration is performed. The THV is deployed.

Pitfalls

Pitfalls include embolization of calcium, difficulty lacerating a heavily calcified raphe, and hemodynamic instability. Technical tips include cerebral embolic protection, precise positioning of the traversal system adjacent to the raphe, balloon dilatation of the traversal channel, and prompt THV deployment.

Take-home message

Transcatheter electrosurgical leaflet laceration may facilitate uniform THV expansion in Sievers type 1 bicuspid aortic valve patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement.

title: Preimplantation Genetic Testing: Patient and Provider Preferences, Ethical Considerations, and Obstetrical and Neonatal Harms Analyses.
authorString: Ontario Health, Ontario Health .
abstractText: Preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) refers to a group of genetic tests that analyze the DNA of embryos for chromosomal or genetic anomalies prior to the transfer to the uterus during in vitro fertilization (IVF). Ontario Health conducted a series of health technology assessments (HTA) of PGT, including assessment of PGT-A, PGT-M, and PGT-SR. In this report, we summarize the findings common to all 3 HTAS, including a rapid review of the qualitative literature, direct patient engagement, and a review of published literature examining ethical considerations relating to PGT. We also undertook a rapid review of the obstetrical and neonatal harms of PGT using trophectoderm biopsy. Reviews of the clinical and economic impact of PGT-A, the clinical impact of PGT-M, and the clinical impact of PGT-SR have been published separately.

title: Large-scale proteomics identifies circulating markers of pulmonary pressure and pulmonary hypertension risk.
authorString: Giugni FR, Santos M, Yang Y, Lamberson V, Claggett B, Hoogeveen R, Ballantyne C, Systrom D, Waxman A, Buckley L, Yu B, San José Estépar R, Hegde SM, Shah AM.
abstractText: Pulmonary hypertension, defined by elevated pressure in the pulmonary circulation, is morbid and diagnosing is challenging as no early-stage blood markers are currently available. Here we show that large-scale proteomic profiling across several independent observational cohorts identifies 22 proteins associated with echocardiography-derived pulmonary artery systolic pressure, several of which are independently associated with invasive measures of pulmonary vascular disease, structural remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature, and subsequent risk of pulmonary hypertension. Genetic analyses support a potential causal role for NOTCH3 and identify a common splice-regulating genetic variant that may modify susceptibility to pulmonary vascular stressors. Protein-based clustering further reveals two distinct biological subtypes associated with increased risk of pulmonary hypertension. Together, these findings identify candidate biomarkers of pulmonary hypertension, implicate pulmonary vascular remodeling in early-stage disease with a potential causal role for NOTCH3, and discover and validate two distinct endotypes of pulmonary hypertension risk in the community.

title: Endovascular Management With a Fenestration Technique of an Iatrogenic Thoracic Chronic Type B Aortic Dissection.
authorString: Mesquita da Cunha H, Landsweerdt S, Possoz J, Swaelens C.
abstractText: We report the case of an 86-year-old woman who developed an intraoperative type B aortic dissection during ascending aortic replacement for an ascending aortic aneurysm. Postoperative imaging demonstrated an uncomplicated dissection extending to the infrarenal aorta. At 10 weeks, follow-up imaging revealed rapid aneurysmal expansion of the false lumen. Thoracic endovascular aortic repair was performed with adjunctive cerebrospinal fluid drainage, rapid pacing, and image fusion guidance. An intimal fenestration technique was used to optimize the distal sealing zone, extending the disruption from a pre-existing re-entry tear. A type Ib endoleak necessitated additional stent-graft deployment, which in turn caused occlusion of the left renal and superior mesenteric arteries. The STABILISE technique (stent-assisted balloon-induced intimal disruption and relamination in aortic dissection repair) with a PETTICOAT (Provisional Extension To Induce Complete Attachment) bare stent restored renal perfusion, and targeted stenting re-established mesenteric flow. A postprocedural pseudoaneurysm was managed conservatively and resolved with spontaneous thrombosis within 48 hours. The patient was discharged on postoperative day seven, asymptomatic, with complete exclusion of the dissection, patent visceral vessels, and no endoleak confirmed at six-week follow-up. This case illustrates that combining distal flap fenestration with STABILISE relamination and a comprehensive endovascular toolkit can successfully manage complex chronic type B aortic dissections, even in elderly, high-risk patients-provided that adequate perioperative safety measures and a broad endovascular armamentarium are available to address unanticipated complications.

title: Atheroembolic Blue Toe Syndrome Progressing to Below-Knee Amputation Despite Attempted Source Control and Revascularization: A Case Report.
authorString: Echavarria DD, Gal I, Espinoza ST, Gershbein A, Gershbein D.
abstractText: Blue toe syndrome is characterized by painful blue or violaceous discoloration of one or more toes caused by impaired digital arterial perfusion. We present a 72-year-old woman with peripheral arterial disease, diabetes mellitus, antiphospholipid syndrome, and prior thromboembolic disease who developed dusky-blue discoloration of the left third toe. Initial arterial duplex demonstrated no major arterial occlusion, while computed tomography angiography with runoff showed distal infrarenal aortic soft plaque and distal tibial/pedal arterial disease. The aortic lesion was considered the suspected proximal embolic source in the setting of concomitant distal tibial and pedal arterial disease. The patient underwent endovascular aortic repair for proximal source control, but the left third toe nevertheless progressed to dry gangrene and required amputation. Over the following months, she developed nonhealing wounds, infections with Pseudomonas aeruginosa and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), worsened distal perfusion, and osteomyelitis. There were multiple limb salvage procedures, including angioplasty, toe amputation, common plantar embolectomy, plantar bypass, transmetatarsal amputation, Achilles tendon lengthening, antibiotic bead placement, and external fixation. Following these procedures, however, the foot developed worsening ischemic and infected tissue loss and needed an emergency left below-knee amputation. Final pathology demonstrated significant findings, including gangrenous necrosis, chronic osteomyelitis, calcific atherosclerosis, and tibial vessel occlusions. This case showcases how blue toe syndrome can progress despite source control when severe distal runoff disease, poor wound oxygenation, and recurrent infections are present.

title: The Many Faces of Familial Mediterranean Fever in Children: Lessons From a Moroccan Cohort and Four Diagnostic Pitfalls.
authorString: Mohamed El Kerim M, Sara A, Elhaddadi H, Elouali A, Rkain M, Babakhouya A.
abstractText:
Introduction

Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is the prototypical hereditary autoinflammatory disease. Inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, it is associated with mutations in the MEditerranean FeVer (MEFV) gene. Its clinical heterogeneity poses a major diagnostic challenge in pediatrics, particularly in developing countries where access to genetic testing remains limited.

Objectives

To describe the clinical, epidemiological, biological, and genetic characteristics of pediatric FMF in the Oriental region of Morocco and to document diagnostic pitfalls through illustrative case reports.

Materials and methods

A retrospective descriptive study including 14 children followed for FMF in the Pediatrics Department of the Mohammed VI University Hospital in Oujda over an 11.5-year period (January 2015 to June 2026). The diagnosis was based on the Yalçınkaya-Özen pediatric criteria and/or genetic confirmation via MEFV gene sequencing.

Results

The mean age at diagnosis was 6.5 years (range: 2-14 years). A marked male predominance was observed in 12 (85.7%); sex ratio (6:1). Parental consanguinity was present in 5/14 (35.7%) of cases. All patients were from the Oriental region 14/14 (100.0%). The predominant clinical manifestations were recurrent fever in 14 (100.0%), abdominal pain in 12/14 (85.7%), and arthralgia/arthritis in 11/14 (78.6%). MEFV gene sequencing was positive in 9/14 (64.3%) of patients, with a predominance of the M694V mutation in 5/14 (35.7%), of whom 3/5 (60.0%) were homozygous. Four illustrative case reports document atypical presentations that resulted in a diagnostic delay of more than two years: a polyarticular form mimicking juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), a coronary aneurysm mistaken for Kawasaki disease, recurrent febrile seizures, and predominantly erysipelas-like erythema. Colchicine was effective in all 14/14 (100.0%) treated cases. No amyloid amyloidosis (AA) was detected during follow-up.

Conclusion

Pediatric FMF is underdiagnosed in the Oriental region of Morocco. Its clinical polymorphism leads to diagnostic delays with harmful consequences. A rigorous clinical evaluation supported by targeted genetic sequencing is essential for early diagnosis and prompt initiation of colchicine therapy.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Corrected Carotid Flow Time for Assessing Fluid Responsiveness in Patients With Septic or Hypovolemic Shock: A Prospective Diagnostic Accuracy Study.
authorString: Cherian D, Jain G, Agarwal A, Kumar B, Bhardwaj BB.
abstractText: Background Predicting fluid responsiveness in patients with hemodynamic instability remains challenging. Corrected carotid flow time (CFTc) is a non-invasive bedside Doppler measure proposed to identify fluid responsiveness, but its reported performance is inconsistent. We evaluated baseline CFTc as a predictor of fluid responsiveness and assessed whether the post-bolus percentage change in CFTc corresponded with the echocardiographic change in stroke volume. Materials and methods This prospective diagnostic accuracy study included 80 adult patients presenting with new-onset shock of presumed septic and/or hypovolemic origin. All received a clinically indicated first bolus of 10 mL/kg Ringer's lactate. Stroke volume (SV) measured by transthoracic echocardiography and CFTc by carotid Doppler were obtained at baseline (T1) and 20 minutes after the bolus (T2). Responders were defined by a ≥15% rise in SV. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to assess the diagnostic performance of CFTc and its percentage change. Results An infective focus was identified in 61 patients (76.2%), with no source documented in 19 patients (23.8%). Thirty-two patients (40.0%) were responders. A baseline CFTc cut-off of ≤324.03 ms predicted responders with 71.9% sensitivity and 47.9% specificity (AUROC 0.563, 95% CI 0.435-0.691; p = 0.343). The percentage change in CFTc showed poor discrimination for fluid responsiveness (AUROC 0.568, 95% CI 0.436-0.700; p = 0.305) and corresponded weakly with the percentage change in SV (Spearman rho = 0.141; p = 0.213). Non-responders experienced recurrent hypotension more often and required earlier initiation of vasopressors. Conclusion In adults with new-onset shock, baseline CFTc did not usefully discriminate echocardiography-defined fluid responders, and the post-fluid change in CFTc showed weak correspondence with the change in stroke volume. CFTc should not be relied on alone to guide fluid resuscitation in this population.

title: Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction Following Significant Weight Loss During Tirzepatide Therapy: A Case Report.
authorString: Roy A, Pabani UK, Kyriakou A, Elliott MK.
abstractText: Tirzepatide is a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist that produces substantial weight loss and improves multiple cardiometabolic risk factors. Current evidence supports its cardiovascular safety, with no established association between licensed tirzepatide therapy and acute coronary syndrome (ACS). As its clinical use continues to expand, reporting unusual cardiovascular presentations remains important for pharmacovigilance. We present a case of a 48-year-old South Asian man with obesity, diet-controlled prediabetes, a history of smoking, and a family history of premature coronary artery disease who had been receiving tirzepatide for approximately 18 months, achieving a weight loss of approximately 30 kg. Following increased physical activity, he developed progressive exertional chest pain and dyspnoea. Electrocardiography demonstrated inferolateral ischaemic changes, and serial high-sensitivity troponin T measurements were consistent with a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Transthoracic echocardiography showed preserved left ventricular systolic function with inferior regional wall motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography revealed severe triple-vessel coronary artery disease involving the left anterior descending, left circumflex, and right coronary arteries. He subsequently underwent successful coronary artery bypass grafting with an uncomplicated postoperative recovery. Although a temporal association existed between prolonged tirzepatide therapy, substantial weight loss, and presentation with NSTEMI, the presence of advanced multivessel coronary artery disease suggests longstanding atherosclerosis rather than a direct adverse effect of tirzepatide. A more plausible explanation is that significant weight loss improved functional capacity, allowing increased physical activity that unmasked previously silent obstructive coronary artery disease. This interpretation is consistent with current evidence demonstrating favourable cardiovascular effects of tirzepatide while acknowledging that causality cannot be established from a single case. This case highlights the importance of thoroughly evaluating new exertional chest pain in patients receiving tirzepatide despite marked improvements in weight and metabolic health. Clinicians should remain vigilant for underlying coronary artery disease in individuals with traditional cardiovascular risk factors. This report describes a temporal association rather than a causal relationship and contributes to the growing body of real-world experience with tirzepatide.

title: Recurrent Pleuropericardial Effusions Following Amplatzer Amulet Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: A Case of Post-Cardiac Injury Syndrome.
authorString: Reece J, Shannon B, Sofka S.
abstractText: Post-cardiac injury syndrome (PCIS) is an inflammatory pleuropericardial syndrome that may follow myocardial, pericardial, or iatrogenic cardiac injury. Although pericardial effusion is a recognized complication of left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO), recurrent pleuropericardial inflammation after LAAO is less commonly described. We report a patient with persistent atrial fibrillation who underwent uncomplicated LAAO with a 28-mm Amplatzer Amulet device (Abbott Medical, Plymouth, MN, USA) following a recent hemorrhagic stroke. Post-implantation transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated appropriate device positioning without peridevice leak or pericardial effusion. Within two weeks, the patient developed chest pain, dyspnea, electrocardiographic ST-segment elevations, markedly elevated CRP, and a large hemorrhagic pericardial effusion with tamponade requiring drainage of 780 mL of frank blood. The subsequent course was characterized by recurrent unilateral left exudative pleural effusions requiring repeated thoracenteses and chest tube drainage, followed by recurrence of both pleural and pericardial effusions. Serial microbiologic and cytologic studies were negative, and imaging demonstrated no evidence of malignancy. Colchicine was discontinued following an interval hospitalization, after which pleuropericardial effusions and systemic inflammation recurred. Following pleural drainage and reinitiation of colchicine, CRP declined from 87.8 mg/L (<8 mg/L) to 22.5 mg/L (<8 mg/L), respiratory symptoms resolved, and the patient was discharged home on room air. The temporal relationship to LAAO, recurrent pleuropericardial involvement, inflammatory response, exclusion of alternative etiologies, and clinical course were consistent with PCIS. This case highlights PCIS as an important consideration in patients presenting with recurrent pleural or pericardial effusions after LAAO while emphasizing the need to exclude mechanical device complications.

title: Management of bleeding and nonelective invasive procedures in patients receiving direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs): a 5-year single-center observational study.
authorString: Pontis A, Mansour A, Maurice A, Rousseau C, Nédelec-Gac F, Guéret P, Soulat L, Maucorps L, Godier A, Gouin-Thibault I.

journal.title: Research and practice in thrombosis and haemostasis

abstractText:
Background

Guidelines exist for managing bleeding or nonelective invasive procedures in patients on direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), but their clinical impact remains unclear.

Objectives

To describe the management of patients who had DOAC concentrations measured for bleeding or nonelective invasive procedures and to assess associations between guideline compliance, outcomes, and DOAC concentrations.

Methods

This retrospective, single-center study (2014-2018) included adult patients receiving dabigatran etexilate, rivaroxaban, or apixaban who required hospital care for bleeding or nonelective invasive procedures and had DOAC concentrations measured at the time of the event. Compliance with French and European guidelines was assessed. Adverse outcomes-a composite of all-cause mortality, worsening or new bleeding, and thrombotic events-were recorded until discharge.

Results

A total of 584 events (432 procedures and 152 bleeding episodes) in 547 patients were analyzed. Guideline compliance was 79% and showed no association with outcomes. Among 95 events treated with prothrombin complex concentrates, one thrombotic event occurred. DOAC concentrations were higher in the bleeding group than in the procedural group (122 [IQR, 57-219] vs 55 [IQR, 25-127] ng/mL), but bleeding severity was not associated with drug levels. In bleeding patients, rivaroxaban concentrations were higher in those with adverse outcomes compared with those without (243 [IQR, 74-367] vs 88 [IQR, 35-199] ng/mL).

Conclusion

In a large cohort of patients who had DOAC concentrations measured at the time of a bleeding or a nonelective invasive procedure, compliance with guidelines was high and not associated with outcomes. In bleeding patients, rivaroxaban concentrations were higher in those with vs without adverse events.

title: Spontaneous Renal Hemorrhage in an Anticoagulated Patient With Prior Large-Vessel Vasculitis: A Wonder of Its Own.
authorString: de Silva D, Peiris A, Patel A.
abstractText: Wunderlich syndrome (WS) is a spontaneous renal or perinephric hemorrhage occurring in the absence of trauma. Renal neoplasms are the most common cause, although vascular, infectious, cystic, and coagulopathic etiologies also occur. When active extravasation is detected on imaging, angiography with embolization is the preferred approach. We report a case of an 81-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation on apixaban and large-vessel vasculitis complicated by aortitis and a prior intramural aortic hematoma, who presented with four days of weakness, nausea, diarrhea, and right-sided abdominal pain, and was hypotensive at 71/56 mmHg. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) demonstrated a 12 × 12 cm right perinephric hematoma with active extravasation from a serpiginous vessel at the lower renal pole. Interventional radiology recommended medical management rather than embolization, citing the procedural risk associated with her aortitis. Treatment consisted of discontinuation of anticoagulation, reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K, transfusion of three units of packed red blood cells, crystalloid resuscitation, and vasopressor support. The course was complicated by oliguric acute kidney injury, with creatinine rising from 1.30 to 3.72 mg/dL, and by Escherichia coli bacteremia of urinary source. Serologic evaluation demonstrated a positive perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (p-ANCA) result, with negative myeloperoxidase (MPO) and proteinase 3 (PR3) antibodies, and pulse methylprednisolone was administered. Urine output was reestablished with intravenous furosemide, vasopressors were discontinued by hospital day 4, and creatinine returned to 1.38 mg/dL before discharge on hospital day 7. This case demonstrates that conservative management can achieve hemodynamic and renal recovery in WS with active extravasation when vascular comorbidity precludes embolization.

title: Severe Rhabdomyolysis With Minimal Muscular Symptoms After Long-Term Rosuvastatin Use: A Case Report and Brief Literature Review.
authorString: Izadian Bidgoli A, Gomez Usatorres A, Gomez Usatorres HA, Gomez Veliz A, Qayum T.
abstractText: Severe rhabdomyolysis may present with limited muscular symptoms despite substantial biochemical injury. We describe a case of suspected statin-associated rhabdomyolysis during prolonged rosuvastatin exposure. A 65-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, peripheral arterial disease requiring bilateral below-knee amputations, and previous rhabdomyolysis presented with generalized weakness, abdominal discomfort, and left flank pain. He had taken rosuvastatin for more than 10 years. Admission investigations demonstrated creatine kinase of 23,107 U/L, creatinine of 7.80 mg/dL, markedly elevated aminotransferases, and brown urine. Creatine kinase subsequently peaked at 38,747 U/L despite limited muscular complaints. Progressive azotemia and encephalopathy prompted hemodialysis. Rosuvastatin was discontinued, and supportive treatment was provided without immunosuppression. The reported myositis panel was negative, while magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated mild, nonspecific muscle edema. By discharge, weakness and encephalopathy had resolved, strength was preserved on focused examination, and creatine kinase had decreased to 1,003 U/L. The patient was advised to avoid all statins. Outpatient hemodialysis, rheumatology follow-up, and serial creatine kinase measurements were arranged, with anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibody testing and muscle biopsy planned if creatine kinase remained persistently elevated after discharge. This case highlights the discrepancy between biochemical severity and muscular symptoms during long-standing statin exposure. Improvement after statin withdrawal and supportive care supported a suspected statin-associated process but did not establish causality or exclude an autoimmune mechanism. Continued clinical and biochemical follow-up was essential to document recovery and determine the need for further investigation.

title: Recurrent Hypoglycemia and Hypercalcemia As Presenting Features of CD30-Positive Peripheral T-cell Lymphoma, Not Otherwise Specified.
authorString: Izadian Bidgoli A, Gomez Usatorres A, Gomez Usatorres HA, Gomez Veliz A, Noriega-Toledo D.
abstractText: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS), is an aggressive mature T-cell neoplasm that may present with nonspecific systemic and metabolic abnormalities. A 73-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with progressive weakness, altered mental status, recurrent hypoglycemia, and hypercalcemia, accompanied by acute kidney injury, pancytopenia, diffuse lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. A complete critical-sample evaluation during hypoglycemia was unavailable, and the mechanism of the parathyroid hormone (PTH)-independent hypercalcemia could not be established because PTH-related peptide and vitamin D metabolite measurements were unavailable. Core biopsy of a left axillary lymph node demonstrated a mature CD4-positive T-cell lymphoma with strong diffuse CD30 expression, reduced CD7, negative anaplastic lymphoma kinase and Epstein-Barr virus-encoded RNA studies, and a Ki-67 proliferation index exceeding 90%, supporting PTCL-NOS after exclusion of other supported mature T-cell lymphoma entities. Classification remained limited by the absence of an excisional biopsy and additional molecular studies. Prednisone cytoreduction was followed by cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisone, with brentuximab vedotin planned but not documented as administered. The course was complicated by profound myelosuppression, Klebsiella pneumoniae pneumonia, and neutropenic septic shock. Formal response assessment was not possible because complete staging and adequate follow-up were unavailable. This case highlights the importance of prompt tissue diagnosis when unexplained metabolic abnormalities coexist with cytopenias and generalized lymphadenopathy. Although hypoglycemia and hypercalcemia occurred in association with PTCL-NOS, the available data do not establish a causal or paraneoplastic relationship.

title: Endovascular management of acute and chronic arterial mesenteric ischaemia: A narrative review of evidence informing interventional radiology treatment.
authorString: Keady C, O'Malley CM, Mohamed SA, Bell J, Crotty C, Patton A, O'Regan D, Keeling A, McGrath A, Given M, Mulholland D, Sheehan M.
abstractText: Mesenteric ischaemia is a potentially life-threatening vascular disorder caused by impaired intestinal perfusion, with treatment selection requiring consideration of clinical presentation, bowel viability and lesion anatomy. This narrative review examines evidence informing interventional radiology decisions in arterial acute mesenteric ischaemia (AMI) and chronic mesenteric ischaemia (CMI). MEDLINE/PubMed was searched from inception to December 31, 2025, supplemented by reference-list screening and targeted guideline searches. Qualitative evidence synthesis considered patient selection, study design, adjunctive treatments, outcomes and follow-up. In AMI, endovascular techniques can restore perfusion, but predominantly retrospective evidence does not establish superiority over surgery in bowel preservation or survival. For CMI requiring revascularisation, European Society for Vascular Surgery guidelines recommend an initial endovascular approach, supported by Cardiovascular and Interventional Radiological Society of Europe consensus-based guidance. Observational comparisons associate endovascular treatment with lower perioperative morbidity, and surgery with less symptom recurrence. By linking individual treatment decisions to society guidance and supporting studies, this review complements existing comprehensive reviews and guidance documents. It distinguishes formal recommendations and consensus-based practice from technical feasibility and demonstrated comparative patient benefit, while identifying unresolved questions concerning AMI reperfusion strategies and device selection, in addition to antithrombotic therapy and restenosis management in CMI.

title: Compressed Branching Geometry in a Bovine-Type Aortic Arch: A Morphometric Cadaveric Case Report and Systematic Review of the Literature.
authorString: Naoun AA, Figueroa Monsanto HL, Veras W.
abstractText: Anatomical variation in aortic arch branching is common and clinically significant, yet specimen-level morphometric characterization of a bovine-type aortic arch (BAA) remains scarce. We report a two-branch bovine-type arch that was identified during cadaveric dissection of a formalin-embalmed male decedent in his late 70s. The left common carotid artery arose proximally from the brachiocephalic trunk, which then bifurcated into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries; the left subclavian artery arose separately from the arch. We contextualized this finding by conducting a systematic review of cadaveric studies reporting the same configuration. Five database sources yielded 191 records, of which 14 cadaveric studies met the eligibility criteria and were appraised using two Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical-appraisal instruments. The specimen's brachiocephalic trunk measured 18.73 mm externally, which falls within the 18.39-18.84 mm external-diameter range reported in the bovine cadaveric literature. Its luminal diameter measured 17.1 mm, which was also within the corresponding 16.85-17.35 mm range. This caliber may reflect a vessel accommodating combined bilateral carotid perfusion, rather than a pathological dilatation. The single interostial distance between the brachiocephalic trunk and the left subclavian artery measured 7.18 mm externally and 8.5 mm endoluminally. The endoluminal measurement was 34.2% below the 12.91 mm reported in a prior cadaveric BAA specimen and 11.5% below the 9.6 mm mean reported in the only bovine cadaveric series that reported this parameter, with both measured endoluminally. The measured carotid take-off length of 8.01 mm fell within, but near the lower limit of, the range reported across five previously published cadaveric bovine studies (6.0-17.3 mm). The mid-arch diameter measured 25.18 mm, 16.1% below the reported male mean that was obtained at the corresponding anatomical plane using outer-wall measurements. The arch showed proximal-to-distal tapering without aneurysmal ectasia, mural thrombus, or atherosclerotic calcification. Four of the prior included studies reported BAA-specific morphometry that could be interpreted against a stated convention. The reported interbranch distances varied by more than sixfold; heterogeneous measurement methodologies likely contributed substantially to this apparent variability, as most studies did not define their anatomical landmarks. Harmonizing three series with disparate measurement conventions to a common landmark framework yielded closely concordant interbranch distances. The compact BAA branching geometry observed here may be relevant to the available anatomical corridor during arch and carotid interventions, although clinical consequences cannot be inferred from this limited dataset. Standardized measurement protocols with explicitly defined anatomical landmarks are therefore necessary to enable meaningful cross-study morphometric comparisons.

title: Delayed Healing and Infection in Elderly Intermediate-Severity Burns: Clinical Predictors and Implications for Care.
authorString: Ghorbel I, Moalla S, Makhlouf H, Gargouri A, Agrebi A, Taieb I, Ennouri KH.

journal.title: Annals of burns and fire disasters

abstractText: Burn injuries in elderly patients within resource-limited settings represent a major therapeutic challenge due to increased vulnerability associated with age-related physiological changes and prevalent comorbidities. This study focuses on intermediate-severity burns and aims to identify clinical predictors of delayed wound healing and burn wound infection in elderly patients in Central Tunisia. We conducted a retrospective study including patients aged 65 years and older who were hospitalized for thermal burns between January 2013 and December 2022. Demographic, clinical and outcome data were analyzed using SPSS v26. Prognostic factors for delayed healing and infection were identified through multivariate logistic regression. Among 414 burn admissions, 31 patients (7.48%) were aged ≥65 years. Flame burns were predominant (77.4%). Key predictors of poor outcomes included: total body surface area burned (TBSA) >10% (OR 3.2; 95% CI 1.4-7.1); full-thickness burns (OR 2.8; 95% CI 1.2-6.5); delayed admission >24 hours (OR 2.1; 95% CI 1.1-4.3). In elderly patients with intermediate-severity burns, early specialized intervention and optimal management of comorbidities are essential to reduce the risk of delayed healing and infection.

title: Libman-Sacks Endocarditis as the First Presentation of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus in a Young Man: A Multisystemic Diagnostic Challenge.
authorString: Waring S, Fletcher JW, Jones A.
abstractText: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a complex, phenotypically varied disorder that possesses wide-ranging cardiac involvement. Libman-Sacks endocarditis (LSE) is one such cardiac manifestation, which results from the deposition of verrucous, sessile lesions favoring the left-sided heart valves. LSE is typically clinically silent without significant valvular dysfunction. Such patients with LSE, however, are those most susceptible to a more severe clinical phenotype resulting from SLE. Here, we report a unique case of a 22-year-old man initially presenting with unilateral leg swelling found to be secondary to a deep-vein thrombosis. He subsequently developed a constellation of acute symptoms, including embolic strokes, splenic infarction, proteinuric kidney injury, and significant mitral regurgitation, all of which mimicked bacterial endocarditis. His complex, multi-systemic disease course presented diagnostic challenges. We highlight the need in such complex cases for a specialist-led multidisciplinary approach, including cardiologists and rheumatologists, to guide serological and radiological investigations. Early use of echocardiography, in particular 3D transesophageal imaging, was paramount in clinching the diagnosis of LSE as an index presentation of SLE and in the transition from intravenous antibiotics to immunosuppression. Our case underscores the importance of the multidisciplinary team and the role of echocardiography in identifying such patients with LSE in SLE and thereby those most vulnerable to significant end-organ sequelae.

title: Short-Term Outcomes of Lower-Extremity Surgical Revascularization for Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia Among Yemeni Patients: A Prospective Observational Study.
authorString: Al-Modwahi NY, Fadhel AM, Hamoud AM, Al-Modwahi YA, Halboob EA, Al-Hashedi A, Al-Mnari MA, Al-Motawakill MA.
abstractText:
Background

Chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) carries a high risk of amputation and mortality. We evaluated short-term clinical, hemodynamic, and quality-of-life outcomes after open lower-extremity surgical revascularization in a Yemeni cohort.

Methods

This single-center prospective observational cohort study was conducted at Al-Thawra Modern General Hospital, Sana'a, Yemen. We enrolled 39 consecutive adults with CLTI (Rutherford categories 4-6) who were selected for and considered fit to undergo open lower-extremity surgical revascularization between December 2022 and September 2024; follow-up was completed in December 2024. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Al-Thawra Hospital Ethics Committee (approval no. 33-2026), and written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The study was not registered. This was an exploratory consecutive cohort; no formal sample-size calculation was performed, and no contemporaneous endovascular, nonoperative, or primary-amputation comparator group was included. Primary endpoints were graft patency and limb salvage at three months. Secondary outcomes were secondary patency, postoperative complications, and changes in ankle-brachial index (ABI) and Vascular Quality of Life Questionnaire-6 (VascuQoL-6) scores. Paired comparisons used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; Fisher's exact tests were used for categorical comparisons.

Results

The mean age was 60.9 years (SD 9.7), and 30 patients (76.9%) were male. Diabetes mellitus and hypertension were present in 34 (87.2%) and 30 (76.9%) patients, respectively. Nineteen patients (48.7%) had ischemic rest pain, and 20 (51.3%) had tissue loss. Great saphenous vein (GSV) and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) grafts were used in 28 (71.8%) and 11 (28.2%) patients, respectively. At three months, primary patency was 84.6% (33/39 grafts; 95% CI 70.3%-92.8%), secondary patency was 89.7% (35/39 grafts; 95% CI 76.4%-95.9%), and limb salvage was 89.7% (35/39 patients; 95% CI 76.4%-95.9%). Given the small cohort, the confidence intervals around these estimates were relatively wide. Among the 35 patients with limb preservation, mean ABI increased from 0.35 (SD 0.11) to 0.55 (SD 0.12; mean difference 0.21, 95% CI 0.19-0.23; p<0.001), and mean VascuQoL-6 score increased from 10.3 (SD 2.9) to 16.6 (SD 4.0; mean difference 6.3, 95% CI 5.6-7.1; p<0.001). Complications occurred in nine patients (23.1%). In an exploratory unadjusted subgroup analysis, GSV use was associated with higher primary patency than PTFE use (92.9% vs 63.6%, p=0.042).

Conclusion

In this single-center prospective cohort, open surgical revascularization was feasible and was associated with 89.7% limb salvage and 84.6% primary patency at three months. Improvements in ABI and VascuQoL-6 were observed among patients with limb preservation. Autologous GSV use was associated with higher primary patency; this finding requires confirmation in larger, adjusted studies.

title: Lithium Toxicity Following Initiation of Semaglutide in a Patient With Bipolar Disorder: A Case Report.
authorString: Dhingra A, Nichols CM, Sanchez E, Ayyagari A, Rateshwar Y, Narvaez N.
abstractText: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists are increasingly prescribed for type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity, including among patients with severe mental illness. Their effects on gastrointestinal motility, oral intake, and volume status raise concern for interactions with drugs with narrow therapeutic indices that are cleared almost entirely by the kidney, such as lithium. We describe a 69-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, stable for several years on lithium, who presented with acute confusion, dysarthria, and expressive aphasia. A stroke protocol was activated, and noncontrast head CT, CT angiography of the head and neck, and MRI of the brain showed no acute infarct or hemorrhage. Semaglutide had been initiated approximately one month earlier for weight management, and she had experienced substantial weight loss with persistent nausea, intermittent vomiting, and reduced oral intake. Serum lithium was elevated above the reference range, accompanied by a reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate and biochemical findings suggestive of volume depletion. Lithium was held, and intravenous fluids were administered; renal function improved and the neurologic deficits resolved. Lithium was subsequently resumed at a reduced dose without recurrence. In this patient, initiation of semaglutide was temporally associated with lithium toxicity in the setting of gastrointestinal intolerance, reduced oral intake, and suspected volume depletion. Although a single case cannot establish causality, this observation supports closer lithium monitoring when initiating GLP-1 receptor agonists and during dose escalation.

title: When Diabetes Mimics Scleroderma: Cheiroarthropathy and Neuropathic Digital Erosions in Type 2 Diabetes.
authorString: Papaioannou J, Wu D, Zembowicz A, Schwager Z.
abstractText: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy is an underrecognized complication of diabetes characterized by limited finger joint extension and thickened, waxy skin of the hands. It can clinically mimic several rheumatologic conditions, particularly systemic sclerosis, creating a diagnostic challenge. We report the case of a 68-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus who presented with hand stiffness and contractures, scleroderma-like skin thickening, and nonpainful crusted digital erosions, raising concern for systemic sclerosis-associated digital ulceration. He underwent rheumatologic evaluation and received immunosuppressive therapy without improvement in the cutaneous findings, prompting further clinical reassessment. His overall clinical phenotype, including a positive prayer sign, skin thickening confined to the digits, absence of Raynaud phenomenon, normal nailfold capillaries, and negative anti-Scl-70 and anticentromere antibodies, favored diabetic cheiroarthropathy over systemic sclerosis. The digital erosions were considered likely multifactorial, with contributions from unrecognized trauma in the setting of diabetic neuropathy and possible vascular compromise related to peripheral arterial disease and tobacco use. This case highlights the clinical overlap between diabetic cheiroarthropathy and systemic sclerosis, particularly when digital erosions accompany scleroderma-like hand changes. Recognizing this presentation may help prevent misdiagnosis and unnecessary immunosuppression while directing management toward glycemic control, prevention of repetitive trauma, local wound care, and occupational therapy.

title: Drug-Disease Interactions Causing Hemorrhagic Cardiac Tamponade.
authorString: Torres-Mercado B, Delgado-Lopez X, Maldonado-Suarez J, Bermudez Nunez DR, Rodriguez Acosta JF.
abstractText: Hemorrhagic tamponade in severe hypothyroidism is an uncommon presentation that warrants evaluation for superimposed pathology. We present the case of a 57-year-old man with nonischemic cardiomyopathy, chronic amiodarone therapy, and atrial fibrillation on apixaban who developed advanced myxedema, complicated by a large hemorrhagic pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade. This case highlights a rare but life-threatening convergence of amiodarone-induced severe hypothyroidism and potentiated anticoagulation, culminating in hemorrhagic tamponade. Recognition of drug-disease interactions is critical in anticoagulated patients with endocrine dysfunction who present with rapidly recurrent pericardial effusion.

title: Adrenocortical Carcinoma: A Case Report on the Diagnostic and Therapeutic Approach.
authorString: Poulios E, Theofilopoulou S, Sidiropoulos T, Schizas D, Christodoulou S.
abstractText: Although the diagnosis of adrenocortical carcinoma might not be challenging, there is still a lack of evidence on the recommended therapeutic options, the extent of lymph node dissection, and the use of chemotherapy and radiotherapy. This is the case of a 43-year-old man who presented to our department with unregulated blood pressure. During the diagnostic workup, he underwent a CT scan that showed an incidental solid, ovoid 7-cm lesion of the adrenal gland with a density of 30 HU pre-contrast, 60 HU right after, and 38 HU in a 15-min delayed measurement after contrast administration. His plasma metanephrines, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S), total and free testosterone, and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) were normal. While his 8.00 am baseline serum cortisol was also within the age-adjusted reference range, the 8.00 am serum cortisol concentration after an overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test was suppressed. Although the aldosterone-to-renin ratio was found to be elevated, this was attributed to concomitant β-adrenergic blockade due to the biochemical evaluation. The patient underwent an endoscopic retroperitoneal left adrenalectomy. Histological examination revealed an encapsulated adrenocortical carcinoma, with a Ki-67 proliferation index of 21%. The patient was discharged and remains under follow-up with no evidence of recurrence. Adrenocortical carcinomas are classified into stages according to their size, local invasion, and metastatic potential. Surgical excision is the treatment of choice for non-metastasized ACCs, while in cases of metastases, chemotherapy and radiotherapy is usually preferred. This case highlights the need for further research into the pathophysiology of this malignancy to facilitate the development of evidence-based guidelines and to optimize management strategies for advanced-stage disease.

title: Intra-aortic Balloon Counterpulsation-Assisted Cardiac Support in the Anesthetic Management of Surgery for Acute Cervical Spine Compression With Severe Coronary Artery Disease in the Prone Position.
authorString: Motiani P, Mallikarjuna S, Chakravarthy M, Shaikh S.
abstractText: Severe coronary artery disease associated with the requirement for urgent cervical spine surgery in an elderly patient in a prone position is challenging for the anesthesiologist. Perioperative hemodynamic parameters are key to surgical success. Intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation (IABC) is a well-established modality for the management of patients with ischemic heart disease. There are very few case reports on management in noncardiac surgery with IABC. Here, we present a case report of a 74-year-old male patient with cervical cord compression scheduled for C3-C7 laminectomy and lateral mass fixation, with severe coronary artery disease and a recent history of severe coronary artery disease with triple-vessel disease and severely impaired left ventricular function, managed with IABC insertion post-induction of general anesthesia for intraoperative hemodynamic management to prevent cervical cord hypoperfusion and perioperative myocardial ischemia/infarction.

title: Right ventricular infarction with a culprit lesion in the distal right coronary artery: incidence and clinical characteristics.
authorString: Takigawa Y, Hoshino N, Hoshino M, Yamada A, Yanase M, Izawa H.
abstractText:
Objectives

Right ventricular infarction (RVI) is commonly observed in patients with inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction and typically results from proximal right coronary artery (RCA) occlusion. However, the occurrence of RVI and its clinical characteristics in patients with distal RCA lesions are not well defined.

Methods

We retrospectively investigated 128 patients with inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction caused by RCA occlusion who underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention at our institution between January 2020 and December 2023. RVI was diagnosed based on echocardiographic evidence and hemodynamic instability. Clinical characteristics and incidence rates were compared between patients with RVI [the RVI (+) group] and those without RVI [the RVI (-) group]. Findings on coronary angiography were assessed in detail for patients with distal RCA lesions.

Results

RVI was identified in 24/128 patients (18.8%), including 3/31 patients (9.7%) with distal RCA lesions. Right ventricular global longitudinal strain (RVGLS) was significantly lower in the RVI (+) group (-14.0% [-16.4, -11.6] vs. -16.4% [-18.7, -13.9]; p=0.004), as was right ventricular free wall strain (RVFWS) (-14.7% [-18.5, -10.6] vs. -17.7% [-20.7, -15.0]; p=0.01). RVGLS and RVFWS values were comparable in the RVI (+) group regardless of whether the RCA lesion was distal or proximal. There was no significant difference in TIMI flow before or after percutaneous coronary intervention or in the distribution of lesions.

Conclusions

RVI can be caused by distal RCA lesions, albeit less often than by proximal RCA lesions. No significant differences in RV strain parameters were observed between distal and proximal lesions.

title: Apparent Diffusion Coefficient Fraction Predicts Endovascular Thrombectomy Benefit in Large Ischemic Core.
authorString: Kim H, Seo BS, Choi KH, Park MS, Kim JT.
abstractText:
Background

Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) is recommended for large ischemic core stroke, but which patients within this population derive meaningful benefit remains uncertain. We investigated whether the fraction of apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC)-defined infarct volume within the ischemic lesion predicts EVT outcomes in large ischemic core stroke.

Methods

This retrospective study included patients with diffusion-weighted imaging volume ≥50 cm3 and large vessel occlusion within 24-hour of onset (2016-2024; EVT:130, no-EVT:192). The ADC fraction was defined as the volume of ADC <540 × 10-6 mm2/s divided by initial diffusion-weighted imaging volume. Overlap weighting (OW) with doubly robust estimation corrected for indication bias. Primary outcomes were modified Rankin Scale shift and favorable outcome (modified Rankin Scale score 0-3) at 3-month. The relationship between ADC fraction and EVT treatment effect was examined using overlap-weighted restricted cubic spline interaction analysis, and treatment effects were subsequently quantified above and below the crossover point.

Results

A total of 322 patients were included (age, 73.8 years, 51.9% men). Before OW, patients with EVT were younger with lower National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score and smaller diffusion-weighted imaging volumes (EVT: 93.8 cm3, no-EVT: 129.9 cm3). After OW, all covariates were well-balanced. The doubly robust-OW analysis demonstrated attenuation of EVT effect on ordinal modified Rankin Scale score shift (odds ratio, 1.37 [95% CI, 0.85-2.21]) and favorable outcome (odds ratio, 1.73 [95% CI, 0.91-3.28]). ADC fraction significantly modified the EVT treatment effect (P interaction=0.009), with a crossover at 48%, identified as a data-derived exploratory threshold. Below this threshold, EVT was associated with a favorable ordinal modified Rankin Scale score shift (odds ratio, 1.85 [95% CI, 1.05-3.26]), whereas above it the direction of the association was reversed (odds ratio, 0.42 [95% CI, 0.19-0.95]).

Conclusions

In large ischemic core stroke, the association between EVT and functional outcome varied according to infarct tissue composition. The ADC fraction distinguished patients in whom EVT was associated with more favorable outcomes from those in whom this association was not observed, supporting its potential as an imaging biomarker to inform individualized treatment decisions.

title: Plug-Anchored Coil Embolization of a Paravalvular Aortic Pseudoaneurysm After TAVR With BASILICA.
authorString: Chan VH, Chu ZHY, Wong GLN, Lai LK, Fong FK, Kam KK, So KC.
abstractText:
Objective

We present a case of aortic pseudoaneurysm after transcatheter aortic valve replacement with BASILICA (bioprosthetic or native aortic scallop intentional laceration to prevent iatrogenic coronary artery obstruction), which was tackled with coil embolization with an Amplatzer Vascular Plug II (AVP) acting as an anchor for entanglement.

Key steps

The steps were as follows. 1) Obtain bilateral common femoral artery access. 2) Advance 8-F JL 4.5 guide catheter through an Agilis large-curl steerable catheter to engage the aortic pseudoaneurysm adjacent to the left aortic cusp. 3) Deliver the AVP to the pseudoaneurysm while leaving it attached to the delivery cable. 4) Advance an EBU-4.5 6-F guide catheter, then an Excelsior SL-10 microcatheter, to deploy coils into the pseudoaneurysm around the AVP, which acts as an anchor. 5) Deploy multiple coils until resistance is met. 6) Final release of the AVP anchor after sealing the pseudoaneurysm.

Potential pitfalls

Coil deployment alone can cause frequent coil prolapse into left ventricle given the high flow state of the pseudoaneurysm. Release of AVP before adequate coil packing of the pseudoaneurysm may result in AVP embolization or pseudoaneurysm rupture.

Take-home message

During coil embolization of a large, high-flow pseudoaneurysm, a vascular plug device can be used as a stabilizing anchor to facilitate controlled coil deployment.

title: Inflammatory burden index and contrast-associated acute kidney injury after iliac artery endovascular intervention: association with renal injury and lesion complexity.
authorString: Keten MF, Bıyıklı K, Sengor BG, Uzel ST, Kılıçarslan MF, Küçük AN, Karaot H, Kaya A, Danışman N, Balaban İ.

journal.title: Postepy w kardiologii interwencyjnej = Advances in interventional cardiology

abstractText:
Introduction

Contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI) is a complication after peripheral endovascular interventions, but the value of the inflammatory burden index (IBI) in this setting is unknown.

Aim

To evaluate the association between pre-procedural IBI and CA-AKI after iliac artery intervention, compare its performance with other inflammatory indices, and examine its relationship with TASC II lesion complexity.

Material and methods

This retrospective study included 417 patients treated between January 2020 and December 2025. IBI was calculated as C-reactive protein multiplied by the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio. CA-AKI was defined as a serum creatinine increase of ≥ 0.5 mg/dl or ≥ 25% within 72 h. Receiver operating characteristic analysis, DeLong testing, multivariable logistic regression with multiple imputation, restricted cubic splines, and bootstrap validation were performed.

Results

CA-AKI occurred in 70 (16.8%) patients. IBI showed the highest discrimination for CA-AKI (AUC = 0.857, 95% CI: 0.810-0.904), outperforming C-reactive protein, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, systemic immune-inflammation index, and aggregate index of systemic inflammation (all p < 0.001). At a cutoff of 40.6, sensitivity and specificity were 80.0% and 80.2%, respectively. Each doubling of IBI was independently associated with CA-AKI (adjusted OR = 3.19, 95% CI: 2.22-4.59; p < 0.001). The association was nonlinear (p for nonlinearity < 0.001). IBI was also independently associated with TASC II C-D lesions (adjusted OR per doubling 2.91, 95% CI: 2.29-3.71; p < 0.001).

Conclusions

Pre-procedural IBI was independently associated with CA-AKI and complex iliac lesion morphology and outperformed the other evaluated inflammatory indices. External validation is required before clinical implementation.
