title: <i>Salmonella</i> aortitis without surgery or fluoroquinolones: Complete resolution with sequential antibiotic therapy.
authorString: Kim A, Navindi D, Kwon J, Hegde S, Lew W, Sarmiento A, Khouzam N.
abstractText:
Background

Salmonella aortitis is a rare, life-threatening infection historically associated with near-universal mortality without surgery. When surgery is not possible, the choice of oral agent, particularly when fluoroquinolones cannot be used, and the conduct of long-term suppression are guided by few reported cases.

Case

An 85-year-old man with diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and atrial fibrillation presented in septic shock from Salmonella Enteritidis bacteremia with infrarenal aortitis. Bacteremia cleared by hospital day 2 on intravenous ceftriaxone. Because operative risk was prohibitive and the patient preferred non-operative care, a multidisciplinary team elected antibiotic therapy alone: six weeks of intravenous ceftriaxone followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, chosen because the isolate was only intermediately susceptible to ciprofloxacin (minimum inhibitory concentration 0.25 μg/mL). On serial computed tomography angiography, periaortic inflammation was unchanged through week 7 despite clinical improvement, improved at week 15, and resolved completely at approximately 9 months, with no aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, or periaortic gas on any of eight studies. Inflammatory markers normalized during that time. After radiographic resolution, and with appetite and weight loss possibly related to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, suppression was stepped down to reduced-dose oral amoxicillin, planned to continue for the foreseeable future.

Conclusion

Carefully selected patients with non-aneurysmal native Salmonella aortitis and prohibitive operative risk may achieve clinical and radiographic resolution with antibiotics alone, even when fluoroquinolones are not an option. This case illustrates susceptibility-guided selection of an oral agent and step-down to a better-tolerated agent after resolution. Radiographic response lagged clinical response by months; unchanged early imaging should not by itself be read as treatment failure.

title: Solitary cerebellopontine angle metastasis from gallbladder adenocarcinoma: A rare clinical entity.
authorString: Chaurasiya M, Bhardwaj S.
abstractText:
Background

Isolated intracranial metastasis to cerebellopontine angle (CPA) is very rare, as CPA tumors are mostly vestibular schwannomas.

Case description

We present here a rare case of isolated brain metastasis in CPA primarily arising from gallbladder. A female patient presented with chief complaints of dizziness, difficulty walking, and nausea. On evaluation with magnetic resonance imaging brain, there was a contrast enhancing heterogenous mass in the right CPA. Patient underwent surgery that tumor was resected and sent for histopathological examination. Histology of tumor was metastatic adenocarcinoma. The patient was evaluated with positron emission tomography scan for possible primary and was found to be arising from the right lateral wall of gallbladder.

Conclusion

Although limited by clinical nature of single case, metastatic adenocarcinoma of gall-bladder origin, despite its rarity, should be considered in the differential diagnosis of CPA lesions, particularly when clinical and radiological features are atypical.

title: Targeted delivery of celastrol and siRNA via macrophage biomimetic nanoparticles for doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy therapy.
authorString: Zhang Q, Guo T, Xue X, Zhang Z, Liu X, Cai Q, Wang N, Zhang B, Peng J.
abstractText: Doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy (DIC) is a severe complication following anthracycline chemotherapy, and its main pathogenesis is inflammatory responses and ferroptosis. This study constructed hyaluronic acid-based macrophage biomimetic nanoparticles (M@HCDA) to co-delivery of Celastrol (Cel) and siADAM17 for the treatment of DIC. This research revealed that Cel exerted an anti-ferroptosis effect by regulating GPX4 and SLC7A11, while siADAM17 inhibited TAK1-MAPK pathway activation by silencing ADAM17. Meanwhile, the synergistic effect of Cel and siADAM17 significantly alleviated oxidative stress, myocardial fibrosis, apoptosis, and mitochondrial dysfunction, thereby relieving myocardial injury caused by DOX-induced cardiotoxicity and providing effective early cardioprotection. In vitro and in vivo experiments indicated that M@HCDA exhibited good stability, biocompatibility, and targeting capability, showing the clinical application potential. The design and development of M@HCDA provide new experimental evidence and candidate strategy for treating DIC.

title: Recognizing a duplicated inferior vena cava during radical nephrectomy for papillary renal cell carcinoma: A case report.
authorString: Siddique MW, Waqas M, Shahzad MH, Javaid MH, Dalir N.
abstractText: Duplication of the inferior vena cava (DIVC) is a rare congenital venous anomaly with important implications during retroperitoneal surgery. A 40-year-old man presented with 3-month hematuria and mild left flank pain. CT revealed a 7-cm left renal mass, pulmonary and osseous lesions, and two separate IVC channels near the aortic bifurcation. PET/CT confirmed DIVC and suspected metastases. Open radical nephrectomy with lymph-node dissection was performed without vascular injury. Histopathology showed papillary renal cell carcinoma, ISUP grade 3, confined to the renal capsule. This case highlights the importance of recognizing DIVC before renal surgery.

title: Opportunistic computed tomography-based vertebral attenuation for osteoporosis screening.
authorString: Atik I, Tashimbekov A, Gul E, Atik S, Yildiz B.
abstractText:
Objective

The aim of this study was to evaluate opportunistic vertebral trabecular attenuation on routine unenhanced abdominal computed tomography for predicting osteoporosis and its relationship with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry parameters.

Methods

This retrospective study inc luded 350 patients (mean age 68.5 years) who underwent both dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry and routine unenhanced abdominal computed tomography for non-oncologic clinical indications within a 3-month interval between 2022 and 2025. Patients were grouped into normal (n=119), osteopenia (n=117), and osteoporosis (n=114) based on L1-L4 T-scores. Two blinded radiologists measured Hounsfield Unit values using regions of interest on high-resolution 0.625-mm sagittal-reconstructed computed tomography images of the L1-L4 vertebral bodies. Interobserver agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis.

Results

Lumbar Hounsfield Unit values decreased progressively from normal to osteoporosis groups (p<0.001). Mean L1-L4 attenuation values for normal, osteopenia, and osteoporosis groups were 148.99±5.54, 120.39±3.84, and 78.53±3.36 Hounsfield Unit, respectively (p<0.001). Interobserver reliability was excellent (intraclass correlation coefficient: 0.90-0.94). L1 Hounsfield Unit measurements showed the highest diagnostic performance for predicting osteoporosis (area under the curve: 0.913; 95%CI 0.870-0.955). An L1 cutoff of ≤95.50 Hounsfield Unit yielded 84.60% sensitivity and 86.40% specificity. Mean L1-L4 Hounsfield Unit also showed high accuracy (area under the curve: 0.881) at a ≤95.00 Hounsfield Unit cutoff (sensitivity: 80.80%, specificity: 77.30%).

Conclusion

Opportunistic sagittal lumbar Hounsfield Unit measurements, particularly at L1, provide high diagnostic accuracy and reproducibility for identifying osteoporosis on routine abdominal computed tomography without requiring additional imaging or radiation exposure. This protocol may facilitate early opportunistic screening for osteoporosis and support timely referral for dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry assessment.

title: Pancreatic involvement in lung cancer: Imaging findings and diagnostic challenges in two cases.
authorString: Bouziane A, Essâdi B, Bekhakh C, Bennani A, Elmqaddem O, Koulali H, Kharrasse G, Ismaili Z, Zazour A.
abstractText: Pancreatic metastases from lung cancer are uncommon and may be difficult to distinguish from primary pancreatic malignancies. We report 2 patients with lung cancer and pancreatic lesions causing biliary obstruction. The first patient was a 58-year-old man with small-cell lung carcinoma and a pancreatic head mass associated with biliary and pancreatic duct dilatation and extensive vascular contact. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass, and endoscopic ultrasound-guided tissue acquisition confirmed a pancreatic metastasis from pulmonary small-cell carcinoma. The patient underwent endoscopic biliary drainage followed by cisplatin and etoposide chemotherapy. The second patient was a 61-year-old man with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma and a progressively enlarging pancreatic head lesion. Two endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspirations performed 1 month apart were nondiagnostic. The patient subsequently developed obstructive jaundice caused by a severe distal common bile duct stricture. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography allowed biliary drainage and biopsy of the infiltrated major papilla. Histological and immunohistochemical findings supported metastatic adenocarcinoma of pulmonary origin involving the major papilla. Although the pancreatic lesion itself was not histologically confirmed as metastatic, the overall clinical and radiological findings were considered suggestive of pancreatic metastatic involvement. These cases illustrate the considerable imaging overlap between pancreatic metastatic involvement and primary pancreatic malignancy. Imaging findings should be interpreted in conjunction with the oncological history and pathological findings. When pancreatic tissue acquisition is inconclusive, biopsy of another accessible involved site may provide diagnostic evidence of metastatic disease.

title: One-stop photon-counting CT angiography for simultaneous assessment of cardio-cerebrovascular lesions: A case report.
authorString: Wan Y, Zou D, Lan J, Yang F, Jiang J, Liu Y, Tian W, Wang G, Zhang Y.
abstractText: We report a 73-year-old male admitted for 2-year progressive dysuria, with incidental detection of abnormal cardiovascular signs on physical examination. Initial evaluation via energy-integrating detector computed tomography (EID-CT) coronary angiography and cranial magnetic resonance imaging identified key vascular abnormalities, while subsequent photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) combined cardio-cerebral computed tomography angiography (CTA) provided more detailed assessment of stenosis severity, plaque composition, and the entire vascular bed. The combined PCD-CT scan delineated synchronous lesions in detail: proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery plaque, ascending aortic dilatation with left coronary sinus aneurysm compressing the left atrium, and occlusion of the intracranial right vertebral artery. Importantly, PCD-CT cardio-cerebral CTA yielded a lower radiation dose compared with standalone EID-CT coronary angiography. With spectral reconstruction, the severity of LAD stenosis was re-evaluated and interpreted as mild stenosis, a lower grade than that assessed by EID-CT; meanwhile, 0.4 mm thin-slice imaging enabled detailed compositional analysis of the coronary plaque, with imaging features suggestive of a stable plaque. Based on multidisciplinary discussion integrating all imaging findings and clinical context, a treatment strategy was formulated: prioritize high-risk aortic lesion management, synchronously perform coronary artery bypass grafting for myocardial ischemia prevention, and electively address intracranial stenosis. This case demonstrates the preliminary clinical value of PCD-CT as a supportive imaging modality for the evaluation and multidisciplinary management of concurrent cardio-cerebrovascular diseases.

title: Pedicle total leg fillet flap of the lower extremity: An extensive orthoplastic trauma reconstruction cases report with hip disarticulation.
authorString: Malan AM, Paraoan VC, McArthur J, Wallace DL.
abstractText: Trauma related, extreme, high-level lower extremity amputations are uncommon procedures and pose complex challenges with soft tissue and bony reconstruction. This case reports presents a challenging ortho-plastic trauma reconstruction with a hip disarticulation and a massive pelvic wound, and soft tissue reconstruction with a full leg pedicle fillet flap. We describe a step-by-step operative plan performing a pedicle full leg fillet flap for a massive pelvic wound.

title: Mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) type VI: A case series to assess the efficacy of enzyme replacement therapy and to guide precision-based medicine in the IRISH paediatric cohort.
authorString: Mathew C, Carey N, Losty E, Crushell E, Monavari A, Elsammak M, Carroll A, Knerr I.
abstractText:
Aims

To assess the diseasecourse in paediatric patients with mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) type VI and efficacy of enzyme replacement therapy, to guide precision-based medicine in the Irish context.

Methods

This was an ethically approved retrospective case series conducted at Children's Health Ireland (CHI) at Temple Street in Dublin, reviewing our paediatric MPS type VI cohort. Informed consent was obtained. Data sources included hospital patient charts, laboratory results and radiological images.

Results

Four patients were included in the study (age 3 years 9 months to 16 years at data cut-off). Age at diagnosis ranged from 2 months to 3 years in our cohort. Presenting features included coarse features, broad ribs, upper airway issues, corneal clouding, hernias, hearing loss and motor delay. All patients were treated with enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with galsulfase. GAG/creatinine ratio at time of diagnosis ranged between 29.2 - 159 mg/mmol creatinine compared to 12.8-26 mg/mmol creatinine following one year of ERT. Two of the patients had hyperintensities noted on MRI brain but, interestingly, these resolved after one year of ERT. All patients had significant disease burden requiring multidisciplinary team input and follow up by multiple medical specialists.

Conclusion

Among the main findings in our study are the resolutions of hyperintensities on MRI brain images in 50% of cases on ERT during childhood. However, disease burden remained high during childhood. Precision-based medicine for MPS type VI requires a multidisciplinary approach, including proactive surveillance. Short abstract: A hospital-based retrospective study was conducted to assess the course of mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) type VI in four young people, to guide precision-based medicine in the Irish paediatric context. All patients were treated with enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with galsulfase, essentially leading to normalisation of GAG/creatinine ratios. Two patients had hyperintensities on MRI brain, but, interestingly, these resolved after one year of ERT. All patients had significant disease burden, requiring tailored multidisciplinary treatment including proactive surveillance.

title: Autonomic nervous system dysfunction in critically ill cancer patients: Hemodynamic consequences and multimodal assessment strategies.
authorString: Gong S, Chu Y, Wang X.
abstractText: In critically ill cancer patients, autonomic nervous system (ANS) dysfunction may contribute to hemodynamic instability and organ dysfunction and may be exacerbated by malignancy-related injury and anticancer treatment. This narrative review summarizes conventional methods for assessing ANS function, including heart rate variability (HRV), blood pressure variability (BPV), baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), and cardiovascular autonomic reflex testing, together with emerging approaches such as high-resolution multimodal monitoring (MMM) and artificial intelligence (AI). Host-organ unregulated response (HOUR) framework is used to integrate interactions among autonomic, neuroendocrine, inflammatory, immune, coagulation, metabolic, bioenergetic, and microcirculatory dysregulation. Collectively, these approaches may facilitate real-time assessment of autonomic function and tissue perfusion, thereby supporting risk stratification and individualized management in critically ill cancer patients.

title: Diet-attributable vascular/metabolic disease burden comparisons and public health implications in Western Europe and North America.
authorString: Li H, Zhang J, Liu Z, Li J, Yin X, Li H, Lu Y, Xu Q, Wang J.
abstractText: Ischemic heart disease (IHD), ischemic stroke (IS), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and lower-extremity vascular disease are leading causes of disability in Western Europe and North America, but their diet-attributable burden remains unclear. Using Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 data, we assessed the association between the Socio-demographic Index (SDI) and the vascular/metabolic disease burden and compared the cross-regional burden through multi-dimensional time-trend, risk contribution, and projection analyses. Mendelian randomization (MR) tested causal diet effects on disease subtypes. Frontier analysis showed diet-related IHD and IS burden declined with SDI, while T2DM increased. By 2023, Western Europe had a lower burden than North America. Processed meat and whole grain dominated T2DM and IHD burden, respectively. Joinpoint analysis revealed declining trends. Projections to 2035 indicated North America remains higher. MR identified several potential causal links. This study provides a basis for vascular/metabolic disease prevention policies and dietary interventions in Western Europe and North America.

title: Clinical manifestations of patients with <i>STAT1</i> gain-of-function variants in Mexico.
authorString: Cova-Guzmán TL, Okada S, Tsumura M, O Farrill-Romanillos PM, Martínez-Barricarte R, Román-Montes CM, Yamazaki-Nakashimada MA, Gámez-González LB, López-Martínez V, Meléndez-Díaz GM, Zuñiga-Lagunes CG, Gómez-Tello H, Nuñez-Nuñez ME, Bayardo Gutiérrez B, Staines-Boone AT, Lugo Reyes SO, Salazar-Gálvez Y, Moctezuma-Trejo C, Alaníz-Flores AK, Gómez-Hernández N, Ortega-Cisneros M, Zárate-Hernández MDC, Bustamante-Ogando JC, Soudée C, Rosain J, Boisson-Dupuis S, Migaud M, Casanova JL, Espinosa-Rosales FJ, Cristerna Tarrasa GH, Palacios-Reyes D, Puel A, Bustamante J, Espinosa-Padilla S, Blancas Galicia L.
abstractText:
Background

Germline Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 1 (STAT1) gain-of-function (GOF) variants enhance cellular responses to IL-27 and type I, II, and III interferons, predisposing to fungal, bacterial, and viral infections and immune dysregulation.

Methods

Mexican patients with pathogenic STAT1-GOF variants identified at referral centers were enrolled.

Results

Thirty patients from 17 kindreds were included. Fifteen variants were identified, including the novel C324W variant, confirmed as GOF by functional studies. All patients developed mucocutaneous candidiasis. Among 25 BCG-vaccinated patients, 24% developed BCG disease. According to the Graham criteria, seven patients (23%) with tuberculosis were classified as confirmed (n=1), possible (n=3), and probable (n=3) cases. Three patients developed both BCG disease and tuberculosis. Autoinflammatory and autoimmune manifestations occurred in 50% and 40%, respectively. Two patients developed infection-triggered macrophage activation syndrome. Seven patients (23%) died.

Conclusions

This cohort illustrates the broad clinical spectrum of STAT1 GOF disease, including infectious, inflammatory, autoimmune, and hematological manifestations. BCG disease and tuberculosis were observed in a subset of patients, highlighting the complexity of clinical presentation and the importance of comprehensive evaluation and follow-up.

title: Progression rates of aortic stenosis in patients with calcific and rheumatic heart disease in Saudi Arabia.
authorString: Elsherif ZT, Elsherif D, Ahmed AM, Ardah HI, Al-Mutairi F, Almaghrabi S, Alanazi F, Alaqeel H, Almohaimeed M, Alklaib R, Aldakhil J, Alturki H.

journal.title: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice

abstractText:
Study objective

Calcific aortic stenosis (AS) is the most prevalent type of AS in developed countries. However, in developing countries, rheumatic heart disease (RHD), which has a low progression rate, remains the prevalent type. This study compared the progression rates of AS between the National Guard cohort and Western populations.

Design

This was a retrospective single-center cohort study.

Participants

Involving patients who underwent two echocardiographic examinations within an interval of at least 2 years.

Main outcome measures

Progression of aortic valve stenosis was assessed by measuring changes in the aortic valve area (AVA), peak aortic velocity, and mean aortic valve gradient.

Results

In total, 1669 patients (median follow-up: 6.9 years) were included in the analysis. The overall annual AVA progression rate was 0.074 ± 0.1 cm2/year (median: -0.061 cm2/year). Patients with RHD had lower progression rates than those without RHD (25%-35%; AVA: -0.036 [-0.042, -0.030] cm2/year). Patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) who exhibited calcific AS had the highest progression rate (AVA: -0.102 ± 0.096 cm2/year). The overall progression rate of AS for the National Guard cohort was lower across all groups compared with that in Western populations (AVA: -0.08 to 0.12 cm2/year).

Conclusions

Patients with ESRD who had calcific AS had the highest progression rate. Meanwhile, patients with RHD exhibited the lowest progression rate. The high prevalence of calcific AS in our study shows the importance of adherence to the American College of Cardiology/European Society of Cardiology guidelines for disease management.

title: Mannitol as a crystalloid substitute for colloid oncotic support in the respiratory active working heart-brainstem preparation.
authorString: Bicakci AO, Hülsmann S.
abstractText: The working heart-brainstem preparation (WHBP) is an arterially perfused in situ rodent model that requires an osmotically or oncotically active perfusate additive to limit edema and maintain stable central respiratory motor output. Ficoll-70 at 1.25% (w/v) is widely used for this purpose, but at this concentration it generates only modest colloid osmotic pressure (∼3-4 mmHg) and presents practical limitations, including batch variability, endotoxin risk, and high cost. We asked whether mannitol at 0.85% (w/v), a small-molecule crystalloid osmolyte and hydroxyl-radical scavenger with an established clinical safety profile, can substitute for Ficoll-70 while preserving WHBP viability. Adult mouse WHBPs (n = 7 Ficoll; n = 9 mannitol) were perfused for 1 h with Krebs-based perfusate containing either 1.25% Ficoll-70 or 0.85% mannitol. Preparations were assessed for phrenic and vagus nerve activity, perfusion pressure, whole-preparation weight gain, brain tissue weight, and single-neuron recording capability. Phrenic discharge frequency increased over time in both groups (Ficoll: 0.15 → 0.49 Hz; mannitol: 0.24 → 0.45 Hz), and amplitude of the integrated phrenic burst did not differ significantly between additives. Perfusion pressure rose modestly over 1 h (Ficoll: 67.7 → 76.7 mmHg; mannitol: 67.2 → 74.1 mmHg), with no significant between-group difference. Whole-preparation weight increased in both conditions, indicating tissue water uptake during perfusion. Brainstem-cerebellum wet weight after 1 h was similar with both perfusates (0.140 ± 0.023 g, Ficoll; 0.124 ± 0.020 g, mannitol; p = 0.18). Juxtacellular recordings from preBötzinger complex neurons confirmed that single-unit activity can be obtained reliably in mannitol-perfused preparations for more than 2 h. Moreover, post-inspiratory activity of the vagus nerve is preserved in mannitol-perfused preparations. Together, these data indicate that 0.85% mannitol maintains WHBP cardiorespiratory function and tissue water balance to a degree comparable with 1.25% Ficoll-70, while providing a lower-cost, endotoxin-free alternative. The use of mannitol as a crystalloid perfusate additive may therefore facilitate wider and more reproducible application of the WHBP and related arterially perfused in situ preparations in integrative physiology and pharmacology.

title: Prognostic Value of the Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index and Controlling Nutritional Status Score in Patients Aged ≥ 75 Years With Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction
authorString: Li Y, Shao H, Liu Y, Wang J, Yin Y, Yang C, Wang X, Zhong Y, Lv L.

title: From cytokine storm to adaptive dysregulation: temporal evolution of the inflammatory network and phase-specific intervention strategies in fulminant viral myocarditis.
authorString: Liu Y, Li J, Xiao G, He C.
abstractText: Fulminant viral myocarditis (FVM) is characterized by acute onset and rapid progression, often deteriorating into cardiogenic shock, malignant arrhythmias, and multi-organ failure within days. Its pathological essence does not lie in the "quantitative accumulation" of focal lymphocytic infiltration seen in ordinary myocarditis, but rather in a "qualitative shift" driven by diffuse myocardial edema compounded by a multi-cytokine cascade. Accumulating evidence indicates that the "inflection point" of myocardial injury is determined not by viral load per se, but by the dysregulated pattern recognition of viral antigens by the innate immune system and the resultant imbalance of the inflammatory network. The organising framework of this review is temporal (hyperacute to acute to reparative immune states). A spatial dimension, contrasting the circulating and the cardiac-resident immune compartments, is developed wherever direct or closely analogous data exist, but it carries far less evidence than the temporal dimension and is treated as secondary to it. Myocarditis that is immune-mediated without a replicating cardiotropic virus, including vaccine-associated and checkpoint-inhibitor disease, is used here as a labelled comparator and not as part of the entity under review. The virus invades cardiomyocytes and vascular endothelium via receptors with non-canonical distribution, subsequently triggering type I interferon responses and necroptosis through endosomal and cytosolic pattern-recognition receptors, and initiating a cascade effect via damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). The driver of cardiomyocyte death does not stay constant across this course: virus-intrinsic cytopathic and ferroptotic death predominates in the first days, myeloid-mediated killing takes over through the remainder of the first week, and cytotoxic lymphocytes become the principal effectors thereafter. The hyperacute phase is characterized by macrophage phenotypic drift, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and a "cytokine storm" whose earliest cellular sources in viral myocarditis are myeloid rather than T-cell derived. The acute phase features the "clearance-injury" paradox of cytotoxic T cells and the failure of immune checkpoint regulation, and a subset of patients may subsequently follow what the authors describe as a candidate immunoparalysis trajectory rather than an established third stage of disease - a state provisionally characterized by regulatory T cell (Treg) expansion, paradoxical elevation of interleukin-10 (IL-10), and downregulation of monocyte human leukocyte antigen-DR (HLA-DR). Its reported association with secondary infection and adverse outcome derives largely from sepsis and critical-care cohorts and has not been demonstrated in FVM. Building on this "inflammatory time window," the authors propose a phase-specific framework intended to generate hypotheses rather than to recommend treatment: in the hyperacute phase, "fire-extinguishing" approaches (complement blockade and cytokine adsorption) may represent a potential alternative to broad-spectrum immunosuppression; in the acute phase, selective blockade of individual pathways according to inflammatory subtype may be worth exploring; and in the reparative phase, measures aimed at restoring regulatory immune capacity may be considered for study. None of these pathways, and none of the biomarker values discussed in the main text, has been prospectively validated in FVM. Finally, this review envisions individualized decision-making guided by multi-omics and dynamic immune monitoring, emphasizing that the prognosis of FVM depends on the capacity for "dynamic phenotyping and real-time switching" of immune status, rather than reliance on any single therapeutic modality.

title: Perioperative Pain Assessment and Medication Safety in Office-Based Dental Anesthesia: A Practical Review.
authorString: McCarthy A, Shapiro FE, Urman RD.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

We examined perioperative pain assessment, medication documentation, toxicity preparedness, emergency medications and preparedness, and discharge readiness in office-based dental practices. By bringing these considerations together, the goal is to provide a practice overview of what providers should consider incorporating into their office-based dental and other similar anesthesia practices.

Recent findings

Office- based dental anesthesia consistently delivers care to children and patients who cannot tolerate hospital treatment. Effective perioperative pain management is critically important for safe patient care in the dental office. Age-appropriate pain assessment, local-anesthetic safety, emergency preparedness, and recovery and discharge criteria are important components of office-based dental anesthesia practices. Dental offices are an important setting for patients who require sedation or general anesthesia; A practical framework may help clinicians consistently integrate safeguard elements into daily office-based care.

title: Aging reshapes cardiac extravascular leukocyte transcription through bidirectional remodeling during LPS-induced endotoxemia
authorString: Yu Q, Gao H, Fang F, Du J, Wang M.
abstractText:
ABSTRACT

Sepsis disproportionately affects older adults and is frequently complicated by cardiac dysfunction. However, how aging alters the transcriptional responses of cardiac extravascular immune cells during systemic inflammation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated aging-dependent transcriptional remodeling of cardiac immune cells using an LPS-induced endotoxemia model in young and aged C57BL/6 mice. Mice received intraperitoneal LPS (5 mg/kg body weight) or vehicle, and cardiac extravascular leukocytes were isolated from ex vivo retrogradely perfused hearts 24 h later for single-cell RNA sequencing. Aging was associated with bidirectional transcriptional remodeling, characterized by both up- and downregulation of gene programs, particularly in cardiac macrophages, monocyte-like macrophages, T cells, and B cells following LPS challenge. A shared feature across these four cell populations was reduced representation of mitochondrial-associated transcriptional programs, indicating aging-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial biology across cardiac myeloid and lymphoid lineages during systemic inflammation. In parallel, cell type-specific transcriptional remodeling revealed distinct functional-associated responses. Macrophages and monocyte-like macrophages exhibited increased tissue-remodeling and repair-associated transcriptional programs. Both T and B cells showed reduced metabolic programs but increased actin cytoskeleton organization. T cells additionally exhibited reduced cytotoxicity-associated and enhanced Th17-associated transcriptional programs, whereas B cells showed reduced antigen-processing and presentation programs. Cell-cell communication analysis suggested aging-associated differences in immune cell interactions following LPS challenge and potential features of cardiac inflammaging at baseline. Together, these findings demonstrate that aging bidirectionally reshapes the cardiac immune response to systemic inflammation, characterized by shared remodeling of mitochondrial-associated programs and cell type-specific changes in inflammatory, metabolic, cytoskeletal, and effector-associated programs. These aging-dependent transcriptional changes occurred in the context of the greater severity of illness observed in aged mice following LPS-induced endotoxemia.

title: A mucosal barrier injury related six gene transcriptomic signature associated with ulcerative colitis using machine learning and public transcriptomic data.
authorString: He S, Sun P, Duan X.
abstractText: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is characterized by epithelial barrier disruption, mucosal immune activation, and sustained intestinal inflammation. We developed a biologically interpretable public-transcriptomic signature using Gene Expression Omnibus datasets GSE75214, GSE38713, and GSE92415. A literature-curated panel of 35 mucosal barrier injury-related genes was integrated with differential expression, LASSO regression, random forest prioritization, and ridge logistic regression. Six genes (LCN2, DEFB1, S100A8, MUC1, VIL1, and TJP3) were retained as a locked transcriptomic score. Because the original feature-selection steps used the complete development cohort, we added 50 repetitions of stratified five-fold outer cross-validation. All preprocessing and ridge tuning were restricted to each outer-training fold; the locked score achieved a mean out-of-fold AUC of 0.9660 (SD 0.0031). A stricter sensitivity analysis that repeated differential-expression filtering, LASSO, random-forest ranking, deterministic six-gene selection, and ridge fitting within each outer-training fold achieved a mean out-of-fold AUC of 0.9600 (SD 0.0094). The refitted locked model retained discrimination in GSE38713 (AUC 0.8974, 95% CI 0.8040-0.9909) and GSE92415 (AUC 0.9894, 95% CI 0.9744-1.0000) when one development-derived cutoff was applied unchanged. The six-gene score did not significantly outperform VIL1 alone in the development cohort (DeLong P = 0.4026). The signature should therefore be interpreted as a molecular pattern associated with UC mucosal inflammation and barrier remodeling rather than as a UC-specific clinical diagnostic test.

title: Translating microRNAs into clinical laboratory medicine: A critical review of biomarker potential, methodological barriers and implementation pathways.
authorString: Stejskal D, Svagera Z, Buzga M, Kusnierova P, Sigutova R.

journal.medlineAbbreviation: Biomed Pap Med Fac Univ Palacky Olomouc Czech Repub
journal.title: Biomedical papers of the Medical Faculty of the University Palacky, Olomouc, Czechoslovakia
journal.isoabbreviation: Biomed Pap Med Fac Univ Palacky Olomouc Czech Repub

abstractText: This critical translational review evaluates the clinical significance of circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) across a broad spectrum of medical disciplines, identifies the main barriers to routine laboratory implementation and proposes a practical roadmap toward clinical use. A structured literature search of PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus covered English-language publications through May 2026. Evidence on preanalytical factors, analytical platforms, absolute quantification, reference interval derivation, clinical validation and translational feasibility of miRNA diagnostics was reviewed across oncology, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, atherosclerosis, ophthalmology, acute kidney injury, sepsis, metabolic disease, liver disease, autoimmune disease, infectious disease, transplantation, reproductive medicine and toxicology. In multiple clinical domains, miRNAs may reflect pathophysiological processes earlier than established laboratory biomarkers; however, single miRNAs rarely offer disease-specific information. Multimarker panels combined with established biochemical markers demonstrate superior diagnostic and prognostic performance, whereas preanalytical standardization, absolute quantification and prospective clinical validation remain critical unmet needs. Reference intervals for eight cardiovascularly relevant miRNAs, determined in whole blood by the miREIA immunoassay, provide a first step toward routine implementation. Routine implementation of miRNA diagnostics therefore requires a five-stage laboratory medicine framework: preanalytical standardization, analytical validation with absolute quantification, biological reference data, prospective clinical validation and demonstration of clinical and economic utility beyond existing biomarkers.

title: Functional Characterization and Genomic Insights into <i>Klebsiella</i> Virulomes, Resistomes, and Mobilome Signatures.
authorString: Li J, Shah T, Yang M, Shah Z, Qin W.
abstractText:
Introduction

Klebsiella is an emerging human pathogen that can cause severe infections, including bloodstream infections, pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and meningitis. Klebsiella spp. are becoming resistant to multiple antibiotics, including carbapenems, making them difficult to treat.

Methods

This study analyzed the complete genome sequence of some closely related Klebsiella spp. including one newly sequenced multidrug resistance (MDR) K. pneumoniae subspecies pneumoniae, and the remaining K. variicola, K. pneumoniae HS11286, K. quasipneumoniae, K. quasivariicola, K. oxytoca, K. africana, K. aerogenes, and K. grimontii retrieved from the publicly available NCBI database for comparative analysis.

Results

PubMLST Klebsiella profiling corresponded to these species for various sequence types (STs). Taxonomic and phylogenomic frameworks highlight the genetic diversity and evolutionary coherence of the K. pneumoniae complex and its close relatives. Additionally, complete genome annotation has revealed AMR phenotypes across the Klebsiella isolates. Moreover, these pathogens harbor several potential virulence factors involved in adherence, invasion, immune modulation, biofilm formation, enterobactin, yersiniabactin, aerobactin, and exotoxins, demonstrating their diverse pathogenic strategies. We also compared the diverse plasmid types among these Klebsiella isolates; K. pneumoniae HS11286 comprised five plasmids carrying multiple AMR genes. Moreover, the identification of distinct prophages, CAZymes, and KEGG annotations revealed functionally dense elements in the Klebsiella genomes. A minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) assay revealed that K. pneumoniae was resistant to several key AMR drugs.

Discussion

The findings of this study help us to better understand the genomic landscapes of clinically important Klebsiella spp. paving the way for antimicrobial stewardship strategies to combat these pathogens.

title: Interactive Pathways and Therapeutic Innovations in Elderly Sarcopenia-Diabetes Comorbidity: Breaking the Negative Self-Reinforcing Loop Through Integrated Care.
authorString: Gong F, Zhang Q, Qu R, Zhou L, Lv Y, Li J, Dai J.

journal.title: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy

abstractText: Against the backdrop of a rapidly aging global population, the prevalence of metabolic dysregulation and degenerative musculoskeletal conditions is escalating. Projections indicate that sarcopenia will emerge as a major public health burden over the next three decades. A robust bidirectional link connects sarcopenia with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM); each condition substantially elevates the risk of the other and may accelerate functional decline and disability. Emerging data demonstrate that older adults with both T2DM and sarcopenia face a markedly higher risk of all-cause mortality than those with T2DM alone. Consequently, unraveling the shared pathophysiological underpinnings of these comorbid disorders holds profound clinical and scientific significance. We reviewed current knowledge on the interactive mechanisms driving the sarcopenia-diabetes nexus and evaluated existing therapeutic approaches through systematic searches of PubMed, Google Scholar, and Science Direct. The high co-occurrence of sarcopenia and T2DM in older adults is not coincidental; rather, it reflects a well-documented pathophysiological interrelationship. By synthesizing contemporary evidence, we aim to guide future research and refine clinical protocols designed to improve quality of life and reduce complication rates among elderly diabetic populations.

title: Early Staged STABILISE Technique Achieves Favorable Aortic Remodeling after Central Repair for Acute Type A Aortic Dissection.
authorString: Takagi S, Goto Y, Inagaki M, Taniwaki M, Imagawa A, Okawa Y.
abstractText: Residual distal aortic dissection often persists after repair of acute type A aortic dissection, and may cause progressive aortic enlargement requiring secondary intervention. We describe a 43-year-old male who underwent an early staged stent-assisted balloon-induced intimal disruption and relamination in aortic dissection repair (STABILISE)-thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) procedure after central repair for an acute type A aortic dissection. Early postoperative computed tomography angiography demonstrated persistent false lumen perfusion, progressive false lumen enlargement, and marked true lumen compression. Thirty-eight days postoperatively, staged STABILISE-TEVAR was performed. Early staged STABILISE-TEVAR was technically feasible and achieved favorable aortic remodeling at 12 months in this patient.

title: Drug acquisition accounts for a minor share of the costs associated with dobutamine-milrinone escalation in cardiogenic shock: a propensity-weighted cost analysis from Indonesia.
authorString: Fajar Respaty R, Purna Sari S, Widyantoro B.

journal.title: Expert review of pharmacoeconomics & outcomes research

abstractText:
Background

Adding milrinone to dobutamine (dobutamine-milrinone escalation) in cardiogenic shock (CS) is reimbursed for a limited duration under Indonesia's national health insurance, but its cost structure is poorly characterized. This study quantified direct medical charges associated with escalation and the contribution of drug acquisition.

Research design and methods

Retrospective cohort of 76 adult CS survivors (20 escalation, 56 dobutamine monotherapy) at Indonesia's national cardiovascular referral center, 2020-2024. Covariate Balancing Propensity Score-based inverse probability of treatment weighting, using pre-treatment covariates, estimated adjusted cost ratios (CR) for intensive cardiovascular care unit (ICVCU) and total hospital costs from institutional billing records.

Results

Escalation was associated with higher ICVCU costs (CR 2.711; 95% CI 1.912-3.844; p<0.001) and total hospital costs (CR 2.321; 95% CI 1.372-3.929; p= 0.002). Combined inotrope costs represented 4.3% of ICVCU expenditure in the escalation group, versus 30.9% for therapeutic and interventional procedures. Baseline vasoactive-inotropic score correlated with total hospital cost (ρ=0.597; p<0.001).

Conclusions

Drug acquisition represented a minor share of costs associated with escalation. The findings support consideration of severity- and resource-based reimbursement approaches rather than focusing solely on duration limits for individual inotropes. Interpretation is limited by the retrospective, single-center, survivor-only design.

title: Efficacy of fludrocortisone for symptom relief in patients with autonomic syncope and hypotensive phenotype.
authorString: Kenny RA, Rice C, Russo V, Parente E, De Lange FJ, Boel TT, Groppelli A, Deharo JC, Maille B, Fedorowski A, Juszczyk M, Maggi R, Francisco-Pascual J, Rivasi G, Laffi M, Brignole M.

journal.title: Europace : European pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac electrophysiology : journal of the working groups on cardiac pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac cellular electrophysiology of the European Society of Cardiology

abstractText:
Aim

To assess the efficacy of fludrocortisone therapy in patients with autonomic syncope and hypotensive phenotype.

Methods and results

Multicentre, prospective, non-randomized study. Fludrocortisone therapy was guided by clinician experience and supported by two 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) assessments-one before treatment start (ABPM 1) and one after drug optimization (ABPM 2). Primary endpoint: reduction of the syncope burden and presyncopal symptoms based on validated semi structured questionnaires. Secondary endpoint: hypotensive episodes on ABPM. In a cohort of 94 patients treated with fludrocortisone (median age 38 [IQR 21-57]) years, 83% females), 16 patients stopped therapy due to side effects, occurring during optimization (#11) or follow-up (#5). A total of 83 patients were analysed. The average 24-hour systolic blood pressure (SBP) increased from 106.3 ± 8.2 mmHg at ABPM 1 to 112.3 ± 9.3 at ABPM 2 (p = 0.0001). The number of daytime SBP drops <90 mmHg and <100 mmHg decreased by 61%, and 45% respectively (p < 0.001 for both). The annual syncope burden was reduced by 50.2%, from 2.0 (IQR 1.0-4.0) before therapy to 0.0 (IQR 0.0-1.8) episodes during a median follow-up of 12.9 months (p = 0.0001). Subjective symptom improvement was reported by 85.6% of patients. The frequency of syncope/presyncope decreased significantly, p = 0.009. The outcome was similar in 42 younger (23 ± 6 yrs) and in 41 older (56 ± 12 yrs) patients.

Conclusion

Fludrocortisone therapy was associated with reduced hypotension and the burden of symptoms both in younger and in older patients. Side effects lead to discontinuation of therapy in 17% of cases.

title: Three-dimensional-printed heart models as medical educational tools in cardiac catheterisation: randomised controlled trial.
authorString: Chao KY, Huang LY, Chen CY, Hung KL, Lin CY.
abstractText:
Background

Simulation-based tools are increasingly used to improve procedural training in medical education. However, access to affordable and anatomically accurate models for teaching cardiac catheterisation remains limited. This study aimed to enhance medical education by developing a cost-effective three-dimensional-printed heart model for teaching basic cardiac catheterisation to medical students.

Methods

This open-label, single-site randomised controlled trial was conducted at Fu Jen Catholic University. Undergraduate and postgraduate medical students were recruited and randomly assigned to either a three-dimensional model group with hands-on practice or a control group receiving slide-based instruction. The effectiveness of a custom-made three-dimensional-printed heart model in teaching cardiac catheterisation was evaluated. A total of 35 participants were enrolled, including 18 in the three-dimensional model group and 17 in the control group.

Results

Overall posttest scores were comparable between groups. However, among undergraduate medical students, posttest scores were significantly higher in the three-dimensional model group than in the control group (P = 0.03). The production cost of each three-dimensional-printed heart model was capped at US＄200, indicating that the model is a cost-effective educational tool.

Conclusion

Three-dimensional-printed heart models provide a feasible and cost-effective approach for teaching cardiac catheterisation in medical education. Their educational benefits appeared more evident among undergraduate medical students. Integrating such models according to learners' training stages and procedural complexity may further enhance training effectiveness.

title: Risk of Postoperative Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events After Dermatologic Surgery After Recent Myocardial Infarction.
authorString: Li HJ, Thatiparthi A, Farahbakhsh N, Torres A.

journal.title: Dermatologic surgery : official publication for American Society for Dermatologic Surgery [et al.]

abstractText:
Background

Dermatologic surgery is classified as very low risk by the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association. Limited evidence evaluates the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events after dermatologic surgery within 1 year of myocardial infarction.

Objective

To determine major adverse cardiovascular event risk after dermatologic surgery within 1 year of myocardial infarction. Outcomes were compared with cataract surgery and endoscopies, which are also considered very low risk procedures.

Materials and methods

Using the All of Us Research Program V8, nationwide database of 633,000 patients, the authors performed a retrospective study from 2018 to 2023. CPT and ICD-10 codes were used to retrieve data.

Results

Out of 308 procedures, 3 (0.97%) major adverse cardiovascular events were observed within the 30-day postoperative window in patients with or without a history of myocardial infarction. Patients undergoing procedures postmyocardial infarction appeared more likely to experience major adverse cardiovascular events than those without prior myocardial infarction (4.9% vs 0%), although not significantly more so than patients with myocardial infarction without procedures.

Conclusion

The authors' findings are consistent with the low risk of dermatologic procedures in patients with myocardial infarction, although they are limited by the low number of major adverse cardiovascular events.

title: Shockwave Lithotripsy for Severe Calcified Extracranial Vertebral and Carotid Disease Treated With Percutaneous Stenting.
authorString: Martinez Gutierrez JC, Gupta AC, Khaldi A, Humphries W, D'Amato S, Zussman B, Gupta R.
abstractText:
Background

Patients harboring heavily calcified concentric or eccentric type lesions in the carotid or vertebral artery pose a challenge in placing a stent to reduce the lesion. These lesions yield suboptimal results due to poor stent expansion. Shockwave lithotripsy offers a potential solution for achieving luminal gain.

Methods

We present a retrospective study of all patients at our institution who were treated with lithotripsy for extracranial carotid or vertebral artery stenosis associated with heavily calcified lesions from July 2022 to February 2026. Data were maintained in our procedural database and retrospectively analyzed for patients treated with lithotripsy. All consecutive patients were analyzed for demographic information, procedural data, perioperative complications, and 6-month midterm follow-up imaging for restenosis.

Results

A total of 41 patients (8 vertebral artery lesions and 33 carotid lesions) were treated with intravascular lithotripsy at our institution between July 2022 and February 2026. The mean age for the cohort was 70.7 ± 8.7. The mean lesion pretreatment for the carotid stenosis was 77 ± 13% and for the vertebral artery treated patients 81 ± 11%. All patients were successfully treated with stenting and lithotripsy, and the mean stenosis posttreatment was 15 ± 14% for the carotid stenosis and 8 ± 5% for the vertebral artery lesions. There were 2 groin complications (5%) with femoral artery pseudoaneurysms treated with thrombin injection and 1 perioperative stroke (3%) secondary to a dissection in the carotid stent cohort.

Conclusions

The current study demonstrates the feasibility of lithotripsy for heavily calcified lesions treated with transfemoral stenting. Future prospective core laboratory adjudicated studies are warranted to determine the efficacy of this technique.

title: Nrf2 Immunohistochemical Expression in Stillbirths: A Potential Marker of Early Fetal Hypoxic Stress.
authorString: Bonasoni MP, Camatti J, Santunione AL, Giorgetti A, Ferretti A, Ishida Y, Kondo T, Cecchi R.

journal.title: Pediatric and developmental pathology : the official journal of the Society for Pediatric Pathology and the Paediatric Pathology Society

abstractText: Stillbirth remains a major challenge in perinatal and forensic pathology, particularly when the timing of fetal death and the mechanisms of hypoxic injury are difficult to establish using conventional morphological criteria alone. Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) is a key regulator of cellular responses to oxidative stress and may represent an early marker of fetal cellular stress. We conducted a retrospective forensic study of stillbirth cases that underwent complete autopsy between 2017 and 2024. Clinical, pathological, and placental data were examined to estimate the timing of fetal distress and the death-delivery interval. Immunohistochemical analysis of Nrf2 expression was performed on fetal cardiac tissue sections, and cases were classified as Nrf2-positive or Nrf2-negative based on unequivocal nuclear immunoreactivity. Nrf2 nuclear expression was identified in 10/44 cases (22.7%) and was observed more frequently in cases with shorter death-delivery intervals and clinicopathological patterns compatible with acute or subacute fetal hypoxic stress, particularly placental abruption and selected acute umbilical cord-related events. These findings suggest that Nrf2 nuclear immunoreactivity may represent a potential ancillary marker of early fetal cellular stress in well-preserved stillbirth tissues. However, tissue preservation may represent an important confounding factor. Further prospective studies with controlled temporal parameters are needed to clarify its diagnostic and forensic value.

title: Early Implementation Performance of the CMS Electronic Clinical Quality Measure for Excessive Radiation Dose or Inadequate Image Quality in Diagnostic CT: An Evaluation of 254 Facilities.
authorString: Smith-Bindman R, Bindman AB, Kohli MD, Stewart C, Szczykutowicz TP, Kline RM, Romano PS.

journal.title: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR

abstractText:
Objective

To evaluate early facility performance on the CMS-adopted Excessive Radiation Dose or Inadequate Image Quality for Diagnostic CT in Adults (ExRad) measure, the first automated radiology outcome measure in CMS payment programs, during the first 16 months of the measure's inclusion in CMS programs.

Methods

ExRad evaluates each adult diagnostic CT examination in three steps: assignment to 1 of 19 CT categories defined by anatomic region and clinical indication; computation of size-adjusted radiation dose and image noise from the DICOM radiation dose-structured report and pixel data; and comparison of both against category-specific thresholds. Because the clinical and radiology data sit in separate systems, translation software inside the health system firewall may be used to perform the linkage. An examination is out of range if its dose or noise exceeds its category threshold; a facility's score is the percentage of eligible examinations out of range (lower is better). We analyzed all facilities reporting between May 2025 and August 2026.

Results

Across 254 facilities and 783,634 examinations in 16 CT categories, 30.7% were out of range: 240,409 (30.7%) exceeded the dose threshold and 446 (0.06%) the noise threshold. Facility scores varied widely: median 29.5% (interquartile range [IQR] 18.4-44.7; range 1.8-82.4), with facilities at the 90th percentile scoring 4.6 times more out-of-range scans than those at the 10th percentile. Median out-of-range percentages by category ranged from 0% (routine and low-dose cardiac) to 82.6% (high-dose head; IQR 23.5-100.0); routine abdomen and pelvis, the highest-volume category, had a median of 43.9% (IQR 30.1-61.3). Within facilities, the median gap between best- and worst-performing category was 74 percentage points (IQR 49-89; intraclass correlation coefficient = 0.12).

Discussion

Early ExRad performance varied widely across facilities and across CT categories within the same facility. Most variation reflected particular facility-category combinations, so facilities need their own category-level results to identify which protocols to target.

title: EMC evaluation in radiation-emitting medical devices: regulatory limits and an integrated safety approach.
authorString: Censi F, D'Agostino S, Apolinio F, Masini EP, Burriesci G.
abstractText:
Introduction

Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) is a fundamental safety requirement for medical devices, ensuring both the limitation of electromagnetic emissions and adequate immunity to external electromagnetic disturbances.

Areas covered

Within the European regulatory framework, EMC is addressed in the Regulation 2017/745 (MDR), which requires manufacturers to minimize radiation emissions, prevent interference with other devices, and provide appropriate information in the instructions for use. The main technical reference standard for EMC is IEC 60,601-1-2, which defines test methods and limits for electromagnetic emissions and immunity. However, this standard evaluates radiated emissions only above 30 MHz, creating a regulatory gap for devices operating at lower frequencies. Moreover, it does not address the assessment of unintended or spurious emissions below this threshold.

Expert opinion

To address these limitations, additional standards and guidelines must be considered. IEC 62,311 provides methodologies for assessing human exposure to electromagnetic fields across the frequency range 0 Hz-300 GHz, while exposure limits can be derived from the ICNIRP guidelines and the European Directive 2013/35/EU. By combining EMC testing according to IEC 60,601-1-2 with exposure assessment based on IEC 62,311 and comparison with ICNIRP limits, manufacturers can demonstrate full regulatory compliance in terms of EMC.

title: Treatment standards for hypotension on hemodialysis - physiology-based phenotyping of acute and chronic scenarios.
authorString: Beige J, Hausschild S, Hecking M, Mussnig S.

journal.title: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association

abstractText: Intradialytic hypotension (IDH) is a pervasive complication of hemodialysis, yet the clinical scenarios in which IDH occurs vary widely. To guide treatment standards, we describe five cases corresponding to typical IDH phenotypes: (i) acute intradialytic allergic event, with abrupt early hypotension reproducible with specific dialyzers; (ii) acute unexpected IDH due to autonomic imbalance (here, postprandial), with disproportionate symptoms despite modest blood pressure drops; (iii) chronic IDH due to hypovolemia from an overly ambitious target weight; (iv) chronic IDH with ultrafiltration-refill mismatch, where blood volume falls despite fluid overload; and (v) chronic hypotension due to limited cardiac reserve. In the acute setting (i-ii), immediate rescue-interruption of ultrafiltration and/or the dialysis session, Trendelenburg positioning, and isotonic fluid bolus-should be combined with rapid bedside phenotyping to identify allergic, autonomic, hypovolemic or cardiac triggers. Material hypersensitivity must be recognized, as rechallenge can be harmful, but is avoidable by dialyzer substitution. In the chronic setting (iii-v), prevention centers on reduced ultrafiltration stress: lower ultrafiltration rates with longer or more frequent sessions, and objective reassessment of target weight. The chronic phenotypes are often clinically indistinguishable yet require different corrections-a higher target weight in hypovolemia, gentler fluid removal that supports refilling in refill mismatch, and acceptance of some fluid overload with limited cardiac reserve-making objective volume assessment the decisive first step. The unifying concern is organ hypoperfusion, not blood pressure. Future trials should enroll phenotype-defined rather than heterogeneous 'IDH-prone' populations and use hard outcomes, end-organ ischemia and patient-reported outcomes.

title: Clinical Variability and Genotype Driven Outcomes in an International Cohort of 14 Pediatric FIG4 Patients.
authorString: Gangfuß A, Gowda VK, Natera-de Benito D, Munot P, Vanegas M, Darling A, Reutlinger C, Carrera-Garcia L, Wunderlich G, Kölbel H, Stüve B, Muhmann D, Monfort Belenguer L, Barca DG, Reddy C VS, Srinivasan VM, Anguita CM, Jungbluth H, Dafsari HS, Rossor T, Böhm J, Schara-Schmidt U, Roos A.

journal.title: Annals of clinical and translational neurology

abstractText:
Background

Biallelic FIG4 variants classically cause distinct conditions characterized by peripheral neuropathy (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4J) or skeletal dysplasia (Yunis-Varón syndrome). However, central nervous system involvement is increasingly recognized. The prevalence and specific characteristics of movement disorders within FIG4-related disease remain poorly characterized, prompting a need to redefine its clinical continuum.

Objective

To delineate the phenotypic spectrum of FIG4-related disorders beyond established entities (Yunis-Varón syndrome, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4J, bilateral temporooccipital polymicrogyria, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis type 11) using an international multicentre cohort.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed clinical, genetic, and neurophysiological data from patients with biallelic FIG4 variants to redefine genotype-phenotype correlations, focusing on motor development, cognitive status, and movement disorders.

Results

Evaluating 14 pediatric FIG4 patients revealed a continuous phenotypic spectrum rather than the clinical entities previously described in the literature. Instead of the typical peripheral neuropathy classically associated with pathogenic FIG4 variants, the predominant clinical picture in this age group was a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. Patients showed profound motor and cognitive delay, with a subset additionally displaying distinct movement abnormalities such as dystonia and bradykinesia.

Conclusion

Loss of functional FIG4 causes a broader and more severe disease spectrum with central nervous system involvement, including intellectual disability and movement abnormalities such as dystonia and bradykinesia. Recognizing these features should prompt clinicians to consider FIG4-associated disorders, allowing for optimized patient care and tailored therapeutic strategies.

title: White matter injury, brain aging, and cognitive decline beyond amyloid/tau.
authorString: Beheshti I, Elkana O.
abstractText: BackgroundWhite matter injury in Alzheimer's disease is etiologically heterogeneous. Brain-predicted age difference (Brain-PAD) may capture structural vulnerability.ObjectiveTo test whether T1-weighted white matter signal abnormality burden (T1W-WMSA) is associated with Brain-PAD and whether Brain-PAD predicts cognitive decline and mild cognitive impairment (MCI)-to-Alzheimer's disease progression beyond white matter injury and amyloid/tau (A/T) status.MethodsHarmonized data from the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project Phenotype Harmonization Consortium (ADSP-PHC) were anchored to the cardiovascular-risk baseline. Cross-sectional regression tested associations between cardiovascular risk and T1W-WMSA and between T1W-WMSA and Brain-PAD. Mixed-effects and Cox models assessed cognitive decline and progression. We also evaluated sex interactions and A/T timing. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery-derived white matter hyperintensity burden (FLAIR-WMH) was examined as a modality comparison.ResultsAmong 601 complete cases, cardiovascular-risk burden was not associated with T1W-WMSA (β = -0.0003, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.0470 to 0.0463; p = 0.989), whereas T1W-WMSA was associated with higher Brain-PAD (β = 6.95 years per log-unit, 95% CI 5.71 to 8.19; p < 0.001). Among 369 participants, higher Brain-PAD predicted faster memory (β = -0.0244 per year; p < 0.001) and executive-function decline (β = -0.0153 per year; p < 0.001). Among 201 participants with MCI, Brain-PAD predicted progression to Alzheimer's disease (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.268, 95% CI 1.191 to 1.351; p < 0.001). The association persisted in the pre-outcome A/T-adjusted subset (HR = 1.333, 95% CI 1.203 to 1.477; p < 0.001). No prespecified sex interaction survived false-discovery-rate correction.ConclusionsWhite matter injury was associated with older-appearing brain structure but should not be interpreted as exclusively vascular. Brain-PAD provided prognostic information complementary to A/T staging and white matter lesion burden.

title: In familial hypercholesterolaemia, remnant cholesterol above 1 mmol/L is associated with 50% higher risk of coronary artery disease.
authorString: Mourre F, Hvid K, Afzal S, Nordestgaard BG.
abstractText:
Aims

Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) leads to lifelong elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and increased risk of coronary artery disease. We tested the hypothesis that elevated remnant cholesterol additionally increases cardiovascular risk in FH.

Methods

In the Copenhagen General Population Study (CGPS) and UK Biobank, 108,751 and 428,625 individuals were classified as with or without FH according to clinical scores and genetic mutations. In the two cohorts, 7,708 and 50,997 experienced coronary artery disease, respectively.

Results

In CGPS and UK Biobank, remnant cholesterol ≥1 mmol/L (39 mg/dL) was observed in 12% and 11% of individuals without FH (N = 104,226 and 403,172), in 33% and 40% with Simon Broome FH (N = 3,923 and 23,860), in 44% and 78% with MEDPED FH (N = 1,005 and 2,465), in 33% and 34% with DLCN FH (N = 744 and 1,207), and in 12% and 21% of individuals with genetic FH (N = 188 and 875). Likewise in the CGPS and UK Biobank, the multivariable adjusted hazard ratios for coronary artery disease by remnant cholesterol ≥1 vs. < 1 mmol/L (39 mg/dL) were 1.49 (95% CI: 1.39-1.59) and 1.47 (1.43-1.52) in individuals without FH, 1.59 (1.31-1.93) and 1.18 (1.10-1.27) in Simon Broome FH, 1.50 (1.08-2.08) and 1.14 (0.89-1.45) in MEDPED FH, 1.60 (1.17-2.21) and 1.59 (1.20-2.09) in DLCN FH, and 1.48 (0.59-3.69) and 1.39 (0.88-2.19) in genetic FH.

Conclusion

In familial hypercholesterolaemia, remnant cholesterol ≥1 mmol/L (39 mg/dL) vs below is associated with ≈50% higher risk of coronary artery disease, that is, above the already high risk due to lifelong genetically elevated LDL cholesterol.

title: PhenX Toolkit: a knowledgebase that enables consistent data collection and facilitates cross-study analysis and data reuse.
authorString: Huggins W, Hendershot TP, Marazita ML, Bakalov VD, Ceger P, Cook B, Cox LA, Ives C, Nelms MD, Quattrone W, Reeve TC, Williams DN, Hamilton CM.
abstractText: The PhenX (consensus measures for Phenotypes and eXposures) Toolkit (https://www.phenxtoolkit.org/) is a publicly available knowledgebase of well-established, broadly validated measurement protocols recommended for use in genomic, clinical, translational, and epidemiological research involving human participants. Consistent use of PhenX protocols, including questionnaires, bioassays, and physical assessments, improves the rigor, transparency, reproducibility, and comparability of research data. The Toolkit was recently highlighted in the National Institutes of Health (NIH) implementation plan, "Leading in Gold Standard Science," as an example of efforts to advance reproducible biomedical research. The Toolkit currently includes 1010 protocols spanning a wide range of diseases, exposures, and study designs. Content development is guided by the scientific community through a consensus-based process involving expert Working Groups, community input, and strategic oversight from the PhenX Steering Committee. Collaborations with NIH Institutes have expanded Toolkit content in priority areas, including substance use and cardiovascular disease. The PhenX Toolkit enhances study design and supports implementation of selected protocols. PhenX also collaborates with resources that facilitate data collection (REDCap), data standards (LOINC), and data repositories to promote interoperability and cross-study analyses. To date, the Toolkit has been recommended in 711 NIH funding opportunities and cited in >1300 publications. Future directions are discussed.

title: Dynamic Supercooled Crystal-Gels for Ultrafast, Reversible Mechanical Adaptative Materials.
authorString: Lv Y, Feng H, Yang Z, Yin J, Li H, Zhou B, Meng Y, Su Y, Zhang X, Pei X.
abstractText: Endowing synthetic materials with adaptability and responsiveness to dynamically optimize their states represents a premier frontier in biomimetic science. However, achieving life-like, rapid yet reversible adaptation under benign triggers remains hindered by high reconfiguration energy or delayed structural recovery. In this work, we present dynamic supercooled crystal-gels that achieve ultrafast, reversible stiffening without requiring continuous energy input. Inspired by the tactile-triggered stiffening of starfish tissues, it utilizes non-equilibrium energy of internal supercooled liquid to realize templated crystallization upon a benign tactile stimulus trigger. Meanwhile, the crystalline structure is reversible under appropriate temperature and humidity perturbations. This synchronously achieves a 2596-fold adjustment in compressive modulus, circumventing the conventional trade-off between energy demands for mechanical reinforcement and structural stability. As a functional validation, microneedles based on supercooled crystal-gels fulfill the divergent requirements for skin adaptation and seconds-scale drug release through their mechanical adaptation, achieving rapid cumulative drug release of ≈37.76% at 10 s and 88.12% within 5 min. This work delineates a strategy for endowing materials with autonomous mechanical adaptation and opens new opportunities for life-like functional evolution in soft robotics and bio-integrated electronics.

title: Crossing subfamily borders: Mechanosensitive TREK-1 and alkaline-activated TASK-4 form heterodimers with unique functional and pharmacological properties.
authorString: Schütte S, Schick F, De Martino E, Schmitz H, Zander KES, Holz F, Sauer P, Mildeberger L, Linder M, Loewe A, Kiper AK, Kauferstein S, Schäfer MK, Rinné S, Decher N.
abstractText:
Background and purpose

The tandem of two-pore-domain potassium (K2P) channels TREK-1 and TASK-4 are expressed in the heart and pancreatic beta-cells. As TREK-1 and TASK-4 belong to distinct subfamilies with different functional hallmarks, heteromerization of these two channels was highly unexpected. However, due to their shared expression in these tissues and their involvement in congenital cardiac arrhythmias, the aim of this study was to probe for a possible formation of TREK-1/TASK-4 heterodimers.

Experimental approach

Two-electrode voltage-clamp and inside-out macropatch clamp recordings, together with immunohistochemistry and chemiluminescence-based ELISA assays, were utilized to describe heteromerization of TREK-1 and TASK-4 channels and elucidate the characteristics of this heteromeric channel complex.

Key results

Here, we show that the mechanosensitive TREK-1 forms heteromeric channel complexes with the alkaline-activated TASK-4. The resulting heterodimers of these only remotely related channels have an enhanced temperature sensitivity, an altered pH dependence and regulation by extracellular sodium. Unlike TREK-1, heteromeric TREK-1/TASK-4 channels are not inhibited via Gs-coupled receptor activation, as the heterodimeric channels are not PKA sensitive. Strikingly, these novel heterodimeric channel complexes are characterized by a unique pharmacology.

Conclusions and implications

The newly described heterodimerization across different K2P channel families is of major relevance for drugs targeting TASK-4 or TREK-1. Their functional co-expression in different tissues raises the possibility of developing drugs against cardiac arrhythmias and Type 2 diabetes by specifically targeting these unique heterodimeric channel complexes.

title: Development and internal validation of a serum ferritin-based prediction model for coronary artery aneurysms in Kawasaki disease.
authorString: Yang P, Zhang J, Yi Q.
abstractText:
Background

Kawasaki disease is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children, and coronary artery aneurysms represent its most important cardiovascular complication. Identifying children at risk for coronary artery aneurysms at 4 to 8 weeks after disease onset is clinically important. Serum ferritin may reflect systemic inflammation in Kawasaki disease, but its incremental predictive value remains uncertain. This study developed a ferritin-based model for predicting coronary artery aneurysms at 4 to 8 weeks.

Methods

Patients with Kawasaki disease were retrospectively identified at a single centre and randomly divided into training and internal validation cohorts in a 6:4 ratio. Predictors were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression and multivariable logistic regression. Model performance was assessed by discrimination, calibration, decision curve analysis, and reclassification metrics.

Results

Among 378 patients, 98 (25.9%) had coronary artery aneurysms at 4 to 8 weeks after disease onset. The ferritin-based model included male sex, platelet count, serum ferritin, albumin ≤ 31.5 g/L, and baseline maximum coronary artery Z score ≥ 2.5. Adding serum ferritin increased the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.853 to 0.899 in the training cohort and from 0.842 to 0.868 in the internal validation cohort, with good calibration, greater decision-curve net benefit, and improved risk reclassification.

Conclusions

Serum ferritin provided incremental predictive value for coronary artery aneurysms at 4 to 8 weeks after the onset of Kawasaki disease. The ferritin-based model improved predictive performance in internal validation and warrants multicentre external validation to assess its generalisability and clinical applicability.

title: Growth failure and nutritional-endocrine adaptations in children with cyanotic CHD: a structured narrative review.
authorString: Soliman AT, Alyafei F, Abdulkayoum AT, AlQadi M, Ahmed S, Alhemaidi N, Alaaraj N, Hamed N.
abstractText: The heart is increasingly recognised as a cardiovascular signalling organ that releases biologically active natriuretic peptides during haemodynamic stress. In cyanotic CHD, chronic hypoxaemia, altered loading conditions, increased energy expenditure, recurrent illness, and delayed repair may disrupt endocrine, metabolic, and nutritional pathways that regulate growth. This structured narrative review synthesises evidence linking cardiac biomarkers, systemic hormonal adaptation, nutritional status, surgical timing, and growth outcomes in children with cyanotic CHD. PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched for human studies published from January 1990 to December 2025 that reported cardiac biomarkers, systemic hormonal measures, growth parameters, nutritional outcomes, or postoperative recovery in paediatric CHD. Thirty-six studies were included and narratively synthesised because lesion types, age groups, assays, and outcomes were heterogeneous. The evidence indicates consistent activation of natriuretic peptide signalling, reduced circulating insulin-like growth factor 1 and insulin-like growth factor binding protein 3 in several paediatric cohorts, appetite-related hormonal changes, impaired weight gain, and frequent linear growth faltering. Longitudinal studies suggest partial improvement in growth velocity and anabolic signalling after timely surgical correction, although incomplete recovery may occur when preoperative hypoxaemia and undernutrition are prolonged. Growth failure in cyanotic CHD should therefore be regarded as a multifactorial cardiovascular-nutritional syndrome rather than isolated primary endocrine disease. Early surgical referral, individualised nutrition, and coordinated cardiology, endocrinology, and dietetic follow-up are central to improving long-term outcomes.

title: Structurally diverse triterpenoid alkaloids from Buxus myrica with cytotoxic and apoptosis-inducing activities.
authorString: Wang Y, Wang M, Zhang Y, Gao H.
abstractText: Sixteen triterpenoid alkaloids, including twelve previously undescribed ones named myribuxines A-L (1-12), were isolated from the twigs and leaves of Buxus myrica H. Lév. To our knowledge, this species has not yet undergone any phytochemical or pharmacological investigation. Their structures and relative configurations were elucidated by comprehensive spectroscopic analysis and DP4<sup>+</sup> probability calculations, with their absolute configurations tentatively assigned on the basis of the biosynthetic origin of Buxus alkaloids. Structurally, 5, 6, 7, and 12 feature a rare C-16 aromatic ester substituent, while 9, 10, and 11 possess a rare tetrahydrofuran ring formed by a C-10-O-C-23 ether linkage. All isolated alkaloids were evaluated for cytotoxicity against HepG2, A549, U251, and HCT-116 cell lines. The active alkaloids showed modest cytotoxicity, with half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC<sub>50</sub>) values ranging from 17.5 to 47.3 μM across the four cell lines. Among them, 2 exhibited modest inhibitory activity toward HepG2 cells. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that 2 promoted apoptosis in a dose- and time-dependent manner. Furthermore, network pharmacology screening predicted HSP90α as its potential molecular target. Follow-up molecular docking further revealed the binding model between compound 2 and HSP90.

title: KARS1-Related Infantile-Onset Progressive Leukoencephalopathy With or Without Deafness: A Novel Variant and Phenotypic Expansion.
authorString: Behroozi J, Khorrami M, Farhadi A, Ghazavi A, Seyedabadi M, Piryaei F.
abstractText: Biallelic variants in the KARS1 gene, encoding lysyl-tRNA synthetase, are responsible for autosomal recessive disorders such as infantile-onset progressive leukoencephalopathy with or without deafness (LEPID; OMIM #619147) and nonsyndromic hearing loss (DFNB89). Common features of LEPID include sensorineural hearing loss, developmental delay, and leukoencephalopathy, but dysmorphic facial features and cardiac anomalies are not commonly reported. This study presents the first documented LEPID case in Iran, expanding the phenotypic and genetic spectrum of KARS1-related disorders. Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed on a two-year-old Iranian boy from non-consanguineous parents, without a positive history of any neurologic conditions. Identified variants were validated by Sanger sequencing, with familial segregation analysis. Moreover, a literature review of 41 KARS1-related cases was conducted to compare clinical and genetic findings. WES identified two compound heterozygous KARS1 variants (NM_005548.3): c.959G > A (p.Arg320His) and c.2T > C (p.Met1Thr), previously reported and novel, respectively, both of which were classified as likely pathogenic according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics criteria. The patient exhibited typical LEPID features (sensorineural hearing loss, developmental delay, seizures, leukoencephalopathy) alongside unprecedented dysmorphic facial features (e.g., synophrys, pointed triangular chin) and cardiac anomalies (pulmonary stenosis, atrial septal defect). Literature review confirmed these dysmorphic features as novel, absent in prior cases, with cardiac involvement in a limited number of patients. This study highlights a novel KARS1 variant and an expanded phenotypic spectrum of LEPID, emphasizing the role of WES in diagnosing rare disorders even in non-consanguineous marriages. These findings advocate for broader phenotypic recognition and functional studies to elucidate KARS1's role in neurodevelopmental, craniofacial, and cardiac abnormalities.
