abstractText: Objective To investigate the association between the endothelial activation and stress index (EASIX) measured within 24 hours of admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) and 30-, 90- and 365-day all-cause mortality in patients with stage 4 cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, and to characterize the shape of this association as it changes with time since admission. Methods Retrospective cohort study; data were obtained from MIMIC-IV. Adults who met stage 4 CKM criteria at ICU admission, survived to 24 hours after admission, and had EASIX measurable within 24 hours were included. The first EASIX value within 0–24 hours was taken, and log₂(EASIX) was used as a continuous exposure. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcomes were 90-day and 365-day all-cause mortality. Cox proportional hazards models were used, with adjustment from M1 (unadjusted) to M4 (fully adjusted); the proportional hazards assumption was tested with scaled Schoenfeld residuals, categorical covariates violating the assumption were changed to stratification factors, continuous covariates were entered with a time-varying coefficient (γ × ln t), and hazard ratios (HRs) were reported at different time points. Restricted cubic splines, quartile analysis and directly standardized survival curves were also fitted, and subgroup analysis and E-value analysis were performed. Patients with stage 4 CKM were identified in eICU-CRD by an approximate definition for external validation; the endpoint in that database was all-cause mortality during hospitalization. Results A total of 9,766 patients with stage 4 CKM were finally included. Median age was 71 (61–81) years, 5,694 patients (58.3%) were male, and median EASIX was 2.1 (1.0–5.0). All-cause deaths at 30, 90 and 365 days were 2,278 (23.3%), 2,938 (30.1%) and 3,802 (38.9%), respectively. In the fully adjusted model, for each doubling of EASIX, the HR for 30-day mortality was 1.243 (95%CI 1.182–1.306) at 1 day after admission and 1.131 (1.079–1.185) at 30 days, and decreased with longer time since admission (γ = −0.0277, P = 0.026); for the 365-day outcome, the HR at the 365-day time point was 1.038 (0.993–1.086). For each 1-standard-deviation increase in log₂(EASIX) (1.861), the HR for 30-day mortality was 1.257 (1.152–1.372). Compared with Q1, the HR for 30-day mortality in Q4 was 1.660 (1.273–2.164), and the differences of Q2 and Q3 from Q1 were not statistically significant. The P values of the non-linearity test were 0.002 to < 0.001. Among the 9 subgroups, at the 30-day time point the interaction was statistically significant for heart failure, SOFA-4 and malignancy (P = 0.003, < 0.001, 0.039), and CKM stage 4a/4b did not reach significance (0.079). In the type 2 diabetes subgroup (n = 3,459), comparing the highest with the lowest quartile, the HR for 30-day mortality was 1.704 (1.061–2.735). The E value estimated at the 30-day time point was 1.40 (1.29). External validation included 1,103 patients, 173 of whom died during hospitalization (15.7%); after full adjustment, the HR of each doubling of EASIX for in-hospital death was 1.121 (1.045–1.203). Conclusions In ICU patients with stage 4 CKM, a higher EASIX calculated within 24 hours of admission was associated with a higher risk of all-cause mortality; the association was strongest early after admission and decreased over time, and was more evident in the higher EASIX range. In eICU-CRD the direction of this association was consistent, but the endpoint in that database was in-hospital mortality, which does not constitute a replication on the 30-day endpoint. The above findings should be interpreted as a descriptive association rather than a validated risk stratification tool; prospective validation on a consistent endpoint is still required before clinical implementation.

title: Transcarotid Artery Stenting Using Flow Reversal for Non-Atherosclerotic Carotid Artery Disease.
authorString: Blackstock C, Yadavalli SD, Jabbour G, Schermerhorn M, Money S.
abstractText:
Objective

We evaluated the use of transcarotid artery revascularization (TCAR) in non-atherosclerotic carotid disease and compared outcomes with transfemoral carotid artery stenting (TFCAS).

Methods

The Vascular Quality Initiative registry was queried for all TCAR and TFCAS procedures performed from 2017-2024. Patients with lesion types categorized as atherosclerosis or restenosis were excluded. The study cohort included dissection, trauma, fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD), and other non-atherosclerotic etiologies. Primary outcomes included major adverse events, including stroke, death, and composite endpoints. Propensity score matching was performed to adjust for baseline differences.

Results

A total of 541 TCAR and 2,348 TFCAS patients met inclusion criteria. TCAR was associated with lower contrast usage and fluoroscopy time across all lesion types. In unadjusted analyses, stroke or death rates were higher with TFCAS than TCAR for dissection (7.1% vs 1.9%, p=0.006), other lesions (8.7% vs 2.1%, p<0.001), and symptomatic (8.1% vs 2.2%, p=0.001) and asymptomatic patients (6.4% vs 1.6%, p<0.001). After propensity matching (527 pairs), TCAR was associated with significantly lower rates of stroke (4.4% vs 1.7%, p=0.0118), death (4.4% vs 0.4%, p<0.001), stroke or death (7.6% vs 1.9%, p<0.001), and stroke, death, or MI (8.0% vs 2.7%, p<0.001) compared with TFCAS (TFCAS vs TCAR, respectively).

Conclusions

This study supports consideration of TCAR for non-atherosclerotic carotid pathology when carotid stenting is indicated and suggests that TCAR may offer important advantages over TFCAS, particularly in reducing the risk of perioperative stroke or death.

title: RyR2-Mediated Ca  <sup>2+</sup>  Leak Drives Progressive Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy
authorString: Zheng J, Ponce-Balbuena D, Estrada S, Xiao L, Ríos Pérez EB, Gowda AM, Korcarz CE, Hansen KM, Blackwell DJ, Thorpe MP, Akers WS, Wu J, Johnston JN, Gómez AM, Benitah J, Knollmann BC, Chen YE, Valdivia HH, Alvarado FJ.
abstractText:
ABSTRACT

Background

Abnormal sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca 2+ release through ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) is a well-established mechanism of ventricular arrhythmias. Whether persistent RyR2 dysfunction can also initiate the structural remodeling characteristic of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) remains unknown. We tested the hypothesis that chronic RyR2-mediated Ca 2+ leak is sufficient to couple electrical instability to progressive cardiomyopathy.

Methods

We generated a rabbit carrying the severe gain-of-function RyR2-V2475F mutation and characterized disease progression using longitudinal cardiac phenotyping, continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, cellular electrophysiology and Ca 2+ imaging, histopathology, biochemical analyses, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). Therapeutic potential was evaluated by continuous treatment with the selective RyR2 inhibitor ent -verticilide for two months.

Results

RyR2-V2475F rabbits developed spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and progressive right ventricular (RV)-dominant fibrofatty cardiomyopathy recapitulating major features of human ACM. Malignant ventricular arrhythmias preceded overt structural remodeling and were associated at the cellular level with early spontaneous Ca 2+ release and early afterdepolarizations. Early disease was characterized by remodeling of excitation-contraction coupling with preserved SR Ca 2+ load and contractile function despite RyR2 dysfunction; upon disease progression, these compensatory changes were accompanied by SR Ca 2+ depletion, impaired RV contractility and reduced left ventricular filling. Single-nucleus transcriptomics identified early fibroblast expansion and predicted cardiomyocyte-centered paracrine signaling before advanced fibrofatty infiltration. Cardiomyocytes also exhibited an altered lipid-metabolic transcriptome and intracellular lipid accumulation, accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake. Selective RyR2 inhibition markedly reduced ventricular tachycardia burden and preserved RV contraction and LV filling during disease progression.

Conclusions

Severe RyR2 gain-of-function can lead to both malignant ventricular arrhythmias and progressive arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in a large-animal model, establishing persistent intracellular Ca 2+ dysregulation as a mechanistic link between electrical and structural heart disease. The ability of selective RyR2 inhibition to suppress arrhythmias and preserve cardiac function identifies RyR2 as a potentially actionable therapeutic target in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

title: CTA-Based 3D Thrombus Radiomics and Machine Learning for Differentiating Stroke Etiology in Acute Middle Cerebral Artery Occlusion
authorString: Huang Y, Chen X, Xin B, Ye Z, Ye H, Kong X, Cai X, Sun J.
abstractText:
Purpose: To develop and evaluate machine learning models integrating three-dimensional (3D) thrombus radiomic features from preoperative computed tomography angiography (CTA) with clinical variables to differentiate large-artery atherosclerosis (LAA) from cardioembolism (CE) in patients with acute middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO).

Materials and Methods:

This retrospective two-center study included 453 patients with acute MCAO who underwent endovascular treatment (EVT). The 3D thrombus region was segmented on preoperative CTA, and radiomic features reflecting intensity, texture, and morphology were extracted. Multiple machine learning models integrating radiomic and clinical variables were developed using the training cohort and evaluated in a held-out test cohort. Discrimination, calibration, SHAP-based interpretability, feature importance, and decision curve analysis were assessed.

Results:

Among the evaluated models, the random forest (RF) model showed competitive performance in the held-out test cohort, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.822, sensitivity of 0.867, and the lowest Brier score (0.171) among the evaluated models. Both clinical and 3D thrombus radiomic features contributed to model predictions. Intraprocedural tirofiban use, admission LDL-C level, sex, admission NIHSS score, and selected thrombus texture and morphological features were important predictors. Decision curve analysis indicated positive net benefit over treat-all and treat-none strategies across threshold probabilities of approximately 0.05–0.60.

Conclusion:

Three-dimensional thrombus radiomics from routine preoperative CTA combined with clinical variables may help differentiate LAA from CE in acute MCAO. The interpretable RF model may serve as a complementary tool for acute-phase stroke etiological assessment.

title: When Winter Comes: Seasonal Patterns in Outcomes After Major Surgery.
authorString: Ejaz R, Alizai Q, Mevawalla A, Angez M, Bega R, Charalampous CM, Elemosho A, Pawlik TM.
abstractText:
Introduction

Seasonal strain may affect perioperative care, yet national evidence on seasonal variation in outcomes after major surgery remains limited. We evaluated whether postoperative outcomes varied by season among older adults undergoing major surgical procedures.

Methods

Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 y or older undergoing abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, coronary artery bypass grafting, colectomy, lung resection, or pancreaticoduodenectomy from 2016 through 2021 were identified using 100% Medicare Standard Analytic Files. Seasons were defined meteorologically, with spring as the reference. Outcomes included 30-d mortality, 90-d mortality, complications, textbook outcome, failure to rescue, surgical site infection, and length of stay. Multivariable regression models adjusted for patient, procedure, and hospital characteristics and were stratified by elective versus emergency admission. Interactions with the nurse-to-bed ratio and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Hospital Star Rating were assessed.

Results

Among 1,165,265 patients, 738,236 underwent elective surgery and 427,029 underwent emergency surgery. Among emergency admissions, winter was associated with higher adjusted odds of 30-d mortality (adjusted odds ratio: 1.10; 95% confidence interval: 1.07-1.13), 90-d mortality (1.10; 1.07-1.13), complications (1.05; 1.03-1.07), and failure to rescue (1.11; 1.07-1.15), as well as lower odds of textbook outcome (0.96; 0.94-0.98) and longer length of stay. Among elective admissions, winter was associated with smaller increases in 30-d and 90-d mortality. No significant interaction was observed by nurse-to-bed ratio or Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Hospital Star Rating.

Conclusions

Winter was associated with worse outcomes after major surgery, particularly among emergency admissions, supporting targeted seasonal preparedness strategies.

title: Left Ventricular Diastolic Dysfunction in Youth with Sickle Cell Disease: Evaluating Genotypic Differences and Effects of Hydroxyurea.
authorString: Igwe C, Kistler I, Schmitt C, Alvarado C, Creary S, Gunsaulus M, Buddhavarapu A, Hor K, Jacobs H.
abstractText: Sickle cell disease (SCD) encompasses a spectrum of genotypes, most commonly Hemoglobin (Hgb)SS and HgbSC. Diastolic dysfunction (DD) is common in SCD and impacts morbidity and mortality. We sought to evaluate if the rates of DD differed by SCD genotype and by hydroxyurea (HU) use among youths. This was a retrospective study of patients with HgbSS and HgbSC who received an echocardiogram, stratifying genotype and HU use. DD was assessed using mitral valve (MV) E/A ratio < 0.8 or > 2, septal E' < 7 cm/s, lateral E' <10 cm/s, E/e' Average > 10; and LA: Aortic root (LA: Ao) ratio > 1.3:1. DD was defined as a diastolic aggregate score ≥ 2 of 5. Multivariable regression models adjusted for age were used to estimate the associations of DD with HU use by genotype. 39% of youth with SCD who had an echocardiogram had DD. DD rates were lower in those on HU (n = 102, 36%) vs. those not on HU (n = 94, 41%). Adjusting for age, youths with HgbSS on HU had lower odds of DD compared to those not on HU, OR 0.22 [95% CI (0.07, 0.59), p = 0.004]. Conversely, youth with HgbSC on HU had slightly increased odds of DD compared to those not on HU, OR 1.36 [95% CI (0.35, 4.98) p = 0.6]. In contrast to previous studies suggesting HU has no impact in reducing DD over time, our study showed DD was less common among patients with HgbSS on HU. Larger, prospective, multi-center studies are needed to assess longitudinal improvement of DD from baseline for SCD patients on HU.

title: Mitochondrial content and intrinsic coupling-related differences shape bioenergetic output and redox responses across striated muscles in rats.
authorString: Chan A, Devaux J, Wen C, Phillips A, Hickey A, Pham T.
abstractText: Striated muscles differ markedly in energetic demand, but whether mitochondrial respiration and reactive oxygen species emission differ intrinsically across muscle types remains unclear. This study compared mitochondrial respiration, hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) emission and antioxidant enzyme expression in heart, diaphragm and hindlimb skeletal muscle from healthy rats. Mitochondrial O2 flux and H2O2 emission were measured simultaneously using high-resolution respirometry coupled with fluorometry in tissue homogenates subjected to substrate-uncoupler-inhibitor titration protocols. Mitochondrial content was estimated by citrate synthase activity, and antioxidant enzyme expression was measured by immunoblotting. Heart tissue displayed the highest mitochondrial respiration and H2O2 emission when expressed per tissue mass, followed by diaphragm and skeletal muscle. However, normalisation by citrate synthase activity eliminated differences in respiratory flux between muscles, indicating that variations in tissue-level respiration were primarily driven by mitochondrial content. Net H2O2 emission was greatest during leak respiration and decreased during oxidative phosphorylation and uncoupled states in all muscle types. Cardiac mitochondria exhibited a higher H2O2/O2 ratio during leak respiration and higher coupling-related ratios than those of diaphragm and skeletal muscle. In association, cardiac muscle showed greater expression of the mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes superoxide dismutase 2 and catalase in a separate cohort. These findings indicate that absolute oxidative metabolism across striated muscles is largely determined by mitochondrial content, whereas respiratory capacity per mitochondrial unit was conserved. Cardiac muscle exhibits elevated leak-associated reactive oxygen species emission but compensates by enhancing antioxidant defences, highlighting coordination between bioenergetic demand and redox regulation in continuously active muscles.

title: Safety of Bioelectric Impedance Analysis Testing in Pediatric Patients With Cardiac Implantable Electronic Devices.
authorString: VanderWilde AJ, Knilans TK, Mays WA, Knecht SK, Powell AW.
abstractText: Bioelectric impedance analysis (BIA) is a useful clinical tool in pediatric heart disease, but concerns regarding cardiac implanted electronic devices (CIEDs) limit its use. This study's goal was to assess the impact of BIA on CIED settings in pediatric patients. This single-center cohort study included two groups: a retrospective cohort of patients under 21 years old who had CIED interrogation within 12 months before and after BIA use, and a smaller prospective cohort who had CIED interrogation immediately before and after BIA use. The prospective group also underwent real-time monitoring for electrical interference during BIA. Exclusion criteria included age, implanted loop recorders, and incomplete data. Analysis used either a paired t-test or a Wilcoxon signed-rank test as appropriate, with p-value < 0.05 considered statistically significant. The retrospective cohort included 55 patients with 80 total tests. A statistically but not clinically significant difference in lead impedance was observed (513 [456, 627] v 513 [399, 593] ohms, p < 0.0001), though no differences were found in electrogram amplitudes, thresholds, or programmed output. When patients with multiple tests were analyzed, there remained a statistically significant difference in lead impedance (513 [399, 614] v 513 [375, 592] ohms, p = 0.0002) but not in other CIED parameters. In the prospective cohort (n = 10), no electrical interference was appreciated during BIA, and there were no before-and-after differences in CIED sensing amplitudes. No inappropriate shocks or premature device failures occurred. BIA was not associated with adverse events or meaningful changes in CIED function in this pediatric cohort.

title: Should Esophageal Temperature Probes Be Used within UK Search and Rescue Helicopter Services?
authorString: Atkinson E, Freshwater ES, Brogan JS.
abstractText: Due to the environment in which they operate, UK search and rescue helicopters (SARH) may encounter patients presenting with accidental hypothermia or hypothermic cardiac arrest. For these patients, accurate core temperature measurement allows thorough assessment of hypothermia severity and determines the recommended clinical interventions and conveyance decisions. Ongoing monitoring of core temperature also provides feedback to clinicians on the effectiveness of rewarming interventions. Currently, SARH paramedics use peripheral thermometers, which some evidence suggests may not be appropriate for assessing hypothermic patients in this environment. The implementation of esophageal temperature probes (ETPs) may allow clinicians to meet the needs of a wider range of patient presentations. This article aims to discuss the demand, practicality, and training required to implement ETPs into SARH paramedic practice and highlights an opportunity for further research.

title: Bare-Metal vs Covered Balloon-Expandable Stents for Transplant Renal Artery Stenosis: A Retrospective Comparative Study.
authorString: Discalzi A, Sanna E, Ruffino MA, Mandolini M, Nardelli F, Brino J, Albarello T, Tallia C, Calandri M, Biancone L.

journal.title: Journal of endovascular therapy : an official journal of the International Society of Endovascular Specialists

abstractText: To compare short- and long-term outcomes of bare-metal (BMS) vs covered (CS) balloon-expandable stents in transplant renal artery stenosis (TRAS). This retrospective study evaluated patients who underwent elective stent placement for TRAS between 2016 and 2023. Short-term efficacy was assessed by clinical improvement (resolution of resistant hypertension/hypervolemia) and reduction in serum creatinine (sCr) within 14 days post-procedure. Long-term outcomes included Doppler ultrasound parameters - peak systolic velocity (PSV), acceleration time (AT) and resistive index (RI) - and restenosis/occlusion rates requiring or not intervention. Graft survival at the latest follow-up was recorded. A total of 40 patients (mean age 58 ± 13 years, 68% male) were treated with BMS (n = 31) or CS (n = 9). Clinical improvement was observed in 71% of BMS and 83% of CS patients (P = 1.00). Median sCr decreased by 26% and 33% in BMS and CS patients, respectively (P = .30). At a median follow-up of 29 months, there were no statistically significant differences between groups in median PSV reduction (47% BMS vs 47% CS; P = .44), AT improvement (36% BMS vs 25% CS; P = .38) or RI increase (15% BMS vs 33% CS; P = .12). In the BMS group, 2 cases of in-stent restenosis occurred (6.5%). In the CS group, 1 stent occlusion occurred (11%), resulting in graft loss. At final follow-up, overall graft survival was 85%. In this pilot study, BMS and CS showed no significant differences in TRAS outcomes. Further studies are warranted to better guide stent selection.Clinical ImpactIn transplant renal artery stenosis, balloon-expandable covered stents achieved clinical, biochemical and Doppler outcomes comparable to bare-metal stents, despite being used in more complex, atherosclerotic and longer lesions. This first direct comparison suggests that covered stents may be a reasonable option when heavy calcification, a friable wall or mural thrombus raise concern for embolisation or rupture, while bare-metal stents remain appropriate for most lesions. The single late covered-stent occlusion with graft loss highlights the need for careful platform selection and antiplatelet management. These pilot data should inform adequately powered multicentre registries rather than directly change practice.

title: Association of breakfast skipping on quality of life among university students in Latin America: A multicenter cross-sectional study.
authorString: Fuentes-Valdes JJ, Parra-Soto S, Gómez G, Carpio-Arias TV, Landaeta-Díaz L, Ríos-Castillo I, Araneda-Flores J, Morales-Illanes G, Meza-Miranda E, Núñez B, Murillo G, Cordón-Arrivillaga K, Nava-González EJ, Mauricio-Alza S, Bejarano-Rocancio JJ, Cavagnari B, Duran-Agüero S.
abstractText: BackgroundSkipping breakfast is a prevalent habit among university students and has been associated with poorer quality of life; however, evidence from Latin America remains limited, particularly from multicenter studies.AimTo analyze the association between breakfast skipping and quality of life across its physical, psychological, social, and environmental dimensions among Latin American university students.MethodsA cross-sectional multicenter study was conducted in ten Latin American countries using an online self-administered questionnaire. Breakfast frequency, sociodemographic variables, and quality of life were assessed using the WHOQOL-BREF instrument. Bivariate and multivariate linear regression analyses were performed, adjusting for age, sex, body mass index, smoking status, physical activity, and socioeconomic status.SummaryA total of 4539 university students participated (67% women; mean age: 21.3 ± 2.5 years). Of these, 38.6% reported skipping breakfast three or more times per week. Breakfast skipping was significantly associated with lower scores in the physical (β = -2.8; 95% CI: -3.9 to -1.6), psychological (β = -2.3; 95% CI: -3.4 to -1.2), and environmental (β = -1.9; 95% CI: -2.9 to -0.9) domains. No significant association was observed with the social domain. In conclusion the frequent breakfast skipping is associated with poorer quality of life among Latin American university students. Promoting regular breakfast consumption may represent an effective strategy to improve overall well-being in this population.

title: Benign Schwannoma of the Coronary Sinus in a Child: Diagnostic Pitfalls and Surgical Management.
authorString: Nokhrin AV, Gvozd EM, Kulemin ES, Kornishina TL, Trizna EV, Krasnogorskaya OL, Malekov DA, Ivanov DO.

journal.medlineAbbreviation: World J Pediatr Congenit Heart Surg
journal.title: World journal for pediatric & congenital heart surgery
journal.isoabbreviation: World J Pediatr Congenit Heart Surg

abstractText: Primary cardiac tumors in children are uncommon, and cardiac schwannomas occur predominantly in adults. Benign coronary sinus schwannoma in a child represents an unusual presentation with important diagnostic and surgical considerations. We report the case of a 5-year-old child presenting with recurrent exudative pericarditis and signs of progressive heart failure. Initial evaluation suggested inflammatory pathology; however, advanced imaging revealed a mass originating from the coronary sinus. Surgical resection was performed via median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass. Due to dense adhesions, the tumor was removed in fragments with radical excision. The coronary sinus was reconstructed using an autologous pericardial patch. Histopathology confirmed a benign schwannoma (S100 and SOX10 positive). The postoperative course was notable for transient right ventricular dysfunction, which resolved with supportive therapy. No tumor recurrence was observed during 48 months of follow-up. Coronary sinus schwannoma in children may mimic inflammatory pericardial disease. Timely surgical intervention with radical resection and anatomical reconstruction is feasible. This case highlights important diagnostic and surgical considerations in managing an unusual pediatric cardiac tumor.

title: Acute mechanical stretch enhances β-adrenergic-protein kinase A signalling and increases susceptibility to ventricular arrhythmias.
authorString: Wang H, Lai EC, Hua Z, Liu C, Sherstnev I, Fu J, Ng FS, Gorelik J.
abstractText: Mechanical stretch can increase ventricular arrhythmia susceptibility during sympathetic activation, but the mechanisms linking stretch to altered β-adrenergic receptor (βAR) signalling, Ca2+ handling and electrical instability remain unclear. We tested whether left ventricular (LV) stretch alters Cav3-associated membrane organisation and enhances βAR-protein kinase A (PKA)-dependent arrhythmogenic signalling. Langendorff-perfused male rat hearts were studied using a fluid-filled LV balloon, with sham hearts fitted with an unstretched balloon. Optical mapping during S1-S2 programmed stimulation showed that LV stretch had limited effects at baseline but altered the response to βAR stimulation, increasing ventricular arrhythmia severity, prolonging APD50, reducing local conduction velocity and steepening APD80 restitution. H89 markedly reduced βAR stimulation-induced arrhythmia severity in stretched hearts, whereas KN93 did not provide comparable protection. LV stretch also increased cardiomyocyte length and altered Cav3 organisation at wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-defined membrane regions. In isolated LV cardiomyocytes, hypoosmotic membrane deformation did not alter basal caffeine-induced Ca2+ release but enhanced isoprenaline-induced irregular activity and Ca2+-transient amplitude, both of which were attenuated by PKA inhibition. Hypoosmotic membrane deformation also amplified isoprenaline-evoked PKA activity and increased RyR2 Ser2030 phosphorylation. These findings indicate that LV mechanical stretch alters the ventricular βAR response in association with altered Cav3-associated membrane organisation and enhanced βAR-PKA-dependent Ca2+ instability. KEY POINTS: Left ventricular (LV) balloon stretch has limited baseline electrophysiological effects but increases arrhythmia severity, slows conduction and steepens APD80 restitution during β-adrenergic stimulation. LV balloon stretch is associated with cardiomyocyte elongation and altered Cav3 enrichment at wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-defined membrane regions. Hypoosmotic membrane deformation enhances isoprenaline-induced irregular activity and Ca2+-transient amplitude without increasing basal caffeine-induced Ca2+ release. PKA inhibition reduces stretch-enhanced irregular activity in isolated ventricular myocytes and β-adrenergic receptor (βAR)-induced arrhythmia severity in stretched hearts. Hypoosmotic membrane deformation enhances isoprenaline-evoked PKA activity and increases RyR2 Ser2030 phosphorylation.

title: Bachmann Bundle Pacing and Acute Changes in Left Atrial Mechanical Function in Patients With Interatrial Block: A Within-Subject Echocardiography Analysis.
authorString: Aiyasiding X, Yang J, Meng Q, Chen Z, Cai M, Chen Y, Chi X, Wan X, Li C, Wang W, Dai Y, Chen K.
abstractText: Interatrial block (IAB) is associated with atrial electromechanical dysfunction and adverse cardiovascular outcomes. Bachmann bundle pacing (BBP) has emerged as a physiological atrial pacing strategy capable of restoring interatrial conduction synchrony. However, its impact on left atrial (LA) mechanical function and hemodynamics remains unclear. To evaluate the acute effects of BBP on atrial mechanical parameters in patients with IAB. In this prospective single-center study, 31 patients with IAB who underwent successful BBP implantation were enrolled. A standardized postoperative evaluation protocol was performed under intrinsic sinus rhythm (SR), right atrial septal pacing (RASP) at atrial lead threshold +0.5 V/0.4 ms, and BBP at 5 V/0.4 ms using a within-subject repeated-measures design. Electrocardiographic and echocardiographic parameters were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, with additional adjustment for heart rate. BBP produced significantly greater P wave duration (PWD) shortening than RASP (p < 0.001). Compared with SR, BBP was associated with lower LA volume indices and higher LA emptying fraction and LA expansion index (all p < 0.001), with consistent superiority over RASP at acute postoperative phase. These associations remained significant after heart rate adjustment. The observed acute changes were consistent across partial and advanced IAB subgroups without significant interaction effects. In patients with IAB, electrical resynchronization during BBP was accompanied by acute changes in LA mechanical parameters compared with SR and RASP. These findings suggest that BBP may represent a promising physiological pacing strategy for patients with atrial conduction disease.

title: The role of methionine-driven epigenetic modulation in the regulation of health and disease: a comprehensive review.
authorString: Nath SK, Rahman N, Roy TK, Ferdous M, Islam MS, Ismail Z.
abstractText: Methionine, a sulfur-containing essential amino acid, plays a pivotal role in epigenetic regulation through its involvement in one-carbon metabolism and as a precursor to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the universal methyl donor. This review explores how methionine availability dynamically influences DNA and histone methylation, non-coding RNA expression, and RNA modifications, ultimately shaping gene expression, cellular identity, and developmental outcomes. Emerging evidence suggests that balanced methionine intake is critical for maintaining epigenetic homeostasis. At the same time, both deficiency and excess can disrupt this equilibrium, contributing to diseases such as cancer, metabolic disorders, neurodevelopmental abnormalities, and cardiovascular dysfunction. Methionine deficiency is shown to impair DNA and histone methylation, alter non-coding RNA profiles, and compromise stem cell pluripotency and neurogenesis. Conversely, excess methionine can trigger aberrant hypermethylation, genomic instability, and metabolic imbalances, with links to oncogenic transformation and accelerated aging. Notably, methionine restriction (MR) enhances stress resilience, promotes healthy aging, and reduces tumor progression by reprogramming the epigenetic landscape. This review highlights methionine's dualistic nature, both as a crucial epigenetic regulator and a potential contributor to disease when imbalanced. It also underscores the need for context-specific dietary strategies and further research into the intricate interplay between methionine metabolism, gene regulation, and long-term health outcomes. Understanding these molecular mechanisms may unlock novel nutritional and therapeutic approaches for disease prevention and epigenetic reprogramming.

title: Knockdown of mitotically associated long non-coding RNA dysregulates endothelial functions, transcriptome and proteome.
authorString: Zhang SY, Zhou C, Zheng J.
abstractText: Preeclampsia (PE) is a hypertensive disorder during pregnancy, which is characterized by a wide spectrum of endothelial dysfunction. However, the mechanisms underlying PE-associated endothelial dysfunction remain poorly understood. Our previous RNA-sequencing analysis showed that PE down-regulated mitotically-associated long non-coding RNA (MANCR) in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). Herein, we tested the hypothesis that knockdown of MANCR dysregulates endothelial functions via disrupting the transcriptome and proteome using HUVECs as a cell model. Reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) was conducted to confirm the down-regulation of MANCR in PE-HUVECs. MANCR was knocked down in HUVECs from normotensive pregnancy using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), followed by functional assays, RNA-sequencing and proteomics. RT-qPCR revealed that PE decreased MANCR in male and female HUVECs. Compared with scrambled ASOs, MANCR ASOs reduced MANCR by 71% and 74% in male and female HUVECs, respectively. Functionally, MANCR ASOs blocked fibroblast growth factor-2 (FGF2)- and vascular endothelial growth factor-A (VEGFA)-stimulated cell proliferation, whereas they did not affect cell chemotaxis and tube formation in responses to FGF2 and VEGFA. MANCR ASOs dysregulated the expression of 37 and 39 genes as well as 97 and 15 proteins in male and female cells, respectively. Bioinformatics analysis predicted that MANCR-regulated genes and proteins in male and female HUVECs were differently associated with diseases and biological functions, many of which are relevant to cell mitosis and hypertension. Thus, down-regulation of MANCR impairs endothelial functions and causes sex-specific disruption of transcriptome and proteome, possibly partially contributing to PE-associated fetal endothelial dysfunction. KEY POINTS: Preeclampsia causes widespread endothelial dysfunction, but the roles of long non-coding RNAs in endothelial cells remain poorly understood. Mitotically associated long non-coding RNA (MANCR) is down-regulated in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) obtained from preeclampsia. We provide the first evidence that down-regulation of MANCR blocks endothelial cell proliferation stimulated by fibroblast growth factor 2 and vascular endothelial growth factor A. We also demonstrate that down-regulation of MANCR disrupts transcriptome and proteome as well as pathways associated with cell division, cardiovascular disease-related processes and immune responses. These findings identify MANCR as a previously unrecognized regulator of endothelial cell function.

title: Small Nucleolar RNAs, Big Impact: Biogenesis, Mechanisms, and Roles in Health and Disease.
authorString: Natarajaseenivasan SM, Rai AK, Pierre N, Joseph ME, Lam M, Sharma P, Garikipati VNS.

journal.title: American journal of physiology. Cell physiology

abstractText: Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) are a diverse class of regulatory molecules classified by their size, localization, and function. Among them, small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) are 60-300-nucleotide small non-coding RNAs that are primarily encoded within intronic regions of protein-coding or non-coding host genes. They are broadly categorized into three types: C/D box snoRNAs (SNORDs), H/ACA box snoRNAs (SNORAs), and Cajal body-specific RNAs (scaRNAs). SNORDs and SNORAs primarily mediate RNA modifications through 2'-O-methylation (Nm) and pseudouridylation (Ψ), respectively, whereas scaRNAs specialize in modifying small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) within the Cajal body, which is crucial for splicing processes. Recent discoveries have broadened the functional landscape of snoRNAs beyond their canonical roles, uncovering non-canonical functions in protein secretion and the identification of snoRNA/scaRNA reads within glycoRNA-associated small RNA populations, suggesting novel mechanisms of cellular communication and pathophysiology. This review offers an integrative discussion of snoRNAs, focusing on their biogenesis, functions, developmental roles, and implications in various diseases, while providing detailed insights into these RNAs.

title: Markers of early cardiac dysfunction in young adults with insomnia disorder: a case-control study.
authorString: Petrov ME, Youngstedt SD, Angadi SS, Jiao N, Mookadam F, Abdalla M, St-Onge MP.

journal.title: Journal of clinical sleep medicine : JCSM : official publication of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine

abstractText: Insomnia is a highly prevalent, chronic disorder that is a modifiable novel risk factor for cardiovascular disease. However, there are fewer physiological data available suggesting that insomnia may be related to early cardiac disease and atherosclerotic progression among young adults (ages 21-44 years). In this case-control study, we investigated the association between insomnia and subclinical cardiovascular disease risk markers in a sample of young adults with ICSD-3-diagnosed insomnia compared to healthy good sleepers. Among a sample of 43 community-based, healthy young adults (18 individuals with insomnia disorder, 25 good sleeping controls; Mage = 28.7 years, range 21-42), we compared indices of cardiac function with 2D echocardiography, endothelial dysfunction with flow-mediated endothelial dilation, and arterial stiffness with carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity, adjusted for body mass index. The insomnia group had worse left ventricular global longitudinal strain in comparison to the good sleeping controls (insomnia M(SD) - 22.8 (2.2), good sleeping controls - 24.3 (1.5), F[1, 39] = 7.42, p = 0.01, ηp2 = 0.16, estimated marginal mean difference = 1.47%, adjusted R2 = 0.18), but no differences in endothelial function, arterial stiffness, or other cardiac function parameters. Young adults with well-defined insomnia disorder and few confounding comorbidities demonstrated worse left ventricular strain than good sleepers. Worse left ventricular strain may reflect subtle, subclinical myocardial dysfunction that could precede changes in other cardiac function parameters or overt cardiovascular disease. Longitudinal studies are needed to evaluate whether this finding heralds future cardiovascular risk. Insomnia disorder is linked to cardiovascular disease, but this connection is rarely explored with markers of cardiac and vascular function in young adults. Young adults with insomnia disorder had worse left ventricular strain, as measured by left ventricular global longitudinal strain, than well-defined good sleeping controls, suggesting early cardiac risk in patients with insomnia disorder.

title: Porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder-type lesions in patients with early fibrotic stages of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
authorString: van Doorn DJ, Schoenmakers L, de Jager S, Lantinga MA, Holleboom AG, Drenth JPH, Kwanten WJ, Francque S, Takkenberg RB, Driessen A, Verheij J.
abstractText: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a rising cause of chronic liver disease. Liver stiffness measurement (LSM) to assess disease stage is gaining popularity but can demonstrate heterogeneous results in clinical practice. Moreover, portal hypertension may develop early in MASLD in the absence of cirrhosis. These observations may be partially explained by features not assessed in the current NASH-CRN liver biopsy staging, including features of porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder (PSVD). We conducted a retrospective cohort study in patients with MASLD who underwent biopsy between 2015 and 2022. All biopsies with NASH-CRN F0-F2 were screened for eligibility and revised in consensus by two expert liver pathologists. Primary objective was to assess the presence and severity of PSVD-type lesions. Secondary objectives included the grading of perisinusoidal fibrosis and to correlate histological features with LSM. We included 136 patients [60% male, median age 50y] with a median BMI of 30 kg/m2, 15% having F1 fibrosis and 85% F2 fibrosis. Median LSM (available in 54%) was 8.2 kPa. Portal venule stenosis affecting ≥50% of portal tracts was present in 26% of biopsies, and muscularisation of portal venules was present in 21% of biopsies. Perisinusoidal fibrosis was present in 97% of biopsies, respectively mild, moderate, and severe in 62%, 32%, and 3%. PSVD-type lesions did not correlate with LSM, but LSM did correlate with the degree of perisinusoidal fibrosis. Portal venule stenosis (≥50%) and muscularisation of portal venules, both major criteria associated with PSVD, were found in 26% and 21% biopsies, respectively. Furthermore, the extent of perisinusoidal fibrosis correlates with liver stiffness and could explain the heterogeneity of LSM in MASLD.

title: Fibroblast growth factor 10 (FGF10) ameliorates pulmonary arterial hypertension by restoring endothelial mitochondrial function and reducing DNA damage via the PPARγ pathway.
authorString: Lu S, Wang N, Zhou Y, Ran T, Deng Q, Zhang H, Du X, Kong X.
abstractText: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is characterized by endothelial dysfunction, but the role of fibroblast growth factor 10 (FGF10) in regulating mitochondrial integrity and DNA damage remains unclear. A monocrotaline (MCT)-induced PAH rat model and MCTP-treated pulmonary artery endothelial cells were used. FGF10 was silenced using AAV- or lentivirus-mediated shRNA and supplemented exogenously. PPARγ involvement was assessed using GW9662 inhibition and Co-IP assays. Hemodynamic analysis, histology, and molecular assays were performed to evaluate vascular and endothelial alterations. MCT exposure induced severe pulmonary vascular remodeling and endothelial mitochondrial injury, including fragmentation, reduced membrane potential, increased ROS, and persistent DNA damage responses. FGF10 knockdown aggravated these abnormalities, whereas exogenous FGF10 significantly restored mitochondrial structure and function, reduced oxidative stress, and attenuated DNA damage. Mechanistically, FGF10 upregulated PPARγ expression in vivo and in vitro. Pharmacological inhibition of PPARγ partially abolished the protective effects of FGF10. Co-IP further confirmed an interaction between FGF10 and PPARγ. FGF10 protects against MCT-induced pulmonary vascular remodeling by preserving mitochondrial homeostasis and limiting DNA damage in endothelial cells via a PPARγ-dependent mechanism. The FGF10-PPARγ axis may represent a potential therapeutic target for PAH, warranting further validation in additional models and translational studies.

title: Association between diabetes-related autoantibody positivity and renal impairment in clinically diagnosed type 2 diabetes: a cross-sectional study.
authorString: Zheng T, Yang R, Li S, Wu X, Jiang L, Li X.
abstractText: To investigate whether diabetes-related autoantibodies are independently associated with renal impairment in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). In this retrospective cross-sectional analysis, 2,010 Chinese patients with clinically diagnosed T2DM were included, and renal parameters (eGFR and UACR) were compared between autoantibody-positive (IAA/GADA/ICA/IA-2A) and autoantibody-negative groups. Multivariable logistic regression assessed independent associations with UACR ≥ 30 mg/g and eGFR < 90 mL/min/1.73 m2, adjusting for confounders. Stratified and interaction analyses were performed. Autoantibody positivity was detected in 804 patients (40.00%), with IAA accounting for 75.25% of positive cases. After adjustment, autoantibody positivity remained independently associated with albuminuria (OR = 1.308, P = 0.007) and reduced eGFR (OR = 1.410, P = 0.003). Hypertension significantly modified the association with reduced eGFR (P for interaction = 0.009) but did not significantly modify the association with albuminuria (P for interaction = 0.054). Among normotensive patients, autoantibody positivity was associated with higher odds of albuminuria (OR = 1.514) and of reduced eGFR (OR = 1.935), while no significant associations were observed in hypertensive patients. Sex (P for interaction = 0.028) and HbA1c (P for interaction = 0.040) also modified the albuminuria association, with a stronger association in males. The full model including autoantibody status and fasting C-peptide yielded the highest AUC for reduced eGFR (0.786), although the incremental improvement over the conventional model was small (ΔAUC = +0.020). Autoantibody positivity was independently associated with renal impairment in patients with clinically diagnosed T2DM, particularly in normotensive and male patients in exploratory subgroup analyses, suggesting that immuno-metabolic factors may be associated with diabetic kidney disease (DKD) beyond conventional clinical factors. However, the incremental discriminatory value of autoantibody status and fasting C-peptide was modest, and these findings require confirmation in future studies.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Inverse Identification of α<sub>1</sub>-Adrenergic Receptor Non-Desensitization Mechanisms.
authorString: Zhou S, Wang X.
abstractText: This study investigates the aberrant activation and "non-desensitization" phenomenon of α1-adrenergic receptors (α1-AR) in hypertension. To systematically elucidate the mechanisms underlying receptor-mediated vascular smooth muscle contraction, a unified kinetic model was constructed, comprising a control group, an endocytic dysfunction group, a conformational change group, and a composite model integrating multiple regulatory processes. The model explicitly accounts for receptor binding, phosphorylation, endocytosis, and conformational transitions. Using rat vascular ring tension measurements, a quantitative mapping between model states and experimentally observed contractile responses was established. A physics-informed neural network (PINN) implementation combining a predefined linear warm-up schedule for the physics-loss weight with sequential Adam and L-BFGS optimization was employed to infer key kinetic parameters while balancing data fitting and kinetic constraints during training. Numerical comparisons based on fitting errors and AIC indicated that the composite model provided the most favorable balance between data agreement and model complexity among the candidate mechanisms. Analyses revealed that α1-AA sustains receptor activation and continuously amplifies downstream signaling by enhancing binding affinity, stabilizing the active conformation, and suppressing endocytosis, thereby promoting persistent vasoconstriction. These findings provide a quantitative explanation for the "non-desensitization" of α1-AR and demonstrates the practical utility of PINNs for parameter estimation and mechanistic analysis in complex biological systems.

title: Rising Prevalence of Metabolic Dysfunction - Associated Steatotic Liver Disease in an urban South Indian screening cohort: a Retrospective Cross-sectional Study.
authorString: Karuppasamy B, Jothimani D, Ramachandran H, Velayuthum D, Simon E, Rela M.
abstractText: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), redefined in 2023 from non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, is highly prevalent globally, but population-level data using 2023 AASLD criteria and FibroScan-based assessment remain scarce in South Asia, particularly among asymptomatic adults undergoing routine health screening. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study of 1,103 asymptomatic adults (mean age 43.1±12.7 years; 64.1% male) undergoing FibroScan-based Master Health Check-up at a tertiary centre in Chennai, India (2023-2025). MASLD was defined as controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) ≥249 dB/m plus ≥1 cardiometabolic risk factor; fibrosis was assessed by liver stiffness measurement (LSM). MASLD was identified in 716 participants (64.9%; 95% CI 62.1-67.7%). Affected individuals were older, had higher BMI, and more frequently had diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia (all p<0.01). In multivariable analysis, age, male sex, BMI, and diabetes were independently associated with MASLD. Notably, 53.4% of cases occurred in adults under 46 years, and 45.3% had normal liver function tests while 31.3% had normal ultrasound, indicating conventional screening substantially underestimates disease burden. Nearly two-thirds of asymptomatic urban South Indian adults screened met MASLD criteria, predominantly working-age individuals under-detected by conventional tools. FibroScan-based screening should be considered in preventive health programmes to enable earlier detection.

title: Longitudinal remodeling of acylcarnitine signatures before and after arthroplasty for osteoarthritis: A 7-year cohort study.
authorString: Sõber-Williams EK, Kilk K, Kals J, Märtson A, Prommik P, Tootsi K.
abstractText: Total joint arthroplasty (TJA) is the most effective treatment for end-stage osteoarthritis (OA). Although systemic acylcarnitine alterations have been reported in OA, long-term metabolic changes after TJA remain poorly understood. Existing metabolomic studies are cross-sectional and have not compared post-TJA changes with age- and sex-matched controls. We examined metabolic markers before and 7 years after TJA to assess long-term systemic metabolic changes relative to healthy aging controls. Fasting serum acylcarnitines were measured using liquid chromatography mass-spectrometry in a longitudinal cohort of participants with end-stage OA undergoing TJA (n = 70) and in age- and sex-matched healthy controls (n = 82) at baseline and 7-year follow-up. Acylcarnitine concentrations were compared between groups and longitudinally within participants, with analyses adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, hypertension status, and corrected for multiple comparisons. A total of 70 patients (age 62 ± 7) with severe OA who were undergoing TJA and 82 matched controls without OA were included in the study. Forty-eight acylcarnitine measures and ratios passed quality control. Fifteen acylcarnitines changed differently between groups over follow-up; six measures differed at baseline and 12 at follow-up. Five baseline differences normalized, whereas 11 new between-group differences emerged. After adjustment for baseline metabolite concentrations, seven acylcarnitines showed differential longitudinal change: four short-chain species (C5-OH, C5-DC, C5-M-DC, C5:1-DC) and three long-chain species (C14:2-OH, C16:2, C18:1). The four short-chain species increased 19.8-32.0% more in the TJA group than in controls. Free carnitine (C0) declined relative to controls, with a 24.8% lower longitudinal change (ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.62-0.91). Several medium- and long-chain acylcarnitines that were lower at baseline normalized toward control concentrations. Total acylcarnitine/free carnitine increased 32.3% more in the TJA group (ratio 1.32, 95% CI 1.17-1.50), with the baseline group difference resolving by follow-up. TJA was associated with partial normalization of select circulating acylcarnitines; however, persistent abnormalities in hydroxy- and dicarboxy-acylcarnitines suggest ongoing alterations in lipid handling. Reduced carnitine buffering capacity and shifts toward alternative oxidation pathways further indicate incomplete restoration of systemic fatty-acid metabolism. Overall, these findings support pathway-specific metabolic remodeling rather than full metabolic normalization following TJA. REGISTERED ON WWW. GOV: NCT06211465.

title: Does Geographic Disadvantage Increase Lower Extremity Amputation Risk in the State of Georgia?
authorString: Stegall A, Hitchcock B, Patrick K, Radcliff J, Solis MM, Jean-Jacques E.
abstractText: Over 100,000 lower extremity amputations are performed annually in the United States, with most related to peripheral arterial disease and diabetes. Rural populations experience greater socioeconomic disparities and higher rates of chronic disease. This study examined socioeconomic differences, prevalence of amputation risk factors, and lower extremity amputation rates between rural and urban residents of Georgia. County-level lower extremity amputation data for 2020 were obtained from the Georgia Department of Public Health. Demographic and socioeconomic data were retrieved from the US Census Bureau, and the prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, peripheral arterial disease, and smoking from the Centers for Disease Control Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System. Rural counties were defined as those with populations <50,000. Bivariate analyses compared rural and urban medians. Nonparametric data were log-transformed to meet assumptions of normality. Significance was set at P < 0.05 with 80% power. Rural counties had higher proportions of males and individuals greater than 65 y. Rural populations had greater socioeconomic disadvantages: higher poverty and lower median income. Risk factors were more prevalent in rural areas: diabetes, hypertension, smoking, and peripheral arterial disease. The incidence of lower extremity amputations per 100,000 residents was higher in rural versus urban counties. Rural Georgians undergo higher amputations of the lower extremities occurring in the context of greater prevalence of chronic disease and socioeconomic disadvantage.

title: Sleep quality, atrial fibrillation burden, and symptom severity in patients with atrial fibrillation: a cross-sectional study.
authorString: Erkal E, Yamantürk YY.

journal.title: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care

abstractText: Sleep disturbances are common in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and may be associated with greater AF burden and more severe AF-related symptoms. However, evidence linking sleep quality to AF-related patient-reported outcomes remains limited. To evaluate sleep quality, AF burden, AF-related symptom severity, and global well-being in patients with AF and to examine the associations between sleep quality and these outcomes. This descriptive cross-sectional study included 122 patients with AF attending the cardiology outpatient clinic of a public hospital. Data were collected using a patient information form, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and the University of Toronto Atrial Fibrillation Severity Scale (AFSS). Analyses included independent-samples t-test, one-way analysis of variance, Pearson correlation, and multivariable linear regression. The mean PSQI score was 7.60 ± 3.29, and 77% of participants were classified as having poor sleep quality. Mean AFSS Global Well-being, AF Burden, and Symptom scores were 4.96 ± 1.93, 13.98 ± 5.40, and 9.42 ± 5.14, respectively. After adjustment for age, sex, BMI, AF duration, additional cardiac disease, and alcohol use, higher PSQI scores were associated with lower Global Well-being (β = -0.231, p = 0.013), higher AF Burden (β = 0.444, p < 0.001), and greater symptom severity (β = 0.453, p < 0.001). Poorer sleep quality was associated with lower global well-being, greater AF burden, and more severe AF-related symptoms. These findings support routine sleep assessment and individualized care in patients with AF.

title: Dietary Vitamin K2 Intake, Musculoskeletal Injury, and Cardiometabolic Health in Service Members.
authorString: Wood RL, McCarthy MS, Salcedo KP, Colburn ZT, Gillette LH, Hung LH, Fukuda BN, Yeung KY.
abstractText: Vitamin K2 (K2) research has demonstrated that with sufficient K2 intake, vitamin K-dependent proteins are activated to regulate bone diseases and inflammation-related diseases, offering an innovative strategy to address ongoing musculoskeletal injury (MSKi) and high adiposity challenges that threaten health promotion, performance, and readiness in service members (SMs). This study aimed to characterize K2 status in a military sample and explore the relationship between dietary K2 intake and bone health, metabolic health, and inflammation status in the context of SM health and operational readiness or deployability. At baseline and 12 months, Army and Air Force units provided data from demographic and food frequency questionnaires, body composition, bone density, cardiometabolic, and biomarker measurements. Activity trackers monitored physical activity and sleep duration continuously. Between August 2023 and July 2024, we enrolled 47 active duty SMs. The sample was predominantly male, racially and ethnically diverse, averaged 27 years of age, and had an average of 6.5 years of service. At baseline, 45% met the criteria for stage I hypertension and 45% exceeded military body fat standards. Participants reported insufficient baseline dietary intake of vitamin K1+K2 and vitamin D. Over the 12 months, fermented food consumption slightly increased, activity behaviors remained unchanged, and participants self-reported 10 noncombat MSKis. Participants reported no significant changes in body composition, body fat specifically, or dietary intake of vitamin D or vitamin K2. Exploratory proteomics analysis identified links between K2 and inflammation, bone architecture, glucose homeostasis, and insulin receptors. MSKi, high body fat, and meeting optimal nutrition goals remain readiness challenges for SMs. Exploring K2 identified meaningful metrics and actionable strategies to address these challenges. Highlighting data-informed interventions adds to nursing's nutritional and cardiometabolic knowledge base and clinical interventions, as the nursing workforce is positioned to influence every step of patient care: conducting research, generating data to inform clinical practice and interventions, and ensuring evidence-based patient education and counseling to optimize SM health and readiness.

title: Effectiveness of Radiofrequency Renal Denervation in the United States: Six-Month Primary End Point Results From the SPYRAL AFFIRM Study.
authorString: Kandzari DE, Kario K, Weber MA, Townsend RR, Schmieder RE, Böhm M, Tsioufis K, Stoler R, Lee DP, Navetta F, Bertolet B, Potluri S, David S, Cohen DL, Lung TH, Anderson K, Carvelli J, Mahfoud F, SPYRAL AFFIRM Study Investigators.
abstractText:
Background

Radiofrequency renal denervation (RDN) is a guideline-recommended therapy for uncontrolled hypertension. SPYRAL AFFIRM is a single-arm, postapproval study assessing the efficacy and safety of radiofrequency RDN using the Symplicity Spyral catheter. We report the 6-month primary end point results in the SPYRAL AFFIRM US population.

Methods

Enrolled patients had an office systolic/diastolic blood pressure (BP) ≥140/90 mm Hg and a home systolic BP ≥135 mm Hg. Patients with type 1 diabetes, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c >8.0%), or an estimated glomerular filtration rate <45 mL/min per 1.73 m2 were excluded. The primary end point was the 6-month change in office systolic BP from baseline compared with a prespecified performance goal (-6.0 mm Hg).

Results

Among 594 patients treated in the AFFIRM study from 73 US clinical sites, baseline clinical characteristics included: mean (±SD) age, 57±12 years; female, 45%; African American, 27%; Hispanic, 11%; type 2 diabetes, 19%; and mean estimated glomerular filtration rate, 79±20 mL/min per 1.73m2. Baseline systolic/diastolic office, home, and 24-hour ambulatory BP (mm Hg) were 169±21/106±13, 158±17/101±13, and 151±18/96±13, respectively. Patients were prescribed an average of 3.6±2.0 antihypertensive medications at baseline that remained unchanged through 6 months. Six months after RDN, the change in systolic BP (mm Hg) was -18.2±22.0, -9.4±13.8, and -9.7±16.8 for office, home, and 24-hour ambulatory measures, respectively (P<0.001 compared with baseline). Adverse clinical events through 6 months were uncommon.

Conclusions

In this US postapproval study, the primary end point was met with significant BP reductions following radiofrequency RDN consistent across different measures. In a broader patient population with uncontrolled hypertension, these results reaffirm the safety and efficacy of radiofrequency RDN.

Registration

URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT05198674.

title: Ocular Considerations for the Department of War's New Testosterone Initiative.
authorString: Clabeaux CE, Narduzzi M, Rana HS.
abstractText: On 15 July 2026, the Secretary of War announced that the Department of War will begin annual testosterone deficiency screening for male Active Duty and Reserve Component personnel aged 30 and older as part of the periodic health assessment, with screening available on request to younger servicemembers. This policy will increase testosterone testing and may increase testosterone replacement therapy (TRT). Primary care, flight, and operational medicine providers will be on the front line of a hormonal intervention with possible ocular implications. This Commentary summarizes the ophthalmic manifestations of low and elevated testosterone states relevant to a military population and proposes pragmatic recommendations for providers implementing this initiative. Screening identifies testosterone concentrations, not symptoms of deficiency, and should not be equated with an indication for treatment. Androgen deficiency is associated with meibomian gland dysfunction and evaporative dry eye, but benefit from replacement remains unproven. The evidence linking testosterone exposure to central serous chorioretinopathy, retinal vascular occlusion, and intracranial hypertension is real but heterogeneous. Cohort findings, case reports, and observations in transgender patients do not establish a common risk in hypogonadal male servicemembers. Glaucoma findings are similarly mixed. We propose a brief, targeted ocular history, symptom counseling and inquiry during TRT follow-up and periodic health assessments, and referral according to clinical urgency. For vision-critical specialties, baseline dilated examination should be coordinated through existing occupational clearance processes when an adequate recent examination is unavailable. These measures are precautionary; screening benefit and an optimal repeat-examination interval have not been established. The Military Health System is uniquely positioned to prospectively answer the ocular questions this literature has only partially resolved.

title: BAG3 genetic variant is associated with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction phenotypes.
authorString: Wungu CDK, Susilo H, Wijaya J, Susanto CR, Kevin K, Nugraha D, Oceandy D.
abstractText: Genetic variations are involved in determining heart failure (HF) phenotypes. While variants within the BAG3 gene have been associated with HF in European populations, the impact of specific single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within the BAG3 gene in determining phenotypes of HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) in Southeast Asian populations is unknown. Therefore, in this study, we identified BAG3 SNPs and investigated their biological and clinical relevance in determining HFpEF phenotypes among an Indonesian HFpEF cohort. We conducted a study involving 36 patients with HFpEF and 30 healthy individuals. We detected the presence of rs196326 and rs2240777 SNPs in our cohort. However, the rs2234962 polymorphism, which has been associated with HF and cardiomyopathy in Western populations, was absent in our Indonesian cohort. We found that the rs196326 SNP was significantly associated with relative wall thickness (RWT), with patients carrying the CG genotype displayed significantly lower RWT. Additionally, the rs196326 CG/GG genotypes were correlated with higher serum N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and lower Caspase-3 levels. Our study showed that the BAG3 rs196326 polymorphism was significantly associated with HFpEF phenotypes in the Indonesian population. This highlights the importance of identifying population-specific as genetic markers of disease severity.

title: Irisin alleviates hypertensive renal injury by suppressing communication between macrophages and tubular epithelial cells.
authorString: Wu F, Li H, Fan Z, Pang Q, Zhang A.

journal.title: Clinical and experimental hypertension (New York, N.Y. : 1993)

abstractText: Hypertensive renal injury (HRI) is characterized by renal inflammation and fibrosis. We investigated whether macrophage-tubular epithelial cell communication contributes to HRI and the renoprotective effects of irisin. HRI was induced by unilateral nephrectomy, angiotensin II infusion, and a high-salt diet. FNDC5 knockout mice and recombinant irisin were used to assess endogenous and exogenous irisin, respectively. Single-cell RNA sequencing and CellChat characterized renal cell populations and predicted intercellular communication. Flow cytometry assessed macrophage Cd209a expression. A macrophage-tubular epithelial cell Transwell co-culture system, together with IL-1 receptor blockade and recombinant IL-1β stimulation, was used for functional validation. Irisin improved renal function and attenuated renal fibrosis and pEMT-related alterations without significantly reducing blood pressure, whereas FNDC5 deficiency aggravated renal fibrosis and macrophage accumulation. ScRNA-seq identified a Cd209a-high Macro-2 macrophage subset that expanded during HRI and was further increased by FNDC5 deficiency. CellChat predicted enhanced communication between Macro-2 macrophages and proximal tubular cells, with further enhancement following FNDC5 deficiency. In vitro, Ang II increased Cd209a expression and IL-1β secretion in RAW264.7 macrophages. Functional experiments suggested the involvement of IL-1β signaling in macrophage-induced pEMT-related alterations in tubular epithelial cells. Irisin pretreatment attenuated Ang II-induced macrophage inflammatory activation and reduced macrophage-induced pEMT-related and profibrotic alterations in TCMK-1 cells. Irisin protects against HRI by improving renal function and attenuating renal fibrosis without significantly affecting blood pressure. Macrophage-associated inflammatory responses and macrophage-tubular epithelial cell interactions may contribute to the renoprotective effects of irisin, supporting the FNDC5/irisin axis as a potential therapeutic target for HRI.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease and Cardiovascular Disease: A Review.
authorString: Rahni S, Lebovics E, Frishman WH, Aronow WS.
abstractText: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists have transformed the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity and have more recently demonstrated clinically important effects across the cardiometabolic spectrum, including metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Earlier cardiovascular outcome trials established reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events by way of injectable forms in patients with diabetes, while newer evidence has expanded these findings to oral semaglutide and to other patient populations. This review summarizes the hepatic, cardiovascular, and heart-failure evidence for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists-based therapies and discusses remaining clinical uncertainties and future directions.

title: Practice variation in mechanical circulatory support: a cross-sectional questionnaire survey of Japanese interventional cardiologists in the CVIT Kyushu-Okinawa chapter.
authorString: Kawakami S, Fujino T, Nakashima T, Kadooka K, Misumi K, Furukawa S, Hongo H, Honda T, Kitazono K, Imamura S, Shimono H, Suematsu N, Hironaga K, Matoba T, Tsujita K.
abstractText: Mechanical circulatory support (MCS) practice for cardiogenic shock may vary with institutional resources and operator experience, but data from Japanese interventional cardiologists are limited. We conducted an anonymous cross-sectional survey of 720 members of 83 Japanese Association of Cardiovascular Intervention and Therapeutics (CVIT)-certified or affiliated training hospitals in the CVIT Kyushu-Okinawa Chapter (September-October 2025); 536 returned questionnaires (74.4%), and consent was confirmed for 385 (53.5%). The primary analysis included 276 respondents who had performed intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP), veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO), or Impella CP insertion within 12 months: 163 at Impella-capable and 113 at non-Impella-capable hospitals. Documented MCS and extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation protocols were more frequently reported by respondents from Impella-capable hospitals (46% vs. 6% and 39% vs. 13%, respectively), as was collaboration with emergency and critical care physicians; no statistically significant difference was detected in perceived need for collaboration. MCS selection varied between groups. At Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) shock stage C, IABP (44%) and Impella CP (48%) were selected with similar frequency among respondents in Impella-capable hospitals, whereas IABP was selected by 79% in non-Impella-capable hospitals. At stage E, ECPELLA (79%) and VA-ECMO plus IABP (84%) predominated, respectively. Among respondents with device-specific operator experience within 12 months, vascular access and anticoagulation practices varied between groups. Procedural anxiety was lower with higher CVIT qualification; however, 19% of board-certified members reported anxiety about Impella CP insertion and 45% about emergency intubation. These findings identify MCS practice variation across several domains warranting further evaluation.

title: Primary Aldosteronism: Evaluation and Management in the Hypertensive Patient.
authorString: Balhara M, Owei L, Demko J, Wachtel H, Cohen JB.
abstractText: Primary aldosteronism (PA) is common, underdiagnosed, and associated with excess cardiorenal risk. We review recent changes in screening, diagnosis, treatment, and implementation. Contemporary guidelines have broadened screening and reduced barriers to aldosterone-to-renin ratio testing through medication-tolerant, assay-aware interpretation. Confirmatory aldosterone suppression testing is increasingly de-emphasized, with selective use or omission in high-probability patients when results are unlikely to change management. Adrenal vein sampling remains standard for most surgical candidates, while molecular imaging is emerging as a noninvasive alternative. Adrenalectomy is preferred for lateralizing disease; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists remain first-line therapy for bilateral or nonoperative disease, with renin response increasingly used to assess dosing adequacy. Finerenone and aldosterone synthase inhibitors are potential emerging options. PA care is shifting from a rigid multistep workup toward earlier detection and treatment-directed evaluation. Future work should define scalable screening pathways and compare outcomes of emerging diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

title: Mitochondrial bioenergetics deficit linked to endothelial dysfunction and ER stress induced by obesity in coronary arteries.
authorString: Olmos L, Gómez Del Val A, Martínez P, Sánchez A, Estévez Á, Muñoz M, Rodríguez C, López M, Rivera L, Benedito S, Prieto D, Contreras C.
abstractText: Obesity and metabolic syndrome are major drivers of metabolic heart disease, characterized by profound cardiac energy deficits, structural remodeling, and progression to heart failure. While myocardial mitochondrial dysfunction in obesity is well established, its impact on coronary arteries remains underexplored. This study investigates how high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity affects coronary bioenergetics, mitochondrial REDOX balance, and endothelial function. Male Wistar rats were fed a HFD (60% kcal fat) for 15-16 weeks after weaning as a model of diet-induced obesity, and tunicamycin-treated rats as a model of chemically-induced ER stress in vivo were used. Myograph experiments to assess coronary endothelial function, reactive oxygen species (ROS) measurements, and mitochondrial respiration experiments in a Seahorse analyzer were comprehensively conducted. After 15-16 weeks of HFD rats developed metabolic syndrome features, including weight gain, hyperglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and elevated lactate. Coronary arteries exhibited endothelial dysfunction, evidenced by impaired acetylcholine- and isoprenaline-induced relaxations, mediated by NADPH oxidase 1 (NOX1)-derived ROS, as selective NOX1 inhibition (NoxA1ds-tat) restored vasodilation. Mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) levels increased in arteries but not myocardium, along with preserved hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-mediated signaling. Protein analysis revealed down-regulated endothelial NOX4 and manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), reduced respiratory complex IV (COX-IV) and uncoupling protein 2 (UCP2), and blunted mitochondrial respiration across basal, ATP-linked, and maximal states. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α) up-regulation indicated adaptive biogenesis. HFD also activated endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. Notably, tunicamycin-induced ER stress recapitulated these deficits, impairing relaxation, H2O2 production, and respiration, yet up-regulating protective NOX4/MnSOD/PGC-1α. These findings couple coronary mitochondrial impairment to obesity-driven heart disease, highlighting impaired coronary bioenergetics, mitochondrial oxidative stress, and ER stress as key mechanisms. Thus, coronary artery mitochondria emerge as therapeutic targets to improve microvascular perfusion and mitigate progression to heart failure in obesity.

title: The acute kidney injury - acute kidney disease - chronic kidney disease continuum: pediatric perspective.
authorString: Karmakar S, Sarkar S, Dasgupta D, Mammen C, Sinha R.
abstractText: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is emerging as a significant contributor to long-term kidney morbidity in children. Advances in critical care have improved survival, but a growing proportion of pediatric AKI survivors remain at risk of progressing to chronic kidney disease (CKD). The concept of acute kidney disease (AKD), defined as persistent kidney dysfunction up to 90 days after AKI, has emerged as a key intermediary phase in this continuum. This review outlines current evidence on the epidemiology, pathophysiology and outcomes of the AKI-AKD-CKD continuum in children and the relevance of AKD within this continuum. Mechanisms underlying AKI-CKD transition include maladaptive hyperfiltration, persistent paracrine signalling and vascular rarefaction, which together drive progressive nephron loss and fibrosis. Pediatric studies, though limited and heterogeneous, consistently demonstrate an increased risk of CKD, hypertension and subclinical kidney dysfunction following AKI. Early risk stratification, structured follow-up and integration of emerging biomarkers may improve outcomes by identifying children at the highest risk for CKD progression. Strengthening post-AKI care pathways should be a priority in pediatric nephrology.

title: Urinary peptidome analysis of kidney failure in children with obstructive uropathy.
authorString: Buffin-Meyer B, Sylla B, Voutsadaki K, Klein J, Siwy J, Nguyen TMN, Breuil B, Delecroix E, Murunga S, Schaefer F, Burgmaier K, Liebau MC, Boeckhaus J, Gross O, McLeod DJ, Becknell B, Schanstra JP.
abstractText: Children with congenital obstructive uropathy (OU) who survive infancy are at increased risk for progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD), but disease onset and severity vary widely, highlighting the need for improved risk stratification. The present study evaluated whether urinary peptidome analysis could predict progression to kidney failure (KF) in children with OU. Urinary peptidome analysis was performed on 151 samples from children with OU enrolled in the Chronic Kidney Disease in Children (CKiD) Study. Progression to KF was defined as a ≥50% decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate or initiation of kidney replacement therapy. Peptides were incorporated into a random survival forest model developed in a training cohort and tested in an independent validation cohort. Performance was compared to the 5-year Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE). Over a median follow-up of 5.6 years, 33% (50/151) of children progressed to KF. Iterative cross-validation identified 47 urinary peptides predictive of KF within 5 years in the training set of 101 patients. The model achieved an area under the curve of 88.6% (95% CI: 75.2-97.8), with sensitivity of 66.7% and specificity of 88.0% in the validation cohort of 50 patients, demonstrating similar overall performance, but higher specificity and lower sensitivity, than the KFRE. Independent and external validation in 162 patients with CKD other than OU confirmed the performance of the peptide model. Urinary peptidomics identifies children with mild to moderate OU-related CKD at risk for KF with high specificity and moderate sensitivity. Although overall performance was comparable to the KFRE, the peptide model's specificity may be particularly useful for stratifying patients at intermediate KFRE risk. A higher resolution version of the Graphical abstract is available as Supplementary information.

title: The Lymphatic System in the Fontan Circulation: Pathophysiology, Imaging and Therapeutic Interventions.
authorString: Cánovas-Galindo C, Segura-Rodríguez D, Ladrón-Abia R, Moreno-Escobar E.
abstractText: The Fontan circulation, the definitive palliation for patients with univentricular hearts, produces a unique haemodynamic state characterised by chronically elevated systemic venous pressure, reduced cardiac output and the absence of a subpulmonary ventricular impulse. Because lymphatic drainage depends critically on the pressure gradient between the thoracic duct and the systemic veins, this physiology has profound consequences for the lymphatic system. Over the past decade, the lymphatic circulation has moved from being regarded as a passive bystander to being recognised as a central determinant of Fontan failure. Chronic systemic venous hypertension drives lymphatic overproduction and impaired central drainage, leading to progressive lymphatic congestion that manifests as chylothorax, protein-losing enteropathy (PLE), plastic bronchitis, lymphoedema and Fontan-associated liver disease. Advances in magnetic resonance (MR) lymphangiography, in particular dynamic contrast-enhanced MR lymphangiography and T2-weighted MR lymphangiography, now permit direct visualisation of abnormal lymphatic flow and precise planning of image-guided interventions. Percutaneous lymphatic embolisation and thoracic-duct decompression, together with surgical decompression procedures and, ultimately, heart transplantation, have shown clinically relevant efficacy in selected patients with complications refractory to medical therapy.
