title: Acute and 6-month vascular effects of a multi-component nutritional supplement: a randomized controlled trial
<i>Cassia fistula</i> L. Fruit Extract Attenuates Renal and Cardiac Toxicities by Reducing Oxidative Stress and Inflammation in Fludrocortisone Acetate-Treated Long Evans Rats.
authorString: Fatima-Tuz-Zahra S, Khan SI, Emran T, Gias ZT, Bepari AK, Ahmed R, Jain P, Reza HM.
abstractText: Renal and cardiovascular diseases are major contributors to death worldwide. We investigated the therapeutic effect of Cassia fistula fruit extract (CFFE) on fludrocortisone acetate (FCA)-induced oxidative stress, renal toxicity, and cardiac fibrosis in rats. Long Evans rats were divided into different treatment groups, and biochemical tests were conducted on plasma, kidney, and heart homogenates to measure oxidative/antioxidative parameters and organ-specific functional markers. The expression of proinflammatory and fibrotic genes in cardiac tissue was also measured. We observed that CFFE administration reduced the elevated levels of oxidative stress markers-malondialdehyde (MDA) and advanced oxidative protein products (AOPPs)-while enhancing the reduced antioxidant enzyme levels of catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and glutathione (GSH) in FCA-treated rats. Similarly, the CFFE treatment significantly reduced the increased plasma levels of cardiac troponin I (cTnI), uric acid, and creatinine in these rats. There was elevated expression of IL-1β, IL-6, TGF-β1, and TNF-α genes in the heart of the FCA rats, which was substantially downregulated by CFFE treatment. Histological investigations further revealed morphological abnormalities and fibrosis in the kidney and heart of the FCA rats, while CFFE treatment markedly ameliorated these signs. Our results suggest that CFFE prevents FCA-induced oxidative stress, renal injury, and associated cardiac damage and fibrosis by enhancing the antioxidant defense system and controlling inflammation.

title: Longitudinal Remodeling and Network Architecture of the Proximal Aorta in Children and Adolescents With Marfan Syndrome.
authorString: Tirado AG.
abstractText:
Background

Aortopathy is the main cardiovascular manifestation of Marfan syndrome, but the joint evolution of the different segments of the proximal aorta during pediatric growth remains insufficiently characterized.

Objective

To evaluate longitudinal remodeling and the interindividual and intraindividual architecture of the proximal aorta in children and adolescents with Marfan syndrome.

Methods

This was a secondary analysis of data from the Pediatric Heart Network Marfan trial. Participants aged <18 years at randomization with acceptable echocardiograms obtained at baseline and at 6, 12, 24, and 36 months were included. The aortic annulus, sinuses of Valsalva, sinotubular junction, and ascending aorta were analyzed using absolute diameters and Z-scores. Partial correlation networks were estimated, separating interindividual and intraindividual components. Uncertainty was assessed using participant-level bootstrap resampling.

Results

A total of 515 participants were included; 445 (86.4%) had five acceptable visits. From baseline to 36 months, all absolute diameters increased, whereas Z-scores decreased (-0.688 to -0.454; all p < 0.001). Exploratory age-stratified analyses showed larger decreases among participants aged 6-11 years. The interindividual network was stronger than the intraindividual network (global strength 1.783 vs 1.020; difference 0.763; 95% CI 0.526-1.101; p < 0.001). Sensitivity analyses using inverse-probability weighting and an alternative Pediatric Heart Network Z-score system showed the same overall pattern of declining Z-scores.

Conclusions

The proximal aorta shows a multisegment architecture in which organization across patients is stronger than within-patient coordination of change. Network findings complement, but do not replace, serial measurement of individual aortic levels, and their prognostic value requires independent validation.

title: Left Atrial Strain and Left Atrio-Ventricular Coupling in Heart Failure Patients with Left Ventricular Hypertrophy and Wild-Type Transthyretin Cardiac Amyloidosis.
authorString: Di Lisi D, Bono G, Puccia G, Macaione F, Bongiorno F, Mesi F, Galassi AR, Novo G.
abstractText: Wild-type transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTRwt-CA) is a cardiomyopathy characterized by myocardial and atrial stiffening. We aimed to assess left atrial (LA) function and left atrio-ventricular coupling index (LACI) in heart failure (HF) patients with left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and evaluate their ability to discriminate ATTRwt-CA from non-amyloid LVH. We conducted a case-control study including 50 patients with ATTRwt-CA and 50 HF patients with hypertensive heart disease. LA reservoir strain (LARS), LA contraction strain (PACS), LA stiffness index (LASI), LA reservoir work (LAWr) and LACI have been measured. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed for interventricular septal thickness (IVS), relative wall thickness (RWT), age, sex, coronary heart disease (CAD) to mitigate confounding. Before matching,  significant differences in IVS, RWT, age, sex, and CAD rates were observed between cases and controls. After PSM, LA functional indices remained significantly impaired in CA patients compared to controls. In the multivariate analysis, only LARS and LASI were independently associated with ATTRwt-CA. A LASI > 1.57 (AUC 0.87) and a PACS  ≤  6.0% (AUC 0.79) demonstrated the highest diagnostic accuracy for identifying ATTRwt-CA, with reduced LARS ( ≤  14.0%) also providing significant discrimination. Incorporating LASI  into the AMYLI (AUC 0.91) and IWT scores (AUC 0.89)  significantly enhances overall diagnostic accuracy for ATTRwt-CA detection. LA function and the atrio-ventricular coupling are more impaired in ATTRwt-CA patients compared to patients with HF alone; especially LARS and LASI are independent predictor for ATTRwt-CA and should be assessed in HF patients with LVH to detect CA.

title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis at Diagnosis is Associated With Adverse Long-Term Glycaemic Trajectories and Retinopathy in Adult-Onset Type 1 Diabetes. A Single-Centre Retrospective Cohort Study.
authorString: Pollis RM, Boscari F, Furlanetto D, Bittante C, Crepaldi MC, Vedovato M, Bruttomesso D, Maran A, Bonora BM, Morieri ML, Fadini GP.
abstractText:
Aims

The long-term significance of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) at the diagnosis of adult-onset type 1 diabetes (T1D) is poorly understood. We investigated the association between DKA at diagnosis and long-term outcomes.

Methods

In this retrospective study, we analysed adults with T1D diagnosed at age ≥ 18 years who attended a single tertiary diabetes centre between 2000 and 2025. Participants were classified according to the presence or absence of DKA at diagnosis. Longitudinal changes in HbA1c were analysed using mixed models. Incident chronic complications were evaluated using Cox regression models.

Results

Among 517 adults with T1D (47.2% women), 112 (21.7%) presented with DKA at diagnosis. The frequency of DKA at diagnosis increased from 13.2% in 2000-2008 to 34.6% after 2016 (p < 0.001). During a median (IQR) follow-up of 9.3 (3.5-15.5) years after cohort entry, individuals presenting with DKA had persistently higher HbA1c levels than those without DKA, with an adjusted between-group difference of 0.37% (95% CI 0.20, 0.53; p < 0.001). When data were aligned to the diabetes onset date, the estimated mean difference was 0.66% (p < 0.001). In exploratory analyses, DKA at diagnosis was associated with a higher incidence of retinopathy (HR 1.61; 95% CI 1.02-2.55; p = 0.041). The association was confirmed after accounting for delayed cohort entry and was attenuated by adjusting for mean HbA1c during follow-up.

Conclusions

Among individuals with adult-onset T1D attending a tertiary diabetes clinic, DKA at diagnosis was associated with persistently less favourable glycaemic control during long-term follow-up. Interpretation is limited by the single-centre retrospective design and delayed cohort entry.

title: A Multimodal Neuroimaging Study of Hyperlipidemia-Induced Abnormal Spontaneous Brain Activity and Cognitive Decline.
authorString: He JH, Wu JJ, Meng FL, Xiang YT, Huang RR, Zheng MX, Ma J, Xu JG.
abstractText:
Objective

To investigate multidomain cognitive performance in older adults with hyperlipidemia and its associations with alterations in spontaneous brain activity and functional connectivity (FC).

Methods

A total of 104 participants were recruited, comprising 50 hyperlipidemia patients and 54 healthy controls. Comprehensive psychological assessments were conducted, and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) data were collected from both groups. Amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), regional homogeneity (ReHo), and FC were calculated.

Results

Compared with healthy controls, hyperlipidemia patients showed significantly lower SDMT scores (p < 0.001), whereas no significant between-group differences were observed in the other neuropsychological measures. Imaging analyses revealed altered spontaneous brain activity and FC involving frontal, temporal, and cerebellar regions. In exploratory correlation analyses, lower SDMT scores and longer STT-B completion times were associated with higher zALFF values in the right inferior temporal gyrus (r = -0.197, p = 0.046); however, the SDMT association was modest and did not survive correction for multiple comparisons (r = 0.257, p = 0.009). Age also positively correlated with zALFF in this region (r = 0.195, p = 0.048).

Conclusions

Hyperlipidemia was associated with lower SDMT performance, altered spontaneous activity, and functional connectivity in the frontal, temporal, and cerebellar regions. The exploratory associations involving the right inferior temporal gyrus suggest a potential relationship between altered regional brain activity and cognitive performance.

title: Quantification of Anti-Ro52, Anti-Ro60 and Anti-La Autoantibodies at High Sample Dilution and Their Predictive Value for Congenital Heart Block.
authorString: Rudolph L, Möller ER, Rodrigues RDS, de Fremont GM, Ottosson V, Lagnefeld L, Gunnarsson I, Svenungsson E, Nordenstam F, Bergman G, Sonesson SE, Thorlacius GE, Wahren-Herlenius M.
abstractText: Maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies confer a risk of congenital heart block (CHB), but current methods for predicting risk relying on the presence or absence of these autoantibodies perform poorly. To identify more accurate biomarkers of CHB risk, we investigated the association between maternal levels of autoantibodies and the risk of CHB. A total of 318 women positive for anti-Ro/SSA autoantibodies were included. Autoantibody presence was obtained from health records for all, and ELISA was used to quantify levels of anti-Ro52, anti-Ro60, and anti-La in a subset of 116 women with samples obtained during pregnancy, including 27 CHB-affected pregnancies. Predictive models for CHB risk were developed using logistic regression and machine learning. Anti-Ro/SSA positive women with anti-Ro60 were more likely to have pregnancies with CHB (p < 0.05). Levels of both anti-Ro60 (p < 0.001) and anti-Ro52 (p < 0.05) were significantly higher in CHB-affected pregnancies and correlated (r = 0.8, p < 0.0001), while levels of anti-La did not differ between groups. Levels of anti-Ro60 were identified as the strongest individual predictor of CHB, with a relative risk of 16.3 (95% CI 1.04-255.0, p < 0.001) for the top versus the bottom decile. In all tested combinations, models that included anti-Ro60 levels outperformed models that did not. Models based on anti-Ro60 levels alone reached an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.76 and an odds ratio (OR) per standard deviation increase of 2.8 (95% CI 1.6-5.3). These findings confirm a strong association between maternal anti-Ro antibody levels and CHB risk in anti-SSA-positive pregnancy, highlighting anti-Ro60 autoantibody levels as a valuable biomarker in risk stratification.

title: Inflammation and Oxidative Damage in Fatty Acids Oxidation Disorders.
authorString: Altenhofen S, Tedesco L, Lopes FF, Acosta M, Sitta Â, Coelho DM, Reis BGD, Wailer L, Tonelotto D, Bottcher AK, Wajner M, Vargas CR.
abstractText: Deficiencies in enzymes and transporters involved in mitochondrial fatty acid beta oxidation results in the accumulation of fatty acids, a condition known as fatty acid oxidation disorders (FAODs). Therefore, the present study aimed to evaluate the oxidative and inflammatory profiles of treated patients with FAODs, comparing those receiving dietary treatment and l-carnitine supplementation with one untreated FAOD patient, to provide new insights into the pathophysiology and treatment of this group of diseases. Samples from 12 treated FAOD patients, 18 age-matched controls, and one untreated patient at diagnosis were included in the study. Levels of 8-isoprostanes, DNA and RNA oxidative damage, nitrite and nitrate, cathepsin D and cytokines were measured in urine and/or plasma samples, depending on the analyte, of FAODs patients under treatment (mean: 3.0 ± 2.9 years) and of an untreated patient with increased levels of several organic acids, who was included as an illustrative case and not considered in the statistical analyses. Levels of 8-isoprostanes, nitrite and nitrate, DNA damage, and interleukins 1β, 8, and 10 did not differ significantly between treated patients and control group, whereas IL-6 levels were increased in FAODs patients. These findings indicate that treated FAOD patients presented oxidative and inflammatory biomarker levels similar to those of controls for most analytes, while IL-6 remained elevated. The results suggest a potential beneficial effect of current treatment on oxidative and inflammatory profiles.

title: A Case of Asymptomatic Carotid Artery Stenosis With Thumb-Sized Calcification Detected on Panoramic Radiograph.
authorString: Shibata K, Kaneko K, Takaya T, Inou T, Hung YC, Kitamura H, Oki E, Nezu H, Ara T, Funaoka S, Higuchi D, Dewake N, Okuda M, Muneyasu M, Yoshinari N, Uchida K.
abstractText: A 73-year-old male with dyslipidemia and chronic kidney disease exhibited carotid calcification on a dental panoramic radiograph. Ultrasonography confirmed 30% asymptomatic carotid stenosis. This case highlights intimal calcification's link to kidney disease and atherosclerosis. Prompt medical-dental collaboration and diagnostic imaging remain crucial to prevent cerebrovascular events, extending healthy life expectancy.

title: Emergent Re-Do Open Aortic Valvular Repair and Foreign Body Retrieval During TAVR: A Case Report.
authorString: Dougherty R, Ong T, Morgan M, Chiang E, Srinivasan A, Ayad S.
abstractText: A 73-year-old man presented for a transcatheter aortic valve replacement after prosthetic aortic valve dysfunction. During the case, the transvenous pacer lost capture, causing the new prosthetic valve to embolize to the ascending aorta. This case details the intraoperative management throughout the valve deployment, attempted retrieval, and subsequent emergent redo open aortic valve repair with foreign body removal. Complications and considerations of a redo open chest, vasoplegia, cardiopulmonary bypass, aortic dissection, right ventricular failure, heart block, and prosthetic valve embolization are discussed.

title: An anatomy-aware spatio-temporal generative extrapolation network for distal ascending aorta restoration in standard echocardiographic views.
authorString: Chen X, Weng H, Cheng H, Qi Z, Shi Z, Guo G, Wang X, Chen H, Chen F, Fang A, Shan C, Chen Y, Luo S, Yao J, Qian S.
abstractText:
Background

In two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), the standard parasternal long-axis (PLAX) view enables reliable evaluation of the aortic valve and aortic root. Owing to the limited field of view of the ultrasound probe and rib-window occlusion, the distal ascending aorta (AA) is frequently truncated, compromising the diagnosis of aortic aneurysm and dilation.

Purpose

We aim to address the incomplete visualization of the distal AA in standard PLAX views. By aggregating fragmented anatomical features intermittently visible in adjacent frames, we enhance the clarity of vessel wall edges and generate the distal AA structure, thereby completing the missing AA imagery in standard PLAX views.

Materials and methods

We retrospectively collected 1160 TTE videos from Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital (August 2022 - December 2024), all showing complete AA anatomy. After de-identification, 1059 cases were randomly split into training/validation/test sets (6:2:2), and 101 cases were reserved for observer agreement experiments. An additional 152 videos from three different device models (EPIQ CVX, GE Voluson E10, Resona A20T) formed an external validation set. Two training data types were constructed: (i) dual-view synchronous data - a standard PLAX sequence and an AO-PLAX sequence acquired after a cranial probe shift, phase-matched at end diastole (ED); and (ii) locally masked data - the distal AA region was masked, forcing the model to infer missing anatomy from left-side context. Input sequences of five frames (ED ± 2) were extracted. The proposed Spatio-Temporal Ascending-Aorta generative adversarial network (STAA-GAN) first aligns adjacent frames using an Edge Boosted Feature Alignment (EBFA) module with multi-stage modulated deformable convolutions. A channel-wise fusion strategy then aggregates temporally aligned features. The fused representation is fed into a Swin-UNet generator enhanced with a Strip based Cross window Prediction (SCP) module to capture long-range structural dependencies. Training employs a composite loss including pixel reconstruction, feature reconstruction, texture consistency, relativistic average least-squares GAN (RaLSGAN), temporal coherence, and structure-aware terms, with data-dependent weighting. Statistical analyzes included Bland-Altman, Passing-Bablok regression, paired t-tests with Cohen's d, Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, and two one-sided tests (TOST, Δ=0.2cm ).

Results

STAA-GAN achieved the best image-quality values among the compared methods, with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) = 22.51 dB, structural similarity index (SSIM) = 0.7574, multi-scale structural similarity index (MS-SSIM) = 0.8598, and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) = 0.1758. All 12 pairwise comparisons (SRN, IOH, and U-Transformer versus STAA-GAN, designated as the reference group) remained statistically significant after Bonferroni correction ( α1=0.00417 ), with absolute effect sizes ranging from 0.255 to 3.439. The per-frame inference time was 203 ms. In clinical consistency validation, the mean difference between measurements on generated and original images was ≤0.01  cm with 95% limits of agreement within ±0.13  cm; TOST with Δ=0.2  cm confirmed clinical equivalence for all comparisons ( p<0.001 ). The segmentation Dice coefficient on generated images averaged 0.913±0.045 across five cross-validation folds. External validation on three different ultrasound devices (Philips, GE, Mindray) maintained consistent equivalence (TOST p<0.001 , Cohen's d<0.2 ). These results demonstrate that STAA-GAN produces clinically interchangeable distal ascending aorta images with high fidelity and real-time feasibility.

Conclusions

STAA-GAN enables extrapolation of the missing distal ascending aorta in standard PLAX views, achieving improved image quality and clinically equivalent diameter measurements on both internal and external validation datasets. These findings support its potential for assisting distal ascending aorta assessment in routine echocardiography.

title: Bicuspid Aortic Valve With Preserved Ejection Fraction: One-Year Changes in Ventricular and Atrial Mechanics.
authorString: Yalman H, Aygün AA, Temiz MK, Raimoglou D, Çimci M.
abstractText:
Purpose

Left ventricular (LV) dysfunction in bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) disease may precede ejection fraction (EF) decline. We assessed 1-year changes in LV global longitudinal strain (GLS), left atrial (LA) strain and myocardial work in BAV with preserved EF.

Methods

This retrospective cohort included 82 adults with BAV and sinus rhythm who had preserved LVEF (≥50%) at two echocardiograms 363 ± 15 days apart without interim surgery; 40 age- and sex-matched controls with tricuspid aortic valves were imaged once. Primary outcomes were changes in absolute GLS and LA reservoir strain (LASr); myocardial work, corrected for the transaortic gradient in aortic stenosis, was exploratory. Reader reproducibility was tested on stored images.

Results

At baseline, patients had lower absolute GLS (17.8 ± 2.8% vs. 21.8 ± 1.0%) and LASr (38.5 ± 5.2% vs. 40.8 ± 3.4%) than controls (p < 0.001 and p = 0.004). At 1 year, mean LVEF and LV volumes did not change significantly, whereas absolute GLS decreased by 0.8% points (95% CI 0.5-1.1) and LASr by 2.4 points (1.7-3.0; both Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Gradient-corrected global work index decreased by 47 mmHg% (27-68). The GLS decrease exceeded the intra-observer minimal detectable change in 22 patients (27%), versus an increase in 4 (5%). The GLS change was not significantly associated with valve lesion type or severity.

Conclusion

In selected patients with BAV who maintained preserved LVEF without valve or aortic surgery, LV GLS and LA reservoir strain decreased slightly over 1 year. Their clinical significance requires validation with longitudinal controls and test-retest data.

title: Clinical Features, Treatments, and Outcomes of an International Cohort of 96 Children with Takayasu Arteritis.
authorString: Bistolarides J, Morishita KA, Sivaraman V, Wagner-Weiner L, Bosman ES, McPhate N, Nocton JJ, Liegl M, Pan AY, Beresford MW, Charuvanij S, de Guzman M, Elder M, Giani T, Gagne S, Harrison K, James K, Jelusic M, Khan A, Martin N, Park J, Rosenberg AM, Shenoi S, Tanner T, Tarvin SE, Twilt M, Yeung RSM, Brown K, Cabral D, ARCHiVe Investigators Network within the PedVas Initiative and the CARRA Chronic Childhood Vasculitis workgroup.
abstractText:
Objective

To characterize the clinical features, treatment, and outcomes of a large, international cohort of childhood-onset Takayasu arteritis (cTAK).

Methods

Patients with a diagnosis of cTAK were identified in A Registry of Childhood Vasculitis and divided into subcohorts by era-of diagnosis: pre-biologic (PB; 1986-2006), early biologic (EB; 2007-2017), and recently diagnosed (RD; 2018-present). Longitudinal patient data were collected at time of diagnosis (TOD), postinduction (PI; 3-6 months after TOD), and 12 months after TOD (12m). Meaningful clinical improvement was defined as at least a 50% reduction in the Pediatric Vasculitis Activity Score. Damage was assessed by the Pediatric Vasculitis Damage Index.

Results

Among 96 patients (69% female, median age 12.8 years [interquartile range 9.8-15.3]) from nine countries, 86% showed clinical improvement at PI and 90% maintained improvement at 12m. Glucocorticoids (GC; n = 84, 88%) and methotrexate (n = 47, 49%) were the two most common medications prescribed at TOD, often together and in combination with another medication. GC use continued at 12m in 79%. Patients more recently diagnosed were more likely to receive treatment with tumor necrosis factor inhibitors (0% PB, 26% EB, and 35% RD; P = 0.007) and reach 70% improvement (59% PB, 81% EB, and 100% RD; P = 0.007) at PI. However, neither improvement nor damage at 12m differed among the subcohorts.

Conclusion

Although treatment approaches for cTAK have evolved and most patients demonstrate sustained clinical improvement at 12m, these advances have not translated into substantial changes in outcomes, highlighting the need for optimized therapeutic strategies.

title: "A Father and Daughter Presentation of Autosomal Dominant Sleep-Related Hypermotor Epilepsy Via a DEPDC5 Deletion in Exon 28".
authorString: Barbaro JL, Benham EM, Ambekar A, Nayak CS.
abstractText: Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE) is a form of focal epilepsy that can be caused by a pathogenic autosomal-dominant DEP domain containing Protein 5 (DEPDC5) variant. Given its variable clinical presentation and etiology, SHE can be challenging to diagnose and treat effectively. This case describes a father-daughter pair who experienced sleep-related seizures with similar semiologies and were later diagnosed with autosomal dominant sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (ADSHE) after genetic test results revealed that they each had a DEPDC5 deletion in Exon 28. Currently, seizures are well controlled in the father with lacosamide plus brivaracetam and in the daughter with lacosamide alone. Due to the technically difficult nature inherent in diagnosing ADSHE, both father and daughter experienced diagnostic and treatment delays. This case report highlights the importance of early pattern recognition and genetic testing in patients with clinical features of ADSHE and expands upon the current understanding of clinical presentations of pathogenic DEPDC5 variants.

title: Mechanical Thrombectomy of a Combined Persistent Primitive Trigeminal Artery and Basilar Artery Occlusion: A Case Report and Literature Review.
authorString: Deprez L, Dasnoy-Sumell G, Abdellaoui R, Schyns O, Moïse M.
abstractText:
Objective

Persistent primitive trigeminal artery (PPTA) is a rare anastomosis between the internal carotid artery and the posterior circulation, most commonly with the basilar artery (BA). It has been associated with neurovascular diseases such as cerebral hemorrhage and ischemic stroke. Its occlusion in the case of ischemic stroke presents multiple challenges, both diagnostic and therapeutic, as the modified vascular anatomy may complicate the initial imaging diagnosis and endovascular treatment with mechanical thrombectomy (MT).

Case presentation

We report here the case of a 64-year-old woman presenting with an altered conscious status and bilateral mydriasis due to an occlusion of a PPTA and the distal part of the BA, which was treated with MT. Complete recanalization was obtained using combined contact aspiration and stent retriever thrombectomy through the PPTA.

Conclusion

PPTA is a rare vascular anatomical variant whose knowledge is important in the setting of stroke. In this setting, MT appears to be a feasible, safe, and effective technique compared to other proximal sites of occlusion.

title: High cardiorespiratory fitness predicts lower risk of progression and higher chance of regression of arteriopathy during a lifestyle intervention.
authorString: Schuth S, Kantartzis K, Machann J, Schick F, Schulze MB, Marx-Schütt K, Marx N, Jumpertz-von Schwartzenberg R, Birkenfeld AL, Peter A, Fritsche A, Lehn-Stefan A, Stefan N.
abstractText: High carotid intima-media thickness (cIMT) is a marker of arterial injury, and cIMT can be used to track the regression, arrest, or progression of arteriopathy. Because high cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) protects from cardiovascular disease and closely associates with mitochondrial function, we determined whether baseline CRF and change in CRF predict change in cIMT during a lifestyle intervention. A total of 208 subjects at risk for type 2 diabetes who participated in the Tübingen Lifestyle Intervention Program underwent measurements of CRF, cIMT, glucose, and lipid metabolism, body fat mass and distribution, and liver fat content at baseline and after 9 months. During the intervention, almost all cardiometabolic risk parameters improved. However, there was a large variability in the change in cIMT. In a multivariable linear regression model, CRF at baseline (std.-β -0.19, p = 0.02) and change in CRF (std.-β -0.18, p = 0.01) were associated with change in cIMT. Subjects in the upper tertile of change in cIMT had a mean (SD) increase in cIMT of 14 (9)%, while subjects in the lower tertile had a mean decrease in cIMT of 16 (7)%. Larger increase in CRF was associated with lower odds of progression of cIMT (OR per SD increase 0.05 [95% CI 0.006-0.42], p = 0.004) and with higher chance of regression of cIMT (OR per SD increase 13 [95% CI 2-111], p = 0.01). We provide novel findings that measuring CRF before and during a lifestyle intervention may help predict the progression and regression of arteriopathy.

title: Community perspectives on Exception from Informed Consent (EFIC) in the intensive care unit (ICU) setting: a mixed methods study.
authorString: Keijer BL, Boggs KM, Habet V, Goldstein S, Mamolea C, Puente BN, Fetch A, Sleeper LA, Ross CE, Kheir JN.
abstractText:
Introduction

The U.S. Exception from Informed Consent (EFIC) regulatory pathway enables clinical research in life-threatening situations where delays may preclude trial participation or reduce treatment efficacy. The use of EFIC in the intensive care unit (ICU) setting remains limited.

Methods

In preparation for a prospective, multi-centre, ICU-based randomised controlled interventional trial, community consultations and public disclosures were conducted at three quaternary paediatric centres to assess the acceptability of an EFIC framework among community members and clinical staff. Session content was standardised, meetings were recorded and transcribed, and surveys with seven-point Likert scales (0-6) were distributed, with scores ≥5 considered affirmative.

Results

We conducted 18 clinician meetings (cumulative attendance n=313) and 26 community meetings (cumulative attendance n=43). Survey responses (n=128) demonstrated strong EFIC support: 100% (24/24) community participants viewed the trial as important; 88% (49/56) of clinicians viewed reperfusion injury as clinically important. Also, 100% (24/24) community members and 93% (97/104) clinicians reported willingness to enrol a relative or patient. In the qualitative analysis, significant concerns about the feasibility, utility, and messaging of the pre-enrolment opportunities to object (OTO) led to it being left to enrolling clinicians' discretion. The post-enrolment OTO to ongoing participation process was considered appropriate.

Conclusions

In this mixed methods study, community members and clinicians across three centres expressed support for use of EFIC in this ICU-based trial. These findings highlight the importance of structured and multi-perspective community engagement in EFIC trials and support its future use in the ICU setting.

title: SDHC Gene is a Potential Player in the Pathogenesis of Congenital Heart Disease and Neurodevelopmental Disorder by Promoting eNOS Signaling, Suppressing Inflammation and Improving Angiogenic Endothelial Function.
authorString: Deng X, Zhao Y, Deng W, Wang Z, Zhou K, Xu Q, Li X, Qin X, Guo L, Tan Y, Qian Y, Xiao Y, Jiang ZS.
abstractText:
Introduction

Congenital Heart Disease (CHD) and Neurodevelopmental Disorders (NDD) frequently co-occur due to shared genetic defects in embryonic angiogenesis and mitochondrial metabolism; however, the regulatory mechanisms linking these pathways remain poorly understood.

Objective

To identify pathogenic genes underlying CHD-NDD co-development and investigate the regulatory role of Succinate Dehydrogenase Complex Subunit C (SDHC) in endothelial angiogenesis.

Methods

Blood samples from 70 children (13 CHD+NDD, 33 CHD, 24 NDD) were analyzed by Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) and Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS). Candidate genes were identified through bidirectional deduplication, multi-library comparison, PPI network analysis, and functional enrichment analysis. SDHC expression was examined by immunofluorescence in the developing mouse heart and brain. In Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) with SDHC overexpression or knockdown, eNOS and TNF-α protein levels were measured by Western blot. Cell migration and tube formation were quantified by scratch and Matrigel assays.

Results

WES identified high-frequency SDHC mutations, including T→TTA (Chr1:161293485, 33.33%) and C→CT (Chr1:161332091, 55.56%) in CHD+NDD. Bioinformatics suggested SDHC involvement in cardiac and neural development. In mice, cardiac SDHC increased age-dependently by 71.83% (P < 0.05), 100.21% (P < 0.01), and 239.89% (P < 0.0001) from 1 to 8 weeks. In HUVECs, SDHC overexpression upregulated eNOS by 103.25% (P < 0.001) and downregulated TNF-α by 45.16% (P < 0.01); knockdown downregulated eNOS by 43.37% (P < 0.05). SDHC overexpression increased migration by 42.96% (P < 0.0001), while its knockdown decreased it by 34.02% (P < 0.001). Tube formation nodes increased by 130.24% (P < 0.0001) and mesh area by 111.82% (P < 0.0001); knockdown reduced mesh area by 80.81% (P < 0.0001).

Discussion

These findings suggest SDHC dysregulation may affect CHD-NDD comorbidity through eNOS modulation and inflammatory responses in HUVECs. The presence of SDHC variants in 7 of 13 patients (53.8%) and functional data indicate SDHC may serve as a candidate angiogenesis regulator linking cardiovascular and neurodevelopmental abnormalities. However, the small cohort (n = 13 CHD + NDD), absence of healthy controls, and lack of patient-derived variant validation limit definitive conclusions. The biological consequences of the identified variants remain unknown because variant-specific functional analyses were not performed. Future studies require expanded cohorts and in vivo SDHC- specific models to investigate potential associations.

Conclusion

SDHC may play potential roles in eNOS signaling, inflammation suppression, and endothelial angiogenic function. These findings suggest SDHC as a candidate gene associated with CHD-NDD comorbidity.

title: What is an ideal mHealth for post-discharge home care of CHD: perspectives from primary caregivers, healthcare professionals, and project technical consultants: a qualitative research study.
authorString: YangLan R, Ma F, Li Q, Yao W, Peng S.
abstractText:
Background

Congenital heart disease (CHD) remains a leading global birth defect with high prevalence, yet advances in diagnosis and treatment have raised survival rates to 90%-95%. This epidemiological shift transforms CHD into a chronic condition demanding long-term post-discharge home management. Although mobile health (mHealth) holds promise for supporting such care, current tools suffer from low adherence, insufficient age-appropriateness, and a lack of emotional and social support, and most evaluations neglect the integrated perspectives of primary caregivers, clinicians, and technical developers.

Objective

This study aims to explore and synthesize the needs for and perspectives regarding an idealized mHealth system for post-discharge CHD home care from the perspectives of primary caregivers (PC), healthcare professionals (HP), and technical consultants (TC).

Methods

A qualitative descriptive design was employed, using semi-structured interviews with seven PC, six HP, and three TC. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's Reflexive Thematic Analysis (RTA) framework.

Results

Six overarching themes were identified: (1) tailored to individual, (2) easy to use, (3) media in convergence, (4) at the ready, (5) one clear voice and (6) emotional support on demand.

Conclusions

These findings provide a stakeholder-informed framework to guide future development of user-centered, clinically relevant, and technically robust mHealth interventions.

title: Association between maternal antimony exposure and offspring congenital heart defects: findings from a large birth cohort study.
authorString: Shao Y, Cao L, Lin R, Ran J, Liu Q, Mao B.
abstractText:
Background

This nested case-control study aimed to investigate the association between maternal blood antimony concentrations and the risk of congenital heart defects (CHDs) in offspring, identify potential risk factors for CHDs, and inform prevention strategies.

Method

The study was conducted within a birth cohort established jointly by Gansu Provincial Maternity and Child Care Hospital and Yale University. A total of 291 women were enrolled, including 97 women who gave birth to infants with CHDs (case group) and 194 controls. Controls were selected from the same cohort using a 1:2 matching ratio and matched to cases by age and community. Maternal whole blood samples were collected during prenatal hospitalization before delivery, and antimony concentrations were measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to determine an antimony exposure cutoff and classify participants into high and low exposure groups. Conditional multivariable logistic regression was performed to assess the association between maternal blood antimony concentrations and the risk of CHDs in offspring.

Results

The mean maternal blood antimony concentration was 13.05 μg/L in the control group and 20.30 μg/L in the CHDs group, and the difference between the two groups was statistically significant. Compared with the low exposure group, the high exposure group was associated with a significantly higher risk of CHDs in offspring (OR = 4.455, 95% CI: 2.029-9.782). Similar associations were observed for the subgroups of isolated CHDs, great arteries malformation, septal defects, and atrial septal defects (ASDs). For each 6 μg/L increment in maternal blood antimony, a 38.9% higher risk of CHDs in offspring (OR = 1.389, 95% CI: 1.110-1.735), with consistent findings in the isolated CHDs, septal defects, and ASDs subgroups. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis showed that when maternal blood antimony exceeded 18.409 μg/L, CHDs risk in offspring increased with rising antimony levels.

Conclusion

Higher maternal blood antimony concentrations were associated with an increased risk of CHDs in offspring. These findings suggest that the prenatal living environment may be a modifiable target for CHD prevention and warrant efforts to minimize exposure to potential environmental sources of antimony.

title: Striatal dopamine transporter binding in adults with 22q11.2 copy number variants: a SPECT study.
authorString: Spapens JCC, van Hooijdonk CF, Schalbroeck R, Sylvester AL, Boot E, van Amelsvoort TAMJ, Vingerhoets C, Booij J.
abstractText: Copy number variants at the 22q11.2 chromosomal locus, hemizygous 22q11.2 deletions or duplications, are associated with a broad spectrum of neuropsychiatric and other medical conditions. Individuals with a 22q11.2 deletion are at increased risk for developing early-onset Parkinson's disease. The catechol-O-methyltransferase gene at 22q11.2 is involved in dopamine metabolism. While previous studies have examined several aspects of dopamine function in individuals with 22q11.2 copy number variants, striatal dopamine transporter availability, a regulator of synaptic dopamine, has not yet been systematically investigated. Therefore, dopamine transporter availability was quantified in nine adults with a 22q11.2 deletion, nine with a 22q11.2 duplication and eight controls using a brain-dedicated single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) system. Specific striatal binding ratios were calculated with the occipital lobe as the reference region. Permutation analysis of covariance controlling for age and sex showed significantly higher striatal dopamine transporter availability in adults with 22q11.2 deletions compared with those with duplications (P = 0.026, η 2 p = 0.30). No significant differences were observed between adults with 22q11.2 copy number variants and controls. These findings suggest distinct nigrostriatal dopaminergic profiles associated with 22q11.2 copy number variant status, which may play a role in shaping frequently occurring neurological and psychiatric phenotypes in these individuals.

title: Dosimetric benefits of deep inspiration breath-hold in postoperative radiotherapy for left-sided breast cancer after breast-conserving surgery: an anatomical parameter-based analysis.
authorString: Cui Y, Xu S, Wang X, Huo L, Wen J, Hao L, Wang X, Zhang Q, Duan H.
abstractText:
Objective

To investigate the dosimetric impact of deep inspiration breath-hold (DIBH) technique on radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery for left-sided breast cancer, and to explore the relationship between patient anatomical characteristics and dosimetric benefits of DIBH, providing preliminary evidence for understanding individual differences in DIBH related dosimetric gains and their personalized application.

Methods

This retrospective study included 17 patients who underwent postoperative radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery for left-sided breast cancer. All patients underwent computed tomography (CT) simulation under both DIBH and free-breathing (FB) conditions, and intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) plans were generated from both image sets. With identical prescription doses and planning optimization objectives, dosimetric parameters for the left lung, heart, and cardiac substructures were compared between the two respiratory conditions. Correlations of the maximum cardiac margin distance (MCMD), cardiac displacement, cardiac displacement volume, heart-to-breast distance (HBD), and changes in lung volume with dosimetric parameters were also analyzed.

Results

Compared with FB, DIBH significantly reduced the mean dose (Dmean), V20, and V30 of the left lung, as well as the cardiac Dmean, V20, V30, and V40 (all P < 0.05). In addition, DIBH significantly reduced the mean doses to of the right ventricle (RV), left ventricle (LV), and left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) compared with FB (all P < 0.05). Correlation analysis demonstrated that MCMD under the DIBH condition was positively correlated with cardiac Dmean. The change in MCMD between DIBH and FB was negatively correlated with cardiac and ventricular dose parameters. Cardiac displacement volume between the two respiratory states was positively correlated with changes in mean heart dose. Further analysis revealed that changes in lung volume were positively correlated with cardiac displacement along the Z-axis and changes in HBD while negatively correlated with LAD Dmean under the DIBH condition.

Conclusion

DIBH can reduce radiation exposure to the left lung, heart, and selected cardiac substructures while satisfying target-dose requirements. Exploratory analyses indicated that cardiac geometric parameters and changes in lung volume were associated with selected dosimetric parameters, suggesting that dynamic anatomical changes during DIBH may help explain interindividual differences in dosimetric benefit. These findings require further validation in larger, multicenter cohorts.

title: Comparative efficacy of esophageal protection strategies during radiofrequency atrial fibrillation ablation: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized trials.
authorString: Ramezani A, Kian N, Sharafi A, Yousefimoghaddam F, Khezrpour A, Ghaffari Jolfayi A, Arya A, Haghjoo M.
abstractText:
Background

Esophageal thermal injury remains a clinically significant complication of radiofrequency catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation (AF), with endoscopically detected esophageal lesions (EDELs) occurring in up to 10-15% of cases and atrio-esophageal fistula carrying high mortality. Multiple protective strategies have been proposed; however, their comparative efficacy remains uncertain.

Methods

We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials evaluating esophageal protection strategies during AF ablation. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception through August 7, 2026. Parallel-group randomized trials in adult patients undergoing radiofrequency ablation were included. The primary outcome was incidence of EDEL. A frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis was performed, with treatment hierarchy assessed using P-scores. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were evaluated using the Cochrane RoB 2 and CINeMA frameworks, respectively.

Results

Twenty-five randomized controlled trials involving approximately 2,500 patients were included in the systematic review. Twelve trials involving 1,077 patients contributed to the connected network meta-analysis. Mechanical esophageal deviation combined with luminal esophageal temperature monitoring (LET) had the most favorable point estimate compared with no dedicated protection (OR, 0.27; 95% CI, 0.02-3.05) and achieved the highest P-score (0.861). The rankogram estimated a 58% probability of ranking first. Visualization-guided strategies also showed a favorable point estimate (OR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.08-3.09), whereas LET alone and active cooling did not demonstrate significant reductions in EDEL. Directly, mechanical deviation plus LET significantly reduced the odds of EDEL compared with single-sensor LET (OR, 0.13; 95% CI, 0.04-0.41). Seven randomized trials involving 990 patients showed no significant association between higher- versus standard-power ablation and EDEL (OR, 1.19; 95% CI, 0.56-2.54), with no observed heterogeneity (I² = 0%). Network heterogeneity was moderate (I² = 46.9%), with no significant evidence of network inconsistency or publication bias.

Conclusions

No single esophageal protection strategy completely eliminates the risk of thermal injury during AF ablation. Mechanical esophageal deviation combined with LET demonstrated the most favorable overall ranking, while visualization-guided strategies also showed a potentially beneficial signal. In contrast, LET or cooling alone did not reliably reduce EDEL incidence. However, overall confidence in the evidence is constrained by small trial samples and reliance on surrogate outcomes. Larger, contemporary trials are needed to confirm clinical benefits and assess the impact on rare but catastrophic complications.

Clinical trial number

Not Applicable.

title: Acute ischemic stroke associated with <i>Moringa oleifera</i> and protein powder consumption in a patient on warfarin: A coagulation paradox and clinical blind spot.
authorString: Kobayashi Y, Onuki A, Horiuchi K, Oinuma M, Munakata R, Segawa B, Saito K, Ito H, Kazama Y, Watanabe Z.
abstractText:
Background

As the global consumption of "superfoods" and fitness supplements surges, active patients on long-term anticoagulation face unprecedented, hidden thrombotic risks.

Case description

We report the case of a 30-year-old male with a mechanical aortic valve who presented with an acute left internal carotid artery terminus occlusion. Despite a history of stable warfarin therapy, his international normalized ratio (INR) plummeted after he began mixing Moringa oleifera leaf powder into his daily protein shakes. He underwent emergent mechanical thrombectomy, achieving expanded Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction 2C recanalization and dramatic neurological recovery. Upon discontinuation of the supplement, his INR rapidly recovered to 2.6 within a week without altering his original warfarin dose.

Conclusion

This case exposes a critical pharmacological paradox: while M. oleifera is widely marketed as a health supplement, it possesses potent intrinsic procoagulant properties and can catastrophically disrupt warfarin efficacy. The concurrent use of protein powder likely enhanced the bioavailability of fat-soluble vitamins, creating a "perfect storm" for rapid coagulation. This evolving dietary trend represents a dangerous clinical blind spot, necessitating proactive dietary screening to prevent life-threatening strokes in anticoagulated patients.

title: Advanced engineering strategies in human organoids for tissue repair and regeneration.
authorString: Zhang H, Yang N, Wu Y, Chen S, Wen Y, Zhu Y, Chen X.
abstractText: Tissue damage and functional disorders due to diseases or trauma can lead to irreversible organ failure. Conventional treatment strategies such as organ transplantation or stem cell therapy are often limited by immune rejection, donor shortages, and poor regenerative effects. Organoids, 3D miniature tissues derived from stem cells, can provide a promising approach for tissue repair and regeneration by recapitulating the complex structure and functional properties of native organs with high plasticity, scalability, and physiological relevance. In this review, we present novel engineering approaches to human organoids such as generation, optimization, and translational applications for tissue repair. We then introduce core technologies including organoid-on-chip, hydrogels, and 3D bioprinting, which collectively address the challenges such as tissue immaturity, inadequate vascularization, and poor host integration. We also discuss applications of engineered organoids to repair multiple tissues (e.g. heart, lung, brain, bone, and skin) and summarize recent advances in preclinical models and their potential clinical translational applications. Finally, we discuss key challenges for organoid-based therapy including functional maturation; integration with vascular, neural, and immune systems; complexity of reproducing native biomechanical environments; and ethical concerns, as well as possible solutions and directions for their application in regenerative medicine.

title: The Present and Future of Transcatheter Pulmonary Valve Implantation: Lessons From the PULSTA Valve Experience.

title: Performance of artificial intelligence versus clinician left-ventricular segmentation of cardiac MRI for mortality prediction: a retrospective, multicentre, prognostic study.
authorString: Joy G, Punjabi K, Searle G, Abdulelah Z, Gantur T, Pierce I, Thornton GD, Meredith B, Shiwani H, Curtis M, Cashin S, Augusto JB, Miranda I, Fontana M, Kellman P, Howard JP, Shun-Shin M, Treibel TA, Manisty C, Orini M, Schelbert EB, Hughes AD, Moon JC, Davies RH.
abstractText:
Background

Ejection fraction, a key measure of cardiac function, is used in health care for clinical decision making and risk stratification. We hypothesised that a deep-learning artificial intelligence (AI) segmentation of ejection fraction obtained from cardiac MRI (CMR) outperforms expert clinician segmentation for the prediction of all-cause mortality.

Methods

In this retrospective, multicentre, prognostic study, we studied a cohort of 27 382 consecutive patients who underwent cardiac MRI (CMR) in the UK and the USA. Patients were referred for CMR from nine hospitals to Barts Heart Centre (BHC), London. Patients were identified from the reporting archive at BHC as having undergone a CMR between Oct 1, 2014 and Dec 31, 2019. A further cohort of patients was also identified from University of Pittsburgh Medical Centre (UPMC), Pittsburgh, PA, USA, as having undergone a CMR between June 1, 2010 and March 31, 2016. Mortality data were obtained from national and local databases. AI segmentation was done on all CMR studies, and Cox proportional hazards models were fitted to compare the prognostic value of AI-measured versus clinician-measured left-ventricular volume metrics. Model fit was compared using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), discrimination using C indices and the incremental value of AI over clinician segmentation using likelihood-ratio tests of nested models.

Findings

27 382 patients received a baseline CMR (26 106 patients from BHC and 1276 from UPMC). The median follow-up was 5·6 years (IQR 4·4-6·9), during which 3458 (13%) of 27 382 patients died. AI ejection fraction showed better model fit (AIC 57 936 vs 58 097, ΔAIC 161 favouring AI) and marginally better discrimination (C index 0·669 vs 0·637; ΔC 0·033 [95% CI 0·026-0·041]). AI ejection fraction significantly improved model fit when added to clinician ejection fraction (χ2=168, p<0·0001), with only slight improvement when clinician ejection fraction was added to AI (χ2=7·5, p=0·023). After adjustment for age and sex, AI-derived ejection fraction showed better model fit (AIC 55 684 vs 55 742; ΔAIC 59) and had marginally better discrimination (C index of 0·781 vs 0·777; ΔC=0·004 [95% CI 0·002-0·006]).

Interpretation

AI-derived ejection fraction shows marginally superior prediction for mortality than clinician-derived ejection fraction in patients who had CMR. Findings support the potential utility of AI for first-line ejection-fraction measurement with clinician oversight, although this should be investigated in prospective studies.

Funding

National Institute for Health and Care Research Clinical Lectureship and the British Heart Foundation Accelerator Award.

title: Mortality prediction using cardiac magnetic resonance: artificial intelligence versus clinicians-Quo vadis?
authorString: Sveric KM, Linke A.

title: The Effect of Perioperative Video Interventions on Postoperative Pain Control: A Systematic Review.
authorString: Danielsson A, Asif S, Forsberg A, Lipcsey M, Kosek E, Bjurström MF.
abstractText:
Introduction

Postoperative pain is a major cause of suffering and is linked to serious complications, including delayed wound healing, increased cardiovascular risk, delayed rehabilitation, and chronic postsurgical pain. Modifiable psychological factors influence pain outcomes, and preliminary evidence suggests video interventions can reduce preoperative anxiety and improve patient satisfaction. We hypothesized that video interventions could improve postoperative pain control. Therefore, the aim of the current systematic review was to summarize all previous research and investigate the effects of perioperative video interventions on pain levels and/or analgesic consumption.

Methods

The review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024596389) and followed the PRISMA Guidelines. We searched PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Academic Search, and the Cochrane Central register of controlled trials from inception to October 2025 for randomized controlled trials in adult surgical patients. Trials assessing any perioperative video interventions reporting on postoperative pain intensity and/or analgesic consumption were included. Data was extracted independently by two authors, and data synthesis was qualitative due to significant heterogeneity. Risk of bias was assessed using the Revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2).

Results

Forty-four trials were included. Of the 42 trials assessing pain, 11 (26%) reported significantly lower pain in the intervention group. Of the 19 trials measuring analgesic consumption, eight (42%) reported significantly lower consumption in the intervention group. Only two trials demonstrated a benefit for both co-primary outcomes. Significant improvements in secondary outcomes, including anxiety, physical function, and satisfaction, were reported in 26 trials. Most trials were judged as having a high risk of bias.

Conclusion

The current systematic review suggests that perioperative video interventions may improve acute postoperative pain control, although effects are inconsistent across trials. Future research should focus on identifying patient and intervention characteristics that predict efficacy to guide clinical implementation.

Editorial comment

This trustworthy systematic review presents an overview of current research findings for application of perioperative video-based treatments as part of managing postoperative pain. While this approach shows promise, more definitive evidence may be needed to justify more widespread implementation.

title: The Rural Ecological Framework of Intimate Partner Violence (RE-IPV): Social-Ecological Factors and Constrained Agency Among Rural Women.
authorString: Kimber F, Abusbaitan H, Munala L, Luebke J, Walton A, Eyedat A, Gondwe KW, Bement K, Jerome M, Clark C, Mkandawire-Valhmu L.
abstractText: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a pervasive public health crisis, with rural social and structural conditions creating additional challenges for survivors seeking safety and support. Existing applications of the Social-Ecological Model (SEM) have helped identify factors influencing IPV, but offer less explanation about how these factors interact to constrain survivors' agency and shape service navigation. This paper introduces the Rural Ecological Framework of Intimate Partner Violence (RE-IPV), a conceptual framework informed by the SEM, structural violence perspectives, and a synthesis of empirical literature, with refinement through engagement with rural community partners, nurse scholars, and public health scientists. RE-IPV illustrates how interacting societal, community, relational, and individual conditions shape the options available for rural women experiencing IPV. Central to the framework is constrained agency, which helps explain how survivors make decisions about safety, disclosure, and service utilization within circumstances that limit their available options. The framework also conceptualizes service navigation as a recursive process in which healthcare and advocacy encounters can influence survivors' trust, perceptions of safety, and subsequent help-seeking decisions. By moving beyond a descriptive categorization of ecological barriers, RE-IPV offers a rural-specific perspective on how structural conditions shape survivors' agency and engagement with services. The framework provides a foundation for future conceptual development, empirical examination, and survivor-centered nursing and healthcare practice. Trial Registration: Not applicable.

title: From Structural Blindness to Structural Perception: Theorizing LUMEN, a Multisensory Pedagogy for the Structural Determinants of Health in Nursing Education.
authorString: Ballout S, Davis S, Jester M, McKinley Yoder C, Kaylor SK.
abstractText: Structural competency has advanced health-professions education by orienting clinicians to the social, political, and economic structures that produce health inequities, yet its nursing applications treat experiential and sensory teaching methods as instructional delivery rather than explaining why such methods work, and assume rather than cultivate the perceptual acts, recognition, and responses that they depend on. This conceptual paper develops LUMEN, a multisensory pedagogy for teaching the structural determinants of health in nursing, and introduces structural perception as the foundational competency it cultivates. Through an argument-based synthesis integrating structural competency, critical pedagogy, transformative learning, embodied and grounded cognition, social theory, and the arts with the nursing literature, we argue that structural determinants are pedagogically difficult because they are imperceptible, abstract, upstream, and naturalized, making the foundational educational task perceptual rather than informational. Because perception is sensory and embodied, multisensory pedagogy is its fitting mechanism. LUMEN operationalizes this through five domains, Look, Uncover, Mirror, Engage, and Navigate, sequenced across a three-phase arc moving learners from structural blindness through critical consciousness to structural action. LUMEN names a competency the field has assumed and theorizes a mechanism it has used but not justified, offering nurse educators a theoretically grounded, testable foundation for teaching structural perception. We also subject the framework to critique, including the risk that adding another model to a crowded field could individualize what is ultimately an institutional problem.

title: Inequalities in Routine BMI Recording in English Primary Care: A Cross-Sectional Study of 628 546 Adults With Implications for Diabetes and Obesity Care.
authorString: Fatima M, Zafar A, Scarlata C, Birch P, Madni B, Saeed A, Chishti M, Akram A, Siddiquie A, Jaleel N.
abstractText: Obesity is a major cause of ill health in the United Kingdom, and access to diabetes prevention and weight-management pathways depends on BMI recording. To quantify the completeness of adult BMI recording in primary care and to determine whether recording is socially and clinically patterned. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of anonymised primary care records from an integrated care board in England. Adults aged ≥ 18 years (n = 628 546) were included. The outcome was ever having a recorded BMI, with no defined time window. Associations with age, sex, ethnicity, deprivation, T2D and CVD were estimated using modified Poisson regression and reported as adjusted prevalence ratios. Overall, 279 585 adults (44.5%) had a recorded BMI. Recording rose with age (31.0% at 18-39 to 60.7% at ≥ 60 years) and was higher in women than men (51.5% vs. 37.5%; 14.0 pp). Recording was highest in adults with T2D (88.2%) and CVD (78.0%) and lowest in adults with no recorded ethnicity (19.5%), White other (32.7%) and mixed (36.8%) groups. Adjusted analyses showed higher recording in adults with T2D (aPR: 1.79, 95% CI: 1.78-1.80), CVD (1.30, 1.29-1.31), female sex (1.37, 1.37-1.38) and older age, but lower recording in the most deprived quintile (aPR: 0.95, 0.94-0.96) and all non-White British ethnic groups. BMI was recorded in fewer than half of adults and was concentrated among those with chronic disease. Recording was less common in younger adults, men and deprived and minority ethnic groups, highlighting the importance of universal BMI recording as an equity metric.

title: Peak Cardiac Mechanical and Haemodynamic Responses During Incremental Exercise Are Temporally Associated With Ventilatory Thresholds: Novel Insight Into the Coordination of Integrative Physiological Responses to Exercise.
authorString: Spahiu F, Lampkemeyer M, Ottlik M, Hagemann M, Helbig LC, Stöhr EJ.
abstractText:
Background

Maximal aerobic capacity (VO2peak) is traditionally attributed to limitations in oxygen transport and utilization. However, it remains unclear whether peak cardiac mechanical and haemodynamic responses occur in temporal association to ventilatory thresholds during incremental exercise, and whether these relationships vary with cardiorespiratory fitness.

Methods

Eighteen healthy, recreationally active adults (26 ± 3.18 years VO2peak 41.87 ± 4.76 mL·kg·min-1) completed two incremental supine cycling tests to exhaustion, with breath-by-breath gas exchange analysis, exercise echocardiography, and continuous blood pressure monitoring. Plateau timing (PT) was defined as the relative heart rate (%HRmax) at which each cardiovascular variable reached its peak or plateau response. Associations between cardiovascular PTs, VO2peak, and the first (VT1) and second ventilatory thresholds (VT2) were examined using correlation analysis. Exploratory k-means clustering was used to descriptively visualize plateau-timing distributions.

Results

VT1 significantly correlated with PT-ejection fraction (EF) and PT-vascular conductance, whereas VT2 correlated with deformation-based parameters including PT-apical circumferential strain, PT-apical rotation, and iCarT (p < 0.05). VO2peak was positively associated with PT-twist and PT-apical rotation (p < 0.05), and negatively associated with PT-EF (p < 0.05). Exploratory clustering yielded two descriptive clusters which differed in VO2peak (p < 0.05) and were characterized by differences in volumetric and rotational plateau-timing distributions.

Conclusions

During exercise, different cardiac parameters are temporally associated with ventilatory thresholds 1 and 2. Cardiorespiratory fitness may influence interindividual differences in the temporal organization of response patterns during incremental exercise.

title: Drug Utilization Patterns and WHO Prescribing Indicators Among Hypertensive Outpatients at Karnali Academy of Health Sciences, Nepal: A Cross-Sectional Study.
authorString: Aryal B, Yadav BK, Sapkota B, Adhikari S.
abstractText: Hypertension is one of the most prevalent non-communicable diseases (NCDs) worldwide. This descriptive cross-sectional study evaluated drug utilization patterns and WHO core prescribing indicators among hypertensive patients attending the Outpatient Department of Karnali Academy of Health Sciences (KAHS), Jumla. A total of 197 hypertensive outpatients were systematically enrolled, and data were collected using a structured WHO-aligned questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics in SPSS version 26. The mean age of participants was 51.6 ± 13.2 years, with a slight male predominance (51.3%). Calcium channel blockers (32.8%) and angiotensin receptor blockers (24.6%) were the most frequently prescribed antihypertensive classes, while dual-drug therapy was the predominant treatment regimen (43.7%). Assessment of WHO prescribing indicators showed an average of 4.05 drugs per prescription (WHO target < 2.0), generic prescribing of 34.4% (target 100%), adherence to the Essential Medicines List of 79.9% (target 100%), antibiotic prescribing of 14.2%, and injection prescribing of 7.6%. Although antihypertensive prescribing practices at KAHS reflected generally appropriate drug selection for hypertension management, substantial deviations from WHO rational medicine use standards were observed, particularly with regard to low generic prescribing and excessive polypharmacy. These findings highlight the need for urgent policy-level interventions, including mandatory generic prescribing practices and regular prescription audits, to improve affordability, promote rational drug use, and enhance patient safety in this resource-limited setting.

title: Polyglycolic Acid Reinforcement for Prevention of Postoperative Air Leak after Pulmonary Resection for Pulmonary Malignancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authorString: Reviano MO, Reviano ADJ, Raditya AF, Pribadi ORS.
abstractText: Postoperative air leak, including prolonged air leak (PAL), remains a common complication after pulmonary resection for pulmonary malignancy. Polyglycolic acid (PGA)-based reinforcement may improve staple-line sealing; however, evidence of its effectiveness remains limited, and PGA application methods vary across studies. This study aimed to evaluate whether PGA-based reinforcement reduces postoperative air leak after pulmonary resection for pulmonary malignancy. This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines. Five databases were searched through April 2026. Studies comparing PGA-based reinforcement with conventional stapling in patients undergoing pulmonary resection for pulmonary malignancy were eligible for inclusion. The primary outcome was postoperative air leak. Five observational cohort studies involving 1,896 patients were included. PGA-based reinforcement was associated with lower odds of postoperative air leak (odds ratio [OR], 0.22; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.11-0.43; p<0.0001) and PAL (OR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.11-0.69; p=0.005). No significant differences were observed in operative time, blood loss, chest tube duration, or length of hospital stay (all p>0.05). The certainty of the evidence was very low. PGA-based reinforcement may reduce postoperative air leak and PAL after pulmonary resection for pulmonary malignancy; however, further high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews, registration number: CRD420261372690).

title: Postdischarge continuity of care and cardiovascular outcomes in acute coronary syndrome.
authorString: Lin YC, Hsu CY, Chen CW, Chen BL, Huang LY, Chang CL, Yasuda S, Jeong MH, Honda S, Huang WC, Wang YC, Shao YJ, Huang CY.

journal.title: Journal of the Chinese Medical Association : JCMA

abstractText:
Background

Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Despite the availability of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), postdischarge continuity of care (CoC) remains suboptimal, and evidence from Asian health-care systems remains limited. The present study examined the association between CoC and clinical outcomes in Taiwanese patients with ACS.

Methods

This nationwide observational cohort study was conducted using data from Taiwan's National Health Insurance Research Database. It included patients who had their first ACS-related hospitalization between 2012 and 2020 and excluded those who died during the index hospitalization or experienced study outcomes within 1 month after discharge. CoC was assessed in terms of physician, specialty, and GDMT continuity. Study outcomes were all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), hospitalization for heart failure (HHF), and major bleeding.

Results

This study included 140 214 patients with ACS. Patients with low physician continuity had significantly higher risks of all-cause mortality (adjusted risk ratio [aRR]: 2.20, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.09 to 2.31), cardiovascular death (aRR: 1.97, 95% CI: 1.81 to 2.15), MACEs (aRR: 1.78, 95% CI: 1.66 to 1.90), HHF (aRR: 1.66, 95% CI: 1.54 to 1.78), and major bleeding (aRR: 1.45, 95% CI: 1.26 to 1.66) than did those with high physician continuity. Low specialty continuity was associated with a 1.28-to-1.95-fold increase in the risk of adverse outcomes. Furthermore, low GDMT continuity was significantly associated with elevated risks of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular death, and MACEs but not HHF or major bleeding.

Conclusion

The findings suggest that lower CoC during the first year after ACS-related hospitalization is associated with poorer clinical outcomes. Future studies should explore strategies to improve CoC.

title: Racial and Ethnic Differences in Pediatric Perioperative Cardiac Arrest Survival.
authorString: Kitio SAY, Jung S, Gbadegesin S, Yeh J, Nafiu OO.
abstractText: Perioperative cardiac arrest (POCA) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Disparities in perioperative outcomes have been reported, but whether similar differences exist following pediatric POCA remains unclear. We evaluated racial and ethnic differences in 30-day mortality after pediatric POCA. Within the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program for Pediatrics (NSQIP-P) registry, we identified 2646 children under 18 who underwent inpatient, noncardiac surgery (2012─2024) and experienced POCA. Race and ethnicity were categorized as Hispanic, non-Hispanic Asian, non-Hispanic Black or African American, non-Hispanic white, or other. Crude and adjusted risk ratios for 30-day mortality following POCA were estimated. Among 2646 children with POCA, 47.9% (n = 1268) were non-Hispanic white, 28.2% (n = 745) non-Hispanic Black, 4.0% (n = 106) non-Hispanic Asian, 16.2% (n = 430) Hispanic and 3.7% (n = 97) Other race. Overall, 30-day mortality was 32.9% (871/2646). Mortality was similar across racial or ethnic groups (P = .72). In adjusted analyses, mortality risk did not differ significantly for non-Hispanic Black (adjusted relative risks [aRR] 1.02, P = .80), Hispanic children (aRR 1.06, P = .43), or children of other race (aRR 1.02, P = .88) compared with non-Hispanic white children. Emergent surgery (aRR 1.62, P < .001) and preoperative inotrope use (aRR 1.41, P < .001) were independently associated with increased mortality. We found no significant racial or ethnic differences in mortality risk following POCA among children undergoing inpatient surgery. Mortality was associated with clinical and perioperative factors, including emergent surgery and preoperative inotrope use. This suggests that efforts to identify drivers of disparities in pediatric postsurgical mortality must look beyond POCA outcomes alone.

title: Refractory Distributive Shock in Complex Spine Surgery: A Rare Entity That Needs Recognition - Case Series.
authorString: Ebenezer SJ, Mariappan R, Pannerselvam S, Basavaraju NV, Raju K.
abstractText: Vasoplegia is a form of vasodilatory shock characterized by low systemic vascular resistance and severe hypotension with normal or high cardiac output that is unresponsive to volume resuscitation and conventional vasopressors. Its occurrence after major complex spine surgery has rarely been reported. Hypotension during complex spine surgery is associated with increased perioperative morbidity. This case series describes the management of refractory distributive shock of unknown cause in patients who underwent complex spine surgery. Three American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA-1) patients underwent complex spine surgery involving spinal cord manipulation/retraction/stretching. All three patients encountered severe refractory hypotension toward the end of the surgery without any obvious causes of hypotension (hypovolemia, anaphylaxis, spinal shock, cardiogenic, embolic, or pneumothorax). All patients were treated with high doses of noradrenaline and vasopressin for 12-36 h after surgery. All patients had good neurological outcomes despite transient severe hypotension. Awareness of this entity helps anesthesiologists manage hypotension by early institution of nonconventional vasopressors (e.g., vasopressin) after ruling out other causes.

title: Subtype-Specific Treatment of Autoimmune Myocarditis: Current Evidence and Clinical Approach.
authorString: Goh ZY, Ahmad R, Chadalavada B, Alhafez Y, Thota AN, Raza M, Ahmad FN, Elbashir R, Kim MG, Abu Hejleh K, Rahimov D.
abstractText: Autoimmune myocarditis presents a distinct therapeutic challenge: similar clinical syndromes may arise from fundamentally different immune mechanisms and therefore require different treatments. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence for the management of giant cell myocarditis, eosinophilic myocarditis, cardiac sarcoidosis, systemic autoimmune disease-associated myocarditis, immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis, and virus-negative immune-mediated lymphocytic myocarditis. We examine how clinical severity, histopathology, infectious exclusion, extracardiac disease, and treatment toxicity shape therapeutic decisions. Although cardiovascular stabilization follows shared principles, immunosuppressive strategies vary substantially across subtypes, ranging from corticosteroids and multidrug immunosuppression to targeted biologic or molecular therapies. We also discuss treatment escalation, monitoring response, and management of fulminant presentations. Across all subtypes, the central challenge is balancing the urgency of suppressing myocardial inflammation against diagnostic uncertainty and treatment-related risk. A subtype-directed approach offers the most clinically meaningful framework for selecting therapy and improving consistency in the management of autoimmune myocarditis.

title: Baroreflex Sensitivity and Exercise Training: From Molecular Mechanisms to Cardiovascular Therapeutics.
authorString: Zhou XJ, Liu QY, Yang YS, Wang WZ, Tan X.
abstractText: Maintaining stable blood pressure is essential for normal physiological function, and the baroreceptor reflex plays a pivotal role in buffering acute blood pressure variability. Reduced baroreflex sensitivity (BRS) is closely linked to the development and progression of multiple pathological processes. Moreover, enhancing BRS has been identified as a promising therapeutic approach for cardiovascular diseases. Both observational and interventional research consistently demonstrate that long-term aerobic exercise training is associated with elevated BRS, regardless of the presence of pre-existing cardiovascular diseases. Additionally, anaerobic exercise and other exercise modalities offer varying degrees of benefits across different populations. Given the well-established therapeutic effects of exercise in various cardiovascular diseases, elucidating the underlying mechanisms is of significant importance. In this review, we integrate recent findings from human and animal studies, which propose that potential mechanisms may involve exercise-induced secretion of bioactive molecules and modulation of the autonomic nervous system. This review systematically summarizes the advances in the regulation of BRS by exercise, elucidates the underlying mechanisms whereby exercise maintains blood pressure homeostasis and protects cardiovascular function, and thus provides a critical theoretical foundation for employing exercise as an interventional strategy in the prevention and treatment of cardiovascular diseases.

title: Acquired Laryngotracheal Stenosis Following Intubation for Acute Cardiac Events.
authorString: Li AC, Dorotan JT, Zhao H, Soliman AMS.

journal.title: The Journal of laryngology and otology

abstractText: Acquired laryngotracheal stenosis (ALTS) is a complication after endotracheal intubation, associated with prolonged intubation and larger endotracheal tube size. However, the relationship with cardiovascular disease has not been explored. We retrospectively reviewed adult patients diagnosed with acquired laryngotracheal stenosis after acute cardiac event intubation at Temple University Health System hospitals from 2013 to 2023. Acquired laryngotracheal stenosis patients after non-cardiac intubation served as controls. Endotracheal tube size and length of intubation were compared between the two groups. Ten patients developed acquired laryngotracheal stenosis in the study group compared to 21 control patients (0.27 percent vs. 1.23 percent; p < 0.0001). Groups did not differ in demographics or length of intubation. Acute cardiac event patients were intubated with a smaller endotracheal tube (p = 0.023) and required fewer intubation attempts (p = 0.04). Acquired laryngotracheal stenosis incidence was lower after cardiac-related intubation, potentially due to a smaller endotracheal tube size and fewer intubation attempts, but additional factors may be responsible.
