An IE isolate of S.oralis and isogenic mutants lacking functional Fap1 were used alongside pharmacological and antibody-based inhibition of platelet receptors and signaling pathways. S.oralis ATCC 10557 induced robust platelet aggregation with a characteristic lag phase and strong dense granule release. Aggregation required integrin αIIbβ3 signaling and was abolished by inhibition of glycoprotein Ibα (GPIbα) or FcγRIIA. Loss of the serine-rich repeat protein Fap1, or mutation of its conserved sialic acid-binding motif, abrogated platelet aggregation. While most donors required a plasma component for aggregation, supplementation of washed platelets with human IgG fully restored aggregation in a dose-dependent manner. Importantly, IgG was unable to bypass the requirement for Fap1-GPIbα interaction, indicating that direct bacterial adhesion is an essential initiating step that enables antibody-dependent FcγRIIA signaling. Substantial inter-individual variability was observed in aggregation kinetics and IgG dependence. S.oralis induces platelet aggregation through a dual, non-redundant mechanism requiring Fap1-mediated engagement of GPIbα and IgG-dependent FcγRIIA signaling. This cooperative pathway drives potent platelet activation and exhibits marked host-dependent variability. These findings provide new mechanistic insight into early events in IE pathogenesis and highlight platelet-bacterium interactions as potential targets for risk stratification and therapeutic intervention.

title: A Finger Worn Ring for On-Demand Measurement of Absolute Blood Pressure.
authorString: Momin MA, Wang S, Jazini M, Freithaler M, Hashemkhani S, Hoover GE, Li Y, Lee I, Xiong F, Mukkamala R.
abstractText: Regular blood pressure (BP) monitoring is needed to manage hypertension. However, cuff devices are not readily accessible, and many adults are living with uncontrolled BP. Furthermore, popular wearable cuffless devices typically require calibration with periodic cuff BP measurements or demographic information. A finger worn ring for cuffless BP measurement without such calibration was investigated. BP ring concepts were conceived based on the oscillometric cuff principle. The user varies their finger pressures similar to a cuff device by performing ring tightening followed by hand lowering or ring tightening only under visual guidance, while the ring obtains oscillometric measurements from the digital arteries for on-demand BP measurement. A prototype device was built to implement the BP ring concepts. The ring included a mechanical actuator to adjust its diameter and a photoplethysmography sensor, force sensor, and inertial measurement unit to make the measurements. The ring is interfaced to a display via a wired data acquisition system to guide the user in performing the ring tightening/hand lowering. An oscillometric algorithm is applied to compute BP from the measurements. The device was tested in 25 volunteers. The ring tightening-hand lowering BP measurement could be learned by new users. The device yielded root-mean-square-errors of 7.1 and 6.9 mmHg for systolic and diastolic BP against a validated arm cuff device. This study demonstrates the feasibility of absolute BP monitoring using a finger worn ring. The BP ring concepts could potentially be incorporated in smart rings to help improve hypertension control.

title: Prevalence of systemic and ocular comorbidities in patients aged 18-50 years with retinal vein occlusion.
authorString: Zhang C, Allaf AM, Ersan S, Sosa-Lockward J, Williams BK, Berrocal AM.
abstractText: Retinal vein occlusion (RVO) is a well-established cause of vision loss in older adults. However, the prevalence and distribution of documented systemic comorbidities in younger adults are not well characterized. This retrospective cohort study utilized the TriNetX US Collaborative Network to identify younger adults (aged 18-50 years) with retinal vein occlusion (RVO), including both branch (BRVO) and central (CRVO) subtypes. The prevalence of predefined systemic comorbidities was evaluated during the period preceding and within 90 days following the diagnosis of RVO to characterize their frequency and distribution among young patients. A total of 5,257 younger adults with RVO were included. Before RVO diagnosis, 66.4% of patients had at least one documented risk factor, most commonly hypertension (25%), obesity (17.4%), and type 2 diabetes mellitus (13.3%). Primary thrombophilia (2.2%) and hematologic malignancy (1.6%) were less frequently documented. Within 90 days following RVO diagnosis, 12.3% of patients received at least one newly coded risk-factor diagnosis, most commonly hypertension (4.5%), obesity (2.3%), and hyperlipidemia (1.9%). Among patients without any previously documented risk factors, 3.7% had at least one risk factor newly documented during this period. Among young adults with RVO, common vascular comorbidities were documented more frequently than hypercoagulable or vasculitic conditions.

title: Radiological characterization across the spectrum of primary aldosteronism.
authorString: Herr FL, Krüger L, Schweizer JROL, Völter F, Mansour N, Williams TA, Ricke J, Seidensticker M, Bidlingmaier M, Schmid-Tannwald C, Cyran CC, Reisch N, Reincke M, Stüfchen I.
abstractText: To define adrenal imaging phenotypes across primary aldosteronism (PA), low-renin hypertension (LRH), normal-renin hypertension (NRH) and controls. This retrospective study included 196 patients evaluated for suspected PA between January 2024 and February 2025. Plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) was measured by LC-MS/MS. Diagnosis and subtype evaluation of PA was conducted according to Endocrine Society Guidelines (n=95). Individuals who did not meet predefined criteria for PA were further categorized as LRH (n=59) or NRH (n=42) based on the direct renin concentration and aldosterone-to-renin-ratio. Age- and sex-matched individuals without known hypertension served as controls (n=50). Imaging features on CT and MRI, independently and blindly segmented by two radiologists, were categorized in diffuse adrenal enlargement, micronodules (< 10 mm), adenoma/indeterminate lesions (≥ 10 mm), and nodular hyperplasia. Median age was highest in PA (50.0 years), followed by LRH (48.0), and NRH (44.0) (p = 0.049). Sex distribution showed female predominance in NRH (81.0%) and LRH (78.0%) compared to PA (49.5%) (p <0.001). Imaging pathologies were rare in controls (2.0%) and increasingly prevalent from NRH (14.3%) to LRH (35.6%) and PA (42.1%) (p < 0.001). The same difference held for lesions ≥10 mm (p < 0.001). Bilateral lesions and nodular hyperplasia occurred exclusively in PA and LRH. Multivariable logistic regression demonstrated that the association between diagnostic group and adrenal imaging pathologies was independent of age, sex, BMI, and imaging modality. These exploratory findings support LRH as a potential intermediate phenotype within the spectrum of aldosterone excess despite not fulfilling classical PA criteria.

title: The Crossroads Between the Kidney and Gastrointestinal Disorders: Core Curriculum 2026.
authorString: Stevens T, Salani M.

journal.title: American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation

abstractText: The kidney and gastrointestinal (GI) tract are closely linked through a bidirectional system involving complex interactions called the gut-kidney axis. Within this system, alterations in the gut microbiome can promote progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) while uremic toxins from advanced kidney dysfunction can adversely affect intestinal health. Incretin hormones, particularly glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), play an important role in this gut-kidney signaling and will be explored here. We also examine how this physiology helps explain the connection between GI illness and IgA nephropathy, along with the kidney manifestations seen in inflammatory bowel disease. Furthermore, we will review how CKD and end-stage kidney disease increase the risk of GI disease and complicate its management, and how CKD therapies affect GI symptoms. In this AJKD Core Curriculum, we use a case-based format to illustrate the intricate interplay between the kidneys and the GI tract.

title: Association of Retinal Microvascular Density with Hemodynamic and Clinical Severity Markers in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension.
authorString: Erdağ M, Çalişkan T, Yildirim H, Kivrak T, Canleblebici M, Dal A, Balbaba M.
abstractText: To evaluate whether quantitative retinal microvascular and structural parameters, measured by optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), are associated with disease severity and right ventriculo-arterial coupling in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). This cross-sectional study included 45 patients with confirmed PAH, stratified by New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class (I-III). Patients with coexisting ocular pathologies were strictly excluded. Vessel density (VD) in the superficial (SCP) and deep capillary plexuses (DCP), foveal avascular zone characteristics, and ganglion cell complex (GCC) thickness were analyzed. These parameters were correlated with functional capacity (6-minute walk test [6-mWT]), NT-proBNP levels, and the echocardiographic TAPSE/sPAP ratio. Retinal VD in both SCP and DCP progressively decreased with worsening NYHA functional class (p < 0.05). Retinal VD showed a significant negative correlation with NT-proBNP levels (r = -0.355, p = 0.017) and a positive correlation with 6-mWT distance (r = 0.499, p < 0.001). Crucially, retinal microvascular density demonstrated a robust positive correlation with the TAPSE/sPAP ratio (r = 0.420, p = 0.004), a surrogate for right ventriculo-arterial coupling. GCC thickness exhibited variations across NYHA classes but lacked a consistent linear progression. Retinal microvascular attenuation in PAH is strongly associated not only with functional and biochemical severity but also with central hemodynamic impairment represented by the TAPSE/sPAP ratio. These findings suggest that OCTA-derived vessel density may serve as a promising, non-invasive biomarker for monitoring systemic microvascular compromise and right heart function in PAH.

title: Does Pain Level Change When Receiving Multiple Intravitreal Injections?
authorString: Geber A, Ivić L, Mrazovac Zimak D, Tomić M, Vukojević N, Kuzman T, Mandić K, Juri Mandić J.
abstractText: The aim of this study was to evaluate differences in pain intensity among patients receiving their first and those receiving multiple (≥10) intravitreal injections (IVIs), and to identify demographic, systemic, and ocular factors associated with pain perception. This cross-sectional study included 86 eyes of 86 patients treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF agents or corticosteroids for retinal vascular and neovascular diseases. Pain was assessed within 5 min after injection using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), ranging from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain imaginable). Patients were grouped according to injection number: group 1 (first injection, n = 19) and group 2 (≥10 injections, n = 67; subdivided into 2a, 2b, 2c). The median VAS pain score among all included patients was 2 (range 0-10). Median VAS score increased with the number of injections, female sex, and urban residence, whereas it decreased with diabetes, arterial hypertension, and smoking habits. However, multiple regression analysis showed that only female sex (p = 0.038) and a greater number of intravitreal injections (p = 0.020) were significant independent predictors of higher VAS scores, whereas urban residence showed a marginal association (p = 0.058). Pain intensity after intravitreal injections was generally low but tended to increase with the number of injections. Female sex and a greater number of injections were independent predictors of higher VAS scores, while urban residence showed a marginal association. These findings suggest that patient-related characteristics and cumulative treatment burden may influence pain perception, highlighting the importance of individualized counseling and comfort-oriented strategies during chronic intravitreal therapy.

title: Placental small-RNA sequencing reveals a distinct microRNA signature and its functional relevance in a preeclampsia rat model.
authorString: Vaka R, Amaral LM, Chambers CL, Campbell N, Zheng B, Roman RJ, LaMarca B.
abstractText: Despite extensive investigations over the last few decades, molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of preeclampsia remain incompletely understood. Emerging evidence suggests that microRNAs (miRNAs) regulate key pathological processes in preeclampsia including endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and oxidative stress. However, a comprehensive profiling of miRNA expression has not been previously carried out. Thus, using reduced uterine perfusion pressure (RUPP) model of preeclampsia, we performed placental miRNA sequencing to identify functional relevance of abnormally expressed miRNAs. Blood pressure was measured via carotid catheterization on gestational day (GD)19. Placental small-RNA sequencing was performed using Illumina NextSeq2000 sequencer. Our analysis identified 142 differentially regulated miRNAs (40 up- and 102 down-regulated) in placenta from RUPP rats. The top upregulated miRNAs included miR-211-3p, miR-628, miR-6324, miR-363-5p, and miR-6329, while miR-3587, miR-29b-3p, miR-3556a, miR-29a-3p, and miR-21-3p were the most downregulated. Functional annotation revealed associations with immune response (miR-363, miR-21, miR-29), B-cell differentiation (miR-628), T-cell activation (miR-21), adipogenesis, and lipid metabolism (miR-211, miR-29, miR-21), and angiogenesis (miR-363, miR-21). Further, gene ontology analysis revealed significant enrichment in biological processes; regulation of transport, cell-cell signaling, and calcium-dependent exocytosis, cellular components; synaptic vesicles, perinuclear cytoplasm, and clathrin-coated vesicles, and molecular functions; glycoprotein binding, protein dimerization, and myosin binding. These findings suggest that robust miRNA dysregulation in RUPP rats may underlie disease pathogenesis.

title: Persistent Skeletal Deficits Following Weight Restoration in a Rodent Model of Anorexia Nervosa.
authorString: Jafari M, Brooks DJ, Swanson B, Bouxsein ML, Breithaupt L, Kaiser UB, Rutkove SB, Rosa-Caldwell ME.

journal.title: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism

abstractText: Purpose: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is associated with significant changes in bone density and microstructure. However, the extent and nature of skeletal recovery following weight restoration is unclear. The aim of this study was to investigate these changes in bone during simulated AN in rats across short- and long-term recovery. Methods: Female Sprague Dawley rats were exposed to 50-60% food restriction for 30 days to simulate AN, followed by recovery periods of 5, 15, and 30 days. Bone parameters were assessed longitudinally using peripheral quantitative computed tomography (pQCT) and micro-computed tomography (µCT). Bodyweight and muscle strength were correlated with bone parameters. Results: AN resulted in significant reductions in total and trabecular bone density, as well as impairments in cortical and trabecular microarchitecture. Even with weight restoration, these deficits persisted and the compensatory responses were not sufficient for bone recovery. Bodyweight showed an association with total and trabecular bone density. Measures of muscle strength also correlated with total and trabecular density and were additive in multiple regression analysis prediction of total and trabecular bone density when combined with bodyweight. Conclusion: Recovery from AN-induced bone disorders is incomplete even after weight restoration and likely requires targeted interventions beyond nutritional rehabilitation. Furthermore, muscle function is an important predictor of bone health when combined with bodyweight.

title: Endothelin 2-Mediated Neuroinflammation Drives Hypertensive Retinal Dysfunction.
authorString: Cui Y, Au MT, Zhang L, Zhang T, Pan L, Li HL, Zhang Y, Wu MM, Li H, Chung SR, Yang K, Feng P, Wen C, Do CW.
abstractText: Systemic hypertension is a risk factor for glaucoma, a leading cause of irreversible blindness, yet the mechanistic basis connecting the 2 conditions remains elusive. A longitudinal assessment of blood pressure, intraocular pressure, retinal function, structure, and perfusion was conducted in spontaneously hypertensive rats and Wistar-Kyoto rats. Transcriptomic analyses and immunofluorescence staining were performed to investigate hypertension-associated retinal biochemical changes. AAV-mediated knockdown of endothelin 2 was used to investigate its mechanistic role. Hypertensive rats develop accelerated retinal degeneration marked by retinal thinning, functional impairment, reduced perfusion, and progressive neuroinflammation. Critically, these changes occur despite persistently low intraocular pressure, indicating an intraocular pressure-independent mechanism underlying the pathology. Biochemical analyses identified robust activation of the retinal endothelin system, with endothelin 2 the most significantly upregulated component. AAV-mediated retinal endothelin 2 knockdown substantially restored retinal function, ameliorated neuroinflammation, and enhanced retinal blood flow in hypertensive rats. Pharmacological blockade of endothelin receptor type A, but not type B, replicated these protective effects without altering intraocular pressure. Our findings establish endothelin 2 as an important, intraocular pressure-independent contributing factor to hypertension-associated retinal neurodegeneration and identify the endothelin-endothelin receptor type A axis as a potential therapeutic target to prevent vision loss in patients with hypertension.

title: Beyond Mitochondrial Fission: Emerging Roles of Drp1 in Skeletal Muscle Physiology and Disease.
authorString: Zou K, Berger NJ, Zhou Z, Kugler BA.

journal.title: American journal of physiology. Cell physiology

abstractText: Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) is best recognized as the primary regulator of mitochondrial fission. However, emerging evidence indicates that Drp1 is a multifaceted regulator of skeletal muscle physiology whose functions extend well beyond its canonical role in mitochondrial fission. Recent studies have identified novel roles of Drp1 in regulating substrate utilization, calcium homeostasis, reactive oxygen species signaling, respiratory complex assembly, and mitochondrial-to-nuclear signaling, including mechanisms independent of its canonical fission activity. Importantly, Drp1 regulation in skeletal muscle is highly context-dependent, as both excessive and insufficient Drp1 activity can disrupt skeletal muscle homeostasis. For example, excessive Drp1 activation and mitochondrial fragmentation are associated with insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and neuromuscular diseases, whereas severe or prolonged Drp1 deficiency impairs mitochondrial quality control, bioenergetics, induce muscle atrophy, and compromise the exercise training adaptations. Therefore, the biological consequences of Drp1 modulation are highly context dependent and influenced by the metabolic and physiological state of skeletal muscle. In this review, we summarize the molecular regulation and emerging functions of Drp1 in skeletal muscle, with particular emphasis on fission-independent mechanisms and Drp1 dysregulation in metabolic and neuromuscular diseases. We further discuss pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies for modulating Drp1 signaling and highlight emerging approaches for skeletal muscle-specific targeting. Collectively, current evidence supports a paradigm in which skeletal muscle Drp1 functions as a multifaceted regulator of mitochondrial and skeletal muscle homeostasis, highlighting the therapeutic potential of modulating Drp1 activity to optimize mitochondrial and muscle health across different physiological and pathological contexts.

title: Coach-BP: Computer Vision-Based Assessment and Correction of Blood Pressure Measurement Technique
authorString: Biswas R, Abad AJ, Nugas J, Shim J, Pletcher MJ, Lamprea-Montealegre JA, Abbasi-Asl R.
abstractText:
Background:

Accurate blood pressure (BP) measurement, essential for hypertension care, requires proper technique. Posture errors can raise systolic BP by more than 20 mm Hg, yet technique is rarely verified objectively. We aimed to develop and evaluate Coach-BP, a computer vision system that detects technique errors from video to support real-time coaching.

Methods:

We enrolled adults attending an academic cardiovascular prevention center between February and April 2026 and filmed BP measurements with front and side cameras. We analyzed 408 encounters from 225 participants. Coach-BP uses machine learning models trained on clinician labels to assess five American Heart Association criteria using pose, visual context, and audio-visual features. We evaluated its accuracy against expert clinician ratings by leave-one-participant-out cross-validation. We then examined robustness to simulated camera artifacts and interpreted the features important for each criterion.

Findings:

At baseline, 138 (62%) of 223 participants had at least one technique error and 54 (24%) two or more. Coach-BP achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.93 (95% CI 0.90-0.94), with 0.97 (0.94-0.99) for legs uncrossed, 0.97 (0.93-1.00) for no talking, 0.92 (0.85-0.98) for back supported, 0.91 (0.86-0.95) for feet flat, and 0.86 (0.81-0.91) for arm supported at heart level. Mean balanced accuracy was 0.88 (0.85-0.90). Performance was robust to simulated camera shift, zoom, and rotation. Its models relied on features clinicians would assess, such as cuffed-hand height and foot position. One model classified back support similarly from either camera. Interpretation: Coach-BP accurately detected errors in the five guideline-recommended criteria of BP measurement technique from clinic video, enabling objective assessment of each criterion.

title: Exploring the Attitudes, Barriers, Concerns, Differences, and Ethics (ABCDEs) of Healthcare Decision Making of Vagus Nerve Stimulation
authorString: Sullivan CR, Caola LR, Johnson RA, Differding C, Randolph A, Mejia A, Balangoy D, Widge AS, Henry TR, Nahas Z, Cabrera LY, Wilson SR.
abstractText: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is an established neuromodulation therapy approved for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and epilepsy, with growing interest in its application to other conditions. Despite demonstrated clinical efficacy, VNS remains underused in psychiatric care. This mixed-methods study examined stakeholder perceptions of VNS, focusing on access, stigma, ethical concerns, and acceptability across epilepsy, depression, heart failure (HF), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). We conducted six focus groups and 20 semi-structured interviews with patients, clinicians, and one support person, and integrated qualitative themes with quantitative data on stigma and treatment barriers. Participants revealed stark disparities in VNS adoption: epilepsy patients reported fewer insurance barriers, while TRD participants faced delayed approvals, high out-of-pocket costs, and limited access to specialty care. Depression stakeholders reported higher stigma scores and expressed greater reluctance to consider surgical treatment, despite possessing comparable knowledge to epilepsy stakeholders. Ethical concerns, particularly regarding informed consent and impaired decision-making, surfaced frequently in the context of TRD. Most participants agreed that the appropriateness of VNS should align with disease severity and impact on quality of life. Many cautiously supported VNS for HF and RA, provided strong efficacy data supports its use. Hope emerged as a consistent theme, especially among TRD participants seeking alternatives after exhausting other treatments. These findings underscore the need to address insurance barriers, reduce stigma, and enhance provider education. As VNS expands into new indications, policymakers and clinicians must implement reforms that promote equitable access, decentralized care, and ethically sound consent practices to ensure inclusive neuromodulation therapy adoption.

title: Development and Validation of an Early Prediction Model for Neonatal Hypoglycemia in Full-Term Appropriate-for-Gestational-Age Newborns within 24 Hours of Birth
authorString: Liu T, Wu F, Guo S.
abstractText: Background: Standardized screening for neonatal hypoglycemia (NH) in full-term, appropriate-for-gestational-age (AGA) newborns is lacking. We aimed to develop a bedside prediction model for early NH (≤24 hours) in this population. Methods: This retrospective study included 1,543 full-term AGA newborns, randomly split them into training and testing sets at a ratio of 7:3. From 51 candidate variables, LASSO and multivariate logistic regression were used to select predictors and construct a nomogram. Model performance was evaluated via area under the curve (AUC), calibration, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Results: NH occurred in 15.4% (237/1,543) of the cohort. LASSO regression identified nine core predictive variables: maternal factors (gestational diabetes mellitus, gestational hypertension, mode of delivery, 1-hour glucose level on the oral glucose tolerance test, total bile acids, and hemoglobin) and neonatal factors (sex, gestational age, and feeding method). It demonstrated good discrimination, yielding an AUC of 0.943 (95% CI: 0.919–0.967) in the training set and 0.934 (95% CI: 0.896–0.971) in the testing set. Calibration curves and DCA confirmed robust predictive accuracy and high clinical net benefit. Conclusion: This bedside nomogram enables accurate, early risk stratification of NH in full-term AGA newborns, optimizing targeted screening in a frequently overlooked population.

title: Optimizing entropy-based heart rate variability metrics: fixed tolerance improves congestive heart failure classification.
authorString: Petaja A, Pukkila T, Kanniainen M, Räsänen E.
abstractText: Objective.Entropy-based heart rate variability (HRV) metrics are widely used to characterize heartbeat dynamics and distinguish physiological from pathological states, but their classification performance is highly sensitive to parameter selection. This study investigated a fixed-tolerance approach derived from a healthy reference population as an alternative to conventional subject-specific tolerance normalization and assessed how entropy-parameter selection influences classification performance.Approach.Approximate entropy (ApEn), sample entropy (SampEn), and multiscale entropy (MSE) were evaluated using both conventional and fixed-tolerance formulations in 24-h Holter recordings from 274 healthy subjects and 946 patients with congestive heart failure (CHF). Classification performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Parameter sensitivity was assessed through systematic sweeps of the embedding dimension, tolerance coefficient, and MSE scale range.Main results.Classification performance varied substantially across the parameter space, and the embedding-dimension and tolerance values commonly used in the literature were generally suboptimal. The fixed-tolerance implementation consistently outperformed the conventional subject-specific approach, achieving AUC values of 0.78 (+0.03) for ApEn, 0.77 (+0.09) for SampEn, and 0.74 (+0.14) for MSE. For MSE, tolerance selection had a substantially larger influence on classification performance than scale-dependent parameterization.Significance.The results suggest that a substantial portion of the classification potential of entropy-based HRV analysis remains unexploited under conventional tolerance normalization and parameter selection. More generally, entropy-based HRV metrics appear to be more sensitive to methodological choices than is commonly assumed. The fixed-tolerance approach provides a simple and computationally inexpensive strategy for improving entropy-based CHF classification, although validation in independent datasets is needed to establish its broader applicability.

title: Fam172a deletion exacerbates hepatic steatosis and alters SRSF3-associated PPARγ isoform regulation.
authorString: Li MH, Wang JW, Xu MR, Zhang YW, Chen MY, Ke JF, Zhang ZH, Wang YJ, Li MF, Li LX.
abstractText: Family with sequence similarity 172 member A (FAM172A) has recently been implicated in metabolic diseases such as obesity and atherosclerosis; however, its hepatocyte-specific functions and downstream mechanisms in hepatic steatosis remain incompletely defined. In this study, we observed significant upregulation of FAM172A in the livers of mice with diet-induced hepatic steatosis. Liver-specific deletion of Fam172a exacerbated high-fat diet (HFD)-induced hepatic steatosis and metabolic dysfunction, accompanied by increased expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) and genes involved in fatty acid uptake and lipogenesis. In vitro, Fam172a overexpression attenuated triglyceride accumulation and reduced PPARγ expression, while the PPARγ antagonist GW9662 attenuated lipid accumulation in Fam172a-deficient primary hepatocytes. Proteomic analysis and co-immunoprecipitation identified serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 3 (SRSF3) as an interacting protein of FAM172A. Fam172a deletion reduced hepatic SRSF3 expression and was associated with altered Pparg splicing in liver tissue. In primary hepatocytes, Fam172a deletion increased the PPARγ2/PPARγ1 ratio at both the mRNA and protein levels. SRSF3 restoration partially rescued lipid accumulation in Fam172a-deficient hepatocytes, while SRSF3 knockdown partially attenuated the protective effect of FAM172A overexpression. CLIP-seq provided evidence of an interaction between SRSF3 and Pparg RNA. Collectively, these findings support a protective role for hepatic FAM172A and implicate SRSF3-associated regulation of PPARγ isoform expression in its effects on lipid accumulation, highlighting FAM172A as a potential therapeutic target.

title: Impact of Documentation Aids on the Inclusion of Salient Left-Ventricular Late Gadolinium Enhancement Characteristics in Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging Impressions.
authorString: Singh K, Fang M, Nakashima M, Nguyen C, Tang WHW, Kwon D, Chen PH, Chen D.

journal.title: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine

abstractText: Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is a key diagnostic and prognostic biomarker in ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) and nonischemic cardiomyopathy (NICM). However, the completeness of LGE reporting in routine CMR impressions remains incompletely characterized. We aimed to evaluate the impact of large language model (LLM)-assisted reporting on the consistency of LGE pattern, distribution, and severity documentation in CMR impressions for ICM and NICM. We analyzed 828 unstructured (1990-2023) and 400 structured (2024-2025) CMR reports to identify documentation of LGE pattern, distribution, and severity. A Llama 3 language model fine-tuned on 27,000 structured CMR reports was used to generate 9650 CMR impressions; LGE attributes were extracted using an LLM judge. LLM reporting behavior was further assessed using quantized low-rank adaptation adapters trained on structured and unstructured impressions. Structured reporting captured LGE pattern more frequently than unstructured reporting overall (85.5% vs. 61.0%, p = 9.60 × 10<sup>-7</sup>) and for ICM (90.0% vs. 69.4%, p = 0.005). LLM-generated impressions demonstrated more frequent reporting of LGE distribution (75.3%) and severity (70.9%) versus structured and unstructured reports (p < 0.001). Fine-tuning with an adapter trained on unstructured impressions significantly improved reporting of all three LGE attributes. Structured reporting improved LGE pattern documentation, but gaps in LGE distribution and severity documentation persisted across human report formats. LLM-generated impressions achieved broader attribute coverage for LGE distribution and severity. Fine-tuning on unstructured data improved model performance, suggesting that passive augmentation with data capturing the documentation styles of multiple providers may help to address reporting gaps.

title: Machine learning improves 10-year prediction of atherosclerotic plaque progression and cardiovascular events in systemic lupus erythematosus.
authorString: Papazoglou N, Sfikakis PP, Tektonidou MG.
abstractText:
Objectives

To evaluate the performance of generic and disease-adapted tools in predicting 10-year cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and atherosclerotic plaque progression risk in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and develop a machine learning-based model to improve cardiovascular risk stratification.

Methods

In a prospective 10-year follow-up carotid and femoral ultrasound study of patients with SLE without prior CVD events, we assessed the performance of 11 CVD risk scores (7 conventional, 4 SLE-adapted) to predict atherosclerotic plaque progression and incident CVD events. We used discrimination (sensitivity, specificity, area under the curve [AUC], Youden index), calibration (Brier Score [BS]) and classification (Matthews correlation coefficient, F1 score) metrics, and logistic regression and time-to-event analyses. A machine learning-based gradient boosting model was developed and internally validated.

Results

Among 111 patients (91% female, median age: 43.0 years) with 10-year ultrasonography follow-up, 53 (47.7%) developed new plaques, and 8 (7.2%) had incident CVD events. All scores demonstrated suboptimal performance; sensitivity: 0.00-0.44, AUC 0.58-0.79, and BS: 0.44-0.71. In multivariable analysis, QRISK3 was the only tool independently associated with CVD events and/or plaque progression (HR:1.87, p = 0.027). A machine learning-based score that integrates QRISK3 with disease-related risk factors (disease duration, cumulative glucocorticoid dose, DORIS achievement, antiphospholipid antibodies, hydroxychloroquine) and additional traditional CVD risk factors (physical activity, waist circumference), demonstrated significantly better performance compared to all evaluated scores.

Conclusion

Conventional and SLE-adapted tools underestimate CVD events and atherosclerosis progression risk in SLE. A machine learning-based model incorporating disease-specific and traditional cardiovascular risk factors into QRISK3 improves CVD risk stratification.

title: Fibroproliferative Remodeling of Immune-Vascular Co-Culture Spheroid Models in Response to Atherogenic Stimulation.
authorString: Naiyeju I, Lehoux S, Tabrizian M.
abstractText: Cell-based models are highly valuable platforms for preclinical studies of atherosclerosis, offering controllable environments to investigate disease mechanisms. Three-dimensional (3D) spheroids, a class of cell-based models, enable the study of atherosclerotic disease phenomena under physiologically relevant yet controlled conditions. In this study, we examined the lipid-induced changes in a co-culture spheroid model comprising THP-1-derived macrophages and primary human coronary artery smooth muscle cells (HCASMCs) following treatment with 20 or 40 µg/mL oxidized LDL (ox-LDL), a known atherogenic agent. Over a 10-day period, we assessed changes in spheroid morphology (size and compactness), cell viability, metabolic activity, intracellular composition, gene expression, pro-inflammatory cytokine release and extracellular matrix deposition, relative to the untreated control. Lipid exposure increased the abundance of macrophages in ox-LDL-treated spheroids (LS20-3 h: 35.5 ± 21.9%; LS40-3 h: 38.3 ± 8.7%) compared with controls (21.8 ± 0.7%) as early as day 3. Upregulation of fibronectin (LS20-3 h: ~1.8-fold; LS40-3 h: ~2.1-fold), CD36 (~1.8-fold), and ABCA-1 (~1.9-fold) was also observed. Moreover, spheroids exposed to 40 µg/mL ox-LDL exhibited reduced viability and compactness compared with those treated with 20 µg/mL by day 10. While lipid-treated spheroids showed non-statistically significantly higher levels of pro-inflammatory IL-1β cytokine expression at day 0 which declined (> 85% decrease) by day 3, all spheroid groups showed comparable global fibronectin ECM secretion indices. Collectively, these findings reveal lipid-induced proliferative changes to spheroid composition & functionality and show their potential as biomimetic models for the study of atherosclerotic disease phenomena.

title: BAHCC1 Drives Smooth Muscle Plasticity and Neointima via Epigenetic Repression.
authorString: Tang R, Huang Y, Shirasu T, Li J, Webb A, Zheng K, Shen C, Guo Y, Auguste G, Hart P, Murach M, Zhou X, Ma J, Kent KC, Wang GG, Yang J, Miller CL, Martin KA, Guo LW.
abstractText:
Background

Vascular smooth muscle cell (SMC) phenotypic plasticity drives neointimal hyperplasia (IH) and contributes to atherosclerosis. Epigenetic mechanisms have been implicated in SMC plasticity, but the roles of epigenetic reader proteins are poorly understood. BAHCC1 (bromo adjacent homology domain coiled-coil 1) is a newly identified reader of the gene-repression histone mark histone-3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3). Its role in vascular remodeling is unknown.

Methods

We investigated BAHCC1 in human restenotic and atherosclerotic arteries and in rat and mouse arterial injury models using BAHCC1 silencing, SMC-specific deletion, and an H3K27me3-binding-deficient knock-in mutation. Mechanistic studies in human aortic SMCs integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling, protein-interaction assays, and single-guide RNA-dCas9-based epigenetic editing.

Results

BAHCC1 was upregulated in human restenotic and atherosclerotic arteries and rat arteries with IH. While BAHCC1 silenc ing reduced IH in balloon-injured rat arteries, SMC-specific BAHCC1 deletion and the H3K27me3-binding-deficient mutation (BAHCC1Y2537A) attenuated IH in wire-injured mouse arteries. In human SMCs, mitogen induced BAHCC1 expression through nuclear factor Y subunit-α, promoting BAHCC1-dependent dedifferentiation. Integrated transcriptomics and epigenomics identified LMO7 (LIM domain only 7), an IH suppressor, as a key BAHCC1-repressed target. BAHCC1 occupancy at LMO7 required BAHCC1-H3K27me3 interaction, and LMO7-targeted H3K27me3 enrichment through epigenetic editing repressed its expression in a BAHCC1-dependent manner. Furthermore, BAHCC1 associated with SAP30 and RBBP4/7 to form a corepressor complex. Functionally, LMO7 silencing reversed the effects of BAHCC1 knockdown on human SMC phenotype and exacerbated IH in BAHCC1Y2537A mice. Human genetic analyses further identified BAHCC1 variants associated with cardiovascular phenotypes and BAHCC1 expression.

Conclusions

BAHCC1 is a previously unrecognized epigenetic driver of vascular remodeling. By reading H3K27me3 and recruiting corepressors to repress gene expression, BAHCC1 promotes pathological SMC phenotypic transition and IH, highlighting the BAHCC1 pathway as a potential therapeutic target for IH-associated vascular disease.

title: VSMC DDR1 Mechanosensation Aggravates Atherosclerosis via Paracrine Signaling.
authorString: Zhou S, Chu X, Zhang J, Zhang J, Xu Y, Fan L, Liang Z, Shen Y, Yao W, Chen Z, Fu Y, Zhang T, Zhou J.
abstractText:
Background

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) increases cardiovascular risk and is linked to arterial stiffening and atherosclerosis. How stiffness promotes atherogenesis remains unclear. DDR1 (discoidin domain receptor 1), a mechanosensory tyrosine kinase receptor, has been implicated in force-regulated arterial remodeling. We investigated whether DDR1-mediated mechanosensation links arterial stiffness to vascular smooth muscle cell (SMC)-endothelial paracrine communication in CKD-related atherosclerosis.

Methods

Single-cell RNA sequencing, secretome proteomics, and bulk RNA sequencing were integrated with stiffness-controlled models, endothelial assays, and a CKD-hyperlipidemia mouse model. SMC-specific Ddr1 deletion and a DDR1 dephosphorylation-targeting chimera (DEPTAC) were evaluated in vivo. Plasma TSP-1 (thrombospondin-1) levels were quantified in a CKD clinical cohort and analyzed in relation to renal function and atherosclerosis severity.

Results

CKD-associated vascular stiffening coincided with SMC phenotypic switching and enhanced THBS signaling. Multiomics integration identified THBS1 as a stiffness-induced SMC secretory effector. Stiff matrices increased SMC THBS1 secretion, promoting endothelial proliferation, migration, and leukocyte adhesion; these effects were attenuated by THBS1 knockdown. DDR1 coupled matrix stiffness cues to THBS1 expression by regulating its transcription via a tyrosine 3-monooxygenase/tryptophan 5-monooxygenase activation protein epsilon-FOXO3 (forkhead box O3) axis. Vascular SMC-specific Ddr1 deletion reduced aortic THBS1 levels, vascular stiffening, and atherosclerotic burden. DEPTAC suppressed aberrant DDR1 phosphorylation, reduced THBS1, and ameliorated vascular stiffening and atherosclerosis. Plasma THBS1 increased with CKD severity and correlated with atherosclerosis.

Conclusions

DDR1-dependent mechanosensing in SMCs drives stiffness-induced paracrine signaling to endothelium via THBS1, promoting CKD-accelerated atherosclerosis. Targeting mechanical DDR1 activation may be therapeutic.

title: The Investing Fascia–Carotid Sheath Mechanistic Hypothesis of Internal Jugular Vein Outflow Obstruction
authorString: Huang X.
abstractText: The clinical association between internal jugular vein (IJV) outflow obstruction and symptoms such as headache, pulsatile tinnitus, and cognitive decline has been repeatedly observed; however, “venous compression” alone is insufficient to explain the marked clinical heterogeneity of the condition. Among 283 patients with nonthrombotic IJV stenosis, the prevalence of headache was 65.02%; however, within the framework of this hypothesis, risk depends more on whether collateral compensatory capacity (and concurrent valvular antireflux function) is adequate than on the anatomical severity of stenosis—severe vertebral vein dilation, as a marker of adequate collateral compensation, was independently inversely associated with headache risk (OR = 0.184, 95% CI 0.092–0.366). Clinical consequences depend more on whether collateral compensation and valvular function remain sufficient to maintain outflow after compression. This hypothesis attributes this difference to whether compensation is adequate when IJV outflow is obstructed and proposes its upstream factor: sclerotic fibrosis of the investing fascia. Core proposition: Fibrosis of the investing fascia, through loss of elastic buffering and transmission of abnormal mechanical stress via the deep cervical fascial network to the carotid sheath, reduces collateral compensatory capacity when IJV outflow is obstructed and may coexist with insufficient valvular antireflux function; this state of inadequate compensation—centered on collateral compensation with valvular function as a parallel dimension—rather than luminal stenosis itself, is the key mediator linking extrasheath fascial pathology to fluctuating elevation of intracranial venous pressure. This framework provides a unified upstream mechanical perspective for understanding diseases and clinical phenotypes that share a common component of venous outflow obstruction, including headache associated with IJV stenosis, pulsatile tinnitus and cerebral tinnitus, exertional headache, Ménière disease, transient monocular blindness, insomnia, autonomic dysfunction, anxiety/depression/brain fog, vertigo, facial pain, and Eagle jugular syndrome. The hypothesis predicts that investing fascial stiffness is independently associated with compensatory indicators during IJV outflow obstruction; collateral compensatory capacity modifies the association between investing fascial fibrosis and symptoms; and relief of extrasheath mechanical constraint produces paired improvements in venous flow parameters and symptoms.

title: Pulse wave velocity measurement assessing the superficial carotid-femoral distance via smartphone-based light detection and ranging.
authorString: Posokhov IN.
abstractText:
Purpose

Carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV) is the gold standard for non-invasive assessment of aortic stiffness. Tape measurement of the carotid-femoral distance typically requires an assistant to hold the tape while the operator maintains the Doller transducer position. This study assessed the concordance and intra-observer reliability of distance measurements obtained via smartphone-based light detection and ranging (LiDAR) technology compared with traditional tape measurement.

Methods

A cohort of 46 adult participants (mean age, 50.0±12.7 years) underwent Doppler ultrasound evaluation to determine carotid and femoral pulse transit times. The operator measured the superficial carotid-femoral distance using tape and smartphone LiDAR in alternating sequences. Duplicate measurements were taken following a washout period to evaluate intra-observer reliability.

Results

LiDAR distance measurements strongly agreed with tape measurements (ICC (2,1) = 0.92, 95% CI 0.81-0.97; mean bias <0.01 m). The resulting cfPWV calculations demonstrated good agreement (ICC (2,1) = 0.94, 95% CI 0.86-0.98; mean bias, 0.03 m/s). Both modalities exhibited high intra-observer reliability (tape ICC (3,1) = 0.98; LiDAR ICC (3,1) = 0.99). The diagnostic classification for elevated cfPWV (> 10 m/s) showed near-perfect concordance between the methods (kappa > 0.98).

Conclusions

Smartphone-based LiDAR telemetry provides distance measurements and cfPWV estimates that are highly concordant with traditional tape measurements, offering a reliable single-operator alternative for superficial distance acquisition. While these findings confirm technical equivalence and intra-observer reliability, further studies incorporating reference standards and quantitative time-motion analyses are required to confirm the clinical workflow advantages of this method.

title: CERVICAL CANCER IN OLDER WOMEN - A NARRATIVE REVIEW OF AGE-SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT ISSUES FROM THE FRENCH CERVICAL CANCER GUIDELINES GROUP.
authorString: Dugast M, Moureau A, Tromelin E, Sousa C, Mercier M, Carcopino X, Lavoué V, Carcopino X, Ouldamer L, Huchon C, Asseeva P, Azaïs H, Bendifallah S, Brun JL, Canlorbe G, Chargari C, Chauvet P, Cordoba A, Courcier H, Dabi Y, de Berti M, Diguisto C, Fuss E, Gaillard T, Gauthier T, Gertych W, Gladieff L, Graesslin O, Kerbage Y, Koskas M, Laas E, Lacorre A, Lavoué V, Lecointre L, Lecuru F, Margueritte F, Martinez A, Maternowski PJ, Mathevet P, Menouer I, Mimoun C, Moureau A, Netter A, Philip CA, Rousset P, Sanson C, Thomassin-Naggara I, Touboul C, Levêque J, members from the FRENCH CERVICAL CANCER GUIDELINES GROUP.

journal.title: Journal of gynecology obstetrics and human reproduction

abstractText:
Objective

To summarize the available evidence on the management of cervical cancer in older women across early and advanced disease stages, with particular attention to treatment selection, feasibility, tolerance, and specific clinical situations, including cervical cancer associated with pelvic organ prolapse.

Methods

A narrative review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library. Studies addressing surgery, radiotherapy, concurrent chemoradiotherapy, brachytherapy, para-aortic lymphadenectomy, cervical cancer associated with pelvic organ prolapse, and pre-treatment geriatric assessment were considered. The evidence was synthesized qualitatively according to six predefined clinical questions.

Results

In early-stage disease, radical hysterectomy is feasible in selected fit elderly patients but is associated with increased perioperative morbidity, with advancing age. The available evidence does not establish whether surgery or definitive radiotherapy provides superior oncological outcomes in this population. In locally advanced cervical cancer, concurrent chemoradiotherapy appears to improve survival compared with radiotherapy alone in selected older patients, but with increased toxicity. Brachytherapy is associated with improved local control and survival, yet its use decreased with advancing age. No age-specific evidence demonstrated a survival benefit form pretreatment para-aortic lymphadenectomy. Data on cervical cancer associated with pelvic organ prolapse are limited to heterogeneous case reports and small retrospective studies. Pretreatment geriatric assessment influences treatment decisions in mixed cancer populations, but cervical cancer-specific outcome data are lacking.

Conclusion

Age-specific evidence remains limited and largely retrospective, and chronological age alone should not determine access to standard treatment. Treatment selection requires integration of tumor characteristics, frailty, comorbidities, functional status, expected treatment tolerance, quality of life, and patient preferences.

title: Dietary (-)-epicatechin protects against impaired vascular homeostasis in fructose-fed rats: the role of thoracic aortic perivascular adipose tissue.
authorString: Hid EJ, Barrientos G, Lista F, Arreche N, Balaszczuk AM, Fraga CG, Galleano M.
abstractText: (-)-Epicatechin consumption has been associated with cardiometabolic benefits, including antihypertensive and anti-inflammatory effects. This study investigated whether dietary (-)-epicatechin prevents perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) dysfunction induced by a high-fructose diet. Male Sprague-Dawley rats (one-month old) consumed for 8 weeks a control diet, with or without (-)-epicatechin supplementation (20 mg per kg body weight per d), and with or without fructose (10% w/v) added to the drinking water. Dietary (-)-epicatechin protected rats from systemic alterations induced by high-fructose consumption, i.e. increases in systolic blood pressure, glycemia, insulinemia, and HOMA-IR index. In terms of changes in PVAT, thoracic aorta PVAT expansion and whitening resulting from a high-fructose diet were attenuated by the intake of (-)-epicatechin. Regarding inflammation, (-)-epicatechin intake reduced the fructose-mediated activation of the NF-κB pathway and the associated increases in IL-6, TNF-α, and NO-synthase. In parallel, (-)-epicatechin decreased NADPH-dependent superoxide anion production, which was accompanied by lower protein levels of the NOX2 subunits gp91phox and p47phox. Consistent with these effects, (-)-epicatechin prevented the fructose-induced increase in protein 3-nitrotyrosine levels, indicating a reduction in peroxynitrite production in agreement with the inhibition of NOX-dependent superoxide anion generation. Overall, these findings indicate that (-)-epicatechin mitigates high-fructose-induced thoracic aorta PVAT dysfunction primarily by preserving adipocyte phenotype and limiting inflammation and oxidative stress.

title: Mental Health of Children with Fontan Circulation: Associations with Maternal Psychopathology and Parenting Behavior.
authorString: Hemetsberger JM, Nicklin N, Göttlicher KL, Gerlach J, Heinzel L, Schöffl I, Kratz O, Eichler A.
abstractText: Children with Fontan circulation face substantial long-term psychosocial challenges. Parental mental health and parenting behavior are known to influence psychosocial outcomes in children with congenital heart disease (CHD), yet data specific for Fontan families are scarce. This cross-sectional controlled study examined child psychopathology in relation to maternal psychopathology and parenting behavior. 31 mothers and their children with Fontan circulation (aged 4-16 years) were compared with a sex-, age- and socioeconomic status (SES)- matched control group. Standardized maternal self-report questionnaires assessed child psychopathology, maternal psychopathology, and parenting behavior. Children with Fontan circulation showed significantly higher psychopathology than controls (F (1,58) = 6.38, p = .014, η<sub>p</sub>² = 0.10). No group differences were found in maternal psychopathology or parenting behavior (all p > .24). No Group × Moderator interaction effects emerged (all p > .35). Significant main effects were observed for maternal total psychopathology, anxiety, and depression (F(1,58) = 13.10, p < .001, η<sub>p</sub>² = 0.19; F(1,58) = 9.94, p = .003, η<sub>p</sub>² = 0.15; F(1,58) = 11.00, p = .002, η<sub>p</sub>²= 0.16), and inconsistent parenting behavior (F(1,58) = 19.20, p < .001, η<sub>p</sub>² = 0.26), associated with higher child psychopathology across groups, underscoring the need for family-focused support in the Fontan population.

title: Opportunistic MRI assessment of skeletal muscle mass in children and adults with Fontan circulation.
authorString: Kong TY, Razavi J, Dillman JR, Hegde S, Somasundaram E, Morin CE, Bonn J.
abstractText:
Background

Children and adults with Fontan circulation are vulnerable to reduced skeletal muscle mass because of altered Fontan physiology, exercise limitation, nutritional challenges, and chronic liver disease. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) performed for Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD) surveillance provides an opportunity to assess muscle mass without additional imaging.

Objective

To determine the frequency of imaging-defined low skeletal muscle mass on clinically acquired abdominal MRI examinations in children and adults with Fontan circulation and, secondarily, to explore associations with available clinical and imaging markers related to FALD.

Materials and methods

This single-center, retrospective, cross-sectional study included individuals with Fontan circulation who underwent abdominal MRI for FALD surveillance. Pediatric total psoas area and adult total skeletal muscle index were measured using age-appropriate published approaches and analyzed separately. Continuous variables were summarized with medians and interquartile ranges and explored using Spearman correlations and Mann-Whitney U tests. Sparse cardiac and outcome data were treated descriptively.

Results

The study included 124 individuals (78 male; 63%), including 57 children (age range 3.2-17.4 years, median=14.1) and 67 adults (age range 18.1-43.7 years, median=22.3). Imaging-defined low muscle mass was present in 17/57 children (30%) and 14/67 adults (21%) using pediatric- and adult-specific measurement approaches. Exploratory analyses did not identify a consistent pattern linking low muscle mass with the available FALD-related measures including liver stiffness measurement, liver biochemistries or liver scoring systems. Several comparisons including ejection fractions and aortopulmonary collateral flow were limited by missing data, small subgroups, and few outcome events.

Conclusion

Clinically acquired liver MRI examinations can be repurposed to identify imaging-defined low muscle mass in individuals with Fontan circulation. The frequency observed in both age groups supports prospective evaluation of standardized MRI measurements combined with muscle function, exercise capacity, and longitudinal outcomes.
