title: Cardiac Arrest After Deceased Donor Kidney Transplant.
authorString: Endo BI, Engels MC, Bunch TJ.
abstractText: A 54-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease and a dual-chamber pacemaker for high-grade atrioventricular block underwent deceased donor kidney transplantation. Her postoperative course was complicated by marked QT prolongation and recurrent torsades de pointes (TdP), resulting in cardiac arrest. Postarrest electrocardiogram demonstrated macroscopic T-wave alternans-a rare manifestation of severe QT prolongation. Treatment with intravenous magnesium and reprogramming her pacemaker to a lower rate limit of 100 beats/min resulted in electrical stability and improvement of the QT interval. This case underscores recognition of macroscopic T-wave alternans as a harbinger of impending TdP, vigilant QT monitoring, and evidence-based TdP management.

title: Beyond reproduction: the emerging role of FSH in postmenopausal aging.
authorString: Vallejo MS, Paradas A, Neira H.

journal.title: Gynecological endocrinology : the official journal of the International Society of Gynecological Endocrinology

abstractText: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) is traditionally regarded as a biochemical marker of menopause and declining ovarian function. However, emerging evidence suggests that its role may extend beyond reproductive physiology. During the menopause transition, FSH concentrations rise progressively, initially due to declining inhibin B and later to loss of ovarian estradiol and inhibin production. Evidence of FSH effects in bone, adipose tissue, the cardiovascular system and brain has raised the possibility of broader physiological actions. Higher FSH levels have been associated with bone loss and hip fracture risk, adverse cardiometabolic and vascular changes, and cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease. Although these associations do not establish causality, they suggest that FSH may contribute to some consequences of reproductive aging rather than simply reflect ovarian failure. Experimental studies indicate that reducing FSH may benefit bone and adiposity, while preliminary clinical evidence regarding cognition remains inconclusive. Thus, FSH may represent not only a marker of menopause, but also a potential marker of risk and, ultimately, a therapeutic target.

title: Routine Chest CTA Reliably Quantifies Left Ventricular Myocardial Mass
authorString: Twohig KC, Jiang D, Pugar JA, Slivnick J, Landeras L, Pocivavsek L.
abstractText:
ABSTRACT

Background

Routine chest computed tomography angiography (CTA) is the primary imaging modality for thoracic aortic disease, yet cardiac information within these examinations remains underutilized. We evaluated whether left ventricular myocardial mass (LVMM) can be reliably quantified from routine non–electrocardiographically (ECG)-gated chest CTA and its application in thoracic aortic pathology.

Methods

CTA scans were obtained from 257 patients without aortic disease and 181 patients with thoracic aortic aneurysm or dissection. LVMM was quantified using automated three-dimensional segmentation. In a separate 10-patient validation cohort, LVMM was compared across end-systolic, end-diastolic, and non-ECG-gated source reconstructions. CTA-derived LVMM was compared with published echocardiographic and cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) reference values using Cohen’s d.

Results

LVMM remained stable across cardiac phases and non-ECG-gated images (mean coefficient of variation, 2.4%), whereas left ventricular volume varied substantially (36.9%). CTA-derived LVMM demonstrated small effect sizes with the Penn method ( d = 0.22) and moderate effect sizes with ASE linear ( d = 0.67), area-length ( d = 0.68), and CMR ( d = 0.63). LVMM increased through young adulthood, with minimal association with age beyond 30 years. LVMM was comparable between patients with thoracic aneurysms and normal adults (140 ± 43 g vs. 141 ± 40 g; adjusted p = 1.0) but significantly greater in acute (199 ± 61 g) and chronic (191 ± 57 g) aortic dissection (both adjusted p < 0.001).

Conclusions

Routine non-ECG-gated chest CTA enables reliable automated LVMM quantification without additional imaging or radiation and may facilitate large-scale investigations of ventricular remodeling in thoracic aortic disease.

title: Distinct Biomarker Signatures of CMR-Defined Myocardial Remodeling in Moderate Aortic Stenosis
authorString: Wrobel J, Janssen JP, Beckmann A, Shamekhi J, Bahaaeldin M, Luetkens J, Hawwari I, Nienaber S, Franklin B, Kelm M, Nickenig G, Maintz D, Baldus S, al Kassou B, Zeus T, Pennig L, Mauri V.
abstractText:
Background

Moderate aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with adverse outcomes, yet the myocardial response to pressure overload varies substantially between patients and is incompletely reflected by valve hemodynamics. We aimed to determine whether circulating biomarkers of myocardial stress, injury, and fibrosis associate with cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)-defined myocardial remodeling in moderate AS.

Methods

Eighty-nine patients with moderate AS prospectively underwent CMR (cine imaging, T1 mapping, extracellular volume fraction [ECV], late gadolinium enhancement [LGE]) with concurrent measurement of NT-proBNP, high-sensitivity troponin T, sST2, TIMP-1, and Galectin-3. Biomarker associations with the phenotype-defining CMR parameters were tested with adjustment for age, sex, and renal function and correction for multiple testing, and patients were additionally classified into 4 hierarchical remodeling phenotypes.

Results

Six of 20 biomarker-CMR associations remained significant after correction for multiple testing. NT-proBNP tracked LV mass index (beta=0.50), ECV (beta=0.35), and LGE burden (beta=0.43, all q<0.05). TIMP-1 and Galectin-3 were selectively associated with native T1 (both beta=0.35, q=0.012), and sST2 was inversely associated with LV mass index (beta=-0.27, q=0.046). TIMP-1 (adjusted OR 2.18 per SD, 95% CI 1.37-3.48, q=0.005) and NT-proBNP (OR 2.10, 1.19-3.69, q=0.026) increased with higher hierarchical remodeling phenotype. No biomarker was associated with echocardiographic mean gradient, peak velocity, or indexed valve area after correction.

Conclusions

Circulating biomarkers showed distinct associations with CMR measures of myocardial remodeling in moderate AS. Matrix-related biomarkers were associated with native T1, whereas NT-proBNP was associated across several remodeling domains. These signals were not measurably related to valve hemodynamics.

Registration

URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05851209 . Unique identifier: NCT05851209 .

Clinical Perspective What Is New?

In patients with moderate aortic stenosis, myocardial remodeling on cardiac magnetic resonance was heterogeneous, and circulating biomarkers showed distinct associations with individual remodeling domains. The matrix-related biomarkers TIMP-1 and Galectin-3 were associated with native T1, whereas NT-proBNP was associated with several remodeling domains.

What Are the Clinical Implications?

No biomarker was associated with echocardiographic stenosis severity, suggesting that circulating biomarkers may add information on the myocardium that valve hemodynamics do not capture. If validated in larger cohorts, matrix-related biomarkers such as TIMP-1 could help select patients with moderate aortic stenosis for advanced myocardial tissue characterization.

title: Dynamical regimes of excitable cells under pulsed electric fields: From excitation to electroporation
authorString: FARIDI MRA, Manchanda R, Thaokar RM.
abstractText: Nanosecond pulse electric fields (nsPEFs) are an established treatment modality for cancer and have emerged as a potential approach for deep brain stimulation and cardiac defibrillation. The concerns in these two applications are at odds. While pulsed-field electroporation applications aim to minimise excitation of surrounding neurons, therapies based on neuronal stimulation demand minimal electroporation of neurons. Although nsPEFs offer various advantages, such as minimising power input and suppressing electrode reactions, they require strong electric fields to reach both the excitation and electroporation thresholds, so maintaining a safety gap between the two is crucial. Because these coupled processes unfold on time scales ranging from nanoseconds to milliseconds and cannot be resolved simultaneously in experiments, a computational approach is used. This study examines the interplay between excitation and electroporation within the Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) framework for a planar two-bilayer model coupled with the Asymptotic Smoluchowski Equation for electroporation, and solves for transmembrane potentials (TMPs), pore statistics and pore size evolution. The model can predict the role of electroporation in modulating neuronal responses and qualitatively explain key experimental observations in the literature. These include excitation with a single action potential (SAP), repetitive spiking (RS), and depolarisation block (DB), and are explained here with detailed mechanisms, including the subtle effects of strong electric fields and electroporating currents on ion-channel dynamics. Importantly, our work establishes a parameter space for strength-duration curves in regimes of safe excitation without electroporation, and vice versa. For a neuron with an equivalent RC time constant of 10 ns, pulses shorter than about 20 ns electroporate the membrane before they excite it, and the safety factor falls below 5% for 1-ns pulses. The work also expands into μs and ms pulses, and delves into possible regimes that could lead to neuronal inviability due to irreversible electroporation or excessive fractional pore area.

title: Cav1.3-C-terminus Restores Electrical and Contractile Functions in hiPSC-derived Cardiomyocytes Model of Heart Failure
authorString: Sleiman Y, Reisqs J, Boutjdir M.
abstractText:
Objective:

Heart failure (HF) is a major global health concern characterized by impaired excitation-contraction coupling and extensive structural remodeling of the myocardium, often modeled using a potent vasoactive and neurohumoral mediator, endothelin-1 (ET-1). This study investigates whether AAV6-mediated delivery of the Cav1.3-C-terminus, acting as an auto-trans-regulator of gene transcription, can restore electrophysiological and contractile functions in an ET-1-induced HF model using hiPSC-CMs.

Methods:

hiPSC-CM monolayers were treated with 10 nM ET-1 for 48 hours to induce HF-like phenotype and then co-treated with an AAV6-Cav1.3-C-terminus. We subsequently evaluated gene expression via RT-qPCR, single-cell electrophysiological properties via patch-clamp, and contractile function using custom video analysis software.

Results:

ET-1 treatment induced a HF-associated remodeling phenotype, characterized by significant upregulation of hypertrophic (NPPA, NPPB, and ACTA1) and extracellular matrix-associated (COL1A1) genes, along with increased cell membrane capacitance. This structural remodeling was accompanied by marked electrophysiological alterations, including downregulation of KCNH2, CACNA1D, CACNA1C, and SCN5A, reduced potassium, calcium, and sodium current densities, and prolonged action potential duration. ET-1 impaired both the spontaneous beating rate and contraction amplitude of the monolayers. Co-treatment with the Cav1.3-C-terminus successfully restored CACNA1D and KCNH2 gene expression to baseline levels, accompanied by normalized L-type calcium and potassium current densities, normalized APD prolongation, and completely restored the chronotropic and inotropic functions to control levels.

Conclusions:

ET-1-treated hiPSC-CMs model effectively recapitulates the electrophysiological and contractile dysregulations of HF. Gene therapy by Cav1.3-C-terminus provides robust functional rescue myocardial contractility, highlighting its potential as a novel therapeutic strategy for HF.

title: Three-Dimensional Fluid-Structure Interaction Reveals Trade-offs Among Oxygen Delivery, Shear, and Washout in Pediatric Roller-Pump Cardiopulmonary Bypass
authorString: Tu Y, Yeh Y, de Lecea A, Charette K, Bohuta L, Nigam V, del Alamo JC, Greene CL.
abstractText:
Objective:

To determine how roller speed, tubing occlusion, and hematocrit jointly regulate oxygen delivery, shear, and washout in pediatric roller-pump cardiopulmonary bypass.

Methods:

A three-dimensional, closed-loop fluid-structure interaction model resolved roller-tube contact, tubing deformation, and blood flow. Forty simulations combined 4 roller speeds (38-95 revolutions per minute), 2 occlusion levels (77% and 83%), and 5 hematocrit levels (15%-50%). Cycle-averaged flow, oxygen delivery, peak shear stress, and viscosity-normalized relative residence time were quantified.

Results:

Roller compression produced retrograde leakage through the occluded gap, localized peak shear stress exceeding 100 pascals, and adjacent stagnation and recirculation. Flow increased nearly linearly with roller speed and was higher at greater occlusion, with little hematocrit dependence. Higher speed and occlusion increased peak shear stress while reducing relative residence time; higher hematocrit further increased peak shear stress. Similar oxygen delivery could arise from substantially different flow environments: among 10 conditions providing oxygen delivery of approximately 9-12 milliliters per minute, peak shear stress ranged from approximately 25 to 70 pascals. Within conditions satisfying an illustrative minimum oxygen-delivery threshold, lower hematocrit permitted speed and occlusion settings yielding lower peak shear stress and relative residence time.

Conclusions:

Pediatric roller-pump settings that provide similar oxygen delivery can expose blood to markedly different shear and washout environments. Joint evaluation of these metrics may guide selection of speed, occlusion, and hematocrit to meet a target oxygen delivery while reducing shear and improving washout.

Keywords:

Cardiopulmonary bypass; roller pump; pediatric cardiac surgery; fluid-structure interaction; shear stress; relative residence time

title: In vivo optical induction of INaL by photoactivation of AaH-II peptide in beating heart using wireless implantable device
authorString: Dereli M, Millet H, Hivonnait A, Persello A, Choteau-Bodor M, Aillerie V, Aumond P, Zoukimian C, Bigot E, Beroud R, Capoulade R, Gutruf P, Charpentier F, De Waard M, Montnach J.
abstractText: Precise spatiotemporal control of pharmacological compounds in cardiac tissue remains an unmet challenge. Systemic drug administration poorly reproduces the localized and transient nature of cardiac events. Photopharmacology, in which light controls drug activity, offers a compelling solution, but its translation to the beating heart requires wireless light delivery to a moving, soft, and electrically active organ. Here, we demonstrate the first in vivo use of a wireless device to photoactivate a peptide that modulates cardiac excitability. Using a flexible, battery-free implantable optoelectronic device, we achieved light-triggered uncaging of AaH-II*, a natural peptide that enhances the late sodium current. We first validated the caged peptide in vitro and ex vivo, showing that caging suppresses its activity and that UV illumination rapidly restores it. In vivo, wireless photoactivation produced a clear modulation of cardiac electrical activity, as monitored by electrocardiography. This work establishes device-based peptide photomodulation as a strategy for remote, temporally controlled pharmacological intervention in the heart. More broadly, it provides a new platform for probing cardiac excitability and developing region-targeted therapies.

title: Weight and Risk Adjusted Perioperative (WRAP) Bundle for Prevention of Cesarean Delivery Surgical Site Infection: A Quality Improvement Initiative.
authorString: Scremin Souza SC, Walker HA, Bowie AC, Champagne C, Rennicks White R, Walker M, El-Chaâr D, Gomes M.

journal.title: Journal of obstetrics and gynaecology Canada : JOGC = Journal d'obstetrique et gynecologie du Canada : JOGC

abstractText:
Objective

Many individual interventions to reduce surgical site infection (SSI) risk after Cesarean delivery (CD) have been identified; however, their collective impact when used as a bundle is not well defined. This quality improvement initiative compared SSI rates before and after the implementation of a weight- and risk-adjusted perioperative (WRAP) bundle, developed to improve CD outcomes.

Methods

The WRAP bundle was designed to standardize care by tailoring evidence-based interventions according to each patient's individual SSI risk category. Risk stratification was based on pre-gravid body mass index (BMI) and the presence of comorbidities associated with increased SSI risk. This quality improvement initiative adopted a before-and-after quasi-experimental design over two years. Post-CD telephone calls by clinical reviewers were made 30-42 days postpartum to identify CD-SSI incidence.

Results

A total of 4014 CDs were performed between July 1, 2022, and March 1, 2024, with 1275 before WRAP bundle implementation and 2739 after. Maternal characteristics were comparable between pre- and post-WRAP bundle groups, except for hypertension in pregnancy, which was more prevalent in the post-implementation period (22.1% vs. 17.1%, P = 0.001). Across all BMI categories, a statistically significant reduction in overall CD-SSI incidence from 8.9% to 5.8% (P = 0.007) was observed. In the high-BMI group, the CD-SSI rate decreased from 13.9% to 6.9% (P = 0.03).

Conclusion

Tailored bundled interventions, such as the WRAP bundle may be effective in reducing the incidence of CD-SSI, particularly among high-risk individuals. Continuous monitoring of post-CD SSI is vital for quality improvement efforts aimed at optimizing postpartum outcomes.

title: Postmenopausal estradiol levels and female sex modulate haemodynamic responsiveness in experimental portal hypertension.
authorString: Schachteli F, Klein S, Schierwagen R, Fischer J, Peiffer KH, Fobker M, Vorona E, Arif S, Zarei S, Brol MJ, Trebicka J, Uschner FE.
abstractText:
Background & aims

Sex and 17β-estradiol (E2) influence outcomes of cirrhosis, yet preclinical studies in portal hypertension are conducted predominantly in males. We investigated sex and E2-dependent differences in G protein-coupled estrogen receptor 1 (GPER1) signalling and portal pressure response to PDE5 inhibition (PDE5i) in experimental cirrhosis.

Methods

We assessed sex inclusion in rodent studies by PubMed literature search and analysed human hepatic GPER1 expression by sex and age using bulk RNA-seq. Bile duct ligation was performed in male, ovariectomised (OVX) and sham-operated female rats. E2 was administered 24h before invasive haemodynamic assessment in males and OVX females. Acute PDE5i effects were investigated during haemodynamic measurement.

Results

Of 510 rat and 1,657 mouse studies, 87.3% and 77.3% respectively included males only. Human bulk RNA-seq suggested lower hepatic GPER1 expression in cirrhotic females aged ≥ 50 vs. < 50 years. OVX reduced hepatic - but not aortic - GPER1 expression. E2 reduced portal pressure (mean +/- SEM; 22.6 +/- 1.4 vs. 14.3 +/- 1.1 mmHg, p = 0.009) by lowering hepatic portal vascular resistance (74.4 ± 12.7 vs. 25.4 +/- 3.1 mmHg·min·ml-1·g-1, p = 0.03) only in OVX females. PDE5i decreased portal pressure in males (21.3 +/- 1.2 vs. 16.9 +/- 1.8 mmHg, p = 0.03) irrespective of E2. OVX abolished the PDE5i response, which was restored by E2 (14.3 +/- 1.1 vs. 10.0 +/- 0.9 mmHg, p = 0.04).

Conclusions

In experimental cirrhosis, estradiol depletion in OVX females was associated with reduced hepatic GPER1 expression and a diminished portal pressure response to PDE5i. This highlights sex and menopausal status as key determinants of treatment response in portal hypertension and supports the need for sex-specific validation.

Impact and implications

Sex and hormonal status likely contribute to clinically relevant variability in the pharmacology of portal hypertension. Our work highlights that haemodynamic drug response varies due to sex and estradiol status in pre- and postmenopausal females, yet preclinical studies predominantly rely on male models. Integrating sex and menopausal status into early drug development could improve translational accuracy and anticipate non-responder populations.

title: Carotid arterial stiffness and strain after treatment in primary aldosteronism: A prospective follow-up study using speckle-tracking ultrasonography.
authorString: Barlas T, Cerit MN, Sendur HN, Altintop SE, Yalcin MM, Altinova AE, Akturk M, Toruner FB, Karakoc A, Cerit ET.
abstractText:
Aim

This study investigated vascular alterations in patients with primary aldosteronism (PA), using speckle-tracking carotid strain (STCS) ultrasonography, which allows simultaneous assessment of arterial structure and function. It also aimed to compare arterial stiffness and strain changes over follow-up between surgical and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) treatments.

Methods

All patients underwent standardized diagnostic work-up for PA. STCS ultrasonography was performed at baseline and 6 months post-treatment. A 5-mm segment of the common carotid artery below the bulb was analyzed to quantify arterial compliance and distensibility (reflecting elasticity); elastic modulus, β-stiffness index and pulse wave velocity (PWV) (reflecting stiffness); and strain-related parameters: displacement, strain and strain rate.

Results

Thirty patients were included. Arterial compliance increased in both transverse and longitudinal planes in the overall cohort (p<0.05). Between-group comparison revealed greater improvement in arterial compliance in the surgical than in the medical group (p=0.033). Arterial distensibility also increased in the transverse plane (p<0.05), whereas no significant changes were observed in β-stiffness index, elastic modulus, PWV, or strain parameters (p>0.05). Carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) significantly decreased after treatment in the overall cohort and medical group (p<0.05). Multivariate linear regression identified younger age, shorter hypertension duration, male gender and surgical treatment as independent predictors of greater post-treatment improvement in arterial compliance (p<0.05).

Conclusion

These findings suggest that STCS may be a feasible tool for assessing treatment-related vascular changes in PA. Arterial compliance improved following treatment, and more particularly after adrenalectomy, while structural stiffness was largely unchanged in this exploratory comparison.

title: Cross-Database Generalization of a Single-Feature Threshold Model for Congestive Heart Failure Detection from Short-Term Heart Rate Variability.
authorString: Song Y, Wu B, Song Y.
abstractText: ObjectiveTo evaluate the transferability of interpretable single-feature threshold models across the five evaluated databases for congestive heart failure (CHF) detection from short-term heart rate variability (HRV), and to compare their performance with optimized multi-feature classifiers.ApproachTwenty HRV features from 60-second inter-beat interval windows in five databases were evaluated using leave-one-database-pair-out nested cross-validation with six outer-test sets and their corresponding outer-development sets. Within each outer-development set, directions and thresholds were fitted on inner-train sets, and features were selected according to mean inner-validation F1 score. The selected model was refitted on the complete outer-development set. The most frequently selected feature was further evaluated across the six outer-test sets with separately fitted directions and thresholds. Eight multi-feature classifiers were optimized and evaluated using the same data splits. Performance was assessed using record-balanced window-level metrics and database-stratified recording-level bootstrap confidence intervals.Main resultsThe short-term detrended fluctuation analysis scaling exponent (f14) was selected most frequently. The f14 threshold model achieved the highest mean test AUC (0.881 ± 0.038), F1 score (0.718 ± 0.079), and sensitivity among the evaluated single-feature and multi-feature models. Among the eight multi-feature classifiers, Random Forest achieved the highest mean test AUC (0.858 ± 0.067). SignificanceAn interpretable single-feature threshold model showed strong CHF-Normal Sinus Rhythm (NSR) discrimination in the five evaluated databases. f14 was the strongest candidate in this evaluation, although its thresholds varied across outer-development sets and its clinical specificity requires further validation.

title: Association of Medicare's ESRD Treatment Choices Model with Timely Access to Kidney Transplantation in the Southeastern United States.
authorString: Drewry KM, Huffman KM, Kim D, Schmid CH, Koukounas K, Shah AD, Mehrotra R, Wilk AS, Trivedi AN, Patzer RE.

journal.title: Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN

abstractText:
Background

In 2021, Medicare's End-Stage Renal Disease Treatment Choices (ETC) Model randomly assigned 30% of U.S. dialysis facilities to financial incentives to increase home dialysis, waitlisting, and living-donor kidney transplantation. Early evaluations found no improvements in waitlisting or transplantation, but whether the ETC influenced upstream transplant access steps controlled by dialysis facilities remains unknown.

Methods

Using linked data from the United States Renal Data System, Early Steps to Transplant Access Registry, and Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients, we assessed the association of ETC implementation with transplant referral within 1 year of dialysis initiation, evaluation initiation within 6 months of referral, waitlisting or living-donor transplantation within 2 years of dialysis initiation, and corresponding time-to-event outcomes. Difference-in-differences analyses compared outcomes at ETC versus control facilities among adult Traditional Medicare beneficiaries initiating dialysis in Georgia, North Carolina, and South Carolina before (2015-2019) and after (2021-2023) ETC implementation. Follow-up extended through December 2024 (referral, evaluation) and June 2025 (waitlisting, transplantation).

Results

Among 26,809 individuals in 706 facilities (mean [SD] age, 57 [13]; 43% female; 53% non-Hispanic Black; 46% dual Medicare/Medicaid eligible), ETC implementation was associated with adjusted differential increases in timely referral, evaluation start, and waitlisting or living-donor transplantation of 3.58 (95% CI, -1.30 to 8.45), 8.52 (95% CI, -1.42 to 18.45), and 3.61 (95% CI, -0.26 to 7.48) percentage points, respectively, relative to control facilities. Time-to-event analyses were consistent with primary results and substantial COVID-era delays in transplant referral across both ETC and control regions.

Conclusions

ETC implementation was not associated with definitive evidence of statistically significant improvements in timely transplant referral, evaluation initiation, waitlisting, or living-donor transplantation in the Southeastern U.S. The absence of detectable changes in transplant access processes directly influenced by dialysis facilities suggests that incentive misalignment alone is unlikely to explain the ETC Model's limited impact on transplantation.

title: Diet Quality Scores are Associated with Sleep Timing and Regularity in Emerging Adults
authorString: Sanchez SO, Culver MN, Linder BA, Hutchison ZJ, Honaker SM, Jenkins ND, Evans EM, Robinson AT.
abstractText:
Background:

Sleep health is associated with cardiometabolic health, potentially due to direct physiological effects, altered diet quality, or a combination of both. However, data on multidimensional sleep health, particularly sleep regularity and holistic dietary patterns, in emerging adults remain limited.

Objective:

To examine associations between sleep health and diet quality in emerging adults.

Methods:

Objective sleep (duration, efficiency, timing [bedtime, waketime, midpoint], regularity) was measured via actigraphy: n=106 (48M/58F, age [median = 22, IQR = 2] years, BMI [24.2, 4] kg/m2). Subjective sleep quality was measured via Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index: n=122 (58M/64F, age [22, 2], BMI [24.2, 5] kg/m2. We collected diet data via daily food and fluid diaries (≥3 days) to determine Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH; 0-9) and Healthy Eating Index (HEI; 0-100) scores. We used hierarchical regressions (model 1: bivariate analysis, model 2: sex, BMI, race) to examine associations between sleep health and diet quality. We compared diet quality between participants obtaining adequate and inadequate sleep for each sleep health metric using Mann-Whitney U tests.

Results:

Sleep midpoint and bedtime were independently associated with DASH (Bs ≥ -0.165, ps ≤ 0.001) and HEI (Bs ≥ -2.180, ps ≤ 0.001) after inclusion of covariates. Group comparisons indicated higher diet quality among participants with adequate sleep midpoint and waketime SD (p ≤ 0.040).

Conclusions:

Higher sleep regularity is associated with better diet quality in emerging adults. These relations may be bidirectional, thus future studies are needed to investigate whether sleep health interventions improve diet quality, or vice versa, among emerging adults.

title: Genetic hallmarks of patients with congenital portosystemic shunts and portopulmonary hypertension: protocol for a multicentre exploratory study
authorString: Schepens I, Wacker J, Pont F, van Steenbeek F, Joye R, Beghetti M, Makrythanasis P, McLin VA.
abstractText:
Introduction

Congenital portosystemic shunts (CPSS) are rare vascular malformations, with an estimated prevalence of 1/30’000 live births, that cause portal blood to partly bypass the liver. CPSS frequently co-occur with congenital heart disease and other malformations, suggesting a shared developmental or genetic basis. Severe acquired clinical manifestations are present in a large proportion of patients with CPSS. Portopulmonary hypertension (PoPH), the most life-threatening, has been reported in as many as 7–14% of CPSS patients. Mounting evidence indicates that PoPH can arise early in life, particularly in children with CPSS, yet paediatric PoPH remains understudied. This project aims to identify genetic variants associated with PoPH in CPSS patients through whole-genomes, focusing primarily on known pathogenic genes for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), congenital heart disease (CHD), Hereditary Haemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT), SNPs previously associated with PoPH in adults, and ultimately novel genomic variants. The overarching goal of the study is to improve personalised risk assessment and inform clinical decisions regarding elective shunt closure in individuals potentially at-risk of developing PoPH.

Methods and analysis

The aim is to perform an international multi-centre exploratory genome analysis of patients with CPSS and PoPH identified through the International Registry of Congenital Portosystemic Shunts (IRCPSS). Whole-genome sequencing will be utilized to analyse both coding and non-coding regions in a predominantly paediatric cohort. Targeted analysis of established pathogenic genes associated with PAH, CHD, HHT, and PoPH will be complemented by a genome-wide approach to identify novel, potentially pathogenic variants, with variant classification assessed according to American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) criteria. Family-based analyses, including trio analyses and segregation studies, will enable the identification of dominant, recessive, and de novo variants, facilitating a comprehensive evaluation of variant inheritance pattern and pathogenic potential.

Ethics and dissemination

This study has been approved by the CCER (Geneva cantonal ethics committee for research) and poses minimal risk to participants, limited to blood sampling performed as part of routine clinical care for patients. Genetic data will be securely stored and analysed in compliance with GDPR. Clinically significant findings will be communicated through recruiting physicians, in accordance with participant preference regarding incidental findings. Study results will be disseminated through open-access peer-reviewed publications and scientific conferences to advance understanding and management of PoPH in individuals with CPSS and potentially other chronic liver diseases associated with portosystemic bypass.

ClinicalTrials.gov

NCT07314814

CCER Ethical approval

2024-01698

STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY

Systematic analysis of established gene panels for PAH, CHD and HHT, to diagnose referenced genetic disorders. The trio-based whole-genome analysis design allows for the detection of novel potentially pathogenic variants and genes. The rarity of CPSS limits recruitment to an expected sample size of ~30 trios, both a realistic target for a rare disease study and appropriate family-based analyses. Leverages the International Registry of Congenital Portosystemic Shunts as a resource for correlating genetic and clinical data

title: The need for and perception of cardiac rehabilitation among people with ischemic heart disease and heart failure in Pakistan: is a digital home-based programme the solution?
authorString: Khan BA, Zadeh Z, Shah SA, Chaudhry IB, Chaudhry N, Blakemore A, Noor U, Innes D, Ahsan U, Hameed A, Tofique S, Rehman AU, Latif A, Ullah I, Naeem M, Sarwar N, Ansari SuH, Singh SJ, Beurden SV, Husain N, Taylor RS, ACROSS Programme Collaborators.
abstractText:
Background:

Cardiac rehabilitation (CR) reduces hospital admissions and improves health-related quality of life in ischaemic heart disease (IHD) and heart failure (HF), but access is limited in low- and middle-income countries, including Pakistan, where previous data suggest home-based CR may be acceptable. We aimed to assess patients’ preferences for, and preferred modes of delivery of, home-based cardiac rehabilitation (CR), as well as their digital readiness, to inform programme development. Methods An interviewer-administered cross-sectional survey, with responses recorded electronically in REDCap, was conducted of adults with IHD or HF, recruited from the Peshawar Institute of Cardiology and through community outreach in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, between April and June 2026. The primary outcome was willingness to participate in a digital home-based CR programme. Free-text responses to a final open-ended question about views on using a digital programme were analysed using inductive qualitative content analysis. Results Among 310 participants (mean age 55.3 years; 79% men), 254 (82%, 95% CI 77% to 86%) were willing to participate in a digital home-based CR programme and 56 (18%) were unwilling or unsure. Participants who expressed willingness, most often chose family-supported home digital delivery (66%), followed by a paper manual (29%) or app/website (28%) with health-worker support, and a digital–hospital hybrid (25%); few chose hospital (7%) or community (6%) group programmes. Only 55% owned a smartphone and 46% had regular internet access, yet 85% of willing participants reported a family member able to support them. Six themes were developed, including comprehension needs, family support and digital barriers. Conclusion Most surveyed Pakistani patients with IHD or HF were willing to participate in digital home-based CR, A digital programme was the preferred format, most commonly with support from a family member, despite relatively limited digital access and lower levels of independent digital readiness.

title: Effectiveness of an Educational Intervention in the Integral Care of Patients with Diabetes Mellitus
authorString: Goicochea-Rios E, Otiniano NM.
abstractText:
Background:

To evaluate the effectiveness of an educational intervention in the integral care of patients with diabetes mellitus. Methods A pre-experimental study was carried out with 103 patients with diabetes mellitus treated at Essalud, La Libertad, during the second semester of 2024. Pre and post educational intervention information was collected about knowledge of the disease, complications, physical activity and diet, adherence to treatment and family support, number of medical and nursing controls per quarter, glycemia values, HbA1c and compliance with treatment after informed consent. The educational intervention included theoretical aspects of diabetes mellitus, self-care, physical activity, nutrition and family support in 2-hour workshops, once a week, with a total of 4 sessions per participant. Results Predominantly female, mean age 63.22 years, higher education, marital status married/cohabiting and main occupation employed/independent. 97.1% had type 2 diabetes mellitus, 38.8% reported disease duration < 5 years, 72.8% were treated with metformin and the main comorbidity was hypertension (58.3%). The educational intervention improved knowledge about diabetes mellitus (p < 0.001), achieved a significant change in eating habits (p = 0.022) and family support (p = 0.043), and homogenized the level of support among families (p = 0.025). 58.3% of the participants were noncompliant with the prescribed treatment. Treatment adherence fell from 54.4% to 41.7 %, whilst non-adherence rose from 45.6 % to 58.3 %; however 76.8% of patients who initially complied with treatment continued to do so after the intervention. The effectiveness of the educational program on glycemic control was not evidenced. Regarding integral control, 83.5 % of the patients received quarterly medical care and 44.7 % received nursing care. Conclusion The educational program was effective in improving knowledge about T2D, adherence to healthy eating and significantly improved the level of family support and compliance with treatment.

title: Salt-Sensitive Hypertension Begins With Intracellular K<sup>+</sup> and Water Loss.
authorString: Minegishi S, Morisawa N, Wild J, Wan Keat Y, Takase-Minegishi K, Marton A, Lim TT, Peukert M, Lohmayer R, Walsh S, Siew K, Rauh M, Luft FC, Kovalik JP, Hoenig M, Puar TH, Kitada K, Titze J.
abstractText:
Background

Na+ and water overload due to inappropriately low renal salt and water excretion is considered the root cause of salt-sensitive hypertension. However, experimental renal and psoriasis hypertension are characterized by chronic predisposition to dehydration. We tested the validity of this alternative hypertension due to loss of water theory in deoxycorticosterone acetate (DOCA) salt-sensitive hypertension.

Methods

We tested the effect of DOCA (25 mg pellet) in mice on a low Na+ diet (0.02%-0.03%) with tap water, or with Na+ in their drinking water (1% NaCl or 1.44% NaHCO3), on body Na+, K+, and water content 2, 6, and 12 days after treatment initiation. We monitored blood pressure with radio-telemetry, food and water intake, and renal electrolyte and water excretion.

Results

At day 2, DOCA NaCl-treated mice elevated blood pressure during a state of isolated body K+ and water loss, indicating substantial intracellular dehydration. Although increasing their fluid intake and urine output, the mice reduced the excretion of free water, indicating renal water conservation. At days 6 and 12, secondary Na+ retention occurred, which replaced the amount of K+ lost and corrected the dehydration, albeit at the expense of an intracellular Na+/K+ redistribution disorder. DOCA NaHCO3-treated mice with Na+-resistant blood pressure showed a comparable Na+/K+ redistribution disorder, but without accompanying early dehydration due to earlier replacement of lost K+ by Na+.

Conclusions

Experimental DOCA salt-sensitive hypertension initiates with a systemic water conservation response in the face of K+-driven intracellular water loss. Both dehydration and blood pressure increase could be causally treated by oral K+ supplementation.

title: Population-Based Assessment of Cardiometabolic Late Effects in 5-Year Survivors of Pediatric Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia.
authorString: Strebeck PV, Tarlan A, Owsley KM, van der Plas E, Farrar JE, Brown CC, Appell LE.
abstractText:
Introduction

Survival rates for pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) have improved substantially, shifting attention toward long-term health. Epidemiologic data on survivors of pediatric ALL from large, population-based cohorts, particularly in early survivorship, is limited. We addressed this gap by examining the prevalence of diagnosed cardiometabolic conditions among pediatric ALL survivors compared with matched cancer-free peers during the fifth year after diagnosis.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study using linked data from the Arkansas Central Cancer Registry (2013-2020) and Arkansas All-Payer Claims Database (2017-2024). Individuals diagnosed with ALL before age 25 years who survived to the fifth year after diagnosis were identified. We matched ALL survivors with three cancer-free peers by exact matching on sex, race, ethnicity, birth year, Medicaid enrollment history, and county of residence. Cardiometabolic outcomes were identified using claims-based diagnoses among the ALL survivors and matched controls. We examined differences in cardiometabolic outcomes between ALL survivors and matched controls.

Results

ALL survivors (n = 142; age range 4-30 years) experienced a significantly higher burden of cardiometabolic conditions compared with matched controls (n = 426; 10.6% vs. 1.2%, p < 0.01). ALL survivors had higher prevalence of hypertension (4.9% vs. 0.9%; p < 0.01) and diabetes mellitus (4.9% vs. 0.2%; p < 0.01). Differences were more pronounced among ALL survivors aged ≥ 14 years, among whom 20.4% (vs. 2.0%; p < 0.01) had at least one cardiometabolic condition.

Conclusions

Pediatric ALL survivors experience elevated cardiometabolic risk as early as five years after diagnosis, particularly during adolescence. Early screening and preventive strategies are needed to reduce long-term cardiometabolic burden among pediatric ALL survivors.

title: OCT‑Detected Endocardial Abnormality and Minimal Tunnel Area in Patients With Patent Foramen Ovale: Associations With Thrombus Formation.
authorString: Liu XQ, Wang XY, Li BY, He L, Zhang YS.

journal.title: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions

abstractText:
Background

In situ thrombus formation represents one of the key pathogeneses of patent foramen ovale (PFO)‑related disorders. This study aimed to explore factors contributing to in situ thrombus in patients with PFO‑related diseases.

Aims

This study aimed to explore factors contributing to in situ thrombus in patients with PFO-related diseases.

Methods

Forty‑six prospectively enrolled patients with PFO‑related disorders underwent OCT imaging to explore potential contributing factors for in situ thrombus. None of the enrolled participants presented with concomitant lower‑extremity venous thrombosis or atrial fibrillation, and no alternative pathogenic factors were detected.

Results

In 63.04% of the cases (29 individuals), an in situ thrombus was present in the PFO tunnel. Patients with in situ thrombus exhibited a notably smaller right PFO area and minimum area, along with a higher incidence of abnormal endocardium than those without thrombus. Multivariate logistic regression analysis identified PFO minimum area and abnormal endocardium as independent factors associated with in situ thrombus.

Conclusions

Our exploratory analysis suggests that endocardial abnormality and a smaller minimal PFO‑tunnel area may correlate with a higher risk of thrombus formation, offering clues regarding possible mechanisms behind PFO‑related diseases.

title: No significant change in urinary sodium excretion within 48h after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery: the weight LUSER study.
authorString: Henry J, Oo S, Lai C, Thakkar R, Bolckmans R, le Roux CW, Welbourn R.

journal.title: Annals of the Royal College of Surgeons of England

abstractText:
Introduction

Metabolic and bariatric surgery is effective in achieving remission of hypertension and metabolic disease. It is unclear whether metabolic changes within the first 48h after surgery can potentially explain underlying mechanisms of hypertension control. We aimed to assess changes in urinary sodium excretion early after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) as a potential weight-loss-independent mechanism of hypertension remission.

Methods

All patients undergoing primary RYGB provided a 24-h urine collection, blood pressure (BP) measurement, and blood sampling both preoperatively and 48h postoperatively. The dietary sodium content was similar at both time points.

Results

Twenty patients were included, of whom 16 met the minimum output urine volume criteria for 24-h urine samples. Mean patient age was 55.2 ± 7.7 years and median body mass index was 48kg/m2 with 13 patients (65%) diagnosed with hypertension and 7 (35%) with obstructive sleep apnoea. Twenty-four-hour urine sodium excretion was similar immediately prior to surgery and 48h postoperatively (72.1 ± 44.0 vs 74.5 ± 65.2mmol/24h, p = 0.45). There was no significant difference in systolic or diastolic BP immediately prior to surgery compared with 48h postoperatively (143.3 ± 15.1 vs 135.9 ± 16.3mmHg, p = 0.09 and 79.8 ± 9.2 vs 79.9 ± 5.8mmHg, p = 0.47). Both findings were confirmed on further sensitivity analysis.

Conclusion

No significant change in urinary sodium excretion or BP was detected in the first 48h post RYGB in normotensive patients or those with well-controlled hypertension.

title: Association between frailty index and self-reported stomach pain among middle-aged and older adults: Evidence from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study and machine-learning analysis.
authorString: Cheng G, Geng Y, Lyu L, Dai F, Huang J, Fu W.

journal.title: The Journal of international medical research

abstractText: BackgroundFrailty reflects accumulated health deficits and reduced physiological reserve across multiple systems. Although frailty has been associated with various adverse health outcomes, its relationship with self-reported stomach pain remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the association between frailty index and self-reported stomach pain and evaluate the predictive performance of frailty index-based models using machine-learning approaches.MethodsIn total, 24,280 participants aged ≥45 years enrolled in the baseline survey of the 2011-2013 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study were included. A frailty index was constructed using multiple health-related deficits. Multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline analyses were performed to assess the association and nonlinear relationship between frailty index and stomach pain. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore potential effect modification by major comorbidities. Machine-learning models incorporating frailty index and clinical characteristics were developed, and SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis was performed to interpret feature contributions.ResultsA higher frailty index was significantly associated with increased likelihood of self-reported stomach pain in the fully adjusted model (odds ratio = 2.17, 95% confidence interval: 1.95-2.42, p < 0.001). Restricted cubic spline analysis demonstrated a significant nonlinear association between frailty index and stomach pain (p for nonlinearity < 0.001). The association was stronger among participants without hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, or cardiovascular disease. The eXtreme gradient boosting model demonstrated good performance in identifying individuals with stomach pain, and SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis indicated that frailty index was one of the most influential features contributing to model predictions.ConclusionA higher frailty index was associated with greater likelihood of self-reported stomach pain among middle-aged and older adults. These findings suggest that frailty represents an important marker of gastrointestinal symptom burden. Machine-learning analyses further demonstrated the value of frailty index in identifying individuals with stomach pain. However, longitudinal studies are needed to clarify causal relationships.

title: Remnant cholesterol predicts progression from prehypertension to incident hypertension: Evidence from a prospective cohort study and Mendelian randomization analysis.
authorString: Qi M, Wang M, Li Y, Cai X.
abstractText: ObjectiveRemnant cholesterol (RC), a marker of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein remnants, has emerged as an important contributor to residual cardiometabolic risk. However, whether RC contributes to the transition from prehypertension to clinical hypertension remains unclear. We investigated the association between RC and incident hypertension among adults with prehypertension and further assessed genetic evidence using Mendelian randomization (MR).MethodsThis prospective cohort study included 2,858 adults with prehypertension from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, followed from 2011 to 2015. RC was calculated as total cholesterol minus low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Multivariable logistic regression, restricted cubic spline analysis, subgroup analyses, and receiver operating characteristic analysis were performed. Two-sample MR, including inverse-variance weighted and Bayesian weighted MR methods, was used to evaluate the genetic association between RC and hypertension-related traits.ResultsDuring 4 years of follow-up, 891 participants developed incident hypertension. Higher RC was independently associated with increased odds of incident hypertension. In the fully adjusted model, each 1 mg/dL increase in RC was associated with a 2% higher odds of hypertension. Compared with participants in the lowest RC quartile, those in the highest quartile had 67% higher odds of incident hypertension, corresponding to an absolute increase of 11.86% in cumulative hypertension incidence during follow-up. Compared with the lowest RC quartile, the highest quartile showed a significantly higher risk of incident hypertension. Restricted cubic spline analysis demonstrated a linear dose-response association, with no evidence of nonlinearity. Subgroup analyses suggested stronger associations among older adults, non-smokers, individuals with normal body weight, and participants without depressive symptoms. MR analyses further supported a positive genetic association between elevated RC and hypertension-related traits.ConclusionsAmong adults with prehypertension, elevated RC was independently and linearly associated with higher risk of progression to incident hypertension. Genetic evidence further supported a potential role of RC in hypertension-related traits. These findings suggest that RC, which can be readily calculated from routine lipid profiles, may complement existing approaches for hypertension risk assessment and targeted blood pressure monitoring among individuals with prehypertension.

title: Impact of artificial intelligence-assisted health management on blood pressure and self-management efficacy in older adults with hypertension.
authorString: Yang X, Huang X, Cui Y, Zhao K.
abstractText:
Purpose

This paper examined the impacts of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted health management on blood pressure control and self-management effectiveness in older adults with hypertension.

Materials and methods

Two hundred hypertensive patients were randomly assigned to a usual care group (routine health management) or an intervention group (AI-assisted health management, including aspects such as intelligent monitoring, early warning and proactive intervention, among others) (n = 100 each). Primary outcomes included blood pressure control rate (<140/<90 mm Hg) and systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP and DBP). Secondary outcomes included improvement in lifestyle behaviors, level of hypertension knowledge awareness, self-management efficacy, medication beliefs, quality of life, and management satisfaction.

Results

Following one year intervention, the intervention group demonstrated a higher blood pressure control rate than the usual care group (88.66% vs. 64.89%), along with lower SBP (128.49 ± 6.63 vs. 135.38 ± 7.31 mmHg) and DBP (77.49 ± 6.07 vs. 81.84 ± 5.44 mmHg) (all P < 0.05). Additionally, the intervention group showed superior improvements in smoking behavior change, alcohol consumption behavior change, low-salt and low-fat diet adherence, and regular exercise attainment, as well as higher scores on the Hypertension Knowledge-Level Scale, Hypertension Patient Self-Management Behavior Rating Scale, Modified Beliefs about Medicines Questionnaire, physical component summary and the mental component summary, and Client Satisfaction Questionnaire-8 (all P < 0.05).

Conclusion

AI-assisted health management enhances blood pressure control, and improves self-management capacity, quality of life, and service satisfaction in older adults with hypertension.

title: T-Cell-Derived IFNγ Instructs ECM Crosslinking by Cardiac Fibroblasts Through LOXL3 in Experimental Cardiometabolic HFpEF.
authorString: Emig R, Robbe Z, Kley C, Smolgovsky S, Bayer AL, Travers J, Blanton RM, McKinsey T, Black LD, Alcaide P.
abstractText:
Background

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a major clinical challenge characterized by diastolic dysfunction. Left ventricular stiffening and inflammation are hallmarks of HFpEF, yet the contribution of ECM (extracellular matrix) stiffness and the immune-stromal mechanisms driving ECM stiffening in cardiometabolic HFpEF remain poorly understood.

Methods

We used the murine 2-hit model of cardiometabolic HFpEF, in which the combination of high-fat diet and hypertension induced by L-nitro-arginine-methyl ester causes diastolic dysfunction. We evaluated diastolic function by echocardiography and ECM mechanics by uniaxial tensile testing of decellularized cardiac tissue. Functional in vivo studies included genetic depletion of T cells, IFNγ (interferon-γ) knockout mice, and pharmacological lysyl oxidase inhibition. We combined cocultures of CD4+ T cells and cardiac fibroblasts with mechanical testing of cardiac ECM and molecular biology to elucidate cellular and molecular mechanisms.

Results

Left ventricular ECM stiffness strongly correlated with impaired diastolic function in experimental cardiometabolic HFpEF. Cardiac CD4+ T-cell infiltration was required for ECM stiffening and upregulation of lysyl oxidase enzymes in cardiac fibroblast. We discovered that CD4+ T-cell-derived IFNγ was required to induce LOXL3 in cardiac fibroblast, which increased ECM stiffness in vitro. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that a signaling axis involving IFNγ, PI3K (phosphoinositide 3-kinase), AKT, and HIF1α (hypoxia-inducible factor-1α) drives LOXL3 expression and subsequent collagen crosslinking. Genetic or pharmacological disruption of this IFNγ-HIF1α-LOXL3 axis attenuated adverse ECM remodeling and improved diastolic function.

Conclusions

CD4+ T cells promote pathological ECM stiffening in cardiometabolic HFpEF through IFNγ-mediated, cardiac fibroblast LOXL3-dependent ECM crosslinking. Targeting this immune-stromal pathway may offer a novel therapeutic strategy for HFpEF.

title: Diastolic Dysfunction in Congenital Heart Disease: A Pressure-Volume Loop Analysis of Borderline Left Heart.
authorString: Thatte N, Liberman M, Hammer PE, Callahan R, Esch J, Farias M, Marx G, Beroukhim RS, Feins E, Emani S, Ghelani SJ.
abstractText:
Background

Diastolic dysfunction is a major driver of morbidity in congenital heart disease, but its mechanisms are poorly understood. It remains unknown whether left ventricular (LV) diastolic dysfunction in borderline left heart patients is caused by a defect in active relaxation or in passive stiffness. We applied gold-standard pressure-volume (PV) loop analysis to define the mechanism of diastolic dysfunction in patients with borderline LV.

Methods

We analyzed invasive PV loops from children with bLV (n=13) and a pragmatic comparison group of patients with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (ccTGA, n=14). PV loops were generated during transient preload alteration. Active relaxation was assessed by the isovolumetric relaxation time constant (τ) and maximal rate of pressure decline (dP/dtmin) indexed to peak systolic pressure. Passive stiffness was quantified by the stiffness constant (β), derived from the multibeat end-diastolic PV relationship. To account for size differences, β was calculated using indexed ventricular volumes (iβ), and also converted to a dimensionless stiffness constant (βw=β×ventricular wall volume).

Results

Active relaxation measures were similar between groups (τ bLV, 28 [23.5-29.5] versus ccTGA, 24 [21-28] msec, P=0.11; dP/dtmin/peak systolic pressure bLV: -10.6 [-11.0 to -9.4] versus ccTGA: -9.9 [-10.5 to -8.7] s-1, P=0.17). In contrast, patients with bLV had markedly abnormal passive stiffness. The end-diastolic PV relationship was shifted upward and to the left, and the stiffness constants were higher in the bLV group (iβ bLV, 0.10 [0.04-0.35] versus ccTGA, 0.03 [0.02-0.04] m2/mL, P=0.003; βw bLV, 4.08 [1.6-7.52] versus ccTGA, 1.21 [0.95-1.77]; P=0.002).

Conclusions

The primary mechanism of diastolic dysfunction in bLV is increased passive ventricular stiffness, while no differences were detected in active relaxation. These findings suggest a limited role for lusitropic medications and therapeutic strategies that focus on mitigating ventricular stiffness (such as surgical endocardial fibroelastosis resection) may be more valuable.

title: RBFOX2 Autoregulation Promotes Cardiomyocyte Transcriptome Maturation and Differentiation.
authorString: Huang M, Ladha FA, Wang Y, Trembley MA, Yin HM, Zheng R, Prondzynski M, Tharani Y, Akerberg AA, Aigner S, Yee BA, Mayourian J, Morton SU, Bezzerides VJ, Pu WT, Yeo GW, Chen K, Burns CG, Burns CE.
abstractText:
Background

Haploinsufficiency of the RNA splicing regulator RBFOX2 has been linked to congenital heart disease, including hypoplastic left heart syndrome, yet its pathogenic mechanisms remain unresolved.

Methods

Human induced pluripotent stem cells heterozygous or null for RBFOX2 were created and their cardiomyocyte (CM) derivatives were characterized in monolayer culture and engineered heart tissues. In addition to cellular phenotyping, molecular profiling by RNA sequencing and enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation sequencing was performed to detect changes in gene expression, exon usage, and RBFOX2 (RNA-binding fox-1 homolog 2) binding. These data sets were integrated to identify RBFOX2-bound RNAs with altered expression and splicing and to compare them with publicly available data sets from progressive CM differentiation time points. Rescue experiments were performed in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived CMs, engineered heart tissues, and zebrafish.

Results

We demonstrate that RBFOX2 is essential for CM differentiation by driving transcriptome maturation through gene expression- and alternative splicing-based isoform switching in transcripts primarily encoding sarcomere, cytoskeletal, and focal adhesion components, including the critical Z-disc factor ACTN2 (alpha-actinin-2). We further find that threshold levels of RBFOX2 facilitate autoregulatory splicing of mutually exclusive exons, generating early and late RBFOX2 isoforms with distinct functions. In heterozygous CMs, this threshold is not reached, resulting in isoform imbalance and production of an aberrant transcript, which further reduces functional RBFOX2 levels to well below 50% of wild-type. Finally, we demonstrate that ACTN2 overexpression rescues heterozygous, but not null, phenotypes, suggesting that ACTN2 activates an RBFOX2-dependent feedback loop that promotes transcriptome maturation.

Conclusions

Our data demonstrate that reduced RBFOX2 dosage and impaired autoregulation stall CM differentiation by inhibiting transcriptome maturation, contributing to congenital heart disease pathogenesis and potentially increasing heart failure susceptibility following surgical intervention.

title: A cascade-targeted nanoplatform for in situ remodeling of the atherosclerotic plaque microenvironment through bidirectional cholesterol regulation and ROS/NO rebalancing.
authorString: Guan Q, Li Z, Qiao G, Du J, Liu M, Zhang L, He L, Yang Q, Liu L, Shen M, Li Y.
abstractText: Atherosclerosis (AS) is driven by intertwined dysregulation of cholesterol homeostasis, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation, limiting the efficacy of single-target therapies. Here, we developed a hierarchically engineered pH/ROS-responsive nanoplatform, TSCA@OL, for plaque targeting and coordinated microenvironment remodeling. CD44-mediated accumulation enhances plaque localization, while simvastatin (SV) and β-cyclodextrin (β-CD) jointly suppress cholesterol synthesis and promote cholesterol efflux. In parallel, suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA) and L-arginine (L-Arg) restore ROS/NO balance, promote endothelial repair, and attenuate inflammatory activation. In ApoE<sup>⁻/⁻</sup> mice, TSCA@OL markedly increased plaque ABCA1 and ABCG1 expression, improved serum lipid profiles, and reduced aortic plaque burden by 62.97% relative to the high-fat diet group. Treatment also suppressed pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization and improved plaque stability. Collectively, TSCA@OL integrates cholesterol regulation with oxidative-inflammatory correction, providing a coordinated biomaterials strategy for reducing plaque burden and remodeling the atherosclerotic microenvironment. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Atherosclerosis is driven by intertwined lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, endothelial injury, and inflammation, yet most therapies address only one process. This study introduces TSCA@OL, a hierarchically engineered nanoplatform that links biomaterial structure with coordinated biological function. A hyaluronic acid-based outer layer recognizes plaque-associated cells through CD44 and responds to acidic conditions, while a reactive oxygen species-sensitive inner module enables local release. The platform combines simvastatin-mediated suppression of cholesterol synthesis with β-cyclodextrin-mediated cholesterol removal, antioxidant regulation, and nitric oxide support. In atherosclerotic mice, TSCA@OL reduced plaque burden, improved lipid profiles, enhanced markers of cholesterol efflux, and promoted features associated with plaque stabilization. This work provides a biomaterials strategy for remodeling complex disease microenvironments through spatially coordinated, multi-pathway intervention.

title: Computational alternative to cardiac biopsy in multiple myeloma: utilizing the shape of routine laboratory data for the classification of AL cardiac amyloidosis
authorString: Cremer MA, Song H, Fradley MG, Rhea IB, Kieslich CA, Ferrall-Fairbanks MC.
abstractText:
Background:

Patients with multiple myeloma (MM) are at increased risk for light chain cardiac amyloidosis (CA) due to high circulating levels of light chains. ALCA is a clinical diagnosis based on biopsy, cardiac imaging findings of restrictive cardiomyopathy, and serum monoclonal proteins. To overcome these challenges, we have developed machine learning models that accurately predict ALCA status while identifying key diagnostic features based on routine laboratory measurements and using limited data.

Methods:

Utilizing electronic medical data (EMR) data, we built support vector machine models (SVMs) using the MISTIC framework. Data including diagnosis history, treatment, and laboratory values for patients with MM or monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS) were collected as a retrospective cohort study at Moffit Cancer Center and Research Institute between 2014 and 2019. To utilize the wealth of information in longitudinal EMR data, we fit regression models to the EMR data and used the parameters and characteristics of the fits as features for our SVMs. We tested three different sets of features: descriptive statistics alone, parameters and characteristics of fit only, and both the descriptive statistics and parameters of fit (DescFits). A classifier using raw data at a timepoint proximal to the date of ALCA diagnostic imaging (EchoAdj), as well as analogous random forest and XGBoost models were used for comparison.

Findings:

SVM classifiers trained on the DescFits feature set (AUC= 1.0) outperformed blind model predictions of the EchoAdj model (AUC = 0.36) and other conventional machine learning approaches in identifying which patients were diagnosed with ALCA. The DescFits model selected features describing the temporal relationship of physiologic parameters including hematologic state, and cardiac and renal function. Interpretation: We demonstrated that the MISTIC SVM framework and the shape of EMR data can aid in identifying patients with cardiac amyloidosis without cardiac biopsy or imaging.

title: Snare-Assisted Retrieval of a Mechanically Locked-Open TEER Device: A Novel Bailout Technique.
authorString: Kaliyamoorthy D, Murugesan K, Mahesh Kumar A, Chandrasekaran K.

journal.title: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions

abstractText: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) is an established intervention for patients having severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with prohibitive surgical risk. Complications during deployment related to device malfunction are uncommon but necessitate prompt decision-making and management. A 54-year-old gentleman with dilated cardiomyopathy, severe left ventricular dysfunction, and severe MR underwent TEER using the MyClip system (Meril Life Sciences Pvt. Ltd., Vapi, Gujarat, India). Initial deployment across the A2-P2 scallops of mitral leaflets achieved partial MR reduction. Significant residual MR required a second clip for optimal leaflet coaptation. While deploying the second clip, it failed to close because of a mechanical locking failure. So, we everted the clip, pulled back to LA, and it stayed in open position and failed to close. We report a novel bailout snare technique that enabled safe retrieval without the need for a second transseptal puncture. The ability to close the clip arms prior to withdrawal minimized the risk of tearing the atrial septum and facilitated the successful completion of the TEER procedure. Another clip was deployed successfully, resulting in significant MR reduction. This case demonstrates a rare complication during deployment, a malfunction of the device, and a novel strategy for safely bailing out a challenging intra-procedural complication.

title: Outcomes of Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillators in Patients Being Considered for Heart Transplantation: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
authorString: Krishnaswamy RJ, Cherrett CA, Adonopulos AA, Macdonald PS, Hayward CS, Muthiah K, Watson AJ, Subbiah RN.
abstractText:
Introduction

Subcutaneous implantable cardioverter defibrillators (S-ICD) are an alternative to transvenous devices (TV-ICD) in patients not requiring bradycardia pacing, resynchronization (CRT) or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP). At our center, S-ICDs are often preferred in patients being considered for heart transplantation (HTx) without pacing/CRT/ATP needs, as their removal post-HTx avoids retained transvenous leads which can preclude MRI surveillance for graft rejection. We assessed outcomes of S-ICDs in this population.

Methods

We retrospectively reviewed 201 S-ICD implants at our center; July 2016 - March 2025.

Results

We identified 33 patients (22 male; age 46 ± 13 years) who, at time of S-ICD implant, had been referred for HTx evaluation or were referred at any time thereafter. Etiologies were nonischemic cardiomyopathy (n = 18), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (n = 5), ischemic cardiomyopathy (n = 4), congenital heart disease (n = 4), and myocarditis (n = 2). Median follow-up was 296 days [IQR = 72-798]. Two patients died, both non-arrhythmic. Four patients received appropriate S-ICD therapies and three had inappropriate shocks due to P- or T-wave oversensing (TWOS) (n = 2), or a rapidly conducted atrial arrhythmia (n = 1). Three patients, all with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, received transvenous device upgrades: one to CRT-P for disease progression, one to TV-ICD for ATP-terminable ventricular tachycardia and one to TV-ICD due to inappropriate shocks from TWOS. Thirteen patients underwent HTx at median 257 days [IQR = 130-453] post S-ICD; three of whom were bridged with HeartMate 3 LVADs. One LVAD patient needed S-ICD deactivation due to electromagnetic interference. There were no retained device components following HTx and S-ICD extraction.

Conclusion

In selected pre-HTx patients, S-ICDs offer arrhythmic protection while avoiding retained leads post-HTx.

title: From Virtual Reality to High-Fidelity Silicone Models: A Pilot Pathway for Training Vascular Surgeons in Robotic Skills.
authorString: Torres IO, Coutinho ML, Saes G, Belon A, Puech-Leão P, Artifon E.
abstractText:
Objective

This pilot study evaluated the learning curve of vascular surgeons undergoing structured VR simulator training and assessed the feasibility of performing a robotic vascular anastomosis within a team lacking prior laparoscopic or robotic experience.

Methods

Three vascular surgeons completed a structured curriculum on the RobotiX Mentor VR simulator, followed by a robotic aorto-aortic bypass with a Dacron graft performed on a high-fidelity pulsatile silicone model using the da Vinci surgical system. These procedures were compared with an open-technique anastomosis performed on the same model, with outcomes assessed via the Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skills (OSATS), operative time, and leakage rate.

Results

Surgeons completed a median of 248 training sessions across 77 distinct cases to reach the 20-hour required for robotic surgery certification, with proficiency achieved after 14-19 hours of training. Robotic anastomosis was associated with lower OSATS scores (34.5 [IQR 33.25-35.375] vs 40 [IQR 40-40]; P=0.003) and longer operative times (47 [IQR 41.5-57.75] vs 12 minutes [IQR 11.0-13.75]) relative to open surgery. Leakage rates did not differ between techniques (2 mL [IQR 0-4] vs 0 mL; P=0.087), and final product quality was considered acceptable, with a median score of 23 out of 25.

Conclusion

Vascular surgeons without prior robotic or laparoscopic experience were able to acquire basic robotic vascular anastomosis skills through a structured curriculum combining VR and high-fidelity silicone simulation. Despite longer operative times relative to open surgery, technical quality and leakage rates were comparable between techniques.

title: Sex-Related Variation in Abdominal Aortic Dimensions and the Effect of Body-Size Indexing: A CT Study in Mexican Adults.
authorString: Castillo C, De la Torre OA, Lemus Colorado VJ, Flores CS, Díaz de León Derby R, Pena-Almaguer E, Fabiani MA.
abstractText:
Background

This study evaluated the relationship between sex and abdominal aortic calibre and assessed whether Aortic Size Index (ASI) and Aortic Height Index (AHI) attenuate sex-related differences in a Mexican cohort without known vascular or aortic disease.

Methods

In this prospective study, 152 adults (58 males, 94 females) without known vascular pathology underwent CT imaging with measurements obtained perpendicular to the vessel centerline. Aortic diameters were measured at eight anatomical levels. ASI and AHI were calculated. Interobserver agreement was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC).

Results

Males had larger absolute infrarenal diameters than females (17.6 ± 2.0 vs. 14.9 ± 1.8 mm, p < 0.001). BSA indexing helped attenuate sex differences, yielding comparable ASI values between sexes (males 0.90 ± 0.14 vs. females 0.89 ± 0.12 cm/m2, p = 0.55; median sex difference 0.010 cm/m2), compared to an unadjusted median difference of 2.9 mm. Height indexing retained a significant sex difference (AHI: 1.01 ± 0.12 vs. 0.94 ± 0.12 cm/m, p < 0.001; median sex difference 0.090 cm/m). Interobserver agreement was excellent (ICC ≥ 0.90) at 6 of 8 anatomical levels.

Conclusion

In this non-pathological Mexican CT cohort, ASI was observed to attenuate baseline sex-related differences in abdominal aortic caliber, whereas height-based indexing AHI retained residual variation. These observations provide baseline reference parameters highlighting body scale and biological sex as relevant variables that warrant further investigation in larger, multi-center, and pathological cohorts to assess their clinical utility.

title: A Scoping Review on Artificial Intelligence for Image-Based Analysis in Aortic Aneurysm Care.
authorString: Hofmann A.
abstractText:
Objective

Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising approach to enhance automated image analysis, quantitative assessment, and clinical decision-making in aortic aneurysm care. This scoping review aims to summarize the current cumulative body of evidence.

Methods

A systematic PubMed search identified 661 records, with 59 studies ultimately included after de-duplication and multi-stage screening based on predefined eligibility criteria, focusing on original research applying artificial intelligence to medical imaging in aortic aneurysm care. Data were extracted on study design, imaging modality, AI methodology, validation, and dataset characteristics.

Results

Fifty-nine studies were included. Deep learning approaches, particularly U-Net-based architectures, were the most frequently applied methods, with AI primarily used for automated segmentation and quantitative analysis of aortic pathology. AI models achieved high technical performance across applications, including vessel segmentation, aneurysm detection, endoleak identification, and risk prediction, with reported improvements in efficiency and diagnostic accuracy. However, external validation, multimodal data integration, and prospective clinical evaluation remained uncommon.

Conclusion

AI demonstrates substantial potential to enhance aortic aneurysm disease assessment through accurate image analysis, automated quantification, and improved procedural support. However, current limitations include lack of external validation, reporting transparency, and clinical integration.

title: A single exposure to the environmental contaminant tributyltin induces oxidative stress and vascular endothelial dysfunction.
authorString: Marques VB, Santos GAC, Silva KM, Ximenes CF, Costa AKN, Hortelan M, Taufner SB, Graceli JB, Fernandes AA, Ribeiro EH, Dedkova EN, Stefanon I.
abstractText: Organotin compounds, such as tributyltin (TBT), are environmental contaminants known for toxic effects. Subacute exposure to TBT leads to vascular dysfunction associated with increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). This study aimed to investigate whether a single exposure to TBT induces endothelial dysfunction. Adult female rats were divided into two groups: control (CT) and TBT-exposed. Vascular reactivity of isolated aortic rings was assessed 24hours after a single oral dose of TBT (500ng/kg). Vasodilator responses to acetylcholine and sodium nitroprusside were not altered by TBT exposure. However, aortic rings from TBT-exposed rats exhibited greater contractile response to phenylephrine and reduced influence of endothelial denudation or L-NAME incubation on vascular reactivity. The impaired nitrergic modulation induced by TBT was prevented by co-incubation with superoxide dismutase plus L-NAME. In vitro DAF-2 assay indicated reduced NO production in the TBT group. TBT-induced vascular hyperreactivity was reversed by incubation with apocynin, TIRON, catalase, allopurinol, losartan, indomethacin, NS-398, SQ-29,548, and SC-19,220. In contrast, the non-selective NOX inhibitor VAS2870 did not modify the response to phenylephrine. Dihydroethidium staining showed increased ROS levels- including superoxide anion and hydrogen peroxide-in aortas from TBT-exposed animals. Scanning electron microscopy revealed endothelial structural damage in the TBT group. Together, these findings indicate that a single dose of TBT (500ng/kg) caused vascular dysfunction, likely resulting from impaired endothelial and nitrergic modulation mediated by increased ROS production derived from xanthine oxidase, activation of the local renin-angiotensin system, and cyclooxygenase pathways in female rats.

title: cGAS-STING activation promotes abdominal aortic aneurysm formation in mice and humans: Therapeutic potential of inhibition.
authorString: Du P, Ma X, Zhu F, Zhu G, Li F, Nie H, Yu M, Tang L, Yan J, Li Y, Sun Y, Huang K, Yang H, Feng J.
abstractText: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a life-threatening vascular disease lacking effective pharmacotherapy. The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) innate immune pathway has been linked to inflammatory conditions, yet its role in AAA remains unclear. Here, we combined single-cell transcriptomics, mouse models, pharmacological inhibition, and human tissue validation to investigate the role of this pathway in AAA. In murine single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data, cGAS-STING activation was predominantly observed in AAA endothelial cells (ECs). Human scRNA-seq and scissor-based classification of stable versus ruptured AAAs showed that cGAS and STING1 were significantly upregulated in ECs from ruptured AAA, implicating pathway activation in rupture risk. Bioinformatic analyses suggested that endothelial cGAS-STING activation correlates with barrier dysfunction and oxidative stress, and that dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) deficiency may link DNA damage to pathway activation. In Angiotensin II (Ang II) -induced murine AAA, cGAS, p-STING, and p-TBK1 were markedly elevated. Pharmacological blockade with RU.521 (cGAS inhibitor) or STING-IN-2 (STING antagonist) reduced AAA incidence, aortic dilation, and structural damage, while improving endothelial mitochondrial morphology. In human AAA tissues, immunohistochemistry (IHC) confirmed increased cGAS, STING, and TBK1 expression. Moreover, RU.521 or STING-IN-2 treatment of patient-derived 3D AAA organoids significantly downregulated cGAS, p-STING, and p-TBK1, confirming target engagement. Collectively, our findings indicate that the cGAS-STING pathway is activated in murine and human AAA, and that targeting this axis may offer a promising therapeutic approach to limit AAA progression.

title: VascFlux-GEO: Comparator selection and auditability in vascular transcriptome module prediction
authorString: You L, Peng Z, Guo Y, Shen L, Ge J.
abstractText:
ABSTRACT

Background

Mathematical coupling and comparator selection are established concerns when a transcriptome response is defined as follow-up minus baseline. We assessed whether apparent within-cohort improvement survives matched constant-follow-up and scalar-shrinkage controls, and whether specified evaluation faults are detectable in an auditable vascular transcriptome benchmark.

Results

Using eight frozen modules, 72 rosuvastatin pairs, 14 peripheral artery disease pairs, 20 repeated subject-held-out five-fold partitions, and 5,000 subject bootstrap draws of fixed losses, we compared 15 explicit specifications.
