Supporting post hoc analyses included 800 known-truth training/test simulations, annotation and input-ablation sensitivities, complete-tuning integrity checks, and an independent-source cross-sectional artery description. In GSE86216, nested follow-up ridge had lower observed repeated-CV mean absolute error than mean follow-up, 0.3280 versus 0.3405 (difference 0.0126; descriptive central 95% percentile range 0.0033–0.0224), while scalar shrinkage had lower observed error (0.3256). These ranges have no validated coverage guarantee. No full-matrix advantage was established; equivalence was not tested. In peripheral artery disease, nested ridge (0.3449) had slightly higher observed MAE than the median follow-up comparator (0.3409), and no advantage was established. Simulations illustrated how mean follow-up can outperform mean change without temporal signal, while the GSE281841 histological stenosis-grade description remained limited by anatomical imbalance, unconfirmed participant identity and an unresolved sample-count discrepancy.

Conclusions

These retrospective, nonconfirmatory comparisons show modestly lower observed within-cohort error than constant-follow-up controls in one cohort, without established full-matrix advantage. They do not partition prediction into mathematical, technical and biological components. Independent longitudinal validation and clinical utility remain unestablished.

title: Emergency thoracoabdominal aortic repair: distal-first approach with two previous aortic repairs.
authorString: Naruka V, Kumar U, Rasheed I, Lopez-Marco A, Adams B, Ye Oo A.

journal.title: Multimedia manual of cardiothoracic surgery : MMCTS

abstractText: Thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm repair after prior endovascular intervention is among the most technically demanding procedures in aortic surgery. We present an emergency thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm repair in a 59-year-old man with a history of preoperative haemodialysis, previous frozen elephant trunk for acute type A aortic dissection, followed by thoracic endovascular stent graft, complicated by partial spinal cord ischaemia and a type Ib endoleak. He presented with chest pain, and imaging demonstrated a 74 mm descending thoracic aortic aneurysm with impending rupture features. Multidisciplinary consensus deemed further endovascular intervention unsuitable, necessitating emergency open repair. A distal-first approach was used to overcome the distal perfusion challenges imposed by chronic aortic dissection. Following infrarenal clamping and the distal anastomosis to a branched graft, left heart bypass was established through its sidearm. Sequential visceral perfusion was performed, followed by anastomosis of the right renal and coeliac arteries to the graft branches. The proximal anastomosis incorporated both frozen elephant trunk and thoracic endovascular aortic repair, reinforced with double Teflon strips. The intercostal arteries were reimplanted. After declamping and de-airing, the superior mesenteric and left renal arteries were anastomosed. Motor-evoked potentials and cerebral monitoring were preserved. The patient recovered well and was discharged home 5 weeks postoperatively with a patent repair on imaging.

title: LGS modified aortic valve reimplantation with neosinus creation for aortic root aneurysm.
authorString: Mitar L, Svensson L.

journal.title: Multimedia manual of cardiothoracic surgery : MMCTS

abstractText: Valve-sparing aortic root replacement is an alternative to composite valve conduit replacement in patients with a morphologically preserved aortic valve and aortic root aneurysm or dilation. This video tutorial demonstrates a modified aortic valve reimplantation technique in which the aortic anulus is sized to the expected normal diameter for the patient's sex and body surface area, using a Hegar dilator as a sizing guide. The aortic valve is mobilized, and pledgeted sutures are passed from inside the left ventricular outflow tract through a straight polyester tube graft, then tied down around the appropriately sized Hegar dilator. This step reduces the annulus to a normal calibre and simultaneously creates neosinuses above the left ventricular outflow tract to accommodate cusp motion. The valve is sewn into the graft, commissures are resuspended as needed, and the neosinotubular junction is recreated by spacing the commissural sutures 4-5 mm apart. The coronary buttons are reimplanted, and the repair is completed with cardioplegia testing for valve competence. This technique has been used in over 500 patients with excellent mid- and long-term freedom from reintervention and low rates of residual aortic regurgitation.

title: Left Subclavian Artery Elongation Technique for a Child with a Vascular Ring.
authorString: Ueda H, Sasaki T, Suzuki K, Amitani R, Akitsuki H, Ishii Y.

journal.medlineAbbreviation: World J Pediatr Congenit Heart Surg
journal.title: World journal for pediatric & congenital heart surgery
journal.isoabbreviation: World J Pediatr Congenit Heart Surg

abstractText: A 4-year-old girl with a vascular ring formed by a Right aortic arch, aberrant left subclavian artery, left ligamentum, and Kommerell diverticulum underwent surgical repair. Although she initially had only mild symptoms, imaging studies during follow-up revealed progressive tracheal compression. Preoperative computed tomography revealed in addition an anomalous origin of the left vertebral artery from the left common carotid artery. Division of the ligamentum, resection of the Kommerell diverticulum, and reimplantation of the left subclavian artery into the left common carotid artery were performed. The anomalous left vertebral artery originating from the left carotid artery meant that the left subclavian artery when reimplanted had to be situated more proximally. Because of this anatomic variant the left subclavian artery was elongated in order to reach the left carotid artery. We describe that elongation technique. Postoperative imaging confirmed improvement in tracheal compression and a patent left subclavain artery. This case highlights a variation in the origin of the left vertebral artery, which required left subclavian artery extension, and a more proximal anastomosis on the left carotid artery.

title: A structured participatory approach to implementation priority setting for neurodevelopmental follow-up care in congenital heart disease
authorString: Donovan T, McPhail SM, Eagleson KJ, Justo R, White N, Sharma P, Parsonage W, Keating J, Abell B.
abstractText: Background: Approaches to prioritising implementation targets in healthcare remain underdeveloped, despite increasing recognition that implementation priorities should be co-created with stakeholders. There is limited guidance and empirical evidence on how to structure co-creation processes to identify and prioritise implementation needs. This study examined whether a structured participatory approach could co-create implementation priorities and how it aligned with established frameworks for successful priority setting and knowledge translation. The approach was trialled at a national meeting on neurodevelopmental follow-up care for children with congenital heart disease (CHD) in Australia. Methods: A mixed-methods study evaluated a multi-component participatory and co-creation process involving 53 stakeholders with lived, clinical, research, advocacy, and policy experience. The structured approach included presentations, a reflexive positionality exercise, 25/10 crowdsourcing, facilitated small-group discussions, an importance–feasibility matrix, and a next-steps panel. Data sources comprised meeting artefacts, 25/10 priority cards and scores, matrix ratings, researcher observations, and a post-event evaluation survey. Qualitative content analysis and descriptive statistics were used to examine the process, outputs, and alignment with conceptual frameworks for successful priority setting and knowledge translation. Results: The 25/10 activity generated 53 ideas, which were consolidated into 14 priorities for further deliberation. Participants rated the 25/10 method as highly acceptable and appropriate for early-stage priority setting, due to its inclusivity, efficiency, and ability to reduce dominant voices. The importance–feasibility matrix was considered somewhat appropriate, but offered limited discriminatory value, with most priorities clustering as high-importance/high-feasibility and substantial variability in feasibility ratings. Overall, the participatory approach aligned strongly with recognised process elements of successful priority setting, including transparency, stakeholder engagement, and information management, and also demonstrated key characteristics of knowledge translation platforms. Limitations included under-representation of some equity-related perspectives. Conclusion: A structured participatory approach can be used to co-create implementation priorities that are actionable, legitimate, and grounded in diverse forms of evidence and stakeholder experience. By combining priority setting with knowledge translation, the approach supported shared understanding, collective ownership, and the generation of contextually relevant priorities. Such approaches may offer a promising method for implementation priority setting in complex health service contexts, although further work is needed to examine downstream uptake, implementation outcomes, and equity-informed adaptation.

title: Multisystem effects of sacubitril/valsartan: clinical evidence, proposed mechanisms and limits of interpretation
authorString: Kasasbeh WH, Zainal H, M RA.
abstractText: Sacubitril/valsartan has established efficacy in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, while its peptide pharmacology has prompted interest in additional therapeutic uses. This structured narrative review evaluates metabolic, renal, inflammatory, fibrotic, vascular, cognitive and cardio-oncology evidence, distinguishing overall treatment effects from proposed mechanisms and evidence for a separate indication. A descriptive framework considers the population, comparator, endpoint, replication and limits of causal attribution. Secondary analyses of randomized heart failure trials show modest glycated haemoglobin reductions and slower estimated glomerular filtration rate decline, but do not establish direct tissue mediation or independent diabetes and kidney indications. UK HARP-III did not demonstrate superior measured filtration compared with irbesartan. Lipid effects are mixed, and most systemic antifibrotic and anti-inflammatory mechanisms remain experimental. Randomized cognitive assessments are reassuring within follow-up, without demonstrating neuroprotection. In cardio-oncology, favourable strain-based prevention outcomes coexist with the neutral primary ejection-fraction result in PRADA II. Vascular studies and PARADISE-MI further limit broad extrapolation from biological plausibility. The review contributes a consistent assessment of what each endpoint can establish, retaining neutral results and distinguishing repeated analyses from independent replication. Future applications require appropriate active comparators, prospective investigation of mediation, and clinically meaningful benefit assessed alongside treatment-related harm.

title: Eosinophilic myocarditis in platelet-derived growth factor receptor α-rearranged myeloid neoplasm with central nervous system involvement: a case report.
authorString: Aloini MC, Segreti A, Melfi R, Grigioni F.

journal.title: Monaldi archives for chest disease = Archivio Monaldi per le malattie del torace

abstractText: Eosinophilic myocarditis is a rare inflammatory condition caused by eosinophilic infiltration of the myocardium, often associated with systemic or hematologic disorders. We report a 31-year-old man with a newly diagnosed platelet-derived growth factor receptor α-rearranged myeloid neoplasm who presented with acute chest pain and elevated cardiac biomarkers. Echocardiography showed Loeffler-type apical involvement, coronary computed tomography angiography excluded obstructive coronary disease, and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) demonstrated acute non-ischemic inflammatory myocardial injury. During hospitalization, neurological symptoms revealed central nervous system involvement by the underlying myeloid neoplasm. Corticosteroids and targeted hematologic treatment resulted in marked clinical and radiologic improvement. On long-term follow-up, CMR showed normal cardiac function with complete resolution of the inflammatory myocardial abnormalities and no residual fibrosis. This case highlights the value of early multimodality cardiac imaging, etiologic diagnosis, and coordinated cardio-hematologic management in recognizing potentially reversible eosinophilic myocardial injury and limiting progression to irreversible cardiac sequelae.

title: An immediate reperfusion sign might increase the likelihood of favourable outcomes in patients with intracranial atherosclerotic disease-related stroke who received stent-retriever-based thrombectomy.
authorString: Wen W, Cui Y, Lin T, Kong X, Du B, Duan W, Zhang X, Han X, Wang W, Xuan X, Lu D, Yu Y, Liu Y, Cai Y, Liu L, Du J.
abstractText:
Objects

To investigate the relationship between the presence of an "immediate reperfusion sign (IRS)" during retrievable stent-based thrombectomy and clinical outcomes in patients with large vessel-occluded acute ischaemic stroke related to intracranial atherosclerotic disease (ICAD) treated with stent retrievers.

Methods

Consecutive ICAD-LVO stroke patients who were treated with stent retrievers and whose imaging records were available for the assessment of the IRS were included. The sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values of the IRS for predicting favourable outcomes were calculated. Univariate analysis and partial correlation analysis were also performed.

Results

Eighty-two ICAD-LVO patients were identified from 421 endovascularly treated AIS patients from 2015 to 2024. Fifty-four of them were ultimately included in the analysis, and an IRS was observed in 41 of these patients (75.9%). Favourable outcomes were significantly more frequent in the IRS (+) group (51.2% versus 7.7%, p=0.005). The sensitivity of the IRS for predicting favourable outcomes was 95.5% (21/22), the specificity was 37.5% (12/32), the positive predictive value was 51.2% (21/41), and the negative predictive value (NPV) was 92.3% (12/13). Additionally, the presence of an IRS, as well as age, baseline NIHSS score and successful final reperfusion, was significantly different between the favourable and unfavourable groups. Partial correlation analysis revealed a moderate correlation (r=0.412; p=0.002) between the comprehensive reperfusion score (in which the presence of an IRS and successful final reperfusion was counted as 1 point) and favourable outcomes.

Conclusion

In our respective cohort of patients, the presence of an IRS during stent-retriever-based thrombectomy appeared to indicate a higher rate of first-pass-effect and a 3-month favourable outcome in acute LVO stroke patients with ICAD.

title: Renal Denervation to Enable Kidney Transplant Listing in Resistant Hypertension Patient on Hemodialysis.
authorString: Desai Y, Ghaner A, Galo J, German C, Bernardo N, Taylor A, Hashim H, Waksman R, Case BC.
abstractText:
Background

Hypertension is often poorly controlled in patients with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and evidence for renal denervation in this population remains limited.

Case summary

We describe a 38-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis because of thrombotic microangiopathy who developed refractory hypertension with recurrent hypertensive emergencies despite 6 antihypertensive agents and aggressive ultrafiltration, precluding kidney transplant listing. After a thorough secondary hypertension work-up, he underwent off-label catheter-based bilateral renal denervation, after which his blood pressure improved substantially, hypertensive emergencies ceased, and he was subsequently added to the transplant waitlist.

Conclusion

Renal denervation may serve as adjunctive therapy to help dialysis patients with resistant hypertension reach transplant candidacy.

Take-home messages

Understand the limitations of pharmacologic and dialytic therapy for blood pressure control in dialysis-dependent patients. Appreciate how refractory hypertension may serve as a barrier to kidney transplant listing and how renal denervation may address it.

title: Topological dependent modifications of gene expression in the preeclamptic placenta under aspirin treatment.
authorString: Vaiman D, Benouda I, Miralles F, Guerby P, Gascoin G, Dubusc C, Attal J, Gonzalez Matatoros S, Mehats C, Hansson SR.
abstractText: Preeclampsia is a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy characterized by systemic endothelial dysfunction and placental inflammatory activation. Low dose aspirin reduces preeclampsia incidence when initiated early, yet its molecular effects on the diseased human placenta remain poorly defined. We performed a topologically resolved transcriptomic analysis of placentas from two independent cohorts of preeclamptic women treated or not with aspirin. Placental samples were obtained either from the villous surface (syncytiotrophoblast rich) or from deep parenchymal regions (stromal and endothelial rich). In villous samples, microarray profiling identified 1,836 differentially expressed genes, predominantly down regulated. Gene set enrichment demonstrated marked suppression of pathways central to hypertensive placental pathology, including TNFα/NF κB signaling, hypoxia responsive programs, glycolysis, and estrogen response cascades. RNA seq analysis of parenchymal samples identified 645 differentially expressed genes, again dominated by down regulation of cell cycle progression, mTORC1 signaling, inflammatory pathways, and metabolic stress responses. Across cohorts, 116 genes were consistently down regulated by aspirin and enriched for hypoxia, NF κB, estrogen response, and inflammatory signatures. Promoter analysis implicated transcription factors central to vascular inflammation and stress signaling, including NF κB1, RELA, HIF1A, PPARG, and PARP1. Functional validation in BeWo trophoblasts confirmed aspirin dependent modulation of key placental transcripts and altered secretion of MMP9, ANGPT2, and soluble endoglin (sENG) molecules directly implicated in endothelial dysfunction and hypertensive disease. These findings demonstrate that aspirin attenuates core inflammatory, hypoxic, and metabolic pathways across multiple placental lineages in preeclampsia, providing a mechanistic framework linking early aspirin administration to improved vascular and placental adaptation in hypertensive pregnancy. The action of aspirin upon differentiation of trophoblasts contribute to explain why aspirin protects only when administered early in pregnancy, before the end of the first trimester.

title: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase mediates atherosclerosis progression by regulating copper metabolism <i>via</i> PHOX2A.
authorString: Xue Q, Feng G, Hu J, Li F, Tang S.
abstractText: Atherosclerosis (AS) is a major cardiovascular disease whose underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This study investigates the role of dopamine beta-hydroxylase (DBH) in AS pathogenesis and its regulation of copper metabolism via the transcription factor PHOX2A. Through transcriptomic profiling of aortic tissues from ApoE⁻/⁻ mice fed a high-fat diet, we identified 2891 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between AS and control mice, with DBH being significantly upregulated. DBH expression was also elevated in the serum of AS patients and in ox-LDL-treated human vascular smooth muscle cells (HVSMCs). Mechanistically, we demonstrate that PHOX2A directly activates the DBH promoter, and that DBH knockdown attenuates ox‑LDL‑induced apoptosis and lipid accumulation in HVSMCs while PHOX2A overexpression exacerbates these effects. Importantly, DBH knockdown in ApoE⁻/⁻ mice not only reduced atherosclerotic plaque burden and improved serum lipid profiles but also restored serum copper concentrations and altered the expression of cuproptosis‑related proteins (FDX1, LIAS, DLAT). These findings identify DBH as a key mediator of AS progression linked to PHOX2A‑dependent regulation of copper metabolism and cuproptosis, suggesting that targeting the DBH/PHOX2A axis may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for AS.

title: A re-tightening suture technique for hemostasis during aortic root remodeling in chronic DeBakey type II aortic dissection.
authorString: Aratame A, Kunihara T, Kaku D, Baba T.
abstractText: We report a 45-year-old man with chronic DeBakey type II aortic dissection, a sinus of Valsalva aneurysm, and severe aortic regurgitation. His atopic dermatitis remained poorly controlled despite topical corticosteroids and injectable anti-inflammatory therapy and he occasionally experienced cutaneous bleeding from unconscious scratching during sleep. He therefore wished to avoid long-term anticoagulation. Valve-sparing root replacement using root remodeling with external annuloplasty was performed. Bleeding from the proximal continuous suture line was controlled using a re-tightening suture technique that lifted the bleeding point, facilitated placement of an additional mattress suture, and secured the redundant continuous suture under renewed tension. Postoperative imaging showed satisfactory root geometry and no residual aortic regurgitation. This technique may provide a simple and reproducible method for controlling difficult suture-line bleeding during root remodeling.

title: Orthotopic heart transplantation associated with hemiarch reconstruction for advanced heart failure and chronic aortic dissection: a case report.
authorString: Sánchez OE, Pérez-Ariza V, Cruz Buitrago RH, Parra JF, Rios W, Nuñez F.
abstractText: Concomitant orthotopic heart transplantation and aortic arch replacement are extremely rare, particularly in chronic Stanford type A dissection. A 43-year-old man with end-stage heart failure and chronic aortic dissection underwent combined orthotopic heart transplantation and hemiarch replacement. Because of concomitant liver donation, the donor inferior vena cava required pericardial patch reconstruction. Despite early right ventricular dysfunction requiring veno-arterial ECMO, the patient recovered completely and was discharged with preserved graft function. This case demonstrates the feasibility of a single-stage combined approach with excellent postoperative outcomes in carefully selected patients.

title: Outcomes of Handmade Tri-leaflet ePTFE Valved Conduits for RVOT Reconstruction: A Propensity-Matched Analysis Compared with PVR.
authorString: Masaki N, Koizumi J, Yamazaki Y, Edaki D, Saito K, Sato A, Takizawa Y, Nakano S, Saiki H, Ikai A, Kin H.
abstractText: We aimed to evaluate the long-term durability and valve function of handmade expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) valved conduits of different calibers and compare their outcomes with those of bioprosthetic pulmonary valve replacement (PVR). We retrospectively reviewed 100 patients undergoing RVOT reconstruction between 2007 and 2025: 66 with ePTFE conduits and 34 with bioprosthetic valves. Patients were categorized into small-conduit, large-conduit, and PVR groups. Propensity score matching was performed to adjust for baseline differences. Mean age was 1.6 ± 1.8, 11.2 ± 6.5, and 26.3 ± 16.9 years in the small-conduit, large-conduit, and PVR groups, respectively (p < 0.0001). Ten-year survival was similar among groups (100%, 100%, and 97%; p = 0.19). In contrast, the small-conduit group showed significantly lower freedom from RVOT reoperation than the large-conduit and PVR groups (53%, 85%, and 93%; p < 0.001), driven by progressive pulmonary stenosis (10-year freedom from moderate pulmonary stenosis: 9%, 55%, and 58%; p = 0.01). Freedom from moderate pulmonary regurgitation remained comparable (80%, 94%, and 85%; p = 0.37). In the matched cohort, conduit and PVR groups demonstrated similar freedom from reoperation (94% vs. 89%; p = 0.34), with numerically better valve function in the conduit group. In conclusion, large-caliber handmade ePTFE valved conduits demonstrated favorable long-term durability, with outcomes comparable to PVR in adolescent- and adult-sized patients. They may be a reasonable option for selected younger patients requiring redo RVOT reconstruction.

title: Effect of Activin Type II Receptor Signaling in Patients With HFpEF and Pulmonary Hypertension: A Critical Analysis of Biological Mechanisms and Clinical Trials.
authorString: Packer M, Gomberg-Maitland M, Tedford RJ, Langleben D, Vachiery JL, Borlaug BA.
abstractText: The totality of evidence indicates that the mechanisms underlying the increase in pulmonary vascular resistance in patients with combined postcapillary and precapillary pulmonary hypertension (CpcPH) associated with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) differ meaningfully from those responsible for the increase in pulmonary vascular resistance in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension. CpcPH-HFpEF is a complex disorder involving the pulmonary veins, left atrium, and pulmonary arterioles, but recent evidence has highlighted a potentially central role for pulmonary venous and left atrial (LA) dysfunction. Epicardial adipose tissue occupies anatomical proximity to both structures, allowing derivative secretory products to influence their structure and function. The most well-characterized proinflammatory adipokine released from an expanded epicardial fat mass is activin A, which causes fibrosis and cardiomyocyte stiffness and senescence in underlying tissues by signaling through activin type II receptor signal transduction. Such signaling regulates pulmonary venular responses to mechanical stretch, and circulating activin A is elevated in patients with HFpEF who have enlarged LA chambers, pulmonary venous hypertension and increased pulmonary vascular resistance. The adipokine hypothesis of HFpEF identified activin A and activin type II receptor signaling as key adipokine mediators in the pathogenesis of HFpEF. Experimentally, activin A signaling promotes the development of both atrial myopathy and HFpEF, and activin type II receptor ligand traps alleviate HFpEF and ameliorate both the pulmonary vascular and left heart abnormalities in experimental models in which CpcPH-HFpEF is induced by obesity. These collective observations led to the prospective hypothesis that adipokine modulation by sotatercept would mediate benefits on the left heart in patients with CpcPH-HFpEF. These expectations were validated when the CADENCE trial showed that sotatercept decreased both pulmonary artery wedge pressures and left atrial volume index in patients with CpcPH-HFpEF, which are effects that could not explained by a decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance. Activin A released from an expanded epicardial adipose tissue promotes both pulmonary venous and left atrial remodeling and fibrosis in vivo, which (in turn) are effects that can be attenuated by an activin A decoy. The efficacy of sotatercept to slow the progression of CpcPH-HFpEF is now being tested in a phase III outcomes trial.

title: Aqueous Extract of <i>Lonicerae japonicae</i> Flos Attenuates Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease by Suppressing Oxidative Stress and Inflammation in Mice.
authorString: Chen L, Zhang M, Zhao D, Wang X, Kang C, Qu X, Dong H, Li Q, Li J.
abstractText: Objectives: This study employed an integrative strategy combining UPLC-MS-based phytochemical profiling, network pharmacology, and transcriptomics to systematically investigate the protective effects and potential mechanisms of LJF against ALD. Methods: An ALD model was established via chronic ethanol liquid diet feeding combined with acute ethanol binge administration over 16 days. Liver function, lipid metabolism, oxidative stress (OS), and inflammatory markers were assessed. UHPLC-Q Exactive HFX MS analysis was performed to tentatively annotate the chemical constituents of LJF. Candidate targets and active constituents were predicted by network pharmacology integrated with transcriptomics, followed by experimental validation using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) and Western blot. Results: LJF extract significantly alleviated ALD, as evidenced by decreased serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, reduced hepatic total cholesterol (TC), triglyceride (TG), and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels, and improved histopathological changes. LJF attenuated oxidative stress by lowering reactive oxygen species (ROS) and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels while elevating superoxide dismutase (SOD) and glutathione (GSH) levels. Furthermore, LJF suppressed inflammatory responses by reducing IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α levels. Integrative analyses pinpointed Hif1a, Ppara, Cyp2b10, Chac1, Nupr1 and Saa1/2, among others, as key targets, with luteolin, apigenin, isorhamnetin, lonicerin, 5-O-caffeoyl shikimic acid, and caffeic acid as major bioactive constituents. Mechanistically, LJF concurrently restored the Nrf2/HO-1 antioxidant defense and suppressed the p38 MAPK/NF-κB pro-inflammatory axis, thereby exerting a dual regulatory effect on redox homeostasis and immune response. Conclusions: These findings establish LJF as a promising multi-target agent against ALD and, more importantly, provide correlative evidence for the involvement of Nrf2/HO-1 regulation and p38 MAPK/NF-κB signaling modulation, which may guide future strategies for ALD pharmacotherapy.

title: Shared Genetic and Regulatory Architecture of Congenital Heart Disease and Autism Spectrum Disorder Revealed by Cross-Tissue Multi-Omic Integration.
authorString: Zhu M, Zhang JF, Hu SX, Wang X, Xu W.
abstractText: Background: Congenital heart disease (CHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) co-occur more frequently than expected, suggesting shared developmental susceptibility. We aimed to identify cross-tissue molecular candidates linking cardiac and neurodevelopmental abnormalities. Methods: CHD- and ASD-associated genes were curated from MalaCards and SFARI Gene, and their intersection was defined as the CHD- and ASD-associated gene set (CAGES). Shared gene enrichment was assessed against the human protein-coding genome. CHD and ASD genome-wide association data were integrated with heart and brain cis-expression quantitative trait loci using Bayesian colocalization and summary data-based Mendelian randomization with HEIDI testing. Candidates were further evaluated using bulk transcriptomics, six machine learning feature selection methods, independent cohorts, and scTenifoldKnk virtual knockout analyses in developing human heart and cerebral cortex. Results: Seventy-three genes were shared between CHD and ASD. CHD7 showed suggestive colocalization for CHD and ASD, while lower genetically predicted CHD7 expression was associated with higher odds of both disorders, with nonsignificant HEIDI tests. MEF2C was downregulated in tetralogy of Fallot myocardium and selected by all six ASD machine learning methods, with consistently lower expression in ASD. CAGES-derived signatures discriminated independent CHD, ASD cord blood, and cortical cohorts. CHD7 virtual knockout analysis identified MEF2C as a computationally predicted regulatory candidate in the prenatal brain, particularly in late-fetal excitatory neurons and intermediate progenitor cells, with cell-type-specific predicted effects also observed in the developing heart. Conclusions: CHD and ASD share molecular susceptibility involving pleiotropic developmental mechanisms. CHD7 and MEF2C emerge as connected cross-tissue candidates across complementary genetically informed, transcriptomic, and developmental regulatory analyses, highlighting prenatal neuronal populations and developmental windows for investigating the heart-brain axis.

title: Structural Fetal Anomalies Identified During First-Trimester Screening: A Single-Centre Experience in Romania.
authorString: Mureșan MC, Mureșan MB, Dumitrașcu Biriș D, Cîtu IC.
abstractText: Background and Objectives: The 11-13+6-week scan has evolved from a nuchal translucency (NT) measurement into an early anatomical survey, and the anomalies it identifies increasingly shape prenatal counselling and management. Data from Central and Eastern European screening populations are scarce. Materials and Methods: Retrospective cohort of all pregnancies undergoing first-trimester combined screening in a single fetal medicine centre in Romania between August 2009 and April 2026, with a crown-rump length of 45-84 mm. The centre provides routine screening but also receives women referred after an abnormal finding elsewhere; the cohort is therefore described as a screening population with referral enrichment. Structural anomalies recorded prospectively in the ultrasound database at the first-trimester scan were classified by organ system and by first-trimester detectability category. NT, combined risk, karyotype and pregnancy outcome were extracted from the same database. Associations were quantified with odds ratios (OR) from logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors by woman. Results: 11,229 pregnancies (10,015 women; 408 multiple pregnancies) were included. A structural anomaly was identified at 11-13+6 weeks in 197 (17.5 per 1000; 95% CI 15.3-20.1); 16.1 per 1000 (13.8-18.7) after exclusion of the years 2009-2012 and 16.9 per 1000 (14.6-19.5) in singleton pregnancies. A further 44 pregnancies had isolated cystic hygroma/hydrops or soft markers only. Cardiac defects (81; 7.2 per 1000) and abdominal-wall defects (74; 6.6 per 1000, of which 67 exomphalos) were present in 145 pregnancies (74%), followed by central nervous system (27), facial (23), skeletal (23), thoracic (10) and urogenital (10) anomalies; 37 pregnancies (19%) had anomalies in two or more systems. NT ≥ 3.5 mm was present in 59/197 (30%) anomalous versus 203/11,032 (1.8%) non-anomalous pregnancies (OR 22.8, 95% CI 16.3-31.9), and in 51% of cardiac defects. Among 37 karyotyped fetuses, 15 (41%) had a chromosomal abnormality. Pregnancy outcome was known for 87 anomalous pregnancies: 46 terminations, 33 live births and 8 fetal or neonatal deaths; 17 of 30 exomphalos cases with known outcome were live-born. Conclusions: In a screening population with referral enrichment, about 1 in 57 pregnancies had a structural anomaly identified at the 11-13+6-week scan, dominated by cardiac and abdominal-wall defects; the figure describes prenatally identified anomalies in this setting and is not a population-based prevalence. One third of these fetuses had increased NT and a high proportion of those tested had an abnormal karyotype, supporting the integration of systematic anatomical assessment and genetic evaluation into first-trimester screening.
