In the lung, influenza sustained a CXCR3-driven chemokine storm, comprehensive Th1, Th17, and exhaustion T-cell activation programs, coordinated monocyte recruitment through Ccl2 , Ccl7 , Ccl8 , and Ccl12 , a broad acute phase response including Saa3 and A2m , alveolar identity collapse through loss of Nkx2-1 and surfactant proteins, and broad metabolic dysregulation involving suppression of fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial function, and circadian metabolic regulators. In the aorta, influenza drove macrophage and DAMP activation through Trem1 , Fpr2 , and S100a8 , cytotoxic T-cell engagement, smooth muscle cell dedifferentiation through Myocd loss, convergent bioenergetic failure, and an ectopic lung-identity gene signature representing a previously undescribed cross-organ communication mechanism. Circadian clock and Hippo/YAP pathway suppression were shared across both tissues, identifying systemic vulnerabilities connecting pulmonary infection to vascular structural compromise. Consistent with the in vivo findings, influenza-infected Apoe −/− bone marrow-derived macrophages exhibited inflammasome activation, DAMP amplification, M1 polarization, and suppression of prostaglandin-mediated inflammatory resolution. Together these findings define a lung-to-aorta inflammatory and metabolic axis driving atherosclerotic plaque destabilization during the post-infection recovery period and identify CCR2/CXCR3 antagonism, NLRP3 inhibition, and YAP pathway activation as candidate therapeutic interventions.

Influenza infection drives atherosclerotic plaque destabilization

title: Chronic Q fever prosthetic valve endocarditis with a retained pacemaker: multidisciplinary and infection prevention considerations
authorString: Im* CR, Kappeler ARM, Allen O, Pocock J, Alam R, Williams L, Odone J, Warne B, De Silva R, Pai* S.
abstractText:
Introduction:

 Chronic Q fever, caused by Coxiella burnetii, is an important cause of culture-negative infective endocarditis, particularly in patients with congenital valvular disease or prosthetic valves. Clinical presentation is often insidious, and diagnosis is challenging, relying predominantly on serology and molecular diagnostics.  Case presentation: A man in his 60s with a bioprosthetic aortic valve for prior bicuspid aortic valve disease and a permanent pacemaker was referred after an incidental echocardiographic abnormality. He reported several years of non-specific symptoms but was afebrile at presentation, and multiple blood cultures yielded no clinically significant pathogen. Imaging demonstrated severe paravalvular regurgitation and dehiscence of the prosthetic aortic valve, prompting redo aortic valve and aortic root replacement. Cultures of the excised valve remained negative, while broad-range 16S rRNA polymerase chain reaction identified C. burnetii. Serology supported a diagnosis of Q fever endocarditis, with a phase I IgG titre of 1:10,240. Following diagnosis, the specialist Q fever multidisciplinary team (MDT) recommended pacemaker retention following a risk-benefit assessment, alongside 24 months of doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine, with a minimum of 18 months. At four-month follow-up, antibody titres remained unchanged, while C-reactive protein had normalised.   Conclusion: This case illustrates the difficulty of diagnosing C. burnetii prosthetic valve endocarditis in the absence of classical clinical features. The postoperative diagnosis also raised challenges regarding pacemaker retention and potential occupational exposure during surgery, emphasising the importance of detailed occupational history-taking and early consideration of Q fever in culture-negative endocarditis.

title: Bridging the Atlantic: converging paths, diverging approaches: a comparative review of the 2025 European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society focused update and the 2026 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association guideline on dyslipidaemia management.
authorString: Miteva K, Mach F.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

The global burden of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) drives lipid-lowering strategies, now undergoing their biggest transformation since statins. In 2025 and 2026, the two most influential guideline bodies, the European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) and the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), both released updated guidance that reflects evolving clinical evidence. This review provides a detailed, head-to-head examination of their recommendations, highlighting areas of convergence, divergence, and the clinical implications for practitioners on both sides of the Atlantic.

Recent findings

The 2025 Focused Update of the 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the Management of Dyslipidaemias builds incrementally on an established framework, incorporating new trial data within its existing risk-stratified, target-driven model. In contrast, the 2026 ACC/AHA Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidaemia represents a comprehensive rewrite, introducing a novel risk calculator, reinstating explicit LDL-C targets for all risk categories, and endorsing a more flexible, individualized selection of nonstatin therapies.

Summary

Both documents embrace the 'lower is better' and 'strike early and strong' paradigms, yet they differ profoundly in how they apply these principles. The review distinguishes the ESC/EAS's structured, stepwise approach from the ACC/AHA's flexible, individualized paradigm (Graphical abstract).

title: Coronary artery calcium scoring and coronary computed tomography angiography in familial hypercholesterolemia: current evidence and future directions.
authorString: de Sousa LMF, Cramer SHM, Schonck WAM, Nurmohamed NS.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

Familial hypercholesterolemia is a prevalent genetic disorder characterized by lifelong elevated LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C), resulting in increased risk of premature atherosclerosis and cardiovascular events. General and familial hypercholesterolemia-specific risk scores (SAFEHEART-RE, Montreal-FH, and FH risk score) are insufficient to capture the interindividual variability in cardiovascular risk. Current guidelines and consensus statements recognize the potential value of coronary computed tomography in familial hypercholesterolemia, although specific guidance on timing and modality remains limited. This review evaluates the evidence and role of coronary artery calcium scoring (CACS) and coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) for improved cardiovascular risk stratification and therapeutic guidance.

Recent findings

Although elevated CACS is highly prevalent among patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) and homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HoFH), younger familial hypercholesterolemia patients may exhibit exclusively noncalcified plaque, and because most are treated with statins, which may increase coronary calcification, CACS should be interpreted with caution. CCTA provides comprehensive assessment of plaque burden, stenosis, and high-risk features, which are associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes. CCTA may support therapy intensification by identifying patients with substantial coronary plaque burden, while the absence of detectable atherosclerosis should not justify withholding guideline-recommended lipid-lowering therapy (LLT).

Summary

CCTA may provide additional information on atherosclerotic burden in familial hypercholesterolemia. In HeFH, evidence is currently insufficient to support routine CCTA screening at specific ages or intervals. CCTA at approximately 30 years of age in men and 40 years of age in women may represent a proposed strategy requiring prospective evaluation. In children with HoFH, screening is recommended at least once after the age of 3. Follow-up imaging should be individualized according to clinical indication, imaging findings, treatment response and radiation-associated risks.

title: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis after pembrolizumab-based chemoradiotherapy for cervical cancer: A case report.
authorString: Makita C, Yin L, Kobayashi S, Kajiura Y, Tanaka O, Matsuo M.

journal.title: Journal of infection and chemotherapy : official journal of the Japan Society of Chemotherapy

abstractText: Listeria monocytogenes is a major cause of invasive infections in individuals with impaired cell-mediated immunity. Recently, the combination of pembrolizumab with concurrent chemoradiotherapy has been established as the standard treatment for high-risk, locally advanced cervical cancer. Nevertheless, characterization of severe infections that occur during this treatment regimen remains inadequate. Herein, we report a case of L. monocytogenes meningitis that occurred during pembrolizumab-based chemoradiotherapy for cervical cancer. A 45-year-old woman with no underlying medical conditions was diagnosed with p16-positive cervical squamous cell carcinoma, involving the pelvic, para-aortic and left supraclavicular lymph nodes. The patient received concurrent chemoradiotherapy with weekly cisplatin and pembrolizumab every 3 weeks. On day 44, after receiving 50.4 Gy of external beam radiotherapy, she developed febrile neutropenia with a temperature of 40.1 °C, white blood cell count of 600/μL, absolute neutrophil count of 408/μL, and worsening diarrhea. She was treated with cefepime, and blood and urine cultures were negative. Immune-related adverse events, including endocrine disorders, were considered unlikely. After clinical improvement, she completed the concurrent chemoradiotherapy phase. On day 73, the patient presented with headache, nausea, and vomiting. Cerebrospinal fluid examination revealed neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein levels, and hypoglycorrhachia. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid cultures yielded L. monocytogenes. She was treated with ampicillin and gentamicin for 3 weeks and recovered. Thus, fever during pembrolizumab-based chemoradiotherapy should not be solely attributed to immune-related adverse events. Severe infections, including Listeria meningitis, should be considered when fever or neurological symptoms occur, particularly in patients with myelosuppression, immune dysregulation, or gastrointestinal toxicity.

title: Inferoseptal Recess Anatomy Predicts Conduction Disturbances After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
authorString: Guan Y, Yan H, Yang L, Pang G, Wang R, Wang X, Liu S, Song J, Shan X, Qiao F, Song Z, Bai Y, Jin Z, Guo Z, Zhu N.

journal.title: Hellenic journal of cardiology : HJC = Hellenike kardiologike epitheorese

abstractText:
Background

New-onset conduction disturbances (CDs) remain the most frequent and clinically relevant complications after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). The anatomical mechanisms underlying conduction injury are not fully understood. This study aimed to investigate the association between inferoseptal recess (ISR) anatomy and post-TAVR conduction disturbances, and to validate its predictive value using an interpretable machine learning algorithm.

Methods

This retrospective study included 307 patients who underwent TAVR between 2017 and 2024. Pre-procedural computed tomography (CT) was used to quantify ISR morphology and aortic root anatomy. The primary endpoint was new-onset CDs (bundle branch block, high-grade atrioventricular block, or need for permanent pacemaker implantation). Machine learning algorithms were applied to integrate CT-derived anatomical and clinical variables and to validate the predictive value of ISR metrics, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) applied for interpretability.

Results

CDs occurred in 57 of 307 patients (18.6%). Wider WOISR (per 1-mm increment) was independently associated with reduced risk of CDs (OR: 0.76, 95% CI 0.66-0.89; P<0.001), along with counter-clockwise aortic root rotation (OR: 0.91, [95% CI, 0.87-0.95]; P<0.001), smaller ΔMSID (OR: 0.83, [95% CI, 0.76-0.91]; P<0.001), larger left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (P=0.004), with pre-existing right bundle-branch block (P<0.001). Among ML models, the RF model achieved an AUC of 0.91 in the temporal holdout cohort and showed favorable net benefit across a range of clinically relevant threshold probabilities. SHAP analysis identified non-coronary sinus calcification score, LVEDD, and WOISR as dominant contributors to model output.

Conclusions

WOISR (≤4 mm) is an anatomical predictor of CDs following TAVR. WOISR was independently associated with post-TAVR conduction disturbances and provided incremental discriminatory information beyond established clinical predictors. These findings support further prospective evaluation of ISR morphology as a complementary component of CT-based conduction-risk assessment before and after TAVR.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps drive immunoinflammatory remodeling in abdominal aortic aneurysm: from inflammatory amplification to precision therapy.
authorString: Wang L, Zhu J, Li Y, Zhu Z.

journal.title: Translational research : the journal of laboratory and clinical medicine

abstractText: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a chronic vascular disorder characterized by progressive aortic wall dilation, extracellular matrix degradation, and an increased risk of catastrophic rupture. Currently, no effective pharmacological therapy is available to prevent or slow AAA progression. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) have emerged as a critical pathological platform linking dysregulated innate immunity to vascular structural deterioration. In the AAA microenvironment, local inflammation, oxidative stress, metabolic disturbances, altered mechanical forces, and platelet activation collectively contribute to the induction of NETosis. Persistent NET formation promotes immunoinflammatory remodeling of the aortic wall by activating inflammatory sensing pathways, including TLR9, cGAS-STING, and NLRP3, modulating macrophage responses, inducing vascular smooth muscle cell ferroptosis and phenotypic switching, and exacerbating proteolytic degradation, oxidative injury, and immunothrombotic responses. During disease progression, NETs may transition from early drivers of inflammatory amplification to sustained regulators of vascular remodeling, while in advanced AAA they may synergize with intraluminal thrombus formation and structural destabilization to accelerate disease progression. Circulating NET-associated biomarkers represent promising candidates for complementing conventional imaging-based risk assessment; however, their specificity and predictive value require further validation. Therapeutic strategies targeting PAD4-mediated NET formation, the oxidative metabolic environment, NET-associated effector molecules, DNase I-mediated NET degradation, and nucleic acid sensing pathways have demonstrated potential in preclinical studies. This review systematically summarizes the emerging roles of NETs in AAA pathogenesis and discusses future precision strategies integrating biomarkers, multi-omics profiling, and imaging-based risk stratification with stage-specific therapeutic interventions.

title: Novel LOX Start-Loss Variant Mimicking Arterial Tortuosity Syndrome in Neonatal Cutis Laxa: A Diagnostic Challenge.
authorString: Sinha P, Holla V, Rawat KS, Aggarwal N, Joshi R, Gahlot A, Puri RD, Yadav A.
abstractText: Cutis laxa comprises a group of rare connective tissue disorders characterized by loose, inelastic skin due to defects in elastic fiber formation, with autosomal recessive forms presenting early with multisystem involvement. Recently, biallelic variants in the LOX gene have been proposed to cause a severe form of autosomal recessive cutis laxa (ARCL), although evidence remains limited. We report a neonate with generalized cutis laxa, dysmorphic features, and extensive vascular abnormalities. Imaging revealed marked tortuosity of the aortic arch, descending thoracic aorta, cervical arteries, and pulmonary arteries, along with involvement of the systemic venous system. Whole exome sequencing identified a homozygous start-loss variant in the LOX gene, predicted to result in loss-of-function. The patient remained under cardiology follow-up but succumbed at 2 years of age. Lysyl oxidase plays a critical role in collagen and elastin cross-linking within the extracellular matrix, and its disruption provides a plausible mechanism for the observed phenotype. While previously reported cases have described predominantly arterial involvement, the additional presence of venous tortuosity in our patient expands the phenotypic spectrum of this emerging entity. This report adds to the limited evidence supporting LOX as a candidate gene for ARCL and highlights the importance of molecular diagnostics in delineating rare connective tissue disorders.

title: Hemodynamic Analysis of a Repaired Ascending Aorta with Preserved Aortic Root.
authorString: Zhai H, Chen Y, Kitada Y, Takayama H, Vedula V.
abstractText:
Purpose

To evaluate the hemodynamic impact of restoring a normal sino-tubular junction (STJ) following a novel Hegar dilator-based procedure in patients undergoing root-sparing ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) repair using computational modeling.

Methods

We retrospectively selected an ATAA patient who underwent pre- and postoperative gated computed tomography angiography (CTA). We developed a novel workflow to segment the lumen, thick-walled aorta, and aortic valve from CTA images for subsequent blood flow analysis using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and fluid-structure interaction (FSI). Morphological and hemodynamic characteristics of the root were quantified and compared against those of a control subject. Sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate the impact of graft properties, leaflet material parameters and heterogeneity, wall compliance, external tissue support, and solid domain annular boundary conditions.

Results

Both CFD and FSI results showed that the postoperative geometry reconstructed with a normal STJ profile reintroduces sinus vortices during peak systole, similar to the control subject, which were absent pre-surgery. Accounting for aortic valve leaflets in FSI studies yielded a similar spatial patterning of the high-velocity jet and wall shear stress compared to the CFD data. However, FSI resulted in substantially elevated velocities, time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS), and energy dissipation, likely due to the dynamically changing orifice area and differing profiles of the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT).

Conclusion

We demonstrated that restoring a normal sinus shape and STJ profile during ascending aortic repair may have potential hemodynamic benefits. The study also highlights the model's sensitivities, particularly the LVOT shape and leaflet morphology and mobility, and may assist planning STJ reconstruction to yield optimal hemodynamics before intervention.

title: Predicting Post-TEVAR Endoleaks: A Pre-operative Hemodynamic Risk Factor from Patient-Specific Fluid-Structure Interaction Simulations.
authorString: Duca F, Tavarone S, Domanin M, Bissacco D, Trimarchi S, Vergara C, Migliavacca F.
abstractText:
Purpose

Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) is a minimally invasive treatment for thoracic aortic pathologies, including thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA). Computational simulations can provide valuable insights into TEVAR outcomes and complications before intervention. This proof-of-concept study proposes a novel risk factor R as a potential predictor of post-TEVAR type I and III endoleaks (ELs) using pre-TEVAR hemodynamic data.

Methods

Fluid-structure interaction (FSI) computational simulations are performed in ten pre-TEVAR patient-specific TAA cases, with known follow-up TEVAR outcomes. Hemodynamic drag forces acting on the aortic wall are quantified and used to define R, which combines parallel and perpendicular drag force components with aortic tortuosity. The patient cohort is divided into a calibration set, used to associate specific R values with three different risk levels, and a test set, used to preliminarily assess the agreement between the predictions derived from R and the post-TEVAR follow-up outcomes.

Results

Based on the R values obtained for the calibration set, R ≤ 0.33 is associated with low risk of EL formation, 0.33 < R ≤ 0.67 with moderate risk, and R > 0.67 with high risk. Once it is applied to the test set, the risk factor is able to correctly identify a type I EL.

Conclusion

The risk factor proposed in this work is capable of identifying all the EL cases analyzed. This study represents a preliminary attempt to determine whether pre-TEVAR hemodynamics can effectively predict post-TEVAR complications and therefore aid clinicians in the pre-operative planning.

title: A splenic reservoir of pro-angiogenic neutrophils supports blood flow recovery after peripheral tissue ischemia
authorString: Amoedo-Leite C, Parv K, Seignez C, Seidler A, Ermesjö H, Pavliuk O, Prendes CF, Mani K, Lindsay R, Christoffersson G, Wanhainen A, Phillipson M.
abstractText:
Background

Neutrophils accumulate at sites of ischemic injury, where a distinct subset characterized by CD49d + CXCR4 hi VEGFR1 hi expression promotes angiogenesis and contributes to blood flow recovery. This study investigated the function, origin, and recruitment mechanisms of these pro-angiogenic neutrophils (PANs) in a murine model of hindlimb ischemia and explored whether a corresponding population responds to acute ischemia in humans.

Methods

Using spectral flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry, PANs and classical neutrophils were characterized in ischemic gastrocnemius muscle following hindlimb ischemia in mice. Blood flow recovery was assessed by laser speckle flowmetry. To determine the origin and mobilization mechanisms of PANs, splenectomy, chemical sympathectomy with 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA), and surgical splenic denervation were performed. Translational studies examined blood samples collected during elective abdominal aortic aneurysm repair to assess PAN mobilization following acute lower limb ischemia induced by aortic cross-clamping.

Results

PANs rapidly accumulated in ischemic muscle through a CD49d-dependent mechanism, and blockade of CD49d impaired blood flow recovery. During homeostasis, PANs were maintained within a splenic reservoir and were rapidly released into circulation following ischemia. Splenectomy and disruption of splenic sympathetic signaling significantly reduced PAN recruitment to ischemic tissue and impaired functional recovery. Mobilization was driven by ischemia-induced sympathetic activation, which decreased CXCL12 levels in the splenic red pulp, disrupting CXCR4-mediated PAN retention. In humans, a phenotypically similar PAN population was identified in peripheral blood, which increased rapidly following lower limb ischemia during aortic cross-clamping. The speed of this response is consistent with release from an extramedullary reservoir, although its anatomical source remains unknown.

Conclusion

These findings identify the spleen as a reservoir of pro-angiogenic neutrophils in mice and reveal a neuroimmune mechanism regulating their mobilization and recruitment after ischemic injury. The rapid appearance of PAN in human circulation after acute ischemia suggests that comparable extramedullary neutrophil reservoirs may also exist in humans.

title: Venous excess ultrasound score (VExUS) in pediatrics: venous flow patterns and inferior vena cava-to- aorta ratio in healthy children
authorString: Gómez-Sánchez R, Clavero-Adell M, Alonso-Ojembarrena A, Boldova VE, Palanca-Arias D.
abstractText: Purpose Venous excess ultrasound score (VExUS) assesses systemic venous congestion using inferior vena cava (IVC) diameter and abdominal venous Doppler patterns, both of which remain poorly defined in children. This study aimed to define their physiological features in healthy children to assess VExUS applicability in pediatrics and explore specific criteria and potential thresholds for its interpretation. Methods Healthy children aged 1 month to 14 years were prospectively recruited at a single center and stratified by age and body surface area (BSA). Abdominal ultrasound was performed to assess IVC and aortic diameters together with hepatic, portal and intrarenal venous Doppler patterns in relation to anthropometric variables. Results A total of 101 healthy children were included. Venous Doppler patterns were broadly comparable to those described in normovolemic adults and consistent with physiological venous flow. IVC diameter increased with age, from 4.4 mm [3.6–5.9] in children aged 0–2 years to 12.9 mm [10.6–15.5] in adolescents. Aortic diameter also increased with growth but showed lower variability. Vascular diameters correlated significantly with anthropometric variables, with no sex-related differences. The median IVC/Ao ratio was 0.959 (95% CI 0.898–1.035), remaining close to 1 and becoming relatively more stable with increasing age and BSA. Conclusion Venous Doppler patterns in healthy children were broadly comparable to those described in adults, supporting the potential applicability of VExUS in pediatrics. Although vascular diameters were influenced by growth, the IVC/Ao ratio appeared relatively more stable beyond childhood. These findings provide a physiological reference framework for pediatric VExUS and suggest that age or BSA-adjusted criteria will be required for its implementation in children.

title: Multi-institutional assessment of practice patterns in the use of cardiovascular magnetic resonance and computed tomography for pulmonary valve replacement planning: A survey-based study.
authorString: Alloah Q, Fishbein J, Cohen J, Christopher A, Beroukhim RS, Lee S, Han BK, Rajagopal HG.

journal.title: Journal of cardiovascular magnetic resonance : official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance

abstractText:
Background

Consensus documents provide recommendations on using cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) and cardiovascular computed tomography (CCT) in pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) planning in congenital heart disease (CHD). However, clinical practice patterns across institutions remain unclear, particularly with the increase in transcatheter PVR options and multi-modality imaging use. We aimed to characterize practice variation in cross-sectional imaging using CCT and CMR.

Methods

A REDCap survey was distributed to Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance and Society of Cardiovascular Computed Tomography members to assess imaging practices for PVR planning in CHD, including imaging volumes, acquisition protocols, right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) measurement techniques, and reporting times, with one response per institution. Wilcoxon rank sum tests, Fisher's exact tests, and analysis of variance were used.

Results

Forty-three institutions (84% US and 16% international) responded. Most centers (29/43, 67%) reported performing CMR first, adding CCT only if the Harmony valve or Alterra pre-stent was under consideration. Only two centers (5%) used CCT without CMR as their standard practice. CCT was performed instead of CMR in patients with pacemakers or intracardiac leads (28/38, 74%). 88% of centers perform functional CCT, with 44% reporting ventricular volumes and function. Eight centers (19%) used a focused field of view on the RVOT, and branch pulmonary arteries, excluding the ventricles. RVOT measurement techniques varied: 84% of centers used angulated multiplanar reformats (MPR) and 28% used centerline technique/curved planar reformats (CPR). 88% used MPR-derived diameters and 24% used perimeter-derived area and average diameters. For CMR, only six centers (14%) reported using a non-gadolinium-based superparamagnetic iron oxide contrast agent. 30% of centers reported performing dedicated RVOT short-axis cine sequences and 16% reported utilizing 4D flow or 3D models. Median reporting times were 60minutes (IQR 60-90) for CCT and 120minutes (IQR 80-142) for CMR with dedicated technologist support available in 14 (33%) for CCT, and 15 (35%) for CMR. Overall, 84% favored a standardized imaging protocol and/or reporting template for PVR planning.

Conclusion

This survey highlights wide variations in imaging practices for PVR planning, with most respondents supporting standardization, which may improve efficiency, quality, and potentially reduce radiation burden in this specific patient population.

title: Tetrahydrobiopterin restores oligodendrocyte maturation after hypoxic white matter injury by reprogramming translational output
authorString: Sarić N, Antonios I, Heiser K, Ballard A, Miller K, Mansoor I, Rajtboriraks MT, Chandran S, Goldstein E, Ishibashi N.
abstractText:
ABSTRACT

Background

Complex congenital heart defects (CHDs) are frequently associated with chronic cerebral hypoxemia, leading to impaired white matter maturation. One proposed mechanism involves hypoxia-induced disruption of the nitric oxide synthase cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), resulting in oxidative stress and impaired oligodendrocyte (OL) development. While our previous studies found BH4 supplementation improves hypoxia-induced white matter dysmaturation, the molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Because OL maturation requires coordinated translational control, we hypothesized that BH4 promotes white matter maturation by restoring translation programs disrupted by hypoxia.

Methods

Translating Ribosome Affinity Purification sequencing (TRAP-seq) was performed on OL lineage cells isolated from transgenic ribosomal reporter mice exposed to chronic hypoxia (10.5% O₂, postnatal day 3–11) with or without daily BH4 treatment. Differential translation, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, pathway enrichment, RNAscope, and immunohistochemistry identified translational programs associated with hypoxia and BH4-mediated rescue.

Results

Developmental hypoxia extensively altered the OL translatome, suppressing transcripts associated with OL maturation while enriching pathways related to translational regulation and cellular stress. Network analyses identified BH4-responsive gene modules enriched for OL maturation, protein metabolism, and translation-related processes. BH4 partially reversed hypoxia-induced translational changes, restored OL maturation gene expression, and normalized nuclear localization of the lineage regulator OLIG1, consistent with recovery of maturation-associated regulatory programs.

Conclusions

Developmental hypoxia disrupts OL maturation through coordinated alterations in ribosome-associated gene expression and post-transcriptional regulatory pathways. BH4 promotes recovery of OL maturation programs, including restoration of translation-related networks and OLIG1 nuclear localization, providing mechanistic insight into BH4-supported white matter maturation under chronic hypoxic conditions.

Research Perspective

What New Question Does This Study Raise?

Developmental hypoxemia in congenital heart disease remodels the oligodendrocyte translatome, raising the question of whether translational dysregulation represents a fundamental and therapeutically targetable mechanism underlying white matter dysmaturation in other forms of perinatal brain injury.

What Question Should Be Addressed Next?

Future studies should determine how BH4 restores ribosome-associated translation of oligodendrocyte maturation programs, establish whether these molecular changes increase myelin protein synthesis and improve long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes, and define the cross-species efficacy for clinical translation.

Clinical Research Implication

These findings provide a mechanistic rationale for evaluating BH4 as a neuroprotective adjunct therapy to preserve white matter development in fetuses and infants with congenital heart disease experiencing chronic cerebral hypoxemia.

title: Acute effects of cardioneuroablation on ventricular arrhythmia inducibility and refractoriness in patients with functional bradyarrhythmias. The Roman 4 study.
authorString: Sikorska A, Nowinski A, Niedzwiedz M, Krynski T, Gawalkiewicz-Mazanska A, Baran J, Kulakowski P.
abstractText:
Background

Cardioneuroablation (CNA) is a promising method to treat functional bradyarrhythmias. However, whether CNA-induced decrease in the parasympathetic drive to the heart may occur proarrhythmic in the future is not known.

Objective

To assess acute effects of CNA-induced total vagal denervation on QT interval as well as invasively measured ventricular effective refractory period (VERP), ventricular action potential duration (VAPD) and vulnerability to ventricular arrhythmias.

Methods

CNA was performed using anatomical approach by means of electro-anatomical mapping and intracardiac echocardiography. Intra-procedural efficacy was assessed using extracardiac vagal stimulation. QTc and QTd intervals were measured from surface ECG. VAPD and VERP were measured from ablation electrode in right ventricle. Measurements were performed at four time-points: at baseline, immediately after CNA, after atropine injection, and finally after isoproterenol bolus.

Results

80 patients (51 females, mean age 42 ± 14 years) underwent CNA. Polymorphic ventricular tachyarrhythmias were induced in 2 females who had pre-existing cardiac conditions. Changes in QTc depended on the method used for correction. Using the Bazett formula, QTc was significantly prolonged, however using the Framingham, Fridericia and Hodges corrections, these changes were much less pronounced or non-significant. QTd remained unchanged across all measurements. The VERP and VAPD values remained unchanged after CNA and after atropine whereas they became significantly shorter following isoproterenol injection.

Conclusion

The present study did not demonstrate evidence of acute electrophysiological changes suggesting increased ventricular arrhythmogenicity after CNA in patients without structural heart disease. However, long-term follow-up is needed to confirm lack of proarrhythmic effects of CNA.
