title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists and Risk of Arrhythmias: A Network Meta-Analysis.
authorString: Barbosa LM, Rodrigues Oliveira VM, Ruelas MG, Nascimento BR, Moreira HG, Nunes MDCP, Darrieux F, Lopes RD, Boriani G, Lip GYH.
abstractText:
Background

Arrhythmias are often associated with comorbidities such as diabetes and obesity, which significantly influence their onset and progression. In this context, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have garnered attention for their potential benefits, with emerging evidence indicating that GLP-1 receptor activation might offer antiarrhythmic effects.

Objectives

This study aimed to evaluate the impact of all GLP-1 RAs and co-agonists on the incidence of new-onset arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation (AF).

Methods

A comprehensive search of databases was conducted from inception to December 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) focusing on patients with diabetes or obesity receiving GLP-1 RAs or co-agonists. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. Interventions were ranked using the p-score cumulative rank, ranging from 0 (worst) to 1 (best).

Results

A total of 94 RCTs involving 155,989 patients were included, comparing 12 GLP-1 RAs and co-agonists. Subcutaneous semaglutide emerged as the most effective intervention, significantly reducing AF incidence compared with placebo (RR 0.82; 95% CI: 0.68 to 0.99), and compared with tirzepatide (RR 0.57; 95% CI: 0.37 to 0.88). In contrast, dulaglutide was associated with an increased risk of AF, while lixisenatide was associated with a decreased risk in atrioventricular blocks. For AF, semaglutide presented a p-score of 0.7885, while tirzepatide and dulaglutide scored 0.1830 and 0.1750, respectively.

Conclusion

Among GLP-1 RAs and co-agonists, subcutaneous semaglutide is highlighted as the most effective intervention for reducing the risk of AF. Further studies focusing on arrhythmic outcomes are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Emerging insights into amino acid metabolism in the heart: implications for cardiovascular diseases and therapeutic targeting.
authorString: Azam T, Zhang H, Zi M, Chen C, Wu J, Papapetropoulos A, Wang X.
abstractText: As a metabolically versatile organ, the heart is capable of generating energy from a wide range of substrates. Although fatty acid and glucose metabolism in the heart have been extensively studied, the contribution of amino acid metabolism to cardiac physiology and disease is gaining increasing attention. A range of amino acids, including branched-chain amino acids, glutamine and glutamate, asparagine, glycine, tryptophan and alanine, play integral roles in signalling pathways that orchestrate key adaptive and maladaptive changes in the myocardium, under both physiological and pathological stress. Dysregulation of these pathways is associated with cardiovascular disease such as heart failure, hypertension, myocardial infarction and atherosclerosis, via mechanisms involving impaired mitochondrial function, oxidative stress and inflammation. This review provides a comprehensive overview of amino acid metabolism in the heart, including sulphur amino acids, their role in relation to cardiovascular disease and emerging therapeutic strategies targeting amino acid metabolism in the heart. Finally, this review also discusses current and ongoing clinical trials targeting amino acid metabolism with the aim of finding potential therapeutic targets in cardiovascular disease.

title: [LDL-c and residual cardiovascular risk in patients with coronary artery disease].
authorString: de Saint Nicolas T, Dromas H, Lemesle G.
abstractText: In secondary prevention, current therapeutic management of dyslipidemia primarily aims to reduce low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-c) levels, as LDL-c is a major driver of atherosclerosis. Elevated LDL-c levels are also one of the main modifiable cardiovascular risk factors. LDL-c lowering is directly, proportionally, and linearly associated with a reduction in cardiovascular events, with no apparent threshold effect. However, patients with chronic coronary syndrome or those who have recently experienced an acute coronary event are still generally undertreated and achieve guideline-recommended targets in only one out of four cases. This article aims to explore the underlying causes of and potential solutions to this therapeutic gap, which is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Treatment adherence varies considerably across studies (randomized controlled trials or real-life studies), as well as across geographical settings, and appears to be approximately 60%. However, non-adherence to treatment alone does not explain the low proportion of patients achieving LDL-c treatment targets, which remains at approximately 25%. The underlying reasons are complex and multifactorial. Paradoxically, although the expanding therapeutic armamentarium allows for increased substantial LDL-c reductions, this has not translated into a corresponding improvement in target attainment. Therapeutic inertia may arise at the patient, physician, and healthcare system levels. Furthermore, patient education and the therapeutic alliance should remain central to patient management and should be regularly reinforced and individualized.

title: Lifetime Management of Aortic Stenosis: Expert Review of Evidence and Consensus Guidelines.
authorString: Centofanti P, Rinaldi M, Di Eusanio M, D'Onofrio A, Gerosa G, Lodo V, Pacini D, Salizzoni S, Stefano P, Pilato M, Italian Cardiac Surgery Working Group.
abstractText:
Background

The 2025 European Society of Cardiology/European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery Guidelines introduced a Class I recommendation for transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) in selected patients aged 70 years or older with tricuspid aortic stenosis and suitable anatomy, while surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) remains recommended in younger low-risk patients. In patients with long expected survival, this framework requires careful consideration of valve durability, future reintervention, and patient preferences. This expert review, developed by the Italian Cardiac Surgery Working Group, examines contemporary evidence and consensus recommendations from a lifetime-management perspective.

Methods

We performed a narrative, evidence-based synthesis of randomized trials, trial-based meta-analyses, and propensity-matched real-world registries comparing transfemoral TAVI and SAVR, with primary emphasis on low-risk patients. Lower-intermediate-risk evidence was included only when directly relevant to lifetime management, durability, or reintervention.

Results

Evidence suggests that treatment effects are time-dependent: early non-inferiority of TAVI may attenuate with longer follow-up, particularly in patients with substantial life expectancy. Randomized durability data remain limited, whereas propensity-matched real-world registries have suggested possible higher late mortality after TAVI in younger, lower-risk populations. Reintervention after a transcatheter-first strategy may be associated with increasing technical complexity and procedural risk over time.

Conclusions

This review supports appropriate application of current guidelines through a pragmatic framework for individualized, Heart Team-based decision-making. Transfemoral TAVI is often appropriate in patients with limited life expectancy or recognized high surgical risk when anatomically feasible. In patients with long expected survival, SAVR should retain a central role as an important reference strategy.

title: Targeting Apolipoprotein C-III in Hypertriglyceridemia: Implications for Pancreatitis and Cardiovascular risk.
authorString: Zimerman A, Marston NA.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

Apolipoprotein C-III (apoC-III) has emerged as a validated target for lowering triglycerides, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, and remnant cholesterol. This review summarizes the biology of apoC-III, the genetic and clinical trial evidence supporting its inhibition, and remaining questions.

Recent findings

Loss-of-function variants in APOC3 are associated with lower levels of triglycerides and reduced cardiovascular risk. Pharmacologic inhibition of apoC-III with RNA-based agents has led to substantial reductions in apoC-III and triglycerides across familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS), severe hypertriglyceridemia (sHTG), and moderate hypertriglyceridemia (mHTG). In FCS, agents volanesorsen, olezarsen, and plozasiran have demonstrated reductions in triglycerides and acute pancreatitis. In sHTG, olezarsen has extended this benefit to a larger, multifactorial population. In mHTG, olezarsen and plozasiran lower triglycerides, remnant cholesterol, non-HDL-cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B, but an imaging study with olezarsen demonstrated neutral findings on coronary plaque composition, and cardiovascular event reduction has not been demonstrated. ApoC-III inhibition provides a potent strategy for lowering triglycerides and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Its most immediate clinical role is in FCS and sHTG, where prevention of acute pancreatitis is the main objective. Its future as a cardiovascular therapy will depend on whether reductions in remnant cholesterol and apolipoprotein B translate into fewer atherosclerotic events in a dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial.

title: From structural repair to biomechanical compatibility: Aortic stiffness after open and endovascular aortic repair.
authorString: Moothathamby T, Jubouri M, Kayali F, Roy S, Roy S, Mohammed I, Williams IM, Bailey DM, Bashir M.
abstractText: Evaluation of aortic repair has traditionally prioritised perioperative safety, exclusion of the diseased segment and durability. As endovascular treatment expands to younger patients, attention is turning towards the biomechanical compatibility of prosthetic grafts with the native aorta. Native aortic compliance supports Windkessel function, whereas grafts create a compliance transition that may accelerate pulse-wave transmission, alter wave reflection and increase left-ventricular load. This narrative review distinguishes established evidence from emerging concepts after open surgical repair, endovascular aneurysm repair and thoracic endovascular aortic repair. Carotid-femoral pulse-wave velocity (cfPWV) is the accepted reference non-invasive measure of regional aortic stiffness; cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR)-derived segmental pulse-wave velocity and distensibility provide complementary information. Brachial-ankle pulse-wave velocity, the cardio-ankle vascular index, and augmentation index assess different territories or haemodynamic properties and are not interchangeable with cfPWV. Left-ventricular strain and mass are downstream cardiac outcomes. Clinical evidence generally reports increases in measured arterial-stiffness indices after endovascular repair, whereas findings after open repair are heterogeneous. Treatment length, landing-zone location, oversizing, anatomy and baseline vascular phenotype may be as important as graft fabric or stent-frame category. Conflicting comparisons of polyester and expanded polytetrafluoroethylene arise from small, non-randomised studies using non-equivalent endpoints and do not support a reliable ranking of commercial devices. Emerging 4D-flow CMR, simulation and compliant graft materials illustrate a shift from structural exclusion alone towards compliance-aware repair, but evidence of improved outcomes remains insufficient. Future studies should use standardised longitudinal stiffness, blood-pressure and cardiac assessments and relate biomechanical changes to hypertension, ventricular remodelling and cardiovascular outcomes.

title: Factors Associated With Primary Patency Loss After Covered Endovascular Reconstruction of the Aortic Bifurcation for Aortoiliac Occlusive Disease: An Individual Patient Data Meta-analysis.
authorString: IJgosse WM, Holewijn S, Reijnen SEJ, de Cort BA, Zacà S, Borghese O, Giudice R, Fujihara M, Kruszyna Ł, Reijnen MMPJ.

journal.title: Journal of endovascular therapy : an official journal of the International Society of Endovascular Specialists

abstractText:
Background

Covered endovascular reconstruction of the aortic bifurcation (CERAB) has emerged as an endovascular treatment option for complex aortoiliac occlusive disease (AIOD). However, factors associated with loss of patency remain insufficiently defined. This individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis evaluated outcomes after CERAB and identified factors associated with loss of primary patency.

Methods

Six retrospective CERAB datasets including 412 patients treated for symptomatic AIOD between 2009 and 2021 were identified through systematic literature review, harmonized, and merged. The primary outcome was loss of primary patency. Secondary outcomes included primary-assisted patency, secondary patency, freedom from target lesion revascularization, morbidity, mortality, and functional outcomes. Kaplan-Meier analysis estimated patency and survival, while Cox proportional hazards regression identified factors independently associated with primary patency loss.

Results

Technical success was achieved in 405/412 procedures (98.3%). Primary patency was 90.9% at 1 year and 76.8% at 5 years, whereas secondary patency remained greater than 95% throughout follow-up. Factors independently associated with loss of primary patency were younger age (hazard ratio [HR], 0.96/year; P < .001), Rutherford category 4 to 6 (HR, 2.06, P = .034), and prior target-area revascularization (HR, 2.44; P = .006). Freedom from target lesion revascularization was 91.8% at 1 year and 80.1% at 5 years. Perioperative complications occurred in 10.4% of patients, and 30-day mortality was 1.0%. Ankle-brachial index and Rutherford classification improved significantly within 30 days, although long-term functional follow-up was limited by incomplete data.

Conclusions

Covered endovascular reconstruction of the aortic bifurcation was associated with favorable mid-term patency, low perioperative morbidity, and meaningful early clinical improvement in patients with complex AIOD. Younger age, advanced Rutherford category, and prior target-area revascularization were independently associated with loss of primary patency.Clinical ImpactThis individual participant data meta-analysis moves beyond descriptive outcome reporting by identifying clinically relevant factors associated with patency loss after covered endovascular reconstruction of the aortic bifurcation for aortoiliac occlusive disease. It identifies younger age, advanced Rutherford stage, and previous target-area revascularization as factors associated with loss of primary patency. These findings add granularity to the existing CERAB literature and may help refine patient selection, inform counseling, and support more individualized follow-up strategies.

title: Characterization and treatment of ischemic stroke in patients with infective endocarditis: a meta-analysis.
authorString: Werring N, Bonberg N, Heidenreich A, Beuker C, Noblejas-Sanchez G, Oswald M, Royl G, Wagner-Altendorf TA, Zeller T, Stiermaier T, Eitel I, Katalinic A, Minnerup H, Minnerup J.
abstractText:
Background

Ischemic stroke is a common and serious complication of infective bacterial endocarditis. This study aimed to characterize the frequency, clinical and pathological features, treatment strategies, and outcomes of patients with stroke due to infective endocarditis.

Methods

We systematically searched PubMed from database inception to October 2022 for studies reporting on stroke in patients with infective endocarditis and performed a meta-analysis.

Results

A total of 122 studies comprising 270,211 patients with infective endocarditis were included. Ischemic stroke occurred in 21% and hemorrhagic stroke in 5% of patients. Stroke was observed in 32% of patients with mitral valve endocarditis, 25% with aortic valve, and 11% with tricuspid valve endocarditis. Stroke was associated with significantly higher mortality (OR 2.35; 95%CI 1.74-3.16). Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species were most frequently associated with stroke (33% and 25%, respectively). The risk of stroke did not differ significantly between patients with and without pre-existing antithrombotic therapy (37% vs. 24%; OR 1.24, 95%CI 0.75-2.06). Successful reperfusion was achieved in 80% of patients undergoing mechanical thrombectomy, although mortality remained high at 49%.

Conclusions

Stroke is a common complication of infective bacterial endocarditis and has a substantial impact on patient outcomes. It occurs most frequently in patients with mitral valve endocarditis and in those with infections caused by staphylococcal pathogens. Stroke risk was not reduced in patients with pre-existing antithrombotic therapy, supporting discontinuation where no other indication exists. Mechanical thrombectomy in patients with endocarditis-related large vessel occlusion achieves high recanalization rates; however, overall clinical outcomes remain poor in this population.

title: Early mitophagy defects and impaired mitochondrial energy metabolism drive target organ damage progression: Lessons from the Fabry heart.
authorString: Gambardella J, Fiordelisi A, Cerasuolo FA, Buonaiuto A, Avvisato R, Viti A, Sommella E, Campiglia P, D'Argenio V, Prevete N, Pezone A, D'Apice S, Altobelli GG, Varzideh F, Pande S, Paolillo R, Perrino C, Riccio E, Pisani A, Bianco A, Sadoshima J, Spinelli L, Santulli G, Sorriento D, Iaccarino G.
abstractText: Increasing evidence supports a pathogenic role for impaired energy metabolism in organ damage. Genetic diseases provide opportunities to investigate these mechanisms, as exemplified by Fabry disease (FD), caused by an α-galactosidase A (GLA) deficiency and globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) accumulation, with cardiomyopathy as the leading cause of death. Beyond Gb3 storage, impaired energy metabolism may contribute to cardiomyopathy. Here, we demonstrate mitochondrial dysfunction in FD heart and its therapeutic targeting. Using a humanized FD mouse model (R301Q-Tg/GLA knockout), embryonic fibroblasts, and neonatal and adult cardiomyocytes, we found impaired mitophagy and mitochondrial respiration, increased reactive oxygen species, and a vicious cycle aggravating lysosomal dysfunction. These defects progressed with age, causing accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria, energetic failure, apoptosis, cardiac hypertrophy, and diastolic dysfunction. L-arginine, promoting NO/PGC-1α-dependent mitochondrial rescue, prevented cardiac abnormalities. Our findings identify mitochondrial dysfunction as a key driver of FD cardiomyopathy and reveal the lysosome-mitochondria axis as a targetable pathway in FD and beyond.

title: Computational Fluid Dynamics Simulations Provide Insights into the Paradox of Newer Prosthetic Aortic Valves.
authorString: Linker DT.
abstractText:
Background

Patient-prosthesis mismatch (PPM) is defined by the estimated orifice area divided by body surface area (BSA), or iEOA. Small iEOA predicts poor outcomes with surgical bioprosthetic valves (SBV), but balloon-expandable valves (BEV) and self-expanding valves (SEV) have more variable results.

Objectives

Assess effect of geometry of the valve on overestimation of gradients and methods for adjusting for body size other than BSA.

Methods

Computational fluid dynamic simulations of SBV, BEV and SEV, with 25 different variations of anatomic and valve sizes for each valve type determined peak stenosis velocity and peak and total valve gradients. The relationship between stroke volume and body size measures was analyzed using data from the Atherosclerosis Risk In Communities study.

Results

Doppler peak velocity correctly estimated the total gradient for SBV (slope = 1.01) but overestimated the gradient for BEV (slope = 1.19) and SEV (slope = 1.42). The gradient across the valves varied even with identical dimensions, with SBV being highest, BEV lower, and SEV lowest. BSA had a fair correlation with stroke volume (r = 0.6030), but lean body mass (r = 0.6494) and fat-free mass (r = 0.6631) were better and left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) area was best (r = 0.7570).

Conclusions

Geometry of the valve has a major impact on hemodynamics with very different results with identical dimensions. LVOT area was better way to adjust for body size than BSA. Two measures based on LVOT velocity and area are proposed as an alternative to implement these results. If these findings are confirmed with in-vitro and in-vivo studies, the approach could allow more accurate prediction and evaluation of PPM.

title: Nanoparticles for cardiovascular diseases: identifying and overcoming barriers in translating preclinical success to clinical applications.
authorString: Ahmadi A, Refaat A, Miao K, Vidallon MLP, McFadyen JD, Wang X, Peter K.
abstractText: Nanoparticles (NPs) have emerged as versatile platforms for drug delivery in cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), demonstrating robust efficacy in preclinical models by stabilizing atherosclerotic plaques, promoting safe and efficient thrombolysis, and mitigating ischemia-reperfusion injury. These advances highlight the maturation of cardiovascular nanomedicine; however, translation to clinical practice remains limited. This gap between laboratory success and clinical adoption reflects broader challenges in nanomedicine design, including suboptimal delivery to diseased tissues, limited efficacy of single therapeutic payload-based strategies in addressing the multifaceted inflammatory pathways driving CVDs, NPs' immunogenicity, and scale-up feasibility. Addressing these barriers is particularly critical in CVDs, where therapeutic success depends on precise engagement with multiple molecular and cellular drivers of disease. This review discusses the evolving landscape of cardiovascular nanomedicine, focusing on four aspects. First, we highlight advances in NPs bioengineering strategies, such as refined targeting moieties, optimized physicochemical properties, and responsiveness to endogenous and external stimuli that enhance organ- and cell-specific delivery in atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, and stroke. Second, we discuss analytical innovations that improve characterization and control of NPs' biodistribution, enabling more rational targeting. Third, we evaluate therapeutic payloads, emphasizing how RNA-based and immunomodulatory agents represent a meaningful step toward clinical translation. Fourth, we outline approaches to addressing persistent challenges in safety and scalable manufacturing. Together, these developments establish a foundation for translating NP design principles into practical cardiovascular therapies. With continued progress in targeted delivery, clinical safety, and production scalability, cardiovascular nanomedicine is increasingly well-positioned to translate preclinical advances to transformative patient outcomes.

title: Outcomes of Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome by Subtype and Presence of Ventriculocoronary Connections: A Fetal Heart Society Multicenter Retrospective Study.
authorString: Barris DM, Freud LR, Day PE, Morris SA, Lopez KN, Kavanaugh-McHugh A, Killen SAS, Peyvandi S, Nuñez Gallegos F, Moon-Grady AJ, Ro SS, McBrien A, Hornberger LK, Lee CK, Hogan WJ, Reeder RW, Chelliah A, Howley LW, Arya B, Keller SB, Krishnan A, Donofrio MT, Taylor C, Husain N, Lemley BA, Ronai C, Zinis S, Tworetzky W, Ikemba CM, Gonsalves C, Geiger MK, Duong SQ, Cohen J.
abstractText:
Background

Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is classified by anatomic subtype: mitral atresia and aortic atresia (MA/AA), mitral stenosis and aortic atresia (MS/AA), and mitral stenosis and aortic stenosis (MS/AS). The MS/AA subtype is associated with ventriculocoronary connections (VCCs). We assessed whether specific HLHS subtypes are associated with an increased risk of mortality and whether this risk is stratified by VCCs identified during fetal or postnatal echocardiography. We also assessed whether the type of neonatal intervention performed modified the risk.

Methods

We performed a multicenter retrospective cohort study of fetuses and infants <2 months old with HLHS who were admitted between January 2012 and December 2016 to participating Fetal Heart Society institutions. Clinical and demographic data were collected. Fetal and transthoracic echocardiograms from a subset of patients with MS/AA and those with suspected VCCs were reviewed. Cox proportional hazards analysis was performed, controlling for cardiac center (random effect), birth weight, genetic diagnosis, extracardiac malformation, and restricted/intact atrial septum.

Results

Among 16 centers, 591 patients were born alive with intention to treat. MA/AA was the most common subtype (261, 44%), followed by MS/AA (200, 34%) and MS/AS (130, 22%). Of those with MS/AA, 115 (58%) had suspected VCCs. Median follow-up was 9.0 (interquartile range: 7.0, 10.8) years. Overall transplant-free survival (TFS) was 55.6% at 5 years and 49.4% at 10 years. When comparing MA/AA, MS/AS, and MS/AA with and without VCCs (reference group: MS/AA without VCCs), MS/AA with VCCs had the lowest TFS (hazard ratio [HR], 1.69 [1.12, 2.57]; 5-year TFS, 44.7%; 10-year TFS, 40.3%). This was followed by MA/AA (HR, 1.40 [0.95, 2.05]; 5-year TFS, 54.1%; 10-year TFS, 46.6%). Survival of MS/AA without VCCs (5-year TFS, 60.4%; 10-year TFS, 56.9%) was similar to MS/AS (HR, 0.91 [0.59, 1.41]; 5-year TFS, 65.0%; 10-year TFS, 58.3%). Among those with a prenatal diagnosis of HLHS (n=532), patients with MS/AA and VCCs suspected on fetal echocardiogram had a lower TFS compared with those with MS/AA without fetal suspicion for VCCs (HR, 1.79 [1.12, 2.85]). Fetal echocardiography was used to diagnose VCCs in 33 of 103 (32%) cases with MS/AA and VCCs suspected postnatally. Of patients with MS/AA and VCCs, type of stage I palliation was not associated with TFS (P=0.784).

Conclusions

In a large, multicenter cohort of HLHS patients, the MS/AA subtype with VCCs had the lowest TFS. Prenatal diagnosis of VCCs was associated with a lower TFS. This study underscores the prognostic value of assessing for VCCs in patients with HLHS both before and after birth.

title: Patterns of Postdischarge Heart Failure, Ischemic, and Bleeding Events After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
authorString: Okita S, Kitahara H, Kuji H, Miyakoda K, Toishi R, Kanda T, Saito Y, Tanaga K, Nakamura Y, Matsuura K, Kobayashi Y.
abstractText:
Background

Although outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) have improved, heart failure (HF) hospitalization, ischemic events, and major bleeding remain clinical challenges in patients with severe aortic stenosis.

Objectives

The objective of the study was to evaluate the incidence, timing, and prognostic impact of these events after TAVR.

Methods

This two-center retrospective registry included 988 patients with severe aortic stenosis who underwent TAVR. Patients were grouped according to the first clinical event after discharge: HF hospitalization, ischemic events (myocardial infarction or ischemic stroke), major bleeding, or the event-free group. The timing of the first postdischarge event and all-cause mortality after the first event were evaluated.

Results

During a median follow-up of 665 days after discharge, 165 patients (16.7%) experienced any of these events. As first events, HF hospitalization, ischemic events, and major bleeding occurred in 80 (8.1%), 32 (3.2%), and 53 (5.4%) patients, respectively, whereas 823 (83.3%) were in the event-free group. Among patients with a first postdischarge event, major bleeding occurred earliest among the 3 event groups. One-year all-cause mortality after the first event was high across groups (HF hospitalization, 31.5%; ischemic events, 30.4%; major bleeding, 25.4%).

Conclusions

Among patients who experienced a first postdischarge event after TAVR, major bleeding occurred earlier than HF hospitalization or ischemic events. Once a first postdischarge event occurred, subsequent all-cause mortality was high across the 3 event groups. These findings suggest that event timing should be considered and careful clinical reassessment may be warranted when a first postdischarge event occurs after TAVR.

title: Sca1⁺ stem cells contribute to β-Aminopropionitrile-exacerbated aortic aneurysm progression in marfan syndrome.
authorString: Gao Q, Cao X, Wang AA, Long C, Zhuang X, Wang Z, Wei Z, Zhang T, Yu B.
abstractText: Aortic aneurysm and dissection (AAD) is the major cause of mortality in patients with Marfan syndrome (MFS), with no currently available effective therapies. FBN1 mutations disrupt extracellular matrix homeostasis through impaired microfibril function, leading to aberrant matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) activity and compensatory lysyl oxidase (LOX) upregulation. Although the β-Aminopropionitrile (BAPN) induced mouse model is widely used to study aortic aneurysms, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we show that BAPN treatment exacerbates aortic aneurysm progression in MFS mice by increasing collagen production, promoting MMP expression and reducing LOX expression in Sca1<sup>+</sup> stem cells, promoting Sca1<sup>+</sup> stem cells differentiation towards synthetic vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) and inhibiting their differentiation into contractile VSMCs and activating the Smad2/3 signaling pathway through increasing TβR1 (TGF-β receptor 1) level and Smad2/3 phosphorylation. Our study highlights the critical role of Sca1⁺ stem cells in the pathological process of vascular remodeling and provides new insight into how their dysfunction contributes to aortic disease. Restoring stem cell reparative function represents a promising therapeutic avenue for treating aortic aneurysms in MFS.

title: AAOLCA in a Child Presenting With Fever and Cardiac Arrest: Diagnostic Overlap With Acute Myocarditis.
authorString: Bui TD, Nguyen YTK, Le TVP, Nguyen BK, Phan LT.
abstractText:
Background

Anomalous aortic origin of the left coronary artery (AAOLCA) is a rare congenital coronary anomaly causing myocardial ischemia and sudden cardiac death. Despite differing in pathophysiology from acute myocarditis, AAOLCA can present with a clinically indistinguishable acute picture.

Case summary

We report an 11-year-old child with no prior cardiac history presenting with fever (40 °C), syncope, cardiac arrest, and cardiogenic shock. Elevated troponin and reduced ejection fraction initially suggested acute myocarditis, which could not be excluded. Atypical features-absent arrhythmia, rapid biomarker normalization, and fluctuating ventricular function-prompted further evaluation. Echocardiography and coronary angiography identified AAOLCA with a hemodynamically significant intramural segment; dynamic ischemia was confirmed during angiography. Surgical unroofing resulted in clinical recovery.

Conclusions

AAOLCA should be considered when pediatric myocarditis presents atypically. Echocardiography is essential. When concurrent myocarditis cannot be excluded, surgical timing should be individualized; here, a period of stabilization preceded definitive repair.

title: Telomere Dynamics in Congenital Heart Defects: Hidden Architects of Cardiogenesis?
authorString: Joshi R, Nath S, Gupta S.
abstractText:
Background

Congenital heart defects (CHDs) represent a significant global health burden, particularly in India, and are among the leading causes of childhood mortality. Despite growing insights into their multifactorial etiology, the molecular mechanisms linking maternal health to embryonic heart development remain elusive. Telomeres, the repetitive DNA-protein structures that cap chromosome ends, are recognized as markers of cellular aging and also as regulators of early embryogenesis. This review examines emerging evidence connecting telomere biology with the risk of CHD in offspring.

Scope of review

This review is aimed at mapping the existing evidence on telomere dynamics in the context of cardiogenesis and CHD. It encompasses studies involving human subjects and experimental models, focusing on telomere length (TL), telomerase activity, and telomere dysfunction in cardiac development and CHD pathogenesis.

Key findings

We highlight the influence of environmental stressors on telomere dynamics and chromosomal stability in gametes and early embryos. Current evidence suggests that altered telomere dynamics may influence cardiomyocyte proliferation, cellular senescence, and genomic integrity, thereby contributing to aberrant cardiac development. Studies indicate potential associations between telomere shortening, impaired telomerase activity, and increased susceptibility to CHD; however, findings remain heterogeneous and fragmented.

Implications

This review highlights the need to explore impaired parental telomere maintenance as a novel risk factor for improper chromosomal segregation and abnormal heart development. Understanding the role of telomere dynamics in cardiogenesis may provide novel insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying CHD. This could aid in identifying potential biomarkers for early risk assessment and open avenues for targeted therapeutic strategies aimed at modulating telomere function.

Conclusion

Telomere biology represents a promising yet underexplored area in CHD research. This study is among the first to conceptualize impaired parental and embryonic telomere dynamics as a unifying mechanistic link in CHD pathogenesis. This review highlights the need for comprehensive and integrative studies to elucidate potential mechanistic links in order to translate these findings into clinical applications. Understanding this telomere-CHD axis may open a new frontier for periconceptional intervention and targeted maternal care to improve overall birth outcomes.

title: Fabry's Disease, Valvular Disease and Infective Endocarditis: A Rare Intersection.
authorString: Awada H, Chawla R, Shepherd Y, Kumar R, Oganesian B, Yetenikyan D.
abstractText:
Background

Infective endocarditis may present with nonspecific systemic symptoms that mimic other conditions, creating diagnostic challenges in high-risk patients.

Case summary

A 44-year-old man with advanced Fabry disease, bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement, and a chronic Port-A-Cath presented with fever, chills, and malaise shortly after pegunigalsidase alfa infusion, initially raising concern for an infusion reaction. Persistent methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia prompted further evaluation, revealing right-sided native tricuspid valve infective endocarditis with septal leaflet perforation and severe tricuspid regurgitation. Prosthetic aortic valve involvement remained clinically suspected despite nondiagnostic imaging. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated multifocal septic embolic infarctions. He received targeted intravenous antibiotics, catheter removal, multidisciplinary care, and cardiothoracic surgical evaluation, with continued medical management recommended.

Conclusion

This case emphasizes maintaining suspicion for infective endocarditis despite a plausible alternative diagnosis and highlights the role of multimodality imaging in guiding management.

Take-home messages

Persistent S aureus bacteremia should prompt evaluation for infective endocarditis in high-risk patients even when symptoms initially suggest a plausible alternative diagnosis. Multimodality imaging and multidisciplinary assessment are essential when initial imaging is nondiagnostic or clinical findings suggest embolic complications.

title: Seven Novel Sonographic Signs
authorString: Ji X.
abstractText: Ultrasound is a widely used imaging modality in clinical practice, and sonographic signs serve as valuable teaching tools that aid in pattern recognition and diagnosis. This review consolidates five novel sonographic signs previously proposed by the author, including the Cracked Earth Sign for subcutaneous edema, the Mushroom Cap Sign for localized gallbladder adenomyomatosis, the LTS Sign for dilated cardiomyopathy, the LTI Sign for endocardial fibroelastosis, and the Three Pipes Sign for the suprasternal long-axis view of the aortic arch. The SFH Sign for advanced cervical insufficiency and the Gentle Upslope Sign for the parvus–tardus waveform are proposed for the first time in this paper. Collectively, these seven signs span the fields of superficial ultrasound, abdominal ultrasound, echocardiography, and obstetric ultrasound. For each sign, its naming logic, definition, clinical implications, and teaching value are described. This review aims to facilitate a better understanding of these signs and to promote their use as teaching aids in ultrasound education.

title: Role of cardiac magnetic resonance imaging in the diagnosis of chronic constrictive pericarditis revealed by Pick's syndrome: A case report.
authorString: Sall F, Meneas C, N'Cho Mottoh MP, Akatchi R, Vy L, Boka BC, Adoubi A.
abstractText:
Introduction

Chronic constrictive pericarditis (CCP), or Pick's syndrome, is a rare but severe inflammatory disease of the pericardium, often difficult to distinguish from restrictive cardiomyopathy without multimodality imaging. In sub-Saharan Africa, tuberculosis remains the leading cause.

Case presentation

We report the case of a 37-year-old woman with a history of post-partum hypertension, admitted for a three-month history of exertional dyspnoea, lower-limb oedema and retrosternal chest pain in a febrile, tuberculosis-suggestive context. Examination revealed isolated right heart failure with a pericardial knock. Echocardiography and cardiac MRI showed pericardial thickening and circumferential detachment, bi-atrial dilatation and a septal bounce, with late gadolinium enhancement and T1/T2 mapping consistent with active pericardial inflammation, confirming an evolving, inflammatory form of CCP. Coronary CT angiography excluded coexisting coronary disease and revealed tuberculous pulmonary sequelae. Under corticosteroids, antituberculous therapy and symptomatic management, the patient improved clinically, allowing pericardiectomy to be deferred.

Conclusion

This case highlights the value of cardiac MRI in the early diagnosis of inflammatory, potentially reversible forms of CCP, helping to avoid upfront surgery and guide targeted medical management, particularly in tuberculosis-endemic regions.

title: Platelet Factor 4 and Corresponding Antibodies in Atherosclerosis and Cardiovascular Disease.
authorString: Bonisoli GL, Wesche J, Schönborn L, Zaninetti C, Friso S, Martinelli N, Thiele T.
abstractText:
Abstract

Antibodies directed against platelet factor 4 (PF4) are increasingly recognized as key mediators of immunothrombosis. In heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), these antibodies emerge following exposure to the polyanion heparin, whereas in vaccine-induced immune thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (VITT), they arise in response to vector-based vaccination or (adeno)viral infections. In both settings, anti-PF4 antibodies promote platelet activation and enhance inflammatory and thrombotic processes. PF4 itself has also been implicated in atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease (CVD), although clinical studies investigating this link have yielded inconsistent results. We review the current knowledge on the roles of PF4 and anti-PF4 antibodies in atherosclerosis and CVD and discuss preclinical and clinical evidence for their relevance in the perioperative setting, for disease progression and antiplatelet therapy.

title: Naxos disease: current insights from early clinical observations to genetics and precision medicine.
authorString: Xylouri Z, Al-Sergani H, Protonotarios I, Vlachopoulos C, Bossone E, Tsatsopoulou A.
abstractText: Naxos disease is the prototype of the Naxos disease cardiocutaneous spectrum, a group of inherited desmosomal disorders characterised by distinctive hair and skin abnormalities that precede the development of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM). Since its original clinical description in 1986 and the subsequent identification of the first ACM-causing gene (JUP), Naxos disease has provided fundamental insights into the pathogenesis, diagnosis and management of inherited desmosomal cardiomyopathies. This review provides current insights into the evolving clinical spectrum, encompassing the characteristic cutaneous signature, early electrical abnormalities, progressive structural myocardial remodelling, inflammatory ("hot-phase") episodes, ventricular arrhythmias and heart failure. We discuss the expanding genotype-phenotype relationships involving JUP, DSP and DSC2, highlighting how distinct genetic substrates influence ventricular involvement, disease severity and clinical outcomes while sharing common desmosomal mechanisms. Particular emphasis is placed on early clinical recognition, multimodality imaging, genetic diagnosis, risk stratification and lifelong multidisciplinary management. Finally, we discuss the emerging role of international collaborative registries, including NAXCARE, in generating prospective real-world evidence to refine genotype-informed surveillance, improve risk prediction and support precision medicine. Nearly four decades after its original description, Naxos disease has evolved from a rare inherited syndrome into the prototype of desmosomal cardiomyopathy, demonstrating how careful clinical observation can drive molecular discovery, precision medicine and improved patient care.

title: Strategies for Managing Obesity and Cardiometabolic Risk in Young Children: Current Evidence and Future Directions.
authorString: Salama M, Kumar S.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

Early-onset obesity is associated with adverse cardiometabolic risk factors and early vascular changes linked to atherosclerosis, yet evidence-based treatment options for young children remain limited. The purpose of the review is to examine current evidence for lifestyle, pharmacologic, and surgical interventions for obesity management in preadolescent children, with emphasis on cardiometabolic and atherosclerotic risk.

Recent findings

Lifestyle and familybased behavioral interventions remain first line therapy but often produce modest and variable weight reduction. Pharmacologic options for children younger than 12 years are limited, emerging data suggest selected agents, including topiramate, lisdexamfetamine, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and metformin can improve weight status and cardiometabolic risk factors in carefully selected patients. Bariatric surgery provides durable weight loss and cardiometabolic benefit and adolescents with severe obesity, though data and younger children are sparse. Available interventions may improve cardiometabolic risk profiles when appropriately applied early in life, but high-quality long-term data and preadolescent children are needed.

title: Catheter-Induced Type B Aortic Dissection After TAVI: Delayed Adverse Remodeling.
authorString: Bargagna F, Casula M, Mori F, Ravani M, Al Jabri A, Berti S, Rizza A.
abstractText:
Background

Catheter-induced type B aortic dissection is a rare complication of transcatheter aortic valve implantation with uncertain long-term behavior.

Case summary

An 85-year-old woman developed a focal aortic isthmus dissection during transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve implantation. Initial computed tomography angiography (CTA) showed no malperfusion or rupture; conservative management and serial CTA surveillance were selected. Despite persistent clinical stability, follow-up CTA demonstrated progressive focal outpouching and pseudoaneurysmal remodeling. At 17 months, elective thoracic endovascular aortic repair achieved complete exclusion of the lesion.

Discussion

Catheter-induced dissection may represent a mechanistically distinct entity from spontaneous type B aortic dissection, limiting direct extrapolation of conventional management pathways. Morphological progression, rather than symptoms or absolute aortic diameter, prompted intervention.

Take-home messages

Clinical stability does not establish aortic wall healing. Long-term serial CTA can identify silent adverse remodeling and guide elective thoracic endovascular aortic repair in selected patients.

title: Early Experience of Fiber Optic RealShape Technology in Endovascular Interventions for Peripheral Artery Disease: A Prospective Single-Center Study.
authorString: Klaassen J, Lodema SN, van Herwaarden JA, Teraa M, Hazenberg CEVB.

journal.title: Journal of endovascular therapy : an official journal of the International Society of Endovascular Specialists

abstractText:
Objective

Interventions in peripheral artery disease (PAD) have changed significantly over the past decades. Most centers have adopted an endovascular-first strategy resulting in an increased radiation exposure, especially for the treatment team. Fiber Optic RealShape (FORS) technology uses laser light instead of fluoroscopy to visualize the specially designed guidewire and catheters. The aim of this early experience overview was to evaluate feasibility and safety of FORS-guided navigation for endovascular interventions in PAD.

Methods

This overview presents prospectively collected, single-center data of FORS-guided PAD interventions. Feasibility was evaluated through technical success in crossing stenotic lesion(s) or occlusion(s). Lesion characteristics were also recorded. Safety was assessed by scoring of intraoperative adverse events related to FORS. Secondary assessments included navigation time, and radiation exposure outcomes (cumulative air kerma [CAK], air kerma-area product [KAP], and fluoroscopy time [FT]) during crossing of the culprit lesion.

Results

In 22 patients (31 lesions) selected for FORS-guided PAD interventions, 22 of 31 lesions (71.0%) were successfully crossed while using FORS-enabled devices, without adverse events. Median length of the treated lesions was 48.0 mm (23.0-87.0). Sixteen lesions (51.6%) had a severe degree of stenosis and 10 lesions (32.3%) had a moderate degree of stenosis, defined according to the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial criteria. Navigation times, CAK, and FT were highest during FORS-guided interventions of most complex stenotic lesions.

Conclusion

Fiber Optic RealShape-guided navigation and lesion crossing in PAD interventions is feasible and safe. Expansion of the FORS portfolio hypothetically in combination with other radiation-reducing technologies might enable a radiation-free interventional environment in the future.Clinical ImpactFiber Optic RealShape (FORS) represents a novel technology that enables visualization of specially designed endovascular devices by utilizing laser light instead of fluoroscopy. These devices facilitate real-time visualization with three-dimensional features to simplify endovascular navigation without the necessity of using fluoroscopy during navigation. This is the first single-center study that presents an overview of 31 peripheral arterial disease (PAD) lesions (in 22 patients) showing that using FORS guided navigation in PAD interventions is safe and feasible. Ultimately, the use of FORS in combination with other radiation reducing technologies might eventually enable a radiation-free interventional environment in the future.

title: Systematic Scoring Differences in Large Language Model-Based Clinical Benchmarking Reveal Evaluator-Dependent Divergence: Controlled Evaluation Study.
authorString: Dinc R, Ardic N.
abstractText:
Background

Large language model (LLM) benchmarking in clinical medicine is increasingly reliant on LLM-based assessment frameworks; in these systems, one AI scores the outputs of another. This practice relies on the assumptions of evaluator neutrality and rubric consistency. These assumptions have not been empirically tested in clinical fields.

Objective

In this study, we aim to directly examine these assumptions by using the PARM (Planning-Action-Reflection-Memory) framework as a theoretical lens to characterize endovascular device selection and clinical reflective reasoning as a clinical field.

Methods

We developed a scoring rubric (C1-C6) with 40 clinical vignettes and 6 criteria across 5 endovascular fields (peripheral artery disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, chronic venous insufficiency, coronary in-stent restenosis [ISR], and cerebrovascular/neuroendovascular; 8 vignettes per field). Four LLMs were evaluated as clinical decision support systems: GPT-4o (M1), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (M2), Gemini 1.5 Pro (M3), and Llama 3.3 70B (M4). Two LLMs served as independent raters with the same evaluation criteria: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (rater 1) and GPT-4o (rater 2). The rater identity was intentionally disclosed; the primary research question concerned rater scoring behavior rather than the absolute performance of the model. Human assessment was intentionally excluded because its inclusion would have shifted the study question from rater disagreement to rater accuracy, a distinct and secondary question. Interrater reliability was measured using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC 2,1) two-way random effects modeling.

Results

The combined ICC(2,1) was 0.153 (95% CI 0.007-0.295). In this exploratory study, the low ICC was not distributed randomly: the magnitude of score differences varied across models (M2 Δ=+5, M4 Δ=+31, M1 Δ=-46, and M3 Δ=-158 points). Scoring behavior analysis identified 2 intrinsically consistent but mutually inconsistent criterion-interpretation models. Rater 1's scores were most consistent with the reasoning quality approach (partial credit to clinical competence independent of vignette context). Rater 2's scores were most consistent with the context fidelity approach (near-zero scores for wrong vignette responses independent of reasoning quality). Contrary to the self-preference hypothesis, both raters placed the other higher-performing model above their own. Under rater 1, C6 (PARM reflection) was the lowest-scoring criterion across all 4 models, whereas rater 2 showed greater model-dependent variation in C6 scoring.

Conclusions

AI raters used in LLM-based clinical benchmarking do not behave as interchangeable scoring tools. Their scoring behavior is most consistent with model-specific criterion interpretation patterns that systematically produce different outcomes. The observed low interrater reliability requires interpretation rather than simply being ignored: it reflects structured, direction-specific disagreement concentrated in models with context-tracking failures, not random inconsistency. PARM reflection showed a notable yet evaluator-dependent scoring pattern that warranted further investigation, rather than being interpreted as an evaluator-independent deficit.

title: Retroperitoneal Nodal Metastasis Detected by Diffusion-Weighted Imaging in Paraspinal Alveolar Rhabdomyosarcoma.
authorString: Kubota H, Arakawa Y, Fujibayashi S, Mori M, Fukuoka K, Fukushima H, Mizumoto M, Tanami Y, Kawashima H, Nakazawa A, Koh K.
abstractText:
Background

Accurate lymph node evaluation is critical in rhabdomyosarcoma, yet small or metabolically inactive nodal metastases often evade detection on conventional imaging, such as fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography-computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT).

Observations

We report a 6-year-old girl with paraspinal alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma whose para-aortic lymph node exhibited diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) hyperintensity but lacked FDG uptake at diagnosis. The node was interpreted as reactive and was not sampled. Nine months after first-line therapy, relapse in the same para-aortic region was histologically confirmed as nodal metastasis.

Conclusions

DWI may reveal nodal metastases not identified by FDG-PET/CT or size criteria, underscoring cautious interpretation of DWI-positive, FDG-negative nodes in trunk rhabdomyosarcoma.

title: The carotid-subclavian artery index (CSAI) in the fetal aortic arch with classic branching and brachiobicephalic trunk in a midtrimester low-risk population.
authorString: Tavares de Sousa M, Hergert B, Gomez O, Crispi F, Hecher K.
abstractText:
Purpose

The carotid-subclavian artery index (CSAI) has shown high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing coarctation of the aorta (CoA) in fetuses and neonates. We investigated whether variations in aortic arch (AA) branching without CoA affect CSAI by comparing fetuses with the classic pattern to those with a brachiobicephalic trunk (BBCT), the most common variant.

Materials and methods

In this prospective cohort study of 335 low-risk singleton pregnancies (19-22 weeks of gestation), standardized fetal echocardiography was used to assess AA branching in a sagittal view. Two blinded observers classified branching patterns and calculated CSAI.

Results

Adequate image quality was obtained in 262/335 (78.2%) cases. 194/262 (74%) fetuses showed a classic pattern and 66 (25.2%) a branching variant. In two fetuses (0.8%), there was disagreement regarding the branching pattern. 50/66 (76.8%) fetuses with isolated BBCT were compared with 194 cases with a classic AA branching pattern. 16 other variants were excluded. The mean CSAI was significantly lower in BBCT (0.71 ± 0.14) than in the classic branching pattern (1.46 ± 0.37; P < 0.001). Interobserver agreement showed an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.852 (95% CI OF 0.814-0.883): . None required cardiac intervention within two years.

Conclusion

Targeted fetal echocardiography showed a lower CSAI in cases with BBCT than in the classic branching pattern. Future studies are warranted to assess the diagnostic impact of our findings in the setting of suspected CoA.

title: Salvage Transcatheter Mitral Valve-in-Valve With Aspiration Thrombectomy in a Young Adult With Repaired CHD.
authorString: Ali R, Naeem M, Tagle Tejeda AP, Pahuja K, Roth T, Boe B, Guyon PW, Ho AH, Khalili H, Saef J.
abstractText:
Background

Prosthetic mitral valve degeneration in adults with repaired congenital heart disease (CHD) can produce rapid hemodynamic collapse and is challenging when surgery and mechanical circulatory support (MCS) are unavailable.

Case summary

A 20-year-old woman with congenital mitral stenosis and multiple ventricular septal defects initially palliated as a single ventricle, then converted to biventricular circulation, with prior mechanical and bioprosthetic mitral valve replacements (the latter for menorrhagia, outside our care), presented in cardiogenic shock with prosthetic mitral stenosis and acute left atrial thrombus. Hypoplastic peripheral vessels precluded MCS. Salvage valve-in-valve was performed with bilateral cerebral protection, FlowTriever thrombectomy (Inari Medical), and a 26-mm SAPIEN 3 valve (Edwards Lifesciences).

Discussion

Transcatheter mitral valve-in-valve can be lifesaving in adults with repaired CHD when intracardiac thrombus is present, and MCS is unavailable.

Take-home messages

In highly selected, life-threatening presentations without alternatives, salvage transcatheter mitral intervention may be considered despite intracardiac thrombus. Peripheral vascular anatomy must be evaluated preprocedurally in complex CHD.

title: Donor-Recipient Sex Mismatch is Associated with Severe Primary Graft Dysfunction after Heart Transplantation.
authorString: Moayedifar R, Zuckerman A, Moayedi Y, Huang R, Dhingra NK, Truby LK, Han J, Henricksen E, Ródenas-Alesina E, Guzman-Bofarull J, Couto-Mallon D, Luikart H, Signorile M, Farr M, Kim G, Crespo-Leiro MG, Hall S, DeVore A, Lerman JB, Sabatino M, Potena L, Rivas-Lasarte M, Segovia-Cubero J, Farrero M, Tremblay-Gravel M, Noly PE, Miller R, Chih S, Takeda K, Ross HJ, Foroutan F, Khush K.

journal.title: The Journal of heart and lung transplantation : the official publication of the International Society for Heart Transplantation

abstractText:
Background

The association between sex and primary graft dysfunction after heart transplantation (HT) remains unclear. We evaluated whether recipient sex and donor-recipient sex matching are associated with severe primary graft dysfunction (PGD) in a contemporary, multicenter cohort.

Methods

We analyzed data from the International PGD Consortium comprised of adult HTs from 2010 to 2024 across 14 centers. Associations between sex-related variables and severe PGD were assessed using multivariable logistic regression, and adjusted for ischemic time, pre-transplant durable left ventricular assist device (LVAD), dialysis, congenital heart disease, and predicted heart mass (PHM) ratio.

Results

Among 3,994 recipients, 1,030 (25.8%) were female. Female recipients were younger (54 vs. 57 years) with fewer comorbidities, and less frequently bridged on a durable LVAD (19.8% vs. 29.1%). Although female recipients had a lower incidence of PGD than male recipients (7.1% vs. 9.4%), recipient sex was not independently associated with PGD after multivariable adjustment. Female donor to male recipient sex mismatching had the highest PGD incidence of 11.5% and was associated with a 43% increase in the odds of severe PGD (p=0.030). While sex-mismatch was associated with an increased incidence of PGD, size mismatch by PHM ratio was not an independent predictor.

Conclusion

In this large international registry, donor-recipient sex mismatch, specifically among male recipients of female donor hearts, was independently associated with severe PGD, even when appropriately size matched. These findings inform risk stratification for development of severe PGD after HT.

title: Comparison of visual estimation of ventricular systolic function with quantitative echocardiographic markers in newborn infants.
authorString: Pereira SS, Yeldo B, Fleming R, Satas S.
abstractText:
Background

Neonatologist-performed echocardiography (NPE) is increasingly practiced. NPE operators typically use visual estimation of systolic function and, if indicated, confirm function using quantitative echocardiographic markers. This exploratory study aims to compare the concordance between qualitative and quantitative echocardiographic markers among NPE and non-NPE operators.

Methods

We studied a cohort of newborn infants, undergoing routine NPE by the authors at Homerton University Hospital and Aberdeen Maternity Hospital from April 2024 to October 2024. Blinded NPE and non-NPE operators independently assessed left and right ventricular systolic function visually. We compared visual estimation with standard quantitative echocardiographic markers such as shortening fraction, Simpson's ejection fraction and global longitudinal strain for left ventricle and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion and fractional area change for right ventricle. We examined the concordance between visual estimation and quantitative echocardiographic markers for biventricular systolic function.

Results

Sixty infants with a mean (SD) gestation and birth weight of 34 (6.2) weeks and 2311 (1319) grams respectively were examined. Sensitivity testing for all echocardiographic parameters ranged from 25% to 80% whereas specificity ranged from 38% to 78%. Sensitivity increased with worsening grades of LV dysfunction defined using shortening fraction. While concordance between NPE and non-NPE operator was generally limited across most echocardiographic parameters, test-retest reliability was acceptable for several quantitative measures, including Simpson's ejection fraction, global longitudinal strain and right ventricular fractional area change.

Conclusion

Visual estimation may be a useful bedside tool for detecting severe ventricular dysfunction in newborn infants; however; quantitative echocardiographic measures are likely to improve the assessment of mild to moderate dysfunction. Further studies should confirm these findings in a larger cohort with a higher representation of infants with ventricular dysfunction.
