title: The macrophage as a neuroimmune sensor and effector: neural control of inflammation across tissues and disease.
authorString: da Cruz RS, Lopes LS, Pachiega ANS, Colombari DSA, Colombari E, Zoccal DB, Katayama PL.

journal.title: Inflammation research : official journal of the European Histamine Research Society ... [et al.]

abstractText:
Background

Once viewed mainly as scavengers of innate immunity, macrophages are now recognized as constitutive partners of the nervous system. In neural tissue their identity is instructed by neurons and glia, and in turn they shape neural function - pruning synapses, tuning neuronal excitability, and executing the autonomic commands that restrain inflammation.

Purpose

Here we advance a mechanistic model built on three principles: that neural and glial signals specify macrophage identity on a shared myeloid template; that the macrophage is a bidirectional sensor-effector node within autonomic reflex arcs, both relaying neural output and generating the cytokine signals that afferent nerves detect; and that this sensor-effector arc is modular, recurring across brain, spleen, gut, heart, and adipose tissue. We give particular attention to the afferent limb of the inflammatory reflex, which now extends beyond the vagus to nociceptors and to the carotid body, an arterial chemoreceptor that senses circulating inflammatory signals and recruits a sympathetic anti-inflammatory pathway, and to the stress-responsive circuitry through which sympathetic outflow drives myelopoiesis, neuroinflammation, and sickness behavior. We then turn to disease, in which macrophage function is altered by a diseased or aged niche in neurodegeneration, chronic pain, gut-brain disorders, and metabolic disease.

Conclusions

Whether the neuroimmune circuits described here are themselves disrupted in these conditions, rather than merely coexisting with them, is largely untested, and we outline what such evidence would require. We close by arguing that tuning these circuits, rather than broadly suppressing macrophage activity, is the more plausible therapeutic goal.

title: Association between perioperative statin-ezetimibe therapy and reoperation following arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: A TriNetX database study.
authorString: Mahatme R, Gangavaram A, Muthusamy N, Moore S, Nayak T, Shao K, Grawe B, Bernholt D.

journal.title: Daru : journal of Faculty of Pharmacy, Tehran University of Medical Sciences

abstractText:
Background

Hyperlipidemia (HLD) impairs tendon healing and is associated with increased revision risk following arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (ARCR). While statins may partially mitigate this effect, residual dyslipidemia may impair healing. Ezetimibe, through inhibition of intestinal cholesterol absorption, has demonstrated favorable effects on tendon healing in preclinical studies.

Objectives

This study evaluated whether perioperative statin-ezetimibe therapy is associated with improved postoperative outcomes following ARCR compared with statin monotherapy and patients without HLD.

Methods

A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the TriNetX Research Network. Adult patients undergoing ARCR were stratified into three cohorts based on HLD status and perioperative (± 6 months) lipid-lowering therapy: (1) documented HLD treated with statin-ezetimibe prescriptions, (2) patients without documented HLD or lipid-lowering therapy prescriptions, and (3) documented HLD treated with statin monotherapy prescriptions. Primary comparisons were predefined between cohort 1 and cohorts 2 and 3. Propensity score matching (1:1) adjusted for demographics and comorbidities. Tear size and presence of fatty atrophy and fatty infiltration were not adjusted for. Outcomes occurring within 5 years included revision rotator cuff repair (RCR), conversion to shoulder arthroplasty, and secondary shoulder arthroscopy.

Results

After matching, 1,066 patients were included in cohorts 1 and 2 and 1,114 patients in cohorts 1 and 3. Compared with patients without HLD, statin-ezetimibe therapy demonstrated similar rates of revision RCR (5.4% vs. 6.4%; RR 0.853; p = 0.358), conversion to shoulder arthroplasty (RR 1.227; p = 0.470), and secondary arthroscopy (RR 0.846; p = 0.260). Compared with statin monotherapy, statin-ezetimibe therapy was associated with lower rates of revision RCR (5.6% vs. 8.0%; RR 0.697; p = 0.023) and secondary shoulder arthroscopy (7.3% vs. 9.6%; RR 0.757; p = 0.048), while arthroplasty rates remained similar (RR 1.261; p = 0.400).

Conclusion

Among patients with HLD undergoing ARCR, perioperative statin-ezetimibe therapy was associated with lower reoperation rates compared with statin monotherapy and postoperative outcomes comparable to patients without HLD. These findings support further investigation of intensified lipid-lowering therapy, while accounting for tear size and fatty infiltration.

title: Transcriptomics Identifies a Small Set of Circulating Biomarkers and Signaling Pathways Dysregulated in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
authorString: Kiyohara Y, Akita K, Fifer MA, Tower-Rader A, Teruya S, Ansari B, Santos AM, Maurer MS, Shimada YJ.
abstractText:
Background

It is sometimes challenging to distinguish hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) from other cardiomyopathies with left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). At present, no circulating biomarkers to distinguish HCM have been established.

Objectives

The authors aimed to identify plasma microRNA (miRNA) biomarkers unique to HCM.

Methods

In this multicenter case-control study, the authors performed comprehensive plasma transcriptomics profiling in cases with HCM and controls with hypertensive LVH, transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), and aortic stenosis (AS). For each disease group, they chronologically split the patients into training and test sets. The authors identified miRNAs that were significantly (Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05) upregulated or downregulated in HCM compared with hypertensive LVH. They made the same comparisons between HCM and ATTR-CM and between HCM and AS. They determined miRNAs that were consistently upregulated or downregulated in HCM throughout all 3 comparisons. Then, they selected miRNAs independently associated with HCM after adjusting for potential confounders. Using the selected miRNAs, the authors developed a logistic regression model to distinguish HCM in the training set. They calculated the area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve in the test set.

Results

The authors analyzed 2,656 miRNAs in patients with HCM (n = 294), hypertensive LVH (n = 321), ATTR-CM (n = 167), and AS (n = 38). They identified 3 miRNAs (miR-454-3p, miR-98-5p, and miR-5581-3p). The logistic regression model using the 3 miRNAs had an area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.93-0.97) with a sensitivity of 0.95 and a specificity of 0.90 in the test set.

Conclusions

Comprehensive plasma transcriptomics profiling identified a small set of circulating miRNAs to distinguish HCM from other cardiomyopathies with LVH.

title: Soil erosion and land-use management influence bioavailable selenium in a highland agricultural landscape in Kenya.
authorString: Isaboke J, Humphrey OS, Osano O, Njoroge R, Watts MJ.
abstractText: Selenium (Se) is an essential micronutrient whose availability in agricultural systems is influenced by geochemical, pedological, and anthropogenic factors. The study aimed to investigate the effects of soil erosion, land-use, and management practices on the bioavailability and redistribution of selenium within a soil-plant continuum in a highland agricultural landscape in Nandi County, Kenya. A stratified sampling approach was applied across three plots representing distinct land-use management practices and varying soil erosion rates. Selenium concentrations were measured both in soils and crops (maize, beans, and pumpkin) collected from the experimental sites. Total and bioavailable Se concentrations in soils were evaluated using a mixed acid digestion (HF, HNO<sub>3</sub>, and H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) and an ammonium chloride (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) extraction, respectively, followed by ICP-MS analysis. Structural equation modelling and regression analyses revealed that soil pH (β = - 0.41, p < 0.001), organic matter (β = 0.29, p < 0.01), and total Se (β = 0.30, p < 0.001) significantly influenced bioavailable Se, although plant uptake showed weak correlation. Temporal comparisons showed a significant increase in bioavailable Se in Plot 3 from 6.74 µg kg<sup>-1</sup> (2021) to 10.03 µg kg<sup>-1</sup> (2023), representing a 42% rise. In contrast, Plot 1 experienced a significant decline (p < 0.05) from 14.72 µg kg<sup>-1</sup> to 9.56 µg kg<sup>-1</sup> over the same period, linked to an increase in erosion rate by 0.58 t ha<sup>-1</sup> yr<sup>-1</sup>. Maize showed significantly higher Se accumulation in Plot 1 (187 µg kg<sup>-1</sup>) compared to Plot 3 (87 µg kg<sup>-1</sup>) (p < 0.05), while beans and pumpkin showed no significant differences across plots (p > 0.05). These findings suggest that appropriate land management and erosion mitigation may help maintain soil Se bioavailability, while targeted agronomic strategies could be considered to enhance crop Se concentrations. However, the relatively low Se concentrations observed in several crops suggest a potential concern regarding Se adequacy, and assessment of dietary intake and human biomarkers would be required to establish nutritional risk.

title: Aortic Arch Morphology Influences Procedural Complexity During Diagnostic Coronary Angiography: Development of a CTA-Informed Procedural Complexity Index.
authorString: Hasan T.
abstractText:
Background

Procedural complexity during diagnostic coronary angiography varies considerably and may result in prolonged fluoroscopy exposure and increased contrast utilization. Although vascular access route and operator experience are recognized contributors, the influence of proximal vascular anatomy remains less clearly defined. This study evaluated the association between aortic arch branching morphology and procedural complexity and explored the development of a CTA-informed procedural complexity index.

Aim

To assess the procedural impact of aortic arch branching morphology during diagnostic coronary angiography.

Methods

This retrospective observational study included 250 consecutive adult patients undergoing diagnostic coronary angiography who had preprocedural computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the thoracic aorta available for evaluation. Aortic arch branching patterns were classified into four configurations (Types A-D) using axial images, multiplanar reconstructions, and three-dimensional CTA analysis. Procedural measures included fluoroscopy time, contrast volume, procedure duration, vascular access route, and access-site crossover. Multivariable linear regression was used to assess predictors of fluoroscopy time, while a separate multivariable logistic regression model for prolonged fluoroscopy was used to derive a weighted CTA-informed procedural complexity index. Discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, with internal validation by 10-fold cross-validation.

Results

Variant aortic arch morphology was identified in 55 patients (22.0%). Patients with variant configurations had longer fluoroscopy times than those with classical Type A anatomy (7.4 ± 2.6 vs 5.9 ± 2.1 minutes; P = 0.002), greater contrast utilization (88 ± 25 vs 78 ± 21 mL; P = 0.01), and longer procedure duration (26 ± 10 vs 22 ± 8 minutes; P = 0.02). Variant arch morphology remained independently associated with longer fluoroscopy time (β = +1.3 minutes; P = 0.003). The derived procedural complexity index demonstrated an apparent area under the curve of 0.72 (95% CI, 0.64-0.80), with a 10-fold cross-validated AUC of 0.68.

Conclusion

CTA-defined aortic arch morphology was associated with procedural complexity during diagnostic coronary angiography. The proposed CTA-informed procedural complexity index demonstrated modest discriminatory performance and may provide additional information regarding anticipated procedural difficulty. The index should be considered exploratory and requires prospective external validation before clinical implementation.

title: Long-Term Stabilization after Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair for a Behçet-Related Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm: A Case Report.
authorString: Oue K, Kinoshita M, Okuda S, Kondo N.
abstractText:
Introduction

Behçet disease is a relapsing systemic vasculitis that can rarely cause aortic aneurysms or pseudoaneurysms. Endovascular repair is increasingly used for Behçet-related aortic lesions, but the long-term interaction between aneurysm remodeling, endoleak, and systemic inflammatory activity remains clinically important.

Case presentation

A 34-year-old man presented with persistent back pain due to an impending rupture of a newly developed saccular descending thoracic aortic aneurysm. Emergency thoracic endovascular aortic repair was performed before Behçet disease was definitively diagnosed. Postoperatively, persistent fever, elevated inflammatory markers, recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, and intestinal ulcerations led to the diagnosis of Behçet disease. The aneurysm initially regressed after corticosteroid therapy but rapidly re-expanded during steroid tapering, in parallel with fever, back pain, and increased C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, despite no demonstrable type I or III endoleak. Additional endovascular reinforcement and intensified immunosuppressive therapy were performed. A type II endoleak from the left first lumbar artery was subsequently detected, but the aneurysm continued to regress under inflammatory control. More than 13 years after the initial repair, the treated aneurysm remains completely regressed.

Conclusions

This case suggests that sac enlargement after endovascular repair for a Behçet-related aortic aneurysm should be evaluated as a potentially multifactorial event, including occult endoleak, persistent sac pressurization, stent-graft-related mechanical factors, and systemic inflammatory activity. In this case, durable stabilization was observed following combined endovascular treatment and sustained immunosuppressive therapy.

title: German multicenter biobank and registry for phenotype-specific genomic research in thoracic aortic disease.
authorString: Erhart P, Körfer D, Simon F, Gombert A, Oikonomou K, von Klitzing E, Oberhuber A, Kerndl H, Hofmann A, Schaaf CP, Hund E, Böckler D.
abstractText:
Purpose

To establish a national multicentre biobank and registry for future genomic and genotype-phenotype studies of distinct thoracic aortic disease entities and to report the study design and current recruitment status.

Methods

A prospective multicenter registry with integrated biobanking was established in May 2024 across eight German vascular and cardiovascular centres. Patients with Stanford type B aortic dissection (STBAD), thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA), intramural hematoma (IMH), or penetrating aortic ulcer (PAU) were enrolled. Clinical characteristics, treatment, imaging parameters, and longitudinal outcomes were collected in a centralized pseudonymized database, and EDTA blood samples were stored at - 80 °C for future genomic analyses. An established retrospective Heidelberg cohort of 118 patients with isolated STBAD serves as a hypothesis-generating cohort, while the prospective multicenter cohort provides an independent population for subsequent validation and extension of genetic findings. No genomic analyses were performed for the present report.

Results

As of May 2026, 274 patients had been included: 118 patients with STBAD from the hypothesis-generating Heidelberg cohort and 156 patients from the prospective multicenter cohort comprising 84 patients with STBAD, 40 with TAA, 13 with IMH, and 19 with PAU. The most prominent descriptive difference between disease entities was age distribution. Among patients with STBAD, 116/202 (57.4%) were younger than 60 years, compared with 6/40 (15.0%) with TAA, 2/13 (15.4%) with IMH, and 2/19 (10.5%) with PAU. A positive family history of thoracic aortic disease was reported in 14 patients (5.1%), and hypermobility or other connective tissue features were documented in 12 patients (4.4%), and two patients (0.7%) had a documented connective tissue disorder. Overall, 217 patients (79.2%) underwent surgical or endovascular treatment. Median imaging follow-up ranged from 1.5 months in IMH to 48 months in the retrospective Heidelberg cohort.

Conclusion

This national multicenter biobank and registry provides a deeply phenotyped platform for future investigation of the genetic basis of distinct thoracic aortic disease entities. The observed difference in age distribution provide a rationale for phenotype-specific genomic investigation but should not be interpreted as evidence of differing genetic contributions per se. Continued recruitment and longitudinal follow-up will enable future future genomic and genotype-phenotype analyses.

title: The intestinal microbiome in inflammatory bowel disease and spondyloarthritides.
authorString: Alizadeh M, Siaton BC, Hudhud D, von Rosenvinge EC, Cross RK, Ravel J.
abstractText: Extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs) of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) can affect any organ system, ranging in presentation, frequency, and severity; the most common EIM is IBD-associated arthritis (IAA), an inflammatory arthritis affecting both axial and peripheral joints. IAA is a form of seronegative spondyloarthritis (SpA), which includes multiple arthritides, and those with IAA are also likelier to have other clinical features observed in those with SpA without IBD, such as increased rates of uveitis, psoriasis, and HLA-B27 positivity. These overlapping features are not limited to clinical disease features; the microbiome has been heavily implicated in the development of both IBD and SpA and is associated with non-SpA EIMs. In this review, we offer an overview of several bacterial taxa and associated metabolites that have been identified as differentially abundant in both IBD and SpA, both in stool and mucosal assessment, and how these taxa are associated with differences in intestinal permeability and immune profiles. We also describe how the overlapping dysbiotic microbiome and associated metabolome in IBD, EIMs of IBD, and SpA may differentially modulate the immune system, thus contributing to the shared underlying etiopathogenesis of these diseases. Further work is needed to characterize causal, mechanistic relationships beyond pure computationally identified associations, and apply these findings towards targeted therapeutic intervention and personalized medicine in IBD.

title: Region-specific associations between dual-Layer spectral detector CT-derived carotid plaque parameters and white matter hyperintensity burden in patients with carotid atherosclerosis.
authorString: Ye Y, Lin L, Liu Y, Wang Y, Wen X, Xu Y.
abstractText:
Objective

White matter hyperintensities (WMH) exhibit region-specific characteristics. Whether dual-layer spectral detector CT (DLSCT)-derived plaque parameters associate with WMH burden region-specifically remains unclear.

Methods

This cross-sectional study enrolled 213 patients with carotid atherosclerotic plaques who underwent carotid CTA and brain MRI within 30 days. Seven DLSCT parameters were measured; WMH was segmented into juxtaventricular, periventricular, deep, and juxtacortical subregions. Multivariable linear regression assessed associations with total WMH burden (FDR correction). Nested models evaluated incremental value. Linear mixed-effects models with region-by-parameter interactions assessed region-specific associations.

Results

In the primary model (Model 2), Z-Zeff was significantly negatively associated with total WMH burden (β = -0.205, 95 % CI: -0.299 ∼ -0.111, FDR-q < 0.001). Adding Z-Zeff to the clinical model significantly increased explained variance (ΔR2 = 0.070, p < 0.001, ΔAIC = -15.09), whereas conventional CTA parameters did not (ΔR2 = 0.001, p = 0.938). Significant region interactions were observed for Z-Zeff, age, and LDL-C. Z-Zeff was negatively associated with all subregions, strongest in periventricular (β = -0.254) and deep (β = -0.172) WMH. Age was most strongly associated with periventricular WMH (β = 0.436). LDL-C and diabetes were associated only with periventricular WMH (β = -0.111 and -0.221, respectively).

Conclusion

DLSCT-derived Z-Zeff was independently associated with WMH burden in a region-specific manner, with the strongest associations in periventricular and deep white matter, and provided incremental value beyond clinical and conventional CTA parameters. These findings support Z-Zeff as a potential imaging biomarker linking carotid plaque composition to regional cerebral small vessel disease.

title: Family Screening and Disease Predictors in Gene-Elusive Dilated Cardiomyopathy.
authorString: Paldino A, Del Mestre E, Gandin I, Stroeks SLVM, Beelen NJ, Treu R, Pio Loco Detto Gava C, Garoia F, Gonzalez-Maniega C, Ramos-Lopez N, Brandão M, Gonzalez-Lopez E, Dominguez F, Dal Ferro M, Muller SA, Riele ASJM, Verdonschot JAJ, Garcia-Pavia P, Merlo M, Sinagra G.
abstractText:
Background

Family screening is recommended in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), but risk stratification of relatives of probands without pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants (gene-elusive) remains uncertain.

Objectives

This study sought to define the incidence, prognosis, and predictors of disease development in first-degree relatives of gene-elusive DCM probands.

Methods

First-degree relatives of gene-elusive DCM probands from 4 international referral centers who underwent baseline electrocardiography and echocardiography were included. The primary outcome was the development of the disease, defined as DCM or isolated left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction (LV ejection fraction: <50%). Major adverse cardiac events were exploratory secondary outcomes. Age-adjusted Cox models with family-clustered robust standard errors were used to identify disease predictors.

Results

Among 292 relatives (median age: 36 years, 48% male), 14 (5%) were affected at baseline. During a median follow-up of 52 months, 21 additional relatives developed disease, corresponding to an incidence rate of 17 per 1,000 person-years. Familial DCM (HR: 4.24; 95% CI: 1.38-13.1; P = 0.012), QRS duration >120 ms (HR: 7.24; 95% CI: 2.25-23.3; P < 0.001), lower LV ejection fraction (HR: 3.73; 95% CI: 2.46-5.65; P < 0.001), and LV dilatation (HR: 6.19; 95% CI: 2.27-16.9; P < 0.001) were predictors of disease development. Age at diagnosis in probands significantly correlated with age at onset in relatives (r = 0.80; 95% CI: 0.55-0.92; P < 0.001). Major adverse cardiac events occurred in 9 patients (4%).

Conclusions

First-degree relatives of gene-elusive DCM probands have a relatively low but non-negligible risk of disease development. Familial clustering, electrocardiographic or echocardiographic abnormalities, and age of disease expression in the proband may help tailor surveillance intensity.

title: Mechanical and Hemodynamic Effects of Balloon-Expandable and Self-Expanding Stents in a Saccular Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Model: Fluid-Structure Interaction Analyses.
authorString: Murakami M, Jiang F, Yamashita T, Mochizuki S.
abstractText:
Objectives

The aim of this study was to compare the effects of balloon-expandable and self-expanding stents on vessel wall mechanics and hemodynamics in a patient-specific saccular abdominal aortic aneurysm model.

Methods

A patient-specific aneurysm model was constructed using computed tomography images, and balloon-expandable and self-expanding stent models were created. Aortic wall stress was evaluated by contact analysis. Fluid-structure interaction analyses were performed at 5 representative phases selected from the cardiac cycle. Mean intra-aneurysmal flow velocity, wall shear stress (WSS), pressure loss, and energy loss were compared.

Results

The balloon-expandable stent produced greater localized aortic wall stress than the self-expanding stent, whereas wall stress was more uniformly distributed with the self-expanding stent. Both stents reduced the mean intra-aneurysmal flow velocity, WSS, pressure loss, and energy loss compared with the no-stent model. However, greater reductions in WSS, pressure loss, and energy loss were noted with the balloon-expandable stent than with the self-expanding stent.

Conclusions

Balloon-expandable and self-expanding stents exhibited different effects on vessel wall mechanics and hemodynamics. The findings indicate the importance of evaluating both hemodynamic and mechanical effects when assessing stent-vessel interactions.

title: The Halo Sign on Cardiac MRI in Recurrent Pericarditis.
authorString: Safdar A, El Roumi J, Ikram J, Ehsan M, Ming Wang TK, Klein A.
abstractText:
Background

Recurrent pericarditis can be difficult to manage. We describe the halo sign, a circumferential or regional rim of increased pericardial signal on T2-weighted imaging and/or late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), and its evolution during rilonacept therapy.

Case summary

Three patients with idiopathic, postcardiac injury, and autoimmune recurrent pericarditis underwent serial cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). Baseline CMR demonstrated the halo sign with concurrent edema and LGE. Edema resolved with near-complete LGE regression in the idiopathic and postcardiac injury cases, permitting therapy discontinuation without recurrence. The autoimmune case showed persistent edema and LGE at 1 year, with improvement by 2 years.

Discussion

Serial CMR demonstrated treatment response. Concurrent edema and LGE suggested active inflammation, whereas isolated LGE may reflect chronic inflammatory remodeling, neovascularization and/or fibrosis.

Take-home messages

The halo sign provides a simple descriptive framework for pericardial inflammation. Serial CMR, integrated with clinical findings and biomarkers, may distinguish active inflammation from chronic inflammatory remodeling and guide individualized therapy.

title: CT-guided iodine-125 brachytherapy for advanced thymic epithelial tumors: a preliminary observational study.
authorString: Tang Z, Qiu S, Liao Y, Wen X, Zhang G, Pu J, Wei X, Li C.
abstractText:
Objective

This study aimed to provide a preliminary description of the application of CT-guided iodine-125 (125I) seed implantation, a form of brachytherapy, in patients with advanced or recurrent thymic epithelial tumors (TETs).

Methods

We retrospectively reviewed seven patients with advanced or recurrent TETs who underwent CT-guided 125I seed implantation. Based on the extent of disease at presentation, one patient had widespread distant metastases, while the remaining six had localized lesions. Treatment planning was performed using a treatment planning system(TPS, Beijing Astro Technology Co., Ltd.) with a prescribed dose of 60-70 Gy. Follow-up evaluations included regular contrast-enhanced CT scans. Tumor response was assessed according to RECIST 1.1 criteria, and safety was evaluated using CTCAE v5.0.

Results

A total of 12 lesions were treated across seven patients. All procedures were technically successful. Over a median follow-up of 46 months (range: 9-69 months),four patients (57.1%) attained a complete response (CR) and three patients (42.9%) attained a partial response (PR) at the patient level. Patient-level response was defined by composite assessment of all target lesions. At the lesion level, six lesions (50%) demonstrated a CR and six lesions (50%) demonstrated a partial response PR. Notably, lesion-level observations are statistically non-independent given that half of treated lesions derived from a single patient. Complications included pneumothorax in three patients (one of whom required drainage) and grade 1 radiation pneumonitis in one patient; all adverse events resolved without long-term sequelae. No severe radiation-related toxicities (e.g., pericarditis) were observed. In a descriptive subgroup excluding the patient with widespread metastases, four of six patients achieved CR and two achieved PR; no local progression was documented during available follow-up, but this finding remains descriptive and non-comparative.

Conclusion

CT-guided ¹²⁵I radioactive seed implantation appears feasible and well-tolerated in patients with advanced or recurrent TETs. The observed objective tumour responses and toxicity profile are hypothesis-generating but must be interpreted with caution given the very small sample size, heterogeneous cohort, non-independent lesion-level data, and lack of a control group. This preliminary study cannot establish durable local control or superiority over external beam radiotherapy. Further larger, prospective studies with standardized dosimetry and time-to-event endpoints are warranted.
