Mitochondrial respiratory capacity did not differ between groups; however, training decreased mitochondria-specific respiration and H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> emission normalized to CS activity and respiration. Endurance training enhances insulin sensitivity and fat oxidation in individuals with T2D and induces favorable mitochondrial adaptations, despite the absence of intrinsic mitochondrial dysfunction.

title: Concept Analysis of Building Rapport in the ICU.
authorString: Eriksson M, Ullsten A, Nordin A, Nilsson J.
abstractText:
Background

Building rapport, understood as establishing a meaningful and trusting relationship through interpersonal interactions between healthcare professionals and patients or their family members, was described in research as early as the 1960s. Although studies highlight its importance in clinical relationships, the concept remains largely undefined, with limited research on experiences of rapport among family members of intensive care unit patients. This concept analysis can help to provide conceptual clarity for future practice and research.

Aim

This paper aimed to analyse and define the concept of 'building rapport' with ICU family members.

Study design

The concept analysis framework of Walker and Avant was used, following the systematic steps of identifying uses, attributes, antecedents, consequences and model cases. Data were obtained from Swedish and English dictionaries and peer-reviewed articles identified through a systematic literature search and screening. Titles and abstracts were reviewed, and six studies were selected based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria.

Results

This analysis clarifies the previously undefined concept of building rapport from the perspective of ICU family members. Building rapport is characterized by empathy and mutual understanding. Key antecedents include communication, time and relationships, while consequences are increased trust and the development of a care partnership. An empirical referent is a shift from family members as passive recipients to active participants in care.

Conclusions

Key features of building rapport with ICU family members are empathy and mutual understanding, supported by communication, time and relationships. The findings suggest that rapport may facilitate family participation and care partnerships in intensive care. However, the findings should be interpreted in light of the limited empirical basis and the absence of formal quality appraisal.

Relevance to clinical practice

Clarifying the concept of building rapport may support communication training, reflective practice and active listening strategies that strengthen partnerships with ICU family members.

title: FXIa inhibitors and secondary stroke prevention.
authorString: Palaiodimou L, Theodorou A, Stefanou MI, Tsivgoulis G.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

Patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke face a substantial residual risk of recurrence despite antiplatelet therapy, while conventional anticoagulation is unsuitable due to an unacceptably high bleeding risk. Activated factor XI (FXIa) inhibition promises anticoagulant efficacy while sparing hemostasis. We appraise the evidence of FXIa-inhibitors in secondary stroke prevention considering the pivotal OCEANIC-STROKE trial.

Recent findings

Phase-2 trials of asundexian and milvexian were reassuring on safety but neutral on imaging-based endpoints, establishing that covert infarcts are a poor surrogate. In the phase-3 OCEANIC-STROKE trial, asundexian added to single or dual antiplatelet therapy reduced recurrent ischemic stroke by 26%, consistently across subtypes, without any excess of major bleeding or intracranial hemorrhage. By contrast, asundexian was inferior to apixaban in atrial fibrillation, a result attributable to dose, comparator, and setting. Consistent with this, the monoclonal antibody abelacimab, which achieves near-complete FXIa-inhibition, reduced bleeding relative to rivaroxaban in atrial fibrillation, though its effect on thromboembolic events has not been established.

Summary

FXIa-inhibition is the first anticoagulant strategy preventing recurrent stroke after noncardioembolic ischemic stroke without a bleeding penalty. Confirmation of a class effect from further trials is awaited, alongside questions of duration, deeper inhibition, and use in other cardiovascular indications.

title: The Role of DEXA Scanning in Secondary Fragility Fracture Prevention.
authorString: Bartolovic G, Aperfine I, Cunningham E, Davison B, Fantoni B, Melott M, Pavlic E, Reed T, Sims M, Schmitt DM.

journal.title: Journal of orthopedics for physician assistants

abstractText: Fragility fractures are often the first clinical sign of osteoporosis and represent a substantial source of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expense in older persons. Despite clear evidence supporting secondary fracture prevention, postfracture care often emphasizes the recovery from the injury itself while insufficiently addressing the underlying skeletal disease. As a result, approximately 6% of patients will have a subsequent fragility fracture within 1 year of the initial injury. In addition, without intervention, osteoporosis will progress in these patients resulting in chronic pain, disability, and decreased quality of life. To slow the progression of osteoporosis, along with lowering the risk of secondary fragility fractures, the aim of this review was to assess the use of dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) in postfracture osteoporosis assessment and monitoring with a focus on its integration with pharmaceutical therapy, fall-prevention techniques, and fracture liaison services (FLS). Without the intervention of FLS, less than one-third of patients will initiate osteoporosis medication therapies within the first year of a hip fracture, despite strong guideline recommendations. DEXA-based bone mineral density evaluation enhances clinical risk stratification, promotes the initiation of evidence-based pharmacologic therapy, and improves osteoporosis detection. The use of DEXA within FLS models improved treatment adherence and subsequently reduced the number of secondary fractures. DEXA-guided postfracture care is essential for lowering recurrent fractures and enhancing outcomes for older persons, especially when incorporated into coordinated care pathways.

title: Psychopharmacological advances in neurorehabilitation after traumatic brain injury.
authorString: Arcani V, Iruthayanathar C, Rauen K.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

Pharmacotherapy is widely used to manage neuropsychiatric sequelae that may interfere with neurorehabilitation after traumatic brain injury (TBI), despite limited TBI-specific evidence. This review summarizes psychopharmacological evidence from the past 18 months and proposes a three-step approach: deprescribing potentially recovery-limiting medications, characterizing individual neuropsychiatric symptoms, and selecting symptom-targeted treatments to support cognitive, emotional, behavioral, and functional recovery after TBI.

Recent findings

Methylphenidate shows the most consistent evidence for selected cognitive outcomes, particularly attention and processing speed. Pharmacological approaches to agitation, sleep-wake disorders, depression, fatigue, and posttraumatic headache have been studied, but TBI-specific evidence remains limited or heterogeneous. Sedative, anticholinergic, and cognitive adverse effects, cardiovascular risks, and dependence require consideration in TBI neurorehabilitation.

Summary

No pharmacological treatment is established as disease-modifying after TBI. Given the limited evidence, psychopharmacotherapy should be individualized, symptom-targeted, and integrated into multidisciplinary TBI neurorehabilitation. Continuous medication review and deprescribing should accompany careful treatment selection and monitoring. Future trials should determine whether symptom improvement translates into better rehabilitation participation, functional independence, and long-term health-related quality of life.

title: Fasting triglyceride-glucose index and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: an observational study of metabolic risk in singleton pregnancies.
authorString: Brenisin M, Lovasova E, Novakova J, Bertkova I, Hubkova B, Pallayova M.
abstractText:
Objectives

To evaluate the association between the fasting TyG index and gestational hypertension/preeclampsia (GH/PE) in singleton pregnancies.

Methods

This observational study included 175 pregnant women with singleton pregnancies examined during routine antenatal care between 11 and 35 weeks of gestation from January 2023 to December 2024. Women with pre-existing hypertension, diabetes, renal disease, gestational diabetes mellitus or major systemic disorders were excluded. Clinical, anthropometric and fasting biochemical data were collected, and the TyG index was calculated as ln [fasting triglycerides (mg/dL) × fasting glucose (mg/dL)/2]. Group comparisons, correlation analyses, logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis were performed.

Results

Thirty-nine women (22.3 %) developed GH/PE. Compared with women with physiological pregnancies, women with GH/PE had higher pre-gestational BMI, gestational weight change, blood pressure, fasting glucose, triglycerides and TyG index values (all p≤0.018). The TyG index correlated positively with mean arterial pressure (r=0.20, p=0.027) and gestational week at assessment (r=0.35, p<0.001). Higher TyG index values were associated with increased odds of GH/PE (OR=3.75, 95 % CI 1.79-7.85). A TyG cut-off of 8.6 showed 58.97 % sensitivity and 69.85 % specificity, with an AUC of 0.69 (95 % CI 0.59-0.79).

Conclusions

In this antenatal cohort, the fasting TyG index was associated with GH/PE and showed moderate discriminatory ability. The TyG index should not be used as a stand-alone diagnostic test, but it may complement BMI and routine clinical assessment in identifying women with increased metabolic susceptibility to hypertensive pregnancy disorders.

title: Comparative Risk of Cardiovascular Adverse Events among Antipsychotic Agents in Adults treated for Schizophrenia: A Systematic Review and Meta Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
authorString: Nepal S, Thapa Y.
abstractText: Background: Adverse drug effects of antipsychotics differ drug to drug. Older typical antipsychotic drugs are associated with greater Extra pyramidal side effects. Among the newer atypical antipsychotic drugs, weight gain has been associated with clozapine and olanzapine. There have been numerous studies reporting increased risk of serious adverse cardiovascular events associated with antipsychotics use but none study has been done evaluating comparative risk of all antipsychotic agents in head-to-head comparison involving randomized controlled trials. Methods: Systematic review was done as per PRISMA 2020 guidelines for all outcomes of all 38 studies included for a full-text review. Meta-Analysis under random-effect model for feasible 7 outcomes were possible. PubMed, Medline, DOAJ, MDPI, Clinicaltrial.gov and Google scholar article repositories were assessed for the review. RoB-2 tool was used to assess the Risk of bias and GRADE Approach was used to grade the certainty of evidence. Results: Antipsychotic agents use showed no statistically significant results with the outcomes of hypertension, serious arrythmia, myocardial infarction, bradycardia, angina, and orthostatic hypotension. Statistically significant risk was found to be associated with antipsychotic use for the outcome of Tachycardia, Risk Ratio (RR) = 2.72, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 1.29-5.68. Conclusion: Antipsychotic use was associated with higher incidence of Tachycardia.

title: Compression Performance of a Novel Leaf-Spring Pocket Compression Device: A Randomized Crossover Evaluation
authorString: Sairaku A, Fukuda Y, Nakano Y.
abstractText: Pocket compression is routinely applied after cardiac implantable electronic device procedures to reduce hematoma formation, but conventional compression bandaging has important limitations, including positional instability of pressure and patient discomfort. We developed a novel leaf-spring pocket compression device designed to provide stable, localized compression. This study was conducted as a preparatory performance evaluation prior to a planned multicenter randomized controlled trial (jRCTs042250188). In this randomized crossover study, 33 healthy male volunteers underwent pressure assessment with both the leaf-spring device and conventional compression bandaging across six clinically relevant body positions. The target compression pressure range was predefined as 8–32 mmHg on physiological grounds. The number of body positions in which compression pressure fell within the target range was higher with the leaf-spring device than with conventional compression bandaging (5 [4–6] vs. 4 [3–5] per participant, P=0.005). Pressure variability across body positions was smaller with the leaf-spring device (P<0.001), and comfort scores were higher (5 [4–5] vs. 3 [2–4], P<0.001). No clinically significant skin complications were observed. These findings demonstrate that the leaf-spring device provided more stable and physiologically appropriate compression than conventional compression bandaging while improving comfort, supporting further clinical evaluation in patients undergoing cardiac device implantation.

title: Characterization of a guinea pig model to evaluate cardiovascular toxicity risk for targeted protein degraders - Insights and lessons learned.
authorString: Kremer JJ, Miranda S, Vicart A, Adachi Y, Neddermann D, Senese PB, Zammit MD, Gralinski MR, Friedrichs GS.
abstractText: Targeted protein degradation is an active area of pharmaceutical research and development with the promise to increase the potential number of druggable targets across numerous therapeutic areas. One challenge in their current development has been unexpected cardiovascular findings that have been reported during clinical trials with some degraders, primarily delayed ventricular repolarization manifested as longer corrected QT (QTc) intervals and potential for increased arrhythmic risk. The objective of this study was to investigate whether guinea pigs might be a suitable small animal model to characterize potential cardiovascular effects earlier in degrader development in alignment with 3R principles. The pharmacokinetics and cardiovascular effects were measured in naïve guinea pigs using 4 distinct degraders previously tested in non-human primates. We found exposures were broadly lower in guinea pigs than non-human primates, and dose-limiting toxicity was observed with some degraders after increasing the dose (mg/kg) in guinea pigs to account for the lower exposures. No consistent CV changes were observed across all 4 degraders, which was not translatable to the QTc interval prolongation observed in non-human primates administered the same degraders. Lastly, an anesthetized guinea pig model was investigated to evaluate acute cardiovascular changes at elevated in vivo exposures beyond those achieved in the conscious preparations. However, no consistent changes were observed in QTc intervals. In this context of this preliminary investigation of 4 degraders, the guinea pig model was not a suitable option for evaluating cardiovascular liabilities.

title: In Vivo Study of Topical Bimatoprost, Latanoprost, Travoprost in Comparison with Minoxidil on Hair Growth in C57BL/6 Mice.
authorString: Navale VS, Marathe PA, Patil SP.
abstractText:
Background

Alopecia significantly affects psychological well-being and social functioning. Standard treatments, like minoxidil and finasteride, are limited by delayed efficacy, need for lifelong use, and adverse effects. Prostaglandin analogs (PGAs), originally developed for ocular hypertension, have shown promise in promoting hair growth. This study compares their effects with minoxidil in a murine model.

Aim and objectives

To compare the effects of bimatoprost, latanoprost, and travoprost on hair growth in C57BL/6 mice, with evaluation of hair density, follicle diameter, and growth rate using minoxidil as the comparator.

Materials and methods

After Institutional Animal Ethics Committee approval, 40 male C57BL/6 mice (aged 6-7 weeks, weighing 20-25 g) were randomized into five groups ( n = 8 in each group): (1) vehicle control, (2) minoxidil 5%, (3) latanoprost 0.005%, (4) bimatoprost 0.03%, and (5) travoprost 0.004%. Drugs were applied topically to shaved dorsal skin daily for 28 days. Hair growth was assessed by follicle density, bulb diameter, and area of regrowth using ImageJ from photographs taken on days 1, 7, 15, and 28.

Results

All PGAs significantly increased hair density compared to vehicle control (vehicle control: 1.50 ± 0.55 vs. latanoprost: 7.50 ± 1.69, bimatoprost: 7.75 ± 2.87, travoprost: 6.87 ± 3.40; P = 0.001). Latanoprost and bimatoprost showed higher hair density than minoxidil (3.75 ± 2.87; P = 0.038 and 0.010, respectively). Hair follicle diameter was greater with PGAs (latanoprost: 53.12 ± 5.30, bimatoprost: 51.87 ± 7.52, travoprost: 48.12 ± 3.47 μm) versus vehicle control (27.91 ± 5.57 μm, P = 0.001) and minoxidil (38.12 ± 5.46 μm, P = 0.001). Bimatoprost showed the greatest regrowth by day 28, while latanoprost demonstrated earlier onset by day 15. PGAs also caused darker pigmentation and longer hair.

Limitations

The present study duration was limited to 4 weeks. Minoxidil (positive control) did not show noticeable hair growth because its effects usually take 6-8 weeks to appear.

Conclusion

Topical PGAs improved key hair growth parameters. Bimatoprost and latanoprost showed early and superior efficacy by day 28.

title: Pulmonary Vein Isolation for Atrial Fibrillation in Brugada Syndrome: A Meta-Analysis.
authorString: Sabahizadeh A, Askarinejad A, Firoozbakhsh P, Kohansal E, Pakmehr SA, Gupta D, Lip GYH, Haghjoo M.
abstractText:
Background

Brugada syndrome (BrS) is an inherited arrhythmogenic disorder responsible for approximately 4% of sudden cardiac deaths. Atrial fibrillation (AF) frequently coexists and increases the risk of inappropriate implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) therapies. Antiarrhythmic drugs are often limited by proarrhythmic effects, creating an unmet therapeutic need.

Purpose

We evaluated whether pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) reduces AF recurrence and provides effective rhythm control in patients with BrS and AF.

Methods

We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies published in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus from inception until February 14, 2026. We included studies reporting outcomes of PVI in patients with BrS and AF. The primary endpoint was freedom from AF after ablation. Secondary endpoints included AF recurrence, changes in inappropriate implantable cardioverter-defibrillator shocks before versus after ablation, and procedural complications. Pooled proportions and risk differences were calculated using random-effects models.

Results

A total of 2149 records were initially identified. After screening and eligibility assessment, Five studies comprising 214 participants overall, including 124 patients with BrS or Brugada-type ECG, were included in the final analysis. The mean age of participants ranged from 45.8 ± 15.5 to 57 ± 10 years, and the proportion of male patients ranged from 33.3% to 100% across studies. PVI significantly reduced inappropriate defibrillator shocks (pooled risk difference -0.35). Freedom from AF was achieved in 82% of patients. The pooled recurrence rate was 36%. A spontaneous type 1 electrocardiographic pattern was present in 10% of patients, and 32% had a family history of sudden cardiac death. Procedural complications were uncommon across studies.

Conclusion

PVI was associated with favorable rhythm-control outcomes and acceptable procedural safety in patients with BrS or Brugada-type ECG and AF. Inappropriate ICD shocks were less frequent after ablation, supporting PVI as a clinically relevant rhythm-control strategy in this challenging population. Larger prospective studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

title: The genetic, clinical and immune landscape of clonal hematopoiesis across adulthood in the multi-ancestry Mount Sinai Million cohort
authorString: Esai Selvan M, Ashraf N, Pradeep R, Giordano L, Dougherty M, Chevelev P, Neuse CJ, Nathan DI, Marcellino BK, Klein RJ, Gümüş ZH.
abstractText: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), the age-associated expansion of blood cell clones carrying acquired driver mutations, remains less well characterized in young adults, across genetic ancestries, and in clinical populations. We analyzed whole-exome sequencing and longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data from 59,598 adults in the Mount Sinai Million Health Discoveries Program, an urban, multi-ancestry hospital-based cohort that includes substantial representation of African (∼35%) and Admixed American genetic ancestry (∼15%) and young adults aged 18-39 years (∼30%). After sample QC, separate analyses were performed in discovery (n = 28,051) and validation (n = 26,938) cohorts defined by sequencing platform and combined by meta-analysis. CHIP was detected in 8.5% of participants in each cohort and in 4.0% of young adults, with  DNMT3A ,  TET2 ,  ASXL1 , and  PPM1D the most frequently mutated genes. Prevalence and clone size increased with age across ancestry groups. After adjusting for age, participants of African ancestry had lower CHIP prevalence than those of European ancestry in both cohorts (discovery: OR=0.86, 95% CI = 0.78–0.95,  p =0.002; validation: OR=0.84, 95% CI = 0.75–0.93,  p =0.001). Participants of Admixed American ancestry showed a similar trend. Higher systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) was associated with CHIP after adjusting for age, sex and ancestry in both cohorts (pooled OR=1.30, 95% CI = 1.15–1.48,  p =4.78e-5). Heterozygosity at an HLA class II locus  HLA-DPA1 was associated with 7% lower odds of overall CHIP (pooled OR=0.93, 95% CI = 0.87–0.99,  p =0.03). Driver-stratified analyses revealed distinct HLA class II nominal association patterns for  DNMT3A - and  TET2 -mutant CHIP. Particularly,  HLA-DQB1 heterozygosity associated with lower odds of  TET2 -mutant CHIP (pooled OR=0.84, 95% CI = 0.70–1.00,  p =0.05),  HLA-DQA1 and  HLA-DOB heterozygosity associated with higher odds of  DNMT3A -mutant CHIP (pooled OR=1.19, 95% CI = 1.00–1.42,  p =0.05; pooled OR=1.12, 95% CI = 1.01–1.25,  p =0.03 respectively). Longitudinal EHR analyses revealed CHIP associations with several incident diseases that varied by driver gene and clone size. The broadest pattern of associations involved high-risk CHIP genes and encompassed hematologic malignancies, solid tumors, cardiovascular outcomes, hypertension, and COPD. High-VAF clones were the main drivers of these associations. Among adults aged ≥ 40 years, phenome-wide analyses identified a Bonferroni-significant association with incident myeloproliferative disease and nominal associations with incident pancytopenia, anemia, cardiomegaly, and chronic renal failure. Young-adult CHIP was nominally associated with incident nodular goiter and esophageal disease. These findings characterize CHIP across adulthood and genetic ancestry and reveal inherited immune variation and systemic inflammation as correlates in a hospital-based population.

title: Clinical Usefulness of Artificial Intelligence–Enabled Electrocardiography for Pulmonary Hypertension Detection: A Meta-analysis Based on Pre- and Post-Test Probability
authorString: EDJIMBI JAC, Kesaf AE, Gajjar A, Allam K, Bakhshi H.
abstractText: Pulmonary hypertension is frequently diagnosed late because its early manifestations are nonspecific. Artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography may provide a scalable method for identifying patients who warrant further evaluation. We searched eight databases from inception through May 2026 without language restrictions for studies evaluating artificial intelligence or machine-learning algorithms applied to standard 12-lead electrocardiograms against invasive hemodynamic or echocardiographic reference standards. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Sensitivity and specificity were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251149532). Five retrospective studies comprising 103,884 individuals were included. Pooled sensitivity was 0.81 (95% CI, 0.79-0.82), pooled specificity was 0.80 (95% CI, 0.76-0.83), and the summary area under the curve was 0.85 (95% CI, 0.81-0.88). The positive likelihood ratio was 4.03 (95% CI, 3.38-4.80), and the negative likelihood ratio was 0.24 (95% CI, 0.23-0.26). At a pretest probability of 20%, positive and negative results corresponded to posttest probabilities of approximately 50% and 6%, respectively. Heterogeneity was substantial, but leave-one-out analyses did not materially alter pooled estimates. Artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography showed good performance for detecting pulmonary hypertension and may support targeted case finding. Prospective studies should determine whether its use improves diagnostic pathways and patient outcomes.

title: Association of MASLD With Atrial Fibrillation Recurrence After Catheter Ablation: A Meta-Analysis.
authorString: Amirat A, Mohamed AA, Alfahmi FK, Harfoush MK, Allahawyah SA, Elhadi A, Roshdy R, Issa EA, Mrouj HS, Mohamed NA, AbuZarifa M.
abstractText:
Background

Atrial fibrillation (AF) recurrence after catheter ablation remains common. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is increasingly recognized as a cardiometabolic condition and has been linked to incident AF, but its association with AF recurrence after catheter ablation remains unclear. This meta-analysis aimed to determine whether MASLD is associated with recurrent AF after catheter ablation METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus till July 2026 for studies that included adults with AF undergoing catheter ablation and compared the risk of AF recurrence between those with and without MASLD. A random-effects model was used to synthesize HRs and corresponding 95% CIs. Between-study variability was evaluated with the I2 measure, with additional subgroup analyses stratified by AF type and MASLD diagnostic method.

Results

Six studies comprising 2921 patients (894 with MASLD) were included. MASLD was significantly associated with an increased risk of AF recurrence after ablation (HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.39-2.64; p < 0.001), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 69.7%). The association remained significant in both paroxysmal (HR 1.78, 95% CI 1.36-2.33) and persistent AF (HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.26-2.05), with no significant subgroup difference (p = 0.58). Studies using imaging-based diagnosis of MASLD showed a significant association, whereas the association was not significant when the Fatty Liver Index was used, with no evidence of a difference between diagnostic-method subgroups (p = 0.47) CONCLUSION: MASLD is associated with a higher risk of AF recurrence after catheter ablation and may help identify patients at greater risk of recurrence. Further prospective studies are needed to provide a more comprehensive understanding of this association.

title: Urban, regional and remote outcomes following TAVR for Queensland patients: a retrospective cohort study
authorString: Cameron P, Brazzale A, Starmer G, Moxon JV.
abstractText:
Background

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) offers a minimally invasive approach to treat severe aortic stenosis (AS) but can only be performed at centres meeting strict regulatory requirements. It remains unclear whether this requirement restricts TAVR access for patients residing in rural Australia, and whether such people experience poorer outcomes than metropolitan counterparts as a result.

Methods

This multicentre retrospective cohort study used Australian Cardiac Outcomes Registry data. All Queensland residents who underwent TAVR between April 2018 and 27 March 2026 were included. Rurality was assigned by postcode using the Modified Monash Model (MMM) and grouped as urban (MMM1), regional (MMM2–4), or remote (MMM5–7). The primary outcome was 12-month mortality and was investigated using Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards analyses.

Findings

Among 6813 patients, 4246 (62%) were urban, 2092 (31%) regional, and 475 (7%) remote. Twelve-month all-cause mortality did not differ by rurality (urban: 211 [5.0%]; regional: 103 [4.9%]; remote: 23 [4.8%]; χ²=0.991, log-rank P=0.929), a finding confirmed in multivariable analysis. At the time of TAVR, regional and remote patients were younger, more comorbid, had more severe AS, and lower STS scores than urban counterparts. Clinical frailty score, non-transfemoral access, STS score, atrial fibrillation or flutter, and moderate–severe chronic lung disease independently predicted 12-month mortality.

Interpretation

TAVR outcomes were comparable between rurality groups, suggesting equitable care within Queensland’s centralised TAVR model. However, registry data only captures patients who underwent TAVR and may miss older rural patients facing barriers to AS diagnosis, referral, or procedural workup.

Funding

There was no funding or sponsor involvement.

Research in context

Evidence before this study

We searched Medline (Ovid) for publications examining the association between rurality and outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). We searched from database inception to September 2026 using the terms “TAVR” OR “transcatheter aortic valve replacement” OR “transcatheter aortic valve implantation” OR “TAVI”, AND “rural*”. We identified two key studies of rurality and TAVR outcomes, one from the USA and one from Australia. Both reported no difference in mortality between rural and urban patients. However, both were single-centre studies with small samples (413 and 142 patients, respectively) and neither used time-to-event analysis. The US study followed patients for only 6 months and used descriptive analysis alone. The Australian study included urban and regional patients but not remote patients.

Added value of this study

In 6813 patients from a national procedural registry, 12-month all-cause mortality after TAVR did not differ between urban, regional, and remote Queensland residents (5.0%, 4.9%, and 4.8%, respectively), including after multivariable adjustment and in sensitivity analyses. This was despite regional and remote patients being younger, having more comorbidity, lower STS scores, and having more severe AS at the time of the procedure. To our knowledge, this is the largest study of TAVR outcomes by rurality and the first in Australia to include remote patients. Remote residents and First Nations people were underrepresented among TAVR recipients compared with the Queensland population.

Implications of all the available evidence

Among people who reach TAVR, a centralised delivery model appears to provide comparable short-term outcomes regardless of where patients live. However, ACOR data only captures patients who received the procedure, and the younger age of rural patients and underrepresentation of remote patients suggests that barriers may exist earlier in the pathway, at diagnosis, referral, or work-up. Future research linking diagnostic and referral data to procedural data is needed to assess access, and the findings should inform planning of non-metropolitan AS services.

title: Understanding widening socio-economic inequities in cardiovascular disease mortality in the Netherlands: A mixed methods protocol
authorString: Thompson K.
abstractText:
Background:

In the Netherlands, there is a substantial social gradient in mortality: individuals with higher socio-economic status are more likely to live longer lives than those with lower socio-economic status. There is evidence that this social gradient has widened since the mid-twentieth century, although why this has occurred is poorly understood. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) provides a particularly useful case study for understanding the mechanisms underlying this widening gradient. While CVD was historically the leading cause of death in the Netherlands, improvements in prevention and treatment have decreased CVD mortality, even as socio-economic inequalities in CVD mortality have increased. In this project, I aim to identify and test the mechanisms driving widening socio-economic inequities in CVD mortality over the last 75 years. Methods and analysis: This project uses mixed-methods. First, in participatory workshops, key stakeholders, e.g. policymakers, healthcare professionals, patient representatives, and individuals with lived experience of poverty, will co-create a conceptual model outlining the explanations linking socio-economic status and CVD in the Netherlands. Second, the conceptual model will provide the structure for the microsimulation, with the former defining which mechanisms will be represented in the latter. The microsimulation will maintain a common model structure across time, although population characteristics and individual trajectories will change to reflect successive twenty-year periods from the 1950s until today. The microsimulation will be validated by comparing simulated outcomes with historical data. Counterfactual scenarios will then be used to estimate the relative contribution of different mechanisms to the widening of socio-economic inequalities in CVD mortality. Ethics and dissemination: This project has been approved by the Social Sciences Research Ethics Committee of Wageningen University (approval number 2026-203). Participants will provide informed consent prior to participation. The microsimulation code will be made openly available, and findings will be disseminated through open-access publications, conference presentations, and a public summary co-designed with stakeholders.

title: Safety of Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) and Colonoscopy Performed Early Versus Delayed After a Recent Vascular Event: A Retrospective Cohort Analysis of a Real-World Database
authorString: Elimeleh Y, Shamah S, Campisi SP, Awadie H, Gorelik Y, Gralnek IM.
abstractText: Background & Aims: A higher American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) classification indicates negative patient outcomes. Guidelines recommend anesthesia-provider support for endoscopy within 90 days of a transient ischemic attack (TIA), cerebrovascular accident (CVA), or myocardial infarction (MI). We evaluated outcomes of esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) and colonoscopy performed early (0–90 days) versus delayed (91–180 days) after such a vascular event. Methods A retrospective cohort study using a population-based database. Patients who underwent a single EGD or colonoscopy 0–90 days after a vascular event (early group) were compared with patients who underwent endoscopy 91–180 days after the event (delayed group). The primary outcome was all-cause 30-day mortality. Results 2,883 patients met inclusion criteria; 1,434 (49.7%) underwent endoscopy in the early window and 1,449 (50.3%) in the delayed window. A total of 85 deaths (2.9%) occurred within 30 days of endoscopy. Early endoscopy was associated with a higher 30-day mortality than delayed endoscopy (HR 2.58, 95% CI 1.82–3.66, p < 0.001). Vascular event type showed a graded association, with greatest 30-day mortality after antecedent CVA, followed by MI and, to a lesser extent, TIA. In the early group, colonoscopy without polypectomy was associated with lower mortality than colonoscopy with polypectomy (HR 0.31, 95% CI 0.11–0.89). Conclusions Among patients undergoing endoscopy after a recent vascular event, mortality correlated with type of antecedent vascular event, patient age, comorbidity burden and procedure type. These findings support individualized decision-making based on indication, urgency, vascular event type and comorbidity, rather than reliance on a fixed time threshold.

title: Factors associated with hypertension among diabetic patients at two tertiary Hospitals in Rwanda: a case-control study
authorString: Nsengiyumva P, Iracyahari E, sebera E, Bitunguhali L, Sebatunzi O, Urengejeho D, Masaisa F, Asfaw EW, Tuyizere A.
abstractText: Background Globally, 60–80% of diabetic patients develop hypertension, leading to increased cardiovascular mortality. In sub-Saharan Africa, including Rwanda, both conditions are on the rise due to urbanization and lifestyle changes. Despite high prevalence, specific risk factors for hypertension in Rwandan diabetic populations remain poorly understood, limiting targeted interventions. This case-control study aimed to identify risk factors for hypertension among diabetic patients at two tertiary hospitals in Rwanda (2020–2024). Methods This retrospective matched case-control study was conducted at two tertiary hospitals in Rwanda from January 2020 to December 2024. The cases consisted of diabetic patients with hypertension (n = 200), and the controls were diabetic patients without hypertension (n = 200), matched for gender. Medical records were reviewed using structured data extraction forms, and we conducted interviews with participants to collect data on lifestyle characteristics. Data analysis employed chi-square tests and multivariate logistic regression using SPSS version 28.0. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant at 95% confidence. Results Among eligible 400 participants in outpatient clinic (200 cases, 200 controls), hypertensive diabetic patients were older (60.3 vs 48.6 years), had longer duration of diabetes (12 vs 10 years), poorer glycemic control (HbA1C 9% vs 8%), and worse lifestyle factors including higher smoking rates (21.2% vs 5.2%) and lower physical activity (17.6% vs 43.8%). In multivariate logistic regression analysis, hypertension among diabetic patients was significantly associated with family history of hypertension (AOR = 3.12, 95% CI: 2.43–22.68), elevated creatinine levels ≥ 88 µmol/L (aOR = 4.23, 95% CI: 1.02–17.48), smoking (aOR = 2.46, 95% CI: 1.15–14.60), and poor glycemic control (HbA1c > 7%) (aOR = 3.46, 95% CI: 1.96–15.81). Engagement in physical exercise was inversely associated with hypertension (aOR = 0.17, 95% CI: 0.05–0.56). Hypertensive diabetic patients also exhibited higher frequencies of chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular complications compared with controls. Conclusion It was revealed that hypertension among diabetic patients is associated with a family history of hypertension, poor glycemic control, elevated kidney function, and smoking, while regular physical exercise has demonstrated a protective effect. These findings support routine risk assessment and integrated diabetes care in service delivery by targeting these associated factors while promoting physical activity.

title: Female Life Stages for Cardiovascular Disease Prevention and Management in Girls and Women: A Case-Based Approach.
authorString: Lau ES, Faubion S, Gangopadhyaya A, Grobman WA, Perak AM, Schulte J, Shim J, Khan SS, Cameron NA, American Heart Association Cardiovascular Health in Girls and Women Science Advisory Group.

journal.title: Journal of the American Heart Association

abstractText: Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death among women in the United States and worldwide, yet current approaches to prevention and management do not fully account for female-specific biology. To address this need, the American Heart Association, in collaboration with the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine, published a Presidential Advisory defining the Female Life Stage construct, which defines four distinct stages across the life course: Perimenarche (Stage 1), Ovarian Cycling (Stage 2), Perimenopause (Stage 3), and Postmenopause (Stage 4), with pregnancy including the time before and after (Peripregnancy period) recognized as a distinct life period when cardiovascular risk may be modified.<sup>1</sup> To provide examples of how this framework and the accompanying consensus guidance published in an accompanying Scientific Statement can be translated into a personalized care approach, this special report presents six hypothetical cases spanning the Female Life Stages, including adolescence and young adulthood, the peripartum period, midlife, perimenopause, and postmenopause.<sup>2</sup> These cases illustrate how a female-specific life course framework that reflects hormonally-mediated physiologic transitions can promote earlier recognition of cardiovascular risk, guide cardiovascular screening and inform cardiovascular management. The cases underscore how hormonal health (e.g., menstrual cycle assessment, pregnancy planning and prevention, assessing and managing perimenopausal and postmenopausal symptoms) and psychosocial health (e.g., anxiety, depression, disordered eating) have cardiovascular implications. Moreover, this approach integrates well-established female-specific cardiovascular risk factors (e.g., premature menopause and adverse pregnancy outcomes), in addition to less well-recognized risk factors (e.g., early menarche, polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome). We also review key evidence to inform a patient-centered approach to exogenous hormone therapy and associated cardiovascular risks for a variety of indications, including management of abnormal uterine bleeding, ovarian suppression, pregnancy prevention, and menopausal symptoms. By contextualizing the Female Life Stage framework within practical case scenarios, this article provides clinicians with a structured, evidence-based approach to improve cardiovascular prevention and management for girls and women.

title: Underrepresentation of women in U.S. occupational cohort mortality studies.
authorString: Johnson CY, Kelly-Reif K, Fujishiro K.
abstractText: Reviews of the occupational epidemiology literature between the 1970s and 2010s found that men were more likely than women to be included in studies of occupational exposures and chronic disease. Our objective was to examine a contemporary sample of occupational cohort mortality studies to determine the extent to which women are underrepresented, how sex is used in analyses, and if the representation of women has improved over time. We searched PubMed for U.S. occupational cohort mortality studies published between 2000 and 2022 with cancer or cardiovascular disease mortality outcomes. We identified 176 U.S. cohort analyses meeting inclusion criteria. Among the cohort analyses that reported the sex of participants, 57% included men and women, 42% included men only, and 1% included women only. Sex was most commonly used in statistical analyses to adjust for confounding (69%) and to exclude women from the study population (26%). Between 2000-2004 and 2015-2022, the proportion of cohort analyses including women increased from 48% to 69%. Women remain poorly represented in occupational cohort mortality studies, although over time fewer studies excluded women. Achieving appropriate representation of women in occupational epidemiology research is essential for fully understanding relationships between occupational exposures and health.

title: Biomolecule-Assembled Materials: Bridging Molecular Assembly Rules and Cardiovascular Applications.
authorString: Liu Q, Liu Y, Zhang Y, Liu K, Su J.
abstractText: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide, and many current drugs and devices are limited by off-target exposure, weak responsiveness to pathological cues, and reduced performance under pulsatile blood flow. Biomolecule-assembled materials, constructed from nucleic acids, proteins/peptides, polysaccharides, and lipids/vesicles, offer a promising way to address these limitations. Their functions arise from sequence- or chemistry-governed assembly rules that encode molecular recognition, transport, and mechanical behavior across multiple scales, from nanostructures to tissue-facing interfaces. This review summarizes recent progress in biomolecule-assembled materials across CVD prevention, diagnosis, therapy, and regeneration. Programmable bio-assemblies support rapid sensing and lesion-localized intervention, while also enabling bioactive coatings, injectable depots, and membrane-mimetic carriers for plaque targeting and drug delivery. By comparing material classes through shared cardiovascular tasks and hemodynamic constraints, modular hybrids suggest potential advantages that merit further investigation under physiologically relevant conditions. Clinical translation will depend on predictive assembly design, standardized manufacturing and quality control, and in vivo validation under physiologically relevant flow. Through converting molecular assembly rules into scalable, hemodynamically robust functions, biomolecule-assembled materials offer a unifying design language for next-generation cardiovascular diagnosis and therapy.

title: CCR2-Dependent Myeloid Cell Recruitment Links Post-MI Heart Failure to Pulmonary Hypertension.
authorString: Gillan JL, Kamp J, Kucherenko MM, Winkler A, Funk-Hilsdorf TC, Jaeschke L, Hegemann N, Bintig W, Wirth EK, Simmons S, Momin N, Foris V, Kovacs G, Kuebler WM, Knosalla C, Grune J.
abstractText:
Background

Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (PH-LHD) is a common complication of myocardial infarction (MI) and heart failure (HF). Myeloid inflammation is a major hallmark of both the local cardiac and systemic post-MI response, with resident and recruited monocyte-derived macrophages orchestrating each step of the ensuing inflammatory cascade, from clearance of dead cardiomyocytes to scar tissue formation. Similarly, myeloid inflammation is a key feature of the PH lung, driving remodeling of small pulmonary vessels. We thus hypothesized that MI-induced systemic myeloid inflammation contributes directly to the development of PH-LHD.

Methods

We assessed expression of inflammatory adhesion molecules, as markers of vascular inflammatory activation and myeloid cell recruitment pathways, in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension, PH-LHD, as well as in a PH-LHD rat model. We then induced MI and subsequent HF in 8- to 10-week-old female C57BL/6J mice via permanent ligation of the left anterior descending coronary artery. HF mice were then treated with a CCR2 (C-C chemokine receptor 2) antagonist to block monocyte recruitment and the development of PH-LHD was assessed at 6 weeks post-MI by a combination of invasive hemodynamics, flow cytometry, echocardiography, and lung histology.

Results

Expression of key inflammatory adhesion molecules, including VCAM1 and SELE, was increased in PH-LHD lungs from humans and rats. Following early post-MI development of HF with reduced ejection fraction, mice exhibited increased numbers of circulating monocytes, lung monocytes, and lung interstitial macrophages, as well as PH-LHD by 6 weeks, characterized by right ventricular hypertrophy, elevated right ventricular pressures, and lung vascular remodeling of small-to-medium-sized pulmonary vessels. Administration of the selective CCR2 antagonist RS102895 from day 10 post-MI to reduce monocyte tissue recruitment attenuated lung vascular remodeling, right ventricular systolic and diastolic pressures, right ventricular hypertrophy, and lung adhesion molecule expression at 6 weeks, compared with vehicle-treated controls, without improving the underlying left-sided HF.

Conclusions

This proof-of-concept study demonstrates a causal role for CCR2-dependent myeloid cell recruitment in the progression from MI-induced HF to secondary pulmonary vascular disease.

title: Comprehensive Centers of Excellence for Women's Cardiovascular Care: A Science Advisory From the American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.
authorString: Cameron NA, Khan SS, Bairey Merz CN, Brewer LC, Davis MM, Ferranti EP, Grobman WA, Hameed AB, Hannon TS, Harrington RA, Johnson HM, Maradik ME, Perak AM, Reynolds HR, Rosen SE, Sanghavi M, Schulte J, Rajgopal Singh R, Sterling MR, Tabak RG, Verma N, Weedn AE, Wood MJ, Kim ESH, American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.
abstractText: Improving cardiovascular health in women is an urgent public health priority given the persistent and pervasive gaps in awareness, prevention, and management of cardiovascular disease in this population. Advances in scientific understanding have led to increased recognition of female-specific considerations in cardiovascular disease, which informed the development of the Female Life Stage construct by the American Heart Association in collaboration with the American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. This construct integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages. However, gaps remain in operationalizing this construct and optimizing the delivery of patient-centered, interdisciplinary care among women. Over the past several decades, women's cardiovascular centers have emerged as leaders, expanded rapidly, and elevated the recognition of cardiovascular diseases that exclusively, disproportionately, or differently affect women (eg, myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, Takotsubo syndrome). In this science advisory, we describe the current landscape of women's cardiovascular centers and propose a national infrastructure to support the expansion of dedicated Comprehensive Centers of Excellence for Women's Cardiovascular Care. These centers are conceptualized as interdisciplinary care models comprising 4 defining pillars: interdisciplinary clinical care, education and training, research, and community engagement. By establishing integrated pathways that span clinical disciplines, these centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research. In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.

title: A Female-Specific Life Course Approach to the Prevention and Management of Cardiovascular Disease: A Presidential Advisory From the American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.
authorString: Khan SS, Grobman WA, Perak AM, Angell S, Brubaker L, Cameron NA, de Ferranti S, El Khoudary SR, Ferranti EP, Hameed AB, Hannon TS, Johnson HM, Kennedy S, Kim ESH, Maradik ME, Martin KA, Miller EC, Reed SD, Tabak RG, Darius Tandon S, Thurston RC, Verma N, Weedn AE, Rajgopal Singh R, Rosen SE, American Heart Association; American Academy of Pediatrics; American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists; and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.
abstractText: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in women, contributes markedly to healthcare expenditures, and is projected to increase substantially by 2050 if current trends continue. There is growing recognition of the complex role of sex as a biologic variable and its influence on cardiovascular health and disease. However, cardiovascular risk remains underrecognized and underaddressed in girls and women, particularly as it relates to female-specific exposure to sex hormones (both endogenous and exogenous), which are systemic modulators of cardiovascular biology. Moreover, girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care spanning specialties, including pediatrics, adolescent medicine, primary care, obstetrics and gynecology, maternal-fetal medicine, cardiology, endocrinology, hematology, and neurology. Consequently, there is a need for a unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health. To address these gaps, the American Heart Association, in collaboration with the American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine, established a Female Life Stage framework to optimize the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women. Physiologic changes in sex hormones define clinically distinct life stages (ie, perimenarche, ovarian cycling, perimenopause, postmenopause), which directly inform female-specific considerations for screening, prevention, and management of cardiovascular disease. This presidential advisory details the framework and its scientific rationale, highlights opportunities for implementation across settings, and identifies priorities for research, clinician education, patient advocacy, and policy. This framework offers a transformative opportunity to equitably improve cardiovascular health for all girls and women.

title: A guide to autophagy-dependent cell death: concepts, criteria, and mechanisms.
authorString: Meng L, Dai M, Zhang X, Kang R, Tang D, Liu N, Guan L, Han L.
abstractText: Macroautophagy (hereafter referred to as autophagy) is generally regarded as a cytoprotective process that maintains cellular homeostasis through intracellular recycling and metabolic adaptation. However, under certain conditions, autophagic machinery can contribute directly to cell death. Defining when autophagy functions as a cause rather than a consequence of cellular demise remains a major challenge and complicates the concept of autophagy-dependent cell death (ADCD). Experimental studies indicate that ADCD can occur through multiple mechanisms, including excessive self-digestion, autophagy-dependent lysosomal injury, selective autophagy-mediated degradation of critical cellular components, and specialized death programs such as autosis. These processes intersect extensively with apoptosis, necroptosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis, placing ADCD within a broader network of regulated cell death pathways. Evidence from cancer, neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, and inflammatory diseases further suggests that ADCD contributes to pathogenesis and may provide therapeutic opportunities. In this review, we discuss the criteria for defining ADCD, the molecular mechanisms underlying its execution, its interactions with other cell death pathways, and its relevance to human disease. Together, we propose a practical framework for distinguishing bona fide ADCD from cell death merely accompanied by autophagy and provide guidance for establishing autophagy as a causal component of the death process.Abbreviations: AACD: autophagy-associated cell death; ADCD: autophagy-dependent cell death; ADF: autophagy-dependent ferroptosis; ATP: adenosine triphosphate; ATPase: adenosine triphosphatase; AUTACs: autophagy-targeting chimeras; BH3: BCL2 homology 3; CAR-T: chimeric antigen receptor T; cGMP: cyclic guanosine monophosphate; CMA: chaperone-mediated autophagy; DAMPs: damage-associated molecular patterns; DHA: dihydroartemisinin; ER: endoplasmic reticulum; ER-phagy: endoplasmic reticulum-selective autophagy; H2O2: hydrogen peroxide; HIV-1: human immunodeficiency virus type 1; I/R: ischemia-reperfusion; LMP: lysosomal membrane permeabilization; MTOR: mechanistic target of rapamycin kinase; PUFAs: polyunsaturated fatty acids; RHIM: receptor-interacting protein homotypic interaction motif; ROS: reactive oxygen species; sGC: soluble guanylate cyclase; SGLT2: sodium-glucose cotransporter 2; TCR-T: T-cell receptor-engineered T; UPR: unfolded protein response.

title: Diastolic Dysfunction Predicts Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Clinical Outcomes in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
authorString: Pepin ME, O’Sullivan J, Gjermeni D, Santana EJ, Mosher B, Malunjkar S, Tso JV, Ashley EA, Lewis E, Christle JW, Myers JN, Parikh V, Kawana M, Wheeler MT, Haddad F.
abstractText:
Background

Echocardiographic indices of diastolic dysfunction are routinely obtained in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), but their relationships with cardiorespiratory fitness and long-term clinical outcomes remain poorly defined.

Objectives

This study therefore sought to determine the extent to which E/e’, left atrial volume index (LAVi), and peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity (TRV max ) relate to peak oxygen uptake, ventilatory efficiency, their longitudinal trajectories, and clinical outcomes in HCM.

Methods

We retrospectively studied patients with HCM who completed cardiopulmonary exercise testing within 7 days of resting echocardiography. Each diastolic index was related to percent-predicted peak oxygen uptake (V̇O 2 ), ventilatory efficiency (V̇E/V̇CO 2 slope), their serial trajectories, and a composite of heart failure hospitalization, transplantation, or death.

Results

Among 441 patients with HCM (mean age 49 ± 16 years; 66% men), each SD higher E/e’, LAVi, and TRV max was independently associated with lower peak V̇O 2 (−6.0, −3.6, and −6.3 percentage points of predicted) and higher V̇E/V̇CO 2 slope (+0.9, +1.0, and +2.5; all P ≤ 0.045), nonlinearly for E/e’ with peak V̇O 2 and LAVi with V̇E/V̇CO 2 slope. On serial testing, only LAVi predicted progressively worsening V̇E/V̇CO 2 slope (+0.4/yr/SD; 95% CI: 0.13-0.68; P = 0.005). Over a median of 4.8 years, 118 of 436 patients (27.1%) reached the composite endpoint, for which LAVi was the strongest echocardiographic predictor (adjusted HR: 1.68/SD; 95% CI: 1.40-2.03).

Conclusions

In HCM, resting diastolic indices were associated with cardiorespiratory fitness, and higher LAVi was independently associated with a steeper rise in V̇E/V̇CO 2 slope and heart failure events. Resting diastolic phenotyping may complement exercise testing.

title: 14-3-3 Enables β-Adrenergic Regulation of the Cardiac Sodium Channel at the Intercalated Disc
authorString: Zheng Y, Lopez Serrano AL, Chorna S, Wan X, Biswas R, Ramirez-Navarro A, Chinthalapudi K, Weinberg SH, Tseng G, Deschenes I.
abstractText:
Background:

Beta-Adrenergic stimulation enables the heart to adapt electrical activity to increased physiological demand. Although the cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5 is essential for impulse propagation, the mechanisms underlying its acute beta-adrenergic regulation, particularly within distinct cardiomyocyte membrane domains, remain poorly understood. We investigated whether the phosphorylation-sensitive adaptor protein 14-3-3 mediates this regulation.

Methods and Results:

Using automated patch-clamp electrophysiology in HEK293 cells and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs), we found that isoproterenol rapidly increased sodium current (INa) and promoted channel activation at more hyperpolarized potentials, whereas PKA inhibition reduced INa. Disruption of 14-3-3 function abolished these responses without substantially altering basal sodium current or Nav1.5 surface expression. Macropatch recordings from ventricular myocytes revealed that isoproterenol preferentially enhanced INa at the intercalated disc, an effect prevented by 14-3-3 inhibition. Proximity ligation assays further demonstrated increased Nav1.5/14-3-3 proximity following beta-adrenergic stimulation. Systematic mutagenesis identified S460 in the Nav1.5 DI-DII linker as a critical determinant of acute PKA-dependent regulation. Molecular modeling predicted that S460 phosphorylation stabilizes the Nav1.5/14-3-3 interaction. In CRISPR-engineered S460A iPSC-CMs, acute beta-adrenergic regulation of INa was abolished, whereas the isoproterenol-induced increase in conduction velocity was significantly attenuated. Computational simulations further predicted that enhanced intercalated-disc sodium current supports increased conduction velocity across varying conditions of electrical coupling and pacing rate.

Conclusions:

Our findings identify 14-3-3 and S460 as critical determinants of spatially selective beta-adrenergic regulation of Nav1.5 at the cardiac intercalated disc. This mechanism provides a molecular link between sympathetic signaling and cardiac sodium current regulation, supporting the concept that localized enhancement of Nav1.5 function contributes to the adaptation of cardiac conduction during increased sympathetic demand.

title: A Local Enrichment Computational Framework to Identify Disease-Enriched Physical Activity Patterns
authorString: qian h, wu c, Li B, Rosenzweig A, Wang M.
abstractText: Wearable accelerometers enable continuous monitoring of physical activity (PA), yet conventional summary measures and population-wide clustering approaches may overlook disease-associated behavioral heterogeneity. Here we introduce LocPA, a computational framework that identifies disease-enriched PA patterns through confounder-adjusted activity profiling, similarity network construction, local disease-enrichment testing and community detection. Applying LocPA to 24-hour accelerometry profiles from the UK Biobank, we identified two recurring PA phenotypes across six diseases spanning cardiometabolic, neurological, psychiatric, renal and cardiovascular conditions: a low-activity phenotype characterized by reduced daytime activity and a sleep-disrupted phenotype characterized by reduced daytime and elevated nocturnal activity. In hypertension and diabetes, the sleep-disrupted phenotype was associated with greater disease burden and less favorable clinical and metabolic profiles, differences not consistently captured by conventional PA summary measures. LocPA also identified disease-specific temporal patterns, particularly in Parkinsons disease. Analyses in an independent National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cohort supported the recurrence of hypertension- and diabetes-enriched patterns across populations and accelerometry measurements. LocPA provides a flexible, disease-driven approach for uncovering clinically relevant temporal PA patterns, with potential applications in disease risk characterization and personalized behavioral interventions.

title: Implications of the 2026 Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Guideline for GLP-1 Receptor Agonist and SGLT2 Inhibitor Eligibility Among US Adults
authorString: Corsi DR, Wang C, Kang YM, Zimerman A, Agbaje AO, Moura F.
abstractText:
Background:

The 2026 cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome guideline broadens recommendations for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), but the increment over pre-2026 standards is unknown. We estimated the number and clinical profile of US adults newly eligible under this guideline. Methods Cross-sectional analysis of adults aged 30-79 years in the 2011-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Adults were newly eligible if they met 2026 CKM guideline indications but not pre-2026 American Diabetes Association, American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association heart failure, Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes, or obesity guideline indications. Sensitivity analyses used 2 US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) label standards. Results Among 175.17 million US adults, 111.84 million (63.8%) were already eligible for either class. The CKM guideline added 7.48 million (95% CI: 6.48 to 8.47), a 6.7% increase, all for GLP-1RA and none for SGLT2i: 6.49 million with overweight (body mass index 27.0-29.9 kg/m2, ethnicity adjusted) and no other cardiometabolic disease, and 0.99 million with type 2 diabetes and 10-year PREVENT cardiovascular risk ?7.5%. Newly eligible adults (86.8% CKM stage 1) were younger (46.2 vs 52.9 years), leaner (27.8 vs 33.0 kg/m2), and at lower 10- and 30-year PREVENT risk (3.6% vs 8.1%; 11.3% vs 19.6%; all P < 0.001). Against FDA labeling, 14.15-25.17 million were newly eligible (7.66-18.20 million for SGLT2i). Assuming a 20% relative risk reduction, the projected number needed to treat per cardiovascular event prevented was 243 over 10 years and 56 over 30 years (ages 30-59) in adults with overweight, versus 61 and 26 in already eligible adults. Conclusions Relative to pre-2026 society guidelines, the 2026 CKM guideline newly confers a GLP-1RA indication on 7.48 million US adults, predominantly at lower cardiovascular risk. Whether treating these adults improves outcomes in a cost-efficient manner remains to be established.

title: Health Literacy and Cardiovascular Health Among Formerly Incarcerated Individuals: Evidence from the JUSTICE Study
authorString: Bouzarjomehri B, Puglisi LB, Wang EA, Aminawung JA.
abstractText:
Background:

Health literacy, defined as the ability to find, understand, and use health information, is a key determinant of cardiovascular disease but remains underexamined among individuals transitioning from incarceration to community life. This study examined the association between health literacy and cardiovascular health among adults recently released from incarceration.

Methods:

Using baseline data from the Justice-Involved Individuals Cardiovascular Disease Epidemiology (JUSTICE) study, a prospective cohort of individuals with cardiovascular risk factors released from correctional facilities, we examined the association between health literacy, as measured by the Short Test of Functional Health Literacy in Adults, and cardiovascular health, as measured by the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 (LE8).

Results:

Among 439 participants (mean age 45 years), 32 (7%) demonstrated inadequate health literacy. Hispanic ethnicity (53% vs. 25%), less than high school education (50% vs. 20%), and homelessness (16% vs. 3.2%) were significantly associated with inadequate health literacy. In bivariate analyses, inadequate health literacy was associated with lower LE8 blood glucose (63.1 vs. 76.8, p = 0.02), and LE8 physical activity (19.4 vs. 32.2, p = 0.03), but higher LE8 diet (55.5 vs. 43.8, p = 0.04) scores. After adjusting for age, gender, race/ethnicity, education level, and housing status, inadequate health literacy remained independently associated with lower LE8 glucose scores (β = -11.9, 95% CI: -22.9 to -0.8, p = 0.04).

Conclusion:

Health literacy is a modifiable determinant of cardiovascular health, particularly glycemic control, in justice-involved populations. Interventions strengthening health literacy may help reduce health disparities among formerly incarcerated individuals.

title: Polygenic risk and genomic signals in premature coronary artery disease
authorString: Laird C, Xing DG, Abrar M, Sinha S, Dewiit A, White C, Modi K, Bhuiyan MS, Yurdagul A, Kevil CG, Orr AW, Rom O, Conrad S, Bhuiyan MAN.
abstractText:
Background:

Premature coronary artery disease (pCAD) is a distinct presentation of CAD. Using the All of Us (AoU) Research Program data, we compared pCAD with later-onset CAD across cardiometabolic, polygenic, and genome-wide domains.

Methods:

We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional case-case analysis of All of Us Research Program (AoU) participants with established CAD. pCAD was defined as first CAD event before age 55 years in males and before age 65 in females; later-onset CAD was defined as the first CAD event at or after age threshold. Pre-index cardiometabolic measures were extracted from electronic health records and modelled with logistic regression. Using 607,719 variants, a CAD polygenic risk score (PRS) was constructed using published summary statistics and short-read whole-genome sequencing data (srWGS). Results were standardized within self-reported race groups, and evaluated overall, by race, and with a PRS x race interaction. A case-case genome-wide association study (GWAS) compared pCAD with later-onset CAD.

Results:

The CAD cohort included 49,919 participants, including 18,455 with pCAD and 31,464 with later-onset CAD. Participants with pCAD had higher BMI, LDL cholesterol and diastolic blood pressure, and lower HDL cholesterol, serum calcium, and systolic blood pressure. Higher BMI and LDL cholesterol were positively associated with higher odds of pCAD, whereas higher HDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, and serum calcium were inversely associated. PRS was associated with greater odds of pCAD in the genomic models (OR per 1-SD higher PRS, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.12?1.17; P<0.001). Analyses stratified by race showed PRS association was present among White participants but was not observed among Black participants. In the case-case GWAS, one variant reached genome-wide significance at 2q24.3 (rs13383835; OR=1.20; 95% CI, 1.13-1.27; P=5.8x10-9). A total of 137 variants met an exploratory threshold of P<1x10-5.

Conclusions:

Premature onset of CAD is characterized by a distinct cardiometabolic profile driven by modifiable risk factors, greater polygenic burden, and genomic signals associated with earlier disease timing. A European-derived PRS did not transfer to Black participants, who were overrepresented in pCAD. Together, these findings support pCAD as a clinically and genetically distinct presentation of CAD and highlight the need for ancestry-specific validation of genomic risk tools in diverse cohorts.

title: Training-free generation of 4D CT and other rare acquisitions improves segmentation across modalities
authorString: Sadée C, Dils A, Hundal NS, Wan K, Chun A, Shukla A, Xi IL, Van Puyvelde M, Hartmann K, Shah P, Hirschvogel M, Zhou W, Lin C, Gangaram V, Er AG, Seweryn M, Van Criekinge W, Nandi TN, Aniegbe JI, Shen L, Ilo AC, Immel-Sadée F, Nnamani AO, Levin DL, Hao M, McDonald ES, Achilefu NC, Iloanusi NI, Poplack SP, Dashevsky BZ, Damrauer SM, Okoye I, Gevaert O.
abstractText:
Rationale: Routine clinical imaging captures anatomy under a limited set of physiologic and acquisition conditions, leaving segmentation models with sparse examples of how lesions and surrounding tissues deform with compression, respiration, or vascular pulsation. Standard image augmentation expands training datasets but does not explicitly model the mechanics underlying these changes. Patient-specific biomechanical simulation offers an approach to generate anatomically consistent images and corresponding segmentation masks under conditions absent from the original scan, without additional imaging or training a generative model. We hypothesized that incorporating this mechanistically grounded variability into training improves segmentation across imaging modalities.

Methods:

We evaluate across three segmentation tasks: breast cancer on 3D digital breast tomosynthesis, lung tumors on chest CT, and carotid plaque on ultrasound. From each routine scan, patient-specific biomechanical models generate acquisitions absent from the original study—a range of breast compressions, the respiratory cycle, and arterial wall distension across the cardiac cycle. The resulting displacement fields deform both images and masks. Segmentation models were trained with and without the generated data across a range of standard image augmentation techniques, evaluated via cross-validation and held-out test sets. Realism was assessed through blinded reader studies, and generated respiratory motion was validated against real 4D CT.

Results:

Training on the generated acquisitions improved segmentation across modalities, increasing Dice scores by 6.6% for breast (p<0.05), 10.1% for lung (p<0.05), and 4.5% for carotid plaque (p>0.05) relative to the routine scans alone. Generated respiratory motion closely matched real gated 4D CT, with Dice of 0.94 ± 0.02 for lung volume overlap. Blinded readers discriminated generated from real images at near chance (AUC: breast 0.61, lung 0.41, carotid 0.46).

Conclusions:

Mechanistic simulation generates imaging acquisitions that clinical systems do not supply, without training data or additional scanning, and improves AI-based disease detection across modalities.

title: Significance of Muscle Health Assessment in Adolescent Fontan Patients: Handgrip Strength as an Early Screening Tool for Fontan-Associated Complications
authorString: Higashi K, Nakajima H, Aotsuka H.
abstractText: Background Skeletal muscle acts as a secondary pump in passive Fontan circulation. However, the prevalence and clinical significance of muscle health abnormalities, such as dynapenia and sarcopenia, remain poorly defined in adolescent Fontan patients. Methods We evaluated 43 adolescent Fontan patients (median age: 11.8 years). Skeletal muscle mass index via DXA and handgrip strength (HGS) were expressed as Z-scores to classify patients into three phenotypes: Normal (N), Dynapenia (D: HGS Z-score < -2 SD, preserved mass), and Sarcopenia (S: both < -2 SD). Peak \(\:{\text{VO}}_{2}\) was defined as the primary outcome, while resting hemodynamics, biomarkers, and Fontan-associated complications were secondary outcomes. Results The prevalence of dynapenia and sarcopenia was 19% (n = 8) and 12% (n = 5), respectively (Normal: 70%, n = 30). Peak \(\:{\text{VO}}_{2}\) showed a significant stepwise decline across the N, D, and S groups (89.6%, 73.8%, and 48.8% of predicted, respectively; \(\:p<0.01\)). Resting cardiac index, central venous pressure, ejection fraction, and BNP showed no significant differences between the N and D groups. However, severe complications (e.g., protein-losing enteropathy) were markedly higher in the D (50%) and S (80%) groups than in the N group (10%; \(\:p<0.01\)). Conclusions Muscle health abnormalities affect nearly one-third of adolescent Fontan patients. Notably, patients with dynapenia may exhibit a high incidence of complications despite normal resting hemodynamics and laboratory data. These findings suggest a cardiac-skeletal muscle crosstalk. Thus, routine handgrip strength measurement serves as a simple, practical tool to identify high-risk patients during routine follow-up.

title: Work Rate Adjustments During High-Intensity Interval Training in the Heat With Active and Passive Recovery
authorString: Yoder HA, Mulholland AM, MacDonald HV, Wingo JE.
abstractText: To test the hypotheses that maintaining target rating of perceived exertion (RPE) with active (ACT) versus passive (PASS) recovery during high-intensity interval training (HIIT) in the heat results in 1) greater thermal and cardiovascular strain, 2) larger work rate adjustments during work intervals, and 3) larger decreases in maximal aerobic capacity (V̇O 2max ). Eight adults completed 4 cycling trials in 35°C, consisting of an 8-min warm-up at RPE 12 followed by 1 (15 ACT , 15 PASS ) or 5 (43 ACT , 43 PASS ) rounds of HIIT (1 round = 4 min at RPE 17 and 3 min recovery at RPE 12 or rest) totaling 15 or 43 min of exercise. Each trial was immediately followed by measurement of V̇O 2max . Rectal temperature was not different between conditions (43 ACT =38.3°C, 43 PASS =38.2°C, p  = 0.003 for interaction, post-hoc both p  > 0.09) but increased over time (both p  < 0.001). HR during work intervals was comparable between conditions ( p  = 0.50) with a 15 b·min ‒1 increase between from interval 1 to 5 (p  = 0.001). Average HR during recovery was 14 b·min −1 higher in the fifth versus first interval across conditions ( p  = 0.003) and + 24 b·min ‒1 during ACT versus PASS ( p  = 0.002). Percent change in work rate from first to fifth interval was larger during 43 ACT (–14%±24%) versus 43 PASS (–1%±16%; p  = 0.04). V̇O 2max was 0.4 L∙min ‒1 (11.5%) lower following 43-min compared to 15-min of HIIT ( p  = 0.008) but was not different between recovery mode ( p  = 0.69). Maintaining target RPE with ACT and PASS resulted in similar physiological strain but averaged 21 W lower power output by the final work interval during ACT. Five rounds of HIIT in a hot environment resulted in small–moderate reductions in V̇O 2max .

title: Primary high-grade malignant epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma of the lung: diagnostic pitfalls of a very rare lung malignancy.
authorString: Rapicetta C, Santandrea G, Lamesta A, Paci M.
abstractText: Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma (EMC) is an exceptionally rare primary lung malignancy arising from submucosal bronchial glands. We report a 55-year-old man with a large paravertebral left lower lobe mass in whom bronchoscopic biopsy suggested metastatic poorly differentiated carcinoma of possible prostatic origin. Clinical work-up revealed a concomitant prostate carcinoma; however, following multidisciplinary discussion, prostatic origin was excluded and the patient underwent left lower lobectomy with mediastinal nodal dissection. Final diagnosis was primary high-grade malignant EMC, confirmed by an extended immunohistochemical panel and EWSR1 rearrangement (22q12) detected by fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH). A prior CT scan, retrospectively reviewed, showed a segmental consolidation four years earlier misinterpreted as pneumonia. This case illustrates the major diagnostic pitfalls of pulmonary EMC-including the coincidental discovery of a second primary tumour-and the indispensable role of molecular profiling when morphology and immunohistochemistry are inconclusive.

title: Medical emergency response related to MedicAtion InciDents (MERRMAID): a case series and lessons to improve medication safety.
authorString: Coombes I, Anderson A, Coombes F, Wong G, Lindsay D, Gowardman J, Donovan P, Carmichael S, Levkovich B, Davies K.
abstractText:
Background

Evidence suggests that some medical emergencies in hospital are associated with preventable medication errors or adverse reactions.

Aim

The purpose of this case series was to investigate and describe the proportion of Medical Emergency Response Team (MERT) activations that are medication-related, the degree of preventability and underlying contributing factors.

Method

This retrospective case series included a review of MERT activations collected from an Australian tertiary hospital by two separate multidisciplinary teams. Initial review by the research team identified those that were potentially medication-related; these cases were then reviewed by an expert panel to determine the degree of causation and preventability and to identify errors within the medication management cycle and their underlying factors. The main outcome measures were the proportion of preventable medication-related MERT activations. The secondary outcome included descriptions of medications, medication errors in the context of the medication management cycle and consideration of factors underlying the errors including pharmacy review contributing to these activations.

Results

Fifteen per cent (17/117) of MERT activations reviewed were medication-related, and 65% (11/17) of those were deemed preventable. The omission of medications due to errors in prescribing, administration, pharmacy review or supply stage was the main contributor to preventable medication-related MERT activations (7/11, 64%). Cardiovascular medications, predominantly metoprolol, were most implicated in preventable medication-related MERT activations.

Conclusions

Medication adverse events due to potentially error-prone steps in medication management processes are a common cause of inpatient MERT activations, presenting a considerable preventable burden to patients and healthcare resources.

title: Loss of PAX6 alters the excitatory/inhibitory neuronal ratio in human cerebral organoids.
authorString: Chan WK, Abdulla S, Zhao L, Negro D, Munro VM, Thomson S, Marshall H, Kozić Z, Brown M, Barbato M, Beltran M, Henderson NC, Price DJ, Mason JO.
