title: Hemodynamic and Functional Outcomes of Rate-Adaptive and Physiologic Pacing in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authorString: Prana Jagannatha GN, Yobel D, Mamangdean CT, Saputra BMI, Yasmin AAADA, Wiryawan IN, Antara IMPS.
abstractText:
Background

Exercise intolerance and poor quality of life remain challenges in HFpEF, driven by chronotropic incompetence and left atrial dysfunction. We evaluated whether rate-adaptive/accelerated pacing (RAAP), targeting these mechanisms, improves hemodynamic, functional, and patient-reported outcomes.

Methods

PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Outcomes included NT-proBNP, Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ) score, 6-min walk distance (6MWD), E/e', and E/A. Within-group pre-post changes and comparisons with usual care were synthesized separately. Effects are reported as mean differences (MD) or odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).

Results

Eight reports involving 380 patients were included with myPACE overlap handled by one report per cohort per analysis. Within-group, RAAP was associated with reductions in NT-proBNP (MD -462.58 pg/mL; 95% CI -891.37 to -33.79), E/A (MD -1.01; -1.19 to -0.83), and E/e' (MD -3.18; -5.65 to -0.72), and improvements in 6MWD (MD +74.10 m; 36.34 to 111.86) and MLHFQ score (MD -17.40 points; -33.06 to -1.74). Compared with usual care, associations favored RAAP for NT-proBNP (MD -108.51 pg/mL; -118.31 to -98.70), 6MWD (MD +73.36 m; 32.23 to 114.48), MLHFQ score (MD -16.52 points; -24.15 to -8.89), and AF burden (MD -6.13; -7.88 to -4.37). MACE also favored RAAP in an exploratory analysis (OR 0.47; 0.23 to 0.93), whereas peak VO2 did not differ significantly.

Conclusions

RAAP was associated with favorable changes in hemodynamic and functional outcomes. These findings support further evaluation of individualized rate modulation in adequately powered randomized trials.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis of an mHealth intervention to improve hypertension control in patients with elevated cardiovascular risk.
authorString: Caputo MT, Lakshminarayan K, Sakboonyarat B, Westberg SM, Everson-Rose SA, McCarthy T, Streib C, Drawz P, Murray TA.
abstractText:
Background

This study evaluates the cost-effectiveness of a mobile health technology (mHealth) based care model to facilitate home blood pressure (BP) monitoring and remote hypertension management.

Methods

We used a Markov microsimulation model to study health and cost outcomes for three hypertension control strategies: an mHealth-based care model (mGlide) vs. Enhanced Usual Care (EUC) vs. No-Intervention. We sampled patient characteristics from the mGlide randomized controlled trial (RCT) and randomly transitioned patients through three possible health states over a 10-year horizon with monthly cycles: 1) No Cardiovascular Event, 2) Cardiovascular Event, and 3) Deceased. We determined transition probabilities from literature, allowing the probabilities to vary by patient characteristics, including BP values. We evaluated health and cost outcomes across a range of plausible deterministic treatment effects (expected BP reductions) supported by the RCT. We performed probabilistic sensitivity analysis to assess cost-effectiveness while randomly varying the treatment effect magnitude.

Results

The mHealth-based care model was cost-effective compared to No-Intervention and EUC across all deterministic scenarios. 10-year mortality absolute risk reductions ranged from 4.9-5.8% (vs No-Intervention) and 0.6-3.3% (vs EUC) across scenarios. In probabilistic sensitivity analysis, mHealth-based care (vs EUC) was less costly in 59.6% of iterations and had better health outcomes in 99.6%. Comparing all care models, mHealth-based care had the greatest net monetary benefit in 95% of iterations at $26,000/QALY and in 99% of iterations at $72,000/QALY.

Conclusions

In the current study, we estimated that mHealth-based care models can be cost-effective approaches to improve hypertension control in patients with elevated cardiovascular risk.

title: Community Health Worker Coaching, Food Insecurity, and Physical Activity in the Healthy Food First Trial: A Causal Mediation and Longitudinal Analysis.
authorString: Anderson RE, Berkowitz SA, Burger KS, Valle CG, Taillie LS, Ammerman AS.
abstractText: To evaluate whether change in food insecurity (ΔFI) mediated the effect of a community health worker (CHW) intervention on physical activity (PA) among food insecure (FI) hypertensive adults, we conducted a secondary analysis of the Healthy Food First randomized clinical trial of food insecure adults with hypertension recruited from 364 North Carolina clinical sites. Participants were randomized to CHW coaching or no coaching within a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial design. FI was measured at baseline and 12 months; total PA (MET-min/week) at 12 and 18 months. Mediation models estimated indirect (ACME), direct (ADE), and total effects (ATE) of CHW assignment on 12-month PA through ΔFI. Generalized estimating equations evaluated repeated PA by CHW assignment. CHW assignment was not associated with PA, and ΔFI did not mediate the relationship. Effects were small (ACME = 16.2; 95% CI -62.6, 121.8; ADE = -214.1; 95% CI -871.7, 484.5; ATE = -197.9; 95% CI -855.6, 500.8 MET-min/week). The proportion mediated was near zero (-8.2%; 95% CI -142%, 124%). GEE analyses similarly showed no association (B = 363.7 MET-min/week; SE = 302.8; P = 0.23). Modest improvements in FI alone may be insufficient to increase PA without additional PA supports. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05048836.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Automated Continuous Quantification of Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction From Standard Adult Transthoracic Echocardiography: A Systematic Review.
authorString: Dembi A, Patankar H, Dhadda S, Hasanovic A.
abstractText: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) guides diagnosis and treatment across cardiovascular disease, but its measurement from transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is operator-dependent and subject to observer variability. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods that estimate a continuous LVEF value have proliferated. This systematic review aimed to summarise how closely they agree with reference measurements at the group and individual-patient level. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and protocol registration on the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO: CRD420261419064), we searched MEDLINE and Embase (via Ovid), Scopus, and IEEE Xplore from January 2015 to 10 September 2026, with forward and backward citation searching, for peer-reviewed journal articles of AI-derived continuous LVEF from standard adult TTE that reported an error or agreement metric against a reference standard. Risk of bias was assessed with a tailored Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Results were summarised as unweighted study-level medians without pooling. We included 108 studies. Most were retrospective (86 of 108), and 34 reported an external or independent test cohort as their main result. EchoNet-Dynamic or CAMUS were used in 54 studies. Systematic bias was small (median absolute bias: 1.5 EF percentage points, interquartile range: 0.5 to 3.4; 68 studies). Typical average error was moderate (median mean absolute error: 4.9 points, 62 studies). The median width of the study-specific 95% limits of agreement was 26 points (interquartile range: 22 to 30; 66 studies). Only 10 of 66 studies (15%) had limits within ±10 points, the usual gap between clinical LVEF decision thresholds. The limits were similarly wide when external results were used wherever available (median width: 26.3 points) and somewhat narrower in studies at low risk of bias (23.6 points). AI methods reproduce reference LVEF with small systematic bias, but individual-patient disagreement in most studies exceeds the difference between clinical LVEF categories and the agreement expected between two expert readers. On current evidence, automated LVEF is better suited to assistive use with expert oversight than to stand-alone measurement, pending prospective, externally validated evaluation.

title: Multi-Omics Insights Into Circulating T-Cell Metabolic Reprogramming and Treg Dysfunction in Moyamoya Disease.
authorString: Zheng Z, He Q, Ma X, Zhang B, Li J, Liu C, Mou S, Sun W, Shi X, Wang W, Zhang D, Ge P, Zhao J.
abstractText: Moyamoya disease (MMD) is a progressive cerebrovascular disease linked to immune dysregulation, yet T-cell metabolic reprogramming and regulatory T-cell (Treg) function remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated multi-omics approaches, including mass cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, metabolomics, and flow cytometry to characterize T-cell metabolic alterations and Treg dysfunction in MMD, uncovering a key metabolic-immune axis. Compared with healthy controls, MMD patients showed chronic immune activation and broad suppression of amino acid, glycolytic, and fatty acid metabolic pathways. Although Tregs were aberrantly expanded, they displayed metabolic inflexibility, together with impaired intercellular communication. Single-cell transcriptomics indicated Treg-to-Th17 conversion, while flow cytometry confirmed increased IL-17A<sup>+</sup> cells within the CD4<sup>+</sup>FOXP3<sup>+</sup> compartment. Besides, these dysfunctional Tregs correlated with advanced Suzuki stages, ischemic stroke, and posterior cerebral artery involvement. Bulk transcriptomic and serum metabolomic analyses further confirmed coordinated immune activation and metabolic suppression at the gene, protein, pathway, and metabolite levels. These findings define a metabolic-immune axis in MMD in which metabolically constrained, functionally unstable Tregs may contribute to neuroinflammation and vascular remodeling, suggesting that restoring Treg metabolic fitness could represent a therapeutic strategy.

title: Prognostic impact of intravascular imaging in percutaneous coronary intervention according to procedural complexity.
authorString: Kim M, Lee JM, Hahn JY, Song YB, Gwon HC, Lee JY, Kim SM, Lee SY, Yun KH, Kim CJ, Nam CW, Park YH, Lee WS, Doh JH, Jo SH, Yoon CH, Koh JS, Lee KY, Lim YH, Cho YH, Cho JM, Jang WJ, Chun KJ, Jeong JO, Song PS, Renovate-Complex-Pci Investigators OBOT.
abstractText:
Background

Data regarding intravascular imaging (IVI) in complex percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remain scarce.

Aims

In this study, we sought to assess the effects of IVI-guided PCI according to procedural complexity.

Methods

This was a post hoc analysis of the RENOVATE-COMPLEX-PCI trial that compared IVI-guided PCI with angiography-guided PCI in patients with complex coronary artery lesions. The study population was stratified into three groups of low, moderate, and high risk, according to PCI procedural complexity, following the European Society of Cardiology criteria. The high-risk group included patients meeting at least one clinical risk criterion and at least one procedural risk criterion. The primary endpoint was target vessel failure (TVF), a composite of cardiac death, target vessel-related myocardial infarction, or clinically driven target vessel revascularisation.

Results

At a median 2.1-year follow-up, TVF risk increased significantly in a stepwise manner from the low (reference) to moderate (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 1.369, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.705-2.660; p=0.353) and high procedural complexity group (adjusted HR 1.619, 95% CI: 0.963-2.723; p=0.069). The benefit of IVI-guided PCI varied by procedural complexity, with significant risk reductions in the moderate-risk group (adjusted HR 0.374, 95% CI: 0.150-0.935; p=0.035) and the high-risk group (adjusted HR 0.633, 95% CI: 0.424-0.945; p=0.025) but not in the low-risk group (adjusted HR 0.735, 95% CI: 0.282-1.914; p=0.528). The interaction between the IVI effect and procedural complexity was statistically significant (pinteraction=0.009).

Conclusions

In patients undergoing complex PCI, an IVI-guided procedure significantly reduced adverse cardiac events, with a greater magnitude of benefit observed in procedures of high complexity.

title: YAP Fuels Cerebral Cavernous Malformations by Regulating KLF4 Transcriptional Activity and Protein Stability.
authorString: Ye T, Zheng Q, Hu Z, Fan H, Sun Z, Li X, Mo H, Chang C, Xu Y, Wang K, Fang D, Song H.
abstractText: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs), which frequently predispose patients to strokes or seizures, primarily arise from endothelial specific loss-of-function mutations in the CCM genes, and occasionally accompanied by gain-of-function mutations in PIK3CA and MAP3K3. While the Hippo pathway is a well-established regulator of tissue homeostasis, its emerging relevance in vascular pathology particularly its precise role in CCM pathogenesis remains poorly understood. In this study, we demonstrate that CCM gene deficiency suppresses endothelial Hippo signaling, as evidenced by diminished LATS activity, alongside concomitant elevation of YAP expression and nuclear translocation in both human and mouse CCM lesions. Notably, endothelial-specific deletion of Yap mitigates CCM lesion formation, reinforces endothelial junctions, enhances inflammatory resistance, and decreases KLF4 protein levels in a CCM mouse model. Conversely, intracranial Adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated inhibition of LATS or activation of YAP promoted CCMs formation under Ccm2 deficiency. Mechanistically, under the dual coordination of negative regulation by LATS and positive regulation by MAP3K3, YAP orchestrates KLF4 transcriptional activity and protein stability. This is achieved through a direct interaction with KLF4 that shields it from β-TrCP-mediated proteasomal degradation, thereby driving CCM progression. Collectively, our findings unveil a novel dimension to Hippo pathway regulation and underscore YAP as a pivotal driver of CCM pathogenesis.

title: Echocardiographic Indices Compared with Galectin-3 and Pentraxin-3 in Stage C Heart Failure
authorString: Oancea A, Morariu PC, Godun M, Jigoranu A, Miftode RS, Mitu O, Simion P, Marcu DT, Bazyani A, Petris AO, Costache-Enache I, Floria M.
abstractText:
Background:

/Objectives: We compared echocardiographic indices with galectin-3 and pentraxin-3 for discriminating established heart failure (HF).

Methods:

This exploratory cross-sectional secondary analysis included 131 coronary angiography patients: 69 with stage C HF and 62 without an established clinical HF syndrome. Patients with HF were clinically stable without symptoms at rest and were classified as New York Heart Association (NYHA) II or III at study evaluation. Tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion/pulmonary artery systolic pressure (TAPSE/PASP), the combined mitral Doppler index E/(Em × Sm), right ventricular systolic annular velocity, and both biomarkers were assessed using paired receiver operating characteristic comparisons and clinically adjusted logistic regression.

Results:

TAPSE/PASP had the highest numerical area under the curve (AUC 0.753; 95% confidence interval 0.671–0.835) and outperformed galectin-3 (AUC 0.500; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0012). Its AUC difference from pentraxin-3 was nonsignificant. E/(Em × Sm) and pentraxin-3 had AUCs of 0.654 and 0.631. TAPSE/PASP retained an association with HF in the joint adjusted model (odds ratio 0.55 per standard deviation; p = 0.0423); E/(Em × Sm) did not. Pentraxin-3 remained associated in its separate adjusted model (odds ratio 1.70; p = 0.0212). NYHA-class and ejection-fraction subgroup differences were nonsignificant after multiplicity correction.

Conclusions:

TAPSE/PASP discriminated established HF better than galectin-3 in this cohort. The separate pentraxin-3 association warrants further investigation of complementary inflammatory information. These exploratory findings, models, and derived thresholds require independent validation before clinical application.

title: Management of Thrombocytopenia in Chronic Liver Disease: From Platelet Transfusion to Thrombopoietin Receptor Agonists
authorString: Radziwon P, Wasiluk T, Tomaszewska J, Radziwon P.
abstractText: Thrombocytopenia is one of the most common hematological complications of chronic liver disease (CLD) and becomes clinically relevant mainly when invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedures are required. Its pathogenesis is multifactorial and includes splenic sequestration secondary to portal hypertension, reduced hepatic thrombopoietin (TPO) synthesis, bone marrow suppression, immune-mediated platelet destruction, and increased platelet consumption. In line with the concept of rebalanced hemostasis, platelet count alone is a poor predictor of procedural bleeding in CLD, and contemporary guidelines increasingly emphasize procedure-specific bleeding risk and patient-related factors rather than correction of an isolated laboratory value. Prophylactic platelet concentrate (PC) transfusion provides only a transient and often unpredictable platelet increment in this population and carries the risk of transfusion reactions, alloimmunization, and platelet transfusion refractoriness. This review summarizes the pathophysiology and clinical significance of thrombocytopenia in CLD, critically evaluates the indications for and efficacy of PC transfusion, and discusses alternative strategies, including recombinant human TPO, TPO receptor agonists (TPO-RAs), splenic interventions, and portal decompression. PC transfusion remains essential when rapid correction is required, particularly in active bleeding or urgent procedures, whereas the TPO-Ras, avatrombopag and lusutrombopag, offer an effective oral alternative in selected patients undergoing elective procedures. A management algorithm integrating these considerations is proposed.

title: Alcohol Non-Abstinence and Hypertension as Independent Risk Factors for Esophageal Cancer Recurrence After Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection: A Multicenter Cohort Study.
authorString: Emori K, Fukunaga S, Mukasa M, Nakane T, Cho T, Minami S, Tanaka H, Ohzono D, Yoshio T, Watanabe Y, Nakano D, Tsutsumi T, Araki T, Morita T, Torimura T, Nouno R, Takedatsu H, Kawaguchi T.
abstractText:
Introduction

Alcohol consumption is a well-established risk factor for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Recently, metabolic abnormalities have been reported as a risk factor for ESCC. However, the impact of these risk factors on recurrence after curative endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) remains unclear. This study aimed to determine whether alcohol consumption and metabolic abnormalities independently contribute to ESCC recurrence following curative ESD.

Materials and methods

We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study including 147 patients with ESCC who underwent curative ESD at four institutions between 2003 and 2021. Independent predictors of recurrence were assessed using Cox proportional hazards regression. Risk stratification was further explored using decision tree analysis and Kaplan-Meier curves.

Results

During a mean follow-up of 2.34 years, 31 patients (21.1%) developed recurrence of ESCC. Cox regression analysis identified alcohol non-abstinence (HR 2.07, 95% CI 1.01-4.76, p = 0.0123) and hypertension (HR 3.04, 95% CI 1.01-9.23, p = 0.0327) as independent predictors of recurrence. Decision tree analysis identified alcohol non-abstinence as the strongest classifier, followed by hypertension. Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated that abstainers or non-drinkers with hypertension had a recurrence risk comparable to that of non-abstainers, with 3-year recurrence rates of 28.2% in non-abstainers, 23.4% in abstainers/non-drinkers with hypertension, and 0.0% in abstainers/non-drinkers without hypertension.

Conclusion

Alcohol non-abstinence and hypertension independently increased the risk of ESCC recurrence after curative ESD. These findings support sustained alcohol abstinence and suggest that hypertension may help identify patients who require careful post-ESD surveillance. Whether blood pressure control reduces recurrence requires prospective evaluation.

title: A bioinformatic approach to investigate placental and fetal gene expression during diabetic stress in pregnancy.
authorString: Larson E, Ullah A.
abstractText:
Maternal diabetes disturbs the intrauterine environment and poses significant risk to fetal development, yet the molecular responses of placental and fetal tissues to diabetic stress remain incompletely characterized. We applied a comparative bioinformatic framework to two publicly available microarray datasets representing placental/decidua and fetal tissue collected at embryonic day 10.5. Both datasets were processed using RMA normalization, differential gene expression analysis, principal component analysis, functional enrichment analysis, and Pathview pathway visualization in R. Placental/decidual exhibited a comparatively constrained differential-expression profile with only two probes reaching BH-adjusted p < 0.05 and one probe meeting both BH-adjusted p < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1. Rank-based GSEA across the complete gene-ranking distribution was used to identify coordinated pathway-level changes. This analysis identified enrichment of gene programs involving ribosome biogenesis, RNA processing and splicing, cell-cycle and DNA-replication processes, and oxidative phosphorylation. In contrast, fetal tissue exhibited substantially broader differential expression with 2,306 probes meeting both BH-adjusted p < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1. KEGG over-representation analysis identified 62 significantly enriched pathways, including pathways associated with axon guidance, Wnt signaling, focal adhesion, MAPK signaling, and PI3K-AKT signaling. Pathview mapping further demonstrated a broader distribution of transcript-level alterations across fetal signaling components compared with the comparatively localized changes observed in placental/decidual tissue. These findings demonstrate distinct transcriptional responses between placental/decidual and fetal tissue under diabetic stress. The comparatively constrained placental/decidual differential-expression profile together with broader fetal transcriptional alterations is consistent with a model in which the maternal-fetal interface may modulate responses to diabetic stress. Collectively, this comparative analysis identified coordinated molecular processes associated with diabetic pregnancy and provides a framework for early biomarker development in diabetic pregnancies.

Supplementary information

The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40203-026-00778-2.

title: Inhibiting MD2 activates AMPK-dependent PPARγ/NOX4 signaling to attenuate mitochondrial oxidative stress and relieve pulmonary hypertension.
authorString: Chen J, Chai M, Liu Y, Zhang Y, Li X, Yang C, Pan H, Xu C, Yao Y, Yu Y, Chen J, Yao D, Huang X.
abstractText:
Aims

Pulmonary hypertension (PH), a severe vascular disorder, is closely associated with chronic inflammatory states and oxidative stress. Myeloid differentiation protein 2 (MD2), a key co-receptor of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), is well established in mediating various inflammation-driven pathologies. However, its role in pulmonary hypertension and its potential involvement in oxidative stress regulation remain unclear.

Methods and results

MD2 expression was upregulated in both PH patients and murine PH models. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of MD2 improved hemodynamic parameters, attenuated pulmonary vascular remodeling, and reduced right ventricular hypertrophy. MD2 inhibition significantly reduced mitochondrial oxidative stress in vivo and in vitro. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that suppression of the membrane protein MD2 activated intracellular AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling, leading to enhanced peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) activity. PPARγ, in turn, suppressed nuclear transcription of NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4), resulting in a marked reduction in mitochondrial oxidative stress.

Conclusion

This study indicates that MD2 may act as an upstream regulator of mitochondrial oxidative stress in PH. Inhibition of MD2 attenuates pulmonary hypertension through activation of the AMPK/PPARγ axis, which suppresses NOX4 mediated mitochondrial oxidative stress. Targeting MD2 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for PH.

title: Therapeutic Reversal of Severe Neuropsychiatric Symptoms in Wilson's Disease: A Case Report.
authorString: Penjor T, Dorji S, Wangchuk S.
abstractText: Wilsons disease is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder of copper metabolism that results in copper accumulation in liver and other organs. Hepatic manifestation tends to occur earlier than the neurological manifestation. We present a case with psychiatric presentation. Following initiation of treatment, the patient showed improvement. Early diagnosis and treatment prevent complications.

title: Neurodegenerative Diseases: Epidemiology, Risk Factors, Classification, Pathophysiology, Clinical Features, Diagnosis, and Therapeutic Strategies.
authorString: He Z, Zeng J, Wang G, Li Y, Zhang F.
abstractText: Neurodegenerative diseases are a growing cause of disability worldwide, particularly as populations age. Although these disorders differ in etiology and clinical presentation, advances in genetics, neuropathology, and biomarker research have identified shared disturbances in protein homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and immune regulation. These processes may contribute to selective neuronal vulnerability and neural circuit dysfunction. These findings are refining disease classification and diagnosis, yet effective disease-modifying therapies remain limited. Disease-specific abnormalities remain essential to clinical interpretation and treatment selection. Existing reviews often focus on individual disorders or isolated mechanisms, leaving the links between shared biology and disease-specific phenotypes insufficiently clear. We synthesize evidence on the epidemiology, risk factors, classification, and pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Friedreich's ataxia, and multiple sclerosis. We compare their clinical manifestations and diagnostic approaches, including the evolving role of biomarkers, and critically assess established and emerging therapies. By distinguishing shared mechanisms from disease-specific abnormalities, we identify key translational gaps and explore how common biological disturbances may lead to distinct clinical trajectories. This cross-disease perspective may inform diagnostic reasoning, treatment development, and future comparative research.

title: Development and Validation of a Prediction Model for Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension in Diabetic Patients: A Retrospective Study of 57,375 Patients.
authorString: Geng Z, Yao J, Wang H, Cao Y, Bao J, Chen J, Yang J, Wang Y.
abstractText: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is an important cardiopulmonary complication in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), yet practical models integrating routinely available clinical, laboratory, and echocardiographic information remain limited. We conducted a single-center retrospective electronic medical record cohort study with a prespecified temporal split. Patients admitted from January 1, 2018 to December 31, 2021 formed the training cohort, and those admitted from January 1, 2022 to July 31, 2025 formed the temporal validation cohort. Among 47,042 pre-2022 records screened, 10,458 eligible patients were included in the training cohort, including 423 patients with PAH (4.0%); among 60,069 later records screened, 14,060 patients were included in the validation cohort, including 600 patients with PAH (4.3%). Nine prespecified clinical domains were initially evaluated. Because tricuspid regurgitation velocity/gradient contributed to the echocardiographic PAH classification, a sensitivity analysis excluded the PAH-related pressure-gradient domain from the exploratory combined model to reduce incorporation bias. In the training-cohort sensitivity analysis, cardiac cavity and vascular dilatation was the strongest remaining individual discriminator (area under the curve [AUC], 0.819), followed by coagulation dysfunction (AUC, 0.697) and cardiac dysfunction (AUC, 0.627); the pressure-gradient-excluded combined model achieved an AUC of 0.823. When applied without refitting to the temporal validation cohort, this sensitivity model achieved an AUC of 0.780. The eight-variable echocardiography-informed nomogram had a C-index of 0.666 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.631-0.699), with a Hosmer-Lemeshow p value of 0.453. Because the nomogram includes echocardiographic predictors, including tricuspid regurgitation velocity and pulmonary valve velocity, it is intended for risk stratification after echocardiography rather than pre-echocardiographic screening or prediction of incident PAH. Diabetes-specific variables such as HbA1c, diabetes duration, treatment exposure, insulin resistance indices, and microvascular complications were not consistently available in the historical records and were not modeled. Prospective multicenter studies with systematic collection of diabetes-specific variables are needed.

title: A review of self-supervised imaging phenotypes for genome-wide association studies.
authorString: Patel K, Zhao X, Xie Z, Zhi D.
abstractText: Biobank-scale imaging-genomic cohorts enable genome-wide association studies (GWASs) of organ structure and function. Traditional approaches rely on expert-defined image-derived phenotypes (IDPs), which capture only a fraction of the biological variation in high-content images. Powered by artificial intelligence, self-supervised learning (SSL) learns representations directly from intrinsic image structures, creating scalable, data-driven traits. Here, we review the technical frameworks and challenges of SSL-based imaging genetics and their applications in brain MRI, cardiac MRI, and retinal imaging. Early studies suggest that these data-driven approaches can complement traditional IDPs and may expand the phenotypic space available for discovery of heritable imaging traits, although broader validation across cohorts, ancestries, scanners, and imaging protocols remains needed.

title: Who should be considered for prostate artery embolization: revisiting the urologic guidelines based on results from over 300 patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia.
authorString: Knight GM, Varadhan A, Benishay E, Rivera-Rodríguez DM, Jenkins K, Hohlastos E, Salem R, Mouli S.
abstractText:
Background

Prostate artery embolization (PAE) has emerged as a minimally invasive therapy which affords improvement in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) symptoms and objective urinary parameters with a favorable adverse event (AE) profile. While PAE was recently included in the American Urological Association (AUA) Guidelines, guidance on its specific use-cases is limited. This study sought to answer remaining questions surrounding the safety and efficacy of PAE across different patient subpopulations where formal guidance for PAE is limited.

Methods

Three hundred two patients with BPH underwent PAE. Key baseline characteristics were gathered. Patients were compared from baseline to follow-ups with regards to (1) objective parameters, including maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax), post-void residual (PVR), and prostate specific antigen (PSA); (2) prostate volume; (3) BPH symptoms, including International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), IPSS Quality-of-Life (IPSS-QoL), and BPH Impact Index (BPH-II); (4) sexual symptoms, including the International Index of Erectile function (IIEF) and Male Sexual Health Questionnaire for Ejaculatory Function Short Form (MSHQ-EjD-SF); and (5) AEs. Additional sub-analyses were performed comparing the safety/efficacy of PAE across key sub-groups.

Results

PAE afforded significant improvement (p < 0.05) in each subjective/objective BPH parameter and sexual function score at nearly all follow-up points. Specifically, IPSS improved by 12.3-13.8 points (52.8-59.2%); IPSS-QoL by 2.3-2.8 points (47.9-58.3%); IIEF by 3.2-5.7 points (15.6-27.8%); PSA by 1.5-2.0 ng/mL (15.6-28.5%); and prostate volume by 16.9%. Twelve (4.0%) AEs were reported; no sexual/severe AEs were observed. PAE was safe and afforded significant improvement in subjective/objective BPH parameters in patients with: prostate volumes ≥ 80 mL; prior BPH surgery/intervention; higher medical comorbidity; pre-procedural catheter-dependent urinary retention; pre-procedural renal insufficiency; and pre-procedural hematuria.

Conclusions

PAE improved subjective/objective BPH parameters and sexual function. Further, it safely afforded significant improvement in subjective/objective BPH parameters in specific contexts/scenarios where current guidance for PAE is limited, including patients with larger prostates, prior BPH intervention, higher medical comorbidity, urinary retention, renal insufficiency, and hematuria. Altogether, PAE can be performed safely and effectively in several real-world contexts in which formal guidance for PAE is limited, and where it may offer unique advantages compared to surgical therapies.

title: Active side branch protection in provisional stenting: techniques, case-based insights, and practical considerations.
authorString: Wong B, Khialani B, Fairley S, Touma G, Ada C, Wu E, Harding S.
abstractText: Provisional stenting (PS) remains the default strategy for most bifurcation lesions, but the risk of side branch (SB) compromise continues to be a concern. Active SB protection strategies were developed to mitigate this risk, as an extension of PS with a jailed wire. They have a common goal: to preserve SB patency while decreasing the need for complex two-stent strategies, particularly in difficult anatomical or clinical situations. This review aims to provide a comprehensive, case-based overview of different contemporary active SB protection methods, including techniques developed in Asia which have not yet been widely adopted elsewhere. We highlight the practical aspects of conventional, contemporary, and modified jailed balloon techniques; active transfer of plaque; jailed microcatheter strategies; and emerging adaptations, such as jailed drug-coated balloon use. Case examples illustrate the mechanisms of stent deformation, rescue manoeuvres, and correction with intravascular imaging. Ultimately, active SB protection may enhance the safety and consistency of PS across a broad spectrum of patients and lesion types.

title: Comprehensive Immune Repertoires of T Cell Receptor and B Cell Receptor Identify Key Immune Features Associated With Disease Activity of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
authorString: Wu J, Zhou Z, Yu A, Lin X, Ren Y, Teng J, Zhu D, Wang F, You Y, Ji X, Wang P, Li H, Yang C, Wang W, Du Y, Ye J.
abstractText: We integrated immune repertoire sequencing (CD4+ and CD8+ T cell receptor [TCR], B cell receptor [BCR]) and transcriptional profiling to characterize the peripheral immune landscape in 32 active systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients, 30 stable SLE patients, and 35 healthy donors. CD4+ and CD8+ TCR α- and β-chain repertoires in SLE patients showed lower diversity, reduced similarity, and more heterogeneous V-J usage, with CD8+ TCR profiles exhibiting relatively consistent stepwise changes across healthy, stable, and active groups. CD8+ T-cell transcriptomics revealed activity-associated upregulation of CD38, S100A11, IFITM3, and LAG3. In addition, BCR immunoglobulin heavy chain (IGH) repertoire analysis showed isotype-specific remodeling in SLE, characterized by contracted IgM/IgD repertoires, increased IgA isotype ratio and richness, and enhanced IgG diversity. Active SLE showed further increased IgG richness with rare-clone enrichment and higher IgM diversity. Among the TCR, BCR, and CD8+ T-cell transcriptomic features evaluated, IGH-derived metrics, particularly IgG- and IgA-associated features, showed apparent within-cohort discrimination between active and stable SLE. Genetic algorithm-based label-guided feature selection followed by hierarchical clustering revealed a multi-omics pattern associated with disease activity within the current cohort. Our study characterized peripheral immune repertoire and transcriptional alterations in SLE and highlighted their value for characterizing disease activity.

title: Neuronal intermediate filament neurologic autoimmunity in a patient with Merkel cell carcinoma receiving pembrolizumab.
authorString: Hijazi A, Guleryuz S, Walshauser MA, Hayat G, Chappidi M.

journal.title: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

abstractText:
Background

Neuronal intermediate filament (NIF) autoimmunity is an uncommon paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome that has increasingly been recognized in association with immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy. Merkel cell carcinoma is among the malignancies most frequently associated with NIF antibodies, although reported cases remain limited.

Case presentation

A 55-year-old female with stage IIIA Merkel cell carcinoma developed vertigo, gait instability, dysarthria, and persistent right hemifacial and cervical spasms after receiving second dose of pembrolizumab for recurrent disease. Brain MRI was unremarkable, while continuous electroencephalography demonstrated encephalopathy without a definitive electrocerebral correlate, raising suspicion for subcortical myoclonus. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein. CSF and positive NIF antibodies using cell-based assay. Pembrolizumab was discontinued, and the patient was treated with high-dose corticosteroids followed by monthly intravenous immunoglobulin, resulting in near complete resolution of her neurologic symptoms after 6 months.

Conclusion

This case expands the growing spectrum of ICI-associated NIF paraneoplastic neurologic autoimmunity complicating Merkel cell carcinoma. To our knowledge, persistent hemifacial and cervical spasm has rarely been reported in this clinical setting. Early recognition of this syndrome, prompt antibody testing, discontinuation of ICI therapy, and initiation of therapy may improve neurological outcomes while informing further oncologic management.
