In addition, this approach may help identify patients whose need for treatment should be discussed within a "Psycho-Cardio-Team" that still needs to be established.

title: Left atrial reservoir strain to identify advanced atrial cardiomyopathy in patients with atrial fibrillation.
authorString: Abbas M, Dziano J, Howie J, Kamsani SH, Fitzgerald J, Evans S, Jayakumar M, Elliott AD, Sanders P, Ariyaratnam JP.
abstractText:
Background

Left atrial (LA) reservoir strain (LASr) is a novel marker of LA function. We hypothesized that LASr can be used to identify atrial cardiomyopathy in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF).

Objective

To evaluate the association between LASr and invasive and noninvasive markers of atrial cardiomyopathy in patients with AF.

Methods

We prospectively recruited patients with symptomatic paroxysmal or persistent AF and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction who were scheduled for catheter ablation. Resting transthoracic echocardiography was performed, focusing on the left atrium. Participants were dichotomized into 2 groups: reduced LASr (<20%) and preserved LASr (≥20%). Markers of LA cardiomyopathy were compared between these 2 groups; invasive markers included mean LA pressure, mean LA voltage, and LA compliance, and non-invasive markers included LA volumes and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP).

Results

A total of 91 patients were enrolled. Patients with reduced LASr (n = 31) were older (69.4 ± 8.9 vs 59.6 ± 11.3 years, P < .001) and more commonly women (45.2% vs 18.3%, P = .007). Reduced LASr correlated with lower LA compliance (0.28 ± 0.16 vs 0.42 ± 0.25 mm/mm Hg, P < .001), higher LA pressure (14.8 ± 3.81 vs 13.1 ± 4.46 mm Hg, P = .031), and lower LA voltage (1.65 ± 1.35 vs 3.12 ± 1.57 mV, P < .01). On noninvasive assessment, reduced LASr was also associated with higher NT-proBNP levels (479 [200-1073] vs 121 [58-256] pg/mL, P < .001) and larger LA volumes (38.5 ± 11.5 vs 32.6 ± 7.7 mL/m2, P < .001).

Conclusion

In patients with symptomatic AF, reduced LASr is associated with a more advanced atrial cardiomyopathy involving hemodynamic, mechanical, and electrical atrial dysfunction. LASr may therefore provide a useful non-invasive marker of atrial cardiomyopathy in AF.

title: Day-Night Patterns of Wearable-Derived Electrocardiographic Age and Left Atrial Remodeling in Atrial Fibrillation-Naïve Individuals.
authorString: Park SH, Jin J, Kim J, Lee D, Kim D, Jang J, Yu HT, Chan You S, Joung B.
abstractText:
Background

Artificial intelligence-derived electrocardiographic (AI-ECG) age is conventionally treated as a static marker. Its diurnal dynamics and structural correlates in individuals without atrial fibrillation (AF) remain unknown.

Objective

To characterize diurnal AI-ECG age patterns, their reproducibility, and associations with left atrial (LA) remodeling.

Methods

We analyzed continuous wearable ECGs from two prospective registries (NCT05119725, NCT05355948). In 499 AF-naïve participants with ≥48-hour recordings, AI-ECG age was estimated every 10 minutes. Unsupervised clustering identified day-night trajectories, summarized by day-night difference (ΔAge) into Restorative (>0.6 years) or Disrupted (≤0.6 years) phenotypes. Reproducibility was evaluated across sequential periods. Age- and sex-adjusted associations of binary and continuous ΔAge with LA volume index (LAVI) were pooled in a cross-sectional echocardiographic substudy (n=122).

Results

Three trajectories emerged in both registries. Restorative prevalence was 47.6%-50.2%. Agreement between two consecutive 48-hour periods was 75.8% (κ = 0.516; 95% CI, 0.395-0.631); 6- to 8-day intraclass correlation coefficients were 0.51-0.54. The Disrupted phenotype was associated with higher LAVI (pooled mean difference, 5.54 mL/m2; 95% CI, 1.11-9.98; P = .014) and greater odds of LA enlargement (LAVI ≥40 mL/m2; pooled odds ratio, 3.68; 95% CI, 1.45-9.29; P = .006). Per 1-SD higher ΔAge, LAVI was lower (β, -2.89 mL/m2; P = .007) and LA enlargement less likely (odds ratio, 0.53; P = .004).

Conclusion

Wearable-derived AI-ECG age exhibits a reproducible day-night pattern. A Disrupted phenotype is associated with adverse LA remodeling. Because reproducibility remains insufficient for individual-level classification, prospective outcome-based validation is warranted.

title: Lipid metabolism and pulmonary arterial hypertension.
authorString: Sun Y, Gao P, Lv C, Li M, Zhang Y, Liu M, Zhu L.
abstractText: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a rare and progressive disease characterized by pulmonary vascular remodeling and progressive narrowing of the pulmonary arteries. Recent studies have shown that changes in lipid metabolism and lipid action play an important role in the pathogenesis of PAH, involving membrane integrity, energy metabolism, inflammatory response, and pulmonary vascular remodeling. Lipoprotein receptor deficiency further exacerbates inflammation, fibrosis, and associated pathological processes in PAH. This review summarizes the role of many lipid-active substances and their signaling pathways in the pathogenesis of PAH, sorting the biomarkers related to the severity and prognosis of PAH and discussing the potential application of drug therapy targeting lipid metabolism in managing PAH. This review aims to identify clinically relevant lipid molecules and candidate biomarkers, and to provide new insights and potential targets for precision oriented diagnosis and treatment of PAH.

title: The functional anatomy of caveolae across cell types.
authorString: Rusu MC, Zamfir IŞ, Varga I, Vintilă B.

journal.title: The international journal of biochemistry & cell biology

abstractText: Caveolae are 50-100nm, cholesterol- and sphingolipid-enriched invaginations of the plasma membrane, assembled from caveolin and cavin proteins. They are not generic vesicles distributed equally across mammalian tissues, but cell-type-specific membrane organelles whose abundance, molecular composition and physiological roles vary widely. This review synthesises the evidence for caveolae across the cellular landscape and treats distribution, signalling and disease as a single axis. Endothelial cells, adipocytes and muscle cells represent the highest-density systems, where caveolae support transcytosis, membrane tension buffering, lipid handling, contractile signalling and ion-channel organisation. Fibroblasts are also a well-supported non-endothelial model, with genetic and functional evidence linking caveolin-1 and cavin-1 to caveola formation, integrin mechanosensing, matrix production and fibrosis; by contrast, direct evidence for fibrocytes remains sparse. In epithelia, glia, immune cells, stromal cells and cancer cells, caveolin expression must be distinguished from the verified presence of bona fide caveolae. This distinction is particularly important for telocytes, mature neurons, lymphocytes and tumour cells, where caveolin-based markers, non-caveolar scaffolds and context-dependent loss of cavin proteins complicate interpretation. Disease phenotypes mirror this cellular specificity: mutations or dysregulation lead to muscle caveolinopathies, pulmonary arterial hypertension, lipodystrophy, vascular and blood-brain barrier dysfunction, fibrosis, altered host-pathogen entry, and cancer phenotypes. A cell-type-resolved view therefore complements mechanism-centred accounts of caveola mechanics and helps explain why one caveolin-cavin module can generate divergent physiological and pathological outcomes.

title: Endoscopic ultrasound in hepatology: A European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ESGE) Technical and Technology Review.
authorString: Fabbri C, Binda C, Iglesias Garcia J, Tarantino I, Larghi A, Laleman W, Arcidiacono PG, Hernandez-Gea V, Berzigotti A, Seicean A, Crinò SF, Anderloni A, Karstensen JG, Vanella G, Samanta J, Santopaolo F, Facciorusso A, Van der Merwe SW, Fuccio L.
abstractText: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided techniques are increasingly applied in hepatology, including for tissue acquisition, vascular access, pressure measurement, and selected therapeutic interventions. However, adoption remains heterogeneous because of variability in technical approaches, devices, outcome definitions, operator expertise, and the quality of available evidence. This European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ESGE) Technical and Technology Review summarizes the current evidence on selected EUS-guided techniques in liver disease and portal hypertension, including liver stiffness assessment, focal liver lesion characterization and sampling, EUS-guided liver biopsy, EUS-guided portal pressure gradient measurement, therapy for gastric varices, and portal vein sampling for liquid biopsy applications. Evidence was identified through a structured literature search up to April 2026, and recommendation statements were graded using the GRADE framework. Eight ESGE statements were developed. The available evidence supports selected use of EUS-guided shear wave elastography and contrast-enhanced EUS as adjunctive techniques; EUS-guided liver biopsy and EUS-guided portal pressure gradient measurement as complementary approaches in selected patients and expert centers; and EUS-guided treatment of gastric varices as a valid alternative to direct endoscopic injection where appropriate expertise is available. Portal vein sampling remains investigational. Across the indications, the evidence base is limited by small studies, heterogeneous techniques, variable outcome definitions, and limited prospective comparative data. This review provides an evidence-based framework for the selective use of EUS-guided techniques in hepatology and portal hypertension. Wider adoption will require standardized techniques, structured training, consistent outcome definitions, and prospective comparative studies.

title: Pulmonary diffusion capacity to select patients for echocardiographic evaluation of pulmonary hypertension in interstitial lung disease: Impact of interstitial lung disease phenotype.
authorString: Ito N, Masuda T, Shimoji K, Yamaguchi K, Sakamoto S, Horimasu Y, Nakashima T, Hamada H, Hattori N, Iwamoto H.
abstractText: Treprostinil inhalation for pulmonary hypertension (PH) with interstitial lung disease (ILD) has increased the importance of PH screening. We aimed to determine whether pulmonary function tests performed for ILD management could identify patients with possible PH on echocardiography, according to ILD subtype. In this cross-sectional study, patients with ILD who underwent pulmonary function tests and echocardiography within three months were enrolled consecutively. The correlation between pulmonary function test results and peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity (TRV) was assessed using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. We defined possible PH as peak TRV > 2.8 m/s. The screening performance for possible PH was evaluated using ROC analysis. In total, 278 patients were analysed. Among pulmonary function test values, percent predicted diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (%DLCO) most significantly correlated with TRV (ρ = -0.468, p < 0.001). In the ROC curve analysis for identifying possible PH, %DLCO exhibited the highest area under the curve (AUC) of 0.750. The AUC for combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema (CPFE), idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (IIPs), and collagen vascular disease-related interstitial pneumonia (CVD-IP) were 0.856, 0.747, and 0.671, respectively. Among patients with IIPs, the AUC was higher when Brinkman Index was ≥600 than when it was <600 (0.881 vs 0.620). Based on numerical trends, %DLCO showed potentially high screening performance in patients with CPFE or IIPs with a history of heavy smoking. Echocardiographic evaluation for possible PH may be warranted in this population with reduced %DLCO.

title: Clinically Motivated Redesign of the Pennsylvania State University Child Ventricular Assist Device.
authorString: Scheib CM, Yeager EE, Xu L, Siedlecki CA, Cysyk JP, Bohnenberger KO, Jhun CJ.

journal.title: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)

abstractText: Building on validated in vitro and chronic in vivo testing of the Penn State University (PSU) Child Ventricular Assist Device (CVAD), the four-bladed prototype rotor (Rev 0.0) was redesigned using established analytical and computational methods to improve hydraulic efficiency while preserving hemodynamic performance and biocompatibility. Applying turbomachinery principles at the nominal operating condition (3 liters/minute [LPM], 8,000 revolutions/minute [RPM]), a five-bladed design (Rev 1.0) was created with an ideal inflow angle (β1 = 41.0°) and outflow angle (β2 = 27.4°). In silico simulations of Rev 1.0 across the prototype's operating range (7,000-9,000 RPM, 1-5 LPM) demonstrated an approximately 40% improvement in hydraulic performance. The Rev 1.0 rotor was then evaluated on a benchtop mock circulatory loop using fresh ovine blood, confirming the in silico gains. The normalized index of hemolysis (NIH), measured at two clinically relevant conditions (1.5 LPM and 3.3 LPM, both at ~80 mm Hg), was 0.052 ± 0.054 and 0.047 ± 0.033 mg/dL, respectively, and high-molecular-weight multimers of von Willebrand factor were preserved within normal to borderline ranges. By achieving target flows and pressures at approximately 1,000 RPM lower speeds, the redesign reduces power requirements and enables longer untethered operation, advancing a fully implantable PSU CVAD toward a critical unmet need in pediatric advanced heart failure.

title: Feasibility of a machine learning model for predicting weight gain after kidney transplantation machine learning and weight gain after kidney transplantation.
authorString: de Freitas JMC, Ballester PL, Pedrollo EF, Corrêa C, Menezes RCR, Leitão CB, Souza GC.
abstractText: Excessive weight gain after kidney transplantation adversely affects patient and graft outcomes. Machine Learning has been increasingly used to improve risk prediction across a range of transplant-related outcomes, yet its application to post-transplant weight trajectories remains unexplored. This study is the first to evaluate the feasibility of using Machine Learning algorithms to identify predictors of weight gain after kidney transplantation. This retrospective cohort study analyzed 374 adult kidney transplant recipients. We developed an Elastic Net regression model with 10-fold cross-validation to predict body weight variation at 12 months post-transplant. The analysis screened a comprehensive set of demographic and clinical variables, including recipient characteristics, donor type, dialysis duration, and pre-transplant hypertension, to identify predictors within the training (75%) and testing (25%) datasets. Mean weight gain was 4.0 ± 7.4 kg. The Elastic Net model retained four predictors in the final model: female sex, deceased donor source, age, and pre-transplant body mass index. However, the model demonstrated limited predictive performance (R2 = 0.10; Mean Absolute Error = 8.7%), indicating that baseline variables explain only a small fraction of the observed variability in weight change. This pioneering study establishes an analytical benchmark and reveals the informational limits of standard clinical datasets for predicting post-transplant weight gain. While Machine Learning application is feasible, current demographic and clinical variables are insufficient for precise individual prediction. Future models must integrate more granular behavioral and pharmacological data to achieve clinically actionable risk stratification.

title: Integrating Scalability and Equity into Hypertension Remote Patient Monitoring Program Design.
authorString: Kronish IM, Bryant KB, Commodore-Mensah Y, Halladay JR, Kim EJ, Margolis KL, Rikin S, West H, Cluett JL.
abstractText: Remote patient monitoring (RPM) for hypertension combines home blood pressure (BP) monitoring with electronic transmission of BP readings and clinical support. RPM has the potential to improve BP control and reduce hypertension disparities, but because it depends on devices, connectivity, digital literacy, and sustained engagement, it may also worsen inequities if not intentionally designed. This review examines barriers to equitable RPM implementation and strategies to address them. RPM can improve hypertension control and extend care beyond traditional clinical settings, but its effect on health equity depends on program design. Equity should be treated as a core design principle. Future research should evaluate differential reach, engagement, effectiveness, and sustainability across populations and identify payment models that support equitable implementation at scale. Barriers to equitable RPM implementation occur at patient, clinician, health system, and policy levels. Key challenges include limited access to technology, language barriers, out-of-pocket costs, inadequate cuff sizing, unmet social needs, clinician workload, referral bias, infrastructure limitations, reimbursement variability, and the digital divide. Emerging evidence suggests that equity-focused strategies can improve reach and engagement, including provision of cellular-enabled devices, reduced patient costs, culturally and linguistically tailored support, team-based care, registry-based outreach, and routine monitoring of enrollment and outcomes across demographic groups. High-resource, low-resource, and hybrid RPM models each offer distinct advantages and tradeoffs in balancing scalability, sustainability, and equity.

title: Effect heterogeneity of loneliness and social support on incident hypertension in older, normotensive populations.
authorString: Nielsen VM, Smith L, Han L, Honda T, Manjourides J.
abstractText: Although social isolation is known to impact those with cardiovascular disease, its relationship with incident hypertension is unclear. In this retrospective cohort study, we used data from the All of Us research program. Participants were enrolled between May 2017-April 2023, aged 50+ years, and had at least 60-days of EHR data pre-index date. We identified incident hypertension during follow-up. Those classified as hypertensive at or prior to the index date were excluded. We defined low social support and loneliness as binary variables. Using causal forests, we estimated treatment effects as unweighted and overlap-weighted risk differences (RD). A total of 24,720 participants with a median follow-up of 2.6 years were included. While loneliness and social support were not significantly associated with incident hypertension in the overall population, causal forests revealed meaningful effect heterogeneity, with socially isolated male (RD: 0.038, 95% CI 0.002 to 0.075; overlap-weighted RD: 0.027, 95% CI -0.005 to 0.059) and Gay or Lesbian participants (RD: 0.108, 95% CI 0.011 to 0.205; overlap-weighted RD: 0.11, 95% CI 0.008 to 0.211) experiencing a significantly elevated risk. This illustrates how machine learning, when embedded within epidemiologic frameworks, can detect subgroup vulnerability that other approaches may obscure, enabling targeting of limited resources.

title: Genetic Pulmonary Hypertension Combined With Biventricular Heart Failure: Role of AQP1 Gene Mutation.
authorString: Danh VD, Nguyen QQ, Nguyen HT.
abstractText: Aquaporin-1 (AQP1) mutations are a rare cause of heritable pulmonary artery hypertension. The clinical manifestation remains poorly defined, and coexisting left ventricular dysfunction has not been reported. A 34-year-old man presented with severe pulmonary arterial hypertension and biventricular dysfunction. Genetic testing revealed a heterozygous AQP1 mutation, c.551T >C (p.Ile184Thr), not previously reported; family screening confirmed the same variant in his mother and daughter. After 6 months of guideline-directed medical therapy and endothelin receptor antagonist therapy, pulmonary artery pressure decreased significantly, and functional capacity improved. Biventricular impairment raises 2 hypotheses: septal dyskinesia secondary to right ventricular overload, or myocardial impairment because of altered AQP1 channel function. The favorable response suggests targeted pulmonary vasodilator therapy may benefit in this rare genetic subset. AQP1 mutations should be considered in genetic workup of pulmonary arterial hypertension and may coexist with left ventricular dysfunction responsive to endothelin receptor antagonist therapy.

title: Clusters of modifiable dementia risk factors at mid-life and late-life and their association with incident dementia: A prospective cohort study of 246,968 adults.
authorString: van Baal TL, Köhler S, Deckers K, Janssen N.
abstractText: BackgroundModifiable dementia risk factors rarely occur in isolation, yet their co-occurrence and clustering remain poorly characterized, limiting identification of high-risk individuals and development of targeted strategies.ObjectiveTo identify clusters of ten modifiable risk factors in mid-life (45-65 years) and late-life (>65 years), and to examine their association with incident dementia.MethodsData were drawn from the 2012 Dutch Public Health Monitor Survey (mid-life: n = 121,120; late-life: n = 125,848), with dementia follow-up through 2023. Ten modifiable risk factors: obesity, hypertension, diabetes, hearing loss, visual loss, physical inactivity, excessive alcohol consumption, smoking, loneliness, and depression, were used to derive clusters using latent class analysis. Cox proportional hazards models examined the association between late-life clusters and incident dementia.ResultsIn mid-life (mean age, 55.7 ± 6.2 years), four risk factor clusters were identified: cardiometabolic, substance use, psychosocial, and lower risk. In late-life (mean age, 73.9 ± 6.4 years), four clusters were identified: cardiometabolic, substance use, psychosocial and physically inactive, and lower risk. After adjustment for sociodemographic factors, the psychosocial and physically inactive cluster was associated with the highest hazard of dementia (hazard ratio (HR), 1.23; 95% CI, 1.16-1.32), followed by the substance use (HR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.09-1.24) and the cardiometabolic cluster (HR, 1.12; 95% CI, 1.07-1.18).ConclusionsDistinct risk factor clusters were identified at both mid-life and late-life; the psychosocial and physically inactive cluster carried the highest risk of dementia. These findings underscore the importance of considering risk factor clustering when designing targeted interventions to reduce dementia risk across the life course.

title: Cardiomonostack: A postoperative heart failure risk prediction model for total hip arthroplasty driven by ensemble learning.
authorString: Cui J, Lim ECN, Lim CED.

journal.title: Technology and health care : official journal of the European Society for Engineering and Medicine

abstractText: BackgroundAccurate perioperative risk prediction remains challenging because of class imbalance, cohort heterogeneity, unstable probability estimates and limited interpretability.ObjectiveTo develop and externally evaluate CardioMonoStack, an ensemble architecture integrating heterogeneous base learners, branch-level monotonicity priors, stacked meta-learning and feature-dependent residual logit correction.MethodsWe conducted a multicentre retrospective cohort study of 1911 patients aged ≥65 years undergoing total hip arthroplasty across five healthcare databases. CardioMonoStack was developed using MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, validated in INSPIRE, and externally tested in eICU and MOVER. Performance was assessed using AUROC, AUPRC, Brier score, threshold-dependent classification measures, calibration plots and decision curve analysis. Interpretability was examined using SHAP, interaction and individual conditional expectation analyses.ResultsCardioMonoStack achieved the highest AUROC point estimates among evaluated models in eICU (0.790; 95% CI 0.711-0.865) and MOVER (0.866; 95% CI 0.761-0.949), with AUPRC values of 0.569 (95% CI 0.415-0.717) and 0.571 (95% CI 0.328-0.792), respectively. Calibration and net benefit varied across cohorts and comparators. Omission of L3 increased Brier-score and log-loss point estimates in both external cohorts; paired confidence intervals supported these differences in MOVER but were inconclusive in eICU. SHAP analyses prioritised blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, age, and metabolic and demographic factors.ConclusionCardioMonoStack is a candidate framework for estimating in-hospital heart-failure risk after total hip arthroplasty. Despite promising external discrimination, prospective validation, local recalibration, and clinical impact evaluation are required before implementation.

title: C5 Inhibition for Anti-Cancer Therapy-Induced Renal Thrombotic Microangiopathy.
authorString: Barbarini M, Chavez CN, Mirkheshti P, Thongprayoon C, Go RS, Sridharan M, Herrera Hernandez LP, Leung N, Herrmann SM.

journal.title: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association

abstractText: Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is increasingly recognized as a complication of both cancer and anti-cancer therapies. C5 complement inhibition is used in selected cases, but evidence supporting its effectiveness, particularly in kidney biopsy-proven disease, remains limited. This retrospective cohort study included adult patients with biopsy-proven TMA attributed to anti-cancer therapies between 2015 and 2026 at Mayo Clinic, USA. Patients were stratified according to treatment with complement inhibition versus no complement inhibition therapy. The primary outcome was renal recovery; secondary outcomes included hematological recovery, composite outcome, overall survival, and longitudinal changes in hematologic and renal function parameters. A total of 31 patients with kidney biopsy-proven TMA related to anti-cancer therapy were included. Nine received complement inhibition, and 22 did not. A higher proportion of patients in the treated group achieved complete or partial renal recovery at 3 months (p = 0.008), hematologic recovery at 1 month (p = 0.007) and composite outcome (complete-partial renal plus hematologic recovery) (p = 0.041). During follow-up, platelet counts increased significantly at 1 month and 3 months (p = 0.045, both) in the treated group. Mixed-effects modeling showed significantly lower longitudinal estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) values in the untreated group (β = -13.9 mL/min per 1.73 m², p = 0.028). In the gemcitabine-associated TMA subgroup, complete-partial renal recovery occurred only in treated patients (p = 0.021) and hematologic recovery was achieved in the whole cohort but occurred significantly faster in the complement inhibition group (p = 0.019). The higher rate of renal recovery persisted in sensitivity analysis (p = 0.021). In this rigorously phenotyped cohort of patients with biopsy-proven, anti-cancer therapy-associated renal TMA, we observed a signal of benefit from C5 inhibition, most consistently for renal recovery and possibly extending to hematologic outcomes, particularly among patients with gemcitabine-associated TMA.

title: The START-SIAPAV-PAD Registry - Rationale, study design, and baseline characteristics of an ongoing Italian multicentre registry.
authorString: Visonà A, Amato C, Biscetti F, Zalunardo B, Favaretto E, Marzolo M, Lotti E, Ghirardini F, Dorigo W, Pignatelli P, Carlizza A, Puccetti L, Porfidia A, Cini M, Antonucci E, Ageno W.
abstractText: Background: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is associated with a high burden of cardiovascular and limb events, yet guideline-directed medical therapy remains suboptimal. The START-SIAPAV-PAD registry was designed to describe characteristics, management and clinical history of patients with PAD in Italy. Baseline characteristics and treatment are reported. Patients and methods: START-SIAPAV-PAD is a prospective, multicentre, observational registry enrolling consecutive adults with PAD managed at 20 Italian Vascular centres, starting in February 2023. Standardised electronic case-report forms collect demographics, risk factors, comorbidities, haemodynamic parameters, vascular anatomy, therapies. Follow-up is planned for a minimum of 3 years. PAD severity is classified according to the Leriche-Fontaine scale, and risk-factor targets follow the 2024 ESC guidelines. Results: The present analysis includes 517 patients (72.0% male; median age 71 years) with a high prevalence of hypertension (79.2%), dyslipidaemia (85.0%), diabetes (36.9%), smoking (96.1% current or former) and chronic kidney disease (21.2%). Nearly half reported a walking distance <200 m, 77.5% had a resting ankle-brachial index ≤.80, and 17.2% presented with Leriche-Fontaine stage IV. Femoropopliteal disease was most frequent (69.8%), with multilevel involvement in 43.4%. Previous revascularisation was common, major amputation was rare. LDL cholesterol target (<55mg dL) was achieved in 27.9% of patients despite lipid-lowering therapy in 82.1%. Dual pathway inhibition, advanced lipid-lowering therapies, supervised exercise and structured smoking-cessation programmes were insufficiently adopted. Conclusions: In a population with advanced PAD and multiple risk factors we observed a substantial gap between guideline recommendations and real-world practice. Longitudinal follow-up will assess outcomes and opportunities to improve PAD management.

title: Clonal expansion of CD8+ effector T cells in patients with calcific aortic valve disease.
authorString: Bartoli-Leonard F, Chelvanambi S, Pham T, Clift CL, Turner ME, Blaser MC, Singh SA, Caputo M, Aikawa M, Pang A, Muehlschlegel J, Aikawa E.
abstractText:
Aims

Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) is a complex cardiovascular pathology, culminating in aortic stenosis and heart failure with no effective treatment strategy, except invasive surgery. While inflammation may contribute to valvular fibro-calcific pathology and T cells have been identified within the leaflets, their contribution to CAVD pathogenesis remains unclear.

Methods & results

Disease-staged whole-tissue proteomics (n=16) confirmed a pro-inflammatory T cell driven signature, with immunohistochemistry (n=10) and immunofluorescence (n=8) conducted on control and CAVD valves to confirm T cell localization to calcified regions. Flow cytometry immunophenotyping (n=20) was was performed using valvular tissue and corresponding peripheral blood from the same individuals. Single cell RNA sequencing and paired single T cell receptor sequencing was conducted on an additional 4 patients on CD45+, CD3+, CD4+ or CD8+ T cells. T cell signaling was identified through unsupervised clustering. Tissue resident memory (TRM) T cells were detected within the valve, exhibiting a highly cytotoxic, activated, and terminally differentiated phenotype. This pan-pro-inflammatory signal was differentially identified in T cells originating from the valve tissue, and not observed in the blood, indicative of an adaptive, local and non-systemic inflammatory signature in CAVD patients. T cell receptor analysis detected hyperexpanded clones within the CD8+ T cell central memory (TCM) population, with TRM cells comprising most of the large and medium clonal expansion within the T cell population. Clonal expansion was more prominent in valve tissue, with expanded clones largely confined to their tissue of origin. Clonal interaction network analysis demonstrated the greatest proportion of clones originating from CD8+ TCM and TRM populations, exhibiting a tissue resident, cytotoxic environment within the valve.

Conclusions

Taken together, the data define distinct T cell subpopulations in CAVD and implicate specific antigenic epitopes driving clonal expansion of valvular T cells, supporting a central role for antigen-driven, autoimmune-like inflammation in disease propagation.

title: Predictive Value of the HALP Score for Post-Operative Atrial Fibrillation After Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery.
authorString: Şaylık F, Kümet Ö, Sezgin M, Sarıkaya R, Çınar T, İçkale UB, Şimşek ÖF.
abstractText: Post-operative atrial fibrillation (POAF) is common after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, occurring in 20% to 40% of patients and significantly increasing morbidity. The hemoglobin, albumin, lymphocyte, and platelet (HALP) score, a composite nutritional-inflammatory index, is a prognostic marker in cardiovascular disease. However, its predictive value for POAF remains unestablished. We aimed to evaluate the predictive performance of 5 nutritional-inflammatory indices (HALP, Naples score, Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index [SII], neutrophil percentage-to-albumin ratio [NPAR], and C-reactive protein-albumin-lymphocyte [CALLY] index) for POAF and internally validate a novel prediction model incorporating HALP. Among 448 patients undergoing CABG, POAF occurred in 131 (29.2%). The HALP score demonstrated the highest discriminative ability (area under curve [AUC] 0.812), significantly (P < .001) outperforming Naples (AUC 0.676), NPAR (AUC 0.730), SII (AUC 0.726), and CALLY (AUC 0.684). Adding HALP to the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO)-derived base model significantly improved discriminative ability (AUC 0.813-0.897; P < .001) and net clinical benefit across threshold probabilities. The combined model achieved a bootstrap-corrected AUC of 0.885 with a calibration slope of 0.909, reflecting excellent internal validity. HALP was the strongest POAF predictor in the combined model. The HALP-integrated model showed excellent performance, offering a practical tool for preoperative POAF risk stratification.

title: Comparative lifestyle factors and outcomes of an intensive interprofessional lifestyle medicine program versus usual care in Medicare and commercially insured musculoskeletal patients with chronic disease.
authorString: Prather H, Bradley E, Mele A, Leupold O, Cheng J.

journal.title: PM & R : the journal of injury, function, and rehabilitation

abstractText: Lifestyle medicine (LM) uses evidence-based interventions to reduce chronic systemic inflammation, a driver of chronic diseases and painful musculoskeletal conditions. Medicare beneficiaries represent a high-risk population for chronic systemic inflammation and may benefit from receiving care through an intensive LM program (ILMP). To compare baseline lifestyle factors and outcomes (1) between Medicare and commercially insured patients completing an ILMP, and (2) between Medicare patients completing an ILMP and Medicare patients receiving usual care (non-ILMP). Retrospective exploratory study of repository data. Tertiary orthopedic center. A total of 204 Medicare and 322 commercially insured patients entered the ILMP from May 2023 to May 2025; of these, 101 Medicare and 130 commercially insured patients completed the program and were included in this study (50% vs. 40% completion rate; p = .040). A third group of 90 Medicare patients with similar conditions received usual care during this same time frame. The ILMP virtually integrates individual and group visits with an interprofessional team, with patient-identified health goals. Goal attainment; changes in weight, pain, physical/mental health, and metabolic labs from program enrollment to completion. Compared to commercially insured ILMP patients, Medicare ILMP patients were older (70 ± 7 vs. 55 ± 10 years, p < .001) and had higher rates of ≥2 lifestyle-related chronic diseases (96% vs. 85%; p = .015), hypertension (72% vs. 54%; p = .010), hyperlipidemia (59% vs. 40%; p = .001), and gastroesophageal reflux disease (33% vs. 18%; p = .015) at baseline. Medicare and commercially insured ILMP patients reported similar use of program services, goal attainment, and outcomes. Compared to the Medicare usual-care group, the Medicare ILMP group had similar baseline characteristics but achieved greater weight loss (10 ± 14 lbs vs. 1 ± 4 lbs; p < .001). An interprofessional ILMP delivered virtually is feasible and effective for Medicare patients with musculoskeletal conditions and lifestyle-related chronic diseases, despite having a greater baseline disease burden compared with commercially insured patients.

title: Self-management barriers in dialysis patients: a target for improving health outcomes.
authorString: Driehuis E, Meuleman Y, Hobo SGD, Bonenkamp AA, Dekker FW, Abrahams AC, van Jaarsveld BC, of the DOMESTICO study group.
abstractText: Adequate self-management behaviours may improve health outcomes, but dialysis patients often struggle to adopt and maintain these behaviours. Therefore, we aimed to 1) identify self-management barriers in dialysis patients, 2) assess their relation to patient characteristics, and 3) assess their effect on clinical and patient-reported outcomes. We conducted a multicentre, longitudinal cohort study in adult incident dialysis patients who filled in the Self-Management Screening questionnaire. Descriptive analyses were performed to assess the extent of self-management barriers. The relation between patient characteristics and self-management barriers was determined using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. The impact of self-management barriers on health outcomes was investigated using linear and Cox regression models. In 1518 dialysis patients, self-management barriers were common across a wide range of domains (eg self-efficacy, coping, and social support). Sex, age, educational level, cohabitation, dialysis modality, and comorbidity were associated with the extent of individual self-management barriers and the total number of barriers. Moreover, a higher number of self-management barriers was associated with poorer mental and physical health-related quality of life, and with a higher symptom number and burden at 6 and 12 months after dialysis initiation. Dialysis patients frequently experience self-management barriers across many domains and the extent differs depending on patient characteristics. Self-management barriers negatively impact patient-reported outcomes over time. Our findings highlight the importance of systematic, personalised, multicomponent self-management support in dialysis care, as this is an important target to improve health outcomes in this population.

title: Association of Diet Quality and Physical Activity through Young Adulthood With Mid-Life Cardiovascular Health Trajectories: The Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) Study
authorString: Rai I, Ning H, Li J, Pettee Gabriel K, Lloyd-Jones DM.
abstractText:
Background:

Young adulthood is a critical life course window during which cardiovascular pathophysiology develops, yet diet quality and physical activity (PA) are typically studied as separate, static exposures. We examined joint associations of diet and PA across young adulthood with midlife cardiovascular health (CVH) patterns.

Methods:

Among 2,806 participants in the biracial Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) cohort, group-based dual-trajectory modeling identified latent classes of joint Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) score and PA from exam Year 0 to Year 20 (mean age range at each exam 25-45 years). Group-based trajectory modeling defined midlife CVH trajectories using Life's Essential 8 (LE8) scores (5 physiologic components) from Year 20 to Year 35 (mean age range at each exam 45-60 years). Multinomial logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, race, and education, related young-adult behavioral groups to midlife CVH status (high ?80, moderate 50-79, or low <50).

Results:

Four joint diet/PA groups from young adulthood behaviors were identified: low DASH/very low PA (Group 1; 10.9%); low DASH/moderate-declining PA (Group 2; 25.6%); moderate DASH/high-declining PA (Group 3; 41.5%); and high DASH/high-declining PA (Group 4; 22.0%). Three non-overlapping midlife CVH trajectories (low, moderate, high) emerged. Compared with Group 1, participants in Groups 2, 3, and 4 had 4.8-, 8.6-, and 21.7-fold higher odds of high versus low CVH. The joint odds ratio (21.7) exceeded those for high diet quality (7.2) or high PA (10.3) individually. Associations persisted after adjustment for baseline LE8 score.

Conclusions:

Sustained simultaneous adherence to high-quality diet and high PA through young adulthood was strongly and synergistically associated with high midlife CVH, supporting early, comprehensive, and sustained lifestyle prevention.

title: Renal adaptation to primary aldosteronism requires GDF15 to control plasma potassium level in mice and human.
authorString: Billiet J, Morla L, Vidal-Petiot E, Wirth E, Laney M, Baron S, Amar L, Cheval L, Crambert G.
abstractText:
Background:

Primary aldosteronism (PA), the most common secondary cause of hypertension, results from autonomous aldosterone production, driving renal Na retention and K secretion. Paradoxically, only 9 to 37% of PA patients develop hypokalemia, suggesting adaptive mechanisms. Growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) promotes intercalated cell type A (ICA) proliferation and K reabsorption in the collecting duct, but its role in PA is unexplored. Methods We measured urinary and plasma GDF15 in 81 PA patients (two centers) and 41 controls. A murine model of chronic mineralocorticoid excess (DOCP treatment) was used in wild-type (WT) and GDF15 knockout (GDF15KO) mice to assess renal adaptation. Results PA patients exhibited 3-fold higher urinary GDF15 and 1.6-fold higher plasma GDF15 than controls, with normalization post-treatment. 24-hour urinary GDF15 correlated with urinary aldosterone (rho=0.35, p<0.01), age, and BMI (Body Mass Index), but not plasma K. WT mice developed hypokalemia following DOCP administration (plasma K 3.5±0.1 mM vs. 4.3±0.1 mM in controls, p<0.01). In GDF15KO mice DOCP-induced hypokalemia was more severe, indicating a protective role of GDF15. In WT mice, DOCP increased 24-hour urinary GDF15 (2-fold) and GDF15 expression in the collecting duct. Transcriptomic analysis revealed an inverted transcriptional response to chronic mineralocorticoid in ICA and PC according to the genotype. This could be related to the increase of ICA number in WT, an effect abolished in GDF15KO mice. Conclusions These results indicate that GDF15 is involved in the renal response to mineralocorticoid excess, likely through stimulation of ICA proliferation, which may promote potassium reabsorption in the collecting duct and help mitigate aldosterone-mediated K loss.

title: Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy Using a Conduction System Pacing Defibrillation Lead in Patients Meeting CRT-D Indications: Six-Month Clinical Outcomes Results From the ASCEND CSP Study.
authorString: Varma N, Burri H, Manrique Garcia A, Singh B, Tse HF, Tam MTK, Nair D, Pierre B, Joza J, Zimetbaum P, Birgersdotter-Green U, Tung R, Sanders P, Feng L, Ganz L, Leclercq C, Lee K, Schaller RD.
abstractText:
Background

Conduction system pacing (CSP) via left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP) is a physiologic alternative to conventional biventricular (BiV) pacing for cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), but prospective data using purpose-built implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) leads are limited.

Objectives

The purpose of this study was to evaluate procedural success, defibrillation efficacy, safety, and 6-month clinical outcomes of left bundle branch-optimized cardiac resynchronization therapy (LOT-CRT) delivered with a purpose-built CSP ICD lead and compare outcomes to conventional BiV-CRT.

Methods

A total of 52 CRT defibrillator patients (age 66 ± 10 years, 31.4% female, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 29.5 ± 6.7%, left bundle branch block [LBBB] 66.7%, QRSd 164.6 ± 25.3 milliseconds, 29.4% ischemic) in the ASCEND CSP IDE (A Stylet-Driven ICD Lead Intended for Conduction System Pacing IDE Study) study underwent attempted implantation of a CSP ICD lead and a coronary sinus lead (LOT-CRT). Implant success, safety and efficacy outcomes, electrocardiographic characteristics, echocardiographic remodeling, heart failure status, patient-reported quality of life, and CRT response were assessed through 6 months. Outcomes were compared with a propensity-matched conventional CRT cohort (BiV-CRT).

Results

Implantation succeeded in 98.1% (51 of 52), with LBBAP capture achieved in all (51 of 51). Freedom from CSP lead-related serious adverse device effects through 6 months was 98.1% (95% CI: 87.1%-99.7%). Defibrillation was successful in all tested patients (100%). Compared with baseline, QRS narrowed by 30.4 ms and LVEF increased by 10.4 points (both P < 0.0001), with a CRT response (≥5%) in 71.1% and super-response (≥14.5%) in 34.2%. Compared with matched BiV-CRT patients from the MORE-CRT MPP (MORE response on Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy with MultiPoint Pacing) study, lead-related events were similar (2.0% vs 2.5%; P = 1.0), LVEF increase was greater (10.4 points vs 4.6 points; P = 0.0005) with more responders (≥5%) and super-responders (≥14.5%) (71.1% vs 48.5%; P = 0.0107 and 34.2% vs 7.8%; P < 0.0001, respectively), and more patients improved by clinical composite score (76.5% vs 52.0%; P = 0.0016). Significant improvements were seen with LOT-CRT in both LBBB and non-LBBB patients.

Conclusions

LOT-CRT with a dedicated CSP ICD lead achieved high implant success, preserved defibrillation efficacy, and had favorable safety, with greater left ventricular systolic function and clinical improvement than matched conventional CRT, supporting CSP-based CRT defibrillator therapy.

title: Epigenetic regulation of vascular smooth muscle cell plasticity in vascular injury, repair, and aging.
authorString: Zheng XL, Sun J, Yin H, Zhou S.
abstractText: Vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) exhibit a remarkable phenotypic spectrum in response to injury, inflammation, metabolic stress, and aging through state changes encoded in chromatin. This review examines how DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation, histone modifiers, chromatin readers, adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-dependent chromatin remodelers, three-dimensional genome organization, and non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) shape VSMC plasticity in intimal hyperplasia, atherosclerosis and vascular aging. Bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4) is used as a case study because it links acetyl-lysine recognition to transcriptional programs and BRD4 inhibition has been reported to affect VSMC biology in vivo. Based on published evidence, we discuss the timing and delivery of potential vascular epigenetic targeting: short-term, local chromatin-directed therapy may help restrain maladaptive VSMC proliferation after acute artery injury, whereas chronic conditions, including atherosclerosis and vascular aging, would require careful long-term dosing that preserves endothelial repair, VSMC contractile state and hematopoietic safety. These therapeutic implications remain preclinical hypotheses, with clinical efficacy remaining to be established.

title: 4D-Flow MRI Assessment of Ascending Aortic Energy Loss in Quadricuspid Aortic Valve.
authorString: Inno G, Nagao M, Nishiya K, Kawase T, Takahashi Y.
abstractText:
Images

Four-dimensional-flow magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated prominent helical and vortical flow in the ascending aorta of a patient with severe aortic regurgitation caused by a quadricuspid aortic valve.

Case summary

Peak systolic energy loss in the ascending aorta was 68.3 mW and decreased to 15.7 mW after surgical aortic valve replacement, accompanied by marked reduction in abnormal flow patterns.

Take-home message

This case demonstrates the ability of 4-dimensional-flow magnetic resonance imaging to visualize abnormal ascending aortic flow and quantify associated energy loss beyond conventional valvular assessment.

title: Novel Mechanometabolic Signaling Cascade Linking Efferocytosis to Inflammation Resolution.
authorString: Kumar D, Pandit R, Frausto L, Governale TA, Yuan S, Nion Fieira J, Quaye A, McGee K, Das S, Anand SK, Pandey N, Kaur H, Ahmed T, Katakia Y, Gomez K, Gates B, White L, Orr C, Sperfslage N, Breitzman MW, Showman LJ, Doran AC, Straub AC, Razani B, Woolard MD, Lively K, Knight FW, Traylor JG, Sugar MA, Dhanesha N, Pattillo CB, Orr AW, Rom O, Yurdagul A.
abstractText:
Background

Apoptotic cell clearance by macrophages, termed efferocytosis, resolves inflammation and promotes tissue repair, whereas defective efferocytosis contributes to chronic inflammatory diseases such as atherosclerosis. Putrescine biosynthesis, driven by the rate-limiting enzyme ODC1 (ornithine decarboxylase 1), has emerged as a key efferocytosis-induced metabolic pathway that promotes inflammation resolution. However, the mechanisms regulating ODC1 during atherosclerosis remain undefined. Here, we investigated the mechanisms controlling ODC1 and putrescine biosynthesis and identified a novel integrin αv-FAK (focal adhesion kinase)-Rac1 (Rac family small GTPase 1)-STAT3 (signal transducer and activator of transcription 3)-MYC (MYC proto-oncogene) signaling axis that becomes progressively impaired during atherosclerosis.

Methods

We performed metabolomic and cytokine profiling of human atherosclerotic plaques and assessed ODC1 expression in lesional macrophages from humans and mice. Mechanistic studies used apoptotic cell- or polystyrene bead-exposed macrophages, Ldlr-/- mice with hematopoietic integrin αv deficiency fed a Western-type diet, single-nuclei RNA sequencing, and bulk RNA sequencing.

Results

Putrescine levels negatively correlated with inflammatory mediators, and ODC1 expression in lesional macrophages declined with disease progression in humans and mice. Engulfment of apoptotic cells or polystyrene beads increased ODC1 expression through an integrin αv- and actin polymerization-dependent mechanism. Hematopoietic integrin αv deficiency exacerbated lesion size and necrosis, reduced efferocytosis, and decreased fibrous cap thickness. Single-nuclei RNA sequencing showed no changes in lesional cell composition but revealed activation of inflammatory pathways specifically in integrin αv-deficient macrophages. Mechanistically, phagocytosis-induced ODC1 expression relied on integrin αv-mediated STAT3 activation and MYC-dependent Odc1 transcription. Bulk RNA sequencing showed that apoptotic cell-exposed human macrophages lacking integrin αv upregulated atherogenic mediators and inflammatory pathways, an effect reversed by restoring putrescine levels.

Conclusions

Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanistic link between phagocytosis and macrophage metabolism, which we identify as a case of mechanometabolism, and demonstrate how its dysregulation compromises inflammation resolution and promotes atherosclerosis.

title: Dual-layer spectral CT-derived iodine and extracellular volume biomarkers for noninvasive assessment of hepatic fibrosis in Fontan-associated liver disease.
authorString: Inmutto N, Srisuwan T, Nimitrungtawee N, Sethasathien S, Kongkarnka S, Na Chiangmai W.
abstractText:
Purpose

To evaluate the diagnostic performance of delayed-phase dual-layer spectral CT-derived normalized iodine concentration and extracellular volume fraction for noninvasive assessment of hepatic fibrosis in patients with Fontan-associated liver disease.

Methods

This single-center exploratory retrospective study included 23 patients with Fontan-associated liver disease who underwent both liver biopsy and delayed-phase dual-layer spectral CT between January 2021 and December 2023. Normalized iodine concentration was calculated as hepatic iodine concentration divided by aortic iodine concentration. Hematocrit-adjusted extracellular volume fraction (ECV) was calculated from delayed-phase iodine-density maps. Histologic fibrosis stage based on the METAVIR system was used as the reference standard. Associations between CT biomarkers and fibrosis stage were assessed using the Kruskal-Wallis test, Jonckheere-Terpstra trend test, and Spearman correlation. Diagnostic performance for advanced fibrosis (≥ F3) and cirrhosis (F4) was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis.

Results

Histologic fibrosis stages were F1 in 4 patients, F2 in 2, F3 in 9, and F4 in 8. ECV was higher in advanced fibrosis stages, with median values of 39.21% in F1, 37.15% in F2, 42.72% in F3, and 46.78% in F4. ECV differed significantly among fibrosis stages (p = 0.014), showed a significant ordered trend (p < 0.001), and correlated positively with histologic stage (ρ = 0.666, p < 0.001). IC-normalized showed a weak positive correlation with fibrosis stage, but the ordered trend did not reach statistical significance. For advanced fibrosis, ECV showed promising preliminary discrimination, with an AUC of 0.902 (95% CI, 0.766-1.000). For cirrhosis, ECV showed an AUC of 0.833 (95% CI, 0.655-1.000), with sensitivity of 87.5%, specificity of 80.0%, and negative predictive value of 92.3% at a cutoff of 43.45%.

Conclusion

In this single-center exploratory study, delayed-phase dual-layer spectral CT-derived ECV showed a significant association with histologic fibrosis severity and promising preliminary discrimination for advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis in Fontan-associated liver disease. External validation in larger, independent Fontan cohorts is required before clinical application.

title: Neonatal Common Atrioventricular Valve Replacement After Failed Staged Biventricular Repair.
authorString: Tanimoto K, Kanaya T, Hayashi K, Asada D, Aoki H, Tsumura S.

journal.medlineAbbreviation: World J Pediatr Congenit Heart Surg
journal.title: World journal for pediatric & congenital heart surgery
journal.isoabbreviation: World J Pediatr Congenit Heart Surg

abstractText: Balanced complete atrioventricular septal defect (cAVSD) with aortic coarctation (CoA) is generally considered amenable to staged biventricular repair (BVR). However, anatomic suitability does not necessarily guarantee functional stability. We report a 3.5-kg neonate with balanced cAVSD (Rastelli type A), severe common atrioventricular valve regurgitation (CAVVR), and CoA. Preoperative echocardiography indicated suitability for BVR. At 9 days of age, arch repair and pulmonary artery banding (PAB) were performed. However, weaning the patient from cardiopulmonary bypass was impossible because of profound hypotension, and transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated worsening of CAVVR. PAB adjustment and removal were ineffective. Intraoperative inspection revealed a severely dysplastic valve morphology incompatible with durable repair. After myocardial recovery with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation support, the patient was converted to a univentricular pathway. The patient subsequently underwent common atrioventricular valve replacement, Damus-Kaye-Stansel anastomosis, and right ventricle-to-pulmonary artery shunt placement. Postoperative ventricular function was preserved without residual regurgitation. This case underscores the importance of flexible intraoperative decision-making guided by direct valve assessment and timely strategic conversion in high-risk neonates with cAVSD and severe CAVVR.

title: Elevated CERS6/C16:0 Ceramide in taPVAT Promotes Aortic Dissection by Driving Macrophage Inflammation via FPR2/NF-κB Signaling.
authorString: Zhuang X, Jiang Z, Li H, Yang X, Tang L, Lei J, Chen X, Tian Y, Chen K, Cheng N, Chen Y, Jiangbin W, Wang Y, Cai Z, Chen L.
abstractText:
Background

Perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) is the endocrine microenvironment closest to the aorta. Using multiomics analysis, we found that Cers6 (ceramide synthase 6) was upregulated and C16:0 ceramide accumulated in thoracic aortic PVAT (taPVAT) from aortic dissection (AD) mice; however, its role and underlying mechanism in AD remain unclear.

Methods

A mouse model of AD was established by combined β-aminopropionitrile and AngII (angiotensin II) administration, followed by proteomic and quantitative lipidomic analyses of taPVAT. Cers6 expression in taPVAT adipocytes was locally manipulated by adeno-associated virus delivery, and exogenous C16:0 ceramide was administered in vivo. Mechanistic studies were performed using adipocyte-bone marrow-derived macrophage (BMDM) coculture and C16:0 ceramide-stimulated BMDMs, combined with transcriptomics, pharmacological inhibition, molecular docking, surface plasmon resonance, cellular thermal shift assay, and small interfering RNA knockdown. WRW4 intervention was evaluated in vivo. Human taPVAT samples were used to validate CERS6/C16:0 ceramide changes and clinical correlations.

Results

Cers6 was selectively upregulated in taPVAT from AD mice, accompanied by increased C16:0 ceramide levels. Specific knockdown of Cers6 in taPVAT adipocytes reduced AD incidence and attenuated aortic ECM (extracellular matrix) degradation and inflammation, whereas Cers6 overexpression or exogenous C16:0 ceramide aggravated disease. In vitro, Cers6/C16:0 ceramide enhanced macrophage inflammatory activation, migration, and Mmp9 (matrix metalloproteinase-9) expression via Fpr2 (formyl peptide receptor 2)/NF-κB (nuclear factor-κB) signaling. WRW4 mitigated these pro-AD effects in vivo. Similarly, in human taPVAT, CERS6 and C16:0 ceramide were elevated, and C16:0 ceramide correlated positively with aortic inflammatory gene expression and maximal thoracic aortic diameter.

Conclusions

taPVAT Cers6-driven C16:0 ceramide accumulation promotes AD through macrophage Fpr2/NF-κB signaling, enhancing inflammation and ECM degradation. Targeting taPVAT Cers6 or blocking the Fpr2/NF-κB axis may offer a tissue-focused therapeutic strategy.

title: Multidisciplinary Collaboration in the Performance of Aortic Surgery: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association.
authorString: DeAnda A, Steppan J, Boskovski MT, Cherry AD, Dickey RA, Gray DeAngelis K, Ibekwe SO, Tseng EE, American Heart Association Council on Cardiovascular Surgery and Anesthesia, Education and Publication Committee; Council on Clinical Cardiology; Council on Cardiovascular Surgery and Anesthesia; Council on Peripheral Vascular Disease; Council on Lifelong Congenital Heart Disease and Heart Health in the Young; and Council on Cardiovascular Radiology and Intervention.
abstractText: Intraoperative management of a patient undergoing cardiac surgery requires continuous and independent interventions by multiple healthcare professionals, including surgeons, anesthesiologists, and perfusionists, among others. Although each clinician performs tasks based on their training and accepted techniques, guidelines, and protocols, an action by one member of the team can have immediate consequences for other team members. Aortic surgery adds a level of complexity, with the need for interventions such as single-lung ventilation, systemic cooling (and subsequent rewarming), and myocardial, cerebral, and visceral protection. Much has been made of the utility of the multidisciplinary team. This scientific statement is intended to approach the patient undergoing aortic surgery from 3 different viewpoints: that of the surgeon, the anesthesiologist, and the perfusionist. This scientific statement is not intended to provide an exhaustive summary of approaches to aortic surgery but rather to illustrate the specific concerns that each member of the team may have.

title: Psychosocial profile of adults with Congenital Heart Disease according to documented history of anxiety disorders.
authorString: Martínez-Quintana E, García-Suárez MI, Alcántara-Castellano M, González-Martín JM, Rodríguez-González F.
abstractText:
Background

Adults with congenital heart disease (CHD) may experience substantial psychological distress. This study evaluated whether a documented history of anxiety disorders is associated with a distinct psychosocial profile in adults with CHD.

Methods

In this cross-sectional study, 45 adults with CHD were included: 21 with a documented history of anxiety disorders and 24 without. Psychosocial assessment included the EuroQol-5D-3L (EQ-5D-3L), Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES), State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI), and Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II). Associations between psychosocial measures and documented anxiety history were assessed using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for sex, NYHA functional class, and CHD complexity. Moderate depression was additionally assessed using univariable logistic regression.

Results

Mean age was 35 ± 9 years in participants with a documented history of anxiety disorders and 31 ± 11 years in those without (P = 0.230); males accounted for 33% and 62%, respectively (P = 0.052). NYHA functional class II-IV was more frequent among participants with a documented history of anxiety disorders (67% vs. 25%; P = 0.018). Compared with those without a documented anxiety history, participants with anxiety history reported greater limitations in usual activities (P = 0.021), higher anxiety/depression scores on the EQ-5D-3L (P = 0.023), poorer self-rated health (P = 0.038), higher trait anxiety (31.2 ± 5.8 vs. 26.5 ± 5.2; P = 0.008), and greater depressive symptom severity (BDI-II median 19 vs. 3; P = 0.001). Self-esteem was also higher (RSES median 27 vs. 25; P = 0.006). After adjustment, BDI-II scores were positively associated with a documented history of anxiety disorders (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.05-1.28; P = 0.011), while EQ-5D VAS scores were inversely associated (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.38-0.97; P = 0.048). STAI-State, STAI-Trait, and RSES scores were not significantly associated with anxiety history. None of the variables assessed in the univariable analysis was significantly associated with moderate depression.

Conclusions

In adults with CHD, a documented history of anxiety disorders was associated with greater depressive symptom severity and poorer self-rated health after adjustment for relevant clinical factors.
