Compared to usual care, DHIs supporting care integration had significant reductions in the odds of CVD events (OR: 0.74 [0.59, 0.92], df=5, p=0.02), but not in all-cause mortality or readmissions. Although this review shows that DHIs supporting care integration were associated with reduced CVD events compared to usual care, the current evidence remains concentrated primarily on person-centred care integration, with limited studies evaluating broader dimensions of care integration at organisational and systemic levels. These findings highlight the important evidence gaps of DHIs in supporting more comprehensive and system-level integration in cardiovascular care. Further research is necessary to understand the influence of DHI modality and function on effectiveness of care integration.

title: Cohort profile: Bushehr Elderly Health (BEH) Program, Phase III
authorString: Khalagi K, Tavassol ZH, Ejtahed H, Shafiee G, Razi F, Haghpanah V, Mansourzadeh MJ, Joukar D, Sanjideh Z, Hesari E, Hajivalizadeh S, Sanjari M, Farhadi A, Heshmat R, Vahdat K, Fahimfar N, Larijani B, Ostovar A, Nabipour I.
abstractText: The Bushehr Elderly Health (BEH) Program is a population-based prospective cohort study, designed to address the increasing health challenges associated with an aging population. The third phase of the BEH program was conducted to repeat measurements from previous phases of the study, assessing the state of non-communicable diseases (NCDs)—particularly cardiovascular and musculoskeletal diseases and cognitive function—as well as their determinants and consequences among older adults. This article presents the study profile for this phase, detailing the methodology, recruitment process, and baseline participant characteristics. The resulting longitudinal data will be used in future analytical studies. Phase III of the BEH Program was conducted six years after the second phase (stage 2), involving repeated measurements among participants aged 60 and above who were residing in Bushehr city and had participated in the previous phases of the first recruitment of the study. Previous phase participants were invited to take part in this phase. This phase repeated the measurements conducted in the previous phases included comprehensive questionnaires, physical and anthropometric examinations, whole body and bone density scan, diagnostic laboratory tests, and biobanking of biological samples including serum, EDP, stool, and saliva. The successful assessment has been completed for participants invited from the earlier phases of the BEH program, yielding extensive data for future analysis. In this phase of the BEH program, a total of 1,345 participants were enrolled in the study, a response rate of 64.7%. The mean (standard deviation) age was 74.3 (4.6) years and 50.4% of the participants were males. The third phase of the BEH program successfully repeated comprehensive measurements and expanded the biobank to include microbiota samples. These repeated measures will provide valuable longitudinal insights once analyzed, enabling researchers to examine changes in health-related variables over time and better understand the needs of older Iranian adults. Future analyses will address the specific objectives related to cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, and cognitive health.

title: Vascular access management after kidney transplantation position paper on behalf of the Vascular Access Society and the European Kidney Transplant Association.
authorString: Akin B, Jemcov TK, Cucchiari D, Malik J, Pettigrew GJ, Hahn Lundström U, Zaza G, Rotmans JI.
abstractText: There is no consensus on whether to ligate or preserve uncomplicated vascular access (VA) after kidney transplantation (KT), as International Guidelines do not address this issue. Enhanced survival rates of kidney grafts may elevate the risk of cardiac morbidity and mortality due to prolonged exposure to the hemodynamic effects of arterio-venous fistulas (AVF). Although VA ligation reduces left ventricle (LV) mass, its impact on cardiovascular (CV) morbidity or mortality is unclear. High-flow VAs can complicate KT patients, and immunosuppressive medication may increase these complications. Despite preserving VA for future hemodialysis (HD) use, central catheters are used in nearly two-thirds of patients. Detecting transplant patients who can undergo AVF ligation and reconstruction when returning to HD allows for flexible decision-making with a multidisciplinary approach, personally tailored to patients at their discretion. Therefore, an algorithm involving Doppler ultrasound and cardiac evaluation is advisable.

title: Unexpected Death in a Preschool Child: Forensic Assessment of Acute Myocarditis on Left Ventricular Hypertrophy.
authorString: Incarnato S, Luta R, Fraternali Orcioni G, Barranco R, Ventura F.

journal.title: The American journal of forensic medicine and pathology

abstractText: Myocarditis is an inflammatory disease of the myocardium with a highly variable clinical spectrum, ranging from mild or subclinical forms to severe manifestations, including heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. In this article, we report a case of sudden death in a 4-year-old child in whom autopsy and histopathologic investigations identified myocarditis developing on a substrate of left ventricular hypertrophy. Given the lack of pathognomonic symptoms in myocarditis, maintaining a high index of clinical suspicion is paramount for ensuring timely admission. Early diagnosis is crucial to initiating treatment before clinical deterioration occurs. Furthermore, implementing standardized and systematic autopsy analysis is essential to maximizing the diagnostic yield in cases of unexpected death in childhood. In the absence of a unified investigative framework and multidisciplinary approach, postmortem examinations risk remaining incomplete, potentially leaving critical pathologic findings undetected.

title: Exploring the application value of preoperative femoral artery and vein cannulation in redo cardiac surgery.
authorString: Yu YH, Zhang XL, Wang L, Xiao LQ, Huang FH, Wang ZH.
abstractText:
Background

To explore the clinical value of preoperative femoral vessel cannulation in redo cardiac surgery.

Methods

A retrospective analysis was performed on the clinical data of 106 patients who underwent redo cardiac surgery in our hospital from January 2022 to December 2024. According to the cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) cannulation technique adopted, the patients were divided into the Femoral Cannulation group (n = 79) and the Traditional Central Cannulation group (n = 37). Preoperative baseline data, intraoperative CPB-related parameters, blood product consumption, and the incidence of postoperative complications were recorded and compared between the two groups.

Results

There were no statistically significant differences in preoperative baseline data or intraoperative parameters between the two groups (all P > 0.05). Similarly, no significant statistical differences were found in postoperative mortality, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) utilization rate, acute kidney injury (AKI) incidence, or cognitive dysfunction incidence between the two groups. However, compared with the Traditional Central Cannulation group, the Femoral Cannulation group had significantly lower intraoperative packed red blood cell (PRBC) transfusion volume and a significantly lower incidence of major cardiovascular injuries (all P < 0.05).

Conclusion

In redo cardiac surgery, preoperative femoral vessel cannulation can significantly reduce the incidence of major cardiovascular injuries and the demand for intraoperative blood transfusion, which is worthy of promotion and application in clinical practice.

title: Acute heart failure in emergency settings.
authorString: Miró Ò, Masip J, Chioncel O, Polyzogopoulou E, Harjola VP, Rosselló X, Peacock WF, Laribi S, Parissis J, Müller CE, Behringer W, Tavares de Oliveira M, Tavazzi G, Pöss J, Verbrugge FH, Platz E, Adamo M, Grand J, Yilmaz MB, Schaubroeck H, Price S, Sionis A, Gambaro A, Tica O, Gualandro DM, Mebazaa A, Arrigo M.
abstractText: Acute heart failure (AHF) represents a major cause of emergency medical care worldwide and continues to carry a substantial burden of morbidity and mortality despite advances in chronic heart failure management. Most patients with AHF present to emergency departments (EDs), where the first hours of care are critical to determine prognosis. Of these, some have been previously evaluated and treated by prehospital emergency medical services before ED arrival. This consensus document summarizes the current evidence and provides practical advice to emergency physicians for the diagnosis, treatment, and disposition of patients with AHF in these emergency settings (emergency medical services and ED). It emphasizes the importance of a rapid phenotypic classification into acute decompensated heart failure, acute pulmonary oedema, isolated right ventricular failure, or cardiogenic shock, as a key tool to guide early management and triage decisions. It reviews evidence on prehospital and ED management, including the use of biomarkers, imaging, ventilatory support, diuretic and vasodilator strategies, and early initiation or continuation of guideline-directed medical therapy. It also discusses risk stratification and disposition decisions supported by validated tools. Finally, it identifies major knowledge gaps and future research priorities, including pragmatic trials to assess prehospital interventions, biomarker-guided therapy, and early initiation of disease-modifying treatments. Ultimately, this consensus document is aimed to contribute to the improvement of outcomes in AHF.

title: Low-grade inflammation and cardiovascular events among patients with chronic kidney disease.
authorString: Motiejunaite J, Benamara L, Moutard E, Halimi JM, Alencar de Pinho N, Danchin N, Aboyans V, Massy ZA.
abstractText:
Aims

Chronic inflammation is associated with cardiovascular disease in the general population, but data on patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are limited. We sought to assess whether systemic low-grade inflammation is independently associated with cardiovascular events in CKD patients not yet on kidney replacement therapy, with or without a history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

Methods

CKD-REIN is a prospective cohort study of adults with CKD stages 2-5, conducted in 40 French nephrology outpatient facilities. Baseline high-sensitivity plasma C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) was centrally measured using an immunoturbidimetric method. Systemic low-grade inflammation was defined as hs-CRP ≥2 mg/L. Cox proportional hazards models estimated cause-specific hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; composite of stroke, myocardial infarction, or cardiovascular death) or hospitalization for heart failure (HHF).

Results

We included 2078 patients: 67% men, mean (SD) age 67(13) years, mean eGFR 36(12) mL/min/1.73 m2, 38% with history of ASCVD, median hs-CRP concentration 2.4 mg/L (inter-quartile range 1.1-5.1). After median follow-up of 5 years, 171 patients had a MACE and 207 had HHF. After controlling for potential confounders, a twofold increase in hs-CRP was associated with a 12% (95% CI 0-26) higher cause-specific hazard of MACE and a 26% (95% CI 13-40) higher cause-specific hazard of HHF.

Conclusion

In CKD patients not yet on kidney replacement therapy, systemic low-grade inflammation, measured through hs-CRP, is associated with occurrence of cardiovascular events independently of traditional risk factors, including a history of ASCVD.

title: Characteristics, Interventions, and Deprivation Patterns in Suspected Opioid-Associated Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrests Attended by North East Ambulance Service NHS Foundation Trust: A 36-Month Service Evaluation
authorString: Kirk B, McClelland G, Scott J.
abstractText:
Background:

Drug-poisoning deaths in England and Wales have more than doubled since 2012, with the North East of England persistently reporting the highest mortality rates. Opioid-associated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OA-OHCA) presents distinct clinical and operational challenges for ambulance services, particularly amid the emergence of potent synthetic opioids and uncertainty over the role of naloxone during cardiac arrest. This service evaluation sought to characterise the incidence, clinical features, and deprivation patterns of suspected OA-OHCA attended by North East Ambulance Service NHS Foundation Trust (NEAS), and to describe their geographic distribution.

Methods:

A retrospective service evaluation was conducted using structured and reported fields from the NEAS electronic patient care record (ePCR) system between 1 January 2022 and 31 December 2024. Inclusion required a documented cardiac resuscitation together with either a reported aetiology of drug overdose, or documented naloxone administration. Data were analysed descriptively.

Results:

351 cases met the inclusion criteria. The mean age was 42.9 years; 69.2% were male. Cases represented a rising proportion of OHCA where resuscitation was attempted by NEAS across the period (4.7% in 2022 to 5.9% in 2024). Naloxone was administered in 87.2% of incidents, adrenaline in 86.9%, and amiodarone in 9.4%. Advanced airway management was recorded in 88.3% and intraosseous access in 75.5%; defibrillation was performed in 16.5%. Cases were concentrated in the most deprived communities, with Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) deciles 1-3 comprising 71.8% of the cohort.

Conclusion:

Suspected drug-related cardiac arrests in the NEAS region predominantly affected working-age adults in deprived communities, and were managed with consistent airway, ventilation, vascular access, and naloxone administration alongside infrequent defibrillation, consistent with a predominantly asphyxial arrest model. This evaluation provides a descriptive baseline that could inform service planning and provides the empirical foundation for a subsequent qualitative study of paramedic clinical decision-making in OA-OHCA.

title: Prediction of in-hospital mortality in acute myocardial infarction patients with left anterior descending artery occlusion
authorString: Zou C, Fang L, Wang D, Tang Q, Zuo H.
abstractText: Objective To identify potential risk factors for in-hospital mortality in acute myocardial infarction (AMI) patients with left anterior descending artery (LAD) occlusion and construct a nomogram for predicting their prognosis. Methods The study dataset was randomly partitioned into a 70% training set and a 30% validation set. LASSO regression and random forest algorithms were used to screen potential risk factors among 32 candidate variables in the training set. Independent risk factors selected by multivariate logistic regression were used to construct a nomogram. The discriminatory performance, calibration performance and clinical utility of the nomogram were assessed using the receiver operating characteristic curve, calibration curve, and decision curve analysis. Results A total of 454 AMI patients with LAD occlusion were enrolled in this study. Age, systolic blood pressure, heart rate, white blood cells, lactate dehydrogenase, fibrinogen, and albumin-to-globulin ratio were independent risk factors of in-hospital mortality in AMI patients with LAD occlusion. The nomogram showed good discriminatory performance with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.953 (95%CI: 0.918-0.989) in the validation set. The calibration curve demonstrated that the nomogram exhibited satisfactory calibration performance for predicting in-hospital mortality in AMI patients with LAD occlusion. The decision curve analysis indicated favorable clinical utility of the predictive model. Conclusion This nomogram can accurately predict in-hospital mortality in AMI patients with LAD occlusion.

title: Development and external evaluation of a routine laboratory-based three-ratio score for in- hospital mortality in older critically ill patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease: a MIMIC-IV and eICU study
authorString: Cui S, Yao X, Zhou X, Tao Y, Zhou L, Xue Y, Chen W.
abstractText: Background Older patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) often develop concurrent changes in renal handling, acid-base balance, and glucose metabolism after admission to the intensive care unit (ICU). A single laboratory measurement may not capture the combined extent of these early abnormalities. Methods We conducted a multidatabase retrospective cohort study using MIMIC-IV 3.1 and eICU 2.0. We included patients aged 65 years or older who had ASCVD, remained in the ICU for at least 24 h, and had the four laboratory measurements required to calculate the three-ratio score (TRS-3). TRS-3 was defined as the equally weighted mean of the blood urea nitrogen-to-creatinine, blood urea nitrogen-to-bicarbonate, and glucose-to-bicarbonate ratios after normalization to clinical reference values. The primary outcome was in-hospital all-cause mortality after the first 24 h of ICU admission. Associations were assessed using multivariable logistic regression, competing risk models, and restricted cubic splines. TabM models underwent patient-level cross-fitting in MIMIC-IV, after which the preprocessing parameters, model parameters, and classification threshold were applied unchanged to eICU. Results The MIMIC-IV cohort included 8037 patients, of whom 714 died in hospital. The eICU cohort included 9686 patients, of whom 1002 died in hospital. After full adjustment, the odds ratios (ORs) for in-hospital mortality per 1-standard-deviation increase in TRS-3 were 1.39 (95% CI: 1.28–1.51) in MIMIC-IV and 1.31 (95% CI: 1.22–1.41) in eICU. Compared with the lowest quartile, the highest quartile had ORs of 3.81 (95% CI: 2.80–5.20) and 2.70 (95% CI: 2.10–3.48), respectively. Both cohorts showed continuous nonlinear risk gradients. Adding TRS-3 to the core clinical TabM model increased the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from 0.788 to 0.829 in MIMIC-IV and from 0.717 to 0.760 in eICU, with paired DeLong P < 0.001 in both cohorts. Net reclassification improvement and integrated discrimination improvement were positive in both cohorts. Conclusions A higher early TRS-3 was associated with a greater probability of in-hospital death among older critically ill patients with ASCVD and provided incremental discrimination beyond the core clinical TabM model. This fixed score can be calculated from 4 routine laboratory measurements, although its probability calibration and classification threshold require evaluation in prospective cohorts.

title: Impact of atrial fibrillation on hemodynamics in a sheep model of the Fontan circulation
authorString: McKittrick MM, Otaki Y, Muralidaran A, Jonker SS, Louey S, Giustini A, Alaniz SM, Balaji S.
abstractText: Arrhythmias are a common cause of morbidity and mortality in patients who undergo the Fontan operation. The impact of atrial fibrillation (AF) on hemodynamics in the Fontan population is unclear. The aim of this study was to describe hemodynamic changes following onset of AF in a sheep model of the Fontan operation. We hypothesized that AF will negatively impact hemodynamics and Fontan pressure. Adult female non-pregnant sheep were anesthetized, intubated, had central arterial and venous lines placed, and underwent an off-bypass extracardiac Fontan operation with epicardial atrial and ventricular pacing wire placement. Data were collected in normal sinus rhythm pre- and post-operatively, and in any spontaneous dysrhythmia throughout the procedure. AF was induced using rapid atrial pacing at atrial rates of 400–600 bpm. Cardiac output was calculated using the Fick equation, with an estimated O 2 consumption of 5 mL/kg/min. Four out of 8 sheep studied developed AF: 2 spontaneously after surgery and 2 with rapid pacing. Compared with sinus rhythm, AF resulted in a significant elevation of the central venous pressure by 2mmHg (p < 0.05) without a change in mean arterial pressure, an increase in arteriovenous O 2 saturation difference by 30% (p = 0.001) and a fall in cardiac output also of 30% (p < 0.05). Atrial contraction contributes about 30% to the cardiac output in sheep who have undergone the Fontan. These findings have significant implications for patients those with Fontan physiology who go on to develop AF.

title: Heat-related mortality by comorbidity and cause of death: a time-stratified case-crossover study of 3.7 million deaths in Brazil, 2014–2025
authorString: Vieira FL.
abstractText: The literature on heat vulnerability has emphasised cardiometabolic conditions — obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease. We evaluated these candidates and alternatives within a single design, over 3,672,003 deaths from the Mortality Information System (12 Brazilian states, January to May, 2014–2025), using a time-stratified case-crossover analysis, defining case days as those in the top decile of daily maximum temperature within each month, based on measurements from the 318 automatic weather stations located in those states, with lags of 0 to 3 days. Comorbidity was obtained from all lines of the death certificate. Two findings stood out, each within its own analytical category and in a different quantity, not on a common scale: effect modification among the comorbidities, and cause-specific relative risk among the external causes. Dementia showed the strongest evidence of greater heat susceptibility among the ten conditions tested: an effect-modification ratio of 1.044 (95%CI 1.029–1.058; p = 1.1 × 10⁻⁹), and 1.035 (1.020–1.050) in an analysis stratified by ten-year age bands among individuals aged 65 years or older; Alzheimer's disease as the underlying cause had a relative risk of 1.093 (1.073–1.114), the highest among the specific natural causes examined. Drowning was the largest external-cause effect: 1.161 (1.117–1.208; p = 8.8 × 10⁻¹⁴), with a gradient across all deciles analysed, from 0.798 in the coldest decile of the month to 1.256 in the hottest, and a log-linear trend of 1.046 per decile (p = 1.4 × 10⁻⁴⁵), peaking on the hot day itself. Adjustment for precipitation did not change the estimate (1.154; 1.104–1.206). Most conventional cardiometabolic conditions showed little or no evidence of greater susceptibility: in the primary analysis, obesity (1.000; 0.976–1.024) and diabetes (1.003; 0.995–1.011) had estimates close to the null, in a study with 80% power, at α = 0.05, to detect modifications of 3.4% and 1.1% or greater. Because deaths without a given condition differ in cause composition from deaths with it, each condition was also compared with deaths carrying another of the studied conditions: the dementia estimate strengthened to 1.050 (1.036–1.065), and cerebrovascular disease reached 1.018 (1.009–1.027), a smaller but statistically robust positive modification. The ICD-10 code for exposure to excessive natural heat (X30) was recorded as the underlying cause in only ten deaths, and anywhere on the death certificate in twelve, among 3.7 million. The patterns observed suggest that behavioural mechanisms may contribute to heat vulnerability alongside the physiological mechanisms traditionally considered.

title: Ventricular repolarization in hospitalized patients with inflammatory bowel disease: a weighted real-world ECG study
authorString: Tan Y, Liao L, Huo J, Gong J.
abstractText: Whether inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is accompanied by a longer QT interval is unsettled: prior clinical studies were small, predominantly involved outpatient or selected populations, and varied in comparators, ECG metrics and findings. We studied hospitalized patients using MIMIC-IV linked to MIMIC-IV-ECG (2008–2019). Adults whose first electrocardiogram of an admission was analysable were included once; patients with an IBD diagnosis code (n = 1,618) were compared with inpatients never coded with IBD (n = 86,913). Overlap propensity-score weights balanced demographics, heart rate, calendar period, clinical setting and timing of the recording, prior cardiac and kidney disease, and ECG device bandwidth class (all standardized differences < 0.02). Mean Fridericia-corrected QT (QTcF) was 415.5 ms with IBD and 416.7 ms without; the adjusted difference, the single confirmatory outcome, was − 1.22 ms (95% CI − 2.74 to 0.29; P = 0.11), and the confidence interval excluded an adjusted mean difference of 5 ms or greater. Fifteen pre-specified supporting analyses gave estimates between − 2.3 and + 0.2 ms. One device bandwidth class was associated with QTcF about 7–9 ms longer. In hospitalized patients selected for electrocardiography, IBD was not associated with a longer mean QTcF after balancing clinical context and accounting for device configuration.

title: Characteristics of hemodynamics and fluid management in severe amlodipine poisoning with shock: a retrospective case series
authorString: Wang C, Cao P, Tan D, Sun J.
abstractText: Background: Shock is a risk factor for mortality in amlodipine poisoning, yet comprehensive hemodynamic characterization including direct invasive assessment remains rare. We characterized the hemodynamic profile and fluid-management patterns in patients with shock due to severe amlodipine poisoning. Methods: This single-center retrospective case series enrolled consecutively admitted adults with amlodipine poisoning from 2019 to 2025. Demographic, ingestion, clinical, hemodynamic, treatment, and outcome data were collected. The primary outcome was hemodynamic profile in shock patients with amlodipine poisoning. Results: Twelve patients (median age 54 years, IQR 47–67; 75% female) ingested 140–1120 mg amlodipine. Five with mild-to-moderate shock required norepinephrine alone (0.1–0.8 µg/kg/min); seven with severe shock required multiple vasopressors (norepinephrine 0.55–2.0 µg/kg/min, terlipressin, and epinephrine in three). Initial CVP was elevated (15–28 mmHg) in 9/11 patients. The predominant findings on complete echocardiography in 11 patients were hyperdynamic left ventricular function, inferior vena cava dilation, and right-heart enlargement. Invasive monitoring in ten patients showed increased or normal cardiac index (3.43–5.66 L/min/m²) and decreased SVRI (621–1647 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵·m²). Initial CVP correlated positively with length of stay (LOS; r = 0.636, 95% CI 0.06–0.89, P = 0.035). Early negative single-day fluid balance within 3 days was associated with shorter vasopressor duration (4 vs 10 days; r = 0.641, 95% CI 0.02–0.91, P = 0.046). Conclusions: Amlodipine poisoning induces severe vasoplegia with hyperdynamic (preserved) left ventricular function, frequently accompanied by elevated CVP and right-heart enlargement. Higher initial CVP predicts longer LOS, whereas early negative fluid balance may accelerate vasopressor weaning.

title: Safety and efficacy of Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonist and Sodium Glucose Transporter 2 inhibitor on major limb adverse events and mortality in peripheral artery disease and diabetes
authorString: Khadija HA, Hellou E, Alnees M, Fisman EZ, Ibraheem K, Najajra D, Raanani E, Hamdeh NA, Masu'd M, Alkrinawi J, Qadan A, Khadija YA, Fraitekh YZ, Darwish A, Hroub O, Kogan A, Sternik L.
abstractText: Background Current guidelines recommend both Glucagon-Like-Peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP1-RAs) and Sodium-glucose-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) for patients with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Patients with peripheral artery disease (PAD) and diabetes are at particularly high risk of major adverse limb events (MALE), amputation, and mortality. While both drug classes have demonstrated cardiovascular benefits, real-world evidence regarding the safety and effectiveness of their combined use in PAD, particularly with respect to limb outcomes and mortality, remains limited. Methods We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study using the Clalit Health Services electronic medical record database. Patients with PAD and diabetes from 2015 to 2026 were classified into four groups: neither GLP1-RA nor SGLT2i, GLP1-RA alone, SGLT2i alone, and both GLP1-RA/SGLT2i therapy. Outcomes included MALE, limb revascularization, major and minor amputation, and all-cause mortality. Multinomial propensity scores and stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting were used to balance baseline covariates, and weighted Cox models were used to estimate hazard ratios. Results The cohort included 13,471 patients. Median follow-up was 5.75 years for MALE and 4.42 years for mortality. Compared with neither treatment, combined therapy was associated with lower hazards of MALE (HR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.33–0.75), major amputation (HR, 0.30; 95% CI, 0.17–0.53), and all-cause mortality (HR, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.19–0.28). SGLT2i monotherapy was also associated with reduced MALE, major amputation, and mortality, while GLP1RA monotherapy was associated with lower mortality; limb-specific estimates were limited by smaller subgroup size and event numbers. Conclusions Among patients with PAD and diabetes, treatment with GLP1-RA and SGLT2i was associated with lower MALE and mortality. SGLT2i showed the same trends. GLP1RA monotherapy showed a survival benefit, while its limb-specific associations should be interpreted with caution, given the limited subgroup size and event numbers.

title: Association Between Postoperative Albumin-Corrected Anion Gap (ACAG) and 28-Day Mortality Risk in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) After Cardiac Surgery: A Retrospective Study Based on Two Large Databases, Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) and eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD)
authorString: Li M, zheng y, Guo D, Wu Z, Peng K, Yan S, Zhou X, Huang Z, Zhan X, Wu S, He J, Pang L, Sun X, Yao F.
abstractText: Background The 28-day mortality rate after cardiac surgery can reach 2%–22%, and existing scoring systems have limited efficacy in early risk identification. Albumin-Corrected Anion Gap (ACAG) can reflect signals of metabolic disorders; however, its predictive value in the acute postoperative period and its cross-center generalizability remain unclear. Methods This multicenter retrospective large cohort study used MIMIC-IV v3.1 as the study cohort and eICU as an independent external validation cohort. Kaplan-Meier survival curves, Cox nested models, restricted cubic spline (RCS), and C-index were used to evaluate the association between postoperative ACAG and 28-day mortality risk in the ICU and model discrimination. Results The MIMIC cohort included 2,206 patients (276 deaths, 12.5%) and the eICU cohort included 2,409 patients (831 deaths, 34.5%). After adjustment for confounders, ACAG was an independent risk factor for death in both cohorts (MIMIC: hazard ratio [HR] = 1.132, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.099–1.167; eICU: HR = 1.037, 95% CI: 1.024–1.052; both P < 0.001). Only the highest quartile group showed a significantly increased risk of death (eICU Q4 vs Q1: HR = 1.54, 95% CI: 1.24–1.93). RCS showed that ACAG was linearly positively associated with mortality risk (nonlinear P = 0.401). The C-index in MIMIC and eICU was 0.822 and 0.700, respectively. Conclusion Higher postoperative ACAG was significantly positively associated with 28-day all-cause mortality in the ICU after cardiac surgery. The risk of death was highest in the highest quartile group (ACAG > 20 mmol/L), and this threshold can serve as a clinical high-risk warning threshold.

title: Left Atrial Ridge Edema After VARIPULSE pulsed field ablation: Correlation With Early Peri-device leak
authorString: Li k, wang R, Jin JQ, Wang M, Duan Q, Zhang Y, Liu z.
abstractText: Background: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) combined with left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is an emerging one-step strategy for atrial fibrillation. Current clinical studies mainly focus on procedural safety and recurrent arrhythmia, while subtle anatomical changes after PFA, especially alterations of the left atrial ridge, are rarely recognized. This cohort represents a preliminary real-world experience of one-stage PFA+LAAO using the VARIPULSE system in Chinese patients, where related anatomical morphological data remain scarce in domestic literature. Methods: In this single-center retrospective cohort study, 40 consecutive patients underwent combined PFA and LAAO. LAA ridge thickness and LAA orifice diameter were measured via transesophageal echocardiography before and after ablation.The primary follow-up endpoint at 90 days was the presence of residual shunt of the LAA occluder. Periprocedural adverse events were analyzed descriptively as secondary outcomes. Results: Implant success was achieved in all 40 patients (100%), with no deaths, strokes, major bleeding events, or intervention-requiring pericardial effusions observed. No complications such as hemolysis, air-bubble stroke, phrenic nerve palsy, or coronary artery spasm occurred intraoperatively. All patients underwent pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) with VARIPULSE, followed by LAAO with Watchman FLX (21/40) or LACbes (19/40) guided by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). Post-PFA, LAA ridge thickness increased significantly by 1.21±0.50 mm ( P <0.001) ,30.45±12.69%. At 90-day follow-up, complete sealing (0 mm peri-device leak) was achieved in 100% of patients, with no device-related thrombus (DRT) or embolization observed. Conclusion: Combined PFA and LAAO was feasible with high implant success, low periprocedural complication rates, and favorable outcomes through 90 days. This integrated approach offers a promising “one-stop” strategy for patients with AF requiring rhythm control and stroke prevention. we observed a mean 30.45% increase in LAA ridge thickness immediately following PFA. This study provides preliminary anatomical evidence for postoperative structural changes after VARIPULSE PFA.

title: A three-axis burden score and in-hospital mortality in ICU patients with heart failure and atrial fibrillation: limited incremental discrimination and transportability in a retrospective cohort study
authorString: Wang¹ J, Yu R.
abstractText: Background ICU patients with heart failure (HF) and atrial fibrillation (AF) have substantial in-hospital mortality. We defined a 0–3 burden score from a low prognostic nutritional index (PNI), a high neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and a low dynamic lactate clearance rate (dLCR), and asked whether the count is associated with in-hospital mortality after adjustment and whether it improves discrimination in a second database. Methods Cut-points were the medians of observed values in MIMIC-IV and were applied unchanged in both cohorts. Derivation used MIMIC-IV v3.1 (n = 7,562; 1,222 deaths, 16.2%) and external assessment used eICU-CRD 2.0 (n = 2,588; 414 deaths, 16.0%). Missing values were handled by multiple imputation (m = 10). Associations were odds ratios from logistic models. Incremental discrimination was the change in area under the curve relative to a 43-variable reference model. Results In the imputed cohorts, in-hospital mortality rose from 10.8% to 24.9% in MIMIC-IV and from 10.2% to 24.0% in eICU-CRD across scores 0 to 3. Among patients in whom all three axes were measured, mortality was higher at every score, and the eICU-CRD gradient was not monotonic. In MIMIC-IV each additional point had an adjusted odds ratio of 1.20 (95% CI 1.08–1.33). The corresponding estimate in eICU-CRD was 1.14 (0.97–1.35). Out-of-fold, the score raised the AUC of a reference model that already contained albumin, the white-cell count and lactate by 0.0028 (0.0011–0.0045), less than the gain from the axes as continuous terms. That increment was not detectable when the models were refitted in eICU-CRD. The reference model kept its rank order after transport (AUC 0.711) but was miscalibrated; two-parameter recalibration, evaluated out of fold, lowered the Brier score from 0.140 to 0.124. Conclusions The count is a descriptive stratification tied to the derivation cut-points. The adjusted association is supported in MIMIC-IV and not in eICU-CRD. It is not a validated or transportable prediction tool, and the absolute risks from the reference model are not available from the three measurements alone.

title: Socioeconomic, Lifestyle, and Dietary Factors Associated with Concurrent Hypertension and Diabetes among Adults in Selected Communities in Southwestern Nigeria: A Cross- Sectional Study
authorString: Adeyemi-Benson, Adeyemi-Benson OA, Olaniyi P, Oladele AO, Jolayemi FT.
abstractText: Background Hypertension and diabetes frequently coexist, increasing cardiometabolic morbidity and mortality. Evidence on the coexistence of these conditions and their socioeconomic, lifestyle, and dietary correlates in Southwestern Nigeria remains limited. This study aimed to assess the burden of concurrent hypertension and diabetes and determine the socioeconomic, lifestyle, and dietary factors associated with their coexistence among adults in selected communities in Southwestern Nigeria. Methods A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted among adults in selected urban and peri-urban communities in Southwestern Nigeria between July and December 2025. Using a two-stage probability-sampling approach, 500 adults were screened for hypertension and diabetes. All 244 participants who screened positive for at least one condition underwent detailed sociodemographic, lifestyle, anthropometric, and dietary assessment. Dietary patterns were derived using principal component analysis. Associations with concurrent hypertension-diabetes screening positivity were evaluated using Firth bias-reduced logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index, with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction across 11 exposure tests. Results Among the 244 screen-positive participants, 14.8% had both conditions. Three dietary patterns, plant-rich traditional, beverage-animal foods, and grain-condiment/snack, explained 39.0% of dietary variation. Higher monthly income showed the strongest adjusted association with concurrent screening positivity (aOR per income-category increase 1.45, 95% CI 1.05–1.98; p = 0.023), but this association did not remain statistically significant after false-discovery-rate correction (q = 0.251). No measured lifestyle or dietary-pattern exposure remained significant after correction. Sensitivity analyses using more specific outcome definitions showed a similar positive income gradient. Conclusion Concurrent hypertension and diabetes represents a meaningful cardiometabolic burden among adults in these Southwestern Nigerian communities. Although higher income showed a consistent positive association across analyses, the finding remains exploratory because it did not withstand multiple-testing correction. Integrated screening and larger prospective studies using confirmatory measurements are warranted.

title: Identification of TREK channels in mouse intracardiac ganglion neurons.
authorString: Campos-Rios A, Herrera-Perez S, Rodriguez-Castañeda M, Ameal-Tedin D, Alvarez-Rodriguez M, Blanco-Remesar D, Rodriguez-Tebar A, De Miguel E, Covelo A, Lamas JA.
abstractText: The intracardiac nervous system is a complex neural network formed by a diffuse plexus, the so-called intracardiac ganglion (ICG). These ganglia locally innervate and control heart function, but little is known about how ICG neuronal activity is regulated. Although various ionic currents have been characterized in cardiac tissue, the expression and role of TWIK-related K+ (TREK) channels in ICG neurons remain unexplored. TREK channels, members of the two-pore domain potassium channel family, are essential regulators of neuronal membrane resting potential and excitability, with recognized neuroprotective functions. In this study, we have characterized different ionic currents present in mouse ICG neurons, including tetrodotoxin-sensitive Na+ currents, delayed K+ rectifiers, Ca+2-dependent K+ currents and A, H and M currents. Notably, we provide the first evidence of functional TREK channel expression in these neurons. Our findings suggest that TREK channels contribute to excitability control and cellular homoeostasis in ICG neurons, highlighting their potential relevance to cardiac physiology and disease. KEY POINTS: This study provides the first evidence of functional TWIK-related K+ (TREK) channel expression in intracardiac ganglion (ICG) neurons. Comprehensive profiling of ionic currents shaping excitability in ICG neurons. Neuroprotective TREK channels might emerge as potential therapeutic targets for cardiac disorders.

title: Human cell models for inherited platelet disorders: strengths, limitations and emerging technologies.
authorString: Ramaekers K, Freson K.
abstractText: Inherited platelet disorders (IPD) comprise a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of conditions affecting platelet number, function, or both. Although next-generation sequencing has accelerated gene discovery, it has also produced a growing number of variants of uncertain significance, creating a pressing need for experimental systems that can establish causal genotype-phenotype relationships. Because megakaryocytes are scarce in the bone marrow and murine models incompletely recapitulate human platelet biology, human cell-based models are indispensable for studying megakaryopoiesis and platelet formation. Here we review the evolution of such models and their application to IPD research. Leukemia-derived megakaryocytic cell lines provided the first genetically tractable models but incompletely reproduce physiological thrombopoiesis. Megakaryocytes derived from primary hematopoietic stem cells remain the gold standard for patient-specific disease modeling, offering high biological relevance but requiring donor material and being subject to significant inter-donor variability. Induced pluripotent stem cells provide a renewable source of megakaryocytes for disease modeling, although efficient platelet production and functional characterization remain challenging. In contrast, the immortalized megakaryocyte cell line offers a scalable and genetically tractable platform that faithfully recapitulates megakaryocyte maturation, supports platelet production, and enables selected platelet function assays. We further discuss emerging three-dimensional and organoid systems that begin to capture the complexity of the bone-marrow niche. Across these platforms we discuss applications in disease mechanism discovery, functional validation of novel variants, and preclinical evaluation of therapies. No single model is universally optimal; rather, model choice should be guided by the biological question, with validation against primary patient material remaining essential.

title: An interval-based approach to measuring eating jet lag in female healthcare shift workers.
authorString: Rico N, Díaz I, G Rúa A, Alonso A, Díaz E.
abstractText: Circadian rhythms regulate physiological and metabolic functions, and their disruption, particularly from shift work, is associated with adverse health outcomes such as obesity or cardiovascular disease. Meal timing variability, or eating jet lag, has emerged as a valuable marker of circadian misalignment. This study introduces a novel method to assess eating jet lag through direct comparison of food intake intervals, addressing limitations of traditional midpoint-based approaches reducing intervals to single values, potentially overlooking meaningful overlap. We conducted a cross-sectional study on 290 female healthcare professionals in Asturias, Spain, from a larger cohort of 679 participants with complete temporal data for meals across morning, afternoon, and night shifts. The proposed method calculates the degree of embedding between intake intervals during work shifts and rest days, and a global index is derived by aggregating alignment values across shifts. Results show that the interval-based method captures temporal overlap not represented by the midpoint-based approach, especially where the midpoint method underestimates alignment. Bland-Altman analysis showed systematic and proportional disagreement between the two approaches, with discrepancies greater at lower levels of alignment. This approach provides complementary information for evaluating eating-window alignment and provides a basis for future studies between eating-window alignment and health-related outcomes.

title: Over-the-counter topical diclofenac in musculoskeletal pain: clinical value, access and responsible use.
authorString: Morlion B, Seefried L, Verhagen E.
abstractText: Topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including diclofenac, are established options for localized musculoskeletal pain, with guidelines supporting their use in knee osteoarthritis, broader osteoarthritis management and acute non-low-back musculoskeletal injuries. For selected indications, topical diclofenac can be highly effective and is generally well tolerated when used as indicated. It provides local analgesic and anti-inflammatory activity with substantially lower systemic exposure than oral NSAIDs, which may be particularly relevant for older adults and people with gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, renal or polypharmacy-related risk factors. As an NSAID, topical diclofenac should nevertheless be used in accordance with product labeling.These clinical benefits sit alongside environmental considerations. Diclofenac may enter wastewater via excretion, and for topical products, through handwashing, wash-off from treated skin, and improper disposal. National exposure estimates suggest that topical formulations can make an important contribution to diclofenac entering wastewater and surface waters, although estimates are setting-specific and depend on assumptions about use, wash-off and wastewater removal.This commentary considers the clinical value of over-the-counter (OTC) topical diclofenac alongside environmental evidence and uncertainties relevant to responsible use. Integrated evidence comparing analgesic options across clinical outcomes, patient safety, environmental burden and substitution effects remains limited, and the net consequences of treatment substitution cannot currently be reliably assessed. Some practical measures can reduce diclofenac release through specific point-of-use pathways, although their uptake and population level impact require further evaluation.Topical diclofenac therefore provides a useful case study for responsible, pharmacist-guided OTC self-care in musculoskeletal pain management. In the authors' opinion, the available evidence and remaining uncertainties call for proportionate stewardship: maintaining clinically appropriate OTC access to topical diclofenac while avoiding unnecessary use and supporting label-consistent treatment, patient education, and feasible measures to reduce avoidable environmental release, alongside formulation and delivery innovation.

title: Causal inference in oral health research: Beyond statistical significance toward a causal framework.
authorString: Wolf JM, Mitra N, Glick M.
abstractText: Oral health research has adopted sophisticated statistical methods, yet studies routinely present adjusted associations as causal effects. The problem is not statistical competence but the absence of explicit causal reasoning. This commentary proposes a principled framework for causal reasoning in oral health research. We conducted a narrative synthesis of foundational and recent literature on causal inference, drawing on texts describing the potential outcomes and counterfactual frameworks, the ICH E9(R1) regulatory addendum on estimands, study design, directed acyclic graphs, and recent applications of causal methods in oral health research; recurring principles were organized into a sequential four-pillar framework, illustrated throughout with a worked example examining periodontal treatment and cardiovascular disease. First, the question is framed through abductive reasoning and translated into a precisely defined estimand. Second, study design is aligned with that estimand by specifying the population, exposure contrast, and time origin so that the data reflect the intended causal comparison. Third, counterfactual reasoning and directed acyclic graphs clarify the conditions under which causal conclusions are warranted, guiding principled adjustment. Fourth, estimation and inference are used to evaluate evidence for the estimand, and results are interpreted with explicit attention to the assumptions required for causal claims CONCLUSION: We propose a cultural shift in oral health research where causal effects are precisely defined, identification assumptions are explicitly defended, and structural uncertainties are acknowledged. This framework reveals that statistical sophistication cannot substitute for careful causal reasoning. Advanced methods such as multivariable regression, propensity scores, and machine learning can allow robust estimation of causal effects but do not replace the need for a prior causal reasoning and identification assumptions. The question is not whether analyses are statistically correct, but whether causal effects are well-defined and assumptions are explicit. Applying this framework would make causal assumptions transparent, acknowledge uncertainty inherent in observational research, and clarify when experimental designs become necessary. This commentary argues that oral health research has a fundamental problem: studies use sophisticated statistics but still present associations as if they were causal findings. Better math alone doesn't fix flawed reasoning. The authors propose a four-pillar framework to address this. First, researchers should use abductive reasoning to frame a precise causal question that specifies the exposure, population, outcome, and comparison of interest. Second, study design should be aligned to that question. Third, causal assumptions must be made explicit using counterfactual thinking and directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), which clarify confounders, mediators, and colliders. Finally, statistical estimation and inference should come last, quantifying uncertainty about a pre-specified causal quantity, not generating causal meaning on their own. The bottom line: no statistical method, however advanced, can substitute for explicit causal reasoning. The real question in oral health research is not whether the analysis is statistically correct, but whether the causal effect is clearly defined and the underlying assumptions are honestly defended.

title: Factors Associated with the Evolution in Quality of Life and Volume During the Maintenance Phase After a Multidisciplinary Intensive Treatment Program in Patients with Lower Limb Lymphedema.
authorString: Heroes AK, De Vrieze T, Fourneau I, Thomis S, Spincemaille L, Bechter-Hugl B, Swinnen C, Geeroms K, Vervloesem K, Cools J, Devoogdt N.
abstractText: To evaluate which factors are associated with change in lymphedema-specific quality of life (QoL) and relative volume difference in the maintenance phase after a multidisciplinary intensive treatment program in patients with lower limb lymphedema(LLL). In this retrospective study, patients received a multidisciplinary intensive treatment followed by a maintenance phase. In this maintenance phase, patients were advised to perform skin care and exercises and to wear compression garments. Circumferential measurements and the Lymph-ICF-LL questionnaires to determine volume and the lymphedema-specific QoL, respectively, were collected at the start and end of the intensive treatment and at 6 months follow-up. Patient-, lymphedema-, and treatment-related variables were collected to investigate their association with change in lymphedema-specific QoL and relative volume in the maintenance phase. Mann-Whitney U and Spearman rank correlation tests were applied. Patients (n = 279) who did not receive physiotherapy between 5 and 6 months follow-up and had a lower %score on the 6-minute walk test at the start of the intensive treatment showed significant better improvement in physical function and general tasks/household in the maintenance phase, respectively. Younger age, concomitant lipedema, and a lower % volume reduction during intensive treatment were significantly associated with less relative volume increase in the maintenance phase. Patients without physiotherapy around 5-6 months follow-up or with limited physical capacity at the start may perceive better improvements in certain lymphedema-specific QoL domains, while younger age, concomitant lipedema, and less initial volume reduction appear to be less predisposed to volume regain during the maintenance phase.

title: Pah in the era of obesity: navigating phenotypes of pulmonary hypertension.
authorString: Tager D, Bernardo RJ, Tonelli AR.
abstractText:
Introduction

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive vasculopathy whose phenotype has shifted over the decades from young women to older patients with cardiometabolic comorbidities. Obesity is among the most prevalent and clinically consequential of these comorbidities, affecting 24-40% of patients in contemporary PAH registries.

Areas covered

We review the epidemiology of obesity and its impact on PAH; the definition of obesity and the limitations of body mass index; the effects of obesity on adipose, cardiovascular and respiratory systems; its association with health disparities; the clinical approach to the patient with obesity and suspected pulmonary hypertension (PH), including right heart catheterization with provocative maneuvers and esophageal manometry; comorbid conditions and the obesity paradox; and management, including weight loss, PAH-specific therapy, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and sleep-disordered breathing. A literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE was performed for articles published from database inception to September 2026.

Expert opinion

Obesity has implications in the origin, symptoms, diagnosis and management of PH. Accurate characterization of PH in obese patients depends first on measuring and reporting pressures that reflect true transmural hemodynamics. Incretin-based therapy and activin signaling inhibition are promising therapeutic directions, but dedicated trials in patients with obesity and pulmonary hypertension are needed.

title: scTraitReg: a single-cell multi-omic database of trait-relevant transcription factor eRegulons.
authorString: Chen H, Liu Y, Rui X, Li S, Sun L, Xiao G, Tang H, Sun Y, Guan X, Cao C.
abstractText: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify loci associated with human diseases and disease-related traits, but the regulators and cellular contexts linked to these signals remain difficult to resolve. We present scTraitReg, a database of trait-relevant transcription factor (TF) eRegulons-TFs with their target genes and linked cis-regulatory regions-at single-cell resolution. scTraitReg integrates 655 sets of curated GWAS summary statistics covering 122 Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) disease terms with 111 human single-cell multi-omic datasets profiling RNA and chromatin accessibility in the same cells. The resource spans 34 tissues, 252 cell types, 2 081 538 cells, and 2208 curated GWAS-single-cell analysis pairs. Across these analyses, it contains 2 840 939 TF-cell-type records for 886 regulators; 67 666 records met all three criteria-cell-type specificity, genetic relevance, and the trait-associated regulon score-and were included as candidate trait-relevant eRegulon records. Each record links to the TF-target regulatory network with its cis-regulatory regions, cell-type-resolved evidence, per-cell regulon module scores, and target-gene enrichment, all available as downloadable tables. Users can search by disease, tissue, cell type, or regulator and examine these associations through interactive visualizations. scTraitReg thus provides a searchable and reusable resource linking genetic associations to cell-type-specific regulatory programs, and is freely available at https://www.sctraitreg.bio/.

title: An early risk prediction nomogram for coronary artery lesions in Kawasaki disease: a retrospective cohort study.
authorString: Cong X, Shen L, Shen F.
abstractText: Coronary artery lesions remain a major concern in Kawasaki disease. This study aimed to develop and internally validate a practical nomogram for early identification of children at risk for Coronary artery lesions. We retrospectively analysed 216 children with Kawasaki disease divided into a training cohort (n = 151) and a validation cohort (n = 65). Coronary artery lesions was defined as early coronary dilatation and/or coronary aneurysm. XGBoost and SHapley Additive exPlanations were applied to explore age's nonlinear effect. Predictors were screened via multivariable logistic regression with elastic-net regression for supplementary assessment. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, calibration curves, and decision-curve analysis. Overall, 46 children (21.3%) developed Coronary artery lesions. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis identified a U-shaped age-risk pattern with cut-off points at 17 and 58 months. Male sex, age group, fever duration, systemic immune-inflammation index, C-reactive protein/albumin ratio, and intravenous immunoglobulin resistance were independent Coronary artery lesions risk factors incorporated into the nomogram. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve reached 0.835 (95% CI 0.804-0.867) in the training cohort and 0.818 (95% CI 0.767-0.869) in the validation cohort. Calibration and decision-curve analysis confirmed good consistency and favourable clinical net benefit. This nomogram integrates routine clinical variables and interpretable machine learning to identify nonlinear age-related Coronary artery lesions risk and provide individualised early risk estimation. External validation in large prospective multicentre cohorts is needed before wide clinical application.

title: Structural Valve Deterioration in End-Stage Renal Disease Patients With Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
authorString: Inan B, Cordoves EM, Ramos-Lemos G, Tagliafierro M, Moos EF, Owolabi G, Lao JY, Mason I, Fatehi Hassanabad A.
abstractText: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has revolutionized the management of aortic stenosis (AS), particularly for high-risk and inoperable populations. Nevertheless, patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) who require TAVR present a unique clinical challenge. These patients tend to have a high burden of comorbidities, as well as chronic uremia, that purportedly predispose them to a higher risk of more frequent and rapid structural valve deterioration (SVD). This narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence regarding the mechanisms, incidence, and clinical outcomes of TAVR SVD in the ESRD population. In doing so, we summarize the pathophysiology for SVD in this patient population, contextualize the reported rates of TAVR SVD, and summarize the limited literature describing the clinical outcomes for these patients. We posit that clinical management for ESRD patients must focus on proactive, multidisciplinary surveillance and the integration of predictive modeling to optimize the timing of rescue interventions. Finally, we underscore the importance of better understanding the underlying mechanisms that accelerate TAVR SVD in uremic conditions.

title: Decoding voltage-gated sodium channels structure: Molecular mechanisms linking architecture, function, and disease.
authorString: Boazinha JP, Carneiro J, Cerqueira NMFSA, Sousa SF.
abstractText: Voltage-gated sodium (NaV) channels are critical transmembrane proteins responsible for the initiation and propagation of electrical signals in excitable tissues. They consist of a large α subunit and auxiliary β subunits. Together, the voltage sensing, ion selectivity, and rapid gating transitions regulate neuronal, muscular, and cardiac excitability. Recent cryo-electron microscopy breakthroughs have transformed the understanding of NaV structure-function relationships, revealing the asymmetric organization of voltage-sensing domains (VSD), the architecture of the DEKA selectivity filter, the mechanical coupling between S4-S5 linkers and S6 gating helices, and the allosteric mechanism by which the IFMT motif mediates fast inactivation. Across the nine human NaV isoforms, subtle structural divergences underlie distinct tissue distributions, biophysical properties, and disease susceptibilities, explaining the diverse channelopathies that range from epilepsy and cardiac arrhythmias to skeletal muscle disorders and painful neuropathies. These high-resolution structures also illuminate isoform-specific pharmacological pockets, including membrane-dependent cavities in VSD4 and dynamic fenestrations that govern state-dependent drug access, enabling the rational design of small molecules, peptide toxins, and hybrid therapeutics with improved selectivity. Advances in structural biology, biochemistry, and computation have established an integrated mechanistic model that connects NaV channel architecture to gating, inactivation, isoform-specific function, and human disease. This growing molecular atlas now supports next-generation precision therapies aimed at selectively modulating NaV channel activity in neurological, muscular, cardiac, and pain disorders.

title: Photoinduced Selective Cyclization Cascades of Unactivated N-alkene-Linked Indoles with the Insertion of Sulfur Dioxide and Its Preliminary Application Investigation.
authorString: Huang J, Li J, Zeng Y, Li Q, Jia Y, Liang F, Hu Z, Mao Y, Tian J, Yang M.
abstractText: Photoinduced selective cyclization cascades of unactivated N-alkene-linked indoles with the insertion of sulfur dioxide were established, generating diverse exo- or endo-trig-cyclization products with a broad substrate scope in moderate to good yields. The mechanistic study revealed that selective radical addition, cyclization and radical-polar-crossover (RPC) process were involved in this transformation. We next deliverd a preliminary application investigation, and found that 3wj exhibited significant inhibitory effect on B16F10 cells, most showed a significant photophysical property, and some were applied as fluorescent dyes into live-cell imaging.

title: Vascularized Organoids Emerge from a Heart-Foregut-like Intermediate Recapitulating Early Human Development
authorString: Wang W, He Q, Xiong Z, Zhang H, Meng Q, Su X, Guo Y, Fan Y, Yang LY, Liu X, Bian X, Lu G, Chan W.
abstractText: During early cardiogenesis, the heart regions lie in close contact with foregut endoderm, which supplies essential nutrients and signaling cues to orchestrate primitive heart tube assembly. Here, we show that self-organized heart/foregut like-structures emerge from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). The initial heart/foregut-like structures, termed the Seed, are encased by surrounding supportive cells termed Soil, which provide a matrix microenvironment; the Seed progressively develops into chambered human cardiac organoids (hCOs) containing cardiomyocytes (CMs), epicardial cells, cardiac fibroblasts, and endothelial cells. Optimization of the induction system further enhanced hCO maturation and vascularization. Therefore, this Soil-Seed system provides a model to dissect human early heart/foregut self-organization.

title: Genetic Determinants of Cell-Type-Specific Responses to Cardiotoxic Chemotherapeutic Agents
authorString: McIntire E, Barr KA, Gonzales NM, Allen OL, Burnett JE, Gilad Y.
abstractText: Doxorubicin (DOX) and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) are effective for treating a variety of cancers, yet many patients taking these drugs experience adverse cardiovascular events that are severe enough to pause treatment, often prolonging the course of chemotherapy and reducing its efficacy. Individual risk for drug-induced cardiotoxicity is likely mediated, at least in part, by genetic variants that control how the heart and vasculature respond to drug-induced perturbations. To identify loci associated with drug-induced cardiotoxicity, we developed an in vitro model that allows us to characterize the effects of chemotherapeutic drugs on a wide range of cardiac cell types, including cardiomyocytes, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts. Using single-cell RNA-seq, we profiled responses to DOX and 5-FU across 46 individuals and 14 cell types, identifying hundreds of expression quantitative trait loci that modify cardiovascular transcription in response to each drug (response eQTLs). Drug-responsive eQTL genes include genes that were previously linked to drug-induced cardiotoxicity and cardiovascular disease, such as ABCB4, HAS3, TNFRSF1A, and OGFR. Over a third of drug-responsive genes are shared between the DOX and 5-FU treatments, suggesting that genes predictive of DOX-induced cardiotoxicity may extend to 5-FU. Among the credible colocalizations we identified between GWAS signals and drug-response eQTLs, we discovered a locus associated with ischemic heart disease that is also a DOX-responsive eQTL for IL6R. IL6R was previously nominated as a druggable target for heart disease, and its binding partner IL6 is a candidate biomarker for anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity. These findings advance the discovery of genetic variants underlying cardiotoxicity and support development of genotype-based predictors for treating cancer.

title: A Clinical Atlas for Phenome-Wide Association Study of Obstructive Sleep Apnea Across Electronic Health Record Domains
authorString: Hwang NH, Mishra S, Westover MB, Thomas RJ, Katwa U, Becker KA, Hwang D, Klimper MT, Jara J, Stevens DR, Gratton MK, Mazzotti DR, Sun H.
abstractText: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a heterogeneous disorder whose associations across the entire phenome remain incompletely characterized by hypothesis-driven outcome-specific analyses. We constructed a multidomain atlas for phenome-wide association study of OSA in 222,109 adults undergoing diagnostic sleep testing in Kaiser Permanente Southern California. Using apnea-hypopnea index, we examined cross-sectional associations across diagnoses, laboratory tests, medications, procedures, healthcare utilization, behaviors, and symptoms; associations with incident diseases; and data-driven cross-domain phenotypes. After full adjustment, 169 prevalent phecodes and 16 incident phecodes remained Bonferroni-significant. Positive associations converged most consistently on cardiometabolic diseases, including hypertension, impaired glucose metabolism, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and heart failure, with concordant laboratory, medication, and cardiac-measurement signals. Multidimensional physiologic, symptom, and comorbidity phenotypes showed heterogeneous disease incidence after adjustment, with patterns not aligned with apnea-hypopnea index severity alone. These findings define the broad clinical landscape of OSA and provide a comprehensive atlas for replication and hypothesis generation.

title: U-Shaped Association Between Preoperative Fasting Blood Glucose and Postoperative Delirium in Elderly Diabetic Patients: A Multicentre Retrospective Cohort Study
authorString: Zhang X, Zhang Y, Yuan M, Xu B, Cao J, Liu Y, Lou J, Shi W, Fu Q, Mi W.
abstractText:
Abstract Objective: The heightened susceptibility of the aging brain to dysglycemia establishes blood glucose as a pivotal risk factor for postoperative delirium (POD) in elderly diabetic patients. This study investigated the association between preoperative fasting blood glucose (FBG) and POD risk in this population to define the optimal FBG range for POD.

Methods:

This study included 2,157 elderly diabetic patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery between April 2020 and April 2022 in 20 hospitals across China. The POD incidence was prospectively assessed using the 3-minute Diagnostic Interview for Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM) within 7 postoperative days. The FBG-POD relationship was retrospectively analysed using restricted cubic splines within Cox proportional hazards model. Thresholds were validated with the machine learning-guided optimal cut-point analysis. A multivariable linear regression model was plotted to compare the distribution of time to POD onset and subgroup analyses were performed based on specific populations.

Results:

A significant U-shaped relationship was observed between preoperative FBG and POD risk (P for nonlinearity=0.03). The hazard ratio identified the risk nadir of FBG at 8.43 mmol L-1. Optimal cut-point analysis defined three risk strata: a hypoglycemic-risk group (FBG ≤5.92 mmol L-1; 13.3% POD), an optimal-glycemic group (FBG 5.92-9.75 mmol L-1; 9.7% POD), and a hyperglycemic-risk group (FBG >9.75 mmol L-1; 18.5% POD). Compared with the optimal-glycemic group, both the hypoglycemic-risk group (HR=1.65, P<0.001) and the hyperglycemic-risk group (HR=1.51, P=0.03) showed significantly increased risk. Interpretation: Preoperative FBG has a U-shaped association with POD risk in elderly diabetic patients with an optimal lowest-risk range as 5.92-9.75 mmol L-1.

Keywords:

Diabetes Mellitus; Elderly; Fasting Blood Glucose; Postoperative Delirium; Risk Stratification; Threshold Analysis.

title: Speaking Progress, Feeling Threat: A Biopsychosocial Approach to Systemic Progressive Social Change
authorString: Colombo M, Scheepers D, Homan M, van Nunspeet F.
abstractText: Progressive values are substantially endorsed across Western Europe, yet concrete engagement with social change remains limited. This gap raises questions about the motivational and physiological processes that may underlie ambivalence toward progressive action. Drawing on the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT), the present study examined whether progressive hierarchy-disruptive social change elicit cardiovascular threat responses even among individuals who support such change. Ninety Western European university students participated in a within-subjects laboratory study in which they discussed the university’s current collaborations (status quo condition) followed by implementing an academic boycott-like change targeting unethical institutional collaborations (social change condition). Cardiovascular responses were assessed via cardiac output (CO), total peripheral resistance (TPR), and the Threat-Challenge Index (TCI), and analyzed using multilevel modeling. In line with preregistered predictions, the social-change condition elicited stronger physiological threat than the status-quo (lower or stable CO, higher TPR, lower TCI). These responses persisted after controlling for political orientation and (progressive) attitudes, and despite participants generally expressing high support for social change. Text analyses revealed heterogeneity in the sources of threat: Participants either showed reluctance to relinquish status-quo privileges or voiced practical concerns regarding the change. By contrast, relative challenge, which was less prevalent, related to perceiving collective resources to deal with the change but also to rationalization of opposition. These findings suggest that even supporting individuals are not always immune to threat responses when confronting material systemic change.

title: Interoceptive Processing in Boredom Proneness: Sensing Without Making Sense
authorString: Trudel C, Danckert J.
abstractText: Boredom proneness has been linked to a disrupted relationship with one's internal states, yet themechanism underlying this disruption remains unclear. One possibility is that this disruptionreflects a difficulty in translating interoceptive signals into meaningful predictions about internalstates, rather than a basic failure to detect them. Across two studies, we examined whether thisdisrupted relationship reflects interpretive challenges, a deficit in cardiac interoceptive accuracy,or both. Study 1 (N = 124) was a direct replication confirming that highly boredom proneindividuals report attending intensely to bodily sensations while struggling to interpret them — apattern that held across a combined sample of 350 adults and yielded moderate-to-strongcorrelations with established measures of self-focused attention and interoceptive sensoryconfusion. Study 2 (N = 121) administered a heartbeat counting task to determine whether thisdisrupted relationship was due to deficient interoceptive processing or interpretive failure.Boredom proneness was unrelated to objective heartbeat counting accuracy but remainedassociated with self-reported interoceptive sensory confusion. Converging with Study 1, thispattern suggests that boredom proneness is best characterized by a difficulty in interpreting internalsignals than by a basic interoceptive perceptual deficit. Together, these findings are consistent withpredictive processing accounts of boredom proneness where those high in trait boredom struggleto generate meaningful predictions from interoceptive cues. Whether this dissociation betweenself-reported and objective cardiac interoception generalizes across different measurementapproaches and populations remains an open question that future work could examine using moresensitive interoceptive tasks and trial-level prediction error metrics.

title: The Road to Liberation is Paved with Threats: A Biopsychosocial Perspective on Minoritized Individuals’ Responses to Hierarchy-Disruptive Social Change
authorString: Colombo M, Scheepers D, van Nunspeet F.
abstractText: When social equates to social mobility, it elicits adaptive (“challenge”) stress responses among low-status individuals. Instead, hierarchy-disruptive social change may impose under-theorized demands on minoritized individuals, eliciting maladaptive (‘threat’) stress. Thus, LGBTQ+ (n = 57) and cisgender-heterosexual (n = 57) participants expressed their opinion about the status quo and the social change (introducing a non-binary constitution) while cardiovascular challenge-threat was measured. As hypothesized, LGBTQ+ participants exhibited threat when discussing change, compared to the status quo; unexpectedly, cisgender-heterosexual participants exhibited challenge. Among LGBTQ+ participants, higher personal, but not ingroup, demands paired with lower personal resources predicted higher threat. Verbal opinions, coded into five clusters of demands and resources mapped onto challenge-threat, endorsement of change, and protest intentions (but not donations). Notably, one cluster combining failure and retaliation demands with moral hope and collective resources revealed that minoritized individuals persist in social change despite threat, potentially at the cost of their well-being.

title: Maternal Stress and Mother-Child Interaction Dynamics: The Roles of Child Age and Maternal Emotion Regulation
authorString: Folz J, Nguyen T, Hoehl S, van Ast VA, Nikolic M.
abstractText: Caregivers often face stressful multi-tasking situations in which household- or work-related tasks compete with engaging with their young child. Caregivers’ experiences of stress can affect how they interact with their children and may also be transmitted to the child. This “stress contagion” may be particularly pronounced with caregivers who have difficulties in regulating stress responses. In the current study, we examined how inducing stress in 62 mothers shaped the dyadic interaction (expression of facial affect and cardiovascular activity) with their 6-38 months-old children, and how stress-induced changes varied depending on self-reported maternal emotion regulation difficulties and child age. Mothers’ and children’s positive and negative facial affect, inter-beat intervals (IBIs) and respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA), as well as synchrony in each measure, were compared between two-minute face-to-face interactions before and after a stress induction in the mother (pre- and post-stress). Maternal stress impacted the dyad differently depending on the child’s age. In interactions with younger children, both mothers and children showed less positive facial expressions and were less synchronized in their expressions post- versus pre-stress. Older children, in contrast, showed stronger physiological arousal (i.e., decrease in IBIs and RSA), but more positive facial expressions post-stress. In addition, mothers with more emotion regulation difficulties expressed more negative affect, and their heart rates were less synchronized with their children’s post- versus pre-stress. Both child age and mothers’ regulatory abilities are thus shaping the impact of acute maternal stress on mother-child interaction quality and should be considered in interventions on parental stress

title: Bringing Interoception Into the Clinical Setting of Alcohol Use Disorder
authorString: Macchiavello F, Morales JP, Villena-Gonzalez M, Campos-Arteaga G, Laferte M, Thomas FR.
abstractText: AbstractBackground. Interoception is increasingly implicated in alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet clinical translationremains limited by construct conflation, dependence on cardiac tasks, and uncertainty about whether atypicalbodily processing reflects a stable deficit or a context-sensitive process.Methods. This critical narrative review integrates AUD-specific behavioral, psychophysiological,neuroimaging, alcohol-administration, and intervention evidence using an explicit hierarchy that separatesdirect interoceptive measures from mechanistic and translational support.Results. Direct studies indicate that lower cardiac-task performance can coexist with heightened subjectivebodily attention, while recent validity work shows that heartbeat-counting scores cannot be treated as pureindices of bodily-signal detection. Acute alcohol, stress-cue, and ambulatory findings further indicate that thebehavioral significance of bodily signals depends on how they are generated, attributed, and linked toalcohol-related action.Conclusions. The central clinical proposition is not to increase bodily awareness indiscriminately, but toimprove the detection, differentiation, attribution, and appraisal of bodily states within context. Thissignal-context-action framework generates testable hypotheses for assessment, relapse monitoring, andtreatment matching within established AUD care

title: Measuring heart and breath: BRAMS-Bio-Box (B3), a wearable open-source physiology recording platform
authorString: Bahadori M, Voix J, Bella SD, van Vugt FT.
abstractText: Psychology and social neuroscience study the biological basis of real-world interactive behaviors, such as dancing or playing music in groups. Autonomic nervous system reactivity, assessed through cardiac and respiratory signals, plays an important role in these behaviors. However, affordable, scientifically validated, research-grade devices for synchronous, real-time physiological monitoring of multiple individuals in natural settings remain scarce. We propose a wearable open-source physiological monitoring device, the BRAMS-Bio-Box (B3), that can record cardiac and respiratory signals simultaneously from multiple individuals. B3 can be built cost-effectively using open-source blueprints and software we provide to yield a transparent, flexible option for research-grade physiological data collection. We empirically validated B3 against a widely used reference device in nine participants performing various motor and guided-respiration tasks. Heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV) were derived from electrocardiographic (ECG) signals, while respiratory sensors were evaluated for respiration rate and the accuracy and consistency of exhalation event detection.
