Integrated 16 S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that high-dose SF partially restored HFD-associated alterations in gut microbiota composition, including normalization of the Firmicutes/Bacteroidota ratio and changes in several atherosclerosis-associated genera, and altered bile acid profiles. In addition, SF reduced intestinal apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter (ASBT) expression, suggesting a potential role in bile acid homeostasis. Collectively, these findings indicate that SF attenuates atherosclerosis and is associated with alterations in gut microbiota, bile acid profiles, and lipid and inflammatory responses, providing insights into its pharmacological effects.

title: Atrial Cardiomyopathy Through the Pathologist's Lens: From Tissue Remodeling to Clinical Expression.
authorString: Corradi D.

journal.title: Cardiovascular pathology : the official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Pathology

abstractText: Atrial cardiomyopathy (ACM) provides a useful framework for understanding structural, architectural, contractile, and electrophysiological disease of the atria. ACM and atrial fibrillation (AF) are closely linked but are not interchangeable: ACM favors arrhythmogenesis, whereas sustained AF can accelerate atrial injury. This review considers ACM from the pathologist's perspective, encompassing primary atrial disease and secondary remodeling associated with valvular disease and classical cardiomyopathies. The histologic spectrum includes cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and myocytolysis, interstitial and replacement fibrosis, endocardial fibroelastosis, adipose and inflammatory infiltration, vascular injury, and amyloid deposition. Structural remodeling is regionally heterogeneous, and appendage specimens may underrepresent abnormalities elsewhere in the atrium. Histologic interpretation requires attention to intrinsic regional architecture, associated lesions, previous interventions, and methods of quantification. At the molecular and cellular level, genetic susceptibility and acquired stressors converge on cardiomyocyte dysfunction, inflammation, fibroblast activation, and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Correlating these tissue changes with mapping, imaging, biomarkers, and clinical outcomes will be necessary to validate noninvasive phenotypes and identify clinically meaningful disease subsets. At present, ACM should prompt etiologic investigation and risk assessment but does not by itself constitute an indication for specific therapy.

title: Bicuspid aortic valve with giant non-coronary sinus aneurysm compressing the sinoatrial node causing arrhythmia and coarctation of the aorta: A case on clinical decision-making and surgical challenges.
authorString: Liu S, Zhang Z, Yang K, Chen W, Cao W, Wang L, Dong S, Zhang Y.

journal.title: Cardiovascular pathology : the official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Pathology

abstractText:
Background

Bicuspid aortic valve, the most common congenital valvular disease, frequently coexists with aortic pathologies. Symptomatic arrhythmias from unruptured giant aortic sinus aneurysm compressing the sinoatrial node are exceedingly rare. The coexistence of bicuspid aortic valve, arrhythmogenic sinus aneurysm, coarctation of the aorta, and right coronary artery occlusion represents an extraordinarily complex malformation with scarce documentation and controversial management strategies.

Case presentation

A 67-year-old male patient presented with chest tightness and palpitations. Echocardiography and computed tomography angiography revealed Type 0 bicuspid aortic valve (two-sinus type) with giant unruptured non-coronary sinus aneurysm (52 mm × 48 mm), descending coarctation of the aorta (14 mm), post-stenotic aneurysm (42 mm), and right coronary artery occlusion. Imaging confirmed direct sinoatrial node compression. First-stage surgery comprised biological aortic valve replacement, sinus repair, and coronary artery bypass grafting. The coarctation of the aorta was managed conservatively based on borderline transcoarctation gradient and favorable clinical status.

Conclusion

Direct mechanical sinoatrial node compression combined with compromised nodal arterial supply constituted the pathophysiological basis for arrhythmia. For bicuspid aortic valve with multisegmental aortic disease, individualized strategy based on anatomical characteristics, hemodynamic parameters (such as transcoarctation gradient, aortic isthmus ratio, and extremity blood pressure difference), and systemic condition is essential. Staged repair prioritizing hemodynamically threatening lesions reduces surgical trauma and spinal ischemia risk, providing clinical guidance for managing such rare complex aortic pathologies.

title: Association Between Lipoprotein A Levels and Vulnerable Atherosclerotic Plaques.
authorString: Mahadevan A, Jog HS, Dhananjaya H, Patel M, Marwah MPS, Gandhi MH, Vasudevan SS, Lekkala SP, Mehdi HK, Desai R.

journal.title: The American journal of the medical sciences

abstractText:
Background

Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an established cardiovascular risk factor, but its association with imaging-defined vulnerable plaque features remains incompletely characterized.

Methods

We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and Embase for observational studies comparing elevated versus lower Lp(a) levels and reporting thin-cap fibroatheroma (TCFA) or lipid-rich plaques. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed, with the primary TCFA analysis restricted to optical coherence tomography (OCT)-based studies. Sensitivity and geography-based subgroup analyses were also conducted.

Results

Seven studies involving 1,008 patients were included. Elevated Lp(a) was associated with greater odds of TCFA in the primary OCT-based analysis (OR 2.90, 95% CI 1.63 to 5.18; I²=51.0%) and with greater odds of lipid-rich plaques (OR 3.03, 95% CI 1.53 to 6.00; I²=76.9%). Including the MDCTA/MRI study in a TCFA sensitivity analysis yielded a similar association. No significant subgroup differences were observed between Asian and Western studies.

Conclusions

Elevated Lp(a) is associated with imaging-defined features of plaque vulnerability, including TCFA and lipid-rich plaques. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given heterogeneity and the limited number of studies.

title: Association of Air Pollution Exposure and Risk of Incident Atrial Fibrillation: The Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis.
authorString: Cannon EJ, Kaufman JD, Austin TR, Misialek JR, Heckbert SR, Jacobs DR, Lutsey PL.
abstractText:
Background

Consistent evidence indicates that air pollution negatively impacts cardiovascular health. However, the relationship between air pollution and atrial fibrillation (AF) is unclear, and exposure measurement error has been a significant concern for prior studies.

Objective

This prospective cohort study aimed to evaluate the association of chronic air pollution exposure and risk of AF.

Methods

We used data from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, a community-based cohort study conducted in 6 U.S. metropolitan areas. Concentrations of 4 pollutants (PM2.5, NO2, NOx, and O3) were assessed from 2000-2018 using hierarchical spatiotemporal models that incorporated cohort-specific monitoring to estimate ambient exposure at participants' residences. In Cox regression models, pollution estimates were represented as time-varying exposures, with 2-year rolling averages updated every 30 days. In our primary model, we adjusted for demographics and health behaviors.

Results

Our study included 6618 participants (mean age 62; 53% female). Over 16.5 years median follow-up, we identified 1055 AF events. In our primary model, an interquartile range increment of NO2 (13.5 ppb) was associated with 29% higher risk of AF (hazard ratio 95% CI: 1.00, 1.67). Associations with PM2.5, NOx, and O3 were weaker but also directionally consistent with higher risk.

Conclusion

We found evidence linking air pollution exposure to risk of incident AF. These results can be used to inform policy and other public health efforts aimed at alleviating the burden of AF, especially given that NO2 exposure estimates (median 17.3 ppb) fell well below the current U.S. Environmental Protection Agency annual standard of 53 ppb.

title: Midlife and Late-Life Alzheimer Disease Blood Biomarkers and 11-Year Cognitive Decline.
authorString: Smith JR, Pike JR, Lu Y, Walker KA, Sullivan KJ, Windham BG, Thyagarajan B, Mielke MM, Lutsey PL, Hughes TM, Knopman DS, Gottesman RF, Mosley TH, Coresh J, Deal JA, Sharrett AR, Palta P.
abstractText:
Background and objectives

Plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer disease (AD) neuropathology (amyloid-β42 to amyloid β40 [Aβ42/40] ratio, phosphorylated tau at threonine [p-tau181]), neurodegeneration (neurofilament light [NfL]), and neuroinflammation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) in late-life are associated with cognitive decline. Whether these biomarkers in midlife are predictive of subsequent cognitive decline, and whether they are associated with different cognitive domains, is uncertain. In this study, we investigated associations of midlife and late-life plasma Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP with late-life change in domain-specific (memory, language, and executive function) and global cognitive function.

Methods

We performed a prospective cohort analysis of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study (ARIC-NCS). Outcome follow-up was from ARIC visit 5 (2011-2013) to visit 9 (2021-2022). We included all individuals from ARIC field centers (Jackson, Mississippi; Forsyth County, North Carolina; Washington County, Maryland; and Minneapolis suburbs, Minnesota) with biomarkers measured from stored specimens in midlife (visit 3, 1993-1995, mean age 59.0 years) and late-life (visit 5, 2011-2013, mean age 76.8 years). Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were measured with the Quanterix Simoa platform and standardized to visit 3 to facilitate cross-biomarker comparisons of their rate of change from midlife to late-life. We estimated change in memory, language, executive function, and global cognition factor scores from visit 5 to visit 9 with linear mixed-effect models.

Results

In 1,515 included participants, 60.7% (n = 920) were female and 25.5% (n = 387) were Black. Each SD increase in p-tau181 in midlife was significantly associated with faster late-life memory decline (β = -0.030 [95% CI -0.059 to -0.001] SD. Midlife Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP were not associated with subsequent decline in any cognitive domain. In late-life, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were significantly associated with faster decline in different cognitive domains, with the strongest associations seen with memory (β = -0.091 [95% CI -0.123 to -0.058] SD; β = -0.064 [95% CI -0.106 to -0.023] SD; and β = -0.048 [95% CI -0.082 to -0.013] SD, respectively).

Discussion

Midlife p-tau181 was associated with faster 11-year memory decline beginning 20 years later in the ARIC cohort, which underscores a potentially long prodromal phase of cognitive decline that could precede dementia onset. In late-life, biomarkers for AD, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation were associated with faster decline across different cognitive domains, but associations remained strongest for p-tau181 and memory.

title: Staged Omental Wrapping for Perigraft Fluid Collection after Total Aortic Arch Replacement: A Case Report.
authorString: Tomita G, Abe S, Tsuchida H, Ando N, Makino Y.
abstractText:
Introduction

Perigraft fluid collection after aortic graft replacement is often self-limiting; however, progressive enlargement or the development of symptoms warrants careful evaluation. The differential diagnosis includes hematoma, abscess, seroma, and lymphatic leakage. However, differentiating among these conditions can be challenging based solely on clinical symptoms and imaging findings.

Case presentation

A 51-year-old man underwent total aortic arch replacement (TAR) for chronic Stanford type A aortic dissection. Nine months later, he developed rapidly progressive swelling and erythema over the upper portion of the median sternotomy incision. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a low-attenuation fluid collection surrounding the prosthetic graft and extending into the subcutaneous mass. Although there was no evidence of active extravasation, anastomotic disruption, or gas formation suggestive of graft infection, exploratory resternotomy was performed under cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) standby because a redo TAR might have become necessary if either anastomotic disruption or gross graft infection had been identified intraoperatively. Intraoperative inspection revealed no evidence of active bleeding. However, graft infection could not be definitively excluded because yellowish-brown turbid fluid was drained from the subcutaneous mass and around the prosthetic graft. Fluid samples were obtained for microbiological culture, and the perigraft space was thoroughly irrigated. Based on the intraoperative findings, fluid characteristics, and negative microbiological culture results, a sterile inflammatory perigraft fluid collection was considered the most likely diagnosis. Omental wrapping was subsequently performed as a second-stage procedure to manage the large residual space and prevent graft infection. No recurrence was observed during 12 months of follow-up.

Conclusions

Perigraft fluid collection after aortic graft replacement has a broad differential diagnosis. When active bleeding or graft infection cannot be confidently excluded, an exploratory resternotomy under CPB standby may be a practical option for direct evaluation and management. Omental wrapping may be a simple and effective option for preventing recurrence and graft infection.

title: Cardiomyocyte-enriched OTUD5 alleviates pathological myocardial hypertrophy by deubiquitinating STAT3 and modulating the STAT3-PGC-1α axis.
authorString: Ye B, Jiang Y, Zheng Z, Jin Y, Liao Y, Jia Z, Lin W, Xu D, Han J, Fang Z, Zhang N, Shan P, Wu G, Liang G.
abstractText: Pathological cardiac hypertrophy presents a important public health challenge, particularly in aging populations, highlighting the urgent need for novel therapeutic targets. This study investigates the role and molecular mechanisms of OTUD5 in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. OTUD5 expression is greatly increased in cardiomyocytes from hypertrophic hearts. Deleting cardiomyocyte-specific OTUD5 exacerbates myocardial hypertrophy induced by angiotensin II (Ang II) and transverse aortic constriction (TAC). By contrast, targeted overexpression of OTUD5 in cardiomyocytes alleviates Ang II-induced pathological hypertrophy. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that OTUD5 regulates STAT3 activity by removing the K63-linked ubiquitin chain at lysine 283 (K283) on STAT3 through its C224 residue. This process inhibits both phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of STAT3, effectively relieving its transcriptional repression of PGC1α and enhancing mitochondrial function within cardiomyocytes. Our research uncovers a new OTUD5-STAT3-PGC1α axis that modulates mitochondrial bioenergetics, suggesting it as a potential therapeutic target for pathological cardiac hypertrophy.

title: MRI-PHYSIOL-NIRS: an integrated platform to study kidney oxygenation.
authorString: Gladytz T, Cantow K, Millward JM, Waiczies S, Tasbihi E, Grosenick D, Seeliger E, Niendorf T.
abstractText: The kidney always operates close to hypoxia, a pathological condition of O<sub>2</sub>-shortage, due to its unique relationship between blood flow and oxygen demand. Renal hypoxia is central to kidney diseases, where progressive loss of renal function ultimately can no longer sustain life. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can assess renal oxygenation non-invasively in vivo via the relaxation times T<sub>2</sub><sup>*</sup> and T<sub>2</sub>, which reflect deoxygenated hemoglobin, but are influenced by several physiological confounders. We developed MRI-PHYSIOL-NIRS, a platform integrating MRI with ground-truth probes that directly measure tissue oxygenation in rat kidneys (PHYSIOL), and near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) to estimate oxygenation-related parameters to dissect the relationship between MRI-based measures and true tissue oxygenation. Using aortic occlusion and hyperoxia interventions within the MRI scanner, we investigated correlations between non-invasive MRI-based oxygenation measures and true tissue oxygenation. These results demonstrate the potential for entirely MRI-based measurement of renal oxygenation in health and disease, with ultimate application in patients.

title: Functional outcome after recurrent laryngeal nerve injury following thoracic aortic surgery.
authorString: Pregaldini F, Potratz P, Seifert E, Nucera M, Mosbahi S, Bartkevics M, Schmidli J, Siepe M, Yildiz M, Schoenhoff FS.

journal.title: The Journal of thoracic and cardiovascular surgery

abstractText:
Objectives

Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury is a recognized complication of aortic surgery, yet data on long-term functional outcomes remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the incidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and to assess voice recovery after thoracic aortic surgery.

Methods

Single-centre retrospective analysis included adult patients undergoing aortic arch or thoracoabdominal aortic surgery between 2001 and 2024. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury was diagnosed by postoperative vocal cord paralysis. Aortic arch surgery included partial and total arch replacement, while thoracoabdominal surgery involved the proximal descending aorta. The primary endpoint was full voice recovery. Secondary endpoints included recovery of normal vocal cord mobility, residual dysphonia, the need for voice therapy, and vocal cord interventions.

Results

Among 2,983 patients undergoing aortic surgery, 70 (2.3%) were diagnosed with postoperative recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. Median follow-up was 17 [IQR: 7-25] months. The incidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury was 1.7% after arch surgery and 5.3% after thoracoabdominal procedures. At final follow-up, 34 patients (50%) achieved full voice recovery, while 20 (30%) had mild dysphonia, 9 (13%) moderate dysphonia, and 5 (7%) severe dysphonia. Voice therapy was performed in 49 (70%) patients, and 10 (14%) required additional vocal cord interventions.

Conclusions

In this large cohort, the incidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury after aortic surgery was lower than previously reported. Functional outcomes were favourable, with most patients achieving full or near-complete voice recovery through conservative or interventional management. Structured follow-up and multidisciplinary care remain essential to optimize outcomes after recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

title: Brachial artery access for endovascular procedures: how safe is it?
authorString: Howroyd LR, Khattar AS, Tam HC, Morgan R, Chun JY.
abstractText:
Purpose

While femoral and radial artery access are routine for endovascular procedures, brachial artery access remains an important alternative in selected cases. This study aimed to evaluate the complication rate of percutaneous brachial artery access at a tertiary centre and identify potential risk factors for access-site complications.

Materials and methods

A retrospective review was performed of all procedures utilising percutaneous brachial artery access over a 12.5-year period. Patient demographics, sheath size, closure technique and complications were recorded. Complications were classified according to the CIRSE classification system.

Results

One hundred percutaneous brachial artery punctures were identified. Sheath sizes ranged from 3 to 9 Fr; the majority (57%) using 6 Fr. Most procedures (84%) were performed for aortic, mesenteric/renal, or peripheral arterial interventions. Overall, 23 complications occurred (23%), including 9 (9%) grade 3 complications requiring additional treatment. No convincing association was identified between complication rate and patient age, gender, or sheath size. Vascular closure devices were used in seven cases, five of which resulted in complications, including three grade 3 events.

Conclusions

The complication rate associated with brachial artery access in this series was higher than that reported in much of the published literature. These findings suggest that brachial artery access may be less safe than commonly perceived and that vascular closure devices should be used with caution, particularly given their off-label status for this access site. Standardised procedural protocols and post-procedural care pathways may help reduce complication rates. Broader auditing and reporting across centres are encouraged to better define best practice.

title: Perioperative B-Cell-Targeted Therapy for High-Risk Valve Surgery in Active Primary Sjögren's Disease.
authorString: Li B, Pan L, Liao H.
abstractText:
Background

Primary Sjögren's disease (SjD) is a systemic autoimmune disease driven by B-cell dysregulation. Clinically significant valvular involvement is uncommon, and evidence guiding perioperative immunomodulation remains limited.

Case summary

A 59-year-old woman with SjD and severe aortic stenosis required valve replacement. Preoperative evaluation demonstrated active SjD with elevated inflammatory markers and hypergammaglobulinemia. Following multidisciplinary discussion, telitacicept, corticosteroids, and hydroxychloroquine were initiated before surgery. After improvement in inflammatory activity, the patient underwent aortic valve and ascending aorta replacement. Histopathologic examination showed degenerative valvular changes with focal inflammatory cell infiltration. The postoperative course was uneventful, with normal prosthetic valve function at 1-year follow-up.

Discussion

This case highlights the challenges of managing severe valvular heart disease in patients with active primary SjD and a multidisciplinary perioperative strategy incorporating B-cell-targeted therapy. Although preoperative immunomodulation may have attenuated the histopathologic evidence of immune-mediated valvular involvement, the case offers insights when guidance is limited.

title: Late Progressive Multivalvular Regurgitation After Heart Transplantation With Preserved Graft Function.
authorString: Fanous N, Abdo RM, Adams C, Healy J, Adonopulos A, Namasivayam M, MacDonald P, Watson A.
abstractText:
Background

Late clinical decline after heart transplantation is commonly attributed to rejection, cardiac allograft vasculopathy, or ventricular dysfunction. Progressive structural valvular disease is less frequently emphasized when graft systolic function is preserved.

Case summary

A 22-year-old woman underwent orthotopic heart transplantation at age 13 for familial restrictive cardiomyopathy. Nearly 10 years later, she developed progressive exertional fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, and dizziness despite preserved graft systolic function and no significant cardiac allograft vasculopathy. Serial imaging demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation, moderate to severe aortic regurgitation, and moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation. She underwent redo sternotomy with bioprosthetic aortic and mitral valve replacement and tricuspid repair, with preserved ventricular function and clinical recovery at early follow-up.

Discussion

This case highlights progressive multivalvular disease as an important valve-level cause of late clinical decline after heart transplantation.

Take-home message

Consider structural valvular disease in symptomatic long-term heart transplant recipients with preserved graft function.

title: Severe Bioprosthetic Mitral Valve Dysfunction: Multimodality Imaging Identifies Structural Valve Degeneration and Guides Valve-in-Valve TMVR.
authorString: McKenna MJ, McCaughey C, Douglas GL, McCreery C, Mulvihill NT, Quinn M, Shand JA.
abstractText:
Background

Severe bioprosthetic valve dysfunction presents a diagnostic challenge because distinguishing reversible leaflet thrombosis from structural valve degeneration may not be possible using echocardiography alone.

Case summary

A patient with end-stage renal disease, previous bioprosthetic mitral and aortic valve replacement, and prior valve-in-valve transcatheter aortic valve replacement presented with heart failure and cardiogenic shock. Multimodality imaging demonstrated severe bioprosthetic mitral valve dysfunction with restricted leaflet motion, raising suspicion for leaflet thrombosis. Empiric intravenous unfractionated heparin was commenced while cardiac computed tomography was arranged. Computed tomography excluded hypoattenuated leaflet thickening and demonstrated severe leaflet calcification, confirming structural valve degeneration. After heart team discussion, transseptal valve-in-valve mitral replacement resulted in rapid hemodynamic and clinical recovery.

Discussion

Serial multimodality imaging guided escalation from anticoagulation to definitive valve intervention.

Take-home messages

Persistent prosthetic valve dysfunction after anticoagulation should prompt reassessment for structural valve degeneration. Transseptal valve-in-valve transcatheter mitral valve replacement is an effective treatment for selected high-surgical-risk patients.

title: Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair in Advanced Heart Failure and Ventricular Dysfunction: An Evolving Heart Team Strategy.
authorString: AlBadri A, Makar M, Burke J, Mannino S, Giuseffi J, Prasad R, Joshi G, Bikak AL.
abstractText:
Background

Patients with severe left ventricular (LV) dysfunction and mitral regurgitation are underrepresented in pivotal transcatheter edge-to-edge repair trials and are often ineligible for transplantation or LV assist devices, leaving limited options when guideline-directed medical therapy fails.

Case summary

We describe 6 patients aged 38 to 82 years with LV ejection fraction 10% to 20% and severe (4+) to torrential (5+) mitral regurgitation, 4 patients presenting in or near cardiogenic shock requiring inotropic, vasopressor, or intra-aortic balloon pump support. All underwent transcatheter edge-to-edge repair as our multidisciplinary heart team strategy evolved.

Discussion

With increasing experience, the heart team incorporated individualized pharmacologic or temporary mechanical support, preprocedural hemodynamic optimization, and anatomy-driven device selection. One patient initially referred for palliative care was subsequently reassessed and treated. This series illustrates how iterative multidisciplinary learning may expand transcatheter edge-to-edge repair candidacy in carefully selected, high-risk patients with advanced heart failure and profound ventricular dysfunction and limited therapeutic alternatives.

title: Argatroban Anticoagulation for Transcarotid TAVR Under Conscious Sedation in a Patient With Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia.
authorString: Delcampe A, Sabatier R, Lacôte C, Repessé Y, Descamps R.
abstractText:
Objectives

To describe argatroban anticoagulation in a patient with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia undergoing transcarotid transcatheter aortic valve replacement under conscious sedation.

Key steps

Vitamin K antagonist therapy was discontinued and intravenous argatroban initiated, with anti-factor IIa monitoring. Procedural anticoagulation consisted of an argatroban bolus followed by continuous infusion guided by activated clotting time. An ultrasound-guided intermediate cervical plexus block with remifentanil sedation maintained consciousness for neurological assessment. Argatroban was resumed postoperatively before transition to vitamin K antagonist therapy.

Potential pitfalls

Surgical carotid access under argatroban requires careful balancing of thrombotic and bleeding risks. Maintaining consciousness for neurological monitoring adds an anesthetic challenge, requiring adequate anesthesia for carotid exposure while avoiding excessive sedation; an intermediate cervical plexus block may cause dysphagia.

Take-home message

Integrating argatroban anticoagulation with locoregional anesthesia may address the competing requirements of surgical carotid access and continuous neurological monitoring in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia undergoing transcarotid transcatheter aortic valve implantation.

title: Valve-in-Root TAVI vs Redo Surgery in a Young Adult With Failed Bioprosthesis.
authorString: Purmessur R, D'Errico L, Costopoulos C, Ali J.
abstractText:
Topic of controversy

Whether valve-in-valve (ViV) transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) or redo surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) is preferred for structural valve degeneration of a Freestyle stentless aortic root in a young adult, and whether a Ross procedure at index surgery would have better served lifetime management.

Case summary

A 30-year-old man with a failed stentless aortic root (implanted at age 20 for bicuspid aortic valve regurgitation) presented with severe bioprosthetic regurgitation and ventricular dilatation. Transfemoral ViV TAVI with a 29-mm Edwards SAPIEN 3 Ultra Resilia was performed successfully.

Pro viewpoint

ViV TAVI avoids redo sternotomy, preserves future options, and aligns with patient preference to avoid anticoagulation.

Con viewpoint

Redo SAVR with a mechanical valve-and a Ross procedure at the index operation-may offer superior lifetime sequencing, avoiding constraints of successive transcatheter implants.

Take-home message

Lifetime planning must begin at the index operation; both ViV TAVI and redo SAVR require heart team deliberation with explicit consideration of all future interventions.

title: Early Introduction and Prolonged Full-Dose Anakinra Reduce Recurrence Risk After Discontinuation in Recurrent Pericarditis: An International Multicenter Cohort.
authorString: Malandrino D, Bettiol A, Andreis A, De Ferrari GM, Scudeler L, Agosti A, Caforio ALP, Canfora M, Cantarini L, Cercek AC, Dagna L, Insalaco A, Gattorno M, Caorsi R, Klein A, Lazaros G, Lopalco G, Luis SA, Maestroni S, Mattioli I, Manna R, Mardigyan V, Simonini G, Silvestri E, Tavoni A, Imazio M, Brucato A, Emmi G, International Pericarditis Anakinra Discontinuation Study Group.

journal.title: Journal of the American Heart Association

abstractText:
Background

Anakinra is effective in recurrent pericarditis, yet optimal treatment duration and strategies for safe drug discontinuation remain uncertain. Identifying predictors of sustained remission after discontinuation is important for clinical management.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed 185 consecutive adult patients with corticosteroid-dependent and colchicine-resistant refractory recurrent pericarditis across 16 international referral centers, who permanently discontinued therapy after clinical remission. The primary end point was pericarditis recurrence after drug discontinuation. Univariate and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression and Kaplan-Meier analyses were performed to identify demographic, clinical, and therapeutic predictors of postdiscontinuation relapse.

Results

Among 185 patients who discontinued anakinra (58.4% women, mean age 50.4±17.8 years, 77% idiopathic cause), treatment was initiated a median of 10 months (interquartile range [IQR], 4.0-19.5) after the first episode and continued at 100 mg/d for a median of 6 months (IQR, 4-12). Over a median follow-up of 7.2 months (IQR, 1.5-23.3) after discontinuation, 68 patients (36.8%) experienced recurrence, with a median time to recurrence of 2.1 months (IQR, 0.7-8.5). Initiation within 12 months from the first pericarditis episode and maintenance of full-dose therapy (100 mg/d) for ≥6 months were independently associated with lower recurrence risk (hazard ratio [HR], 0.33 [95% CI, 0.18-0.66]; P=0.001 and HR, 0.48 [95% CI, 0.23-0.86]; P=0.017; respectively).

Conclusions

Early initiation of anakinra and maintenance of full-dose therapy for at least 6 months are associated with a significantly lower risk of relapse after discontinuation and may inform treatment duration and discontinuation strategies in recurrent pericarditis.

title: Combined Karyotyping, Copy Number Variation Sequencing, and Whole Exome Sequencing in the Prenatal Diagnosis of Congenital Heart Disease: Detection Rates and Phenotypic Associations.
authorString: Xie J, Huang Y, Yao X, Zhang L, Zhou Y, Wang W, Zhang J, Ge Y.
abstractText:
Objective

This study aimed to assess the value of genetic testing in the prenatal congenital heart disease (CHD) diagnosis and evaluate the relationship between genetic variants and prenatal phenotypes.

Methods

A total of 235 fetuses with CHD were classified into three groups: A: isolated simple CHD, B: isolated complex CHD, and C: non-isolated CHD. All patients underwent karyotyping and copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq), with whole-exome sequencing (WES) performed when indicated. Statistical analyses conducted using IBM SPSS assessed the diagnostic performance of the genetic testing and detection rates across CHD subtypes.

Results

Karyotyping and CNV-seq revealed that chromosomal abnormality detection, particularly numerical abnormalities, was significantly associated with extracardiac anomalies (p < 0.05). In contrast, the detection rates of pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) CNVs (CNV-seq, p = 0.384) and pathogenic gene variants (WES, p = 0.624) did not differ significantly among the three groups. The severity of intracardiac abnormalities, the presence of extracardiac anomalies, and the detection of genetic abnormalities significantly influenced parental decisions regarding pregnancy termination (p < 0.05). The combination of karyotyping and CNV-seq increased the detection rate by 5.11%. In karyotyping/CNV-seq-negative fetuses who underwent WES, WES increased the detection rate by 37.21% (16/43).

Conclusion

Combined genetic testing significantly improved the detection rate and the detection of chromosomal numerical abnormalities was strongly associated with the presence of extracardiac anomalies. Parental decisions regarding pregnancy continuation were significantly influenced by the severity of intracardiac abnormalities, the presence of extracardiac anomalies, and the identification of genetic abnormalities.

title: Septal dysfunction and Abnormal Systolic Stretch Are Associated with Right Ventricular Dysfunction in Repaired Tetralogy of Fallot.
authorString: Fournier E, Joye R, Bitterman Y, Hui W, Mueller B, Runeckles K, Pozza A, Hascoet S, Mertens L, Friedberg MK.

journal.title: Journal of the American Society of Echocardiography : official publication of the American Society of Echocardiography

abstractText:
Aims

Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is a major determinant of outcomes after Tetralogy of Fallot repair (rToF). Although right bundle branch block is present in most patients and electro-mechanical dyssynchrony (EMD) has been associated with RV dysfunction, only a subset of patients ultimately develops RV dysfunction. We hypothesized that septal dysfunction is a key feature associated with the development of EMD-induced RV dysfunction in rToF.

Methods

We retrospectively studied 126 pediatric rToF patients (median age 14.7 years) with contemporaneous ECG, echocardiography, and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) between 2019-2025. Septal mechanics were quantified by strain-derived systolic rebound stretch (SRS) and further combined with RV free-wall mechanics into a systolic stretch index (SSI). RV mechanical dyssynchrony was visually classified, with septal contraction abrogation and systolic stretch as key features. Multivariable models evaluated associations between systolic stretch parameters and RV dysfunction (CMR-derived RV ejection fraction (EF) ≤ 46%), adjusting for relevant covariates.

Results

RV dysfunction was present in 24.6% of patients. Patients with >moderate RV outflow tract obstruction (peak gradient >40 mmHg) were excluded, median pulmonary regurgitant fraction was 35% (IQR, 26-44%). Median SSI was higher in patients with RV dysfunction than in those without (8.9% (IQR 3.2-11.3) vs 2.9% (IQR 1.5-5.5), p<0.001). Premature termination of septal deformation with subsequent stretching, quantified by SRS, was associated with RV dysfunction (p<0.001). Worse septal stretch patterns were associated with RV dysfunction, larger RV end-systolic indexed volume, and longer QRSd (p<0.001). Higher SSI was independently associated with lower RVEF (p<0.001) after adjustment for age, QRSd, RV dilation, and surgical substrate (p<0.001), whereas QRSd lost significance on RVEF after adjusting for SSI. RVEF was lower at SSI values >4%. SSI demonstrated excellent intraobserver and interobserver reproducibility (ICC 0.996 and 0.997, respectively).

Conclusions

In pediatric rToF, RV dysfunction was associated with abnormal septal contraction and systolic stretch. RV-SSI, integrating inefficient RV mechanics via septal and RV free-wall systolic stretch, was independently associated with RV dysfunction beyond QRSd, RV volumes and pulmonary regurgitation severity. These findings may help characterize RV electromechanical phenotypes and provide a rationale for future studies evaluating RV resynchronization therapy.

title: Are we Adhering to Guidelines for Follow-up Imaging in Neonates with Simple Congenital Heart Defects? What are the Healthcare Costs of Non-adherence?
authorString: Hammad ZAA, Coo H, Suntharalingam H, Alhamwi S, Penslar J, Alsalehi M.
abstractText: Simple congenital heart defects (CHDs) are frequently identified via neonatal echocardiograms ("echos"). In 2020, the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology issued guidelines for follow-up imaging of CHDs. In this retrospective study, we evaluated adherence to these guidelines at an academic health center in Southeastern Ontario. The cohort included neonates who had one or more simple CHDs diagnosed in the first 30 days of life between April 1, 2020, and March 31, 2024. We reviewed electronic medical records up to September 30, 2025 to examine (a) rates of non-adherence to guideline-recommended follow-up imaging; (b) factors that may contribute to non-adherence; and (c) the costs of excessive imaging. Among 248 patients, 376 echos were performed over the study period. Adherence status could be determined for 320. Follow-up for 39.7% of echos did not adhere to the guidelines, primarily because repeat echos were performed earlier than recommended. Non-adherence was substantially higher for lesions requiring surveillance imaging, as per guidelines, compared with lesions where follow-up imaging is not recommended or findings were normal (91.9% vs. 12.0%; OR = 83.4, 95% CI: 37.5-185.5). The pediatric cardiologist's recommendation was documented for 74.5% of echos, but only 48.9% of recommendations aligned with the guidelines. Non-adherence was higher when recommendations were not documented or deviated from the guidelines. Sixty-two echos were deemed excessive, corresponding to $13,339 in extra imaging costs. The high rate of non-adherence to guideline-recommended follow-up imaging for simple CHDs highlights an opportunity to reduce unnecessary healthcare costs through consistent documentation of guideline-aligned follow-up recommendations by pediatric cardiologists.

title: Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance Predictors of Residual Pulmonary Regurgitation and Biventricular Recovery After Pulsta Valve Implantation.
authorString: Baek SM, Ahn C, Lee SY, Park WY, Lim HG, Lee W, Seo J, Son KH, Kim GB.
abstractText: Current recommendations for pulmonary valve replacement are based primarily on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR)-derived right ventricular (RV) volume thresholds established in repaired tetralogy of Fallot. However, patients undergoing self-expanding percutaneous pulmonary valve implantation (PPVI) often have mixed pulmonary regurgitation (PR) and pulmonary stenosis with heterogeneous right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) anatomy. We investigated CMR predictors of residual PR, residual RV enlargement (RVE), and residual biventricular imbalance (BVI) after Pulsta PPVI. We retrospectively analyzed 98 patients with paired pre- and post-procedural CMR. Residual PR was defined as post-procedural PR fraction (PRF) ≥10%, residual RVE as RV end-diastolic volume index (RVEDVi) ≥130 mL/m<sup>2</sup>, and residual BVI as an RV/LV end-diastolic volume ratio ≥1.5. Multivariable regression and restricted cubic spline analyses identified predictors of post-procedural remodeling. Residual PR occurred in 40.8% of patients, residual RVE in 38.8%, and residual BVI in 40.8%. Pyramidal/convex main pulmonary artery morphology and higher baseline PRF independently predicted residual PR, whereas reverse pyramidal/concave morphology was associated with lower residual RVE risk. Higher pre-procedural RV/LV ratio independently predicted residual BVI. RVEDVi z-score remained independently associated with RVEDVi reduction after adjustment for baseline RVEDVi. Although RV volumes decreased substantially after PPVI, LV remodeling varied considerably, and both RVEDVi and LVEDVi change independently contributed to recovery of ventricular balance. After Pulsta PPVI, anatomical factors influence residual PR and RV remodeling. RVEDVi z-score and RV/LV ratio provide complementary information that may improve patient selection.

title: In Vitro Models to Study Fibroelastic Remodeling of the Endocardium in Congenital Heart Disease.
authorString: Gaal J, Zajac C, Doettl SC, von Piechowski M, Saraci K, Weixler V, Diaz-Gil D, Del Nido PJ, Friehs I.
abstractText: Congenital heart defects (CHD) are characterized by pathological intracardiac blood flow, exposing the endocardium to disturbed shear stress. This contributes to the development of endocardial fibroelastosis (EFE), a restrictive fibrotic remodeling process associated with diastolic dysfunction. Despite the pathomechanistic role of the endocardium in CHD, EFE-derived endocardial endothelial cells (EdEECs) remain largely understudied. No standardized protocol exists for isolating and purifying them from human pediatric tissue. Tissue from N = 15 pediatric patients with (1) hypoplastic left heart syndrome, (2) pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum, and (3) pulmonary vein stenosis was included. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT). EdEECs were isolated from resected EFE tissue using CD144-based magnetic separation. Enrichment of the endocardial phenotype was evaluated by flow cytometry, immunocytochemistry and RT-qPCR. To mimic disease-like conditions, EdEECs were exposed to in vitro shear stress and transforming growth factor beta 1. EFE driven by fibrogenic activation of EECs through EndMT was observed in the left ventricle, right ventricle, and left atrium in patients with different CHDs. Magnetic CD144-based isolation provided a reliable, gentle approach to purify EdEECs from cardiac tissue, achieving > 95% purity while reproducibly preserving endocardial identity at both the protein and gene expression levels. Isolated EdEECs retained their intrinsic, disease-specific predisposition and vulnerability to EndMT under static, and high shear stress. Unlike healthy EECs (HEECs), physiological, low shear stress alone was not sufficient to restore the intrinsic fibrogenic vulnerability of EdEECs. EndMT-mediated EFE was observed across different CHD entities. A reproducible protocol for isolating and purifying EdEECs from EFE tissue preserves their endocardial phenotype and disease-specific characteristics. This provides a disease-mimicking in vitro model to study EdEEC-specific signaling pathways.

title: Ablation in Dextrocardia With Interrupted Inferior Vena Cava and Azygos Continuation to Coronary Sinus.
authorString: Liao X, Hu L, Ren L, Su X, Ma C, Guo X.
abstractText:
Background

Atrial fibrillation ablation in dextrocardia with interrupted inferior vena cava presents formidable technical challenges, particularly when anomalous systemic venous return distorts interatrial septal relationships.

Case summary

A 58-year-old man with drug-refractory paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, situs inversus totalis with dextrocardia, and inferior vena cava interruption with azygos continuation to the coronary sinus underwent catheter ablation. Lacking an inferior route, a superior approach through the left internal jugular vein was selected. Under intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) guidance, transseptal access was obtained using a dedicated wire-based system. Pulmonary vein isolation and roofline ablation were safely completed using radiofrequency energy.

Discussion

Azygos continuation to the coronary sinus drastically distorts interatrial geometry. ICE-guided, wire-based transseptal access via a superior route is a safe, practical alternative when conventional inferior access is unavailable and needle-based puncture poses high risks.

Take-home messages

In situs inversus, the left internal jugular vein offers an optimal trajectory for transseptal puncture via a superior approach. Using a dedicated transseptal guidewire instead of a rigid needle, strictly guided by ICE, reduces the risk of mechanical complications during atypical transseptal punctures in complex congenital heart disease.

title: Prenatal Diagnosis of Distal Aortopulmonary Window by Fetal Cardiac MRI.
authorString: Verley M, Anquetil S, Ferreira LN, Hamon M, Labombarda F.
abstractText:
Image

Prenatal diagnosis of a distal aortopulmonary window by fetal cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

Case summary

A fetus referred for cardiac MRI because of suboptimal visualization of the great vessels on ultrasound. MRI demonstrated a distal aortopulmonary window with a characteristic heart-shaped appearance of the great vessels.

Take-home message

Fetal cardiac MRI may provide complementary anatomical information when echocardiographic visualization is suboptimal and may help characterize complex fetal outflow tract abnormalities.

title: Sex-Specific Adaptations in Placental Mitochondrial Biogenesis and Function in babies Born with Critical Congenital Heart Disease.
authorString: Demonceaux M, Baruteau AE, Cloteau C, Gourdel M, Romefort B, Benbrik N, Vincke M, Devarenne G, Winer N, Ferchaud-Roucher V.
abstractText: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is the leading cause of birth defects; most critical (c)CHD newborns will develop neurodevelopmental disorders. Abnormal placental development may be involved, as genetics explains only 30% of sporadic CHD cases. Growing evidence suggests that placental dysfunction may result in heart and brain defects, as it shares a common early development. We hypothesized that newborns with critical CHD exhibit sex-specific alterations in placental mitochondrial biogenesis and function which may affect the fetal growth trajectory. Term placenta and paired umbilical cord (UC) blood were collected at birth from cCHD (n=16) and matched control (n=20) neonates. Mitochondrial lipid complex (phosphatidic acid (PA), phosphatidylglycerol (PG), cardiolipin (CL)), acylcarnitine metabolites and organic acids were determined in placenta by LC-MS/MS. Gene expressions of enzymes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics and lipid pathway were measured in placenta by RT-qPCR. Placental protein expressions of β-oxidation and OXPHOS were determined by Western Blot. Mitochondrial dynamics were reduced in cCHD placentas, particularly in male infants. Long-chain acylcarnitine (LC-acar) metabolites decreased in female cCHD placentas and increased in males, while they increased in both sexes in UC plasma. Malonate levels increased in cCHD placentas, affecting the TCA cycle. CL de novo synthesis was dysregulated in the cCHD placentas, though CL concentrations were similar in both groups. The cCHD placenta may compensate for cardiac defect in a potential sex-dependent manner, leading to an accumulation of LC-acylcarnitine in the UC plasma. Placental mitochondrial adaptation to metabolic needs may have a cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects.

title: Evolution of Tined Leadless Pacemaker Implantation: Patient Selection, Implant Volume, Center Characteristics, and Safety Trends.
authorString: Piccini JP, Higuera L, Yang Y, Crossley G, El-Chami MF.
abstractText:
Background

As leadless pacing approaches a decade in clinical practice, we sought to assess how device complications have changed over time, and how variations in patient, implanter volume, and facility characteristics are associated with these changes.

Objective

To examine rates of cardiac perforations after leadless pacemaker implantation over time, and the associations between patient, implanter volume, and facility characteristics with these outcomes, including the extent of variation attributable to implanters and facilities.

Methods

Medicare claims linked to a manufacturer's device registration data were used to identify patients implanted with a tined leadless pacemaker from 2017 to 2024. Patient selection across implanters and facilities was evaluated by examining differences in patient characteristics and their impact on patient-adjusted model estimates. Random-intercept models were fitted to estimate variation attributable to implanters and facilities.

Results

Among 46,698 implants, 19,446 (41.6%) were Micra AV; patients had a mean age of 80.4 years and a high Charlson Comorbidity Index (4.7±3.4). Cardiac perforation rates declined over time (adjusted Coefficient -0.13, 95% CI -0.19 - -0.06, p-value<0.01). Higher implanter volume was associated with fewer perforations (OR 0.93 per additional 10 implants, 95% CI 0.88-0.98; p-value<0.01). Differences in patient characteristics across providers and facilities were observed; however, adjustment for these differences did not materially alter the associations between implanters and facility and perforation rates.

Conclusion

In Medicare patients with tined leadless pacemakers, cardiac perforation rates declined over time and were lower in those implanted by more experienced implanters. Variation in outcomes was more closely associated with implanters than facilities.

title: Practical Approaches to Coronary Venous Ethanol Ablation for Refractory Ventricular Arrhythmias: Technique Selection and Clinical Outcomes.
authorString: Mori T, Ishikawa M, Kitamura K, Fukuju M, Funasaka T, Kaneshiro M, Ishiguro N, Tanaka A, Ando M, Goto H, Miyata S, Kato K.
abstractText:
Background

Coronary venous ethanol ablation (CVEA) is a promising alternative for refractory ventricular arrhythmias (VAs); however, it has limited availability, lacks guideline support, and comprises heterogeneous procedural techniques.

Objective

To evaluate the acute efficacy, safety, and long-term outcomes of CVEA in refractory VAs and outline practical techniques of CVEA.

Methods

Consecutive patients undergoing VA ablation at our center between December 2017 and December 2025 were screened; CVEA was performed after unsuccessful endocardial RFA. We performed CVEA using either tip injection, conventional double-balloon, or modified double-balloon techniques based on venous anatomy.

Results

Among 204 consecutive patients undergoing VA ablation, 55 had VAs refractory to endocardial RFA. Of these, 42 with a coronary venous electrogram preceding VA onset by >20 ms underwent CVEA, including 33 with premature ventricular contraction (PVC) and 9 with ventricular tachycardia (VT). Acute success was achieved in 32/33 patients with PVC and all patients with VT. During a median follow-up of 1,024 days, long-term success was achieved in 22 patients with PVC and 5 with VT. No association was observed between intraprocedural findings and long-term recurrence. CVEA-related procedural complications occurred in 13 patients, with no fatal events reported. Exploratory analyses suggested favorable outcomes for the modified double-balloon technique in anatomically selected cases and an association between higher ethanol volume and ethanol-related complications.

Conclusion

In patients with VAs refractory to endocardial RFA, CVEA was associated with favorable acute and long-term outcomes, with no fatal complications. Technique selection should be tailored to the venous anatomy, with judicious ethanol volume adjustment.

title: Unipolar Electrograms at the Pulmonary Vein Antrum: Spatial and Directional Heterogeneity with Distinct Postablation Morphologies.
authorString: Do U, Nam GB.
abstractText:
Background

Disappearance of the near-field S-wave in the unipolar electrogram (U-EGM) is commonly used to assess lesion formation during pulmonary vein (PV) isolation; however, interpretation of U-EGMs in anatomically complex atrial regions remains uncertain.

Objective

We aimed to characterize spatial, directional, and postablation changes in antral PV U-EGMs, and evaluate the limitations of conventional waveform interpretation.

Methods

In 15 patients undergoing radiofrequency ablation for atrial fibrillation, U-EGMs were recorded at 116 antral PV sites during sinus rhythm and distal coronary sinus (CS) pacing before and after ablation. U-EGM morphology and R- and S-wave amplitudes were analyzed.

Results

Baseline U-EGMs showed spatial heterogeneity, with a small r and deep S in the right anterior PV antrum transitioning to a positive-dominant morphology (Rs) in the left-lower PV antra. Distal CS pacing altered the activation sequence, causing direction-dependent changes, most prominently in the right PV antrum. After ablation, overall S-wave amplitude decreased from -0.94 ± 0.70 to -0.08 ± 0.55 mV (P<0.001). Residual negative deflections ≥0.5 mV persisted in 18.1% (21/116) of recordings, frequently in association with direction-dependent far-field activity. Newly developed positive deflections ≥1.0 mV were observed in 17/116 sites (14.7%; mean 1.42 ± 0.42 mV), predominantly in the right-sided antra.

Conclusions

Antral PV U-EGMs frequently represent composites of near- and far-field signals with spatial heterogeneity and direction-dependent variation. Postablation responses are diverse, including S-wave disappearance, residual negativity, often reflecting contributions from overlapping far-field components, and newly developed positive deflections. PV-antral U-EGMs should be interpreted in the context of their composite nature.
