title: The Red Blood Cell–Liver Axis: A New Framework for Iron Homeostasis and Liver Biology
Pathogenicity assessment of a bicuspid aortic valve-associated <i>ELASTIN</i> variant using a zebrafish model.
authorString: Bernard VG, Théron A, Drouard A, Avierinos JF, Jopling C, Zaffran S, Faucherre A.
abstractText:
Introduction

Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is one of the most common congenital heart defects but its genetic basis remains incompletely defined. Extracellular matrix components play key roles in outflow tract (OFT) and valve development, but their contribution to BAV is not fully established. Following the analysis of a cohort of BAV patients, we identified a family harbouring a rare human ELASTIN (ELN) variant (p.Gln691X). Here, we investigated the pathogenicity of this variant using an in vivo zebrafish model.

Methods

We generated a zebrafish elna/b double knockout (KO) using an RNAless CRISPR Cas9 strategy to avoid genetic compensation. Cardiovascular morphology and function were assessed in mutant embryos. To evaluate pathogenicity of the human ELN p.Gln691X variant, mutant and control embryos were rescued by mRNA injection encoding either WT human ELN or the p.Gln691X variant.

Results

elna/b double KO zebrafish exhibited cardiovascular defects including OFT anomalies, reduced stroke volume and dysmorphic aortic valves, highlighting Elastin's critical role in cardiac development. We then used this model to test the ELN variant identified in the BAV family. We found that wild-type ELN mRNA was able to restore normal cardiac function and morphology, whereas the variant ELN mRNA failed to do so.

Discussion

Our study establishes a robust in vivo model to assess ELN variant pathogenicity and provides evidence linking ELASTIN to BAV, opening new avenues for uncovering the genetic mechanisms underlying BAV.

title: Olfactory dysfunction and submicroscopic abnormalities: unveiling hidden pathologies.
authorString: Bilińska K, Pasińska M, de Castro F.
abstractText: Recent advances in high-resolution genomic technologies have revealed that several syndromes are associated with submicroscopic chromosomal deletions and, less frequently, duplications, thereby substantially contributing to the functional annotation of the human genome. Among these structural variants, recurrent microdeletions or microduplications often disrupt dosage-sensitive genes, leading to shared phenotypic outcomes in affected individuals. While features such as congenital heart defects, neurodevelopmental delays, and intellectual disability (ID) have been extensively studied, phenotypes resulting in olfactory dysfunction remain largely underexplored. Here, we review reported cases of copy number variants (CNVs) in patients with isolated or syndromic olfactory impairment and stratify the strength of associations between CNVs and olfactory dysfunction using predefined evidence levels. The available evidence ranges from well-supported loci with documented human olfactory phenotypes and mechanistic evidence to hypothesis-generating observations based primarily on isolated cases or biological plausibility. By distinguishing these levels of evidence, we highlight both established dosage-sensitive pathways involved in olfactory development and major limitations of the current literature, including incomplete olfactory phenotyping and the difficulty of interpreting large multigenic CNVs. This framework may facilitate more rigorous genotype-phenotype interpretation in congenital and syndromic olfactory disorders.

title: Neonatal and pediatric nutritional care: a modified Delphi consensus on dietary management for infants with congenital heart disease in four Middle Eastern countries.
authorString: Kotby A, Adel A, Hussein BA, Moustafa EBO, Al-Harby F, Moustafa HSH, Al-Husseiny M, Al-Soufi M, Assiri M, Al-Gasmi M, Metwally MH, Matter M, Al Farsy MS, Abdul Rahim RK, Abdelkarim R.
abstractText:
Background

In the absence of localized guidelines for the Middle East region, management of infant malnutrition secondary to congenital heart disease (CHD) can lead to suboptimal outcomes and may aggravate patient conditions. In this consensus document, we aimed to guide health care professionals on care pathways and establish regionally relevant recommendations for the nutritional assessment and management of infants with CHD.

Methods

Fifteen experts from four Middle Eastern countries participated in a two-round modified Delphi process. The included statements were initially developed following a literature review and subsequently refined based on feedback from a steering committee of five experts preselected from the panelists' group for the first voting round. The second voting round, involving the other ten panelists, determined the final voting results. Follow-up discussions were utilized when needed. Consensus was predefined as ≥80% agreement, and statements meeting this threshold were included in the final document.

Results

Consensus was reached with a total of 43 statements, representing 87.8% of the suggested statements. The consensus statements established essential components and cut-off points for diagnosing malnutrition, specified values for enteral and parenteral feeding, caloric and fluid requirements and management, feeding practices and use of formula, and care in acute and critical settings. The highest agreement level was associated with the perioperative nutrition recommendations, while nutritional support recommendations faced the largest variability in response. In the latter, areas where a heterogeneity in clinical practice was observed, reflected by the lack of consensus, were identified.

Conclusion

This consensus document provides a general framework for the assessment, management, and follow-up of infants with CHD with compromised nutritional status in four Middle Eastern countries, bridging the gap between existing international guidelines and real-world clinical practice.

title: Impact of social determinants of health on perioperative and interstage outcomes in congenital heart surgery a systematic review.
authorString: Sakowitz S, Nelson JS, Robinson J, Rossi CS, Shahian DM, Cooke DT, Jacobs JP, Aughtman S, Schultz M, Nathan M, Beaty C, Shafer M, Kozik D, Pelletier GJ.
abstractText:
Importance

Social determinants of health (SDoH)- conditions in which patients live, grow, and age,-are increasingly recognized to influence the health of patients with congenital heart disease (CHD).

Objective

To explore the impact of SDoH on short-term mortality and morbidity, interstage outcomes, and resource utilization, among patients following congenital heart surgery.

Evidence review

A systematic review was completed according to PRISMA guidelines. Relevant studies evaluating the association of SDoH with surgical outcomes of pediatric and adult CHD patients were identified from five databases queried including PubMed, SCOPUS, CINAHL, PYSCINFO, and Cochrane between January 1999 and February 2024. Inclusion criteria incorporated prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses, secondary analyses of prospectively collected trial data, and prospective or retrospective cohort studies. Subsequent reference searches identified 39 related articles. SDoH included patient and neighborhood level metrics. Two independent reviewers screened studies for full-text review, with data extraction by an expert panel.

Findings

Among 1,224 studies identified, 157 articles underwent full-text review and 121 were ultimately selected for data extraction. Eighty-Five articles did not address acute postoperative outcomes and were excluded. Thirty-six studies focused on acute or interstage outcomes following congenital heart surgery and served as the source information. The remainder were retrospective cohort studies using various databases. The number of study participants ranged from 98 to 174,352 (median = 6,979). Factors found to be linked with greater likelihood of in-hospital mortality included Black race, Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, Medicaid insurance, and lower neighborhood socioeconomic status. Both individual and neighborhood level determinants were associated with longer interstage periods, higher complication rates, as well as greater resource utilization and hospital readmissions. Two critical timespans for intervention to reduce inequities in care were the neonatal period and young adulthood.

Conclusions and relevance

SDoH impact both acute and interstage outcomes in patients following surgery for CHD. Developing interventions to increase access to and engagement with quality care and out-of-hospital support may improve both short-term outcomes and reduce systems-level financial burden. Systematic Review Registration.

title: Changes in birth certificate-reported prevalence of congenital anomalies at live birth during the COVID-19 pandemic: a nationwide study of 26 million United States live births.
authorString: Chen Q, Liang D, Wang S.

journal.title: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

abstractText:
Background

Although the majority of studies have indicated that maternal severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) vaccination are not associated with neonatal birth defects, it is relevant to examine whether the disease burden changed during the COVID-19 pandemic, as other influencing factors may have also changed. We aimed to compare the birth certificate-reported prevalence of congenital anomalies at live birth before and during the pandemic.

Methods

Using public birth data, all live births from 2016 to 2022 in the United States of America (USA) were retrospectively included. The birth certificate-reported prevalence at live birth of selected congenital anomalies identified from the birth certificate, including anencephaly, meningomyelocele/spina bifida, cyanotic congenital heart disease (CCHD), congenital diaphragmatic hernia, omphalocele, gastroschisis, limb reduction defect, cleft lip, cleft palate, Down syndrome, chromosomal disorder, and hypospadias, was estimated and compared by calendar year of birth using logistic regression.

Results

A total of 26,345,765 live-born infants from 2016 to 2022 were included. The mean gestational age of the infants was 38.4 weeks (SD = 2.1 weeks), 48.9% were female babies, and 96.7% were singleton. The overall reported prevalence of congenital anomalies was highest in 2018 (3.51‰, 95%CI = 3.45‰-3.57‰) and has since shown a decreasing trend [3.38‰ (95%CI = 3.32‰-3.44‰) in 2019 and 3.35‰ (95%CI = 3.29‰-3.41‰) in 2022]. Using 2019 as a reference, it did not differ in 2020 and 2021 [odds ratio (OR) = 1.01 (0.98-1.03) and OR = 1.00 (0.98-1.03), respectively, after adjusting for maternal age, ethnicity/race, and socioeconomic status] and was slightly lower in 2022 [OR = 0.97 (0.95-0.99)]. For the majority of the congenital anomalies, the reported prevalence during the pandemic (2020-2022) remained unchanged or showed a decreasing trend (i.e., gastroschisis and Down syndrome) compared with that in 2019. The reported prevalence of CCHD was higher in 2021 and 2022 than in 2019. However, the increase had begun before the pandemic, and after correction for multiple comparisons, only the 2021 contrast remained significant. Segmented regression confirmed a significant pre-pandemic upward trend in CCHD with a level change dated to infants born in March 2020. When exposure was re-indexed by estimated year of conception, neither pandemic conception cohort differed from the 2019 conception cohort [2020: OR = 1.03 (0.97-1.09); 2021: OR = 1.02 (0.97-1.08)]. The direction of these results was consistent when stratified by gestational age (≥37 or <37 weeks), with wider intervals in the preterm stratum.

Conclusions

The birth certificate-reported prevalence of congenital anomalies at live birth did not increase during the COVID-19 pandemic in the USA and decreased for several specific anomalies. The higher reported prevalence of CCHD continues a trend that began before the pandemic and is null once exposure is aligned with organogenesis.

title: Immune profiling of anti-SSA-positive at-risk individuals reveals increased type I IFN activity preceding lymphocyte abnormalities in Sjögren's disease.
authorString: Ritter J, Stefanski AL, Aue A, Rincon-Arevalo H, Rapino L, Eren AN, Chen Y, Nitschke E, Dang VD, Wiedemann A, Schrezenmeier E, Lino AC, Szelinski F, Dörner T.
abstractText:
Objectives

Identifying immune features that distinguish asymptomatic autoantibody-positive at-risk individuals from patients with established autoimmune disease is key to understanding the evolution from autoreactivity to established autoimmune disease. This study investigated immune characteristics of anti-SSA-positive at-risk individuals, including pregnant women, compared with patients with Sjögren's disease (SjD) and healthy donors (HDs).

Methods

Peripheral blood samples were obtained from asymptomatic anti-SSA-positive women (at-risk individuals; n = 7, including two ongoing pregnancies with congenital heart block [CHB] and one woman with a prior CHB pregnancy), patients with SjD (n = 10), and age- and sex-matched HDs (n = 21; median age 35.1 years; 100% female). T- and B-cell subsets and IFN signaling molecules, including STAT1, phosphorylated STAT1 (pSTAT1), STAT2, IRF1, and IRF9, were analyzed by flow cytometry. In addition, circulating IFN subtypes were quantified in available plasma samples using the NULISA platform.

Results

At-risk individuals showed lower ANA and rheumatoid factor titers and lacked anti-SSB autoantibodies compared with patients with SjD. At-risk individuals had B-cell distributions similar to HDs, whereas patients with SjD showed a typical increase in naïve B cells and reduced pre-switched and switched memory B-cell frequencies, together with increased CD8+ T-cell frequencies and a non-significant trend toward reduced double-negative T-cell frequencies. At-risk individuals also showed significantly increased IFN activity, reflected by Siglec-1 (CD169) expression on CD14+ monocytes, compared with HDs, while levels tended to be lower than in patients with SjD. Two of three women with a current or previous CHB pregnancy had the highest Siglec-1 levels within the at-risk group. Cytokine profiling revealed a stage-associated IFN pattern, with IFN-α1 and IFN-ω already increased in at-risk individuals, whereas IFN-γ, IFN-β1, and type III IFNs showed a trend toward higher levels in established SjD. Intracellular STAT1 expression was elevated across CD19+ B-cell subsets in at-risk individuals compared with HDs, but was generally less pronounced than in SjD. IRF9 was also increased in B-cell subsets from at-risk individuals and patients with SjD compared with HDs. Similar findings were observed in CD3+ T-cell subsets, where STAT1 and IRF9 expression were elevated in at-risk individuals compared with HDs and were largely comparable to levels observed in patients with SjD.

Conclusions

Our data suggest that increased type I IFN activity and IFN-associated signaling in T- and B-cell subsets are already present in anti-SSA-positive at-risk individuals. In contrast, altered B- and T-cell homeostasis was restricted to established SjD, indicating progression from autoreactivity toward overt autoimmune disease.

title: Nutritional potential of invasive <i>Rugulopteryx okamurae</i>, of <i>Gelidium corneum</i> industrial by-product, and of five native Atlantic macroalgae as feedstocks for alternative protein production.
authorString: Zhao K, Cameselle C, Costas C, Orzechowska W, Woźniak Ł, Rodríguez-Martínez B, Cesário MT, Simal-Gandara J, Otero P.
abstractText: Macroalgae are increasingly considered sustainable resources for protein-oriented food and bioprocessing applications due to their rapid growth, wide availability, low freshwater and fertilizer requirements, and potential as natural sources of proteins and bioactive compounds. However, integrated assessments comparing native, invasive, and industrial side-stream macroalgal biomasses under the same nutritional and safety framework remain scarce, limiting the identification of suitable candidates for protein-oriented valorization. In this context, this study assessed seven Atlantic macroalgal biomasses from Spanish and Portuguese sources: the invasive brown seaweed Rugulopteryx okamurae (R. okamurae), the underutilized Cystoseira usneoides (C. usneoides), an industrial Gelidium corneum (G. corneum) by-product, and four commonly studied species, Saccharina latissima (S. latissima), Porphyra umbilicalis (P. umbilicalis), Gracilaria gracilis (G. gracilis), and Ulva rigida (U. rigida). A common analytical framework was applied to determine proximate composition, carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, amino acid and fatty acid profiles, nutritional indices, mineral and phenolic contents, heavy metals and in vitro cytotoxicity. The results showed that the red algae P. umbilicalis and G. gracilis exhibited the highest protein content among the evaluated macroalgae, with values of 30.78 and 22.69%, respectively, together with relatively low C/N ratio indicating nitrogen-rich compositions. Leucine, isoleucine, and phenylalanine were the predominant essential amino acids, whereas the G. corneum by-product displayed the highest total essential amino acid content (44.8 g/100 g protein) and essential amino acid index (141%). Most biomasses exceeded an essential amino acid index of 90%, supporting their nutritional relevance. Fatty acid analysis revealed unusually high monounsaturated fatty acids levels in R. okamurae and C. usneoides, with R. okamurae being the only brown alga containing both EPA and DHA. Moreover, in vitro cytotoxicity assays confirmed satisfactory biocompatibility and safety for most algal extracts. Overall, G. gracilis, P. umbilicalis and the G. corneum by-product emerged as the most promising candidates for protein-oriented valorization, providing a basis for the development of alternative protein ingredients and higher-value uses of macroalgal resources.

title: Liver Viscosity Imaging and Disease Severity in Alcohol-Associated Hepatitis: A Prospective Cross-Sectional Pilot Study

title: Complex surgical management of right-sided infective endocarditis following ventricular septal defect closure with residual shunt and ascending aortic pseudoaneurysm: a case report.
authorString: Katsui Y, Kato Y, Koyano T, Konno N, Oka N, Tatsuishi W.

journal.title: International journal of surgery case reports

abstractText:
Introduction and importance

Right-sided infective endocarditis is an uncommon condition, especially in patients with surgically repaired congenital heart disease. A residual shunt after ventricular septal defect closure can act as a substrate for late-onset infection, but such cases are rarely reported. High-velocity jet flow from a residual shunt may contribute to endothelial injury and subsequent infection. Furthermore, differentiating a late pseudoaneurysm at a prior cannulation site from an infectious aortic aneurysm is essential for guiding the appropriate treatment strategy.

Case presentation

A 49-year-old man with a history of ventricular septal defect closure in infancy presented with persistent fever and severe systemic inflammation. Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a highly mobile, filamentous vegetation measuring 12 × 56 mm attached to the tricuspid subvalvular apparatus. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed multiple septic pulmonary emboli and a saccular protrusion along the anterior wall of the ascending aorta, suggestive of an ascending aortic pseudoaneurysm. Blood cultures yielded methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Following clinical improvement and multiorgan stabilization with targeted antimicrobial therapy, the patient underwent elective surgery on hospital day 49, including residual defect closure, tricuspid valve replacement with a mechanical prosthesis, and localized pseudoaneurysm repair using a Hemashield patch.

Clinical discussion

This complex combination of pathologies highlights the pathophysiological impact of residual shunt-jet lesions. The clinical decision-making illustrates the challenges of balancing guideline recommendations for early surgery with the need for clinical stabilization.

Conclusion

This case highlights the importance of lifelong follow-up in adult congenital heart disease and provides important considerations for individualized surgical planning in complex cardiovascular pathologies.

title: "It's Not Like My Old Life, But It's Still Freedom": An ACTION learning network mixed methods analysis of the adolescent ventricular assist device experience at home.
authorString: Rea KE, Greiner E, Flaspohler K, Jenkins MC, Karahalios DS, Mijon M, Oliver S, Hutchinson Z, Joong A, Spinner J, Cousino MK.
abstractText:
Background

Pediatric patients supported with durable ventricular assist devices (VAD) are increasingly discharged home on device. Little is known about adolescent and young adult (AYA) experiences during this unique time. This study aims to further understand AYA VAD experience to improve supports and interventions upon discharge.

Methods

An 8-domain, 34-item semi-structured interview guide was developed, informed by prior adult VAD interview, pediatric literature, and multidisciplinary VAD team review, including patient/family advocates. AYAs currently or recently discharged home on durable VAD at an ACTION site were approached. Two authors independently coded qualitative responses using a priori codes for thematic analysis. Inter-rater reliability was achieved.

Results

Seventeen AYAs (M=17.40 years) completed semi-structured interviews. The majority were male (76%) and half were White race (53%). All were supported on HeartMate3, most commonly with underlying diagnosis of dilated cardiomyopathy (76%). Length of heart failure ranged from 2 weeks to 9 years prior to device implant. AYAs provided insights across several domains. Most common worries were emergency situations (82%), infection (71%), and bleeding (71%). All reported some limitations, including engagement with friends (71%), sports (59%), and freedom of movement (47%).

Conclusion

Significant life disruptions and coping challenges are prevalent among AYAs discharged home on VAD. Robust psychosocial supports are indicated, including access to multidisciplinary care providers who are aware of the intricacies of managing VAD outpatient. Given remarks from AYAs regarding importance of peer connection, results highlight AYA peer and caregiver support groups and online communities as future directions.

title: Neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging for preoperative evaluation of cerebral microstructure and neurodevelopment in children with congenital heart disease.
authorString: Xu S, Zhang J, Wang S, Qian J, Zhu D, Zhang J.

journal.title: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery

abstractText:
Background

Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a type of heart structure defect caused by the abnormal development of the heart and major blood vessels during the embryonic stage. With the continuous innovation of surgical treatment techniques and the improvement of perioperative management, the survival rate of children with CHD has significantly improved. However, accompanying central nervous system development problems have become increasingly prominent. This study investigated the clinical utility of neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) in evaluating preoperative cerebral microstructural features and neurodevelopmental status in children with CHD.

Methods

Fifty-five infants with CHD were prospectively enrolled in the CHD group, and 55 age- and sex-comparable typically developing infants were included as the control group. All participants completed the Gesell Development Schedules assessment. The developmental quotient (DQ) and domain-specific subscale scores for five core developmental domains were recorded: adaptive behavior (AB), fine motor (FM), gross motor (GM), language (L), and personal-social behavior (PSB). Diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI) was acquired in all participants, and multiparametric NODDI maps were generated on a postprocessing workstation (Siemens Healthineers). The derived quantitative parameters included extracellular volume fraction (ECVF), neurite density index (NDI), isotropic volume fraction (ISOVF), and the orientation dispersion index (ODI). Intergroup differences in NODDI parameters and Gesell developmental scores were statistically analyzed. Pearson product-moment correlation analysis was then applied to evaluate associations between region-specific NODDI parameters and individual Gesell domain scores within the CHD group.

Results

The ECVF in the splenium of the corpus callosum (SCC) of the CHD group was significantly lower than that of the control group (t=-2.261; P=0.026), whereas the ECVF in the frontal white matter (FWM) was significantly higher (t=2.242, P=0.027). ODI measurements in the posterior limb of the internal capsule (PLIC) were significantly lower in the CHD group than in the control group (t=2.401; P=0.018). Intracellular volume fraction (ICVF) values in the PLIC and SCC were also significantly higher in the CHD group (PLIC: t=4.489, P<0.001; SCC: t=2.388, P=0.019). ODI measurements in the occipital white matter (OWM) were significantly lower in the CHD group than in the control group (t=3.707; P<0.001). Compared to the control group, the CHD group had significantly lower ISOVF measurements in the PTR (t=-2.119, P=0.038), FWM (t=-2.825, P=0.006), OWM (t=-2.253; P=0.028), and temporal white matter (t=-2.164; P=0.034). Correlation analysis further showed that Gesell scores, including DQ, AB, FM, GM, L, and PSB, were consistently lower in the CHD group than in the control group. Within the CHD cohort, the NDI value of the PLIC showed a positive correlation with DQ, AB, FM, GM, L, and PSB, whereas the ODI value of the PLIC showed a positive correlation with PSB. The ISOVF value of the genu of the corpus callosum showed a positive correlation with DQ, AB, L, and PSB. The NDI value of the SCC showed a positive correlation with AB and L.

Conclusions

NODDI sensitively detects preoperative cerebral microstructural changes in children with CHD, and its key parameters correlate with preoperative neurodevelopmental performance. Thus, NODDI-derived parameters may serve as candidate imaging biomarkers for evaluating brain microstructure and development before surgery, offering objective imaging-based support for early clinical assessment and timely intervention.

title: Holt-Oram syndrome presenting with failure to thrive due to a hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus: the importance of early cardiac evaluation in infants with radial ray abnormalities.
authorString: Ibrahim R, Al-Dairy A, Ibrahim R, Srour S.

journal.title: International journal of surgery case reports

abstractText:
Background

Holt-Oram syndrome (HOS) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the TBX5 gene and characterized by radial ray malformations associated with congenital heart defects and/or cardiac conduction abnormalities. Although atrial and ventricular septal defects are the most common cardiac manifestations, other congenital cardiac lesions may occur. Early recognition of cardiac involvement is essential to prevent complications and improve outcomes.

Case presentation

We report the case of an 8-month-old female infant presenting with failure to thrive, feeding difficulties, and mild respiratory distress. She had unilateral radial ray abnormalities, including complete absence of the left thumb and index finger with associated radial, carpal, and humeral hypoplasia. Physical examination revealed bounding peripheral pulses and a continuous machinery murmur. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with pulmonary hypertension and left-sided volume overload. Computed tomography angiography confirmed the diagnosis and excluded associated great vessel anomalies. Based on the characteristic upper limb abnormalities, congenital heart disease, and sinus bradycardia, a clinical diagnosis of HOS was established. Surgical ligation of the PDA was successfully performed without complications. At 6-month follow-up, the patient showed complete resolution of heart failure symptoms, satisfactory catch-up growth, and normal postoperative cardiac findings.

Discussion

This case expands the recognized cardiac phenotype of HOS by describing a hemodynamically significant PDA presenting with failure to thrive and pulmonary hypertension. It also illustrates that the severity of skeletal abnormalities does not predict the type or severity of associated cardiac disease, emphasizing the need for comprehensive cardiovascular assessment in all infants with radial ray abnormalities.

Conclusion

Early recognition of HOS and prompt cardiovascular evaluation are critical for identifying treatable congenital heart defects. Timely intervention, combined with multidisciplinary long-term care, can significantly improve clinical, functional, and developmental outcomes in affected children.

title: Multimodality imaging and surgical management of a rare combination: type 2A bridging bronchus, pulmonary artery sling, and atrial septal defect, a case report.
authorString: Liu J, Song J, Pei X, Li C, Li D, Lu Y, Chen J, Liu C.
abstractText: We report the case of a 15-year-old female presenting with exertional syncope and a history of refractory respiratory symptoms. Comprehensive preoperative multimodality imaging-including echocardiography, multi-detector computed tomography (MDCT) with three-dimensional reconstruction, and bronchoscopy-revealed a rare complex of congenital anomalies: a type 2 A bridging bronchus (BB), a pulmonary artery sling (PAS), and an atrial septal defect (ASD). Crucially, imaging confirmed the absence of significant tracheal stenosis, thereby obviating the need for tracheoplasty. The patient successfully underwent surgical repair via median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass, which included reimplantation of the left pulmonary artery and patch closure of the ASD. Postoperative MDCT confirmed patency of the reconstructed pulmonary artery and the patient's symptoms resolved. This case underscores the indispensable role of advanced imaging in the diagnosis and surgical planning of complex congenital cardiopulmonary anomalies, particularly for guiding a tailored surgical approach in the setting of rare associations like BB and PAS.

title: Advancements in echocardiography for congenital heart defects (CHDs): a literature review.
authorString: Humayun MA, Jammal C, Zhou A, Ali A, Maqbool H, Zaib Khan A, Zaheer A, Shreshtha J, Akbar A.
abstractText: Congenital heart defects (CHDs) are the most prevalent congenital condition globally, affecting approximately 1% of live births and contributing to significant morbidity and mortality. While advancements in diagnostic imaging have improved early detection and management, CHDs remain a leading cause of infant mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income regions. Echocardiography has evolved as a cornerstone in CHD diagnosis, with traditional modalities such as 2D echocardiography, M-mode, and Doppler imaging providing essential structural and hemodynamic assessments. However, these conventional approaches have limitations in visualizing complex congenital anomalies. The emergence of advanced echocardiographic techniques, including three-dimensional echocardiography, fetal echocardiography, speckle tracking echocardiography (STE), and stress echocardiography (SE), has significantly enhanced diagnostic accuracy, preoperative planning, and long-term monitoring. Furthermore, recent innovations in artificial intelligence (AI), deep learning, digital signal processing, and contrast-enhanced echocardiography are revolutionizing the field by automating image analysis, improving image quality, and enabling predictive modeling for CHD prognosis. This review critically compares traditional and advanced echocardiographic modalities, evaluating their respective strengths, limitations, and impact on early CHD detection. Additionally, it explores emerging AI-driven technologies and their potential to optimize echocardiographic workflows, reduce diagnostic variability, and enhance patient outcomes. By synthesizing current evidence, this review aims to provide clinicians, researchers, and healthcare policymakers with insights into the evolving role of echocardiography in CHD diagnosis and management.

title: Native Spleen T1 Mapping for the Assessment of Hepatic Congestion in Children With Congenital Heart Disease.
authorString: Tao K, Yamamura K, Sato M, Sagawa K, Ishikawa Y.
abstractText:
Background

Congestive hepatopathy in congenital heart disease (CHD) can lead to portal hypertension. Liver native T1 relaxation time (LT1) was reported to be associated with elevated central venous pressure and liver injury in CHD. This study investigated the utility of spleen native T1 relaxation time (ST1) in children with CHD, particularly those with Fontan circulation, and its association with hemodynamic parameters and biomarkers of liver injury.

Methods and results

This study included 120 patients with CHD (biventricular repair, 39; bidirectional Glenn shunt, 31; and Fontan circulation, 50) who underwent blood tests, cardiac catheterization, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging performed within 48 h. Age-corrected ST1 (cST1; expressed as a percentage of normal) was calculated based on data from 22 control subjects (healthy children: no structural heart disease, normal cardiac function, normal systemic hemodynamics). cST1 was significantly correlated with net inferior vena cava (IVC) flow in both the overall cohort (r=0.364, P<0.001) and Fontan group (r=0.368, P<0.009). Multiple linear regression analysis showed that aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (P=0.011), LT1 (P=0.005), and net IVC flow (P=0.041) remained independent predictors of cST1 in the overall cohort, whereas AST (P<0.001) and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease fibrosis scores (P=0.029) were independent predictors in the Fontan group.

Conclusions

Age-corrected ST1 may serve as a non-invasive surrogate marker of systemic venous congestion and hepatic involvement in children with CHD.

title: Oxidative Stress in Neonatal Disease: Established Organ Injury and Emerging Evidence for Skeletal Involvement.
authorString: Cannavò L, Beretta V, Petrolini C, Raitano V, Scarpa E, Dell'Orto V, Carloni S, Albertini MC, Perrone S.
abstractText: Reactive oxygen and nitrogen species participate in physiological signaling and adaptation during fetal and neonatal development, whereas excessive, prolonged, or spatially dysregulated production may contribute to oxidative and nitrosative tissue injury. Redox dysregulation has been extensively investigated in neonatal conditions, including bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), congenital heart disease (CHD), and hyperbilirubinemia. Its relationship with bone metabolism is well established in adult and pediatric disorders, including osteoporosis, inflammatory bone loss, and iron-overload-related bone disease. However, the potential contribution of perinatal redox imbalance to early skeletal development remains comparatively underexplored. This narrative review critically examines the biochemical mechanisms of reactive species generation, their interaction with inflammatory pathways, and the experimental and clinical evidence linking redox dysregulation to neonatal organ injury. Particular attention is given to the developing skeleton as a potentially underrecognized target. Experimental studies indicate that excessive reactive species can impair chondrogenesis, alter osteoblast and osteoclast activity, disrupt collagen and osteogenic signaling, and interfere with skeletal growth. Human evidence is predominantly observational. Preliminary longitudinal data show inverse associations between cord-blood markers of oxidative DNA and protein modification and REMS-derived skeletal Z-scores during the first year of life. These findings suggest that early redox imbalance may impair bone quality and growth trajectories in newborns. Prospective studies integrating standardized redox biomarkers, bone-metabolism indices, imaging, nutrition, medication exposure, growth, and fracture outcomes are needed to determine whether redox dysregulation independently contributes to impaired skeletal development.

title: Physiological Significance and Functions of AA.
authorString: Das UN.

journal.title: Reviews of physiology, biochemistry and pharmacology

abstractText: AA has several physiological functions. Its various metabolites also have many significant actions and thus participate in innumerable physiological and pathological processes. There is strong evidence to suggest that AA and its metabolites play a significant role in the pathophysiology of diabetes mellitus (DM), hypertension (HTN), and coronary heart disease. In addition, high-fat diet (HFD), high-cholesterol diet (HCD), calorie-dense foods (CDF), high-salt and low-potassium diet, low magnesium, lack of exercise, sedentary lifestyle, and aging alter the generation of AA from its dietary precursor linoleic acid (LA) by altering the activities of desaturases. This may enhance the occurrence of a pro-inflammatory milieu in the cells/tissues/organs that can be ameliorated to a certain extent by AA.

title: AA in Brain-Memory, Dementia, Depression, Anxiety, Alzheimer's Disease, Affective and Psychiatric Disorders, and Coronary Heart Disease (CHD).
authorString: Das UN.

journal.title: Reviews of physiology, biochemistry and pharmacology

abstractText: The human brain is rich in AA and DHA, which are crucial for normal brain growth and development and memory. They form a major structural component of neurons of the cerebral cortex and photoreceptor cells in the retina. AA and DHA support synaptic plasticity and contribute to efficient neurotransmission. Adequate amounts of AA and DHA support neuronal growth and the formation of new synapses and thus are crucial for memory and cognitive function.Depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, and other neurological diseases occur more frequently in those with coronary heart disease (CHD) and vice versa. Transient depression and anxious mood can trigger acute cardiac events and fatal arrhythmias. Serotonin and catecholamines play a significant role in depression and anxiety and are known to activate platelets, which increases the risk of cardiovascular events. Both serotonin and catecholamines modulate inflammation, while levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines are elevated in anxiety and depression and other psychiatric conditions and CHD. Depression, anxiety, and CHD involve altered essential fatty acid metabolism, particularly of AA and DHA, whose metabolites can inhibit platelet activation, suppress inflammation, and enhance acetylcholine levels. Acetylcholine, in turn, regulates the concentrations of serotonin and catecholamines. Acetylcholine and catecholamines have a modulatory influence on inflammation. Exercise is anti-inflammatory in nature, by virtue of its ability to enhance the formation of anti-inflammatory lipoxin A4, resolvins, protectin, and maresins and suppress pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-α. AA and DHA enhance acetylcholine release and augment the formation of endothelial nitric oxide (NO). These results imply that anxiety, depression, and CHD are low-grade systemic inflammatory conditions that could benefit from the administration of appropriate amounts of AA and DHA. Risk factors for CHD such as obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and atherosclerosis are all considered pro-inflammatory conditions.Since both neuropsychiatric conditions and recovery from CHD need the generation of new neurons and myocardial cells respectively that need to get integrated to the existing cells/tissues, it is proposed that a combination of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) (that is needed for neuronal cells to survive), growth hormone (GH) (needed for growth of the newly generated neurons and myocardial cells), resolvins/lipoxins/protectins/maresins (needed to suppress inflammation and enhance wound healing), retinoic acid (needed for vertebrate development), and 1,4-DPCA that inhibits the excessive deposition of collagen and an inducer of formation of new blood vessels (angiogenesis) may be of significant benefit both in the prevention and management of neuropsychiatric conditions and CHD and their associated conditions such as obesity, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and atherosclerosis.

title: Conclusions and Therapeutic Implications of AA.
authorString: Das UN.

journal.title: Reviews of physiology, biochemistry and pharmacology

abstractText: AA is essential for several tissues in the body, as they are involved in many physiological and pathological processes. Its regulatory role in inflammation, immune response regulation, cell cycle, and membrane structural organization and its ability to control the expression and function(s) of several receptors and convey messages to and from the nucleus are of particular significance. Fine-tuning the metabolism of AA may lead to the development of prevention and management strategies for several diseases, including but not limited to sepsis, inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes mellitus, cancer, coronary heart disease, atherosclerosis, MASLD (NAFLD), hypertension, metabolic syndrome, uveitis, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, glomerulonephritis, ischemia-reperfusion injury, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and drug-resistant infections and cancer. AA is needed for normal brain growth and development, pregnancy, regeneration of the liver and heart, and hematopoiesis. AA can be administered orally, parenterally as needed, and as lipid nanoparticles to target specific tissues.

title: AA in Hypertension and Preeclampsia.
authorString: Das UN.

journal.title: Reviews of physiology, biochemistry and pharmacology

abstractText: Human essential hypertension is driven by a network of interacting nutritional, metabolic, inflammatory, and endothelial mechanisms in which AA and other PUFAs play a critical role. Beyond excess sodium intake, population data supports the role of inadequate calcium, potassium, and magnesium intake and low antioxidant vitamin status in shaping blood pressure regulation. These nutrients influence vascular smooth muscle tone and act as cofactors that support Δ<sup>6</sup> and Δ<sup>5</sup> desaturase activities, thereby governing tissue availability of AA, EPA, and DHA and downstream formation of vasodilator and antiplatelet mediators (e.g., PGE1, prostacyclin), as well as inflammation-resolving lipid mediators (lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, maresins, and nitrolipids).Endothelial dysfunction characterized by reduced endothelial nitric oxide (eNO) bioavailability and increased oxidative stress seems to play an important role in the pathobiology of HTN. High salt intake, asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA), and activation of NAD(P)H oxidase and angiotensin II signaling promote superoxide generation that quenches NO and shifts the vascular balance toward vasoconstriction. Clinical and experimental observations indicate that antihypertensive therapies can partly restore NO and antioxidant defenses, while dietary patterns rich in n-3 fatty acids (particularly DHA) and balanced n-6/n-3 intake may lower blood pressure by suppressing thromboxane formation and enhancing vasoprotective, pro-resolving pathways.Preeclampsia can be considered as a model of reversible hypertension linked to oxidative stress and angiogenic imbalance (sFlt1, soluble endoglin), highlighting mechanistic overlap with essential hypertension. Hypertension is a low-grade systemic inflammatory condition whose origins may be present in the perinatal period through long-term programming of PUFA metabolism and endothelial function.

title: AA and Pregnancy.
authorString: Das UN.

journal.title: Reviews of physiology, biochemistry and pharmacology

abstractText: AA is a crucial fatty acid in pregnancy, especially for the growth and development of the fetus and its central nervous system (CNS). As already discussed in the previous chapters, AA regulates inflammation, immune response, and cell signaling. AA has a modulatory action on gene expression, serves as a mechanotransducer, and regulates cell membrane fluidity. By regulating cell membrane fluidity, AA modulates the expression and binding of several receptors located on the cell membrane. Eicosanoids derived from AA have both beneficial and harmful effects on pregnancy. For instance, (i) AA metabolites such as 14,15-EET and 15-HETE are associated with gestational hypertension and preeclampsia, (ii) AA in association with DHA is crucial for the fetal nervous system and neurocognitive development of the newborn, and (iii) for the growth and development of the fetus, especially during the third trimester. LA and AA are involved in human fertility and in the pathobiology of gestational diabetes.

title: [THE DEVELOPMENT OF CARDIO-SURGERY IN THREE FEDERAL OKRUGS: SIGNIFICANCE OF THE NATIONAL PROJECT].
authorString: Golukhova EZ, Semenov VY.

abstractText: The Federal project The development of network of National medical research centers and the implementation of innovative medical technologies supposed to improve accessibility, including high-tech medical care, at the expense of organizational methodological cooperation of specially organized National medical research centers with health care management bodies and profile medical organizations of the Subjects of the Russian Federation. As a result, 73 new structural divisions were organized and 205 new surgical technologies for treatment of the heart and blood vessels were developed in alone 3 Federal Okrugs supervised by the Federal State Budgetary Scientific Institution The A.
