title: Feasibility of continuous finger arterial pressure recording with synchronised facial video in a hypertension clinic cohort: the BP-WAVE pilot study
authorString: Singh J, Feeney A, Teh JW, Mannion E, Murphy R, Coen E, Sharif F, Judge C.
abstractText:
Introduction:

Whether the arterial pressure waveform carries structural vascular information that brachial pressure does not, and whether its shape can be read from facial video, are both uncertain, and recording a continuous pressure reference with synchronised video in a hypertension clinic has not been reported. We sought to determine whether continuous finger arterial pressure recording with synchronised facial video, linked to existing coronary calcium imaging, is feasible in adults attending a hypertension clinic, whether a consumer camera recovers heart rate and pulse shape in that setting, and to generate exploratory estimates of association between waveform morphology and coronary calcium. Methods. BP-WAVE is a single-site prospective observational pilot study. The primary outcome was feasibility, pre-specified as recruitment, consent, completeness of waveform recording, imaging availability and data completeness. Secondary outcomes were waveform quality, device agreement, feature extraction, and recovery of heart rate and pulse shape from video. The exploratory outcome was the Spearman correlation of 14 waveform features with the Agatston calcium score, with exact permutation p values adjusted within each family of tests. Results. Nine of ten planned participants were recorded over 12 days (median age 55 years, range 40 to 74; five women); all nine completed the recording with video and had a calcium score (median 351, range 33 to 1816). Of 4,178 detected beats, 2,965 (71%) passed quality control. Video recovered heart rate within 0.4 to 4.1 beats per minute in eight of nine participants and pulse shape above a phase-randomised noise bound in six of nine (held-out r 0.48 to 0.76). Form factor had the strongest correlation with calcium (rho −0.68, exact p 0.050, q 0.68); no feature was associated with calcium after Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment within any of the nine families of 14 tests (126 tests in all; smallest q 0.17). Conclusion. In this single-site pilot of nine adults from a hypertension clinic, continuous finger arterial pressure recording with synchronised facial video and linkage to coronary calcium was feasible, a consumer camera recovered heart rate in eight and pulse shape in six participants, and no waveform feature was associated with coronary calcium after correction for multiple testing.

title: Systematic Review on Predictive Utility of Electrocardiographic Correlates for Cardiovascular Disease
authorString: Osarenkhoe J, Nwokedi M, Udo SI, Iroabuchi F, Musa TK, Ovih K, Luke IE, Okeke LK, Alex-Hart B, Otorkpa O.
abstractText: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of global mortality. Electrocardiography (ECG) is widely accessible and non-invasive, and its abnormalities may carry prognostic value beyond diagnosis. Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded ECG's risk-prediction potential, though its incremental value remains debated. This systematic review evaluated the predictive utility of conventional (non-AI) and AI/deep learning-enhanced ECG approaches for cardiovascular disease incidence, mortality, and major adverse cardiovascular events, comparing the two directly. The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies were identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Eligible studies were cohort studies, systematic reviews, or validated AI-based ECG investigations reporting risk estimates or predictive performance metrics. Findings were synthesized narratively and tabulated descriptively rather than statistically pooled. Thirty core studies were included across general, elderly, hypertensive, diabetic, and coronary artery disease cohorts. Conventional ECG abnormalities QT/QTc prolongation, QRS duration, left ventricular hypertrophy, ST-T abnormalities, and atrial fibrillation were consistently associated with cardiovascular disease, mortality, and MACE (hazard ratios generally 1.2–2.5). Adding ECG variables to conventional models yielded modest gains (ΔAUC ≈ 0.02–0.06); AI/deep learning models outperformed conventional interpretation (ΔAUC ≈ 0.10–0.15), including via ECG derived biological age. Conventional and AI-enhanced ECG correlates both carry meaningful, independent prognostic information.

title: Sympathetic Neural Coupling with the Investing Fascia, Deep Cervical Fascia, and Carotid Sheath: A Hypothesis
authorString: Huang X.
abstractText: The deep cervical fascial system consists of three layers: the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia (investing fascia), the pretracheal fascia (middle layer), and the prevertebral fascia (deep layer). This hypothesis proposes that chronic forward head posture or sustained cervical stress may lead to fibrotic remodeling of the investing fascia, resulting in abnormally elevated passive tension. This abnormal tension may be transmitted indirectly to the carotid sheath region through the interwoven collagen fiber network among the layers of the deep cervical fascia, or through intermediate interfaces such as the visceral fascia, thereby contributing to fibrotic thickening of the sheath wall and surrounding tissues. Thickening of the posterior wall of the carotid sheath may exert sustained mechanical compression on the cervical sympathetic trunk immediately posterior to it, thereby causing sympathetic dysfunction and autonomic imbalance. It should be noted that the fascial composition of the carotid sheath remains controversial. The investing fascia and the sheath wall may not be directly fused; instead, they may be indirectly connected through intermediate interfaces such as the visceral fascia. Zhao et al. confirmed in a rabbit model that the carotid sheath has a three-layered fascial architecture: the inner fascial layer on the arterial side appears earliest and is the thickest, and the outer fascial layer shows potential fusion between adjacent structures, suggesting a possible spatial gradient in sheath wall thickening. However, that study was performed at a developmental stage and in an animal model, and it cannot directly prove that pathological fibrotic thickening causes compression of the sympathetic trunk. Lyons and Mills found during human cadaveric dissection that the cervical sympathetic trunk was located inside the carotid sheath in some individuals. Park et al. further integrated the anatomical features of the middle cervical ganglion through meta-analysis, and Salazar-Orellana et al. reported a clinical case in which venous dilation within the sheath compressed the sympathetic trunk and caused sympathetic overactivity. He et al. confirmed in a rat model that atlantoaxial misalignment can cause hypertension, and blood pressure decreased after removal of the implant. Cassaglia et al. confirmed in anesthetized lambs that mechanical elevation of blood pressure can directly increase sympathetic activity in the superior cervical ganglion, suggesting that the causal chain from upper cervical mechanical misalignment or an altered mechanical environment to sympathetic activation and elevated blood pressure is verifiable in animal models. Lee et al. reported a case in which scar formation after rhabdomyolysis of the longus colli and scalene muscles compressed and tethered the cervical sympathetic trunk, causing Horner syndrome, providing direct human clinical evidence for the pathway from cervical soft tissue pathological change to mechanical compression of the sympathetic trunk and sympathetic dysfunction. Okamoto et al. and Farage et al. respectively reported cases of marked fibrosis around the carotid artery and inflammatory pseudotumor of the carotid sheath, providing histological and imaging evidence that fibrosis can occur in the carotid sheath region. Langevin et al. used ultrasound to confirm that fascial thickness and echogenicity increased by approximately 25% in patients with chronic low back pain, providing a methodological precedent for ultrasound quantification of pathological fascial thickening. If this mechano-neural coupling pathway holds true, it may contribute to the peripheral drive of distal pathological conditions such as cervicogenic hypertension, cerebral hypoperfusion, and ocular disorders. However, its core components have not yet been directly validated in animal or human models. This hypothesis is based on evidence from anatomy, histology, biomechanics, molecular biology, pathophysiology, and clinical research. It constructs an evidence integration framework spanning anatomical structure, histological basis, mechanical properties, molecular transduction, pathological experiments, physiological effects, human epidemiology, alternative mechanism controls, and interventional validation, and it proposes testable predictions and a validation framework. At the same time, this hypothesis incorporates negative control evidence and alternative mechanism evidence to define the boundary conditions of the effects of cervical sympathetic trunk intervention. Currently, no animal model or human study has directly simulated sympathetic trunk compression caused by fibrotic thickening of the carotid sheath wall. This is the main evidence gap of this hypothesis, rather than a gap in the literature.

title: Personalised normative cardiac phenotyping reveals clinically relevant heterogeneity in cardiac shape and outcome risk
authorString: Li Z, Bai W, Matthews PM, Kainz B, Qiao M.
abstractText: Standard cardiac biomarkers such as ejection fraction, ventricular volumes, and strain compress complex three-dimensional heart dynamics into a small set of predefined measurements, leaving clinically important heterogeneity unrecognised. Here we propose a personalised normative cardiac framework in which each individual is compared to a digital twin representing expected healthy cardiac function given their age, sex, and body habitus. We show that structured patterns of deviation from these normative twins, discovered through systematic exploration of a generative cardiac dynamics space, constitute novel dynamic phenotypes that are not captured by conventional biomarkers. Applied independently to two UK Biobank cardiac cohorts with distinct shape representation, a 128-dimensional four-chamber statistical shape descriptor (HeartSSM, n = 52,365) and a 64-dimensional deep generative latent space from a conditional variational mesh autoencoder (MeshHeart cVAE, n = up to 39,376), we identify reproducible, continuous deviation-from-normative-twin scores (three discrete deviation phenotypes in the HeartSSM cohort) that improve cardiovascular risk stratification beyond ejection fraction, ventricular volumes, myocardial mass, and strain. The strongest effect was seen for incident atrial fibrillation among individuals with preserved ejection fraction (at least 50%): incremental C-index delta C = +0.068 (5-fold cross-validated delta C = +0.063; likelihood-ratio P = 3.3 x 10^-8), with a separate, smaller effect for incident stroke in the same preserved-EF subgroup in the independent MeshHeart cVAE representation (which showed no signal for atrial fibrillation) (delta C = +0.024, P = 2.6 x 10^-4). Both effects were checked against placebo controls in which the deviation scores were replaced by Gaussian noise. To test whether the normative twin generalises beyond UK Biobank's specific scanning and processing pipeline, we applied the MeshHeart cVAE normative twin, unmodified, to an independent external cohort of healthy volunteers imaged at a different hospital (GenScan/Hammersmith, n = 315): deviation scores in this cohort were of comparable magnitude to the UK Biobank healthy reference (ratio of means = 1.09; Mann-Whitney P = 1.4 x 10^-5), indicating that the normative twin captures cross-site-transferable structure rather than a scanner- or pipeline-specific artefact. Our findings suggest that cardiac phenotyping can move beyond predefined measurements toward data-driven dynamic phenotypes that better capture the heterogeneity underlying cardiovascular disease risk, even among individuals whose ejection fraction appears normal.

title: Targeting Cardiac Fibrosis with Chimeric Antigen Receptor Neutrophils Derived from Human Pluripotent Stem Cells
authorString: Jin G, Fang S, Chang Y, Shao K, Li H, Tan Y, Lian X, Deng Q, Huang Y, Bao X.
abstractText: Heart failure remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, with cardiac fibrosis contributing to disease progression. Following myocardial injury, activated cardiac fibroblasts orchestrate adverse extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, which leads to tissue stiffening and compromised contractility. Despite the clinical importance of cardiac fibrosis, current pharmacological interventions modulate disease progression without directly eliminating activated fibrogenic cells. To target these cells directly, we engineered human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived neutrophils expressing a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) directed against fibroblast activation protein (FAP). In vitro, FAP CAR neutrophils exhibited increased reactive oxygen species-associated fluorescence during fibroblast co-culture and dose-dependent cytotoxicity in 2D cultures, while reducing fibroblast-associated fluorescence in 3D cardiac organoids without a significant reduction in cardiomyocyte-associated cardiac troponin T staining. FAP CAR neutrophils also showed increased iNOS and decreased Arginase-1 expression compared with unmodified neutrophils, consistent with a shift toward an N1-associated polarization profile. Analysis of public cardiac single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing datasets identified temporal patterns of immune-associated expression and fibroblast activation that informed treatment timing. In a murine myocardial infarction (MI) model, mice treated systemically with FAP CAR neutrophils showed higher day 7 left ventricular ejection fraction than PBS-treated mice in an exploratory comparison. Together, these findings support further evaluation of hPSC-derived FAP CAR neutrophils as an immunotherapeutic approach to cardiac fibrosis.

title: Successful Trastuzumab Deruxtecan Treatment After AdjuvantTrastuzumab-Induced Heart Failure: A Case Report
authorString: Fuchikami H.
abstractText: Background : Trastuzumab-induced cardiotoxicity is a well-recognized complication that may lead to discontinuation of adjuvant HER2-targeted therapy. Evidence regarding subsequent treatment strategies for recurrence in patients with a history of trastuzumab-related heart failure remains limited. Case presentation : A woman with HER2-positive early breast cancer received adjuvant trastuzumab after surgery. Her baseline left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) was in the 60% range. During therapy, she developed acute heart failure with LVEF decline to 30%, requiring a one-week hospitalization and discontinuation of trastuzumab. Her cardiac function gradually recovered to the 60% range under standard heart failure management. Approximately 43 months later, she developed recurrence with liver metastases and multiple lymph nodes metastasis. Her cardiologist didn’t allow re-anti-HER２therapy, and we kept chemotherapy without anti-HER2 drugs. Two years later, given her recovered cardiac function and disease progression, trastuzumab deruxtecan (T‑DXd) was started. She received 13 cycles over 10 months, achieving durable tumor response without cardiac deterioration. Conclusion : This case illustrates that T‑DXd can be a feasible and effective option for recurrent HER2-positive breast cancer in patients with prior trastuzumab-induced heart failure, when cardiac function has sufficiently recovered and careful cardio-oncology monitoring is ensured.

title: Evaluation of Short- and Long-Term Outcomes of Patients with Carotid Artery Stenting: 16-Year Experience at a Single Center
authorString: Erdoğan T, Nazlıel B, Batur Çağlayan HZ, Altıparmak T, Önal AB, Akkan MK, Öncü F, Ilgıt ET.
abstractText:
Background:

/Objectives: Carotid artery stenting (CAS) is a preventive treatment for symptomatic moderate-to-severe and asymptomatic severe carotid stenosis. This study evaluated short- and long-term complications and outcomes of CAS.

Methods:

We retrospectively analyzed 584 patients who underwent CAS at our Neurology Clinic between January 2004 and December 2020.

Results:

Of 584 patients, 271 (46.6%) were symptomatic and 311 (53.4%) asymptomatic. At 30 days, myocardial infarction (MI) occurred in 2.2%, major stroke in 2.4%, major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) in 4.1%, and vascular death in 1.4%. Mean Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) was higher in patients with 30-day MACCE (p=0.014) and vascular death (p=0.003). Atrial fibrillation (AF) independently predicted 30-day MACCE (OR 3.57, 95% CI 1.17-10.89) and vascular death (OR 10.17, 95% CI 2.18-47.42); CCI independently predicted MACCE at 5 and 10 years. Diabetes mellitus (69.7%) was not independently associated with MACCE, restenosis, or mortality after adjusting for CCI. Smoking, rather than sex, independently predicted 5-year restenosis (OR 4.61, 95% CI 1.80-11.79); the higher crude restenosis rate in men appears attributable to smoking prevalence. Actuarial analysis showed 10-year overall survival of 81.0%, MACCE-free survival of 75.3%, and restenosis-free survival of 73.4%.

Conclusions:

CAS is generally safe, but close follow-up is necessary to monitor complications, and careful preoperative risk assessment is essential. CCI and AF status should be considered alongside stroke history, carotid anatomy, and smoking status for perioperative risk assessment.

title: Cardiomyocyte-Derived Cell-Free DNA in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
authorString: Kamna D, Davis B, Layman CE, Wiedrick J, Avaylon S, Wheeler K, Jahan I, Carbone L, Masri A.
abstractText:
Introduction

In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), wall stress and subclinical myocardial injury related in part to pathological hypercontractility, which in turn are associated with worse outcomes. Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is released from cardiomyocytes (cfDNA-CM) through irreversible cellular injury and death. We investigated the feasibility of quantifying cfDNA-CM and its relationship to HCM patient characteristics.

Methods

We analyzed 57 plasma samples from stable patients with HCM and 10 plasma samples from patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Plasma cfDNA was isolated from both groups. Whole genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) libraries were generated and sequenced with short-read sequencing. Methylation patterns were used for tissue deconvolution analysis and cell-specific cfDNA quantification.

Results

Yields of cfDNA (p = 0.003) and cfDNA-CM (p = 0.002) fractions were higher in AMI controls than HCM, supporting the validity of the assay. Within the HCM cohort, the median cfDNA yield was 12.22 ng [IQR: 7.77, 18.94]. The cfDNA-CM fraction in this cohort ranged from 0% to 6.4% of total cfDNA. Higher cfDNA-CM tertiles were associated with higher body mass index (BMI, p=0.001), a greater prevalence of BMI ≥30 kg/m² (p<0.001), and a higher prevalence of obstructive sleep apnea (p=0.038). No significant differences were observed in other demographic, genetic, and laboratory characteristics. Higher cfDNA-CM tertile was numerically associated with higher New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class and left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction, while circulating biomarkers of wall stress (NT-proBNP) and myocardial injury (troponin) did not differ across tertiles (p=0.83 and p=0.29, respectively).

Conclusion

Isolation and quantification of cfDNA as well as detection of cfDNA-CM in chronic stable patients with HCM are feasible. Higher cfDNA-CM fraction was associated with increasing BMI and cardiometabolic comorbidity burden. The absence of association with traditional circulating biomarkers suggests that cfDNA-CM may reflect a distinct domain of myocardial health, injury, and adverse remodeling.

title: A cell death-independent role for MLKL in TGF-β receptor recycling in Marfan syndrome
authorString: Nemade H, Guthoff H, Zimmermann O, Riemen S, Stiller H, Hedbawny M, Agbowo B, Zahnow D, Holtkamp F, Arkenberg P, Mehrkens D, Jahn P, Nettersheim FS, Schelemei P, Picard FR, Lagunas KM, Jayachandran J, Sengle G, Ros U, Winkels H, Riffelmacher T, Baldus S, García-Sáez AJ, Adam M, Mollenhauer M.
abstractText: Marfan syndrome (MFS) causes thoracic aortic aneurysm through mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene and subsequent dysregulated TGF-β signalling. Mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL) executes necroptosis after RIPK3-dependent phosphorylation, but also functions in endosomal trafficking. Here we show that MLKL phosphorylation sustains TGF-β receptor recycling and aortic wall integrity without causing cell death. Phosphorylation-dead MLKL  S345A/S347A (  Mlkl AA ) mice developed aortic root dilation with disorganised collagen architecture and a secretory-pathway proteomic signature. Crossing them with  Fbn1  C1039G /+ MFS mice aggravated aortic dilation, disrupted collagen fibril ultrastructure and prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation, and caused lethal rupture under angiotensin II. Complete MLKL deficiency reproduced this phenotype. Phosphorylated MLKL was increased in MFS aortas, yet cleaved caspase-3, TUNEL positivity, smooth muscle cell content and leukocyte infiltration were unchanged. In smooth muscle cells, MLKL depletion dysregulated collagen-modifying enzymes, altered TGF-β-driven matrix remodelling and impaired RAB11-dependent TGFβR1 recycling. These findings suggest that phosphorylation-dependent, non-lytic functions of MLKL may contribute to the maintenance of thoracic aortic integrity in MFS.

title: Oligodendrocyte stress response as a driver of vascular dementia
authorString: Merour E, Ghatage T, Corbett C, DeBerge M, Kunjamma R, Ian Steckler IS, Heidari M, Sorond FA, Flanagan ME, Thorp EB, Popko B.
abstractText: Vascular dementia (VaD) is a prevalent and devastating neurocognitive disorder characterized by profound white matter damage, yet the precise cellular mechanisms linking cerebrovascular stress to demyelination remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize the impact of a chronic cardiometabolic stress regimen combining a high-fat diet and hypertension (HF/HBP) on central nervous system structure and function. Adult HF/HBP mice exhibit progressive oligodendroglial cell loss and myelin thinning, followed by cognitive impairments, anxiety-like behavior, and memory deficits that recapitulate clinical features of VaD. Mechanistically, we identify the integrated stress response (ISR) as a central driver of this pathology; pharmacological inhibition of the ISR restores myelination, while cell-specific genetic deletion of the ISR-activating kinase PERK from oligodendrocytes fully protects mice from HF/HBP-induced pathological and behavioral defects. Furthermore, we provide translational evidence that the ISR is activated in oligodendrocytes in human cases of cerebrovascular disease. Together, these findings reveal a critical, cell-autonomous role for oligodendroglial ISR activation during cerebrovascular stress and position this pathway as a viable therapeutic target to mitigate VaD pathogenesis.

title: Atrial fibrillation begets atrial fibrillation - serum-driven amplification of atrial electrical instability
authorString: Bögner M, Ramesh G, Fahjen P, Hüttemeister J, Kirk M, Heil E, Bock M, Zhang K, Boehm G, Eichelmann L, Gerds-Li JH, Hilgendorf I, Falk V, Mertins P, Hindricks G, Hohendanner F.
abstractText:
Rationale: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is sustained by electrical triggers and atrial substrate, but whether AF itself generates circulating factors that acutely reinforce arrhythmogenesis is unknown.

Objective:

To determine whether rhythm-dependent serum bioactivity directly destabilizes atrial electrophysiology and to identify associated cellular mechanisms and circulating mediators.

Methods and Results:

Cardiac samples were obtained from patients with persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) during AF and after restoration of sinus rhythm (SR) using electrical cardioversion. In isolated Langendorff-perfused mouse hearts, AF serum increased the duration, frequency, and cumulative burden of spontaneous atrial depolarizations compared with paired control perfusate. In human induced pluripotent stem cell derived atrial cardiomyocytes, AF patient serum decreased Ca2-transient amplitudes without significant effect on kinetics or Ca2 spark activity. Moreover, AF serum reduced peak sodium current without materially altering voltage-dependent gating or paced action-potential properties. Data-independent acquisition proteomics identified rhythm-associated changes in extracellular-matrix, proteolytic, inflammatory, and signaling proteins, including MMP9, Ccathepsin G, and 14-3-3 family members. Targeted pathway perturbation differentially modified serum-induced Ca2 phenotypes, indicating context-dependent, multifactorial bioactivity. Serum-induced Ca2 responses were not associated with indices of atrial disease severity, including low-voltage substrate burden and left atrial pressure.

Conclusions:

Persistent AF is accompanied by rhythm-dependent circulating bioactivity that acutely promotes atrial electrical instability and Ca2-dependent trigger formation. These findings extend the concept that AF begets AF beyond tissue-intrinsic remodeling and identify a potentially reversible serum-mediated feed-forward mechanism linking rhythm status and circulating proteomic signals in an atrial substrate severity independent fashion.

Keywords:

atrial fibrillation; serum; atrial cardiomyopathy; calcium signaling; circulating factors; proteomics

title: Age-, sex-, and ethnicity-stratified CMR strain reference ranges and centile-based categories from the Healthy Hearts Consortium
authorString: Salatzki J, Condurache D, Roy R, Szabo L, Westbury L, Akilu T, Salih AM, Chadalavada S, Buelow R, Aquaro GD, Le T, Sucha D, Aung N, Harvey NC, Leiner T, Chin CW, Barison A, Doerr M, Friedrich MG, Andre F, Petersen SE, Raisi-Estabragh Z.
abstractText:
Background:

This study presents reference ranges for cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR)-derived myocardial strain from the Healthy Hearts Consortium, while evaluating variations by demographic characteristics (age, sex, and ethnicity) and technical factors (scanner vendor, magnetic field strength). We derived reference ranges and centile-based categories for ventricular, atrial, and rapid strain parameters. The prognostic relevance of these categories was assessed by examining their associations with incident cardiovascular events. Methods The dataset included 9,088 CMR studies. Automated image analysis pipelines were established using suiteHEART (NeoSoft Inc.) and cvi42 (Circle Cardiovascular Imaging). A three-step quality control framework was applied including exclusion of incomplete data, visual assessment of image and segmentation quality, and statistical outlier removal. Ventricular strain and strain rate were measured using both software solutions. Additional cvi42 derived metrics included velocity and displacement, annular plane systolic excursion metrics, and rapid strain parameters. Age- and sex-specific reference ranges were generated using lambda-mu-sigma (LMS) modeling with penalized splines. Reference ranges were defined as values between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. For lower-tail classification, values below the 2.5th percentile were considered mildly out-of-range and values below the 0.5th percentile at least moderately out-of-range. Differences across scanner vendors (Siemens, Philips, GE) and magnetic field strengths (1.5 T vs. 3 T) were evaluated using adjusted linear models. The prognostic relevance of selected cvi42-derived categories was evaluated in approximately 45,000 UK Biobank participants using Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Results After quality control, 8,975 CMR examinations (cvi42) and 8,992 (suiteHEART) were available for analysis; these represent software-specific analytic cohorts. Most exclusions occurred during visual quality control. Women had higher absolute ventricular and atrial strain values than men across all age groups. Left ventricular (LV) longitudinal strain and strain rate were slightly lower in older ages, whereas circumferential and radial parameters remained largely stable. Left atrial strain was also lower in older age groups, while right atrial strain did not vary by age. Annular plane systolic excursion and rapid strain metrics showed similar sex-specific patterns, with modestly lower atrial and displacement values in older groups. Ethnicity-related differences were modest, heterogeneous, and substantially smaller in magnitude than age- and sex-related differences. Technical effects were parameter specific. While LV longitudinal and circumferential strains were largely unaffected, radial strain was higher at 3 T and showed vendor-related differences. LMS-derived reference ranges and centile thresholds were applied both across all ethnicities and within ethnicity-specific analyses, and are presented stratified by age and sex. In the prognostic analysis, centile categories were most consistently associated with incident heart failure. LV longitudinal, circumferential, and radial strain below the 0.5th centile were associated with significantly increased risk of incident heart failure (HRs: 9.9 to 12.4, 95% CIs 7.00-13.90 to 8.49-18.06). Conclusion This study provides age- and sex-specific reference ranges and centile-based categories for CMR-derived strain parameters in a large reference population. Age and sex represent the primary determinants of myocardial deformation, whereas scanner-related effects are parameter-specific. Values in the lower extremes of the healthy reference distribution, particularly for LV strain, are associated with increased risk of incident heart failure. These findings enable standardized, centile-based classification of myocardial strain, facilitating consistent interpretation and improving risk stratification in research and clinical practice.

title: Machine Learning–based Prediction of Pacing-Induced Cardiomyopathy in Patients with Atrioventricular Block Underlying Heart Failure with Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction
authorString: Lee J, Do U, Kim HM, Choi MJ, Shin SY, Park S, Kang K.
abstractText:
Background

Pacing-induced cardiomyopathy (PICM) is a major complication of chronic right ventricular pacing and develops in up to 25% of patients. Reliable prediction of PICM may facilitate individualized pacing strategy selection; however, currently available approaches demonstrate limited discriminative performance. This study aimed to develop and validate machine learning (ML) models for predicting PICM in patients with atrioventricular block (AVB) underlying heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction.

Methods

In this multicenter prospective study derived from the RISK-PICM registry (January 2002 to January 2026), 125 patients with AVB who underwent pacemaker implantation were analyzed. PICM was defined as a ≥10% reduction in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) resulting in an LVEF <50%. Four ML algorithms, including logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost, were trained using stratified 4-fold cross-validation with hyperparameter optimization and model discrimination was evaluated.

Results

PICM developed in 41 patients (32.8%) during a median follow-up of 4.8 years. Male sex, pre-implant minimum QTc interval, and post-implant maximum QRS duration were significantly associated with PICM in univariable Cox regression. XGBoost achieved the highest discriminative performance (AUROC 0.831; sensitivity 0.805; specificity 0.845). Feature importance analysis identified baseline LVEF and post-implant maximum QRS duration as the most influential features. Model-derived risk stratification significantly differentiated high-risk and low-risk groups on Kaplan-Meier analysis ( P < 0.001).

Conclusions

ML-based models, particularly XGBoost, demonstrated clinically meaningful performance for PICM and may support individualized pacing strategy selection in patients with AVB and underlying heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction.

Clinical Perspective

What Is New

In pacing-dependent AVB patients with HFmrEF or HFpEF, ensemble ML (XGBoost) predicted PICM with an AUROC of 0.831. Model-derived risk stratification separated PICM-free survival (log-rank P<0.001).

What Are the Clinical Implications

An ML model combining baseline LVEF, paced QRS duration, and the full parameter set may guide individualized choice between right ventricular and conduction system pacing in AVB patients with HFmrEF or HFpEF. Using paced QRS duration combined with baseline LVEF during temporary pacing in AVB patients with HFmrEF or HFpEF, this risk estimate could inform pacing-strategy selection before permanent implantation, enabling pre-emptive use of conduction system pacing in high-risk patients.

title: Blood Pressure and Heart Rate Stationarity in Predicting TEVAR Response
authorString: Alakhdar A, Washburn NR, Pocivavsek L, Bohr NL.
abstractText:
Background

Hypertension is a major risk factor for type B aortic dissections and rupture, with guidelines recommending systolic blood pressure (SBP) control below 130 mmHg to improve outcomes. While post-TEVAR blood pressure is often managed with a focus on mean SBP, little is known about temporal hemodynamic patterns and their association with surgical success. This study investigates blood pressure and heart rate (HR) time-series metrics within 24 hours post-TEVAR and their predictive potential for outcomes.

Methods

Blood pressure (n = 560) and HR (n = 680) time-series data from 31 patients were analyzed alongside preoperative aortic geometry metrics. Exploratory data analysis identified correlations between BP variability and outcomes. Stationarity tests were performed on time-series data to assess statistical properties. Logistic regression models incorporating hemodynamic metrics, along with CT-derived features, were used to predict TEVAR outcomes.

Results

Successful outcomes correlated with greater diastolic blood pressure variability and strictly stationary SBP. Logistic regression models combining these metrics along with heart rate standard deviation and preoperative aortic geometry achieved 96.67% 5-fold cross-validation accuracy in predicting outcomes.

Conclusion

Post-TEVAR behaviors of hemodynamic variables are critical predictors of TEVAR success, with higher DBP standard deviation and strict stationarity of SBP significantly associated with favorable outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of hemodynamic variability and stationarity in optimizing post-TEVAR patient care.

title: Development and Validation of a Sleep Disorder Risk Prediction Model in Young and Middle-Aged Adults With Anemia
authorString: Liu Y, Zhang C.
abstractText:
Objective:

This study aimed to develop and validate a predictive model for sleep disorders in young and middle-aged adults with anemia, providing evidence for early identification, risk stratification, and individualized sleep management. Methods Data in the NHANES were analyzed and randomly divided into development and validation cohorts. LASSO regression was used to screen optimal predictors in the development cohort, followed by univariate and multivariate logistic regression to identify independent predictors and construct a nomogram. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration curves, Brier scores, and decision curve analysis. Results The weighted prevalence of sleep disorders among young and middle-aged adults with anemia was 10.19%. Multivariate logistic regression identified seven independent predictors: sex, monocyte count, asthma, overweight, arthritis, congestive heart failure, and hypertension. The model showed good discrimination, with area under the curve values of 0.817 in the development cohort and 0.791 in the validation cohort. Calibration was satisfactory, with Brier scores of 0.074 and 0.075, respectively. Decision curve analysis indicated favorable clinical net benefit in both cohorts. Conclusion The proposed predictive model demonstrated good discrimination, calibration, and may help healthcare providers identify young and middle-aged adults with anemia who are at high risk for sleep disorders.

title: Glycaemic Burden and Cognitive Screen-Positive Status in Younger Indian Adults with Long-Standing Type 2 Diabetes: A Cross-Sectional Study with a MoCA Cutoff Sensitivity Analysis in a Lower-Education Population
authorString: Lodha SM, Kumar S, Acharya S, Baweja R, Garg S.
abstractText: Background Structured cognitive screening in diabetes is recommended only from age 65, leaving younger adults with prolonged type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) exposure unmonitored. We quantified the association of HbA1c and diabetes duration with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) screen-positive status in adults aged ≤ 60 years with T2DM of ≥ 5 years, and examined against matched controls how the MoCA cutoff (< 26, < 24, < 23) affects the group contrast in a lower-education population. Methods Cross-sectional study at a tertiary-care centre in North India: 110 adults with T2DM and 50 controls frequency-matched for age, sex, and education. Within diabetics, HbA1c and duration were modelled continuously by modified Poisson regression at each pre-specified cutoff and by Spearman correlation with MoCA total score. Prevalence ratios (PR) for diabetics versus controls at each cutoff were adjusted for age, sex, education, BMI, and hypertension. Results Within diabetics, MoCA total score correlated with HbA1c (ρ = −0.456) and duration (ρ = −0.318; both p < 0.001). Screen-positive prevalence rose 5% per 1% HbA1c at < 26 (PR 1.05, 95% CI 1.02–1.09), 12% at < 24 (PR 1.12, 1.06–1.18), and 17% at < 23 (PR 1.17, 1.09–1.26), and 11% per year of duration at < 23 (PR 1.11, 1.06–1.17). Median education was 10 and 9 years; 76.0% of controls screened positive at < 26, and the diabetes association was cutoff-dependent: adjusted PR 1.08 (0.89–1.29) at < 26, 1.70 (1.10–2.63) at < 24, and 6.72 (2.23–20.23) at < 23, where 44.5% of diabetics versus 6.0% of controls screened positive (absolute difference 38.5 percentage points, 95% CI 25.0 to 48.7). Conclusions In working-age adults with long-standing T2DM, screen-positive prevalence rose continuously with HbA1c at every cutoff, a glycaemic signal independent of threshold choice. The standard < 26 cutoff flagged over three-quarters of both groups and could not triage; < 23 separated diabetics from controls. Screen-positive status is not a diagnosis; MoCA triage at a population-appropriate cutoff in this group warrants prospective validation against a neuropsychological reference standard.

title: Circulating miRNA Signatures in Preeclampsia: Potential Biomarkers for Differentiating Preeclampsia from Gestational Hypertension
authorString: Kurmanova A, Nurmakova A, Salimbayeva D, Ayazbekov A, Ashirbekov Y, Kan N, Tyutyunnik V, Kypshakbayeva Z, Khalmirzaeva M, Amirtayeva S.
abstractText:
Background:

and Objectives: Preeclampsia (PE) and gestational arterial hypertension (GAH) are major hypertensive disorders of pregnancy with overlapping clinical manifestations, which may complicate their differential diagnosis. Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) are emerging as potential minimally invasive biomarkers reflecting placental dysfunction, hypoxia, impaired trophoblast invasion, angiogenic imbalance, and endothelial dysfunction. This study aimed to evaluate the expression profile of circulating miRNAs in women with PE and GAH and to identify candidate molecular markers capable of differentiating these conditions.

Materials and Methods:

A case-control study included 101 pregnant women: 39 women with physiologic pregnancy (control group), 23 women with GAH, and 39 women with PE. Plasma levels of 15 candidate miRNAs were quantified using TaqMan-based quantitative reverse-transcription PCR.

Results:

Twelve of the 15 investigated miRNAs demonstrated significant differences between PE and the control group and between PE and GAH after multiple-testing correction. The most pronounced decrease in PE was observed for miR-210-3p, with a log2 fold-change of −2.06 versus controls and −2.12 versus GAH. In ROC analysis, miR-210-3p showed the highest discriminatory performance for both comparisons, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.830 (95% CI, 0.735–0.925) for PE versus controls and 0.823 (95% CI, 0.720–0.925) for PE versus GAH. Other miRNAs, including miR-144-3p, miR-363-3p, miR-29a-3p, and miR-16-5p, also demonstrated moderate-to-good discriminatory performance.

Conclusions:

PE is characterized by a distinct circulating miRNA profile that differs from both physiologic pregnancy and GAH, whereas the molecular profile of GAH was broadly comparable to that of controls. Among the investigated candidates, miR-210-3p demonstrated the most consistent discriminatory performance and may represent a promising biomarker candidate for differentiating PE from GAH. A combination of several miRNAs may provide greater diagnostic value than individual markers.

title: AT1R-Selective Negative Allosteric Modulator Targeting the Epitope for Pathogenic Autoantibody Activation
authorString: Singh KD, Pardhi TR, Harford TJ, Laishram L, Ravi T, Desnoyer R, Maroo AP, Tang WW, Karnik SS.
abstractText: A major therapeutic strategy for managing cardiovascular and renal diseases is the use of angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs). These drugs block both pathogenic and physiological signaling by the angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) by preventing angiotensin II (AngII) binding to orthosteric pocket in transmembrane portion of AT1R. However, in many autoimmune diseases, AT1R activation is chronically driven by pathogenic autoantibody binding to a distinct extracellular surface located allosteric site. Currently, there are no allosteric inhibitors of AT1R available to mechanistically prevent the autoantibodies and preserve the orthosteric hormonal functions of AngII. Here, we report the structure-guided hit-to-lead optimization of TP1, a first-in-class AT1R allosteric chemotype and negative allosteric modulator (NAM) with improved potency and drug-like properties. Computational docking and site-directed mutagenesis identified a TP1 binding mode that is distinct from the orthosteric-site binding of ARBs and AngII. Synthetically pure TP1 significantly reduced the capacity of AT1R to bind AngII without affecting AngII binding to AT2R, demonstrating an AT1R selective effect. TP1 reduced AngII-induced calcium signaling and migration in AT1R-expressing cells, arterial contraction, and increases in blood pressure in AngII-infused mice, demonstrating its activity as a NAM. Crucially, TP1 blocked binding of pathogenic autoantibodies to AT1R-expressing cells from the serum of patients with preeclampsia and dilated cardiomyopathy, a function distinct from ARBs. Together, these findings establish TP1 as a proof-of-concept, AT1R-selective NAM chemotype with therapeutic potential for AT1R autoantibody-driven conditions such as preeclampsia, where ARBs are strictly contraindicated. Developing AT1R-targeted NAM antihypertensive drugs may offer therapeutic advantages over ARBs and expand the pharmacological toolkit for this important CVD receptor. Key words: AT1R, AngII, AT1R-AAb, NAM, Allosteric ligand, GPCR, blood pressure, pharmacokinetics, antihypertensives

title: Cardiometabolic stress induces atrial myopathy in mice, characterized by structural remodelling, metabolic dysfunction, and incomplete transcriptional recovery.
authorString: Couet J, Teou DC, Morin-Grandmont A, Le Bos N, Le Bos T, Labbé E, Thibodeau S, Joseph V, Arsenault M.
abstractText:
Background:

The mechanisms underlying atrial remodelling and recovery following the withdrawal of cardiometabolic stress remain incompletely understood. We investigated the functional, metabolic, and transcriptional consequences of metabolic-hypertensive stress (MHS), a murine model of cardiometabolic HFpEF, in the left atrium (LA) and assessed the reversibility of these alterations following myocardial recovery.

Methods and Results:

Male and female mice underwent a two-hit HFpEF-inducing protocol consisting of angiotensin II infusion and a high-fat diet combined with physical inactivity (metabolic-hypertensive stress, MHS). Following 4 weeks of MHS, mice underwent a 4-week myocardial recovery (MR) phase involving stress withdrawal, dietary normalization, and voluntary exercise. We assessed LA function by speckle-tracking echocardiography, mitochondrial respiration by high-resolution respirometry, and transcriptomic remodelling by bulk RNA sequencing. MHS markedly reduced LA reservoir, conduit, and contractile strain, consistent with atrial myopathy. Transcriptomic analyses revealed substantially greater remodelling in the LA than previously observed in the left ventricle under comparable experimental conditions. Hallmark pathway analysis showed activation of extracellular matrix remodelling and profibrotic signalling pathways, along with suppression of oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid metabolism. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified a structural remodelling module enriched for extracellular matrix organization and angiogenesis pathways, as well as a bioenergetic module enriched for mitochondrial respiratory functions. Although inflammatory and structural remodelling pathways largely normalized following myocardial recovery, mitochondrial and metabolic programs exhibited incomplete restoration. Persistent transcriptional alterations were concentrated within a stress-responsive gene network enriched for adaptive cellular response pathways. In parallel, a discrete regulatory module displayed significant sex-dependent expression patterns.

Conclusions:

Metabolic-hypertensive stress induces profound atrial functional, metabolic, and transcriptomic remodelling, consistent with the development of cardiometabolic atrial myopathy. While many stress-induced changes resolve following myocardial recovery, key bioenergetic and stress-responsive transcriptional programs persist, suggesting that cardiometabolic stress leaves a lasting molecular imprint within the atrium.

title: A robust and scalable image analysis framework for phenotyping human thoracic aorta
authorString: Chen J, Qian L, Gong R, Sun C, Pham T, Martin C, Zafar M, Elefteriades J, Sun W, Liang L.
abstractText: Large-scale phenotyping of the thoracic aorta requires a workflow in which every step, from segmentation to phenotype extraction, runs without manual intervention. We present a robust and scalable framework that converts contrast-enhanced CT into anatomical landmarks, a patient-specific quadrilateral mesh, a wall-stress field and regional phenotypes of the thoracic aorta. Four nnU-Net segmentation tasks delineate the aorta, its anatomical regions and two partitions of the aortic root. A surface-curve-point procedure derives the annulus, the sinotubular junction, the ostia of the supra-aortic branches, the cusp nadirs and the commissures from the interfaces between segmented regions. We fit a structured template of 24,882 quadrilateral elements to the segmented aortic surface by staged, differentiable mesh deformation and compute the transmural mean wall stress with PyTorch-FEA. The structured mesh provides node-to-node correspondence across patients, anchored to the anatomy by the landmarks, from which the framework extracts regional morphological and biomechanical phenotypes.

title: Single-Cell Multimodal Profiling Reveals Maternal Diabetes- Nkx2-5 Interaction in Congenital Heart Disease in a Genetic Model Recapitulating Human Embryopathies
authorString: Ibrahim S, Maurizio J, Ved N, Brunet T, Humbert C, Conrozier D, Ameur S, Collod G, Szumska D, Miller JJ, Ashcroft FM, Thienpont B, Kahlert A, Sparrow DB, Stefanovic S.
abstractText: The etiological complexity of congenital heart disease (CHD) arises from the interaction between genetic and environmental factors. We hypothesized that environmental exposure could potentiate a genetic susceptibility, leading to an increased incidence of specific cardiac defects. To test this hypothesis, we used ßV59M+ female mice exhibiting severe hyperglycemia (>28 mmol/L) without dyslipidemia, a model we characterized that faithfully recapitulates human diabetic embryopathy. These females were crossed with males haploinsufficient for  Nkx2-5 , a transcription factor essential for cardiac development and implicated in human CHD. Our results show that the combination of genetic susceptibility and a hyperglycemic maternal environment (G×E) leads to a higher frequency and severity of cardiac malformations, including ventricular septal defects specifically involving the muscular septum, univentricular morphologies, and dilation with thinning of the myocardium. These structural abnormalities were associated with transcriptional changes affecting the contractile identity of the chamber myocardium. Single-nucleus multiomic profiling (snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq) of the E9.5 cardiac region revealed that the interaction between maternal diabetes and  Nkx2-5 haploinsufficiency profoundly reshapes transcriptional and chromatin accessibility landscapes. These changes affect not only metabolic pathways, but also cell cycle progression in second heart field (SHF) progenitors, likely contributing to the observed structural cardiac defects. Multiomic integration further identifies a disrupted indirect  Nkx2-5–Aldh1a2 regulatory axis in posterior SHF progenitors, while demonstrating that maternal diabetes selectively affects a restricted subset of  Nkx2-5 -dependent regulatory elements associated with cardiomyocyte maturation. Our findings establish a comprehensive single-cell multiomic resource that will facilitate the integration of human GWAS and other genomic datasets, enabling the identification and functional interpretation of disease-associated loci.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Modeling to Aid in the Identification of Genetic Conditions in Infants with Congenital Heart Disease
authorString: Caiola M, Thompson T, Stephens SB, Salamat B, Harris K, Lara C, Coban Akdemir Z, Zhang L, Roth M, Milosavljevic A, Weitz AC, Morris SA.
abstractText:
ABSTRACT

Background

Genetic conditions are common in congenital heart disease (CHD) and affect care, but are often missed or diagnosed late. We asked whether routine clinical data can shortlist the most likely genetic conditions.

Methods

Retrospective single-center cohort of children with CHD and an echocardiogram who had either a confirmed genetic diagnosis or negative cytogenetic testing and CHD gene sequencing. Echocardiogram images and serial medical record data were added as model inputs in the order they become clinically available. Class-balanced logistic regression (LR) and a multimodal deep learning fusion network were fitted to the same inputs at each step. The primary metric was balanced top-3 accuracy (correct diagnosis among the top three, averaged across conditions), with bootstrap intervals.

Results

The cohort included 1,720 children (988 with common CHD-associated genetic conditions, 231 rare diagnoses, 501 negative testing). Using only inputs generated at the echocardiogram visit, LR reached a balanced top-3 accuracy 0.758 (chance 0.429). Serial records, radiology notes and ICD-10 codes, raised this to 0.809. Multimodal fusion performed similarly at each stage. With a genetic condition withheld from training, the fusion embedding placed affected children nearest to others sharing a gene group in 0.37 of cases versus 0.10 without the embedding (+0.268 [95% CI +0.242, +0.295]).

Conclusions

Routine clinical data available at first echocardiogram can help identify likely genetic diagnoses, and later coded inputs ceiling. Multimodal fusion added no accuracy over LR, but places children sharing a genetic cause near one another, making nearest-neighbor retrieval informative for undiagnosed children.

title: Variability in Resting Oxygen Consumption Estimation in Adult Patients After Fontan Operation
authorString: Dolenc J, Kuzmanovski A, Benedik E, Pavšič N.
abstractText: The hemodynamics in patients after Fontan operation are commonly evaluated through cardiac catheterization, where accurate assessment depends on reliable estimation of the resting oxygen consumption (rVO₂). In clinical practice, rVO₂ is frequently estimated using predictive equations rather than measured directly. In this prospective observational study, we compared rVO₂ measured by indirect calorimetry with rVO₂ measured during pre-exercise rest phase on routine cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) or estimated using commonly applied predictive equations. To illustrate the potential consequences of rVO₂ variability on hemodynamic calculations, pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) was modeled using a hypothetical patient scenario. Twenty-six clinically stable adult patients after Fontan operation were included (mean age 26.6 ± 5.8 years, 46% female, 73% extracardiac conduit, 42% open fenestration). Substantial variability in rVO₂ was observed depending on the method used. Measured rVO₂ by indirect calorimetry (246.2 ± 45.1 ml/min) differed significantly from that acquired by CPET (n = 22; 355.5 ± 74.4 ml/min) or calculated using predictive equations (n = 26 for all; LaFarge: 146.0 ± 31.9ml/min; Dehmer: 229.3 ± 28.1 ml/min; Bergstra: 264.6 ± 38.8 ml/min; p < 0.05 for all comparisons against indirect calorimetry). The Dehmer and Bergstra equations showed the smallest systematic differences and strongest correlations with measured rVO₂. Modeled PVR varied markedly and inversely with the rVO₂ estimation method used, reflecting its direct mathematical derivation from the rVO₂ values. Given the observed limitations of predictive equations and CPET-derived estimates in this population, direct measurement of rVO₂ by indirect calorimetry should be the preferred method for hemodynamic calculations in adult patients after Fontan operation.
