title: Radial Artery Versus Saphenous Vein Grafts in Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery: A Grade- Assessed Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
authorString: Hamza M, Khalid AA, Shah Z, Saqib HW, Ashfaq A, Ahmad M, Fazal TB, Chaudhry IUH.
abstractText: Background This systematic review and meta-analysis compared the long-term efficacy and clinical outcomes of radial artery (RA) versus saphenous vein grafts (SVG) in coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, databases were searched through March 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing RA and SVG for non-left anterior descending coronary arteries. The primary outcome was graft failure, defined as a composite of complete or functional occlusion (string sign). Results Four RCTs assessing 1,219 grafts (621 RA; 598 SVG) were included. No statistically significant differences were found between RA and SVG in overall graft failure (12.4% vs. 14.9%; P = .11) or patency rates (87.6% vs. 85.1%; P = .11). However, RA grafts demonstrated significantly lower odds of complete occlusion (7.1% vs. 13.9%; P = .046) but a 6-fold higher risk of functional occlusion (6.1% vs. 0.8%; P < .001). Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis revealed that omitting one outlier study eliminated heterogeneity and shifted primary outcomes significantly in favor of RA grafts. No significant differences were observed for all-cause mortality (P = .13) or repeat revascularization (P = .37). Conclusion Neither conduit is universally superior. RA grafts reduce complete anatomical occlusion but are highly susceptible to competitive flow-induced functional occlusion. Graft selection should be individualized based on patient demographics and target vessel characteristics.

title: Persistent Rather Than Variable Short Sleep Associates With Cardiovascular Events in Middle-Aged and Older Chinese Adults: A CHARLS Cohort Study
authorString: Wang Z, Fan X, Chen L, Shi Y, Shao Q.
abstractText: Background Short sleep has been linked to cardiometabolic disease, but single-time sleep assessments cannot separate persistent short sleep from recurrent variable short sleep. Whether these sleep-trajectory phenotypes predict incident cardiovascular events in middle-aged and older adults, and whether the cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein, and glucose (CHG) index identifies higher-risk sleep-metabolic profiles, remains uncertain. Methods We analysed 11,050 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) participants aged 45 years or older who were free of heart disease and stroke through 2015, had sleep-duration data from at least two of the 2011–2015 survey waves, and had 2018 or 2020 follow-up. Sleep trajectories were classified as persistent optimal, variable short, persistent short, optimal-to-short, or other patterns. Incident cardiovascular events were self-reported physician-diagnosed heart disease or stroke. Multivariable Cox models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, clinical, depressive-symptom, and physical-activity covariates; sensitivity, CHG, joint-exposure, and exploratory sex-stratified analyses were performed. Results During 51,330 person-years, 1,923 incident cardiovascular events occurred. Compared with persistent optimal sleep, persistent short sleep was associated with higher cardiovascular risk (hazard ratio [HR] 1.22, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.05–1.42; p = 0.009), whereas variable short sleep was not (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.88–1.21; p = 0.701); estimates were similar across sensitivity analyses. CHG was modestly associated with events after adjustment for sleep trajectory (HR per standard deviation 1.06, 95% CI 1.01–1.11; p = 0.024). High CHG combined with persistent short sleep identified the highest joint-risk group (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.08–1.69; p = 0.008). In exploratory sex-stratified analyses, persistent versus variable short sleep carried higher risk among women (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.04–1.64) but not men, with a significant sex-by-CHG interaction (p = 0.027). Conclusions Persistent short sleep, but not variable short sleep, was associated with incident cardiovascular events after multivariable adjustment in this national cohort of middle-aged and older Chinese adults. The CHG index may help characterise higher-risk sleep-metabolic subgroups, particularly among women in exploratory analyses. Repeated sleep assessment and routine metabolic markers may support prevention-oriented cardiovascular risk assessment in ageing populations. Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: Pressure is not flow: Rethinking blood pressure as a surrogate for cerebral blood flow during general anesthesia
authorString: Österlind J, Holmlund P, Birnefeld J, Hultin M, Wåhlin A, Zarrinkoob L.
abstractText:
Abstract Background: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is pharmacologically augmented in selected perioperative and critical care settings, including acute neurological conditions and after cardiac arrest, with the aim of improving cerebral perfusion, although it remains uncertain whether higher arterial pressure translates into increased cerebral blood flow (CBF). We investigated the CBF response to MAP augmentation with norepinephrine (NE), a commonly used vasopressor in perioperative and critical care settings, during propofol-based general anesthesia.

Methods:

In this prospective within-subject interventional study, 16 neurologically intact patients with ASA physical status I-II undergoing elective surgery were studied using phase-contrast magnetic resonance imaging. CBF was quantified in the awake state and during propofol-based general anesthesia before and after NE-induced MAP augmentation. During general anesthesia, NE was titrated to increase MAP by approximately 25% from baseline. Concurrent systemic hemodynamics were assessed.

Results:

General anesthesia was associated with a 50.1% (interquartile range, 42.1?55.7%) reduction in CBF and a 24.2% (20.3-29.2%) reduction in MAP compared with the awake state (both P<0.001). During general anesthesia, NE-induced MAP augmentation increased MAP by 25.7% (21.9-32.0%; P<0.001), whereas CBF remained unchanged (P=1.000). Cardiac output remained unchanged (P=0.163), whereas systemic vascular resistance index and cerebrovascular resistance increased by 40.0% (28.7-45.2%) and 36.2% (17.7-42.8%), respectively (both P<0.001). Changes in CBF during MAP augmentation were not associated with concurrent changes in MAP, cardiac output, or systemic vascular resistance index.

Conclusions:

In neurologically intact patients undergoing propofol-based general anesthesia, clinically relevant NE-induced MAP augmentation did not increase CBF despite an approximately 50% lower CBF than in the awake state. These findings challenge the assumption that pharmacological elevation of an otherwise adequate MAP improves cerebral perfusion in this setting. While maintaining adequate arterial pressure remains essential, further MAP augmentation should not be assumed to increase CBF. Clinical Trial Registration: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/ NCT06855407 ; NCT06855407 .

title: BCKDK Inhibitors Directly Antagonize Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor and Induce Vasodilation Independently of BCAA Catabolism or BCKDK
authorString: Kawakami R, Deleye Y, Akkaya E, Pham U, Jung JW, Lai L, Chundi A, Darbha S, Murashige D, Gaspar R, He W, Zhang G, Kahsai A, Rajagopal S, White PJ, Arany Z, McGarrah RW.
abstractText: Branched-chain amino acids (BCAA) have been implicated in diabetes and heart failure, leading to ongoing clinical trials with inhibitors of BCKDK, a key regulator of BCAA catabolism. We have previously shown that these inhibitors promote vasodilation and lower blood pressure, well-known cardioprotective effects, but how this occurs remained unclear. We show here, using explanted vessels, in vivo hemodynamics and telemetry, and genetically modified mice, that the vasodilatory effect of BCKDK inhibitors is direct, rapid, independent of nitric oxide, independent of BCAA catabolism, and most strikingly, independent of BCKDK itself. Instead, we demonstrate, using structural and biochemical studies, that BCKDK inhibitors directly antagonize the angiotensin II type I receptor (AT1R) and consequent angiotensin-mediated vasoconstriction. These data demonstrate a strong off-target effect of BCKDK inhibitors, independent of BCAA or BCKDK, which may explain their cardioprotective effects but also questions if this protection would be additive to existing AT1R blockers.

title: Prognostic Value of Prediabetes for Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Patients with Coronary Heart Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authorString: Ding C, Gao Y, Taylor R.
abstractText: Background Coronary Heart Disease (CHD) is a leading cause of death among adults, incurring high socio-economic burdens. Prediabetes is highly prevalent in patients with CHD and may be associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). This study aims to systematically evaluate the effects of prediabetes on the risk of MACE in patients with established CHD and to explore variations in this association across different prediabetes diagnostic criteria. Methods Six bibliographic databases (Embase, PubMed, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang Data, and VIP Chinese Journals Database) were systematically searched to 1 January 2026 for prospective and retrospective cohort studies investigating the association between prediabetes (defined by the ADA, WHO or IEC criteria) and MACE in adult patients with CHD. Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. The risk of bias was assessed by ROBINS-E tool. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were conducted to explore potential sources of statistical heterogeneity. Results Twenty cohort studies involving a total of 63,425 patients with a median of 3 years follow-up were included. Compared with normoglycemic group, coexisting prediabetes was significantly associated with higher risk of MACE in patients with CHD (pooled HR = 1.22, 95% Cl = 1.12–1.33, I 2  = 44.0%). Consistently, elevated risks were observed for all-cause death: HR = 1.30 (95% CI: 1.12–1.50, I 2  = 0.0%) and cardiac death: HR = 1.24 (95% CI: 1.08–1.42, I 2  = 1.4%). Subgroup analysis by prediabetes diagnostic criteria showed consistent risk elevation across ADA, WHO, and IEC criteria, and suggested that these criteria contributed to the observed statistical heterogeneity. The pooled HRs of glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) were: ADA-HbA1c: HR = 1.28 (95% Cl: 1.17–1.41, I 2  = 0.0%); IEC-HbA1c: HR = 1.41 (95% Cl: 1.21–1.65, I 2 = 0.0%). The ADA composite criteria (HbA1c + FPG): HR = 1.19 (95% Cl: 1.07–1.33, I 2  = 51.0%); WHO and IEC composite criteria (WHO-FPG, IEC-HbA1c): HR = 1.53 (95% Cl: 1.26–1.85, I 2  = 0.0%). No statistical differences ( P  > 0.05) were found across a range of population and study characteristics. Conclusions This meta-analysis of cohort evidence indicates that prediabetes is associated with an increased risk of MACE in patients with coronary heart disease, and the magnitude of risk differs by prediabetes diagnostic criteria. However, pooled estimates for 2h-OGTT were unavailable due to insufficient data. Future studies with more diverse CHD populations and complete outcome reporting are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Quantifying Systematic Bias in Observational Causal Estimates Using Negative Controls: The Bias Attribution Fraction
authorString: Zeng Z, Wang J, Zuo H, Shu L.
abstractText: Importance. Observational studies dominate evidence in cardiovascular outcomes research, yet no widely adopted reporting standard requires authors to disclose how much of an observed association is attributable to systematic error. The negative-control calibration framework of the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics consortium returns a binary answer: a calibrated P-value either crosses 0.05 or it does not. That answer conflates "is there a signal" with "is the signal credible."  Objective. To define the Bias Attribution Fraction (BAF), a continuous estimator in [0, 1] that quantifies the fraction of an observed log relative risk that is attributable to systematic bias, together with its 95% credible interval, and to evaluate whether reporting calibrated P-value plus BAF plus interval width produces more defensible decisions than reporting the calibrated P-value alone.  Design. Three-part study: (i) metric definition and interval construction; (ii) Monte Carlo simulation across 1920 conditions by 1000 repetitions = 1,920,000 simulated target estimates (a primary grid plus a sign-flipped companion grid of identical size, pooled for all analyses), with truth known by construction; (iii) two-arm beta-blocker target trial emulation in MIMIC IV, adhering to the TARGET guideline, with targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) and 12 negative-control outcomes.  Setting. MIMIC IV (critical care) and MIMIC IV ECG, 2008 to 2019.  Participants. Adults with a first intensive care unit stay and a recorded 12-lead ECG.  Exposures. Two clinical questions are evaluated: (1) reaching at least 50% of guideline-recommended target dose of an index beta-blocker within 7 days of admission, sustained to 12 months, versus lower or no exposure; (2) receiving guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) with at least two of three foundational drug classes at adequate dose for 12 months versus fewer.  Main Outcomes and Measures. One-year all-cause mortality. Primary analytic outputs: (i) the calibrated P-value from a negative-control empirical null distribution with 12 outcomes; (ii) BAF-hat with a Markov chain Monte Carlo 95% credible interval; (iii) a verdict drawn from a truth-calibrated lookup table mapping the BAF-hat by interval-width cell to a probability of being bias-dominated.  Results. Across 1,920,000 simulated repetitions, the calibrated P-value alone yielded a misuse rate (declared usable while truth was bias-dominated) of 36.02%. Adding the BAF point estimate reduced misuse to 16.48%, and requiring the whole credible interval of BAF to lie below 0.5, clear of the bias-dominated zone, reduced misuse to 10.16%. Requiring in addition a calibrated probability of bias dominance below 15% reduced misuse to 3.02% at the cost of declaring 22.1% of estimates usable (versus 61.8% for the calibrated P-value alone). Read from the bias-dominated view, meaning that withholding a repetition is a positive call and being truly bias-dominated is a positive truth, the BAF estimator achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.922, compared with 0.787 for the calibrated P-value. In MIMIC IV, question 1 produced a calibrated P-value of 0.894 and BAF-hat = 0.875 (95% credible interval 0.385 to 0.992); the apparent one-year mortality reduction of 16.9% was entirely attributable to systematic bias and the association was not usable as effect evidence. Question 2 also failed layer 1, with a calibrated P-value of 0.1026, and BAF-hat = 0.460 placed it in the "competitive, no verdict" zone.  Conclusions and Relevance. Pairing the calibrated P-value with BAF and its 95% credible interval turns a binary credibility judgement into a three-channel report (signal existence, effect size, and bias fraction). Despite TARGET-adherent design, doubly robust TMLE, and 12 negative controls, both clinical questions in this study still failed to qualify as effect evidence, with question 1 demonstrating complete bias domination and BAF quantifying the systematic error that remained. The reporting standard proposed here can be applied to any observational study that includes negative controls, without requiring additional data.

title: A Novel Digital Phenotype of Physical Activity: Associations with Heart Rate Fragmentation
authorString: Pae BJ, Cousineau B, Zeng Z, Li Y, Mathew L, Chang S, De Leon K, Wilson L, Alexander A, Santana E, Alagar N, Colon-Motas K, Murtala A, Karimi S, Li Q, Sameni R, Ko Y, Lobelo F, Lampert R, Bremner JD, Vaccarino V, Clifford GD, Shah AJ.
abstractText:
Background:

Heart rate fragmentation (HRF) has emerged as a novel marker of sinoatrial instability and neuroautonomic dysregulation and is a predictor of incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and cardiovascular mortality. Leveraging heart rate fragmentation as a novel measure may help us better understand the prognostic significance of physical activity. Physical activity (PA) patterns are multidimensional and difficult to study holistically, however. We sought to examine for novel PA clusters in a cohort of veteran men and evaluate their prognostic significance based on their associations with neuroautonomic dysregulation.

Methods:

In this cross-sectional study, we examined 602 male veterans from the Vietnam Era Twins Study of Electrophysiology in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (VETS-EP) who were enrolled between 2022 and 2026. Accelerometry data were used to derive physical activity parameters across 6 domains: volume, sedentary behavior, intensity, diurnal pattern, fragmentation, and variability. Heart rate fragmentation was assessed using percentage of inflection points (PIP), inverse average length of segments (IALS), percentage of short segments (PSS), and percentage of alternating segments (PAS). Gaussian mixture models were used to derive digital phenotypes of physical activity, and associations with heart rate fragmentation were assessed using linear mixed models.

Results:

Participants had a mean age of 73.8 ± 2.9 years and 93.2% reported White race. Two overlapping phenotypes of physical activity patterns were identified: a compact-early phenotype, characterized by earlier activity timing and slightly greater overall activity, and a diffuse-late phenotype, characterized by later activity timing and greater heterogeneity in activity volume. In fully adjusted models, the diffuse-late phenotype was associated with higher PIP, the primary outcome (β: 1.199, 95% CI: 0.034 to 2.363, p-value: 0.044), and higher IALS (β: 0.01210, 95% CI: 0.00048 to 0.02373, p-value: 0.041), but not PSS or PAS, compared with the compact-early phenotype.

Conclusions:

In older male veterans, Gaussian mixture model phenotyping identified two overlapping physical activity phenotypes, differing mainly in diurnal timing and in the dispersion of overall activity, that were associated with modest differences in heart rate fragmentation. These phenotypes provide a framework for capturing complex physical activity patterns. Future prospective studies representing diverse populations are needed to validate such phenotypes.

title: Persistent Hypertension After Asymptomatic Elevated In-Hospital Blood Pressure: The INDEBP Study
authorString: Hausknecht K, Mayr M, Breidthardt T, Burkard T, Vischer AS.
abstractText:
Background: Elevated blood pressure (BP) is common during hospitalization. Despite recommendations to avoid routine changes in antihypertensive therapy, clinical practice remains variable. Prospective data on whether elevated in-hospital BP identifies patients with hypertension after discharge are limited.

Methods:

Adults hospitalized for non-cardiac conditions with asymptomatic routine in-hospital BP ?140 and/or ?90 mmHg on at least two occasions separated by ?24 hours were prospectively enrolled. Antihypertensive therapy was managed at the discretion of treating physicians. Routine in-hospital BP, standardized research BP, and changes in antihypertensive therapy were recorded. Four weeks after discharge, participants underwent 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM).

Results:

Among 50 participants, 42 (84%; 95% CI, 70.9 ? 92.8) had hypertension on follow-up ABPM. Among 21 participants without known hypertension, 18 (86%) had previously unrecognized hypertension on follow-up ABPM; among 29 participants with known hypertension, 24 (83%) had uncontrolled hypertension. Antihypertensive therapy was changed during hospitalization in 26 participants (52%), with de-escalation more frequent than intensification. Hypertension on follow-up ABPM was present in 88.5% of participants with and 79.2% without in-hospital therapy changes. Standardized research BP, but not routine in-hospital BP, correlated with follow-up ABPM.

Conclusion:

Asymptomatic elevated routine in-hospital BP identified a population with a high prevalence of hypertension four weeks after discharge, including patients with and without previously diagnosed hypertension. These findings support structured post-discharge BP reassessment rather than assuming that elevated in-hospital BP is transient. URL: www.ClinicalTrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT06132451

title: Autonomic neurons are intrinsically hyperexcitable in a Friedreich ataxia iPSC model
authorString: (Max) SL, Lees J, Zhang H, Li L, Dottori M, Pebay A, Corben L, Delatycki M, Wilcox S, Pullin J, Choi J, McCarthy D, Napierala J, Napierala M.
abstractText: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is an inherited multisystem disorder caused by a GAA repeat expansion in the FXN gene and consequent frataxin deficiency, causing progressive neurodegeneration and heart disease. Clinical studies have documented autonomic dysfunction in FRDA, including elevated resting heart rate, raised plasma catecholamines and a high burden of urinary, bowel and sexual symptoms. Consistent with this, autopsy studies show degeneration of the cardiac conduction system and its associated ganglia in FRDA. Whether these features are intrinsic to FRDA autonomic neurons has been untestable without a human cellular model. Here, a human model of FRDA autonomic neurons was established by differentiating induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from individuals with FRDA and from their CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. FRDA autonomic neurons expressed canonical autonomic lineage markers and retained reduced FXN mRNA and frataxin protein levels. Electrophysiological analysis revealed pronounced hyperexcitability, with an approximately five-fold increase in spike number, shortened interspike intervals, and longer bursts. FRDA autonomic neurons also exhibited increased cell death, elevated mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and a shift from networked to tubular mitochondrial morphology. Bulk RNA sequencing of all three isogenic pairs revealed loss of extracellular matrix programs and activation of stress response pathways. The top differentially expressed gene was MEG3, a maternally imprinted long noncoding RNA, which was consistently upregulated across all three isogenic pairs. MEG3 sits within the imprinted 14q32 DLK1-DIO3 locus, whose maternally expressed noncoding transcripts were co-ordinately de-repressed in FRDA autonomic neurons. Competitive gene-set testing of 43 imprinted genes across 20 domains showed this to be specific to 14q32: no other imprinted domain was co-ordinately altered. Together, these findings establish hyperexcitability of autonomic neurons as a cell autonomous consequence of frataxin deficiency, accompanied by mitochondrial dysfunction. This provides a cellular basis for the increased sympathetic tone observed in clinical studies.

title: Cardiopulmonary phenotypes as markers of high risk in patients with COPD in primary care: the MASTER-EPOC study
authorString: Calderón-Montero A, Alonso-Avilés R, Sanz-García A, Sheila M, Millares-López C, Gómez-López M, Benito-Fernández R, José-Gallego R, Pérez-Laorden A, LM R.
abstractText: Background Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is managed primarily with respiratory-based algorithms, even though cardiovascular comorbidity is a major determinant of adverse outcomes. We aimed to identify and characterise cardiopulmonary phenotypes defined by exacerbator profile and cardiovascular risk (CVR) in patients with COPD managed in primary care. Methods Cross-sectional, multicentre, retrospective study of 1,307 patients with COPD across 52 primary care centres in six Spanish regions. Phenotypes cross-classified the exacerbator profile (GOLD) with cardiovascular burden (established cardiovascular disease [CVD] / high risk / low-to-moderate risk). We used mixed-effects logistic regression, intraclass correlation, ROC curves, collinearity analysis and a preliminary unsupervised clustering analysis (machine learning). Results Median age was 72.6 years; 65.7% were men, 58.8% had moderate airflow obstruction, 31.2% were exacerbators and 36.8% had established CVD. The most frequent phenotype was the non-exacerbator with high CVR (40.6%), whereas the exacerbator phenotype with established CVD carried the greatest burden of hospitalisations and disease severity. We identified a hidden-risk phenotype—non-exacerbators with CVD—with a higher risk of hospitalisation and poorer clinical control (adjusted OR 1.99; 95% CI 1.21–3.25; p = 0.006 vs non-exacerbator phenotypes; sensitivity analysis). Clustering confirmed the clinical findings. Conclusions In COPD, jointly considering exacerbations and cardiovascular burden defines clinically relevant phenotypes, including a hidden-risk group of non-exacerbators with CVD. These practical, readily available axes complement the eosinophil count and support an integrated cardiopulmonary assessment.

title: Whole-Cardiac-Cycle ECG Dynamics in Critical Illness: The Spatial QRS- T Angle as a Prognostic Marker, an Early-Warning Signal for Arrhythmia and Myocardial Injury, and an In-Vivo Pharmacodynamic Readout
authorString: Hui Y, Qian Z, Song C, Peiwu L, Jian W, Hao Y.
abstractText: Background. Electrocardiographic prediction in critical illness has relied on single parameters measured once — most often the corrected QT interval — with modest and inconsistent results. Whether quantitative parameters spanning the whole cardiac cycle (depolarization through repolarization), measured from every ECG of an ICU stay, carry independent prognostic and mechanistic information is unknown. Methods. We linked MIMIC-IV v3.1 to the MIMIC-IV-ECG waveform subset and built a cohort of 14,319 adult ICU stays without known coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, or pacing (25,112 analyzable ECGs from a 72,166-ECG linked pool). We assembled a whole-cycle parameter panel per ECG: machine-derived intervals and axes (heart rate, PR, QRS duration, QT/QTc, frontal QRS-T angle) and waveform-measured amplitudes from a validated median-beat engine (ST amplitude, J-to-Tpeak amplitude, QRS voltage, ST-T area, Tp-Te). Analyses: (1) 48-hour landmark Cox models for 28-day mortality; (2) linear mixed models of day-by-day trajectories by survival; (3) new-onset repolarization abnormalities as exposures for ECG-specific outcomes (new atrial tachyarrhythmia, new myocardial injury) with cause-specific and Fine–Gray models; (4) within-patient difference-in-differences ECG responses to ICU interventions, with amiodarone as a positive control. Results. The spatial QRS-T angle was the strongest whole-cycle predictor of 28-day mortality: per-SD HR 1.125 (95% CI 1.068–1.185; P < 0.0001) for the 48-h maximum, with dose-response across strata (90–120° vs < 60°: HR 1.23; ≥120°: HR 1.35), independent of age, sex, SOFA, lactate, and MAP. QTc was null (HR 0.95; P = 0.08), as were QRS duration and T-wave amplitudes; J-to-Tpeak amplitude (HR/SD 1.121; P < 0.0001) and low QRS voltage (HR 0.905; P < 0.01) added independent signal. Trajectories separated from day 1 (mixed-model survival main effect + 15.3°; P = 1×10⁻³⁴) without subsequent divergence (day×survival P = 0.40), and adding within-stay change to the first ECG gave no incremental discrimination (ΔAUC − 0.0005) — the first ECG carried essentially all prognostic information for mortality. For ECG-specific outcomes, by contrast, new-onset abnormalities were strongly predictive: new-onset ST depression → new atrial tachyarrhythmia HR 3.10 (1.51–6.36) and → new myocardial injury HR 2.69 (1.32–5.49); new-onset QRS-T angle ≥ 90° → atrial tachyarrhythmia HR 3.77 (2.03–7.01); QTc ≥ 500 ms predicted nothing. In the pharmacodynamic analysis, amiodarone initiation produced the expected + 16.4 ms QTc prolongation (P = 0.0006) and − 15.6 bpm heart-rate reduction (P < 0.0001), validating the framework; norepinephrine initiation was followed by + 5.7 ms QTc (P < 0.05), and renal replacement therapy initiation by + 6.4 ms QTc, + 7.5° QRS-T angle, and + 3.6 ms QRS widening. Conclusions. In critical illness, spatial depolarization–repolarization mismatch — not repolarization duration — is the dominant ECG prognostic axis. It is measurable from the first ECG, static information suffices for mortality prediction, but new-onset electrical abnormalities precede arrhythmia and myocardial injury with 3–4-fold hazard ratios, and the same panel reads out drug and organ-support effects in vivo. Whole-cycle ECG dynamics are a quantitative, reproducible, and clinically actionable monitoring layer for the ICU.

title: High prevalence of cardiovascular comorbidity in multiple myeloma. A Swedish register study with matched controls
authorString: Larsson K, Sverrisdóttir I, Einarsdóttir S, Karma M, Villegas-Scivetti M, Knut-Bojanowska D, Juliusson G, Carlson K, Larfors G, Blimark CH.
abstractText: Introduction Multiple myeloma (MM) is a hematological malignancy with a median age at diagnosis of 72 years. Consequently, cardiovascular comorbidity is a concern. Using Swedish population-based registries, we aim to describe cardiac comorbidities among patients at time of MM diagnosis, the incidence of new cardiovascular events (CVE) at 2-year follow-up and the risk of death, in comparison with matched controls. Material and methods All MM patients (n=8 672) in the Swedish myeloma registry (SMR) diagnosed 2008-2021 were included. Matched controls (n=34 561) and data on cardiovascular disease (CVD) and CVE were collected from nationwide registries. Differences in incidence and mortality were evaluated with chi-square tests and Cox regression. Ethical consent was obtained from the Swedish Ethical Review Board. Results At time of MM diagnosis, 45.8% of the MM patients had a registered CVD vs 35.7% of the controls, p<0.0001. The most frequent comorbidities were hypertension and atrial fibrillation (AF) among both patients and controls; hypertension 32.5% vs 23.3%, p<0.0001 and AF 11.1% vs 9.1%, p<0.0001. At 2-year follow-up, 17.7% of patients had AF vs 8.5% of controls, p<0.0001. Occurrence of AF in patients >80 years was substantial, 30.1%, vs 17.7%, p<0.0001. Among patients with no prior CVD, new-onset CVE was seen among 43%. Patients with CVE at 2-year follow-up had an increased risk of death vs patients without a CVE, HR 1.30 (95% CI 1.21-1.40, p<0.0001). Conclusion Almost 50% of patients had a CVD at the time of MM diagnosis. Among patients >80 years, 30% had a diagnosis of AF at 2-year follow-up. Almost half of MM patients with no CVD at time of MM diagnosis, had a CVE at 2-year follow-up. Among MM patients, CVE was associated with inferior survival, calling for awareness and guidelines for management of CVD among MM patients.

title: Association of Body Roundness Index with Cardiovascular Diseases in Middle-Aged and Older Chinese Adults with Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Stage 0-3: Evidence from the CHARLS Study
authorString: Lian P, Wu X, Xie F, Liang S, Cheng S, Yin L, Zhang S.
abstractText: Objective This study aimed to evaluate the association between the body roundness index (BRI) and the risk of incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) among middle-aged and older Chinese adults in cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome stages 0–3. Methods A total of 7,566 participants from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), free of baseline CVD and classified as CKM stage 0–3, were included. Multivariable Cox models, restricted cubic splines, mediation analyses, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to assess associations, dose-response relationships, potential mediators, and predictive performance. Results During a maximum 9.0-year follow-up, 1,836 incident CVD cases were documented. Each 1-unit increase in BRI was associated with a 15.4% higher risk of CVD (HR: 1.154, 95% CI: 1.112–1.199), 13.4% for heart disease, and 18.7% for stroke. Participants in the highest BRI quartile had significantly elevated risks compared to the lowest quartile. A linear dose-response relationship was observed. Hypertension and dyslipidemia mediated 10.8% and 11.6% of the association, respectively. BRI demonstrated superior predictive ability for CVD (AUC=0.71) compared to body mass index (BMI) and A Body Shape Index (ABSI). Conclusion Higher BRI levels are independently associated with increased CVD risk in CKM stages 0–3, with a dose-response relationship. BRI outperforms BMI and ABSI in risk prediction, partially mediated by hypertension and dyslipidemia, supporting its use for early CVD stratification in this population.

title: Electronic Health Record-Based Machine Learning Models for Predicting Revascularization, Amputation, and Cardiovascular Mortality in At-Risk Patients
authorString: Browder SE, Laivuori M, McIntee T, Leese PJ, Alabi O, McGinigle KL.
abstractText: Patients with peripheral artery disease (PAD), chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), and/or diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) are at increased risk for limb loss and death. Existing risk calculators lack consistent clinical adoption; therefore, we aimed to identify vascular and non-vascular predictors of revascularization, amputation, and cardiovascular death using data from the OMOP CDM plus vascular extension. We assembled a cohort of adults with PAD, CLTI, or DFU receiving care within the UNC Health System from 2014–2024 (n = 178,995). Using 127 vascular-specific and thousands of non-vascular HER variables, we used logistic regression with inverse probability weighting and MCMC-based dimensionality reduction to predict revascularization, amputation, and cardiovascular death. The mean age was 72.5 ± 13.9 years; 50.9% were female and 23.5% Black. The revascularization and amputation models performed well (AUC = 0.984 and 0.926, respectively), while cardiovascular mortality prediction was modest (AUC = 0.772). Revascularization predictors were dominated by arterial disease, amputation prediction was driven by treatment interactions with dementia and frailty, and cardiovascular events and risk factors were the strongest predictors of cardiovascular mortality. Prediction models derived from harmonized EHR data demonstrated strong performance for revascularization and amputation. These findings support harmonized EHR-based vascular prediction modeling and warrant multi-institutional validation.

title: Social isolation, loneliness and functional transitions among middle-aged and older adults with cardiometabolic multimorbidity: a multistate Markov analysis of CHARLS
authorString: Sun J, Xue Z, Cheng A.
abstractText: Background Isolated or lonely older adults are more likely to become disabled; whether these exposures shape the direction of functional change — deterioration versus recovery — in cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM) is unknown. We examined how the two exposures relate to functional-state transitions and death in middle-aged and older adults with CMM. Methods We studied 1,731 adults aged ≥ 45 with CMM (≥ 2 of hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, heart disease or stroke) from waves 1–5 (2011–2020) of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. Isolation was a four-item index (unpartnered, living alone, no weekly child contact, no social activity); loneliness came from the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) item. Crossed, they defined four groups (G1 low isolation/no loneliness, G2 loneliness only, G3 isolation only, G4 both). Multistate Markov models estimated associations with nine transitions among independence, instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) limitation, activities of daily living (ADL) limitation and death. Results Over 9 years, 286 participants (16.5%) died. Loneliness was linked to deterioration onset (G2 vs G1: independence→IADL limitation hazard ratio [HR] 2.83, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.09–7.31; independence→ADL limitation 2.01, 1.28–3.15). Dual exposure carried a distinct signature: faster early deterioration (1→2 HR 2.66, 1.62–4.37), 66% lower recovery from ADL limitation (3→1 0.34, 0.17–0.70) and higher post-disability mortality (3→4 1.57, 1.04–2.39). Expected years independent between ages 60–90 were 4.83 (G1) versus 0.65 (G4): a 4.18-year gap. Conclusions In CMM, loneliness acted mainly at deterioration onset; dual exposure was marked by lost recovery and excess post-disability mortality. Social connection may be a modifiable target for preserving function across CMM trajectories.

title: PCR-based co-detection of respiratory bacterial pathogens among hospitalized COVID-19 patients: Early-pandemic data from Golestan Province, Iran
authorString: Vaez A, Jalali H, Izanloo A, Hamrahjoo M, Nikoo HR, Tabarraei A, Moradi A, Azimi S, Hashemi A, Rafiee M, Yasaghi M, Ardebili A.
abstractText: Background The presence of opportunistic bacterial pathogens may complicate patients with coronavirus disease-2019 (COVID-19), and characterizing their prevalence and spectrum during the early phase of the pandemic is epidemiologically relevant. This study estimated the frequency and distribution of respiratory bacterial pathogens detected by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in hospitalized COVID-19 patients during the first period of the pandemic in Golestan Province, Iran. Methods This retrospective study was performed on patients with COVID-19 confirmed by real-time reverse transcription (RT-PCR) who were hospitalized between June and November 2020. Nasal and nasopharyngeal swabs were tested by PCR for eight respiratory bacterial pathogens. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, and outcome data were extracted from medical records. Because upper-airway PCR cannot detect colonization, non-viable DNA, and true lower-respiratory tract infection, all positive results were interpreted as bacterial detection, not clinically confirmed co-infection. Results Among 254 hospitalized patients with confirmed COVID-19, 154 patients (60.6%) had detectable DNA from at least one bacterial target. Monobacterial and polybacterial detection was found in 111 (43.7%) and 43 (16.9%) patients, respectively. Staphylococcus aureus was the most common (22.8%) detected organism, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae (21.3%), Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (20.5%), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (11.4%). No significant associations were found between overall bacterial detection and age group, gender, clinical severity, ICU admission, mortality, length of hospital stay, or major laboratory parameters. In the unadjusted organism-specific analyses, P. aeruginosa detection was significantly associated with age group (P = 0.006), COVID-19 severity (P = 0.032), fever (P = 0.028), and ICU admission (P = 0.04). After multivariable adjustment, severe or critical COVID-19 remained independently associated with P. aeruginosa compared with mild disease (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 6.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.02–46.46; P = 0.048). Hypertension was identified as a suggestive marker for polybacterial detection (AOR = 3.08; 95% CI, 0.98–9.7; P = 0.054). Mild COVID-19 was associated with lower odds of polybacterial presence compared with severe or critical COVID-19 (AOR = 0.16; 95% CI, 0.03–0.95; P = 0.04). Conclusions Bacterial DNA of several respiratory organisms was frequently detected by PCR in upper-airway specimens from hospitalized COVID-19 patients during the early pandemic. However, these results should be interpreted cautiously; the observational nature of the study precludes causal interpretation. Because respiratory sampling occurred at variable times during hospitalization and PCR positivity cannot distinguish colonization from infection, our findings suggest a prevalence of bacterial DNA detected during the hospital stay rather than active infection. Prospective studies using lower-respiratory specimens when clinically indicated, culture and susceptibility testing are needed.

title: Polycystic kidney disease in pregnancy: A retrospective study on obstetric and neonatal outcomes
authorString: Frayret Z, Badeghiesh A, Baghlaf H, Dahan MH.
abstractText: Objective : The pregnancy, delivery and neonatal outcomes of pregnancies complicated by polycystic kidney disease have yet to be investigated in a population-based study. Most available research consists of case reports or case-control studies limited by small population sizes. 11-13 We sought to evaluate the obstetric and neonatal outcomes in pregnant patients with polycystic kidney disease using a national population database. Methods : This is a retrospective population-based cohort study utilizing the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project, Nationwide Inpatient Sample (HCUP-NIS). All women who delivered or had a maternal death (2004–2014 inclusive) were included in the study. Pregnancy, delivery, and neonatal outcomes were compared between women with an ICD-9 diagnosis of polycystic kidney disease to those without. While this paper uses the term “women” to reflect the framing of the original data set, we wish to acknowledge the distinction between biological sex, the ability to carry a child, and gender identity. Results : In total, 9,096,788 women met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 1690 (18.6/100000) had polycystic kidney disease (PKD), and the rest acted as controls. Patients with PKD, compared to those without, were more likely to be older ( P =0.0001), Caucasian ( P =0.0001), and to use private medical insurance plans ( P =0.0001). Patients with PKD were also more likely to be obese ( P =0.0001), to have chronic hypertension ( P =0.0001), and thyroid disease ( P =0.0001). When controlling for confounding effects, patients with PKD, compared to those without, were more likely to develop pregnancy induced hypertension (aOR 2.81 [95% CI 2.48,-3.19], P = 0.0001), gestational hypertension (aOR 2.20 [95% CI 1.77-2.73], P = 0.0001), preeclampsia (aOR 2.95 [95% CI 2.45-3.56], P = 0.0001), preeclampsia or eclampsia superimposed on pre-existing hypertension (aOR 2.62 [95% CI 2.10-3.26], P = 0.0001), to experience preterm delivery (aOR 1.51 [95% CI 1.29,-1.76], P =0.0001). Babies born to mothers having PKD were at a higher incidence of being born small for gestational age (aOR 1.45 [95% CI 1.13-1.86], P = 0.0001). Conclusions : PKD was associated with many pregnancy complications, including hypertensive disorders and neonatal complications. Pregnancy monitoring should be tailored to these issues and patients with PKD should be informed of warning signs.

title: Predicted fat mass index and incident stroke in adults aged 65 years or older: heterogeneous associations across three national ageing cohorts
authorString: Li S, Chen X, Chen R, Yang Z, Hou Y, Yu J.
abstractText: Background Predicted fat mass index (pBFMI) can be calculated when direct body-composition measurements are unavailable, but it is a deterministic transformation of body mass index (BMI), age, and sex. We examined whether its association with incident stroke was consistent across three national ageing cohorts. Methods We analysed stroke-free adults aged 65 years or older in CHARLS (2011–2020), ELSA (2004–2018), and HRS (2006–2020). Because stroke onset was known only between survey waves, the primary analysis used discrete-time complementary log-log models. Model 2 adjusted for age, sex, education, marital status, smoking, and an alcohol-use indicator; hypertension, diabetes, and heart disease were added in Model 3 as potential intermediates. Sex-specific standardization was recalculated within each cohort's age-65-or-older sample. We assessed mathematical coupling with BMI, compared apparent model fit and discrimination, and treated random-effects synthesis as descriptive. Results Model 2 included 3,241 CHARLS participants (317 strokes), 2,494 ELSA participants (205 strokes), and 3,614 HRS participants (413 strokes). Per sex-specific standard deviation higher pBFMI, hazard ratios were 1.247 (95% CI 1.165–1.334) in CHARLS, 0.924 (0.800–1.067) in ELSA, and 0.987 (0.892–1.091) in HRS. A one-stage discrete-time model showed cohort heterogeneity (joint interaction P < 0.001), which persisted when all Model 2 covariate effects were allowed to vary by cohort (P < 0.001). Hartung–Knapp descriptive synthesis gave an HR of 1.051 (0.709–1.560), I²=89.8%, and a 95% prediction interval of 0.491–2.250. pBFMI correlated strongly with BMI (r = 0.977–0.988) and did not materially improve apparent AIC or C-index. Conclusions Among adults aged 65 years or older, pBFMI was positively associated with incident stroke in CHARLS but not in ELSA or HRS. The findings do not support a consistent cross-population association and provide no evidence of materially improved apparent model fit or discrimination over BMI.

title: Impact of Prolonged Obesity Across the Lifecourse on Myocardial Stress and Injury in Older Age: Birth Cohort Study
authorString: Johnson W, Norris T, Hughes AD, Hamer M, Bell S, Batty G.
abstractText:
Background:

The consequences of prolonged exposure to obesity on biomarkers of myocardial stress and injury remain unclear. We examined associations of duration and cumulative severity of obesity from childhood to later adulthood with concentrations of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI), and growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15) at age 62 years. Methods The sample comprised 4,901 participants in the 1958 National Child Development Study who had measurements of NT-proBNP, hs-cTnI, or GDF-15 at age 62 years and at least four BMI assessments between 7 and 62 years of age. Individual BMI trajectories were modelled, from which total duration of obesity and mean excess BMI (area between the trajectory and the age-specific obesity threshold divided by duration) were derived. Associations of ever versus never having been obese, obesity duration, and mean excess BMI with biomarker concentrations were examined using general linear regression models with progressive adjustment for early-life characteristics; contemporaneous cardiometabolic factors; and health behaviours, socioeconomic position, and psychosocial factors. Nonlinear associations of obesity duration were estimated using restricted cubic splines and subsequently approximated using linear splines. Results Overall, 26.3% of participants had ever experienced obesity. There was no evidence of an association between ever versus never having been obese and NT-proBNP. Among men, ever having been obese was associated with 11.00% (95% CI, 4.62-17.37) higher hs-cTnI in the fully adjusted model, whereas there was no evidence of an association among women. Ever having been obese was associated with higher GDF-15, although the association attenuated substantially after adjustment for contemporaneous cardiometabolic factors. Longer obesity duration was associated with higher concentrations of all three biomarkers in fully adjusted models, but the pattern differed by biomarker: hs-cTnI increased approximately linearly with duration, whereas NT-proBNP and GDF-15 remained relatively stable up to approximately 25 years of obesity before increasing with longer duration. In fully adjusted models, each additional year of obesity beyond 25 years was associated with 1.80% (95% CI, 0.54-3.06) higher NT-proBNP and 0.81% (95% CI, 0.25-1.36) higher GDF-15, while each additional year across the full range of obesity duration was associated with 0.41% (95% CI, 0.07-0.76) higher hs-cTnI. Among participants who had ever experienced obesity, each 1 kg/m2 higher mean excess BMI was associated with 4.02% (95% CI, 1.79-6.24) higher NT-proBNP and 2.00% (95% CI, 0.49-3.51) higher hs-cTnI in fully adjusted models; there was no evidence of an association with GDF-15. Conclusions Longer duration of obesity was associated with higher concentrations of biomarkers reflecting myocardial stress, injury, and cellular stress at age 62 years, with associations particularly evident after approximately 25 years of obesity for NT-proBNP and GDF-15. These findings suggest that duration of obesity may provide clinically relevant information beyond current obesity status, supporting its consideration as an additional dimension of cumulative obesity burden in cardiovascular risk assessment.

title: Decomposing polygenic risk of coronary artery disease into distinct biological processes
authorString: Morze J, Smith K, Kierczak M, Bergstrom G, Li H, Gummesson A, Fall T, Soderberg S, Ebbers T, Smith JG, Landberg R, Franks P, Lappalainen T, Udler M, Wittenbecher C.
abstractText: Standard polygenic risk scores capture overall genetic liability to coronary artery disease (CAD) but do not reveal the biological processes contributing to risk in an individual. Here, we applied data-driven latent factor decomposition to 526 genome-wide significant CAD-associated variants, using their associations with 78 CAD-related phenotypic traits. We identified eight genetic components corresponding to cholesterol-enriched lipoproteins, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, lipoprotein(a), metabolically unhealthy normal weight, obesity, endothelial dysfunction, coagulation and cardiac remodeling. Process-specific polygenic risk scores (pPRSs) captured biological profiles beyond those reflected by conventional risk factors. In UK Biobank (n = 458,905), the Swedish CArdioPulmonary bioImage Study (n = 24,904) and Mass General Brigham Biobank (n = 53,848), pPRSs were consistently associated with clinical and subclinical CAD and showed distinct biomarker, proteomic and comorbidity profiles. These findings establish a framework for biologically resolved genetic CAD risk and may inform process-specific approaches to precision prevention.

title: Extracting meaningful features from time series analysis of plasma analytes in clinical research
authorString: Blank P, Golding AE, Morales I, Waters H, Mekhedov E, Bezrukov L, Wachter RD, Mikhailenko I, Brown RH, Bonnemann C, Demidowich A, Jain M, Yanovski JA, Zimmerberg J.
abstractText: While absolute blood biomarkers have long guided diagnosis, their rate of change often provides greater diagnostic value. For the Limb Girdle Muscular Dystrophies studied here, increased muscle weakness is associated with abnormal sarcolemma repair. Time course analyses were made to changes in muscle-derived plasma enzymes after modest physical activity of ambulatory inpatients. Blood samples at 20 selected time points at variable intervals were obtained at rest, and before and after routine morning activities and motor function testing. After these activities, plasma enzyme levels increased in a similar way, suggesting damage and leakage from skeletal muscle. The levels then decreased in a similar way, suggesting that muscle cells stopped leaking and enzymes were subsequently cleared from the blood. The complex temporal changes were modeled using both continuous time and data features to reduce the number of parameters required to describe the irregularly sampled, interrupted, time series data. Unlike individuals with cardiac muscle ischemia or following intense exercise, there was no extended post-injury rising phase of enzyme levels. In contradistinction, levels fell once activity ceased. Time series analyses of blood biomarkers most likely provide an assay and index of sarcolemma fragility and by extension skeletal muscle damage.

title: CardioNeural-SoC: An Indigenous RISC-V-Based Mixed-Signal System- on-Chip for Multi-Modal Cardiac and Neurological Monitoring — Architecture, RTL Verification, and Pre-Silicon Synthesis Results
authorString: M NJ, Vishwajith R, Sreelakshmi M.
abstractText: Cardiovascular and neurological disease together impose one of the largest preventable disease burdens in India, yet every application-specific integrated circuit used in the cardiac and neurological monitoring devices sold domestically is currently imported. This paper presents CardioNeural-SoC, an indigenous, mixed-signal System-on-Chip architecture designed to consolidate a 4-channel electrocardiogram (ECG) front-end, a 2-channel electroencephalogram (EEG) front-end, a photoplethysmography (PPG) interface, a 16-bit analog-to-digital converter array, a RISC-V-based digital signal processing core with hardware accelerators for arrhythmia and seizure-onset classification, an AES-128-secured Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE 5.3) interface, and an ultra-low-power management unit onto a single 28 nm CMOS die. We report the system-level architecture, the full register-transfer-level (RTL) functional verification of the integrated design (a 9-test-case regression covering multi-channel ECG acquisition, multi-rate clock generation, ADC/DAC sequencing, arrhythmia classification, on-chip AES-128 encryption, and BLE transmit/power-gating handshakes, all of which passed), and gate-level synthesis results for the discrete-wavelet-transform-based sub-band energy feature extractor (layer1_top) that feeds the on-chip classification accelerators. Post-synthesis results for this block show 21,703 standard-cell instances (299,895 µm² total cell area), zero-slack timing closure on the dominant accumulator path at a 200 MHz reference period, and an estimated total power of 46.06 mW dominated by sequential register switching (74.8% of total power). The full chip-level netlist comprises seven hierarchical modules and approximately 129,000 leaf cells. We further present an import-substitution and commercialization analysis indicating an addressable Indian market of approximately ₹427 crore/year in currently imported monitoring ICs across five device segments. All reported quantitative results in this paper are simulation- and synthesis-stage findings; no silicon has yet been fabricated, and the design has not undergone post-silicon or clinical characterization.

title: Complicated Sigmoid Diverticular Disease Presenting as Extensive Retroperitoneal and Thigh Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infection: A Case Report
authorString: Samara M, Rajabi S, Madi M, AL-Khateeb Y, Dibas Y, Zaydeh OA.
abstractText: Introduction: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection (NSTI) is a rare, rapidly progressive, and potentially fatal surgical emergency. Early diagnosis is challenging due to its nonspecific presentation, and prompt recognition followed by urgent imaging and surgical intervention is essential to improve outcome. Case presentation: A 57 year old woman presented with generalized weakness, poor oral intake, lower abdominal pain, and oliguria. She was hypotensive, hypoxic, and in acute kidney injury with metabolic acidosis. Non-contrast CT revealed complicated sigmoid diverticulitis with extensive extraluminal gas extending through the left retroperitoneum, psoas, pelvis, and thigh, consistent with an extensive necrotizing soft-tissue infection. Emergency laparotomy with resection of the diseased sigmoid colon, upper rectum, distal ileum, and cecum, followed by end ileostomy and colostomy, was performed along with extensive left thigh exploration and debridement. Despite initial improvement following source control and intensive care, she developed wound infection with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae and progressive hemodynamic deterioration, ultimately dying of cardiac arrest on postoperative day 19. Conclusion This case highlights the challenges of recognizing deep necrotizing infection from an intra-abdominal source, emphasizing the importance of early imaging and surgical source control.

title: Salt-Sensitivity Trait and Coronary Microvascular Function in New-Onset Hypertension
authorString: Ak AP, Celik FB, Güvenç TS, Caliskan AE, Kapcik M, Ismayilzada N, Yilmaz Y, Kul S, Yilmaz AS, Caliskan M.
abstractText: Background Salt sensitivity is a trait observed in up to 50% of hypertensive patients. This study examined the link between salt sensitivity and coronary microvascular dysfunction in new-onset hypertension to clarify its broader cardiovascular impact. Methods 54 individuals with hypertension were included. Patients consumed a high-salt diet followed by a low-salt diet, and those with a greater than 5 mmHg change in mean blood pressure or systolic blood pressure were classified as having salt-sensitive hypertension. Coronary flow reserve was measured using echocardiography. Results Patients with salt-sensitive (2.51 ± 0.42) and salt-resistant (2.61 ± 0.47) hypertension had a lower Coronary flow reserve compared to controls (3.12 ± 0.33, p < 0.001). However, there were no statistically significant differences between the two hypertensive groups in crude or adjusted analyses. When the alternative definition was applied, patients with salt-sensitive systolic hypertension had a lower Coronary flow reserve (2.41 ± 0.31) compared to both controls (3.12 ± 0.33, p < 0.001) and patients with salt-resistant hypertension (2.71 ± 0.51, p = 0.017). These findings remained consistent after covariate adjustment. Conclusions Coronary microvascular function was altered in new-onset hypertensive patients with salt sensitivity; however, the magnitude was similar to salt-resistant patients. In systolic BP salt sensitivity, dysfunction was more pronounced.

title: Pulsed Field Versus Radiofrequency Ablation For Repeat Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation: Evaluation of Outcomes
authorString: Patel V, Ashur C, Adewumi J, Padalia K, Zipse M, Tumolo A, Garg L, Sabzwari R, Sandhu A, Rosenberg MA, Tzou WS.
abstractText:
Background:

Pulsed-field ablation (PFA) has recently been approved in the USA as a new method for treating atrial fibrillation (AF). PFA provides a promising new approach in the treatment of atrial fibrillation (AF), which historically has a high recurrence rate post-ablation. Of significance, PFA has shown promising data in terms of safety and procedural efficiency to radiofrequency ablation (RFA). Objective The purpose of this study was to compare the procedural and health outcomes in patients with recurrent AF undergoing ablation using PFA or RFA. Methods Consecutive patients with a history of previous radiofrequency ablation and recurrent AF undergoing redo ablation with PFA or RFA were included. Patients were seen for follow-up in the clinic ranging from 4 months to a year and we reported ablation strategy and arrhythmia type. The primary outcome was recurrence of any atrial arrhythmia after a 90-day blanking period. Results A total of 242 patients with recurrent AF underwent redo ablation using PFA (n = 54, 22.5%) or RFA (n = 188, 77.5%). The PFA cohort was younger on average (66 vs. 70 years) with a lower mean CHA2DS2-VASc score (2.2 vs. 3.06, p=0.001) compared to the RFA cohort. PFA procedures were shorter (162±53 vs 206±60 minutes, p<0.001) but required more fluoroscopy (13.9±8.9 vs 8.7±6.3 minutes, p<0.001). Among patients seen on follow-up, recurrence occurred in 28% of PFA versus 55% of RFA patients, with longer arrhythmia-free survival after PFA (log-rank p=0.03). PFA remained associated with lower recurrence after multivariable adjustment (HR 0.4, 95% CI 0.2?0.9, p=0.04). Adverse events, predominantly vascular access?related, were similar. Conclusion Among patients with recurrent atrial arrhythmias after prior RFA, repeat PFA was associated with shorter procedures, greater fluoroscopy use, and lower arrhythmia recurrence, with comparable safety.

title: Transcutaneous Skin Perforation by a Protruding Xiphoid Process in a Bedbound Patient With Post-Traumatic Cervical Myelopathy: A Case Report and Review of the Literature
authorString: Ali HA, Joulani W, Abdulbaqi N.
abstractText: Background The xiphoid process is the smallest and most morphologically variable component of the sternum, and anterior (ventral) deviation is a recognized anatomical variant. Symptomatic xiphoid disease typically presents as localized pain (xiphodynia). Cutaneous complications are exceedingly uncommon, and only a single previous report describing an ischemic xiphisternal ulcer associated with a protruding xiphoid has been published. To the best of our knowledge, we identified no previous English-language report describing complete transcutaneous perforation of the skin by a protruding xiphoid process associated with chronic sinus formation and secondary infection. Case presentation A 71-year-old bedbound man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and post-traumatic cervical myelopathy with spastic weakness developed progressive protrusion of the xiphoid process. The angulated xiphoid tip gradually eroded through the overlying skin, producing a chronic midline ulcer with sinus tract formation and superimposed infection. Lateral radiography demonstrated marked anterior angulation of the xiphoid process with prominent ventral protrusion and irregularity of the distal tip. The patient underwent xiphoidectomy with en-bloc excision of the ulcer and debridement of devitalized soft tissue. Intraoperative culture of the resected xiphoid specimen yielded extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli, and culture-directed carbapenem therapy was administered. Histopathological examination revealed extensive ulceration with inflamed granulation tissue and a sinus tract, accompanied by reactive squamous epithelial hyperplasia (pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia), whereas the underlying bone was unremarkable and showed no evidence of malignancy. Conclusions A protruding xiphoid process can rarely progress beyond pain and superficial ulceration to cutaneous breach with sinus tract formation and secondary infection, particularly in debilitated patients with chronic immobility, diabetes mellitus, and reduced soft-tissue padding. This process appears mechanistically analogous to a pressure ulcer developing over an atypical bony prominence. Xiphoidectomy combined with debridement and culture-directed antimicrobial therapy appears to provide definitive treatment. Histopathological examination is essential because reactive pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia at the ulcer margin may mimic cutaneous malignancy.

title: Carotid Body Paraganglioma Presenting With Paroxysmal Hypertension: A Case Report
authorString: Lu C.
abstractText:
Background: Carotid body paragangliomas（CBP）generally lack clinical manifestations of catecholamine excess. some patients may exhibit a dopaminergic biochemical phenotype characterized by elevated dopamine levels. Case Report: We report a patient with a CBP who presented with paroxysmal hypertension and recurrent syncope. Biochemical evaluation revealed elevated plasma dopamine and 3-methoxytyramine (3-MT) levels, whereas other catecholamines remained within the reference ranges. The symptoms improved following tumor resection.

Discussion:

Elevated dopamine alone cannot fully explain the paroxysmal hypertension. Transient catecholamine release during symptomatic episodes may have contributed. Because dynamic monitoring during episodes and postoperative biochemical reassessment were unavailable, the underlying mechanism remains unclear.

Conclusion:

Dopaminergic CBP may exhibit heterogeneous hemodynamic presentations. Individualized preoperative assessment based on the patient’s clinical presentation may help optimize perioperative management.

title: Normotension as a Red Flag: A Proposed Framework for Early Recognition of Masked Preeclampsia in Couvelaire Uterus – A Case Report and a Teaching Tool
authorString: Mostafa K, Ismaiel H, Shaar H, Allosh A, Jamalih M.
abstractText: Background Couvelaire uterus (CU) is a rare, life-threatening complication of placental abruption, occurring in about 1% of cases. Preeclampsia is a major risk factor; however, its diagnosis becomes difficult when concealed hemorrhage hides typical hypertension, delaying recognition. Additionally, the critical impact of the time from symptom onset to surgical intervention on uterine preservation is not well understood in the literature. We present a case of CU with masked preeclampsia and evolving disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) to propose a new time-based framework for early recognition and surgical decision-making. Case presentation: We report a 19-year-old unbooked primigravida at 35 + 5 weeks presenting with absent fetal movements. On admission, she was normotensive (110/60 mmHg) with a relative rise in heart rate (HR: 88 bpm), severe proteinuria (1000 mg/dL), thrombocytopenia (78×10⁹/L), and a woody uterus. Coagulation revealed PT 17.7s (INR 1.42) and fibrinogen (3.38 g/L), consistent with non-overt DIC (ISTH score 2/8). Ultrasound confirmed intrauterine fetal demise. Over seven hours, labor did not progress, necessitating emergency cesarean section. Intraoperatively, a retroplacental hematoma and CU were identified, and a prophylactic B-Lynch suture was placed (estimated blood loss 1500–2000 mL). Postoperatively, rebound hypertension to 150/100 mmHg responded promptly to magnesium sulfate, confirming masked PE. She recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day four. Discussion Based on this case, we propose three educational frameworks: (1) a three-phase hemodynamic model (occult compensation, rebound surge, therapeutic stabilization) to unmask PE during hemorrhage; (2) a "window of opportunity" concept, advocating surgical intervention within 6–8 hours of symptom onset to avoid irreversible DIC (ISTH ≥ 5) and preserve the uterus; and (3) a counterfactual analysis of two similar cases, demonstrating that timely intervention is the single most modifiable factor for uterine salvage. Conclusion Normotension in PA with proteinuria is a red flag, not reassurance. Magnesium responsiveness confirms underlying PE. B-Lynch suture is effective for uterine preservation, even in resource-limited settings. Clinicians must prioritize early evacuation, especially in conflict-affected areas.

title: Stage at Presentation and Clinical Characteristics of Breast Cancer Patients at the Butaro Cancer Centre of Excellence, Rwanda: A Retrospective Chart Review
authorString: Majyambere JP, Fenta BA, Gemechu NB, Hsu PJ, Belachew AG, Niyigena A, Fehr A, Huang AYZ, Tenna M, Cohen Y, Bempong-Ahun N, Williams W, Riviello R, Bekele A, Ibbotson G, Alayande BT.
abstractText: Background Breast cancer is the leading cancer among women in sub-Saharan Africa, where late-stage presentation contributes to poor outcomes. Understanding the risk-factor profile, comorbidity burden, and functional status of patients at presentation is essential to guide early-detection and management strategies in resource-limited settings. Methods We conducted a retrospective chart review of patients who underwent surgery for breast cancer at the Butaro Cancer Center of Excellence (BCCOE), Rwanda, between 2018 and 2023. From 422 patients identified, 300 charts were selected through simple random sampling and reviewed using a pretested REDCap tool drawing on electronic and paper-based records. Data was analyzed in IBM SPSS Statistics (version 29), and disease was staged according to the AJCC TNM system. Results The mean age at presentation was 50.8 years (SD = 11.8; range 28–82); 98% of patients were female, 94% had health insurance, and 74% were farmers. At least one risk factor was present in 65% of patients, with alcohol consumption (55.3%) and tobacco smoking (21.7%) the most common modifiable factors, followed by family history (5.3%) and nulliparity (3.7%). Comorbidities were frequent, affecting 60.3% of patients; hypertension (25.7%) and HIV/AIDS (7.0%) predominated. Most patients had good functional status at diagnosis (ECOG 0, 81.5%; ECOG 1, 16.4%). Of 281 staged patients (19 of 300 lacked complete TNM staging data), Stage III (38.4%) and Stage II (37.0%) were most common, and late-stage disease (Stage III–IV) accounted for 47.3% of cases. Conclusion Breast cancer patients at BCCOE are diagnosed at a younger age than the global average and carry a high burden of modifiable risk factors and comorbidities. The substantial proportion presenting at late stage may complicate treatment and compromise survival, emphasizing the need for strengthened awareness and early-detection efforts. By centering on a rural referral hospital, this study adds to the limited literature on breast cancer presentation in Rwanda.

title: Retinal arteriolar tortuosity as a candidate genetic window to inner-ear microvasculature: distributed sharing with blood pressure at CSK and PAWR and a roadmap for larger hearing GWAS
authorString: Yang L, Liu Y.
abstractText:
Background

The inner ear is supplied by the labyrinthine artery, which is functionally close to an end artery with limited collateral reserve. Microvascular abnormalities have been implicated in sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) and age-related hearing loss, yet inner-ear microvasculature cannot be assessed in vivo and current hearing genome-wide association studies (GWAS) are underpowered. We evaluated the shared genetic architecture of retinal arteriolar tortuosity (retina_AT) with blood pressure, cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) and hearing phenotypes, and examined whether retinal microvasculature could serve as a candidate genetic window to inner-ear microvasculature.

Methods

We used linkage-disequilibrium score regression (LDSC) to estimate SNP heritability for 19 phenotypes and genome-wide genetic correlations (rg) for 11 prespecified pairs. We ran approximate Bayes-factor colocalization (coloc.abf) between 19 independent retinal loci and systolic blood pressure (SBP), together with 95% credible-set fine-mapping, UCSC gene annotation, colocalization with GTEx aortic and tibial-artery expression QTL (eQTL) data and with white-matter hyperintensities (WMH), hearing-GWAS power calculations, and univariable and multivariable Mendelian randomization (MR) of blood pressure and heart rate on hearing.

Results

Only retina_AT with SBP was significant genome-wide (rg = 0.10, P = 4.2×10⁻⁵, FDR q = 0.00042). The strongest retinal locus, 13q34, did not colocalize (PP.H3 = 0.996; peaks about 267 kb apart; allelic heterogeneity), whereas two secondary loci colocalized strongly—CSK at 15q24 (PP.H4 = 0.98; 3/3 credible variants within CSK) and PAWR at 12q21 (PP.H4 = 0.99; 3/5 within PAWR)— supported by tissue-matched, moderate eQTL evidence (PP.H4 = 0.71–0.75). At 13q34, retina_AT with WMH was an adequately powered null (PP.H4 = 0.019; only this region and phenotype were tested). On the hearing side, sharing of the blood-pressure magnitude (rg ≈ 0.10) was a near-powered null (about 1.5-fold larger sample needed for 80% power under that assumption, versus about 15-fold for weak rg ≈ 0.03 sharing), and rg ≥ 0.12 was excluded; MR found no robust causal effect.

Conclusions

Retinal arteriolar tortuosity shows limited, distributed genetic sharing with blood pressure at the vascular-tone genes CSK and PAWR; no sharing with WMH was observed at 13q34 (only this region was tested). Retinal microvasculature may serve as a candidate genetic window to inner-ear microvasculature, but this analogy awaits direct testing by larger, vessel-oriented hearing GWAS and inner-ear tissue functional studies.

title: A Prediction Model for In-Hospital Sternal Wound Complications After Aortic Dissection Surgery Based on Rewarming Time, Drainage Output, and Hemoglobin: A Retrospective Study
authorString: Xiao Y, Ma W, Feng Y, Wu J, Liu J, Yin J, Wei H, Luo J.
abstractText: Background Currently, early and simple tools for assessing the risk of in-hospital sternal wound complications (SWC) following aortic dissection surgery remain lacking. This study aimed to develop and internally validate a prediction model based on early postoperative objective indicators. Methods Between January 2020 and December 2023, we consecutively enrolled patients with Stanford type A aortic dissection who met the inclusion criteria and underwent surgical treatment at our institution, following predefined exclusion criteria. A total of 243 patients were finally included, of whom 58 (23.9%) developed in-hospital SWC. Variables with P < 0.1 in univariate analysis were screened for collinearity and clinical relevance before entry into a multivariable logistic regression model using the Enter method. A nomogram was constructed based on the multivariable analysis results. The model‘s performance was evaluated via bootstrap internal validation (1000 resamples) in terms of discrimination (AUC), calibration, and clinical utility (DCA). A simplified scoring system was derived as an exploratory analysis. Results Multivariable logistic regression identified three independent predictors of in-hospital SWC: rewarming time (OR = 0.983 per minute, 95% CI: 0.970–0.996, P = 0.012), postoperative day 2 drainage output (OR = 1.22 per 100 mL, 95% CI: 1.10–1.35, P = 0.002), and postoperative day 1 hemoglobin (OR = 0.976 per g/L, 95% CI: 0.954–0.998, P = 0.035), all three of which were incorporated into the final nomogram. The constructed nomogram demonstrated moderate discriminative ability (AUC = 0.702, 95% CI: 0.630–0.775) and good calibration (calibration intercept = -0.115, slope = 0.888, Brier score = 0.170). The simplified scoring system showed an AUC of 0.699 (95% CI: 0.635–0.763). When patients were stratified into low- (0 points), intermediate- (1–2 points), and high-risk (3 points) groups, the event rates were 6.7%, 21.7%, and 38.6%, respectively, showing a significant increasing trend (P for trend = 0.004). Conclusion This study identified rewarming time, postoperative day 2 drainage output, and postoperative day 1 hemoglobin as independent predictors of in-hospital SWC after aortic dissection. The nomogram incorporating these three variables demonstrated moderate discriminative ability and good calibration upon internal validation, supporting its potential utility as an internally validated exploratory model for early risk stratification. The simplified scoring system derived from the model showed modest performance as an exploratory tool and requires prospective external validation before clinical application.

title: Cardiomyocyte Perm1 sustains cardiac bioenergetic reserve and exercise capacity
authorString: Tachibana S, Le T, Schenk S, Feng W, Chen J, Ross R, Lange S, Cho Y.
abstractText:
Objective:

Mitochondrial oxidative capacity in striated muscle is governed by the PGC-1/ERR transcriptional axis, which controls not only steady-state respiration but the capacity to expand energy production when demand rises. Whether this reserve function requires dedicated downstream effectors, and whether its loss is detectable at rest, remains unclear. We asked whether Perm1, a striated muscle-specific PGC-1/ERR-induced regulator, is required cell-autonomously for cardiac bioenergetic reserve.

Methods:

We generated cardiomyocyte-specific Perm1 knockout mice using alphaMHC-nCre, complemented by an adult tamoxifen-inducible alphaMHC-MerCreMer model, and assessed cardiac development, structure, and function longitudinally through 12 months of age in both sexes. We evaluated mitochondrial function by high-resolution respirometry, transmission electron microscopy, and molecular profiling. We tested energetic capacity under load by treadmill exercise with tissue ATP quantification and by beta-adrenergic stimulation of cultured neonatal cardiomyocytes.

Results:

Perm1 deletion did not perturb embryonic cardiac development, and neither constitutive nor adult-onset deletion impaired cardiac structure, systolic function, or diastolic function through 12 months. Despite this preserved resting phenotype, mitochondrial respiration was reduced by 20 - 25% across complex I- and complex I+II-supported conditions, without changes in citrate synthase activity, mtDNA copy number, or OXPHOS subunit abundance. Instead, the MICOS components IMMT (MIC60) and CHCHD3 (MIC19) were selectively reduced, and mitochondrial subpopulations shifted toward fewer subsarcolemmal and more interfibrillar mitochondria, with unchanged total mitochondrial density. Functionally, Perm1-deficient mice of both sexes showed reduced treadmill capacity at 6 and 12 months and failed to maintain cardiac ATP during exercise at a submaximal workload, while skeletal muscle ATP and plasma lactate were unaffected. This deficit was cardiomyocyte-autonomous: beta-adrenergic stimulation increased ATP content in control cardiomyocytes, but Perm1 knockdown reduced this response. Conclusions. Perm1 is a cardiomyocyte-intrinsic determinant of bioenergetic reserve, dispensable for resting cardiac function but required to expand ATP production under increased demand. These findings identify a mode of metabolic regulation that is invisible to resting functional phenotyping.
