title: How confounding factors distort clinical phenotyping in Sjögren's syndrome
authorString: Lacasta K, Gandara-Alvarez A, Rus MJ, Cantiga-Silva C, Navarrete VM, Quesada CD, Venegas JJP, Ortega JA, Simon-Soro A.
abstractText: Importance Clinical phenotyping in Sjögren's syndrome is complicated by non-specific symptoms that overlap with aging, comorbidities, and medication effects. Understanding how these confounding factors affect diagnostic accuracy is essential for valid observational research. Objective To evaluate how age, comorbidities, and xerogenic medications influence clinical phenotyping and diagnostic performance in Sjögren's syndrome. Methods Cross-sectional study of 196 women (97 Sjögren's syndrome, 99 controls). Principal component analysis identified latent phenotypic structure. Random forest classifiers with SHAP values assessed variable importance. Multivariable regression estimated independent associations with stimulated salivary flow. Results A classifier using all variables achieved AUC 0.92 but relied on diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and medication use. A systemic-only model achieved AUC 0.78. An oral-only model retained AUC 0.82. In regression, Sjögren's diagnosis (-0.52 mL/min; 95% CI -0.73 to -0.29) and xerogenic medication (-0.45 mL/min; 95% CI -0.75 to -0.15) were independently associated with lower stimulated salivary flow; age showed a smaller effect (-0.018 mL/min/year; 95% CI -0.027 to -0.010). Diagnostic accuracy declined after age 70. Interpretation Confounding factors can inflate apparent diagnostic performance in Sjögren's syndrome studies. Researchers should consider control-group heterogeneity and audit models for reliance on systemic variables rather than disease-specific oral pathology.

title: Genome-wide identification and spatiotemporal expression analysis of the CYP82 gene family in Corydalis yanhusuo
authorString: Zhang L, Zhang W, Li L, Li H, Yang R, Huang Z, Liu J, Zhao X.
abstractText: Corydalis yanhusuo is a traditional Chinese medicinal herb whose analgesic and cardiovascular activities depend mainly on benzylisoquinoline alkaloids (BIAs). CYP82 family cytochrome P450 monooxygenases are key catalysts governing BIA structural diversification, yet the family has not been characterized at the genome level in this species. Field sampling of C. yanhusuo bulbs was performed during 2025 at a germplasm nursery in Chenggu, Shaanxi Province, China. Based on the recently released chromosome-level genome, we performed the first genome-wide identification and spatiotemporal expression analysis of the CYP82 family and identified 48 CyCYP82 genes. All encoded proteins are hydrophilic; the genes are unevenly distributed across 20 chromosomes and were assigned to three (clusters Ⅰ, Ⅲ and Ⅴ) of six phylogenetic clusters. WGD rather than tandem duplication drove family expansion, with 87.8% of duplicate pairs under purifying selection. Collinearity revealed orthologous relationships exclusively with Papaver somniferum . Promoters were enriched in stress-responsive (notably MYB/MYC), hormone and light responsive elements. CyCYP82N30 and CyCYP82N33 are highly correlated (Cor > 0.9) with the accumulation pattern of protopine and allocryptopine biosynthesis, suggesting that CyCYP82N30 and CyCYP82N33 are candidate genes involved in the regulation of protopine and allocryptopine biosynthesis. Different clusters speculate interact with specific regulatory proteins associated with G-protein signaling, ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis and jasmonic acid biosynthesis. We systematically characterized the full CyCYP82 family at the chromosome-scale genome level and deciphered its evolutionary and regulatory features. The identified BIA-related candidate genes offer critical genetic resources for subsequent functional verification and molecular breeding of high-quality C. yanhusuo .

title: Activation of macrophage pyroptosis via NLRP3 inflammasome: a novel mechanism underlying calpain-mediated septic cardiomyopathy
authorString: Xu S, Lu Z, Xiao Y, Zhu M, Feng X, Xi R, Zhao C, Long Z, Xu Q, Zhou J, Wu J, Jiang Y.
abstractText: Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (SCM) is a life-threatening complication with limited therapeutic options, characterized by a pronounced inflammatory cytokine storm. Although NLRP3 inflammasome–dependent macrophage pyroptosis has emerged as a critical contributor to cytokine release, its upstream regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study investigated whether calpain promotes macrophage pyroptosis via NLRP3 inflammasome activation, thereby exacerbating SCM. A cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) rat model was employed for in vivo studies, and THP-1-derived macrophages stimulated with LPS plus ATP (LA) were used in vitro. CLP rats developed severe cardiac dysfunction and elevated myocardial IL-1β and IL-18 levels, all of these pathological alterations were markedly reversed by calpain inhibitor MDL28170. Notably, CD68⁺GSDMD⁺calpain⁺ macrophages were detected in cardiac tissues of CLP rats. In THP-1 cells, LA triggered GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis, as evidenced by reduced viability, increased IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, and enhanced plasma membrane localization of GSDMD-NT; these effects were abrogated by GSDMD siRNA or MDL28170. Knockdown of CAPN2 (m-calpain subunit), but not CAPN1, significantly rescued LA-induced pyroptotic phenotypes. Mechanistically, CAPN2 silencing suppressed LA-induced ASC upregulation, cleaved caspase-1 production, and caspase-1 enzymatic activity, with affecting NLRP3 expression, indicating that CAPN2 acts upstream of canonical NLRP3 inflammasome activation to trigger caspase-1-mediated GSDMD cleavage. Functionally, conditioned medium from LA-stimulated macrophages markedly reduced H9c2 cell viability, an effect prevented by calpain inhibition in macrophages. Collectively, our findings provide the first evidence that calpain-2 (CAPN2) drives macrophage pyroptosis via the NLRP3 inflammasome/caspase-1/GSDMD axis to exacerbate septic cardiomyopathy, highlighting calpain as a promising therapeutic target for SCM.

title: Night-shift frequency and loneliness among NHS employees: a multi-site cross-sectional analysis of the INTERACT study
authorString: El-Osta A, Haoran L, Altalib S, Jerjes W, Pattani S, Majeed A, Klaber B.
abstractText: Background Night work is fundamental to continuous healthcare delivery but may disrupt biological rhythms and participation in social and family life. Although shift work has been extensively studied in relation to sleep, fatigue, cardiovascular health and mental wellbeing, loneliness has received substantially less attention as a potential occupational-health outcome. We examined whether increasing monthly night-shift frequency was associated with loneliness among National Health Service (NHS) employees and explored whether social interaction frequency, social fulfilment, work-life balance and emotional exhaustion were associated with this relationship. Methods We conducted a secondary cross-sectional analysis of a multi-site online survey undertaken within the Measuring Loneliness in England (INTERACT) study. Monthly night-shift frequency was categorised as 0, 1–2, 3–5 and ≥ 6 shifts and analysed as an ordered exposure. The primary outcome was the three-item UCLA Loneliness Scale (range 3–9). Multivariable linear regression with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors estimated the mean change in loneliness per one-category increase in night-shift frequency. The principal model adjusted for age, gender, study site, survey month, occupational group, department, NHS tenure, weekly working hours, overtime and employment status. Secondary ordered logistic models examined a direct loneliness item and an ordinal specification of the UCLA-3 score. Exploratory pathway analyses used coefficient-product estimates with bootstrap confidence intervals. Results The fully adjusted analytical sample comprised 809 NHS employees: 535 (66.1%) reported no night shifts, 36 (4.4%) 1–2 shifts, 101 (12.5%) 3–5 shifts and 137 (16.9%) ≥ 6 shifts per month. Mean UCLA-3 loneliness was 5.41 (SD 1.97) overall and 5.19, 5.94, 5.62 and 5.95 across increasing night-shift categories. In the fully adjusted model, each one-category increase in night-shift frequency was associated with a 0.211-point higher UCLA-3 score (95% CI 0.055 to 0.368; P = 0.008). Associations were directionally consistent when UCLA-3 was treated as an ordered outcome (OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.42; P = 0.005) and for the direct loneliness measure (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.35; P = 0.050). However, the global proportional-odds test indicated departure from this assumption for the ordinal UCLA-3 model (P = 0.022), warranting cautious interpretation. Exploratory coefficient-product estimates, calculated without adjustment for multiple comparisons, had confidence intervals excluding zero for lower social fulfilment (0.085, 95% bootstrap CI 0.002 to 0.167) and poorer work-life balance (0.097, 95% bootstrap CI 0.038 to 0.161), but not for social-interaction frequency or emotional exhaustion; because all variables were measured contemporaneously, these estimates should not be interpreted as causal indirect effects. Conclusions Greater night-shift frequency was associated with higher loneliness among participating NHS employees after adjustment for demographic and occupational characteristics. Exploratory findings identified work-life balance and social fulfilment as candidate constructs for longitudinal investigation; they do not establish their relative importance or causal roles. Because the design is cross-sectional and the sample volunteer-based, the findings do not establish causality or population prevalence. Longitudinal studies using objectively recorded rosters and repeated measures of social wellbeing are needed to establish temporal relationships and identify modifiable organisational factors.

title: From Erythrocyte P₅₀ and 2,3-BPG to PHD–VHL/FIH–HIF-1α Signaling: Glycohypoxia as a Systemic Oxygen-Unloading Modifier of Tissue Hypoxia in Diabetic Complications
authorString: Akl MM, Ahmed A.
abstractText:
Background:

Tissue hypoxia and dysregulated hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) signaling recur across diabetic complications, yet a circulating determinant linking chronic hyperglycemia to organ oxygen stress remains incompletely defined. Glycohypoxia proposes that impaired erythrocyte oxygen unloading constitutes an additional systemic pressure superimposed on tissue-specific microvascular and metabolic vulnerability. Evidence synthesis: In T2DM, increasing HbA1c was associated with lower P₅₀ (27.0 ± 0.5 to 26.2 ± 0.7 mmHg) and 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG; 4.8 ± 0.4 to 4.2 ± 0.5 μmol/g Hb) despite preserved arterial PO₂, while modeling predicted a 1.5–3.9% cumulative unloading deficit across HbA1c 6–9%. Independent mechanistic models demonstrate that ADORA2B–AMPK–BPGM, SphK1–S1P–Band 3/glycolytic, and ENT1–AMPD3–purine/redox signaling dynamically regulate erythrocyte 2,3-BPG/P₅₀ and tissue oxygenation. During hypoxia, SphK1-dependent adaptation increased P₅₀ by approximately 20% in humans; genetic failure of erythrocyte unloading increased renal and myocardial hypoxia, whereas AMPK activation restored BPGM/2,3-BPG signaling and reduced tissue hypoxia. Downstream, oxygen availability interfaces with PHD–VHL/FIH–HIF signaling, but diabetes can uncouple hypoxia from effective adaptation. Methylglyoxal promotes HIF-1α degradation through Hsp40/Hsp70–CHIP and disrupts HIF-1α–p300 transcriptional competence, while diabetic myocardial fatty-acid metabolism limits succinate-dependent PHD inhibition. Accordingly, diabetic kidney, retina, myocardium, peripheral nerve, and wounds exhibit distinct combinations of tissue hypoxia, HIF dysregulation, VEGF signaling, metabolic remodeling, fibrosis, and defective repair.

Conclusions:

Glycohypoxia is therefore best considered a mechanistically grounded but unproven systemic oxygen-delivery modifier whose expression depends on organ-specific reserve. Definitive validation requires within-subject linkage of P₅₀/2,3-BPG to directly measured tissue oxygenation, PHD/FIH–HIF state, and organ dysfunction independently of glycemia, hemoglobin concentration, arterial oxygenation, and perfusion.

title: The Vagus in Autonomic Function Testing: A Functional Framework for Understanding and Evaluating Vagal Modulation
authorString: Herlekar SS, Siddangoudra S, Doyizode AR.
abstractText: The vagus nerve is a major component of the autonomic nervous system and contributes to dynamic regulation of cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal and other visceral functions through complex afferent and efferent pathways. Although cardiovascular measures such as heart rate, heart-rate variability (HRV) and autonomic reflex responses are widely used to characterize vagal influence, these measures represent integrated physiological outputs rather than direct recordings of vagal nerve activity. This distinction is particularly important in the interpretation of autonomic function testing (AFT), where abnormalities may arise from altered afferent signalling, central autonomic integration, efferent pathways, cardiovascular mechanics or end-organ responsiveness. This review examines the physiological basis, methodological principles and interpretive boundaries of AFT in relation to cardiovagal function and vagal regulation. The roles of paced deep breathing, the Valsalva manoeuvre, orthostatic testing, baroreflex assessment, HRV and complementary measures are considered alongside their physiological contributions and limitations. Clinical patterns of autonomic dysfunction are discussed to illustrate why individual test abnormalities should be interpreted as components of integrated reflex pathways rather than isolated evidence of vagal injury. The review further examines the emerging relevance of vagus nerve stimulation and broader approaches to vagal modulation. In this context, AFT may extend beyond its conventional diagnostic role by providing standardized physiological challenges through which changes in autonomic responsiveness, reflex integration and recovery can be characterized. Such an approach may support functional response phenotyping and longitudinal assessment of neuromodulatory interventions, while avoiding the assumption that cardiovascular responses directly quantify vagal activity.

title: CRISIS RESOURCE MANAGEMENT (CRM) COURSE FOR UNDERGRADUATE MEDICINE AND NURSING STUDENTS
authorString: Mateos Rodriguez A, Espinosa Ramirez S, Cervera Barba E, Fernandez Lebrusan L, Denizon Arranz S.
abstractText: Background Crisis Resource Management (CRM) is a key framework for optimizing team dynamics, communication, situational awareness, and non-technical skills in high-pressure healthcare environments. Although well established in postgraduate medical education, its implementation in undergraduate curricula remains limited. This study aims to describe the educational design, implementation, and outcomes of a simulation-based CRM program for final-year medical and nursing students. Activity Development (Methods) Conducted annually since the 2018–2019 academic year at Universidad Francisco de Vitoria, the mandatory program is structured around 15 core CRM principles across five domains: role clarity, communication, seeking/managing help, resource utilization, and global assessment. Sessions are facilitated by trained instructors and simulation technicians. The educational format includes pre-course materials, an introductory psychological safety and video analysis session, equipment familiarization stations, and four high-fidelity simulation scenarios (cardiac arrest, hypoglycemia with altered consciousness, acute pulmonary edema, and major trauma). Interprofessional teams (two medical and three nursing students) participate actively in scenarios followed by structured  plus/delta/plus debriefings. Perceptions and satisfaction are gathered via post-activity surveys. Discussion & Practical Implications The interprofessional approach is identified as one of the program’s most valuable aspects, fostering collaborative problem-solving, shared leadership, and mutual role understanding prior to independent clinical practice. Participants report high satisfaction and express strong support for increased interprofessional training. Study limitations include the absence of a control group, reliance on self-reported perception data, and lack of long-term objective evaluation in real-world clinical settings. Conclusions High-fidelity simulation-based CRM training provides an effective, highly accepted educational framework for undergraduate medical and nursing students, promoting teamwork competencies and fostering a patient safety culture early in clinical training.

title: Burden of Non-Communicable Diseases Attributable to Polygenic Risk and Its Association with Healthcare Utilization in Taiwan
authorString: Shih M, Ke Y, Chang X, Wang L, Feng YA.
abstractText:
Background:

Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) impose substantial population burden. Their polygenic architecture informs early risk stratification through polygenic risk scores (PRS). Previous studies reported elevated-PRS burden comparable to some modifiable risk factors (MRFs), yet evidence remains confined to European populations. We quantified the PRS-attributable NCD burden in Taiwan. Methods Linking Taiwan Biobank and National Health Insurance Research Database (N = 140K), we analyzed 42 high-burden NCDs. Elevated genetic risk (PRSe; top 10%) was assessed using Cox models. We estimated population attributable fractions (PAFs) and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) using Taiwan-specific estimates from Global Burden of Disease 2023, and examined associations between an integrated PRS (iPRS) and healthcare utilization. Findings Strongest PRSe associations occurred for atrial fibrillation (AFib; HR = 3.56 [95% CI: 3.23-3.92]) and gout (2.41 [2.33-2.49]), yielding PAFs of 20% and 12%, respectively, while population-level attributable DALYs were largest for type 2 diabetes (T2D), intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), and lung cancer. At the individual level, PRS_e corresponded to 1.50 [1.42-1.57] healthy life-years lost for T2D and 0.57 [0.40-0.76] for ICH, approaching 2.4 years for the top 1% PRS. Polygenic attributable burden was overall greater in men. For several diseases, PRS_e-associated PAF and DALYs exceeded those of individual MRFs (e.g., smoking, alcohol use). Top-decile iPRS was linked to 23.9% (15.0-33.6%) more hospital days, 19.1% (13.2-25.3%) more inpatient visits, and 9.6% (6.9-12.4%) more outpatient visits. Interpretation Polygenic risk accounts for a measurable—and for several diseases, MRF-comparable—share of NCD burden in Taiwan, providing a quantitative foundation for integrating genetic liability into preventive care and health planning.

title: Development and Validation of a Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Model for Riociguat and Its Active Metabolite M1
authorString: Zhang W, Lu H, Pan J, Qiao K, Li Z, Zhang X, Liu J, Liu J, Zhao T, Gong J.
abstractText: Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator for pulmonary arterial hypertension and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, has complex pharmacokinetics involving enterohepatic circulation (EHC), multiple metabolic pathways, and dual renal/biliary elimination. We developed and validated the first physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model for riociguat and its active metabolite M1 using PK-Sim 12.2, incorporating EHC based on biliary excretion and gallbladder emptying. The model was built with literature physicochemical/ADME parameters and clinical data from seven studies (0.5–2.5 mg single oral doses), then externally validated; over 90% of predictions fell within 0.5–2.0-fold error. Food-effect simulation predicted C max reduction to 53.4% and T max prolongation from 1.05 to 3.40 h, consistent with clinical reports. In virtual Child-Pugh A/B populations, riociguat AUC inf increased by approximately 23% and 35%. DDI simulations showed clarithromycin increased AUC inf by 37.5% (clinical: 41.5%), while rifampicin reduced it by 85.9%. This mechanistic PBPK platform showed robust predictive performance across healthy, food-effect, hepatic impairment, and DDI scenarios, supporting dose optimization and DDI risk assessment for riociguat, with clinical translational value.

title: Prevalence and Predictors of Chronic Kidney Disease of Undetermined Cause (CKDu) among Small-Scale Fishers in Northwest Tanzania: Application of DEGREE Protocol
authorString: Kapaga¹˒³˒⁶ KH, Maro¹˒³ V, Boer⁴˒⁵ MS, Kilonzo²˒³ K.
abstractText: Background Chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology (CKDu) has emerged as a significant public health problem among disadvantaged populations engaged in physically demanding occupations in tropical regions. Evidence on CKDu among small-scale fishing communities in sub-Saharan Africa remains limited. This study estimated the prevalence of reduced kidney function suggestive of CKDu and identified associated factors among small-scale fishers in Northwest Tanzania using the Disadvantaged Populations eGFR Epidemiology (DEGREE) protocol. Methods A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 422 small-scale fishers in Northwest Tanzania. After applying the DEGREE protocol age criterion, 379 participants aged 18–59 years were eligible for further analysis. Kidney function was estimated using the 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation. Participants with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or heavy proteinuria were excluded to identify reduced kidney function not explained by common causes of chronic kidney disease; a modified DEGREE analysis additionally excluded participants living with HIV. Multivariable linear regression was used to assess factors associated with continuous eGFR, while multivariable logistic regression examined factors associated with reduced kidney function (eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m²). Sensitivity analyses assessed the potential influence of dehydration, urinary tract infection, haematuria, and urogenital schistosomiasis. Results The prevalence of reduced kidney function was 16.6% in the overall population, 13.8% in the DEGREE subset, and 13.6% after additionally excluding participants living with HIV. In multivariable analyses, increasing age was consistently associated with lower continuous eGFR and higher odds of reduced kidney function, whereas male sex was independently associated with higher eGFR and lower odds of reduced kidney function. Occupational heat exposure, dehydration, daily working hours, body mass index, Schistosoma haematobium infection, sugary drink consumption, and energy-drink consumption were not independently associated with kidney function. Sensitivity analyses showed stable prevalence estimates after excluding participants with urinary abnormalities suggestive of acute kidney insults. Conclusions Reduced kidney function suggestive of a CKDu-compatible phenotype was relatively common among small-scale fishers in Northwest Tanzania. The persistence of elevated prevalence after excluding conventional causes suggests that other locally relevant occupational, environmental, infectious, biological, or socioeconomic factors may contribute. Because kidney function was measured once, CKDu could not be confirmed. Longitudinal studies with repeated kidney-function measurements and objective exposure assessment are needed.

title: The Synergy Framework: A Four-View, Domain-Self-Calibrated Instrument for Measuring the Structure of Complex Systems
authorString: Li W.
abstractText: Complex systems in different disciplines are described by variables with different units and reference scales, so a single numeric index computed on one system cannot in general be compared with the same index on another. In practice, analysts rely on one estimator at a time—an estimated Lyapunov exponent, a variance threshold, a pairwise correlation, or a higher-order information statistic—and each fails in a documented way when its operating assumptions are violated. This paper presents a method, not a new physical or mathematical law: a four-view measurement instrument that reports (V1) pairwise structural coupling via the non-diagonal energy fraction, effective rank and participation ratio, (V2) multibody organisation via O-information with weak and strong estimators, (V3) dynamical stability and causal asymmetry via the leading Jacobian eigenvalue, and (V4) perturbation recovery, together with an explicit input class (white-box A versus observed-only B), domain-self-calibrated significance tests, and premise gates. No single view is allowed to determine a conclusion. The method is calibrated analytically: for an m-ary nested hierarchy the participation ratio scales as PR ~ N^a with a = 2 log_m ?, and numerical points fall on these predicted slopes. It is validated out of sample on ten known-answer systems and on a natural physiological domain (heart-rate variability, healthy n=54 versus congestive heart failure n=29), where it honestly records that V1 and effective rank separate the groups while O-information does not and the final classifier consequently does not—a single-point dependency reported as a known boundary rather than hidden. Cross-level correspondence is carried by V2, while V4 is insensitive to inter-layer meshing, a remaining limitation. The contribution is an instrument plus a catalogue of thirteen reproducible failure modes.

title: Spatial organization of fibroblast subpopulations and niches across acute repair and chronic fibrotic remodeling of the human myocardium
authorString: Micu A, Matei A, Li Y, Pecher A, Filla T, Bruch P, Dietrich S, Henes J, Zweck E, Eckstein M, Klingel K, Distler JH, Györfi A.
abstractText:
Myocardial fibrosis is a common end point of acute and chronic cardiovascular injury, yet the spatially organized fibroblast (Fb) and immune-cell states that sustain fibrotic remodeling across etiologies remain incompletely defined. We applied cyclic in situ hybridization (cISH)-based spatial transcriptomics to myocardial biopsies from patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI), ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), postviral myocardial fibrosis (PVMF), and systemic sclerosis associated primary heart involvement (SSc-pHI). CODEX-based protein imaging provided orthogonal support for cell subpopulations and cellular neighborhoods. Spatially informed clustering identified six Fb subpopulations: COL1A1 hi /POSTN hi , NOTCH3 + , TIMP1 hi , GSN hi /DCN hi , AP1 hi Fbs, and myofibroblasts. COL1A1 hi /POSTN hi and NOTCH3 + Fbs were enriched in AMI, whereas GSN hi /DCN hi Fbs and myofibroblasts predominated in chronic fibrotic remodeling. These subpopulations displayed distinct extracellular matrix, inflammatory, and vasoregulatory programs. Infarction-associated reparative niches were enriched in COL1A1 hi /POSTN hi or NOTCH3 + Fbs and SPP1 + or APOE + macrophages (MФ), whereas chronic fibroinflammatory niches were enriched in GSN hi /DCN hi or AP1 hi Fbs or myofibroblasts with C1Q + MФ and plasma cells. The GSN hi /DCN hi Fb niche marked areas of subendocardial fibrosis, whereas the AP1 hi Fb niche localized to perivascular fibrosis. In SSc-pHI, the actively fibrogenic COL1A1 hi /POSTN hi Fb state characteristic of infarct scar formation was present at higher frequency than in other chronic entities and was individually associated with cardiac dysfunction, whereas the chronic GSN hi /DCN hi Fb niche was associated with the extent of interstitial fibrosis and anti-topoisomerase I autoantibodies. These data show that human myocardial fibrosis is organized into spatially distinct Fb subpopulations that assemble into context-specific fibroinflammatory niches across chronic fibrotic remodeling and repair after AMI.

What Is New?

Spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomics of myocardial biopsies from acute myocardial infarction, ischemic and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, postviral myocardial fibrosis, and systemic sclerosis-associated primary heart involvement (SSc-pHI) resolves six fibroblast subpopulations assembling into context-specific fibroinflammatory niches. Infarct scar formation and chronic fibrotic remodeling are organized by distinct fibroblast-macrophage circuits: COL1A1 hi /POSTN hi and NOTCH3 + fibroblasts with SPP1 + macrophages in infarct scar, versus GSN hi /DCN hi and AP1 hi fibroblasts with C1Q + macrophages and plasma cells in chronic disease. Subendocardial fibrosis maps onto GSN hi /DCN hi and perivascular fibrosis onto AP1hi neighborhoods. SSc-pHI is distinguished by increased actively fibrogenic COL1A1 hi /POSTN hi fibroblasts, transient during infarct scar formation, indicating ongoing fibrogenesis.

What Are the Clinical Implications?

Spatial profiling links histological patterns of myocardial fibrosis to distinct fibroblast and immune-cell environments, providing a basis for investigating how these cellular relationships contribute to myocardial remodeling. In SSc-pHI, infarct scar-associated COL1A1 hi /POSTN hi fibroblasts occur alongside GSN hi /DCN hi fibroblasts. These findings provide a basis for functional and longitudinal studies to define their contributions to myocardial remodeling and evaluate their potential as markers of disease activity or therapeutic targets. Prospective studies integrating these tissue findings with cardiac imaging and circulating biomarkers should establish whether the observed cellular patterns provide additional information about disease progression or treatment response.

title: From Effusion to Diagnosis: Integrating the FIP Effusion Index and Cell Tube Block Immunohistochemistry in a Geriatric Cat
authorString: Lopes R, Fernandes C, Lima de Carvalho H, Barros G, Sampaio F.
abstractText: Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) can be overlooked in older cats with competing causes of effusion. An older female domestic shorthair cat with hyperthyroidism and a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy phenotype developed abdominal effusion in December 2023. Initial effusion total protein was 5.46 g/dL, the albumin-to-globulin ratio was 0.48 and delta total nucleated cell count ratio (ΔTNC) was 60.58, yielding an FIP Effusion Index of 126.2. Coronavirus RT-PCR detected FCoV RNA, with M1058L mutation positivity, and cell tube block immunohistochemistry (CTB-IHC) demonstrated viral antigen within macrophages. A second effusion sample collected 9 days after the first had ΔTNC of 2.15 and a FIP Effusion Index of 7.17, despite higher total protein and a lower albumin-to-globulin ratio. GS-441524 treatment began on 20 December 2023 and ended on 22 March 2024. Abdominal fluid was no longer detected at the assessment on 25 January. No confirmed FIP relapse was documented before death during cardiopulmonary decompensation in January 2026. This case illustrates complementary contributions of the FIP Effusion Index and CTB-IHC, with an exploratory observation of serial FIP Effusion Index change. Threshold comparison is retrospective, and the serial measurements do not establish a validated marker of treatment response.

title: Rank-based integration identifies convergent disease mechanisms across omics
authorString: Luo Y, Qiu Z, Palmer D, Jostins-Dean L, Lewis A, Bull K, Nanchahal J.
abstractText: The rapid growth of omics studies offers new opportunities to uncover disease mechanisms, yet findings from individual studies or single omics may be influenced by cohort-, platform- and layer-specific variation. Integrating evidence across studies and omics layers can reveal robust biological signals that are reproducible across molecular layers, but differences in assay platforms, sample sizes and feature coverage complicate direct combination of summary statistics. Here we present the Omics Rank-Based Integration Tool (ORBIT), a direction-aware framework for prioritizing concordant signals across omics layers using only within-dataset feature ranks and effect directions. ORBIT tests directional rank consistency across omics layers against a closed-form variance-gamma null distribution while accounting for inter-dataset correlation and incomplete feature overlap. Simulations show that ORBIT maintains well-calibrated false-positive rates under inter-omics correlation, increasing numbers of omics layers and missingness, while detecting concordant signals with increasing power as the number of layers grows. We applied ORBIT to tubulointerstitial transcriptomic data from patients with chronic kidney disease in the C-PROBE cohort and proteomic data from the Kidney Precision Medicine Project, identifying a concordant injury programme marked by inflammatory and fibrotic remodeling together with impaired energy metabolism. We also used ORBIT to integrate ten transcriptomic, four proteomic and one translatomic datasets in dilated cardiomyopathy heart tissue, identifying extracellular matrix remodeling and mitochondrial energy failure as the dominant concordant biological programmes. In both diseases, ORBIT prioritized concordant genes and identified pathways that were not significant in any single omics layer alone. These results show that directional rank integration can be used for integrating heterogeneous omics summary data and prioritizing robust molecular mechanisms.

title: The dilated cardiomyopathy E525K mutation stabilizes the cardiac myosin interacting-heads motif while activating the isolated motor domain
authorString: Gautam R, Somavarapu AK, Robeson KZ, Childers MC, Regnier M, Ge J, Yengo CM, Craig R, Padrón R.
abstractText: Mutations in β-cardiac myosin are a common cause of inherited cardiomyopathies. The dilated cardiomyopathy E525K mutation alters both thick filament regulation and motor activity, yet the structural basis for these effects has remained unclear. Here, we combined cryo-EM and MD simulations to determine how E525K affects the conformational landscape of cardiac myosin in both its autoinhibited interacting-heads motif (IHM) and isolated myosin head states. E525K-mutated myosin exclusively adopted a single S2 conformation in IHM, in contrast to the conformational heterogeneity observed in wild-type myosin. Structural and electrostatic analyses revealed that the mutation increased positive charge density at the blocked-head (BH) – S2 (subfragment-2) interface, strengthening interactions with negatively charged residues within S2. 3D variability analysis and MD simulations of the E525K IHM demonstrated reduced S2 mobility, consistent with strengthened BH – S2 interactions, and decreased conformational flexibility, providing a structural mechanism for stabilization of the IHM state. To investigate the isolated myosin head, we determined cryo-EM structures of wild-type and E525K subfragment-1 (S1). The mutation induced local conformational rearrangements in the activation-loop and Loop 3 region, the SH3-like domain, and the essential light chain of S1, revealing structural changes that support the enhanced motor activity previously reported for isolated E525K myosin motors. These findings show that E525K stabilizes the autoinhibited IHM through electrostatic stabilization of the BH – S2 interface while inducing structural changes consistent with activation of the isolated motor domain, providing structural insights into how a single DCM mutation differentially regulates cardiac myosin S1 and IHM structure and function.

title: Angiotensin II Promotes Mitral Valve and Left Atrial Pathology in Fibrillin-1  <sup>C1041G/+</sup>  Mice
authorString: Franklin MK, Howatt DA, Pettey AC, Moorleghen JJ, Levitan BM, Mullick AE, Saffitz JE, Lu HS, Daugherty A.
abstractText:
ABSTRACT

Background

Activation of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) contributes to aortic diseases caused by fibrillin-1 haploinsufficiency ( Fbn1 C1041G/+ ). However, whether RAS activation influences mitral valve disease associated with FBN1 variants remains undefined. This study determined whether inhibition or augmentation of the RAS affects mitral valve pathology in Fbn1 C1041G/+ mice.

Methods

Angiotensinogen (AGT) antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) were administered for 12 weeks to inhibit the RAS in male and female Fbn1 C1041G/+ mice. To augment the RAS, mice were infused with angiotensin II (AngII; 1,000 ng/kg/min) for 28 days. Mitral valve and heart function were monitored by ultrasound. At termination, hearts were dissected free and tissue sectioned to assess mitral valve leaflet thickness and pathology.

Results

Mitral valve leaflet thickness was significantly increased in Fbn1 C1041G/+ mice compared to Fbn1 +/+ littermates of both sexes. ASO-mediated AGT inhibition did not alter this phenotype despite markedly reduced plasma AGT concentrations. AngII infusion increased mitral valve leaflet thickness in Fbn1 C1041G/+ mice with increased proteoglycan and collagen content, while exerting minimal effects in Fbn1 +/+ mice. Twenty-five percent of AngII-infused Fbn1 C1041G/+ mice died of non-vascular causes. Ultrasound showed mitral valve dysfunction in AngII-infused Fbn1 C1041G/+ mice. Grossly expanded left atria were common in AngII-infused Fbn1 C1041G/+ mice. These markedly enlarged left atria contained increased fibrosis, macrophage accumulation, and platelet-rich masses.

Conclusions

Mitral valves of Fbn1 C1041G/+ mice did not respond to AGT inhibition but were markedly more susceptible to AngII infusion, with greater increases in thickness and compositional changes than mitral valves of Fbn1 +/+ mice. In addition, AngII promoted mitral valve dysfunction that were associated with pronounced left atrial pathology.

What are the Clinical Implications?

Manipulation of fibrillin-1 in mice leads to vascular pathology that is attenuated by sustained inhibition of the renin-angiotensin system and exacerbated by its activation. However, whether modulation of the RAS influences mitral valve disease in mice harboring fibrillin-1 variants remains unknown. This study demonstrated that the presence of a missense variant of fibrillin-1 greatly augments the effects of renin-angiotensin system activation on mitral valve pathology compared with wild-type mice, with increased leaflet thickness and enhanced accumulation of proteoglycan and collagen. These structural changes are accompanied by mitral valve dysfunction and pronounced left atrial pathology, likely attributable to angiotensin II-induced mitral valve prolapse. These findings provide an experimental basis for determining whether inhibition of the renin-angiotensin system attenuates the development or progression of mitral valve dysfunction in humans with fibrillin-1 variants.

title: Proteomic markers of colorectal cancer risk: results from the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition
authorString: Lee MA, Viallon V, Muller DC, Wang Z, Murphy N, Yarmolinsky J, Cross AJ, Ferrari P, Jakszyn P, Jenab M, Kolijn PM, Masala G, Pali D, Panico S, Peters U, Sacerdote C, Smith-Byrne K, Travis RC, Tsilidis KK, Tumino R, Van-Guelpen B, Vermeulen R, Verschuren M, Wareham N, Chatterjee N, Platz E, Riboli E, Gunter MJ.
abstractText:
Background:

Circulating proteins are promising biomarkers of colorectal cancer risk. Most studies combine colon and rectal cancer despite their biological differences.

Objective:

To identify proteins associated with colorectal, colon, and rectal cancer risk and triangulate findings using cross-cohort confirmation and Mendelian randomisation (MR).

Design:

We profiled 6,402 proteins, using the SomaScan 7K assay in a case-cohort study nested within the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC; 658 colon and 319 rectal cancers). Cox models identified proteins associated with cancer risk at a false discovery rate <5%. Findings were confirmed in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study (ARIC; SomaScan; 235 colon, 36 rectal) and UK Biobank (Olink Explore; 321 colon, 164 rectal). MR and genetic colocalisation evaluated potential causality.

Results:

We identified 36 proteins associated with colorectal cancer, 50 with colon cancer, and 2 with rectal cancer; 20 of the 36 were also associated with colon cancer and none with rectal cancer, and no protein was associated with both sites. Seven of the 40 colon cancer proteins available in ARIC were confirmed, including COMP, MIC-1/GDF15, TFF3, and THIK. Of these, MIC-1/GDF15 and TFF3 were also confirmed in UK Biobank. COMP was inversely associated with colon cancer risk observationally and in MR analyses.

Conclusion:

Colon and rectal cancers have different pre-diagnostic proteomic profiles, underlining the need for site-specific analyses. COMP, MIC-1/GDF15, and TFF3 were the most robustly supported biomarkers of colon cancer risk. Future work should prioritise experimental validation of these associations and use of repeated measures to define timing.

title: Pathogenic Enterococcus cecorum in Broiler Chickens in Bulgaria: Clinical, Microbiological, and Molecular Characterisation- Pilot Study
authorString: Marutsov P, Boneva-Marutsova B, Dimitrov K, Pandova M, Kizheva Y, Hristova P.
abstractText: In November 2025, an outbreak of Enterococcus cecorum in two commercial broiler flocks in southern Bulgaria were investigated. Clinical signs, including lameness and recumbency, appeared at approximately 20 days of age, and mortality reached 2.8% and 3.7%. Necropsy revealed systemic and osteoarticular lesions, including fibrinous pericarditis, hepatitis, splenomegaly, and osteomyelitis. E. cecorum was isolated in pure culture from 11 of 13 examined birds and confirmed by sodA-targeted PCR. The isolates carried the virulence-associated genes psaA, gelE, and ace, five tetracycline resistance genes (tetM, tetK, tetC, tetS, and tetT), and the macrolide resistance gene ermB. This study documents early-onset systemic E. cecorum disease in Bulgarian broilers and highlights the need for further phenotypic and genomic investigation of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Vascular Aging and Bladder Health: Associations Between Peripheral Arterial Disease and Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms in Mid-Life Women from CARDIA-PLUS
authorString: Markland AD, Hendrickson WK, Arguedas A, De S, Adams K, Lewis CE, Hellemann G, Fok CS, Brady SS.
abstractText:
ABSTRACT

Objectives

To describe associations between peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and bladder health (BH) and lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) among a subset of women in the Coronary Artery Risk Development In Young Adults (CARDIA) study.

Methods

Women from CARDIA at Birmingham, AL and Minneapolis, MN were eligible if they completed a questionnaire about bladder symptoms in 2022-23, an ancillary study post-year 35 called CARDIA-PLUS, including the global BH scale (possible range, 0-100) and the LURN-SI 10 (0-38) and the AUASI (0-35). A subset (n=216) completed an inperson examination, including the ankle brachial index (ABI) procedure (n=194). ABI scores were clinically categorized as normal (1.00-1.40), borderline abnormal (0.91-0.99), and abnormal (≤0.90; evidence of PAD). Continuous BH and LUTS variables were regressed on ABI category, adjusting for sociodemographics, obstetric/gynecologic variables, co-morbidities, and physical activity.

Key Results

Among women who completed BH/LUTS questionnaires and the ABI (n=192), the mean age was 63±4 years and racial composition was 47% Black and 53% White. ABI results were normal (74%), borderline abnormal (20%), and abnormal (6%). After adjusting for covariates, women with abnormal ABI scores had higher LURN-SI scores (4.1 points, 95% CI 0.7, 7.5) and did not have higher AUASI scores (1.4 points, 95% CI −3.1, 5.7) or lower BH scores (−9.6 points, 95% CI −24.0, 4.9) compared to women with normal ABI scores. Borderline abnormal ABI was not associated with BH or LUTS.

Discussion/Conclusion

In this cohort, PAD was associated with greater LUTS severity. PAD and LUTS may share common etiologies and risk factors that need additional research.

title: Autolysosomal enhancer GHF201 attenuates pathophysiology in a mucopolysaccharidosis type I mouse model
The Fetal Cardiac Care Pathway: Organization, Standards, and Clinical Practice: A Narrative Review and Organizational Perspective for the Italian Context
authorString: Piacentini G.
abstractText: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is increasingly diagnosed before birth, but the benefit of prenatal diagnosis depends on the care pathway that follows detection. This narrative review traces fetal cardiac care from obstetric screening to neonatal stabilization and follow-up and proposes an organizational framework adapted to the Italian healthcare context. International guidelines, consensus statements, cohort studies, organizational surveys, and quality-improvement studies were interpreted alongside the experience of a fetal cardiology center in Rome. Published evidence supports structured pathways based on hub-and-spoke referral, a multidisciplinary Fetal Heart Team, lesion-specific surveillance, physiology-based Level of Care (LOC) stratification, and standardized delivery planning. A multi-institutional implementation study has associated standardized delivery planning with higher rates of vaginal delivery and delivery at ≥39 weeks. The Italian perinatal system presents specific challenges, including numerous birth centers, separation between delivery hospitals and cardiac surgical centers, and variable neonatal resuscitation readiness. Proposed adaptations include mapping LOC categories onto Italian Level-I and Level-II birth centers, telemedicine-supported regional networks, a dedicated cardiac care coordinator, minimum monitoring and simulation-training requirements, a three-tier model of parental psychological support, and a national outcome registry. These organizational hypotheses require prospective evaluation in multicenter Italian settings.

Pretreatment Pan-Immune-Inflammation Value and Corrected Prognostic Nutritional Index for 24-Month Recurrence Risk Stratification After Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy and Surgery in Stage III Endometrial Cancer.
authorString: Lin R, Hu X, Zhou L, Ye K.
abstractText:
Objective

To evaluate pretreatment pan-immune-inflammation value (PIV) and corrected prognostic nutritional index (PNI) as exploratory markers of postoperative 24-month recurrence risk after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) and interval surgery for stage III endometrial cancer.

Methods

This retrospective single-center cohort included 362 consecutive women treated from January 2014 through December 2022. Complete blood count and albumin values were obtained within 7 days before the first NACT cycle. The fixed-window analysis included 311 patients with definitive 24-month recurrence status; all 362 patients were retained for recurrence-specific and recurrence/death time-to-event analyses. Internal validation used 100 repetitions of stratified 10-fold cross-validation, nested penalty tuning for comprehensive models, training-fold threshold selection, and 1000 bootstrap resamples for optimism correction.

Results

Among 311 patients with definitive status, 119 (38.3%) had documented recurrence. The PIV-corrected PNI model had a mean repeated-cross-validation AUC of 0.762 and a bootstrap-corrected AUC of 0.763. A penalized comprehensive clinical-pathological-molecular-treatment model had a mean held-out AUC of 0.787; adding PIV and corrected PNI increased it to 0.828 (paired held-out ΔAUC 0.042; bootstrap interval 0.013-0.070). The combined-biomarker model had a repeated-cross-validation calibration slope of 0.828 and intercept of -0.085; its bootstrap-corrected slope and intercept were 0.961 and -0.015. In full-cohort Cox analyses, higher PIV and lower corrected PNI remained associated with documented recurrence and with the composite recurrence/death endpoint. Seventeen deaths without prior documented recurrence were included as composite events, whereas 34 patients censored before 24 months were retained in time-to-event analyses.

Conclusion

Pretreatment PIV and corrected PNI provided complementary internally validated prognostic information and improved risk stratification within this cohort. The thresholds and models remain exploratory because model development, calibration, and decision-curve assessment were performed in the same single-center cohort; independent external validation is required before clinical use.

title: Public availability of trial-design and clinical-context information in contemporary lipoprotein(a)-targeted cardiovascular trials: A cross-sectional meta-research study.
authorString: Tan S, Gu J, Yow D, Zheng L.

journal.title: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice

abstractText: Direct lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)]-lowering therapies are advancing toward cardiovascular outcomes testing, but the amount of publicly available trial-design and clinical-context information varies across development stages. To characterize contemporary patient-enrolling direct Lp(a)-targeted pharmacologic trials and describe fixed-date public availability of predefined trial information. We conducted a cross-sectional meta-research study anchored in ClinicalTrials.gov with linked public protocols, statistical analysis plans, design/baseline reports, supplements, and peer-reviewed manuscripts available through May 2, 2026. Contemporary trials started on or after January 1, 2017. Two reviewers independently abstracted 12 prespecified public-information elements. Elements were classified as publicly identified or not publicly identified; no composite score or trial ranking was used. Fourteen trials met inclusion criteria, representing 5 agents, 3 therapeutic platforms, and 56,983 planned or reported participants. Seven trials had Lp(a) biomarker primary endpoints, 5 had clinical cardiovascular outcomes, 1 assessed apheresis burden, and 1 assessed calcific aortic valve stenosis progression. Seven trials were published/protocol-supported and 7 registry-only. Cardiovascular/risk phenotype, prevention or special-population setting, and geographic scope were identified in all trials. Other elements were identifiable less consistently: Lp(a) unit (13/14), background lipid-lowering therapy (9/14), numeric Lp(a) threshold (8/14), PCSK9/inclisiran handling (8/14), demographic information (8/14), CKD/eGFR criteria (6/14), heart failure criteria (6/14), diabetes criteria (5/14), and LDL-C context (3/14). Public availability varied across contemporary Lp(a)-targeted trials at the data lock, particularly for registry-only programs. These findings describe fixed-date public retrievability and should not be interpreted as protocol deficiency, registry noncompliance, trial quality, efficacy, safety, or regulatory readiness.

title: Routine versus deferred percutaneous coronary intervention in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation: a frequentist and Bayesian meta-analysis of randomized trials with trial sequential analysis.
authorString: Ibrahim A, Shalabi L, Giamundo DM, Aboueisha H, Enani A, Assi M, Mojahed A, Granata LG, Meyer DM, Sabouret P, Andò G.

journal.title: International journal of cardiology. Heart & vasculature

abstractText: The optimal management of concomitant coronary artery disease (CAD) in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) remains debated. Therefore, we performed this meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to compare routine percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) versus deferred PCI in patients with severe aortic stenosis and significant coronary artery disease undergoing TAVI. We systematically searched major electronic databases for eligible RCTs. The primary efficacy outcome was spontaneous myocardial infarction (MI); the primary safety outcome was major bleeding. Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis models were fitted using weakly informative prior distributions. Effect estimates are reported as posterior median risk ratios (RR) with 95% credible intervals (CrI). The posterior probability of benefit (PPB) for efficacy outcomes or harm (PPH) for safety outcomes was calculated (RR < 1 or RR > 1, respectively). Three RCTs comprising 1156 patients were included. Routine PCI did not demonstrate a convincing posterior probability of benefit for spontaneous MI (posterior median RR 0.84, 95% CrI 0.43-1.73; PPB: 70.2%) or all-cause mortality (posterior median RR 0.91, 95% CrI 0.60-1.43; PPB: 69.6%). However, routine PCI was associated with a reduced risk of urgent revascularization (posterior median RR 0.37, 95% CrI 0.15-0.91; PPB: 98.1%). For safety outcomes, routine PCI was associated with an increased posterior probability of harm for major bleeding (posterior median RR 1.56, 95% CrI 0.91-2.71; PPH: 95.6%) and life-threatening or disabling bleeding (posterior median RR 1.74, 95% CrI 1.00-3.07; PPH: 97.4%). Among patients undergoing TAVI with concomitant CAD, routine PCI did not reduce ischemic events or mortality but increased bleeding complications. These findings suggest that a selective revascularization strategy, rather than a routine one, may be preferable. CRD420261386909.

title: Monotropein mitigates atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability through circ_0140736/miR-495/SIRPα-mediated efferocytosis.
authorString: Liu Y, Wu Z, Huang B, Ye W, Xu S, He W, Lan Y, Xiao C, Qin C, Gao W, Ye Z.
abstractText: Efferocytosis is a biological process in which phagocytic cells engulf and degrade senescent, damaged, or dead cells to prevent secondary necrosis and inflammation. This process is implicated in various diseases, including atherosclerosis (AS). Enhancing efferocytosis efficiency may offer a promising therapeutic strategy for managing AS. Consequently, increasing attention is being paid to pharmacological agents that can promote efferocytosis. Monotropein (MON), the predominant iridoid glycoside in Morinda officinalis, has demonstrated anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties in previous studies. However, its role in regulating atherosclerotic plaque stability remains unclear. In this study, we show that MON enhances plaque stability in AS. The expression of circ_0140736 was found to be elevated in unstable atherosclerotic plaques. MON suppressed circ_0140736 expression and alleviated miR-495 sequestration via a competing endogenous RNA mechanism, thereby increasing miR-495 levels and downregulating signal regulatory protein α (SIRPɑ) expression. In conclusion, MON exerts its anti-atherosclerotic effects by promoting efferocytosis through the circ_0140736/miR-495/SIRPɑ axis, suggesting its potential as a promising therapeutic candidate for AS.

title: Percutaneous brachial plexus peripheral nerve stimulation for cancer-related upper extremity pain: a novel technical approach.
authorString: Nguyen L, Singh N, Sanghvi C, Saldanha U, Chen A, Pier M, Thompson A, Copenhaver D, Pritzlaff S.
abstractText:
Background

Peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS) is a well-established therapy for neuropathic pain syndromes. Emerging literature suggests that PNS is effective for treating oncologic pain.

Objective

This case report presents a novel ultrasound-guided, dual-lead PNS neuromodulation of the brachial plexus for upper-extremity cancer pain, with a focus on technical considerations.

Methods

Temporary, percutaneous, brachial plexus PNS was implanted in a patient with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma who was hospitalized for refractory pain from a pathologic humeral fracture. A novel approach is presented via the DAVIS (Dual-Lead Approach with Vectoring in the Subclavicular Plane) technique. This technique uses a parallel, subclavicular trajectory to optimize parallel lead positioning and minimize migration. Nerve localization, procedural technique, and patient-specific considerations are discussed.

Results

Following PNS implantation, the patient achieved complete cessation of opioid use with substantial and sustained pain relief, highlighting the clinical potential of the DAVIS technique.

Conclusion

Brachial plexus PNS presents a promising strategy for extremity oncologic pain. Novel approaches focusing on dual-lead placement with a parallel trajectory may expand the efficacy of PNS in anatomically complex or opioid-refractory cases.

title: The silent dialogue between cells: regulatory roles of non-coding RNAs in cardiovascular disease.
authorString: Zhang Z, Yang Y, Liu M, Zhang H, Li Z, Zhang J, Zhang H.

journal.title: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

abstractText: Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) are involved in the occurrence, progression, and repair of cardiovascular disease By post-transcriptional regulation, epigenetic modification, cell-fate determination, and metabolic homeostasis-related pathways, microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and circular RNAs (circRNAs) regulate the development of atherosclerosis heart failure and hypertension The stability in circulation and cell type-specific expression of these molecules have important implications for early disease detection, risk stratification, and prognostic prediction. The development of more sensitive detection techniques facilitates accurate quantification of ncRNAs in different sources including exosomes, plasma or tissues and promotes translational research. Interventions directed toward the regulation of ncRNAs, such as miRNA inhibition or replacement and modulation of lncRNAs and circRNAs are being developed. Despite existing challenges related to ncRNA delivery, specificity, and methodological standardization, ncRNAs represent promising molecular signatures for personalized medicine. Integrated use of multi-omics, clinical phenotypes and computational algorithms is anticipated to optimize an ncRNA-guided precision management pipeline from diagnosis to prediction and treatment.

title: Pilot study of Wilms tumor 1-targeted human platelet lysate-induced antigen-presenting cells in advanced solid cancer patients.
authorString: Togi M, Koya T, Yoshida K, Kawaguchi H, Takano T, Yamada S, Yeh TJ, Liu YC, Sugiyama H, Koido S, Shimodaira S.
abstractText:
Introduction

For the wide implementation of dendritic cell-based cancer immunotherapy, a clinical phase I study was conducted to explore its safety and tolerability using Wilms' tumor 1 (WT1) antigen-targeted human platelet lysate-induced antigen-presenting cells (WT1-HPL-APCs), developed by our team, in patients with advanced solid cancers.

Methods

WT1-HPL-APCs were manufactured from apheresed peripheral blood mononuclear cells administered at 4 × 107 cells biweekly for three sessions (one course). Adverse events and the induction of WT1-specific T cells (WT1-Cytotoxic T lymphocytes [CTLs]) were evaluated. Furthermore, the potential immunoinducibility of WT1-HPL-APC was examined in vitro and regulatory T cells and monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (M-MDSCs) in the tumor microenvironment (TME) and peripheral blood were assessed to monitor immune cells.

Results

The adverse events associated with WT1-HPL-APC vaccination included fever, erythema at the injection site, arthralgia, and chills, all of which were lower than grade 2 in two patients who completed three sessions. The WT1 expression levels and infiltration of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and macrophages in the TME differed among the patients. In only one of the two patients with HLA-A*24:02, WT1-HPL-APC induced WT1-CTLs in vitro. Although a WT1-CTL response could not be detected following three sessions of WT1-HPL-APC administration, the percentage of M-MDSCs in the PB tended to decrease.

Conclusions

As this pilot study included only three patients with different cancer types, evidence supporting the effectiveness or functionality of WT1-HPL-APCs remains limited. WT1-HPL-APC vaccination was tolerable among patients with advanced solid cancers. Our findings suggest that the immunoinducibility of WT1-HPL-APC vary across individuals and that the preexisting immunosuppressive environment could limit WT1-CTL induction. Future studies are warranted to determine whether WT1-HPL-APC vaccination can improve the patient's immunosuppressive environment and induce WT1-CTLs in combination with optimized chemotherapy or adjuvant therapy in large-scale clinical trials involving multiple doses.
